A house and a garden with a detached garage, has the boundary between billing authorities “X” and ”Y” passing down exactly down the middle of the house.
The existence of the garage in “Y” will not affect the decision because the calculation is made by reference to the superficial area of the “principal structure”, i.e. the house and not any structures which do not touch the main building.
As no part of the superficial extent of the house can be reasonably be ascertained to be greater that the other, the billing authorities and not the LO must decide within which area the dwelling is to be treated and situated.
A house and granny annex which are disaggregated into two dwellings
1. Background
The VOA has reviewed its policy on the identification of domestic assessments with hospitals and has received legal advice that;
A domestic assessment would only arise within a hospital hereditament if a person was in hospital for 60 days or more and was not receiving treatment. The new policy co mes into effect on the 1st October 2015.
Separate self contained units requiring disaggregation and separate bands may be present on the geographical site of a hospital such examples may include, staff accommodation where the hospital is in paramount control.
Where the occupant is in paramount control each dwelling may constitute its own separate hereditament and hence attract its own council tax banding.
These two categories require separate assessment and banding.
2. Council Tax, hospitals and composites
Hospitals that are exclusively non domestic will fall to be assessed only in the non domestic rating list. Where they contain a proportion of domestic property, they will form a composite hereditament.
3. Identification of domestic areas
The LO / VO will receive FORs from hospitals, which will give details of the non domestic / domestic split.
The identification of domestic and non domestic areas within a hospital is based on the number of days which patients spend in hospital either in a domestic capacity or a non domestic capacity, as a proportion of the total number of bed days in the hospital. A bed day is the number of days each bed is occupied by a patient, so the total number is multiplied by the total number of beds in the hospital.
The proportion of domestic patient days is then applied to the area of the hospital deemed to have domestic use, and this area is deducted from the total area used to determine the non domestic assessment. The domestic area is then valued in accordance with the valuation basis described below to arrive at a capital value as at 1 April 1991 for England and 1 April 2003 for Wales. The capital value will fall within the usual banding ranges and this will determine the band. .
The test for domestic use is whether active treatment is being administered in hospital wards, if it is then that part of the hospital does not meet the definition of domestic at s66(1) . If patients in hospital are not receiving active treatment , their stay is domestic unless it is non domestic due to the application of s66(2) ( short stay, taken as less than 60 days.)
4. Guidance as to what constitutes treatment;
The following is intended to be a guide as to what treatment is for the purposes of ascertaining domestic property,
“Treatment” means treatment in its normal sense and therefore includes, but is not limited to, any medical intervention, diagnostic care or observation undertaken by professional staff in hospitals, including doctors, nurses, midwives, therapists and psychologists, designed to improve or modify patients’ physical and/or mental abilities and social functions. This definition includes, but is not limited to nursing (which includes aiding convalescence), psychological interventions, physiotherapy and other sorts of therapy including habilitation and rehabilitation.
5. Practical valuation or banding application
The VOA has received legal advice that a split between non domestic and domestic could be carried out on an apportionment of the number of patient days falling into or outside the definition of domestic above.
It is recognised that the split between domestic and non domestic will be fluid. In order to provide certainty the operational approach is to review the banding in conjunction with the identification of non domestic that occurs at the AVD for each Non Domestic Rating List.
To find the domestic portion of a hospital the number of patient days fulfilling the domestic definition should be divided by the total number of patient days. This will provide a fraction which is then applied to the area of the hospital deemed to have domestic. For practical purposes a fraction less than 2.5% is considered de minimis and would not trigger a domestic apportionment.
Unlike traditional domestic dwellings like houses there is no market to derive the valuation from in order to reach a band. In the case of hospitals the application of the contractor’s basis is used where cost is treated as being equivalent to value.
If a hospital has a domestic proportion, this will be translated into a band by use of the contractor’s basis of valuation using the appropriate building costs for the appropriate Valuation List. For England the appropriate date tor the ascertainment of building costs is 1st April 1991 and for Wales 1st April 2003. This calculation is applied where there is only one “dwelling” identified , where more are found please see below.
Tables of building costs are shown at Appendix 1 .
6. Process for banding, using contractor’s basis of valuation
For an English hospital, the contractor’s basis stages are
Stage 1 - Build Costs:
Multiply domestic a rea of hospital(calculated as a nominal proportion of the whole) by the unit build cost for 1991 (price per square metre) from table supplied by Building Surveyors
Stage 2: Apply age and obsolescence allowances provided by Building Surveyors and taken from the NDR valuations.
Stage 3: Add Land
Land is added as a percentage of the stage 2 building costs (ie after the application of the age and obsolescence allowance)
To find the Band
The total cost based on the above process will be treated as being equivalent to capital value and the band will be taken from normal band ranges.
7. How to deal with Disaggregation of domestic dwellings within the composite.
Where a hospital hereditament contains both domestic and non domestic its will be a composite hereditament.
There are specific rules that determine the identification of dwellings within domestic accommodation. Like other composites, d omestic accommodation in hospitals can, on the specific facts, be required to be treated as separate dwellings under Article 3 of the CT Chargeable Dwellings Order 1992 . This process is known as “disaggregation”.
Statute requires that where a single domestic hereditament contains a , “building or part of a building constructed or adapted for use as separate living accommodation” then it shall be classed as a “self contained unit” (SCU) and form a dwelling in its o wn right
Where a SCU is found, there will always be a counter-part so in the example of a simple house with annexe there would be two SCU’s; the annex and the remainder. Both parts need to be self contained units , the presence of one cannot prevent the residue from being a self contained unit.
8. Disaggregation – practice
For a SCU to be identified within the domestic part of a hospital there must be specific physical accommodation that fulfils the following criteria;
- 
    100% domestic usage AND
- 
    Physical characteristics
In relation to (b) , for detailed guidance on what constitutes a self contained unit see CTM link …
Council Tax Manual _ Disaggregation of dwellings
The main characteristics of an SCU are;
- 
    Self contained
- 
    All living functions possible, including washing , toilet , food preparation and eating and sleeping.
(There is case law showing that the absence of one element of an SCU may not prevent an SCU from existing)
Typical hospital examples of SCUs are ;
(i) A block containing all living functions possible; washing , toilet , food preparation and eating and sleeping. Where each of these elements are available on each floor of a block then each floor will comprise a SCU.
(ii) A self contained flat for use by medical staff provided it does not constitute a separate hereditament. If it did, it would comprise a separate dwelling in its own right and require separate assessment.
Where two or more SCU s are found, each must be banded . The dwelling disaggregated from the notional apportioned area of the hospital will be banded specifically on its physical characteristics , primarily its area. In the case where there is only one disaggregated dwelling the remaining domestic accommodation calculated by reference to the notional apportionment less the disaggregated area, becomes the physical extent of the accommodation to be banded .
9. Disaggregation if no domestic entry in Valuation List
The legislation requires that a SCU must be identified from an existing dwelling. This therefore requires the presence of an existing dwelling.
Where the Valuation List shows an entry reflecting the domestic part of a composite hospital, the SCU can be disaggregated so the existing entry would be split into two or more entries in the Valuation List.
However, if two or more dwellings should be shown in the list following the application of Article 3 “disaggregation”, but there is no existing entry in the Valuation List, then an entry reflecting a “notional” single dwelling (comprising both areas to be disaggregated) should be inserted first. Once this entry is in the Valuation List then it can be disaggregated from date of schedule (DOS) to reflect the SCU determined by the LO and its counterpart entry.
10. Example of application of disaggregation of domestic area within composite hereditament.
A hospital hereditament has an area of 10,000m2 which contains an element of long stay where no treatment occurs. The notional apportionment of the domestic patient days shows 10% domestic. This gives an area of 1000m2 to be treated as domestic. Within the hospital a block has been identified that satisfies the conditions of a SCU. This block is 300m2.
There are therefore two dwellings to be banded. The first is the disaggregated block of 300m2. The second is the “counterpart” SCU identified as the remainder ( 1000m2 less 300m2) giving 700m2.
Two bandings are therefore required using the contractors basis described above.
11. Effective dates - practice
For composite hereditaments effective dates are derived from the specific event.
If a hospital becomes a composite, then the date of the event is taken as the effective date for the introduction of the domestic element into the List; likewise if a hospital ceases to have any domestic use. If the balance of the domestic / non domestic use within the composite changes, then the date of the change, if evidenced, becomes the effective date. In practice this will generally be the date indicated in the FOR..
12. Effective dates and disaggregation
Under the The Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (England)
Regulations 2009
(6) Subject to regulation 3(2), where an alteration—
(b) the inaccuracy was to show as one dwelling property which should have been treated as
two or more dwellings by virtue of article 3 of the Council Tax (Chargeable Dwellings)
Order 1992(a),
** “the alteration shall have effect from the day on which the alteration is entered in the list.”**
This has the effect that effective date for disaggregation will be the date of the next schedule (DOS)
If there is no existing domestic entry in the valuation list and disaggregation appearsto be appropriate then it is more complex. In this situation a notional dwelling needs to be created that runs from the same effective date as the domestic was first evidenced to have existed and this may be back to the beginning of the Valuation List if appropriate. Then the notional dwelling needs to be disaggregated from DOS.
Wales - Effective dates and “ 6 year rule”
In Wales the above formulation of effective dates applies but there is intervention of the “6 year rule “ This (Reg 14(6) of 1993/290 applies) prevents the reduction of a band where the alteration occurs 6 or more years ago in terms of the effective date. So for example, if the band of domestic part needed to be reduced from C to B, then the effective date of the alteration to B can only occur from a point 6 years before the schedule that carries out the alteration.

Summary
The Valuation Office Agency's (VOA) technical manual for assessing domestic property for Council Tax.
The Valuation Office Agency’s Council Tax manual is primarily provided as practice guidance for Valuation Officers. The contents of the manual represent the Valuation Office Agency’s (VOA) understanding of the law at the time it was prepared and whilst it is carefully compiled, the VOA does not guarantee the completeness or accuracy of the information in it. From time to time the contents may be revised in the light of changes in legislation and decisions of the tribunals and higher courts or to reflect changing policy.

Inside the defense investing boom fueled by drones, AI and Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:04:29 UTC
21:04:29 KST

- The Defence Blog interviewed four defense investors, including a retail researcher, a venture fund CEO, and a procurement expert, on where capital is flowing.
- Sources discussed defense industry consolidation, Ukraine's export restrictions, and counter-drone technology as key investment themes.
Money is flowing into defense technology at a pace that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago, and the people writing the checks are not just Pentagon program managers anymore. Individual investors, boutique venture funds and family offices are increasingly betting on drone makers, artificial intelligence startups and companies building weapons for a war in Ukraine that has become, whether intentionally or not, the world’s most closely watched proving ground for next-generation battlefield technology.
To dig into those questions, The Defence Blog spoke with four people who each bring a different vantage point to defense investing: an independent retail investor who researches drones and space technology in his spare time, the CEO of a Swedish venture firm actively funding Ukrainian defense startups, a defense procurement expert who tracks the industry from a U.S. investor’s perspective, and an early investor in Anduril Industries who agreed to share his views only on condition of anonymity, citing the sensitivities of his ongoing business relationships in the sector.
The retail investor, who goes by Chrispy online and describes himself simply as an individual investor and researcher covering drones, space and defense technology in his free time rather than an industry insider, sees the market heading toward consolidation. Asked whether future market leaders will be companies building complete drone systems or those specializing in individual components like autonomy software, sensors and electronic warfare, he pointed to a structural squeeze forming in the middle of the market.
“Rollups and components. There will be waves of consolidation and competitive pressure, execution speed and supply chain management will be the differentiator as far defense premiums move towards commercial numbers and economics (delivery, consumer, etc),” said Chrispy.
A rollup, in industry terms, describes the process of acquiring and merging smaller competitors into a larger combined company, a pattern that has already reshaped industries from waste management to veterinary clinics and appears increasingly likely to sweep through the fragmented drone sector as investors push for scale. Chrispy also offered a framework for evaluating a defense startup before it has locked down major government contracts, pointing new investors toward established business analysis tools rather than hype-driven pitch decks.
“Porters 5 forces analysis, readiness levels (technical, manufacturing, integration, etc) these are great frameworks for LLM assessments, but always validate assumptions before taking them as gospel,” said Chrispy.
Porter’s Five Forces is a business strategy framework, originally developed by Harvard economist Michael Porter, that evaluates a company’s competitive position by examining supplier power, buyer power, the threat of new entrants, substitute products and rivalry among existing competitors, a tool increasingly useful for sorting genuine defense innovators from companies riding investor enthusiasm without a durable competitive moat. On where the strongest long-term opportunity sits within the drone and AI market specifically, Chrispy described a market splitting toward two extremes rather than clustering in the middle.
“I see it as a bit of an inverse bell curve, with ‘neoprime’ players on one side offering diversified ecosystems, and tier II suppliers on the other. Individual drone producers may get squeezed if they fail to differentiate or move to either end,” said Chrispy.
The term neoprime has emerged in defense circles to describe a new generation of venture-backed contractors, companies like Anduril Industries and Palantir Technologies, that aim to compete directly with legacy prime contractors such as Lockheed Martin and Raytheon by building integrated hardware and software ecosystems rather than single products, a structural shift Chrispy’s answer suggests will keep squeezing narrowly focused drone manufacturers caught in between.
Jonas Malmgren, CEO of the Swedish venture firm Front Ventures AB and a Swedish Army Reserve Officer, brought a different lens to the conversation, one shaped by direct experience funding early-stage Ukrainian defense companies through an active war. Asked what motivates investors to take on the financial, regulatory and physical risks of financing Ukrainian defense firms, Malmgren pointed first to the sheer speed at which Ukraine’s homegrown defense industry has matured under combat pressure.
“Main reason is that a new defence industry is being formed in Ukraine across several areas: Drones and drone components, SW for command and control, EW systems, UGV’s etc are all driven from Ukraine and also battle proven and has short and effective ‘development to real usage’ cycles. And valuations so far have been attractive even if the increased in last year. By investing in early stage ukraine companies you get access to proven innovation at a lower comparable cost vs investing in european and US legacy defence companies,” said Malmgren.
Malmgren also pointed to a broader shift underway inside NATO budgets, arguing that traditional heavy armor procurement is already losing ground to drone and electronic warfare investment, citing Estonia’s decision to cancel its planned purchase of CV90 MkIV infantry fighting vehicles as a concrete example of that pivot in action. He described the moral dimension of the calculation as well, acknowledging that some investors accept elevated risk specifically because they want to support Ukraine, and noted that investors are increasingly helping Ukrainian companies establish production sites inside the European Union as a way of securing manufacturing capacity that sits outside an active war zone.
On how investors actually evaluate a Ukrainian company’s technology and growth potential, Malmgren described a deliberate focus on either unique intellectual property or foundational component manufacturing capable of scaling across the industry.
“We either look for unique solutions and IP like Molfar Defence Technologies (C-UAV radar, new design of a radar) or Black Forest Systems (specialized drone for infantry and special forces solidiers) or companies that has knowledge to produce components used by many other companies and can scale fast. Example is Aeromotors who makes full inhouse production of drone motors. Here its also a benefit if the company is not export restricted and can sell outside of Ukraine. Its also for us important there is an initial confirmed need / test agreement in place. So we have focused on supporting companies that has initial LOI’s or test orders and needs to scale up production,” said Malmgren.
An LOI, or letter of intent, is a preliminary agreement signaling that a customer plans to purchase a product once it meets certain conditions, a document investors often treat as an early signal of real demand before a company has secured a binding contract. Malmgren was direct about what he sees as the single biggest obstacle holding back international investment in Ukraine’s defense sector, describing a bureaucratic bottleneck that he argued actively pushes innovation and revenue toward Ukraine’s competitors.
“Easier export approvals. As of August now in 2026 there is only one export approval made for strike drones. No export approvals for interceptors. This limitis sales for ukraine defence companies and makes the investment case lass attractive. Its also a risk ukraine missed the innovation leader benefit of exports are restricted. Then NATO, middle east and Asia is forced to buy from other suppliers at higher cost / less capable systems, but that then fuels innovation outside of Ukraine. So easier export approvals and international joint venture approvals should be prrio 1 for ukraine government,” said Malmgren.
Jeff Gabel, a defense procurement expert, framed the current wave of defense investing partly as a cultural phenomenon layered on top of a genuine strategic shift, cautioning new investors against mistaking public enthusiasm for sound analysis.
“I think investing in defense has become a new way of showcasing support around American sovereignty with a focus on leading the global industry in both manufacturing and might. You see this in swag drops from Palantir and other defense brands, building advocacy around individual investors interested in supporting this space and investing in growth. I think it can be easy to be sucked up into the hype of the investing wave but it’s also critically important to understand the implications around the industry and where legislation is going to back these critical needs. Investors need to pay close attention to earnings call language, geopolitical news, DoW announcements, FAA/FCC regulation and track supply chain cycle to really understand defense investing. While the bucket of defense companies can feel the same in theory, they are not all created equal and require a more in-depth understanding of where each company fits into the value chain,” said Gabel.
On where he sees the strongest opportunity within drones and artificial intelligence specifically, Gabel pointed toward counter-unmanned aircraft systems, technology built to detect and defeat hostile drones, as the space with the clearest dual civilian and military application.
“I believe the biggest threat and most critical dual use opportunity is c-uas as we see it deployed to both the frontline and commercially at home to protect infrastructure (most recently FIFA World Cup) and we need to address future needs to build airspace infrastructure and protect it from those who wish to disrupt it. There’s an important concept around layered defense in that we need to build up a variety of methods in deterrence and there’s no golden bullet that can address all situations. I believe companies are moving to a more complete view of the c-uas landscape, producing products meant for dual use and combining complete needs from software to sensor to system, so agencies can procure off the shelf solutions from one supplier and have complete command and control. The industry as a whole is consolidating to support scaled manufacturing,” said Gabel.
The fourth perspective came from an early investor in Anduril Industries, one of the most closely watched defense technology companies to emerge from Silicon Valley in the past decade, who agreed to speak only if his identity remained withheld, citing the sensitivity of his ongoing business relationships across the sector. Asked what motivates him to fund defense startups in the first place, he argued that chasing this kind of investment purely for financial return misses the point entirely.
“Investing money in defense startups and companies like Anduril or Shield AI just for the money is pointless. This should be done by people who want to change the world, who want to make it safer and better,” he said.
He went on to describe why evaluating early-stage defense startups pursuing genuinely novel technology demands real technical depth, arguing that the ideas most likely to reshape the industry often sound the least credible at first.
“You need to have real technical expertise to judge the prospects of startups proposing revolutionary things, because sometimes they sound like fairy tales or the dreams of nerds from university labs, but those are exactly the people who change the world. They drive revolutions, and the defense sector specifically is the foundation that then moves other industries forward too. So I don’t advise people who don’t understand physics to get into these kinds of ventures, unless they have a few extra million they wouldn’t mind losing,” he said.
He was equally direct about the current enthusiasm surrounding his own biggest success.
“As for Anduril, I put money in at a stage when nobody was even dreaming about this venture, and now I’m watching the hysteria around the company and a bunch of fly-by-night funds promising easy, fast money. Be careful with that. The market for companies like this is usually fairly conservative and doesn’t let newcomers in, and when it does open up, it’s often because of some kind of trouble, and the risk of losing money there is often greater than investing in a small, unknown startup out of Florida or Texas,” he said.
Taken together, these four perspectives point toward a few practical takeaways for anyone actually weighing money on defense technology right now. Watch for consolidation rather than betting on standalone drone makers that lack a clear technical edge or a defined place in the value chain. Treat export policy, not battlefield risk, as the real variable to track when evaluating Ukrainian companies, since a country’s regulatory posture can cap a startup’s growth far more decisively than the war itself.
Look toward dual-use technology, particularly counter-drone systems, where military necessity and civilian demand for protecting infrastructure genuinely overlap rather than merely coexist. And perhaps the hardest advice to follow: the easiest money was made by people who backed unproven ideas before anyone else believed in them, which means the crowded, hyped opportunities getting the most attention today are, almost by definition, no longer where the outsized returns are likely to come from.

Afghanistan five years of Taliban rule: Has Germany kept its promises?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:03:00 UTC
21:03:00 KST

Afghanistan, the Taliban and German promises
August 11, 2026
It is hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."
By June this year, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.
For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.
Hundreds of Afghans still waiting
Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."
In August 2026, 5 years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.
In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany. He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.
"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park, or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable."
New government does not want to take in any more local staff
Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.
Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter calling for help: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.
But the German government remains firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.
German Foreign Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2500 ($2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.
Fate of local staff also depends on German courts
Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Courtruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission programme for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.
In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry maintains it is in the right: "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."
According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.
German aid organization continues support
For Javad Niazi, the trepidation about his and his family's future continues. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport 5 years ago, the German non-governmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.
Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning to DW: "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people. And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be 4 weeks has now become 5 years."
Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans. With success: They have won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.
"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," Beyer said.
She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was cancelled."
This article was translated from German.

The Walking Dead star Jeffrey Dean Morgan says former manager fired him for ‘aging out’ in Hollywood
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
13:02:58 BST

The Walking Dead star Jeffrey Dean Morgan says former manager fired him for ‘aging out’ in Hollywood
Morgan found fame later in life, breaking out in ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ in his mid-30s
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Jeffrey Dean Morgan has revealed how close he was to quitting acting before landing three major roles on the bounce.
Morgan was in his mid-30s when he finally booked his breakout roles in Grey’s Anatomy, Supernatural and Weeds. He went on to land his best-known role as Negan in AMC’s hit horror series The Walking Dead in 2016.
However, he told Josh Horowitz on the latest episode of his Happy Sad Confused podcast that his former manager had given up on him before he became successful.
“I remember being in my mid-30s going, ‘This didn’t work out,’” the now 60-year-old recalled. “And my manager had just fired me right before I got the three shows. I’d been with her forever. And she was like, ‘You’ve aged out, bro. You missed your window.’ And she got rid of me and Max Martini at the same time and said the same thing to both of us.”
Unfortunately for Morgan’s manager, “I got Supernatural, Grey’s Anatomy and Weeds all at the same time, like within a week of each other,” he told Horowitz.
At the time, Morgan said he was “always hustling” to make ends meet.
“I would, you know, build fences or whatever,” he said. “Usually, it had involved hammers. There was always something to build for somebody.
“The problem was, I was in my mid-30s and I didn’t have an education and I didn’t know what else to do.”
Morgan went on to gain recognition as Denny Duquette, the charming heart transplant patient whose doomed romance with Katherine Heigl’s Izzie Stevens became one of Grey’s Anatomy’s most iconic storylines. He went on to star as John Winchester in Supernatural and Judah Botwin in Weeds before landing his career-defining role as baseball bat-wielding villain Negan in The Walking Dead.
Morgan said the role on Grey’s changed his life. “TV was so different and 30 million people a week were tuning in to watch that show,” he recalled. “I went from an unknown nobody to I couldn’t leave my house.”
He continued: “I was just so happy. I felt like, ‘Okay, even if I die in Grey’s’ — and I knew that I was dying in Grey’s when I got the job —but I also knew that 30 million people a week were — actually I didn’t know that was going to happen — but that I was going to have a regular job. I was going to do at least five episodes.
“I could pay my rent and then as that built, I remember when it all was airing because they were all airing at the same time. Grey’s was airing and Supernatural was airing at the same time, and it was two totally complete audiences with very little bleed-over. But people realized that I could do two things. It was doing two different things. All of a sudden, where did this actor come from?”
Morgan has gone on to build an impressive television career, appearing in acclaimed series including The Good Wife, Watchmen and The Boys, as well as the superhero film The Losers.
He is currently promoting Amazon Prime Video’s new hit teen romance, Sterling Point, in which he plays a complicated father figure. It follows 17-year-old Annie Jacobson (Ella Rubin), raised in New York City with her twin brother (Keen Ruffalo) and loving adoptive father (Jay Duplass), whose life takes a turn when she inherits her mysterious grandfather’s island in Canada.

Budapest’s ever-burning icon lamps — a bridge between generations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:02:24 UTC
21:02:24 KST

Author
Aleksandra Karamihaleva
Budapest’s ever-burning icon lamps — a bridge between generations
Tuesday 11 August 2026 12:16
Tuesday, 11 August 2026, 12:16
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
Font size
Rumyana Ivanova is a member of the church council of the Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius and an active member of the Bulgarian community in Hungary. It is beneath the dome of this church that the story unfolds of how children from mixed marriages in Budapest learn and preserve their mother tongue, and why many of them choose to pursue higher education at Bulgarian universities after completing their schooling. We also discover how the community is tracing the lost names of the first donors who helped build their church more than a century ago.
This is a story of a unique partnership between the church, the school, and the Cultural Centre in the Hungarian capital.It is a story about the living threads of the Bulgarian spirit beyond the country's borders, about the mission to preserve the memory of our ancestors, and about the power of the Orthodox faith to carry us through the vicissitudes of time and the transience of this world.
For decades, the Bulgarian school has connected Rumyana Ivanova’s life with Hungary. Before devoting herself to serving the church, her life journey first took her through the classroom.
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
“I came to Hungary in 2002 and worked as a teacher at the Bulgarian-Hungarian School. When my work there came to an end, I stayed because I am married to a Hungarian, and I continued my life here in Budapest”, said Rumyana Ivanova.
The connection between Rumyana Ivanova and the educational cause is by no means accidental. In Budapest, the school and the church have always gone hand in hand, from the very founding of the community to the present day.The predecessor of today’s Bulgarian church was a chapel housed in the Bulgarian School on Lónyay Street, where Hieromonk Boris—the founder of the Saints Cyril and Methodius church community and the future Metropolitan of Nevrokop- conducted the community’s first religious services.
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
“The church has always been a place that brings our community together,” Rumyana Ivanova recalls in an interview with Radio Bulgaria’s specialized podcast ''Bridge of Faith’’. “Our beautiful Cultural Centre is located right across from the church. We gather there for every celebration”, said Rumyana Ivanova.
The vibrant collaboration between the school, the church, and the Cultural Centre—the successor to the former Bulgarian community centre—is reflected in numerous joint initiatives. It can be felt in everything, from the shared joy and small gifts for the kindergarten children at Easter to the large-scale events held in the parish. A symbol of this unity is the specially built stage in the schoolyard, which every spring becomes the beating heart of the Bulgarian diaspora.
Saints Cyril and Methodius Church in Budapest
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
“For Easter, we welcomed the children from the kindergarten and their teachers”, Rumyana Ivanova recalls with a smile. “We gave each child a kozunak (sweet bread), a dyed Easter egg, some chocolate, and a toy. And for 24 May we put up a large stage in the schoolyard, where we hold the festivities every year. We invite all our children and their parents and grandparents, as well as fellow Bulgarians from other towns across Hungary. We all gather in this courtyard to celebrate the Day of the Holy Brothers Saints Cyril and Methodius.”
PHOTO Bulgarian School and Kindergarten in Budapest
Right next to the Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius stands the new building, completed in 2024, which now houses the Bulgarian School. It offers a wonderful modern learning environment where children of different ages study Bulgarian language, history and literature.The building also houses the kindergarten, with all the necessary facilities, including teachers’ rooms and offices. This shared courtyard is where the everyday lives of children growing up between the sound of the school bell and the ringing of the church bell unfold.
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
At the height of summer, the children set off by bus for Bulgaria. These traditional annual educational trips give them a firsthand experience of the monasteries, cities, and places of historical and spiritual significance.
PHOTO Bulgarian School and Kindergarten in Budapest
“Our children travel every year”, said Rumyana Ivanova. “They take extensive trips around the country to discover Bulgarian history up close. They visit cities, villages, and monasteries so they never forget where they come from and can immerse themselves fully in our native culture.”
Thanks to the strong sense of community among Bulgarians in Hungary and the excellent organization of their educational, cultural and religious life, even children from mixed marriages speak fluent Bulgarian and maintain a strong sense of national identity.
The flourishing of modern community life is rooted in a deep historical foundation, in which honoring the ancestors is a key element. Caring for the church today goes hand in hand with the noble task of restoring the memory of its first builders, because building the future requires first knowing and cherishing the past. This year, the community faces a great historical duty:
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
“This year, the church celebrates its 110th anniversary. It was built with funds from the Bulgarian state, but also with the contributions of many donors. It is our duty to honor these people, who truly did something for the house of God. That is why we are now planning to have the names we have uncovered engraved on special plaques. We are still searching for the others, so that we can display their names inside or outside the church. We are doing our best to ensure that history is not forgotten.Together with our parish priest, Father Tancho, and our new chairman, Alexi Andonov, we are trying to do more for this church, which is the strongest means of bringing Bulgarians together and helping us remember our faith, culture and heritage.”
In Budapest, church life exists in a unique and harmonious partnership with the other pillars of Bulgarian identity- the Association of Bulgarians in Hungary and the National Bulgarian Self-Government. Today, they all work side by side to preserve the house of God. This shared commitment also includes preserving the memory of the first donors who helped build the church.
“That is exactly what we intend to do”, Rumyana explains. “We want the names of these people, who did so much for our parish, to be mentioned during the Divine Liturgy celebrated by Father Tancho.”
PHOTO Aleksandra Karamihaleva
Another expression of the unbroken bond between generations is the specially arranged memorial space in the church’s northern apse, where portraits of deceased members of the Bulgarian community are displayed. For today’s parishioners who stand before these photographs, their ancestors are not merely a memory of the past, but active participants in the present.
Because church life beyond the homeland’s borders is not simply about preserving traditions, and the church is not merely a monument to times gone by, but an ever-flowing source of Living Water, faith and hope.

Sexual orientation to be included on Australia’s census for the first time

Sexual orientation to be included on Australia’s census for the first time
- Australians will be asked about their sexual orientation and gender identity for the first time in the 2026 national census.
- The mandatory census of nearly 28 million people determines how federal and state governments allocate funding for healthcare, education, and transport over the next five years.
- Everyone aged 16 and above will answer questions on sexual orientation, gender, and sex recorded at birth, while gendered wording has been removed from family relationship questions.
- Demographers have described the update as the most significant change to the census since Indigenous status was introduced more than 50 years ago.
- The policy change follows a 2022 human rights complaint by Equality Australia, highlighting the need for LGBTQ+ representation in national service planning.

Anthropic to embed hidden watermarks in Claude AI content to meet new EU transparency rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:01:01 UTC
21:01:01 KST

Beril Canakci
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
Anthropic said this week it will begin embedding hidden digital markers into text and files produced by its Claude artificial intelligence models, a move the company tied to new transparency obligations under the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act.
In a notice published on its Claude Help Center, the San Francisco-based AI company said Claude models launched in the EU on or after Aug. 2 will support machine-readable marking at launch, with generated text carrying embedded watermarks and generated files, including digitally signed provenance metadata where supported.
The obligation stems from Article 50 of the EU's AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to make synthetic content identifiable through technical means.
Coverage of the new markings extends beyond Europe.
Anthropic said the markings cover output from supported models everywhere Claude is used, including its API-based Claude Platform, its consumer chat product, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and Claude Tag.
Text watermarks are designed to be invisible during normal reading and to persist when content is copied or pasted, though multiple reports on the announcement noted the company has cautioned that heavy editing can weaken or erase the signal. Files in supported formats, including common image types, are expected to carry signed provenance metadata built on the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, or C2PA, standard -- an industry framework already used by other technology firms, including Google, for labeling AI-generated images.
The EU AI Act's transparency requirements form part of a broader regulatory rollout in Brussels aimed at governing artificial intelligence systems by risk level, with obligations phasing in on a staggered timetable through 2026 and beyond.

🔴 Lebanon becomes first Middle Eastern country to abolish death penalty

Lebanon becomes first Middle Eastern country to abolish the death penalty
Lebanon on Tuesday became the first Middle East country to formally abolish the death penalty. Lebanon had not carried out an execution since 2004.
Lebanon's parliament on Tuesday abolished the death penalty, making the country the first in the Middle East to formally end the practice.
"The draft law aimed at abolishing the death penalty in Lebanon was approved after amendments were made to it," the speaker of parliament's office announced.
Lebanon had not carried out an execution since 2004.
Justice Minister Adel Nassar called the abolition "historic", and said the spectre of capital punishment had previously prevented Beirut from obtaining the extradition of suspects from countries where it has been outlawed.
Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch, told AFP the move was "a monumental step for human rights in the country, representing a clear break from a cruel and arbitrary sentence that should never be imposed".
The abolition came as part of a series of bills to be discussed in the current legislative session, including a general amnesty law that has been debated for years.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The Meaning of Roots at 50
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Two days before my 39th birthday, I sat in a small boat making its way up a deep river lined with rooty mangrove trees. Though I had never been to this place, it felt hauntingly familiar, like an unlived memory. This was the River Gambia, and it was taking me to the village of Juffure.
It was February 2001. Three years earlier, President Bill Clinton had appointed my father, George W. Haley, U.S. ambassador to the Republic of Gambia. Like an act of poetic atonement, America sent the great-great-great-great-grandson of a slave back, as a diplomat, to the country whence his ancestor had been kidnapped. From my first breath of Gambian air, every step felt like an introduction to my whole self. But the most extraordinary moment was when I walked into Juffure, as my uncle, Alex Haley, had done 33 years earlier on his journey to writing Roots: The Saga of an American Family, and discovered our beginning.
As soon as the boat reached shore, I gazed into some three dozen eyes that looked like mine, many belonging to my cousins, unmet and however many times removed, and imagined how Uncle Alex felt when he first set foot there. I thanked him silently for his sacrifice and perseverance.
How does a single book at once condemn and captivate a nation? Fifty years ago this August, Roots did just that. In 1976, the bicentennial of the United States of America, Alexander Murray Palmer Haley saw the story he had carried since childhood, then researched and written over 12 years, sit atop the New York Times best-seller list for 46 weeks, spending 22 at No. 1. A U.S. Coast Guard veteran and freelance writer had dispelled any notion of it having been born the land of the free that its anthem professed, and the entire country, it seemed, was now on notice.
Alex Haley was my father’s older brother, and a significant presence in my life. He called me his “beloved niece” and “Little Bertha,” the second a loving attribution to his mother. He flew in for ballet performances and piano recitals, sent flowers for a good report card, and bought me my first car. He delivered the commencement speech at my high school graduation, and sat front and center at my college and law-school graduations. I adored him.
And now, all of those conversations around the Thanksgiving table had finally come to fruition. At 14, I innocently felt that his accomplishment was mine too. I had been raised on this story that was now the world’s to know. This was my family. And this is my love letter to him.
Roots sold 1.5 million copies in its first seven months and eventually 8 million, collecting a National Book Award, a special Pulitzer Prize, and an NAACP Spingarn Medal. It was translated into more than 35 languages and adapted into a ratings-smashing TV miniseries. You would be hard-pressed to find anyone born in America before 1980 who does not remember a copy of Roots on the bookshelf or the miniseries playing on the TV. In his Feb. 2, 1977, monologue for the Tonight Show episode on which Uncle Alex appeared, Johnny Carson remarked, “If there’s anyone watching who does not know about Roots, you must have either been out of the country or on Mars someplace.”
But none of this had been Uncle Alex’s wildest dream. All he had set out to do was to find out for himself who the African was. Uncle Alex and his brothers spent most summers on their maternal grandparents’ front porch. There, they would sit rapt, listening to the stories their grandmother Cynthia and her sister friends told late into the night. One such story told of a man brought to America on a boat from Africa that had landed in “’Naplis.” The African’s name was “Kinte.”
The African had been sold to a plantation in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, where he married Bell, the plantation cook. The two had a daughter named Kizzy, which in his native tongue meant “stay put.” So much more the devastating irony when she was sold to a plantation in North Carolina at 16. There, her enslaver fathered her child, George, who became known as Chicken George because of his skills working gamecock fights.
The stories became livelier at this point, and more rich with detail, as these were characters the women had known personally—Chicken George was Cynthia’s grandfather—and they stayed with Uncle Alex. Haunted him, really. Who was this Kinte? Where had he come from? There was no 23andMe then, but there were reams of microfiche at the Library of Congress and ample records in basements of the Churches of Latter-day Saints. There was also, and first, Cousin Georgia.
When my uncle would land in Kansas City, Kans., where my family lived, it was like a rock star on a sold-out tour. We knew he had come to sit at the knee of his grandmother’s cousin, Georgia Anderson, decades after he’d watched her rocking chair keep time on a porch. Now in her 80s, she was the last living repository of the stories of the African, including some of the words of his native tongue: she knew that kamby bolongo meant river, and kora was a stringed instrument like a banjo.
Her recounting, alongside his research, enabled Uncle Alex to learn that these cherished words were of the Mandinka language, spoken primarily in the Republic of Gambia. He made multiple trips on his meager budget, traipsing around a country the size of Connecticut. Had he too much audacity in believing he could reverse the Middle Passage?
Perhaps he was feeling that way when he stepped into Juffure in April 1967, and the griot recited a history that included a 17-year-old Kunta Kinte, who had left the village almost exactly 200 years earlier to gather wood to make a drum for his younger brother and never returned. Uncle Alex carried the other end of that story: where that firstborn son of Binta and Omoro Kinte had ended up on a British slave ship named the Lord Ligonier that set sail from the Gambia River on July 5, 1767, and arrived in Annapolis, Md., on Sept. 29, 1767. One hundred and forty Africans had been smuggled onto that ship. Ninety-eight survived the journey.
Uncle Alex’s arrival in Juffure was a feat of ancestral home revealed and personal mystery solved. James Earl Jones made that moment his own in the Roots miniseries. In his portrayal of Alex Haley there in Juffure, Jones exclaims with bass-toned exuberance: “You old African! I found you, Kunta Kinte!” I always smile at this scene. Knowing Uncle Alex, I imagine that his reaction would have been no less dramatically felt, but more understated. I see him sitting there, knee to knee with the griot. Upon hearing the name Kinte and then calculating the data, I envision him folding in on himself, a gut punch quietly and gratefully received; a recognition of origin, a recompense for every African American back home, a proof of life: before.
This flood of emotions must have ranged from relief to euphoria to mind-splitting fury. Perhaps it inspired the title Uncle Alex originally had in mind Before This Anger. The story we heard was that the publishers were likely apprehensive about putting off a white audience with this title. But its layers of meaning demand excavation. If there was an anger before this one, the inference is that there was a present anger. And was there not, for Black folks in America’s mid–20th century? (And every century before, and today?)
But there is another way to read it. One that reveals that before this anger—before this truncated knowledge that people of African ancestry had been enslaved for 400 years, stripped of their culture, their liberty, and their personhood, then denied civil rights—there was another place across the waters where their forebears were not property but kings and queens. Before this anger was a place where the culture of these people was wholly intact, centuries old, with a foundation so deep that when stripped from its shores, a man had carried it with him and remembered it to those in the place where he landed.
Not long after Roots’ publication, Uncle Alex was challenged by critics who questioned the accuracy of his timeline and suggested the griot told him what he wanted to hear. But as many historians pointed out, to focus on specific dates or dialogue is to miss the larger truth. The “before,” the lineage Uncle Alex uncovered, came to him by way of oral history. This tradition is, almost by definition, imperfect in its translation, especially across centuries. The very nature of the oral tradition, which is decidedly African and characteristically unburdened by the rules of Western record-keeping, is the spirit of its truth, even more than its detail. One’s trust in a griot’s accounting derives from centuries-old reliability. To counter the critics, Uncle Alex himself said while his work was informed by extensive research, the book was not without errors, and certain details were his own literary creation. Today, we call this historical fiction. But for my family, and all those who see their lineage in Roots, this genre designation changes its meaning not one bit. As my uncle told one journalist, “Neither you nor I know exactly what happened. But I stand by Roots as a symbol of the fate of my people.”
Before Roots, most every depiction of our origin had begun with enslavement, as if we had sprung up spontaneously on this soil with sun-kissed skin and woolen hair. Both captor and captive knew that all had not begun here. But the captor would not have been inclined to tell that story, and the captive was not allowed, being not permitted to learn to read or write.
All the more prescient, then, that Kunta would be inclined to tell his daughter his origin story, and teach her words in his native tongue. He likely would not have imagined that those words would lead his descendants back to his beloved homeland. Or perhaps that was his very design. Alex Haley: his ancestors’ wildest dream.
It was a game of generational telephone that allowed the world to know the history of the African American before slavery. Uncle Alex always said Roots was not just the story of the Haley family, but of every African American: “In all of us there is a hunger, marrow-deep, to know our heritage—to know who we are and where we have come from. Without this enriching knowledge, there is a hollow yearning.” Roots gave Americans of African descent an origin that began not in servitude but in freedom.
White America’s fascination is less legible. Maybe it was a need to not be called out, as by Carson. Or maybe people were more open to national truths following the Vietnam War and civil rights movement. The most common memory Black people around my age have shared with me is how, on the days after watching a Roots episode, they would go to school angry. Mean-mugging white classmates who, in turn, were sheepish and chastened. Roots was not intended as a condemnation, but for some, it played like one.
That the TV deal was struck almost before the ink on the manuscript was dry speaks to the inevitability that Roots would be an economic powerhouse, though the book’s immediate popularity surprised even the publishers, selling out an initial print run of 200,000 copies, with Doubleday forced to push out 14 more printings.
ABC must have been surprised too. The network decided to run the miniseries, originally slated to run weekly, on consecutive nights, to avoid a falloff in viewership, but also to get it all in before the ratings period. Some say it was the inclement weather that had people fixed to their TV sets. But maybe America was actually interested in learning about this 11.5% of its population whose culture it had long appreciated. And so, more than half the U.S. population and 85% of all U.S. homes with televisions watched Roots, most every night, for eight sequential nights.
Since Roots was published our country has seen vast increases in Black businesses and Black academia, a Black superhero and a Black President, even as we continue to fight the battles of institutional racism. A 2022 Pew study reported that of the Black Americans who have delved into genealogical research, 77% did so by speaking to their families. I like to think of that as a nod to Kunta, Kizzy, and the art of oral history.
I have a slightly tattered, no matter how lovingly preserved, copy of the Reader’s Digest excerpt of Roots. On its title page is a message from my uncle that reads: “To the next writer in the family. Love, Uncle Alex.” As we mark the nation’s sesquicentennial, I carry that booklet with me like a talisman, a call to arms: Keep telling our story, he tells me. Keep our ancestors alive.
History may depend on it. Earlier this spring, Knox County, Tennessee—the county where Uncle Alex spent his final years, the home of the university where he would donate the majority of his papers and where a public park holds a 13-ft., 4,200-lb. bronze statue of him, in the state that cradles the porch that birthed the book—banned Roots, requiring that copies be removed from school libraries. Ten days later, following swift backlash, the county reversed its decision. The work of the ancestors, or just better minds prevailing? Either way, the lesson is clear. The surest way to preserve one’s story is to keep telling it.

‘I feel motherly towards them’: the nature reserve manager sharing her office with a wasp nest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

When wasps began streaming through a rusted gap in her office door one June morning, Eilish Rothney’s first instinct was the same most people would have: get rid of them. The reserve manager for the Trinity Broads, part of the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, had discovered a wasp colony taking up residence in her office, a converted shipping container.
“They just built the nest inside my door,” she says. “My first thought was: ‘Oh no, I have to get rid of that now.’ But then I realised: ‘Wait, why? Why do I have to do that?’”
Two months on, Rothney is in a co-working arrangement with the nest, which is now more than a metre tall and swallows an entire bookshelf of ring binders. It has papered the inside of her office in what she calls “lovely layers of colours”, with thousands of chewed wood pulp cells stacked like the world’s strangest filing system.
Rather than evict her new colleagues, Rothney adapted. She opened the window to give the wasps a clear flight path. “I just stroll past like I’m a browsing cow, calmly going about my day,” she says. “The wasps were fine with me being there. The longer I was there, the more I felt relaxed being alongside them.”
The queen lays eggs continuously, while worker wasps forage and bring food back to feed the larvae. That, in turn, exudes a sugary liquid that the adult workers drink. Rothney describes a low purring sound rising off the nest, which she believes comes from thousands of wings beating to keep the colony cool. “It’s almost like the colony in itself is a living organism,” she says.
She says she isn’t worried about being stung – “it wouldn’t be a whole lot worse than mosquito bites” – and her advice for anyone less enthusiastic than her is: “Insects learn that certain individuals won’t harm them. Just keep calm, they will sense that and won’t feel threatened.”
Rothney traces her convictions about wildlife back to an ecology field trip at university, and to what she describes as “a kind of poetry and beauty in understanding the intricate relationships between everything”. She says she has become increasingly frustrated by how easily the label “pest” becomes a green light for extermination. “It’s fair enough if people don’t like wasps,” she says, “but we need to move away from things just being killed out of convenience. We cause a lot of damage with that approach.”
She is quick to defend the wasps which interfere with picnics every August, too. By late summer, the larvae stop producing their sugary secretion, leaving the adult workers suddenly cut off from their main food source, she says. “The poor things are starving. It’s not a battle between them and me. They’re desperate. Let’s provide them with that sugar and maybe draw them away from someone’s real ale in the evening.
“All I want is for people to be more tolerant of wasps, and of nature generally. I’m proud to be working where I am, and it’s our 100th anniversary this year – so maybe the wasps are celebrating too!”
As the weather turns this autumn, Rothney says, the queen will stop laying, the males and worker wasps will die off, and next year’s queens will leave to hibernate alone. By winter, the nest will be empty.
“It’ll be sad when they leave. I do feel motherly towards them,” she says. “It’ll be odd when they’re gone, because even the noise itself is amazing.”
And when the nest is empty? “I’m going to try to take it apart very carefully when they leave so I can see what it looks like inside.”
Until then, the shelves belong to the wasps.

Lithuanian priest accused of sexual crimes against minors over 23 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

A Lithuanian priest whose criminal case has been referred to court is accused of committing sexual offenses against minors over a 23-year period, with 11 people recognised as victims, prosecutors said Tuesday.
The Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office said the priest faces charges related to 34 intentional offenses, including crimes against sexual self-determination and integrity, offenses against children and crimes against public morality.
“The data in the case indicate that these crimes were committed, as stated in the indictment, from 2002 until 2025 – 23 years,” said Justas Laucius, chief prosecutor of the Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office.
According to prosecutors, the priest is accused of 13 incidents involving providing alcohol to a child or children, nine incidents involving the exploitation of children for pornography, four cases of sexually abusing people under 16, and three cases of satisfying sexual desires for payment while violating a minor’s sexual freedom.
He is also accused of two incidents of raping a minor and one incident involving the rape of a young child.
“Eleven people have been recognized as victims in this case. At the time of the alleged offenses, they were between 12 and 18 years old,” Laucius told reporters.
The case has been referred to the Vilnius Regional Court.
Prosecutors said most of the alleged offenses occurred in residences belonging to the Roman Catholic Church where the priest lived at the time.
“Not all of the crimes were committed within the territory of the Archdiocese of Vilnius, but most of them were,” Laucius said. “We are talking about six separate locations in Lithuania.”
Lithuania’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to 15 years for the most serious sexual offense alleged in the case, prosecutors said.
The priest has been ordered not to leave Lithuania and has surrendered his passport. His rights to dispose of real estate have also been restricted to secure potential civil claims by the alleged victims.
Second priest faces pornography charge
Prosecutors also said another criminal case involving a Catholic priest was referred to the Vilnius City District Court in June. The priest is accused of possessing child pornography.
He has also been ordered not to leave Lithuania. Prosecutors said there are no victims in that case.
“The case concerns pornographic material depicting a child or a person presented as a child,” Laucius said, describing the evidence as visual material.
Laucius said prosecutors had cooperated constructively with the Archdiocese of Vilnius in both cases. Both priests have been removed from their duties and are no longer engaged in public pastoral work, he said.
The Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference said in July that five canonical investigations into possible sexual abuse cases were underway in the country’s dioceses at the end of 2025. Two had been launched in 2025 and three in earlier years.
Laucius said alleged crimes of this nature can take decades to come to light because victims often do not report them.
“There is a high level of latency – nobody complained,” he said, adding that criminological factors may also play a role. “In my opinion, that is one of the main reasons.”
Archdiocese in cooperation with law enforcement
The Archdiocese of Vilnius said Tuesday it was cooperating with law enforcement and conducting canonical investigations.
“The Archdiocese of Vilnius has cooperated responsibly with law enforcement agencies and, out of respect for the judicial process, taking into account the sensitive situation of the victims and seeking to protect their privacy, will continue this cooperation,” it said in a statement.
It also said it had initiated canonical investigations and notified the Holy See about the suspected crimes.
“We have no doubt that the court and the canonical process will answer all questions, and those who have committed crimes will be punished accordingly,” the archdiocese stated.
The priests against whom charges have been brought have been and remain suspended from their duties, it assured.
“Every report of possible inappropriate behaviour toward a child or a vulnerable person is shocking and painful. Behind every such report is, first and foremost, a person – their experiences and pain, and sometimes years of suffering and trauma. It affects not only the victim and their loved ones, but also wounds the entire community,” Archbishop Gintaras Grušas of Vilnius is quoted in the statement.

14 suspected illegal miners die at abandoned mine in South Africa, scores injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:59:43 UTC
20:59:43 KST

Hassan Isilow
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
At least 14 suspected illegal miners have died in an abandoned mine shaft in South Africa’s North West province, with several others believed to be injured, police said Tuesday.
The South African Police Service (SAPS) said the group had been operating at the disused mine in the Nkaneng informal settlement near the city of Rustenburg, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) from Johannesburg.
Authorities did not provide detailed information on the circumstances surrounding the miners’ deaths or the number of people injured or trapped, as investigations were still underway.
South Africa, one of the world’s largest producers of gold and other precious minerals, faces a major challenge from illegal mining, with many unemployed people entering abandoned mines in search of remaining precious metals.
It is illegal to enter an abandoned mine shaft in South Africa, but many illegal miners still find ways to access them.
There are many closed mine shafts scattered across the country, and cases of miners becoming trapped, killed or injured are common.
Abandoned mines have attracted large numbers of illegal miners from both within the country and elsewhere in the southern African region.

Singer Assala Nasri prepares for long-awaited return to Damascus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:59:06 UTC
20:59:06 KST

Breadcrumb
After 14 years, Syrian singer Assala Nasri prepares to return to Damascus
Exclusive information obtained by The New Arab confirms that Syrian singer Assala Nasri will hold a concert in Damascus at a festival on 17-19 September.
Sources said she has agreed to return and hold concerts, pending the announcement of the visit programme and details.
Assala's return to Damascus carries particular significance given her political stance during the years of the Syrian revolution in which she declared her support for the opposition from its outset and attacked Bashar al-Assad's regime.
In the first months of the revolution, Assala wrote, "We must revolt, we must rise for ourselves, and if the self becomes insignificant to the whole world, it must not become insignificant to us."
Her support for the revolution led to her being removed from the Artists Syndicate.
The syndicate's former head, Zuhair Ramadan, said she "is not a member of the Syrian Artists Syndicate" and that she was practising her artistic work through a work permit, along with several other artists.
The possible return to Damascus comes as Assala strengthens her artistic presence connected to Syria.
A week ago, Rotana music channel released her new song "Al-Assala", arranged by Fouad Junaid, in a collaboration that brings the singer back to the company that handles some of her concerts.
Assala is also preparing to release a full album in the Syrian dialect, featuring 14 songs inspired by Syrian folklore, to celebrate the cultural identity of her homeland.
She has also sought to extend this approach to the visual aspect, appearing in the album's music videos in outfits inspired by the traditional clothing of several Syrian provinces.
The album is scheduled for release after the end of her current tour, which began in Tunisia and Jordan, with expectations that its release will coincide with, or come around the same time as, her return to Damascus and her reunion with her audience.
Her possible return comes as part of a new phase in which the singer is seeking to reconnect her artistic work with her Syrian roots, whether through music, visual presentation or appearing directly before audiences in Damascus.
Assala's latest album is "Dareebat al-Buad", released in summer 2025. It featured 10 diverse songs that achieved notable success.

Philippine VP Sara charged over Marcos assassination threat
She was hit with a ‘grave threats’ charge in an ongoing Senate impeachment trial over an alleged assassination plot against the president
The charge of “grave threats” was filed on Tuesday afternoon in a Quezon City courtroom, Department of Justice spokesman Polo Martinez said.
Lawyers for Duterte-Carpio on Tuesday argued the case could not be pursued while she was being impeached.
“As a sitting impeachable officer, the Vice-President may not be prosecuted for an alleged offence that is also the subject of an impeachment case,” defence lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim said in a statement.
Asked if the justice department believed the case could be pursued simultaneously alongside the impeachment trial, Martinez said: “That’s correct”, adding it was now in the court’s jurisdiction.
“That’s for the prosecutors in that ongoing trial to present,” he said, adding they had met a “high threshold” before moving forward with the case.
Professor Dante Gatmaytan, of the University of the Philippines College of Law, said there was nothing to prevent the cases from proceeding independently of each other.

Transparency data: Small boat activity in the English Channel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:57:45 BST
20:57:45 KST

Small boat activity in the English Channel
Data on the number of migrants arriving in the UK in small boats and those who were prevented by French authorities from crossing the English Channel.
Documents
Details
Data on small boat arrivals for the last 7 days is updated every day.
The time series for small boat arrivals is updated weekly on Friday. The time series goes back to 2018.
The figures for French prevention are updated weekly every Friday. French prevention activity includes individuals who are prevented from departing France, those who return to France and finds of maritime equipment.
The data published here is provisional and subject to change, including reduction. Finalised data on small boat crossings since 2018 is published in the quarterly Immigration system statistics under the topic “How many people come to the UK by illegal entry routes?”.
If you have any questions about the data, please contact migrationstatsenquiries@homeoffice.gov.uk.

Qatar rejects using Strait of Hormuz as an instrument of political pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:57:02 UTC
20:57:02 KST

DOHA, August 11. /TASS/. Qatar supports any agreements that will ensure the security of the Strait of Hormuz and prevent its use as an instrument of political pressure, said Foreign Ministry’s Spokesman Majed bin Mohammed al-Ansari.
"We in the state of Qatar support any formula of mutual understanding that guarantees the security of the strait and that it will not turn into an instrument of political pressure in the future," he said at a briefing.
Commenting on the statements of Iranian officials on the status of the Strait of Hormuz, the diplomat said that the position of the members of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf is that there is a need to return to the pre-war situation and ensure freedom of navigation.
"The management format in the future and after the current crisis is a matter for the respective regional states, it should reflect a full regional consensus within the framework of unconditional respect for international law," al-Ansari added.
On August 8, Oman's Foreign Ministry said that negotiations with Iran on shipping arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz were taking place in a positive and constructive atmosphere. On the same day, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that the parties were nearing an agreement on the legal aspects of managing the strait and defining new routes. US Vice President JD Vance also noted progress in indirect contacts with Iran, adding that Washington is working to maximize energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

====================================================================================================

Latvia discovers secret migrant tunnel at Belarus frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:56:59 UTC
20:56:59 KST

Latvian authorities have discovered a tunnel used by migrants to cross the border from Belarus illegally amid long-standing concerns that Minsk is weaponizing migration against the EU.
On Monday, border guards detected 15 people who had come through a 10-meter-long tunnel near the border fence between Belarus and Latvia, Riga’s Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said Tuesday.
Belarusian ruler Alexander Lukashenko is a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his regime has supported Moscow’s war of aggression against Ukraine and taken a hostile stance toward the EU.
Advertisement
Tunnels have previously been found in Lithuania, according to Baltic media, but this is the first time one has been used to cross into Latvia.
“This is the first case in which a tunnel has been used for illegal crossing of the state border into Latvia. No signs of violations had previously been detected in this exact location, and no detentions of persons illegally crossing the state border had occurred there,” Dombrava wrote on X.
Authorities returned all 15 people to their “country of departure” and are continuing to inspect the area around the tunnel.
Latvia launched an operation Tuesday to strengthen border security. Dombrava has described illegal border crossings from Belarus as a “hybrid threat.”
Authorities have prevented more than 9,000 illegal attempts to cross the border from Belarus so far this year, the Latvian State Border Guard said in a press release.
