US transgender woman returns home after failed Dutch asylum bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:26:24 UTC
20:26:24 KST

US transgender woman returns home after failed Dutch asylum bid
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A transgender woman from the US who sought asylum in the Netherlands has returned home after her application bid failed and she suffered serious intimidation at the Ter Apel refugee centre.
Jane-Michelle Arc, from California, was one of approximately 76 Americans that sought asylum in the Netherlands last year. She flew to Schiphol airport and was instructed by customs officers to report to the immigration service IND at Ter Apel, which houses roughly 2,000 asylum seekers.
Her reason for leaving the US was the change in policy enacted by the Trump administration, which in an executive order denounced “ideologues who deny the biological reality of sex”, and ended the federal recognition of any gender identity besides male and female, rolling back anti-discrimination policies and protections on employment, housing and healthcare protections for trans people.
But the conditions at Ter Apel, which Arc described as “dire”, were life-threatening, she said, citing anti-trans hostility from other people at the camp.
Dangerous conditions 
 “This is the dumbest thing I’ve ever done”, Arc told the Guardian. “The situation I have in the US as a trans person, not good, right?. But here, I will be hurt or killed,” she separately told outlet Powned last month.
She said it was too dangerous to even walk to the supermarket, and spoke of the rising violence around the centre that has occurred this summer amid an overflow of refugees who were sleeping outside the facility gates in the heat.
After numerous fights, including two stabbings, aid organisations temporarily stopped working there for their own safety. Asylum minister Bart van den Brink subsequently enacted new measures including more security guards, CCTV cameras, and rooms for people without beds at the centre to stay indoors during the day.
US asylum claims 
 Arc estimated there are roughly 35-50 other trans people at the centre, housed in a special block away from other residents. It is unclear how many are seeking asylum on the grounds of gender discrimination, but Dutch group LGBT Asylum Support said in mid-2025 it was assisting around 20 US trans individuals with pending asylum claims.
“The IND generally states that discrimination by authorities and fellow citizens can be considered an act of persecution if it is so severe that victims can no longer function socially and societally,” the group said in a statement reported by Reuters.
 “But the IND maintains that there are no grounds for exceptional treatment of transgender and queer refugees from the US.”
Another US asylum seeker, Lisa Gayle Carter-Stewart, who fled Montana with her 14-year old transgender daughter said their application was automatically rejected because America is considered a safe country, according to the Guardian.
The IND dismissed her daughter’s statement that they would commit suicide if forced to return to the US, Carter-Stewart said. Her daughter did not feel safe to ever leave her room at Ter Apel and attempted suicide three times while staying there, before they were moved to a more family-friendly camp near Leiden. Despite their experiences in the Dutch camps, they still feel unsafe returning to the US.

Tehran, whose representatives had sought compensation for five months of US and Israeli bombardment, says the Strait of Hormuz will stay shut until Washington lifts its naval blockade, ends sanctions and releases frozen Iranian assets.

Since yields move inversely to prices, the rise means investors are selling government debt as they expect that costlier oil will feed into inflation and strengthen the case for higher interest rates.
Money markets now put roughly even odds on a Federal Reserve rate hike in September, with July inflation data due on Wednesday.
Control claimed, traffic missing
The current stalling of US-Iran negotiations is deliberate as US President Donald Trump appears to have been favouring a slower approach as of late.
The US president told Axios in an interview published on Sunday that the US is "low-keying it," meaning Washington was only semi-negotiating and content to watch Iran's inflation and empty coffers do the work, a signal he is prepared to let economic pressure mount rather than order a fresh military campaign.
In the Oval Office on Monday, he struck a triumphant note, claiming the US controls "100%" of the Strait of Hormuz, that only the US Navy holds sway in the region, that American forces have swept it clear of Iranian mines and that the blockade of Iranian ports is impenetrable.

Britons warned of permanent eye damage from looking at solar eclipse
- Britons have been warned that even brief exposure to the sun during the upcoming partial solar eclipse on 12 August can cause permanent vision damage.
- Royal Museums Greenwich said that it will be the most complete solar eclipse visible in the UK since August 1999, an event that resulted in 70 reported cases of visual loss.
- Experts from the Royal College of Ophthalmologists warned that retinal damage is painless, meaning symptoms such as central blind spots or blurred vision may only appear hours later.
- Standard sunglasses, cameras and binoculars do not offer adequate protection, so experts recommend using verified ISO-certified eclipse glasses, indirect projection, or watching live broadcasts.
- The eclipse will be visible across the UK between 6.08pm and 8.10pm on 12 August, reaching its peak between 7.05pm and 7.16pm.

Yerevan has recently announced its intention to pursue integration with the EU. On March 26, 2025, the Armenian parliament adopted a law launching the republic’s accession to the union. At the same time, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said the country does not intend to withdraw from the EAEU and expects to combine its membership there with integration into the EU for as long as possible. Russian President Vladimir Putin noted that integration into the EU automatically entails the cessation of Armenia’s cooperation with the EAEU and the loss of all related preferences from which Yerevan has benefited during its membership in the union.
At an EAEU summit in Astana on May 29, the leaders of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan adopted a joint statement saying that they agreed that Armenia should hold a nationwide referendum on accession to the EU or continued membership in the EAEU.

British girl who died on Caribbean family holiday was ‘killed in boat explosion’

A 16-year-old British schoolgirl who died on a family holiday in the Caribbean was killed in a boat explosion that left 24 others injured, according to reports.

The family was on an excursion in the waters around Saona Island when tragedy struck, The Sun reports.
“It was an accident at sea and was very tragic,” an official in the Dominican Republic told the newspaper. “The young lady and her injured siblings were moved immediately to the hospital in the city of La Romana, but sadly she did not survive.
“Despite the best efforts of medical staff, she did not make it. Her injured siblings are continuing to be looked after in the hospital.”

The couple described the panic and chaos of the scene as flames and bits of debris blew up around them. They said passengers jumped into the surrounding waters to protect themselves before being rescued by other boats.
The pair said they were treated for first degree burns while Mr Torres also received stitches after being struck by debris.
“The three Puerto Rican girls, one of them had a broken foot,” said Gisell. “There was these other two men from New York, one of them has spinal injuries and he doesn’t know if he’s paralyzed. His friend has a broken foot.”
An Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office spokesperson told The Independent: “Our thoughts are with the Lainton family during this difficult time.
“We are providing consular support to the family and assisting other British nationals and their families affected by the incident. We are in contact with the local authorities.”
Tributes have poured in for Abbie, who was awaiting her GCSE results when she was killed.
“Abbie had her whole life ahead of her,” read the GoFundMe page, which has now raised more than £21,000. “She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results. She was so loved by her family, friends and everyone who knew her.”

Heatwaves set to drive prices higher, food producers warn
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:24:39 BST
20:24:39 KST

Heatwaves set to drive prices higher, food producers warn
The Food and Drink Federation said ‘fruit, vegetable and grain supply’ are being hit by recent hot weather and droughts.
- Bookmark
Soaring temperatures and droughts across the UK and Europe are set to drive prices higher, food and drink producers have warned.
The Food and Drink Federation (FDF) said “fruit, vegetable and grain supply” are being hit by recent heatwaves, with these crop shortages then set to feed into supermarket prices.
Economists from the trade group suggested that this will put upward pressure on food inflation going into 2027.
It is understood that the supply of a number of UK-grown fruit and vegetables has already come under pressure, such as broccoli and cherries.
Meanwhile, poor grain harvests are driving the cost of animal feed higher, with predictions that this could lead to more expensive meat as farmers are forced to reduce herd sizes.
It comes ahead of a fresh heatwave in the UK, with the Met Office warning that temperatures will soar to the mid-30s in some areas on Thursday.
Dr Liliana Danila, chief economist at the FDF, said the weather conditions have caused concern across most of Europe.
She said: “Competition for fewer resources will in turn push up the price of ingredients for manufacturers.
“The UK’s food and drink manufacturers work hard to absorb costs where they can, but are already grappling with rising costs as a result of war in Ukraine and in Iran, so we expect the additional upward pressure of reduced crops will be reflected in retail prices into next year.”
FDF Scotland’s David Thomson also told the BBC that price rises are “inevitable” because of “significant concerns” over the availability of many fruit and vegetable products.
Meanwhile, the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (ADHB) has said that milk production has already been impacted by the extreme hot weather, with production yields impacted by heat-stressed cows and poor conditions for grass grazing.
Andrew Opie, director of food and sustainability policy at the British Retail Consortium, said: “Climate change continues to create challenges for retailers and their suppliers.
“Extreme weather, including drought, can affect crop yields and place upward pressure on prices.
“Retailers are experienced in managing supply disruptions and will take all necessary steps, including sourcing from alternative suppliers where appropriate, to minimise any impact on customers.”

Australian PM urged to apologise over joke about melons gifted by Japan’s Takaichi
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:23:03 BST
20:23:03 KST

Australian PM urged to apologise over joke about melons gifted by Japan’s Takaichi
Anthony Albanese appeared to gesture in front of his chest while talking about the gift on a podcast last month
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Australia’s prime minister has refused to apologise over an apparent joke about a gift of expensive melons from his Japanese counterpart.
Anthony Albanese was asked in the parliament on Tuesday whether he would say sorry to Sanae Takaichi, Japan's first female prime minister, who gifted him two crown melons when she visited Australia in May.
“I reject the assertion in the question,” he replied.
The remarks were made on Bush Deep, a comedy podcast recorded at his residence and broadcast in July.
Discussing the melons, Mr Albanese appeared to gesture in front of his chest, and the host, comedian Nikki Osborne, replied that Ms Takaichi had come in looking like Pamela Anderson.
Crown melons are among Japan’s most expensive fruit, grown one to a vine in greenhouses in Shizuoka and given as formal gifts at weddings, funerals, or business meetings. A single melon can cost more than 30,000 yen, or about £150.
The remarks attracted little attention at the time but resurfaced this week after Shingo Yamagami, Japan's ambassador to Australia until 2023, wrote in the Australian that the comments were a sexist joke that betrayed the bond between the two countries.
"So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," Mr Yamagami wrote, adding that the last thing Ms Takaichi expected was to be casually mocked by the leader of Japan's closest strategic partner.
Mr Yamagami had a frosty relationship with sections of Mr Albanese's Labor party during his posting, largely over differences on China.
Pressed again in the parliament, Mr Albanese said that Australia and Japan had never been closer or more strategically aligned and that his government had taken the relationship to new heights.
"Why didn't you say that in the podcast?" one opposition MP interjected.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor called the joke insulting and demanded a personal apology while his deputy, Jane Hume, described it as “grubby” and “beneath the office of the prime minister”.
Labor ministers defended Mr Albanese. Finance minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks were not intended to be taken the way political opponents and some media outlets had reported them, while resources minister Madeleine King said they had been mischaracterised.
Assistant minister Pat Gorman told reporters there was no need for an apology. "I don't know why we're still talking about this,” he said.
Japan’s government sent a diplomatic cable to Canberra in July, days after the podcast episode aired, complaining about sensationalised reporting in the Australian media and saying that it detected no ill intention in Mr Albanese's remarks, according to the Australian.
Shiro Armstrong, director of the Australia-Japan Research Centre at the Australian National University, told Radio National that the remarks had gone unmentioned in Japan until weeks afterwards, calling it a “non-issue” there.
Mr Yamagami later claimed that the row was being debated in Japan and suggested Mr Albanese visit Tokyo this year.
The same podcast episode had already caused trouble for Mr Albanese, who had to apologise after naming Kylie Minogue when Ms Osborne asked him to play a game of "shag, marry, date".
Ms Osborne, best known for crude comedy sketches on YouTube, describes herself on the podcast's website as a wildly inappropriate journalist who asks questions no one else would dare.
Australia and Japan signed a security agreement in 2022 allowing their forces to train on each other's soil. Japan is also one of Australia's largest export markets, taking about a fifth of its liquefied natural gas.

Super Cup: PSG vs Aston Villa, UEFA vs FIFA and the Somali ref barred from the World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:23:02 UTC
20:23:02 KST

Super Cup: PSG vs Aston Villa, UEFA vs FIFA and the Somali ref barred from the World Cup
Barely three weeks after the World Cup final, the first trophy of the new European soccer season is up for grabs in the UEFA Super Cup between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa in Salzburg on Wednesday.
The annual match between the most recent winners of the Champions League and Europa League also offers another chance for more grandstanding by UEFA at the expense of FIFA at a time of a growing disconnect between the two powerful soccer governing bodies in light of the recent conduct of Gianni Infantino.
That’s because refereeing the game will be Omar Artan, the Somali referee who was barred by the United States from officiating at the World Cup days before the start of the tournament because of vetting concerns. U.S. officials claimed Artan had connections to terror organizations, though without providing proof.
UEFA responded by picking Artan — a referee judged the best in Africa last season — to take charge of the Super Cup, a move that was widely celebrated in the soccer community and also was regarded as a clever political ploy by the European association.
The disharmony between UEFA and FIFA has increased since, with UEFA leading the campaign to oust Infantino from the FIFA presidency over his recent — aborted — plan to sell an interest in the World Cup.
And so, the referee taking charge of the match is proving to be as interesting as the players involved, as PSG looks to become the second team in the modern era to retain the Super Cup, after Real Madrid (2016 and 2017).
PSG beat Tottenham in a penalty shootout in last year’s match.
PSG’s World Cup stars return
PSG’s players came back to preseason training in scattered order over the summer, largely depending on how long they played at the World Cup — or not at all in one noteworthy case.
Ballon d’Or winner Ousmane Dembélé, who stood out for France with six goals and two assists, returned on Monday along with international teammates Désiré Doué and Bradley Barcola. They were joined by Spain’s World Cup-winning midfielder Fabián Ruiz, whose clinical performance was key to the semifinal victory against France.
Star winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia didn’t play at the tournament because Georgia did not qualify, and has been back training for considerably longer. He looks certain to start in his favored position on the left flank, with new signing Maghnes Akliouche possibly on the right wing.
Akliouche’s arrival from Monaco could coincide with Barcola’s departure, with the fleet-footed winger — who scored three goals at the World Cup — heavily linked with a move to Premier League giant Liverpool.
Coach Luis Enrique’s team may also feature former Villa player Lucas Digne.
Back to the future
Villa sold Digne to PSG on Sunday for a reported free of 10 million euros ($11.6 million), returning the 33-year-old left back to one of his first clubs.
Digne was among the first signings when PSG began its new era after being bought by Qatari investors QSI.
He was born in the Paris suburbs and joined PSG in 2013 from Lille. He then represented Roma and Barcelona before spending eight years in the Premier League with Everton and Villa, where he played 182 games in total and was one of coach Unai Emery’s most consistent players.
Emery has lost key Villa midfielders
There’ll be a different look to Villa at the start of its fourth full season under Emery, a former PSG coach.
Departing over the summer were key midfielders Morgan Rogers to Chelsea and Youri Tielemans to Manchester United, along with Digne.
Among the new signings are Swiss World Cup star Johan Manzambi and Brazilian midfielder Joao Gomes, who has joined from relegated Wolverhampton. Manzambi is missing because of a knee injury.
Villa won the Europa League by beating Freiburg 3-0 and in the final will be in the Champions League for the second time under Emery.
Artan’s ‘very challenging’ time
Artan, who oversaw the African Champions League final in 2025, is the first non-European to take charge of the Super Cup and said the honor comes after a “very tough period”.
“A lot of people have sympathy for me,” he told UEFA, “because when someone has been working a lot of years and is supposed to do something, and then can’t do it, it’s very challenging. I really appreciate the support I received throughout the world, though. I’m so grateful.”
Artan said he had been undertaking lots of research on PSG and Villa for his first match in Europe.
“The standard in Europe is fantastic and the football they play is very, very good,” he said.

Authorities say 10 Nigerian police officers were killed in gunbattle with rebels in the north
ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — A gunbattle between rebels and Nigerian security forces has left 10 police officers dead in a remote part of the country’s conflict-battered north, authorities said Tuesday.
The clash, which occurred on Monday in the Sakaba council area of Kebbi state, also left two civilians and 17 of the rebels dead, police spokesperson Bashir Usman said in a statement.

“Tragically, we lost 10 gallant police personnel in the engagement, while two others sustained injuries and are receiving medical attention,” the police spokesman said.
The attack is the latest in a cycle of violence in Africa’s most populous country, where gangs compete for territory and control of natural resources in villages where they outnumber the country’s overstretched security forces. Dozens have been killed in recent weeks across the north, and security forces are often targeted.
The U.S. government is providing military support to Nigeria under an agreement it says aims to protect Nigerian Christians, though much of that support is restricted to logistics and intelligence-gathering at the heart of the violence in the north.

Lebanon: Abolition of death penalty a landmark victory affirming justice must be rooted in human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:21:15 UTC
20:21:15 KST

Responding to the Lebanese parliament’s approval of a law that abolishes the death penalty for all crimes, Heba Morayef, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa at, said:
“Lebanon’s decision to abolish the death penalty marks a major milestone and a victory for human rights in the country. Justice must be rooted in human rights, not in an irreversible and cruel punishment. After more than two decades without executions, today’s step transforms a precarious hiatus in executions into lasting legal protection upholding the right to life and bringing Lebanon in line with the global trend towards abolition.
Justice must be rooted in human rights, not in an irreversible and cruel punishment.
Heba Morayef, Amnesty International.
“The passing of this law is testament to the decades of tireless advocacy by Lebanese human rights defenders and organizations, as well as the leadership of key officials who recognized the death penalty as a cruel and inhuman punishment, often imposed after unfair proceedings and the burden of which frequently falls on those at most disadvantage.
“To turn this law from paper to practice, Lebanese authorities must now ensure that all death sentences are commuted and ratify the key international treaty on abolition, while advancing broader reforms to strengthen a justice system based on dignity, fairness and respect for human rights. Authorities must accompany this law with broader legislative reform, including to ensure that any criminal justice punishments are consistent with human rights principles.”
Background
On 11 August the Lebanese parliament approved a law that abolishes the death penalty and replaces it with life imprisonment with hard labour as an alternative sentence.
Lebanon has not carried out any executions since 17 January 2004. As of the end of January 2026, 85 people remained on death row, according to the Directorate of Prisons at the Ministry of Justice. The adoption of this law follows sustained efforts by Lebanese and international civil society. At the forefront of the advocacy efforts have been the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights (LACR), the National Campaign for the Abolition of the Death Penalty in Lebanon and the Association Justice and Mercy (AJEM).
On 7 October 2025, seven members of parliament submitted the draft law to the Parliamentary Human Rights Committee. After seeking the government’s opinion, the cabinet issued a favourable advisory on 20 November 2025. The draft law was approved by the Parliamentary Human Rights Committee on 23 February 2026 and subsequently adopted by the Parliamentary Justice Committee and by the Joint Committee on 2 June and 9 July 2026, respectively, before being approved by the full session of parliament on 11 August 2026. The law is due to be transmitted to the President for final signature and published in the Official Gazette before entering into force.
To make the abolition of the death penalty irreversible under international human rights law, the Lebanese authorities must ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty.
Amnesty International opposes the death penalty in all cases without exception, regardless of the nature of the crime, the characteristics of the individual, or the method used by the state. Lebanon is poised to become the 114th country that has abolished the death penalty for all crimes once the law comes into effect. A total of 145 countries worldwide are abolitionist in law or practice, while 54 countries continue to retain it.

====================================================================================================

EXPLAINER - Cook Islands election emerges as test of China-West rivalry in Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:21:09 UTC
20:21:09 KST

The Cook Islands will hold a general election Wednesday that on paper is about choosing 24 lawmakers for a nation of scattered islands in the South Pacific.
Increasingly, however, the vote is being watched as something larger.
It will be a test of how a small island nation in the South Pacific Ocean navigates intensifying competition between China and its traditional Western partners.
The election comes after an unusually turbulent period in the Cook Islands’ foreign relations, driven by Prime Minister Mark Brown’s effort to broaden the country’s international partnerships, most controversially through a comprehensive strategic partnership with Beijing.
The Cook Islands Parliament says the 18th Parliament was dissolved on June 25 and the election for its successor will be held on Aug. 12.
The country uses 24 single-member constituencies, meaning candidates compete for individual seats rather than through a nationwide proportional system. A party or coalition needs 13 seats for a parliamentary majority.
Brown’s Cook Islands Party enters the election as the dominant force. In 2022, it secured 12 seats compared with five for Tina Browne’s Democratic Party, three for the Cook Islands United Party, one for the One Cook Islands Movement and three for independents.
But this election has become considerably more fragmented.
Asia Pacific Report, citing Cook Islands News, said 63 candidates are running for the 24 seats, with independents accounting for roughly one-fifth of them. One independent, Agnes Armstrong, has already retained the Ivirua Constituency unopposed.
The governing Cook Islands Party is fielding 20 candidates, the Cook Islands United Party 14 and the Democratic Party 12. Smaller groups include the Progressive Party, Independent-Enuamanu and the new Independence Party.
Veteran former politician Norman George told Cook Islands News that political parties appeared to have lost their traditional “attraction, drawcard and magic touch,” arguing that independent candidates were increasingly filling the space.
Cook Islands United Party leader Teariki Heather disputed that assessment, while Democratic Party leader Tina Browne has ruled out pre-election coalition agreements.
The Cook Islands Party, meanwhile, has previously relied on independent support to form governments and is seeking a fifth consecutive term, according to Asia Pacific Report.
The Cook Islands is self-governing but exists in free association with New Zealand, an arrangement dating to 1965. Cook Islanders are New Zealand citizens, and Wellington retains important responsibilities in areas including defense and foreign affairs when requested.
That relationship was strained in 2025, when Brown’s government signed a five-year Action Plan for a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with China.
The agreement covers areas including deep-sea minerals, hydrography, disaster management and cultural cooperation. New Zealand complained that it had not been adequately consulted before the agreement was signed, while opposition groups in the Cook Islands questioned its transparency.
RNZ reported at the time that New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon stressed the expectation that the two governments would consult transparently on matters touching defense and security. Brown rejected suggestions that his government was acting secretly and said its international agreements would serve Cook Islands interests.
Hundreds of people subsequently protested in Rarotonga amid concerns about the China agreement and a separate, later-abandoned proposal for a Cook Islands passport. The government maintained that closer relations with Beijing were intended to complement rather than replace its established relationships with New Zealand, Australia and other partners.
The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), the world's oldest and the UK's leading defense and security think tank, described the China-Cook Islands partnership as part of a broader transformation of Pacific geopolitics.
The Cook Islands has a land area that is tiny by global standards but an exclusive economic zone covering nearly 2 million square kilometers. RUSI said that maritime territory and its resources have increased the islands’ strategic importance as competition between China and Western powers intensifies.
The Chinese state-run Global Times has presented the election and surrounding debate from Beijing’s perspective, against criticism that Western powers are increasingly treating Pacific island countries as arenas for geopolitical competition rather than independent states pursuing their own diplomatic and economic interests.
That competing interpretation goes to the heart of the election’s international significance: whether closer Chinese engagement represents an erosion of the traditional regional order or simply the Cook Islands exercising greater diplomatic autonomy.
The competition is not only about diplomacy.
Some of the world’s potentially important deposits of polymetallic nodules lie on the Cook Islands seabed.
The Cook Islands Seabed Minerals Authority estimates that the country's continental shelf contains about 6.7 billion metric tons of nodules potentially holding roughly 20 million metric tons of cobalt alongside manganese, nickel, copper and other materials important for batteries, advanced manufacturing and defense technologies. Commercial extraction has not been approved.
That has drawn Washington more deeply into the picture.
In February, the Cook Islands and the US established a non-binding framework for cooperation on critical minerals and rare earths, including deep-sea minerals. The agreement covers research, exploration, investment, processing and supply-chain development while explicitly preserving Cook Islands sovereignty over decisions concerning its seabed.
US Ambassador Jared Novelly said in July that Cook Islands seabed minerals had become a top American priority as Washington seeks alternative supplies of critical minerals and tries to reduce dependence on supply chains dominated by China.
American scientific involvement is expanding as well. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced in May that it would work with the Cook Islands Seabed Minerals Authority to map and explore deep waters around the country, including abyssal plains and the Manihiki Plateau.
The result is an election taking place at the intersection of unusually large forces for such a small electorate.
Cook Islanders will vote principally on domestic questions—government performance, public services, representation and the appeal of individual candidates. But the government they produce will also inherit decisions about how closely to engage China, how to manage the country's unique relationship with New Zealand and how far to pursue emerging cooperation with the United States.
And beneath those choices lies another question that could shape the Cook Islands for decades: who, if anyone, will eventually develop the mineral wealth sitting thousands of meters below its surrounding ocean.
For Beijing, Washington and Wellington, Wednesday’s election therefore carries significance far beyond the 24 seats being contested.
For Cook Islanders, the challenge may be precisely the opposite, ensuring that an election about their country does not become merely another contest between much larger powers.

"하루 3시간 이내 수면" 다카이치 여름휴가도 생략
South Korea

2026-08-11
20:20:52 KST
20:20:52 KST

(도쿄=연합뉴스) 조성미 특파원 = 다카이치 사나에 일본 총리가 역대 총리들이 해외 순방이나 여름 휴가로 사용해 온 국회 폐회 기간 별도의 휴가 일정 없이 업무에 전념한다고 요미우리신문이 11일 전했다.
 다카이치 총리는 8월 중순인 일본의 추석(오봉) 연휴 중 여름휴가를 가지 않고 구마모토 강진 사후 수습과 가을 임시국회 준비를 할 방침으로 전해졌다.
 고향이자 지역구인 나라현으로 귀성할 계획이 있었지만 취소했고 해외 순방도 하지 않을 계획이다.
 다카이치 총리와 가까운 한 관계자는 요미우리에 "긴 여름휴가 계획은 없다. 출근 여부는 그날 처리해야 할 업무가 있는지에 따라 판단할 것"이라고 말했다. 
 다카이치 총리는 취임 이후 업무 자료를 읽고 와병 중인 남편 돌봄, 가사를 직접 하느라 수면 시간이 극도로 짧다고 밝혀왔는데 휴식 기회인 장기간 휴가도 갖지 않는 셈이다.
 다카이치 총리가 지난달 자신의 엑스(X·옛 트위터)에 "총리 취임 이후 0∼3시간 수면이 일상화됐다"며 새벽까지 자료를 읽고 집안일을 하는 일상에 대해 소개하자 건강에 대한 우려와 적절한 시간 관리에 대한 요구가 함께 제기된 바 있다.

New Hong Kong trade office in Malaysia a bridge to Greater Bay Area: minister
Commerce chief Algernon Yau calls launch of Economic and Trade Office in Kuala Lumpur ‘highly strategic move’
Hong Kong has opened a new trade office in Malaysia, with a minister saying the move is part of a strategic push to deepen regional ties and will help position the city as a bridge between the country and the Greater Bay Area.
Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah said on Tuesday that the opening of the Economic and Trade Office (ETO) in Kuala Lumpur would strengthen Hong Kong’s presence in the region.
“The establishment of the new [ETO] in Kuala Lumpur is a highly strategic move,” he said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post.
“By setting up a dedicated office in Malaysia, the Hong Kong government can better manage regional resources and provide targeted support across Southeast Asia.”
Yau, who officiated the office’s opening ceremony, noted that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or Asean, continued to serve as Hong Kong’s second-largest merchandise trading partner.
The Asean bloc comprises the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor.

Bluetongue: latest situation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:19:33 BST
20:19:33 KST

Bluetongue: latest situation
Overview of current bluetongue cases, risk level, vaccinations and restrictions.
Be vigilant for signs of bluetongue and report it if you suspect it.
Total number of cases
There have been 334 cases of bluetongue serotype 3 (BTV-3) in the UK in the 2026 to 2027 bluetongue season. This includes:
- 326 cases in England
- 7 cases in Wales
- 1 case in Scotland
- 0 cases in Northern Ireland
There have been no cases of bluetongue serotype 8 (BTV-8) in the 2026 to 2027 bluetongue season.
Where animals with suspect clinical signs are reported, Defra funds the cost of diagnostic testing for up to 3 affected animals.
The bluetongue case map shows the location of all premises in Great Britain where one or more animals have tested positive by PCR for bluetongue.
Latest updates
10 August 2026
Forty-two new cases of BTV-3 were confirmed in England on 10 August 2026. All were tested following reports of suspicious clinical signs. Of these, 39 cases involved sheep and 3 involved cattle. All cases presented with clinical signs typical of those seen in recent cases.
One new case of BTV-3 was confirmed in cattle in England on 10 August 2026, following a non-negative voluntary pre-movement test.
Two new cases of BTV-3 were confirmed in Wales on 10 August 2026. Both cases were in sheep and were confirmed following reports of suspicious clinical signs.
Summary of cases
Cases (number of premises) by county
10 July to midnight 10 August 2026
See our bluetongue cases map.
Species involved
Method of detection
Ongoing cases
There are currently 1,524 potential cases of bluetongue under investigation. These are premises that have reported suspicious clinical signs and are under investigation.
2025 to 2026 season
See historical cases for earlier cases.
Risk level
The risk of bluetongue virus incursion from:
- all routes – is medium (occurs regularly)
- airborne routes – is low (event is rare, but could occur)
This includes serotypes that are not currently circulating in England.
The midges that spread bluetongue became active again on 31 March 2026.
Temperatures are consistently high enough in parts of the UK and nearby continental Europe for the virus to develop inside the midges. This means onward transmission is now occurring and there is increased risk of transmission from midges blown across the Channel. Animals can also get infected through germinal products (semen, ova or embryos).
Control zones
There are bluetongue restricted zones across the whole of England and Wales.
You can check the restricted zones using the bluetongue zone map.
England: country-wide restricted zone
The whole of England is in a bluetongue restricted zone. You can move animals within England without a specific bluetongue licence or pre-movement testing.
You need a specific licence to freeze germinal products (semen, ova and embryo) anywhere in England and testing is required. Keepers are responsible for the cost of sampling, postage and testing. There is more detail in the declaration.
Wales: country-wide restricted zone
An all-Wales restricted zone was introduced on 10 November 2025. This has the following effects:
- free movement of livestock – livestock movements between England and Wales do not require bluetongue vaccination or mitigation measures
- restrictions on germinal products – you must test donor animals before freezing and marketing germinal products, as this provides quality assurance and reduces the risk of longer-term bluetongue transmission
Moving live animals from a Restricted Zone (RZ) to Scotland (including shows, markets, gatherings, even if temporary)
England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man all have bluetongue virus BTV RZs, and any movement of bluetongue susceptible animals from a BTV RZ to Scotland must comply with the conditions set out in the general movement licence EXD608(EW). These controls came into force on 1 June 2026 and will remain in force until at least 9 September 2026. Check the rules on movements to and from Scotland.
Moving animals and animal products
Find out about:
- moving animals within the restricted zone
- general licences to move animals and germinal product from the restricted zone to Scotland or Wales
- moving, freezing and storing germinal product
- moving certain animals from Northern Ireland to Great Britain

Contact the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) if you keep camelids (such as llamas or alpacas) or you’re unsure about the rules.
Importing animals and animal products
Check the rules on imports, exports and EU trade of animals and animal products.

Watch recordings of bluetongue webinars.
Find leaflets, videos and posters about bluetongue.
Defra’s bluetongue control strategy
Defra controls cases of bluetongue by following the Bluetongue: disease control framework in England.
Historical cases
The first cases of bluetongue virus serotype 3 (BTV-3) of the 2026 to 2027 outbreak season was confirmed on 10 July 2026.
2025 to 2026 outbreak season (1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026)
There were 348 cases of bluetongue in Great Britain in the 2025 to 2026 bluetongue season. In:
- England, there were 324 cases of bluetongue – including 311 cases of only BTV-3, 5 cases of only BTV-8, 7 cases with both BTV-3 and BTV-8 and 1 case of BTV (serotype unknown)
- Wales, there have been 24 cases of BTV-3
- There were no cases in Scotland
These cases were confirmed between 11 July 2025 and 23 June 2026.
There were 5 confirmed cases of BTV-3 in Northern Ireland.
2024 to 2025 outbreak season (1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025)
Defra confirmed 160 BTV-3 cases in England and 2 from high risk moves in Wales. One case of bluetongue virus serotype 12 (BTV-12) was confirmed in England on 7 February 2025 Giving a total of 163 cases.
These cases were confirmed between 26 August 2024 and 31 May 2025.
2023 to 2024 outbreak season (1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025)
Between 10 November 2023 and 3 March 2024 Defra confirmed 126 BTV-3 cases in England on 73 premises (119 cattle and 7 sheep). These BTV-3 cases were the first UK BTV incursions for over 15 years.
Prior to these cases the last confirmed outbreak of bluetongue was an outbreak of bluetongue virus serotype 8 (BTV-8), which took place over 2007 to 2008.

Ukraine and Moldova discuss rail corridor for grain amid Russian Black Sea attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:18:30 UTC
20:18:30 KST

Ukraine and Moldova are discussing transporting Ukrainian grain by rail through Moldovan territory to the Romanian port of Constanta, an option driven by intensified Russian attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, according to unnamed sources in both countries cited by Reuters.
The talks come as Russian strikes on vessels using the Black Sea corridor have disrupted traffic during the harvest season and forced Ukraine to cut its export forecast. On 22 July, no ship passed through the corridor at all, and the country's agriculture ministry has already lowered its projection for the 2026–2027 season by up to five million tons.
Discount sought, volume guarantees demanded
Kyiv is asking for a discount of 50 percent off the nominal rate to transport its grain, according to the agency's sources. A source at Moldovan Railway said Moldova responded with a counterproposal: guarantees from Ukraine on the volumes of grain it would transport through the route.
"We are currently collecting information on potential volumes from interested shippers. The information-gathering process has not yet been completed," a senior Ukrainian industry official told Reuters.
Ukraine expects corridor to cover 10 percent of exports
Ukraine estimates the Moldovan corridor could handle 10 percent of its grain exports. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said earlier that his ministry had lowered its grain export forecast for the 2026–2027 season from 43 million tons to 38–40 million tons because of Russian attacks on ports.
Ministers discuss rail links
A day before the Reuters report, Moldova's Minister of Infrastructure and Regional Development, Vladimir Bolea, visited Ukraine's Odesa region and met with his Ukrainian counterpart, Mykola Kalashnyk, to discuss improving rail connections and expanding the transit network between the two countries.
Moldova's premier defends transit revenue
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said his country should not pass up the opportunity to earn millions of euros from transiting Ukrainian grain cargo. He dismissed suggestions by Moldovan farming groups that Ukrainian grain prices would depress the value of their own produce.
"Let's not look for enemies where there are none," he said on Moldovan television.
Russian attacks on shipping
Russia intensified strikes on vessels using the Ukrainian Black Sea corridor in July. On 13 July, Russian forces struck a civilian ship flying the flag of Togo while it was unloading mineral fertilizer off the coast of Odesa region, killing five crew members and injuring five others.
The following day, 14 July, Russia attacked two civilian vessels in the Black Sea — cargo ships flying the flags of Tanzania and Liberia. The captain of one of the ships was killed. On the evening of 17 July, a vessel flying the flag of the Marshall Islands was struck. Attacks continued afterward.
On 22 July, no vessel passed through the sea corridor. The Ukrainian government called the disruption "deliberate economic and humanitarian terror," coming at the height of the harvest season.
Ukraine convened an urgent session of the UN Security Council over the attacks, calling on all states — particularly those "which this directly concerns" — to demand that Russia stop striking shipping. Separately, the Southern Mining and Processing Plant (Pivdennyi HZK) announced it was suspending extraction and temporarily scaling back operations.

Wife’s childhood memory inspires Chinese husband to build world’s largest hollyhock garden

Wife’s childhood memory inspires Chinese husband to build world’s largest hollyhock garden
After 35 years of marriage, the childless couple live amid their flourishing garden, surrounded by their beloved pets
A casual remark from his wife inspired a man in southwestern China to transform a barren valley into a breathtaking sea of hollyhocks spanning 80 hectares.
Zhou Xiaolin and his wife, Yin Jie, now live amid the vibrant blooms in Chengdu, Sichuan province, where they personally tend to their sprawling garden.
Their love story drew national attention after they featured on a China Central Television programme and were celebrated as a “dream couple.”
The idea for the garden took root in 2013 when Yin, reminiscing about her childhood memories of hollyhocks in Beijing, mentioned her fondness for the flowers. Zhou, eager to make her wish come true, promised to create a garden for her.
Despite having no prior gardening experience, he sold his house, bought land in Zhuanlong Town, and taught himself how to cultivate hollyhocks. Over the years, he sourced seeds both locally and internationally, dedicating a decade to transforming the site into what is now considered the world’s largest and most diverse hollyhock garden.

Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows

Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows
Published August 11, 2026last updated August 11, 2026
What you need to know
- Economic experts expect cuts to industrial production because of reduced cargo shipping on the Rhine river
- All shipping past the town of Kaub has now stopped due to record low levels
- Wildfires caused the temporary closure of a major autobahn in northern Germany
- The number of children involved in road accidents has increased
Join us as we cover these and other stories hitting the headlines in Germany on Tuesday, August 8.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Some shipping stops on Rhine as level keeps dropping
New record-low water levels have been measured on the Rhine, a vital transport waterway, with some cargo vessel owners stopping shipping on river sections in the south.
The inland navigation agency WSV reported that the gauge at Kaub, near Koblenz, had fallen to an all-time low of 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) on Tuesday, indicating that the river depth is about 115 centimeters at its deepest point .
A commodity trader told the Reuters news agency that it was "no longer to book cargo shipments on the Rhine past Kaub."
"Most sailings there have stopped," the trader said.
Traders said that sailings on northern sections of the river were continuing.
Germany, along with much of Europe, has experienced a series of heat waves and a long period without meaningful rainfall this summer, leading to low water levels in several rivers.
The situation is having not only an environmental but also an economic impact, with companies that are reliant on goods normally transported via water suffering supply shortfalls.
The ships that are still sailing are carrying much lighter loads than usual and at higher prices.
In pictures: Rhine water levels hit historic low
Endurance athlete to swim 200 kilometers from Frankfurt to Cologne for child water safety
The 31-year-old endurance swimmer Nathalie Pohl took to the water in the Main River in Frankfurt on Tuesday at the start of a planned 200-kilometer (125-mile) swim to Cologne.
Pohl intends to swim via the Main and Rhine rivers to her destination over four days in a feat aimed at drawing attention to the importance of safe swimming, particularly for children.
According to figures from the German Livesaving Association (DLRG), at least 261 people have died by drowning this year up to the end of July.
The action is intended to raise money for swimming projects and education.
Swim not without risks
She is being accompanied by other swimmers who will put in one-hour sessions between her two-hour stints in the water.
Ahead of the start, Pohl showed herself unfazed by the possibility that low water levels in the Rhine could mean a weaker current at her and her team's back.
"Enough water is there and it shouldn't be a problem," she told the German DPA news agency, saying, however, that she hoped the algae that thrive in low water would not affect her health.
Pohl received a special permit for her action, with German authorities fundamentally warning against swimming in large rivers.
"Ultimately, something can always happen," she said, while stressing that she and her team had a comprehensive safety concept.
What you need to know about low river water levels
Water levels in several rivers in Germany, including the Rhine, have hit record lows that are well below normal for this time of year, causing severe disruptions to river traffic, with ships cutting their loads by about 80%.
The water shortage comes during a prolonged dry period in Germany, accompanied by frequent heat waves, both of which are attributed by scientists partly to the effects of human-induced climate change.
But why is the situation so serious for Germany, and what are the key terms in connection with low water levels?
The Rhine: A vital transport waterway
The Rhine has been used as a transport corridor for much of western Europe since Roman times.
It is the most important waterway in Europe, connecting industrial regions in Germany, Switzerland and other countries with big North Sea ports, including Rotterdam in the Netherlands.
Although only one in 10 tons of freight in Germany is transported via rivers such as the Rhine, they are much used for certain goods, including ore, oil, chemical products and coal.
As a result, industries that depend on these for their production are likely to be forced to cut their output, as not only is supply reduced in the current situation, but transport prices have also gone up massively.
What are river gauge measurements?
The depth of water in German rivers is measured by gauges (Pegel) situated at strategic points on their course.
These gauges, which are mostly located near the banks of a river, measure the depth of the river over an arbitrarily selected baseline.
This means the measurements are only an indication of the actual navigable depth, which can be much more.
For instance, although the gauge at the town of Kaub currently measures 16 cm (6.3 inches), the depth of the river in the channel used by shipping there is around 129 cm.
Why is the gauge at Kaub so important?
Kaub is situated on the Middle Rhine between St. Goar and Budenheim.
This section of river is seen as a chokepoint for shipping on the Rhine, as the navigable channel is not as well developed as in other places.
It has also long been used since 1856 as a key location to measure low water levels in the Rhine.
The previous lowest measurement in Kaub was 25 cm (9.8 inches) on October 22, 2018.
The present measurement of 16 cm is thus already a historic low — and it is expected to sink to single figures in the next few days.
Child road accidents rising steadily
More children were killed or injured in road accidents in 2025 than in in the previous year. That represents a renewed rise in road deaths and injuries affecting children since a decline during the coronavirus pandemic, statistics show.
Altogether 29,270 children under the age of 15 were injured in traffic accidents in Germany last year, a 7% increase over 2024, the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Monday.
The number of children killed in such accidents also rose from 53 in 2024 to 74 in 2025.
Of those fatalities, 30 were children under 6, well up on the number of children in that age group that were killed in 2024 (18).
The largest increase in deaths was seen in children travelling in cars (21 to 31).
The number of children killed on their bicycles in 2025 rose to 13 from 8 the previous year, while 4 were killed riding e-scooters, compared with none in 2024.
Most of the children involved in road traffic accidents in 2025 were riding a bicycle (34%). Altogether 31% were in a car, 20% were on foot and 8% were travelling on an e-scooter when the accidents occurred
"On average, a child was injured or killed in a road traffic accident every 18 minutes in 2025," Destatis said.
Germany needs planned intelligence agency reforms, top politician says
The chairman of the parliamentary panel overseeing Germany's secret services, Marc Henrichmann, has defended the new powers planned for intelligence agencies.
"The latest security incident at the Leipzig freight airport has shown once again that we are dealing with a new quality of hybrid threats," Henrichmann told the daily Rheinische Post.
An explosives-laden unmanned aerial vehicle was flown into the airport last week.
Henrichmannsaid that cyber attacks, sabotage and unauthorized drone overflights were "now part of a reality for which we have to be better prepared."
For this reason, he said, both the foreign intelligence agency (BND) and the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) needed the "necessary legal and technical options" to detect threats early on and identify their sources.
The reform plans have met with criticism from civil liberty activists.
The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) has voiced fears that they could lead to a "massive increase in power for intelligence agencies.
"The BND and BfV are to be allowed to intervene profoundly in basic rights with expanded use of government spyware, AI analyses practically without protective measures, access to private video cameras and even hack-backs although the legal hurdles often remain vague and too low," the organization's Kai Dittmann said.
He called for the draft bill to be thoroughly revised, calling it "unconstitutional in many parts."
The draft reform bill is set to be approved by the German Cabinet on Wednesday.
Autobahn reopens after closure because of wildfire
A highway in the northern state of Lower Saxony has reopened after being closed for over 12 hours as wildfire smoke dangerously reduced visibility.
Police closed the A7 autobahn to traffic between Göttingen and Kassel on Monday afternoon after thick smoke from the fire near Hannoversch Münden engulfed the road.
A police spokeswoman said some clean-up operations on a section of the motorway went on until the early hours of Tuesday morning but that both sides could now be used.
Low water in Rhine will cause production cuts — IW research institute
The reduction in cargo being shipped via the Rhine because of low water levels will lead companies to cut production, a leading economic research institute reports.
"Transport routes south of Kaub are now threatening to become completely severed, meaning the Rhine is cut in two," Thomas Puls, the transport expert from the German Economic Institute (IW) told the daily Rheinische Post.
"Because neither road nor rail are able to take the goods needed, the most likely reaction of primary industries will be to reduce production," he said.
This assessment appeared to be confirmed by a spokesman for the chemical company Covestro, who told the paper that the shortfalls in supply caused by the disruption to Rhine shipping was already affecting production.
The spokesman said that the current lifting of a ban on trucks using the motorway on Sundays would be of only temporary benefit.
"Ship transport via the Rhine can barely be compensated on the road, as a cargo vessel that can carry 1,500 tons is the equivalent of around 60 trucks," he said. "So ship transport cannot be completely shifted to roads."
The record low water levels on the Rhine caused by a prolonged shortage of rainfall in Germany mean that ships are currently able to carry only around a fifth of the load they usually transport.

“We’re literally on an hour-by-hour basis hoping that Mr. Gilman hangs on and that we can secure for him some kind of lifesaving medical evacuation out of Russia,” Ramsey told PBS Newshour.
Gilman, 32, was arrested in January 2022 in Voronezh after an incident in which he was accused of assaulting a police officer. A court sentenced him to two years in prison that October.

(요하네스버그=연합뉴스) 나확진 특파원 = 아프리카 콩고민주공화국(민주콩고)에서 에볼라 발병을 선언한 지 3달이 안 돼 누적 사망자가 2천명이 넘었다.
 11일(현지시간) 민주콩고 정부에 따르면, 지난 9일 기준 자국 내 에볼라 누적 확진자는 4천381명으로 집계됐다.

 역대 최대 규모로 에볼라가 유행했던 2014~2016년 서아프리카 유행 때는 확진자 2만8천616명과 사망자 1만1천310명이 발생했지만, 당시엔 기니에서 발병 선언 이후 사망자 1천명에 이르기까지 약 5개월이 걸린 것으로 파악됐다.
 아프리카 질병통제예방센터(아프리카 CDC)의 장 카세야 사무총장은 최근 에볼라 발병 선언 이후 첫 12주 동안 확진자와 사망자 수를 비교하면 이번 발병이 서아프리카 유행 때에 비해 확진자는 8배, 사망자는 6배에 이른다고 말했다고 DPA 통신은 전했다.

Ebola death toll in DR Congo outbreak rises to more than 2,000, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:12:38 UTC
20:12:38 KST

The Ebola outbreak, which has hit the DRC's conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on 15 May but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks.
An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has killed 2,011 people out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus, Congolese officials said on Tuesday.
The latest toll puts it close behind the DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak in 2018-2020 when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases.
The Ebola outbreak, which has hit the DRC's conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on 15 May but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks.
It is the DRC's 17th surge of the highly contagious disease and is already considered the largest in the country's history "and could well become the largest outbreak ever," Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, said.
The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9%.
Aid workers say the outbreak continues to outpace response that’s been expanding across the five eastern provinces affected.
Many health workers have gone on strike to protest lack of payment for their work since the outbreak was declared.
On Friday, World Health Organisation (WHO) vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of the only existing approved Ebola vaccine to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DRC against which no specific vaccine currently exists.
The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DRC.
Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage.
The WHO regional director for Africa, Doctor Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told a news conference that officials are "chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us."
Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever.
The first Ebola virus to be identified was in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now Congo.

Türkiye's Arctic expedition brings scientists together to compare Earth's polar regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:12:04 UTC
20:12:04 KST

International researchers who participated in Türkiye’s sixth National Arctic Scientific Research Expedition have conducted studies ranging from the effects of climate crisis on polar ecosystems to the distribution of Arctic bird species and microplastic pollution.
The expedition, known as TASE-VI, concluded after bringing together 12 scientists to carry out 12 projects and studies in oceanography, biology, chemistry, atmospheric dynamics, meteorology, geodesy and satellite systems.
The expedition was conducted under the auspices of the Turkish Presidency, coordinated by the Industry and Technology Ministry and led by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye’s Polar Research Institute, or TUBITAK KARE.
Travelling aboard a research vessel as far as 82 degrees north, the team examined priority scientific issues of national and international importance under Türkiye’s National Polar Science Strategy.
The research focused on global climate crisis, threatened ecosystems and environmental pressures caused by human activity.
Three international researchers from Argentina, Bulgaria and Uruguay joined the expedition to study the effects of climate crisis on polar ecosystems, the geographical distribution of Arctic bird species and airborne microplastic pollution.
Impact of retreating glaciers on ecosystems
Paula Arbiza, a biologist and Earth sciences master’s student representing the Uruguayan Antarctic Institute, studied Arctic fjord ecosystems affected by glaciers.
Arbiza said the researchers would compare data collected during the expedition with findings from their work in Antarctica.
The study aims to determine how glacier retreat caused by climate crisis affects the health of surrounding ecosystems.
Researchers collected sediment samples and examined small organisms as biological indicators of ecosystem health while also analysing environmental variables in the region.
Comparisons between the Arctic and Antarctic are expected to help scientists better understand how polar ecosystems in the two hemispheres are responding to rising temperatures and shrinking glaciers.
Arctic bird populations observed
Boyan Michev of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences studied the structure of Arctic bird communities and the geographical distribution of species found only in the region.
Michev said researchers were able to observe approximately 30 to 40 bird species over the open sea during the expedition.
Although the birds nest on land, many travel over the sea to feed, allowing researchers to record their presence and distribution along the expedition route.
The observations are expected to contribute to research on how environmental changes affect the habitats, feeding areas and movement patterns of Arctic bird populations.
Microplastics collected from polar atmosphere
Arturo Huber of the Argentine Antarctic Institute investigated microplastic pollution in the atmosphere over the polar region.
Huber said the system used during the expedition collected airborne particles on filters. The samples will be examined in laboratories to determine the concentration of microplastics in the Arctic atmosphere.
The same method was previously used in Antarctica, enabling researchers to compare microplastic pollution in the two polar regions.
Microplastics can be transported over long distances through atmospheric and oceanic circulation, allowing particles originating far from the poles to reach remote Arctic and Antarctic environments.
The comparative research is expected to provide further insight into the scale, sources and movement of microplastic pollution across the planet’s polar regions.

Colombia earthquake rescuers race to find survivors in rubble as death toll rises to at least 169

At least 169 people died and more than 600 were injured in the earthquake, according to a tally released Tuesday by the Association of Mayors.
By Monday night, more than 2,700 people had been reported missing. Many families posted information about loved ones online, hoping for information about their fate.
The 7.4-magnitude quake struck cities across Colombia's western region shortly after 7:30 a.m. local time Monday, sending panicked residents onto the streets.
The city of Pereira, one of the hardest hit, was plunged into darkness Monday evening as volunteers combed through the remains of collapsed buildings searching for survivors.
"We're without power. This seems honestly like a zombie city," resident Juan David Gaitan told French news agency AFP.
At the airport in Pereira, videos showed pieces of ceiling falling down on travelers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic.

Around 1,600 buildings across the country were reported damaged or collapsed, with rescue workers and volunteers seen clearing rubble by hand in some places. The mayors association said 165 structures collapsed.
The Vatican said Tuesday that Pope Leo XIV is "deeply saddened" by the earthquake.
"The Holy Father, deeply saddened to learn the painful news of the earthquake that has seriously affected several areas of Colombia ... offers prayers for the eternal rest of the deceased and raises his prayers to the Lord for the prompt recovery of those affected by this tragedy," the Vatican's secretary of state, Pietro Parolin, wrote in a note to the archbishop of Cartagena, Francisco Javier Munera Correa.

"We are afraid. We hope that is not the case, that he is all right and that it is only a communication failure. But we haven't heard anything from him," Zamora said.
De la Espriella announced Monday night that he had mobilized "the entire military and police apparatus" to respond to the temblor.

South Florida organizations are among U.S.-based humanitarian groups mobilizing to send aid to Colombia.

Colombia continues search and rescue operations after earthquake, over 160 killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:11:43 UTC
20:11:43 KST

Rescue efforts across western Colombia carried into a second day on Tuesday as emergency workers dug through collapsed buildings and flattened homes, amid expectations that the death toll from the country's most powerful earthquake in decades could rise.
The 7.4-magnitude earthquake tore through Colombia's coffee-growing heartland early on Monday, killing at least 164 people.
The quake reduced multi-story buildings to rubble in cities such as Pereira and Cali, and cracked apart one of the towers of a historic cathedral in the city of Manizales.
Emergency teams aided by police, soldiers and volunteers worked through the night with excavators and, at times, their bare hands, hunting for survivors beneath debris.
In Cali, home to about 2.2 million people, at least 85 people were killed. Dozens of buildings were left leaning precariously or destroyed outright, forcing residents into the streets.
Cali hospital floors collapse, patients trapped inside
Several of the top floors of one of the city's hospitals - some dedicated to pediatric care - collapsed upon themselves, leaving some patients trapped and forcing some 600 others to be tended to on a street strewn with rubble, hospital director Irne Torres Castro told Caracol television.
Carmen Yasmin Garcia, 43, a Cali resident volunteering with rescue teams, said on Monday afternoon that her group had freed seven people from a collapsed building, but four others and a dog remained trapped.
"A moment ago there was scratching, but now we can't hear anything; we still have faith that the dog is alive and we can get these people out," Garcia said. "We need people with sticks and spades; the more people lending a hand, the better."
In Pereira, capital of the hard-hit state of Risaralda, authorities reported 66 dead.
The city also bore some of the most visible destruction, with entire residential blocks reduced to piles of concrete and twisted steel. Video posted on social media and verified by Reuters showed the city's airport violently swaying during the quake, with large chunks of the ceiling collapsing as people sheltered.
Another 13 people died in Choco, the rural province closest to the quake's epicenter.
Colombian president to deploy security force members after looting reports
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella, who assumed power just days ago, said 35 people died in Cali alone, while 188 were missing. He said 1,000 members of the security forces would be deployed to the city by dawn, following reports of looting. Cali, as well as Pereira, implemented curfews on Monday night.
"Our intention is to cooperate in any way necessary. Here, there are no distinctions or ideological divisions when it comes to defending our people or showing solidarity," De La Espriella told journalists on Monday evening.
The disaster has drawn comparisons to a deadly 1999 earthquake that devastated the same coffee-growing region, killing more than 1,000 people, as well as to catastrophic quakes that killed more than 6,300 in neighboring Venezuela in June.
