What Andy Burnham could do to keep the killers of Pc Andrew Harper behind bars
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:54:42 BST
19:54:42 KST

What Andy Burnham could do to keep the killers of Pc Andrew Harper behind bars
Justice secretary Alex Norris will now look at ways to keep ‘a greater number of the most serious offenders’ behind bars
- Bookmark
Andy Burnham has stated he is "increasingly confident" that those convicted of killing Pc Andrew Harper will serve their full terms without being released early.
It comes as the prime minister pledged to resolve the "long-running injustice" of indefinite prison terms, combining efforts to ease overcrowding in jails with measures preventing PC Andrew Harper’s killers from leaving prison prematurely.
Writing on Facebook, Mr Burnham said he called on justice secretary Alex Norris to expedite proposals for creating more headroom across the prison estate.
Here we look at the key questions.
How did we get here?
Sir Keir Starmer’s government passed the Sentencing Act, paving the way for criminals to be released after serving as little as a third of their custodial term if they are jailed for less than four years.
For those with terms of longer than four years, many could be released at the halfway point in their sentence, rather than after two-thirds.
The changes are being phased in from later this year as part of the plan to ease a crisis in prison places. Labour blames the Tories for not building enough new cells during their 14 years in power.
How do Pc Andrew Harper’s killers fit in?
The 28-year-old police officer sustained fatal injuries after being dragged down a country road by three teenagers fleeing the scene of a burglary in a car in 2019.
The driver of the car, Henry Long, was not eligible for inclusion in the early-release scheme because he had received an extended sentence of 16 years, after the judge deemed him “dangerous”.
That remains the case, and he will be in prison until at least 2030 when he becomes eligible for consideration by the Parole Board for release.
But his accomplices, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, received standard determinate sentences for manslaughter.
They were each jailed for 13 years and were initially due to be released automatically after serving two-thirds, meaning they would have been behind bars until about 2028, but under the Sentencing Act’s changes they would be eligible next year.
What has Andy Burnham’s government done?
In the face of a public outcry over the potential early release of two of the police officer’s killers, Mr Burnham ordered a review of the measures.
Prisoners serving sentences for rape or child sex offences were exempted from the changes, and Mr Burnham pushed back the date when the first early releases would begin, from September to October, to give the Probation Service more time to prepare.
But despite the furore over Pc Harper’s killers prompting the review, the changes did nothing to alter their position.
What did Mr Burnham say?
The prime minister said he had “pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do” in making the change, and “I know I can look people in the eye and say to them there is nothing more I could have asked for without risking the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing within months”.
He began his holiday as the changes were announced, leaving his ministers facing a week of difficult questions.
What has happened now?
Having returned from his overseas summer holiday, Mr Burnham has ordered justice secretary Alex Norris to find a way to prevent the early release of Pc Harper’s killers.
How could that be done?
Downing Street has been clear that it would not be possible to narrowly exempt the killers of police officers from the early release provisions, meaning that Mr Norris may be forced to ensure all offenders convicted of manslaughter – or those with sentences of, for example, 10 years or more – are not included in the measures.
Mr Norris will be forced to strike a balance, knowing that the wider the exemption is drawn, fewer prisoners will be released early and more pressure will be placed on jails in England and Wales.
The latest figures show there were 1,015 people in prison for manslaughter as of June 2026, made up of 950 males and 65 females.
How could prison capacity be freed up?
One idea that has been considered by ministers is releasing more female prisoners – about 70% of the approximately 3,650 women in custody are serving sentences for non-violent offending – in order to repurpose their prisons to hold male offenders.
There are 12 women’s prisons in operation in England and Wales.
On average, a woman goes to prison for just over 12 months, according to Ministry of Justice data.
Are any other ideas being considered by Mr Norris?
There are about 10,000 foreign national offenders in prisons in England and Wales. The Government could seek to speed up the rate at which they are deported, freeing up cells.
What else?
Mr Burnham wants to end the “long-running injustice” faced by inmates still serving indeterminate sentences of imprisonment for public protection (IPP), which were scrapped in 2012.
More than 2,000 people are still in prison serving an IPP sentence.
A complex resentencing exercise would be needed to reduce the IPP prison population.

For Fauda fans from around the world, the suspense is over, or rather, it’s about to begin: Netflix announced Monday it will show the fifth season of the acclaimed Israeli series around the world beginning on September 8.
The fifth season of this series about an Israeli counterterrorism unit aired in Israel on Yes starting in May. But with the September 8 Netflix release, viewers in 190 countries will be able to see the new episodes, which are in Arabic, Hebrew, French, and English, with subtitles in their native languages.
The series, co-created by Avi Issacharoff and Lior Raz and starring Raz, debuted in 2015 in Israel. It was picked up by Netflix and became a worldwide sensation, hitting the coveted Netflix top 10 charts all over, including in Arab countries. In Lebanon, the fourth season hit the number one spot in January 2023.
It also reached the Netflix top 10 in Jordan, Qatar, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates in early 2023. Reportedly, Fauda is something of a guilty pleasure for Palestinian audiences in the West Bank and even in Gaza, who enjoy seeing the many Palestinian characters.
Fauda’s creators had much of the fifth season written by the fall of 2023, but scrapped these scripts following the Hamas massacre in Israel on October 7, 2023, which led to the outbreak of war. Raz and Issacharof have said in interviews that they needed to incorporate the new reality into the series.
Fauda devotes two episodes to Oct. 7 massacre
In the fifth season, two episodes are devoted to the massacre, and feature violence so graphic that they were shown with warnings in Israel that advised audiences that they could skip the episodes, which came in the middle of the season, if they were afraid that they might be too upsetting.
Yes also took the unusual step of making the episodes available for free online, for those who felt they needed to see them.
Speaking to Deadline, Issacharoff said, “This is a TV show, not reality. But we thought that there is still a story here to be told. We wanted to ask very tough questions to people all over the world, not only in Israel. Is the revenge worth it? Is continuing this very endless cycle of bloodshed worth it? Where is it taking you? I think these are the questions that are at the heart of this season.”
Cast joined by Melanie Laurent
In addition to Raz, the fifth season stars the original cast members, Doron Ben-David and Yaakov Zada-Daniel, who are joined by French star Melanie Laurent, who played the heroine of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds. Much of the early season five episodes are set in Marseille.
Fauda is still available on Yes VOD in Israel.

Lebanon abolishes death penalty, first Arab state to do so
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:54:16 UTC
19:54:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon becomes first Arab state to abolish death penalty in milestone parliament vote
Lebanon's parliament Tuesday abolished the death penalty, making it the first country in the Arab world to replace the sentencing with life imprisonment with aggravated hard labor.
The tiny Mediterranean country has committed to an unofficial moratorium on executions since January 2004. However, dozens of death sentences since then have been issued, but later suspended or commuted.
A majority of Lebanon's 128-member parliament voted in favor of ending the death penalty, with the exception of the parliamentary bloc of Hezbollah.
Justice Minister Adel Nassar, who was in Parliament, called it a "historic step" for the country.
Rights groups that have called for formalising the moratorium or ending the death penalty altogether have also celebrated the vote.
Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon Researcher at Human Rights Watch, says Lebanon is "marking a final break from a cruel sentence that should never be imposed."
"Capital punishment is unique in its cruelty and finality and is plagued with arbitrariness, prejudice, and error," he said.
It's unclear how aggravated hard labor would be enforced, as some legislators said the terms of the new punishment are not yet clear. Lebanon does have the punishment of hard labor written into law and court decisions, but even those have been rarely enforced in recent years due to cash-strapped Lebanon's lack of resources and capacity within its overcrowded prisons.
Lebanon's abolition of the death penalty comes as parliament is debating a controversial general amnesty law, the largest since the end of its 15-year civil war in 1990, that could reduce sentences or even release convicted militants and drug dealers, with some exceptions.
Family members of Lebanese soldiers and servicemen killed or attacked by Islamist militant groups have repeatedly protested against the law, some saying they had hoped to see the perpetrators who killed their family members executed rather than be issued reduced prison sentences.
Hezbollah did not immediately issue a comment about the landmark vote. Neither did Lebanon's diverse religious institutions, where the death penalty is considered legal in some their respective court systems.

‘Gerard of Andalus’: Turkish novelist traces translator who carried Islamic science to medieval Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:54:03 UTC
19:54:03 KST

- Gerard translated more than 80 works from Arabic into Latin, helping lay foundations for Europe’s scientific transformation, author says
A medieval scholar who traveled across Europe in pursuit of a single book eventually came across a vast body of knowledge that would help transform intellectual life in the Latin-speaking world, according to Turkish academic and historical novelist Beyazit Akman.
Akman, known for research-based historical novels and his years of academic work in the US, has brought the story of Gerard of Cremona to contemporary readers in his new novel, Gerard of Andalus.
He describes Gerard as “one of the most important figures who brought the Renaissance to the West,” arguing that his unusual journey and decades of translation played a central role in transferring scientific knowledge from the Islamic world to medieval Europe.
Akman told Anadolu that Gerard’s story began with his determination to find one of the foundational works in the history of astronomy: Ptolemy’s Almagest.
Unable to locate the work anywhere in the 12th-century Latin world, Gerard abandoned his life in Cremona, in present-day Italy, and embarked on a dangerous journey toward Al-Andalus.
“When Gerard arrived, he discovered not only an Arabic copy of the Almagest but also an extraordinary treasury of knowledge extending from Aristotle and Hippocrates to al-Khwarizmi and Ibn Sina,” Akman said.
“With immense determination, he learned Arabic so that he could translate these works and began working with an Andalusian scholar named Galib.”
Gerard spent approximately four decades translating more than 80 works on astronomy, medicine, mathematics and philosophy into Latin, Akman said.
The translations included works by Euclid, Ibn al-Haytham, al-Farabi and al-Kindi.
“From the numerals we use today to astronomy, traces of these priceless works that he introduced to the Latin world can be found in many fields of modern science,” he added.
 
A figure left in the shadows of history
 
Despite Gerard’s influence on the history of science, Akman said the translator remained largely forgotten for centuries.
Akman first encountered Gerard while conducting doctoral research in the US and examined his life more closely while working on his novel 1492: The Gates of Heaven, published in 2012.
“He continued to appear at different stages of my academic research for nearly 15 years,” Akman said. “Despite this, I saw that he was usually mentioned only in encyclopedia entries consisting of a few lines.”
“Gerard left behind the world he knew to find a single book. In the end, he reached a great treasure accumulated by humanity over centuries.”
Akman said he was deeply impressed by Gerard’s complete devotion to knowledge and believed the true story deserved to reach a wider audience.
The role of scholars such as Ibn Sina, al-Khwarizmi and al-Farabi in transmitting knowledge between civilizations also makes the story particularly meaningful for Turkish readers, he added.
 
Translation movement helped prepare ground for Renaissance
 
Discussing intellectual life in Latin Europe before Gerard’s translations, Akman cautioned that the term “Dark Ages” should be used carefully.
During centuries when intellectual production was relatively limited in Latin Europe, the Islamic world had a vibrant scientific and cultural life, he said.
“Direct access to the ancient Greek heritage was restricted in Latin Europe at the time, and intellectual life was largely shaped around religious institutions,” Akman said.
“It would not be correct to describe all Christian thought as hostile to reason, but there were serious disputes about the boundaries between faith and reason.”
Figures such as Peter Abelard, who emphasized questioning and critical inquiry, faced strong opposition, while some works by Aristotle and Ibn Rushd were prohibited in 13th-century Paris, he noted.
“The acceptance of scientific thought was neither easy nor linear. Galileo’s trial is the best-known example of this long tension,” he said.
“This is precisely where Gerard’s importance emerges. By transferring into Latin the knowledge that had been preserved and developed in the Islamic world for centuries, he established a powerful foundation for Europe’s scientific transformation—in other words, the Renaissance.”
 
‘Behind today’s AI and algorithms stands al-Khwarizmi’
 
Akman said portraying Ibn Sina, al-Khwarizmi and Ibn Rushd merely as intermediaries who preserved ancient Greek learning would be a serious injustice to their contributions.
“They did not simply translate the knowledge that came before them. They interpreted it, criticized it, and advanced it through their own original methods,” he said.
Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine systematically classified diseases and remained among the most important textbooks at European universities for centuries, Akman noted.
The work of al-Khwarizmi, meanwhile, was instrumental in establishing algebra as an independent field of study.
The spread of Hindu-Arabic numerals and zero also made calculations that had been extremely difficult with Roman numerals far easier, he said.
“The word ‘algebra’ comes directly from the title of his work, while ‘algorithm’ derives from the Latinized form of al-Khwarizmi’s name,” Akman said.
“So behind today’s artificial intelligence and algorithms stands al-Khwarizmi. The name of a mathematician who lived more than a thousand years ago continues to exist at the heart of modern technologies, from artificial intelligence to banking.”
 
Can one book change a civilization?
 
Akman said his novel, published this year, offers readers a historical adventure built around Gerard’s pursuit of knowledge.
The story begins with the search for a single book unavailable in Europe, but its protagonist soon finds himself following clues to a much larger secret.
“Gerard pursues a greater mystery hidden in the dark corridors of monasteries, burned libraries and forbidden manuscripts,” Akman said.
“On one side are those who have declared war on knowledge; on the other are those who risk their lives to protect it.”
Every text Gerard encounters begins a new search, while every truth he learns exposes him to greater danger, according to the author.
The novel takes readers through Rome, Paris, Cordoba and Toledo while exploring the routes through which numerals, medicine, astronomy and philosophy reached Europe.
Akman said one central question follows readers until the final page: Can a book truly change the fate of one person — or even an entire civilization?
“Gerard of Al-Andalus is a true story that conceals its answer in the shadows of history, in the ashes of burned manuscripts and in the pages of a book that remained closed for centuries,” he said.

US House takes up Graham sanctions bill targeting Russia’s oil money and shadow fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:54:01 UTC
19:54:01 KST

A bipartisan group of US House members introduced the House version of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on 10 August, advancing the sweeping sanctions package during the chamber's summer recess just days after the Senate passed it.
The move puts the bill one chamber from becoming law. If the House passes it, it would hand the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the biggest buyers of Russian crude and gas—China and India chief among them—and to blacklist the aging tankers of Russia's shadow fleet, the vessels that move sanctioned oil around Western restrictions. The target is the oil revenue that pays for Russia's war on Ukraine, at a moment when Ukrainian deep strikes have already knocked a large share of Russian refining capacity offline.
What the bill would do
The package imposes primary and secondary sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, entities propping up Russia's defense-industrial base, and foreign actors that materially aid Moscow's military operations. It targets major Russian banks and the foreign financial institutions that do significant business with them, and it goes after the shadow fleet and sanctions-evasion networks—ships, owners, operators, insurers, and ports that knowingly move Russian oil. The tariff framework, up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil and the top five buyers of its gas, replaces an earlier plan for a blanket 500% tariff, with the US trade representative setting the specific rate for each country. The bill also folds in Iran, extending the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996.
Sanctions could be lifted only if the president certifies to Congress that Russia has signed a peace deal accepted by a free and independent Ukrainian government and has halted hostilities and efforts to subvert Kyiv.
A bill born from a stall—and a death
Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the measure in 2025 with 500% tariffs. It drew more than 80 Senate cosponsors and went nowhere for over a year, as the White House kept it off the floor while betting on negotiations that never delivered. Graham secured President Trump's sign-off, then died on 11 July of an aortic dissection, a day after his last visit to Kyiv. The Senate renamed the bill in his honor and passed it 86-11 on 7 August.
The House is not a rubber stamp
The House text is identical to the Senate-passed version, so the companion functions largely as a whip count—a way for members to signal support before a floor vote expected this fall, once the chamber returns from recess on 31 August. Passage is not guaranteed: some House members have voiced fundamental concerns about handing the president broad tariff powers that could raise costs for US importers and consumers.

2 ex-Chinese military personnel arrested in South Korea for alleged espionage
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — Two former Chinese military servicemembers were arrested in South Korea for alleged espionage, accused of acts including intercepting communications between fighter jets and ground control and collecting information on movements of U.S. armaments, police said Tuesday.
Police said that one of the suspects, a Chinese national in his 60s, set up an interception device consisting of an software-defined radio receiver, an antenna and a laptop at a hotel near an air base jointly used by South Korean and U.S. air forces in southern South Korea.
Police said the man is accused of intercepting communications between fighter jets flown by South Korean and U.S. pilots and air traffic controllers at the base several times since 2024.
Police said he previously served in the Chinese military but refused to disclose further details about his identify. The police statement said the man was arrested Monday for violating laws on aiding the enemy and protecting communication secrets.
Police said they were conducting a forensic examination of his laptop to find if he relayed any of the intercepted communications to Chinese authorities.
The man told investigators that it was his hobby to listen to communications between civilians planes and air traffic controllers and he wanted to listen to communications involving fighter jets as well.
Police said they also arrested another Chinese man in his 40s on Monday on accusations of illegally collecting information from the U.S. military headquarters near Seoul, including information on U.S.-South Korean military drills, photos showing the movements of weapons at the headquarters, and personnel changes of top U.S. military officers, according to police.
Police allege that he obtained some of the information from a South Korean woman working at the U.S. command. Police say he gave her money in return for the information and they suspect the pair had a romantic relationship.
The man, who runs a military supply store near the U.S. command, argued during questioning that he sought the information believing it would help his business.
Police said the man also previously served in the Chinese military. Police said he violated laws on aiding the enemy and protecting military installations in South Korea.
Calls to the Chinese Embassy in Seoul were unanswered after business hours Tuesday.
The police announcement came a day after South Korean and U.S. militaries said they would start large-scale annual exercises next week. The U.S. stations about 28,500 troops in South Korea to help deter potential aggressions from North Korea.

DRC Ebola death toll passes 2,000 amid fastest-growing outbreak on record
A total of 4,381 cases across five provinces have been confirmed in the Democratic Republic of Congo as of Tuesday.
More than 2,000 people have died of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since its outbreak was declared fewer than three months ago.
At least 1,000 of the deaths have occurred in the last three weeks, according to official government data, as the virus continues to spread at an alarming rate.

A total of 4,381 Ebola cases across five provinces of the DRC have been confirmed as of Tuesday, including 2,011 deaths. It is the fastest-growing outbreak on record in the Central African country and is second in size only to the West African outbreak from 2014 to 2016, during which 11,310 people died.
The response to the outbreak has been complicated by several factors, including strikes by unpaid health workers, misinformation and cultural traditions. These have included intimate family burials of some of those killed by the virus, potentially increasing the risk of further transmission.
There is currently no approved treatment or vaccine for the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola responsible for the DRC’s current outbreak. The World Health Organization (WHO) announced last week that vaccine trials were under way but that it would likely take months before the results were received.
On Monday, the WHO said the virus first surfaced in the country in February, three months before an outbreak was officially declared in the country and neighbouring Uganda on May 15.
Meanwhile, the Israeli Ministry of Health announced on Tuesday that it had been alerted to a potential case of Ebola within its borders after one of its citizens returned from the DRC. In a series of posts on X, the ministry said tests had been performed after the person developed a fever. The results are expected within the next 24 hours, and the person remains in isolation.

Syria Sentences Bashar al-Assad to Death in Absentia Over Atrocities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:50:24 UTC
19:50:24 KST

A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former ruler Bashar al-Assad to death after a trial in absentia, convicting him of atrocities committed during the country’s nearly 14-year civil war.
It is the first such ruling under Syria’s transitional leaders who ousted Assad in December 2024, vowing to provide justice and accountability for crimes committed under his rule.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Assad fled to Moscow as Islamist-led forces closed in on Damascus after a lightning offensive.
At a court in Damascus, Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan convicted Assad for crimes including “premeditated murder, the intentional killing of more than one person, the intentional killing of children under 15 years... torture, torture leading to death, and deprivation of liberty on multiple occasions -- classified as crimes against humanity and war crimes”.
“He is therefore sentenced to death.”
Syria in April began proceedings against Assad and other officials accused in person and in absentia of atrocities during the country’s civil war, which erupted with the former authorities’ brutal repression of pro-democracy protesters.
More than half a million people were killed and millions displaced, while tens of thousands of people disappeared, many into the country’s brutal prison system.
The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death including Assad’s brother Maher, who ran the army’s elite Fourth Division and also fled the country.
Russia Resumes Military Cargo Shipments to Syria for First Time Since Assad’s Ouster
Those convicted included former defence minister Fahd al-Freij and Louay al-Ali, who headed military intelligence in Daraa province in 2011.
- Torture -
The court convicted the officials for crimes including murder, incitement to murder, torture leading to death and repeated deprivation of liberty, also considered “crimes against humanity” and “war crimes”.
Former security official Atif Najib -- the only one in the dock -- was also sentenced to death for “crimes against humanity” committed when he was head of political security in Daraa province, the cradle of the country’s 2011 uprising.
Najib, a cousin of Assad who was arrested in January last year, was convicted for crimes including murder, “the intentional killing of children under 15”, and “torture leading to death”.
The acts attributed to him are “crimes against humanity”, the court said as it handed down “the harshest punishment against him, which is the death penalty”.
Syria’s uprising began in Daraa in March 2011, after 15 students were arrested for allegedly writing anti-government slogans on the city’s walls.
Residents said the students were tortured, leading to a protest to demand their release that ended in bloodshed.
Security personnel suppressed peaceful demonstrations with force and fired live ammunition to disperse sit-ins at several locations.
Najib was dismissed after the crackdown, as the protests spread to other provinces.
Aryan said Najib had denied the charges against him and showed “no remorse”.
Assad took the Syrian presidency in 2000 after the death of his father Hafez.

Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:50:12 UTC
19:50:12 KST

Hotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century.
Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday.
Tourists there have been shelling out $793 (£587) on average to secure a room on Wednesday, a 98% jump compared with the same day last year, according to data from the travel and hospitality data group Lighthouse Intelligence.
Spain is also steeling itself for an influx of tourists, as one of the best places on the European continent to view the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry said on Monday that it expected 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse.
The rate for a room in A Coruña in the north of Spain was up 135% compared with last year to $451 on average, while prices in Mallorca, where the eclipse is expected to be visible on the horizon at sunset, were up by 24% at about $448. In Santiago de Compostela and Bilbao, hotel room prices have risen 34% and 67% respectively.
Accommodation in small towns and villages in the eclipse’s path, as well as makeshift observatories set up by local enthusiasts, have been booked for months. There have been reports of US travellers taking part in house exchanges with people living in Spain’s Castilla y León, which is one of the best regions to view the eclipse.
However, authorities in Spain are worried about an increased risk of fires, with police expecting 1.5m more car journeys than usual on Wednesday. They have warned that extraordinarily dry temperatures mean the smallest spark could lead to devastating forest fires, while traffic could end up blocking access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas.
Authorities will undertake out a massive police operation and safety campaign, with plans to deploy 35,000 officers to help minimise risks. Virginia Barcones, the secretary general for civil protection and emergencies at Spain’s interior ministry, said: “We’ve had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That’s why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark.”
Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned in Spain, as have barbecues and fireworks. The València region has closed its natural parks and banned walking on rural footpaths.
As of Monday evening, three large wildfires were burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Fires have already scorched about 200,000 hectares this year – six times more than by the same date in 2025, according to the environment ministry.
For those unable to make the journey, the US space agency Nasa has installed four high-powered telescopes in the small village of Villalibado in north-west Spain in order to livestream the eclipse to more than 10 million people.
A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the UK on Wednesday, where it will reach its maximum coverage at 7.12pm in London.

Trump Walks Back Promise to Let Ukraine Build Patriots Over Russia Fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:49:59 UTC
19:49:59 KST

US President Donald Trump has backed away from plans to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles under license, raising new doubts over Kyiv’s ability to strengthen its ballistic missile defenses before Russia’s expected winter campaign, The Telegraph reported.
According to the magazine on Tuesday, the dispute centers on the Patriot’s highly sensitive Ka-band Active Radar Seeker, a small radar component that guides the interceptor toward incoming ballistic and cruise missiles during the final stage of flight.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump initially said in July that the US would license Patriot production to Ukraine, but later reversed course, citing concerns over transferring sensitive military technology.
“It’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology ... People that you give that technology, they can some day turn on you,” Trump said.
Why the Patriot radar is so important
The Ka-band radar seeker, produced by Boeing in Huntsville, Alabama, acts as the Patriot interceptor’s final guidance system.
The component is housed inside the missile’s nose, which is around 10 inches in diameter, with the radar itself estimated to be about eight inches wide.
When the interceptor approaches its target, the radar allows it to locate and track fast-moving ballistic or cruise missiles and guide the Patriot into a direct collision.
The technology is tightly controlled by Washington. Although around 20 countries operate Patriot systems, Germany and Japan are the only countries currently licensed to manufacture their own missiles, according to The Telegraph.
‘Don’t Go Outside or Look Through Windows’: Russian City Locked Down for Putin Visit
Even Japan, which received a production license in 2005, was not permitted to manufacture the highly sensitive Ka-band radar seeker.
Ukraine needs hundreds of interceptors
The licensing dispute comes as Ukraine faces an urgent shortage of Patriot interceptors ahead of another expected winter campaign of Russian missile and drone attacks.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has sought around 300 Patriot missiles to strengthen the country’s defenses.
Ukraine’s need is particularly acute because Patriot remains the only system in its arsenal capable of intercepting some of Russia’s ballistic and hypersonic missiles.
During a Russian attack in early August, Ukrainian air defenses reportedly failed to intercept any of the 24 ballistic missiles launched at the Kyiv region, according to The Telegraph.
“Every anti-ballistic missile package saves the lives of our people. And every night that we lack them results in casualties,” Zelensky said.
Production could take years
Even if Washington approves licensed production, Ukraine would not be able to start manufacturing Patriots quickly.
The US would have to approve the transfer of technical drawings, software, and manufacturing expertise while also certifying a new network of suppliers and production facilities.
Michael Cadenazzi, the US assistant secretary of defense for industrial policy, said the process would require finding and certifying new suppliers.
“There’s only so many engineers that know how to do this stuff. There’s only so many qualified parts [already available],” he said.
Japan took around three years to successfully test its first domestically produced PAC-3 missile after receiving the necessary license, as per The Telegraph.
Washington fears technology could reach Russia
A major concern behind the US hesitation is the possibility that sensitive Patriot technology could be obtained by Russia.
Licensing production would require Washington to determine which Ukrainian factories, employees and subcontractors could access the technology and establish safeguards against espionage or unauthorized transfer.
Retired US General Philip Breedlove said the concern was real.
“I do believe that there is a fear that if we give this technology to Ukraine, that it will somehow make its way to Russia,” Breedlove told The Telegraph.
Another potential problem is the location of production. A Patriot factory in Ukraine would likely become a major target for Russian missile strikes.
One alternative under discussion is manufacturing the interceptors in Germany or another European country. But European production would also take time and require additional licensing arrangements.
Boeing expands radar production
Boeing is meanwhile increasing production of the Ka-band radar seeker.
The company reached a seven-year framework agreement in April aimed at tripling annual production. Boeing expects to produce significantly more seekers under the agreement than it manufactured during the previous 26 years combined.
However, growing US demand is adding pressure to already limited Patriot stocks.
The Telegraph reported that the war with Iran is believed to have significantly depleted US interceptor inventories, further complicating Washington’s ability to supply Ukraine.
For Kyiv, the combination of limited missile stocks, slow production expansion, and US concerns over technology transfer leaves little time to strengthen its air defenses before another winter of Russian attacks.

Russia develops Darwin-D protective net to shield roads from UAV attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:47:00 UTC
19:47:00 KST

MOSCOW, August 11. /TASS/. Russian specialists have developed the Darwin-D protective capture net, designed to shield highways, roads, and other transportation infrastructure facilities from attacks by FPV drones and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the manufacturer, Mechanical Protection Systems, told TASS.
"The Russian company Mechanical Protection Systems has introduced the Darwin-D protective and intercepting net, developed specifically for highways, roads, and other long stretches of transportation infrastructure. This new solution was developed following an initiative by the Russian Ministry of Transport to authorize the use of road fund resources to finance the installation and repair of protective structures on roads," the company stated.
The new product is a modification of the Darwin protective capture net. It is designed to shield highways, major roads, and transportation arteries at least 12 meters wide from attacks by FPV drones and fixed-wing UAVs. "Unlike conventional rigid barriers, the polyamide net expands upon collision with a drone, absorbing its kinetic energy. Thanks to this ‘soft’ deceleration, the drone becomes caught in the netting or veers off course, and the likelihood of its warhead detonating upon contact with the barrier is reduced," the company added.
CEO of Mechanical Protection Systems Dmitry Dorofeyev noted that to effectively protect highways from UAV attacks, "it’s not enough to simply take an existing anti-drone net and lay it out over several kilometers." "The economics and operational requirements here are completely different: it is necessary to quickly cover large areas, minimize the load on the supports, be able to promptly repair damaged sections, and avoid blocking traffic for long periods. That is why we have developed a dedicated version specifically for roads," he said.
According to the developer, one of the key features of the Darwin-D net is the size of the net panel. "It is 38 meters wide, and a single transport set contains 6,000 square meters of netting. The weight per square meter is 83 grams. Thanks to its low weight, the netting can be installed on quickly erected supports, which is especially important when it is necessary to protect tens of kilometers of roads. The system also allows for localized repairs. If a section is damaged, it can be cut out and patched with a piece of spare mesh, securing it with polyamide cord or special ties. This allows the protective barrier to be restored without having to fully replace the mesh along a large stretch of the road," the company added.

The Welsh actor, 57, explores claims of chemical contamination across his homeland in a two-part series, Buried with Michael Sheen. The show begins with Sheen meeting farming consultant and whistleblower Douglas Gowan, who claims people in Wales have been poisoned by decades of exposure to toxic chemicals in the environment.
Gowan says thousands of tonnes of chemicals known as Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) have been dumped at sites across Wales and north west England.
PCBs were regarded as wonder chemicals in the 1960s but are now designated as a Group 1 carcinogen and banned globally.
In the documentary, Sheen discovers that residents living near the waste sites have abnormally high levels of PCB in their blood, while many have been diagnosed with rare cancers.
In a new interview with The Daily Telegraph, the star explains that he agreed to be tested as a control – but discovered he had the chemicals in his blood.
“I wasn’t quite expecting how shocked I’d be by that,” he said. “I thought ‘of course I’ll be tested because you won’t find anything’, and then when you get the results, you realise there is no safe level, we all have it in us.”
Sheen, a keen environmental activist, began investigating forever chemicals after coming across Gowan’s research on Brofiscin Quarry, in south Wales, while browsing online.
The Underworld actor has also recalled how “paranoid” he felt after visiting the quarry during filming.
“There was a moment when we'd been to Brofiscin, and I'd been in the field and I hadn't been wearing the wellies at that point,” he said. “I was wearing my own boots, and I remember going back in my car and stopping at the garage to get petrol and then taking my boots off and hosing them down in the garage because I got so paranoid that I might be taking this home.
“There’s moments like that where it is really daunting. It is scary.”
Wales’s environmental regulator, Natural Resources Wales, told the BBC it previously investigated PCB leaks at Brofiscin Quarry, but concluded they did not pose enough of a risk to warrant further action.
Sheen is hoping the documentary will lead to “the people who dump this stuff [being] made responsible”.
“I think it's important to say that the biggest injustice here is that the people who are responsible for this have got away with not having to take responsibility,” he said.
“The next thing, in my opinion, is that local councils – where this potentially contaminated land is – are terrified that if they're financially responsible for doing something about this, that it will bankrupt them. Because they don't have the budgets available.
“Somehow we have to make sure that we are able to move past that point.”
The actor has frequently used his platform to highlight environmental and social injustices, and last year paid off £1m worth of debt for neighbours in his local community of Port Talbot.
The move was part of a two-year project to highlight issues with the current credit system, as part of his documentary Michael Sheen’s Secret Million Pound Giveaway.
The film saw Sheen purchase the credit for £100,000 from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), and wipe off debt to the value of £1m, to help over 900 people in south Wales where he grew up.
Sheen has had a busy 2026 and recently took part in the second series of Celebrity Traitors, which is scheduled to air later this year. In September, he’ll also make his debut as the new host of BBC Two quiz show House of Games, having taken over from Richard Osman.
Buried with Michael Sheen comes to BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from Monday 17 August at 9pm

EXPLAINER – What to know about the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:41:33 UTC
19:41:33 KST

- This is the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999
- Nearly 1 billion people could see at least part of the eclipse, while about 15 million live within its narrow path of totality
- Scientists will use the fleeting darkness to study the Sun's corona and atmospheric changes
A total solar eclipse will pass over parts of the Northern Hemisphere on Wednesday, briefly turning day into night along a narrow path from the Arctic through Iceland and into northern Spain.
The Moon will pass directly between Earth and the Sun, completely blocking the Sun’s bright face for observers inside the path of totality.
Outside that band, a partial eclipse will be visible across much of Europe, northwestern Africa and portions of North America.
 
When and where?
The greatest eclipse will occur at about 17:46 UTC, with maximum totality lasting 2 minutes and 18 seconds near 65 degrees north latitude in the North Atlantic, west of Iceland, according to NASA.
The path of totality, roughly 294 kilometers (183 miles) wide at its broadest, crosses remote areas of northern Russia and the Arctic, eastern Greenland, western and northern Iceland, the Atlantic Ocean, northern Spain and a sliver of northeastern Portugal.
Cities expected to experience totality include Reykjavik, Leon, Zaragoza, Bilbao, Valencia and parts of the Balearic Islands. In Spain, the event occurs low on the western horizon shortly before sunset.
Nearly 1 billion people are in areas where at least part of the eclipse could be visible, including about 15 million living within the narrow path of totality.
Coverage reaches more than 90% across much of western Europe and approaches 99% near Madrid and Barcelona, which lie just outside the total path. Partial views also extend to parts of Alaska, northern and eastern Canada, and the northeastern US.
This is the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999 and the first over the Iberian Peninsula in more than a century. It is the only total eclipse Iceland will experience this century.
Anyone outside the path of totality — including in Türkiye — will not see the eclipse.
 
Why it matters
Total eclipses briefly expose the Sun's outer atmosphere, or corona, which is normally invisible against the Sun's glare.
Scientists use the rare alignment to study solar activity that shapes space weather on Earth.
NASA-funded teams plan to track the Moon's shadow using a high-altitude research jet and scientific balloons launched from Iceland to study how the sudden darkness affects the atmosphere.
"From our unique perspective on Earth during a total solar eclipse, scientists can study the Sun’s corona in a way we can’t from anywhere else in the solar system," Kelly Korreck, eclipse program manager at NASA headquarters, said in a statement last month.
"The Sun impacts our daily life, satellites, and astronauts in space, and we can take advantage of this moment to advance our understanding of that influence.”
Amir Caspi, a researcher involved in NASA's eclipse studies, said each eclipse offers new data. "The Sun is always changing," Caspi said. "Every eclipse is different. So we could see things we didn't see before."
 
How to watch safely
Experts stress that it is never safe to look directly at the Sun without certified eclipse glasses, except during the brief seconds of full totality.
Regular sunglasses do not offer adequate protection.
NASA recommends eclipse glasses that meet the ISO 12312-2 international safety standard, or an indirect method such as a pinhole projector.
Cameras, telescopes and binoculars require their own solar filters to avoid eye and equipment damage.
 
On the ground
Iceland has leaned into the rare event. In Hellissandur, on the Snaefellsnes Peninsula, organizers are hosting the Iceland Eclipse festival, from Aug. 11-15 with live music and talks from scientists and astronauts timed around totality.
Cruise operators have also scheduled voyages timed to the eclipse along the Iceland-Spain corridor, and tourism authorities in both countries have published viewing guides as hotels and rental cars near the path have filled up in recent months.
The eclipse also falls during the annual Perseid meteor shower, which peaks around Aug. 12-13, giving skywatchers a second celestial event that night.
NASA said it would stream the eclipse live starting at 1:15 p.m. EDT (1715GMT) on Wednesday.
The next total solar eclipse will occur on Aug. 2, 2027, crossing Spain, the Middle East and parts of North Africa.

‘Like a city of zombies’: 166 dead, thousands missing after devastating Colombia earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:41:12 UTC
19:41:12 KST

In Colombia, rescue teams were racing against the clock Tuesday in an effort to find survivors in the ruins of buildings that collapsed Monday in the powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake that shook the country’s west and center. 
Overnight, the official death toll climbed to 166 and the number of injured to 570, and it became clear that significant damage had been caused to more than 1,500 buildings, dozens of which collapsed completely. As of Monday night, the official number of missing and unreachable people stood at more than 2,700.
In Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city and one of the places that suffered the worst damage, at least 85 people were killed. Overnight, professional rescue workers and volunteers could still be seen clearing debris with their bare hands in search of signs of life. In that city alone, home to 2.2 million people, the number of missing stands at 188. There and in other cities, rescuers were seen forming human chains to clear debris from buildings using pickaxes and basic tools, and from time to time raising their hands in the air to signal everyone to be silent, hoping to hear cries for help from beneath the ruins. “We are carrying out all the necessary actions to rescue people alive,” said Andrés Felipe Mejía, one of the volunteers, overnight.
Another volunteer, Nelson Moreno, arrived at one of the disaster sites in Cali to search for a friend trapped under two collapsed five-story buildings. Her father and baby had earlier been rescued injured but alive. “Now we need flashlights and goggles because of the dust so we can continue the operations at night,” he said, surrounded by hundreds of volunteers. 
Carmen Yasmín García, a 43-year-old Cali resident who also joined the volunteers, said her team rescued seven people from a collapsed building, but four others and a dog remained trapped. “A moment ago we could still hear scratching sounds, but now we don’t hear anything,” she said. “We still have faith that the dog is alive and that we can get these people out. We need people with rods and shovels. The more people who lend a hand, the better.”
Dozens of buildings in Cali were completely destroyed or left dangerously tilted, forcing residents to remain in the streets and preventing them from returning home. Several upper floors of the city’s university hospital, some of them designated for children’s care, also collapsed inward with a roar, leaving patients trapped and forcing about 600 others to evacuate into the debris-strewn streets and receive treatment there.
'People came out naked, jumped from rooftops, like a scene from a movie'
The powerful earthquake struck Monday at 7:34 a.m. local time, 3:34 p.m. in Israel. Its epicenter was at a relatively deep 96 kilometers in San José del Palmar, about 400 kilometers west of Bogotá. The tremor was so powerful that buildings also shook in Colombia’s capital, and residents fled in panic into the streets. No significant damage was caused there, but destruction was reported in dozens of other cities and towns, including Cali, Quibdó, Pereira and Manizales. In one of them, the town of El Cairo, home to about 7,000 residents, about 80% of the buildings were damaged. Significant damage was also caused to seven airports, and their operations were suspended.
Monday’s major quake was also felt in neighboring Ecuador, including in its capital, Quito, as well as in Venezuela and Panama, but no tsunami warning was issued. Since the quake, more than 50 aftershocks have hit Colombia, forcing rescuers to constantly take precautions.
In Pereira, a city located in Colombia’s tourist coffee-growing region, which was already hit by an earthquake that killed 1,200 people in 1999, at least 66 people were killed Monday, and heavy destruction was reported. “We are without electricity. Honestly, it really feels like being in a city of zombies. Honestly, it is very sad,” said Juan David Gaitán, a self-employed worker. Mónica Sánchez, the owner of a small company that makes workplace uniforms, said she and her 12 employees managed to escape from their factory in Pereira at the very last moment, and that one of the factory walls collapsed. “It was shocking — the city simply collapsed around us,” she said.
Even before dawn, stunned residents were still describing the apocalyptic scenes they encountered in the moments after the quake. Wilmer Cuesta, a law student who came to help those trapped, said he saw “people coming out naked, jumping from rooftops, from the second floor, desperate people.” Andrés Hernández, who works as a tattoo artist, admitted he still cannot process what happened: “I felt like I was in a scene from a movie, when I just saw the poles, the cables, everything moving. I am worried about my family, my friends.”
President flies to epicenter: 'Chocó will never again be the land of the forgotten'
Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office only three days before the earthquake and is already facing one of the worst disasters to hit the country in decades, declared a state of emergency Monday night and pledged to lead a coordinated rescue operation. “You are not alone!” he told Colombian citizens. After initial reports of looting in Cali, de la Espriella announced that about 1,000 security personnel would be deployed there, and overnight a curfew was declared in Cali and Pereira.
Chocó, the province where the epicenter was located, is one of the poorest and most neglected areas in Colombia, and frequently suffers from clashes between armed groups. Most parts of Chocó can be reached only by boat, through the jungle or by plane, and very little was known about the extent of the damage there. 
Overnight, President de la Espriella flew to Quibdó, the provincial capital, to assess the damage there, and announced that he had mobilized the entire military and police apparatus to address the needs of the region’s residents. He also announced rent subsidies for those displaced from their homes. “Chocó will never again be the ‘land of the forgotten,’” he said.
Monday’s earthquake in Colombia came less than two months after the pair of deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June. The quakes, with magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5, killed more than 5,000 people and destroyed hundreds of buildings. Colombia and its neighbors are located in the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” an area characterized by intense seismic and volcanic activity caused by the movement of tectonic plates.
Light earthquakes are common in central and western Colombia, but earthquakes with magnitudes above 6 are rare. In 1999, such a quake, with a magnitude of 6.2 near the city of Armenia, killed about 1,200 people. The deadliest earthquake in Colombia’s history occurred in August 1868, killing 70,000 people.

Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:40:45 UTC
19:40:45 KST

A Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died.
The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days.
The former president and his brother, who commanded the feared fourth division and was considered the regime’s top security official, oversaw a brutal crackdown in which government forces killed, arrested and tortured indiscriminately to crush protests that started in 2011.
The court said Bashar al-Assad had been sentenced to death for crimes of “premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children” as well as “torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity”.
It said it would pursue international legal avenues to try to prosecute the two men, but Russian officials have previously declined requests to extradite its former Syrian allies.
The court also sentenced Atef Najib, Assad’s cousin and the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. Najib was responsible for the torture of a group of 15 young boys who had graffitied anti-Assad slogans on a wall in 2011 – an event that kicked off mass protests in the southern Syrian province, which then spread to the rest of the country.
Najib’s trial was highly publicised, with pictures of him listening to proceedings while dressed in a prison uniform and held in a cage in court. The Syrian government has presented his trial as a landmark case in its pursuit of transitional justice, something experts say is key to healing divisions in the country.
Syria has experienced explosions of violence in the post-Assad era. About 1,500 mostly Alawite civilians were killed in a wave of retaliatory killings in March 2025 after militants loyal to al-Assad attacked security forces. Al-Assad belonged to the Islamic Alawite sect – a minority group in Syria – and enjoyed strong support in the group’s coastal heartland during his rule.
In July 2025, more than 1,700 people were killed in massacres in the Druze-majority province of Suweida when local fighting evolved into sectarian killings. Low-level violence has continued in northern Syria until the present day, particularly targeting Alawite civilians.
Syrian authorities have taken steps towards transitional justice, establishing committees and arresting Assad-era officials, in an effort to end intercommunal violence.
Al-Assad became president in 2000 at the age of 34, inheriting power from his father, Hafez. He had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and was not initially supposed to be president, but became the heir after his brother, Basil, died in a car accident.
Though styled as a young reformer who was supposed to allow some liberalisation in Syrian politics and its economy, his legacy was largely defined by his brutal response to the country’s revolution. Under his rule, Syria’s fearsome security apparatus was given a free hand to arrest, torture and kill civilians on an industrial scale.

Iraq shuts 71 fake PMF offices, bans unauthorised drone flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:39:01 UTC
19:39:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq closes 71 fake PMF offices, bans unauthorised drone flights
Iraq's Interior Ministry said on Monday, 10 August, that it had closed at least 71 fake offices claiming to belong to the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), while stressing that any drone flying without authorisation would be treated as a "terrorist threat".
Security measures in Iraq have entered a more stringent phase, following top-level directives to intensify searches at security checkpoints inside cities and between provinces.
The move indicates an Iraqi security strategy aimed at tightening control over the movements of armed factions.
Iraq's Interior Ministry spokesman, Maj Gen Miqdad Miri, said during a press conference for the National Permanent Committee for Regulating and Restricting Weapons to State Control that "the committee currently has an information database containing 6 million weapons across the country".
"There was initially a lack of trust, and registration for free weapons registration was low, but the situation has now changed, and participation has become high," he added.
Miri stressed that "reports about imposing a curfew across the country, coinciding with the end of the deadline for restricting weapons to state control at the end of next September, are incorrect (..). There was a precautionary technical measure, and currently there are no instructions concerning this matter".
"The deadline for registering weapons will end on Dec. 31, 2026, after which an unregistered weapons holder will be treated as being outside the law," Miri said.
"The ministry established 845 offices for weapons registration in all provinces, granted weapons and possession licences to more than 160,000 people, and seized and confiscated 143,000 weapons," he added. "It also uncovered the theft of 2,668 weapons, in addition to registering more than half a million weapons belonging to citizens."
He noted that at least "71 fake PMF offices were closed, and security forces will treat any drone flying without authorisation as terrorism, as well as those who launch them, regardless of their affiliations".
In response, the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) said in statements to the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that the fake offices announced by the Interior Ministry "have no connection whatsoever to them".
It stressed that "measures to close and monitor these offices were carried out as part of an operation conducted by the authority's General Directorate of Security and Discipline, within the framework of the work of the Permanent Committee for Restricting Weapons, formed by the commander-in-chief of the armed forces".
Strategic affairs expert Brig Gen Adnan al-Tamimi told TNA that "the decision to close offices falsely claiming affiliation or connection to the Popular Mobilisation Forces represents an important step towards controlling weapons and ending the practice of some armed factions exploiting the name of official institutions".
"The presence of such offices, particularly those spread across the capital Baghdad and several central and southern provinces, poses a challenge to the authority of the state and the rule of law," he added.
Al-Tamimi further said that "closing illegal or fake offices is based on precise legal and security procedures, after verifying the identity of entities using names and addresses that suggest an affiliation with state institutions".
He continued, "The Popular Mobilisation Forces are an official institution. Therefore, any entity without clear legal authorisation cannot use its status, symbols or offices to provide official cover for armed activities."
He added that "these measures will help restrict armed activity to legally authorised institutions, prevent multiple centres of security decision-making, and curb the exploitation of official status in carrying out activities that could endanger Iraq's security or its relations with neighbouring countries".
Al-Tamimi stressed that "security forces must treat any drone flying over areas of the country without official authorisation or clear identification as a potential security threat, regardless of the entity behind it or its affiliation".
He argued that "the danger posed by drones lies in how easily they can be used to carry out attacks, reconnaissance operations or transport materials".
"Dealing with them should be in accordance with the rules of engagement and applicable security laws and instructions, and legal accountability should extend to those who launch them and those behind their operation when their responsibility is established, without exceptions based on affiliation or political or factional status," he added.
The strategic affairs expert concluded: "Applying these rules equally to everyone sends a clear message that the decision to use force and weapons in Iraq must rest exclusively with the state and its authorised security and military institutions and that any violation of this principle should be met with deterrent legal and security measures".

Government should cut stamp duty to boost housing market, says Bellway
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:33:25 BST
19:33:25 KST

UK housebuilder urges Andy Burnham to slash stamp duty to boost housing market
Burnham previously vowed his government would oversee the ‘biggest council house building programme since the post-war period’
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Residential developer Bellway has urged the Government to introduce an immediate cut to stamp duty to help kickstart a recovery across the UK property market.
The appeal comes as the FTSE 250 business warned that short-term demand remains "uncertain" due to persistent building cost inflation and widespread consumer caution.
Based in Newcastle, the housebuilder is among several firms facing subdued interest for new properties amid high mortgage rates and squeezed household budgets.
Prime minister Andy Burnham last month dismissed prospects of a significant overhaul of stamp duty in the Autumn Budget.
However, Bellway chief executive Jason Honeyman stressed that swift policy changes are necessary to stimulate activity and assist aspiring home buyers.
“With the near-term outlook remaining uncertain, we call on the Government to act now to improve access to housing across all tenures, both by helping first-time buyers onto the property ladder and supporting the delivery of affordable and social housing for those who need it most,” he said.
“In order to ease affordability constraints and stimulate demand, an immediate reduction in stamp duty alongside a Government-backed deposit support scheme for first-time buyers would both drive economic growth and accelerate the delivery of much-needed new homes across the country.”
On Tuesday, the company reported that housing competition grew by 10.8 per cent to 9,695 homes over the year to 31 July, compared with a year earlier.
It also revealed that underlying operating profits are set to have increased to around £320 million from £303.5 million last year.
Bellway said it saw positive trading in the early part of the spring selling season, but has seen a “moderation” in customer demand since April due to the uptick in mortgage rates.
Mr Honeyman added: “Bellway has delivered a robust performance and growth in volume output, despite ongoing headwinds for our industry.
“Our sharp focus on operational improvement and drive for capital efficiency has provided resilience and supported a strong increase in cash generation and shareholder returns.”
In an address in Manchester last month, Mr Burnham said that “the country is in a housing trap” and called for a huge “council house building programme” to be brought in.
He vowed that a Burnham government would oversee the “biggest council house building programme since the post-war period”, using vacant public land to reduce costs.
The new prime minister has indicated that he will focus on higher-density development in existing towns, to both reinvigorate high streets and protect green spaces from development.

Gold prices rise again as Middle East conflict and interest rate fears ease
After hitting record high prices early in 2026, gold suffered a surprise sharp dip when the Iran war broke out
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The price of gold has been on the rise once more, reversing a months-long downward trend which saw the precious metal’s value fall by more than a quarter.
Investors have had a tough time predicting what markets will do this year, with uncertainty from the Iran war hitting inflation, currency markets remaining volatile and and growing concerns over the amounts the largest firms are spending on artificial intelligence.
In such times, previously investors might have turned to gold, seen as a safe haven in troubled times - but instead, the precious metal appeared to mirror some of those other markets with a steep decline in the first half of 2026.
Gold hit an all-time record price of more than $5,600 (£4,147) per ounce in late January. Through to mid-March it still traded at above $5,000 - but across the following five months it fell to a few dollars below $4,000, more than a 28 per cent drop from high point to low.
However, since the start of August it has started to rally once more, up 8 per cent over the past week alone to sit at $4,373.
“One of the stranger developments of recent days has been the pick-up in precious metals. After two months of outflows, gold ETFs attracted inflows in July, and the price of gold increased by more than 7 per cent last week,” said Jemma Slingo, investment expert at Fidelity International.
“It is tricky to pin down exactly what is driving the bounce, which follows a tough few months for gold. The metal did not behave like a traditional safe haven during the early stages of the Middle East conflict, but the changing outlook for interest rates could be moving the dial. If the last year is anything to go by, however, investors should be prepared for a bumpy ride.”
Interest rates potentially moving up in the US and beyond - analysts are split over the Bank of England’s likely movement - can decrease the likelihood of people buying gold, as it is easier to get a return from holding cash because gold pays no dividend.

Others are also suspected of assisting in the crime.

Currently, products from Verkhnedvinsk Butter and Cheese Factory and Belfood Production are being supplied to Uzbekistan. Details

The Kremlin's apple of discord

Meta glasses banned from courts in England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:29:29 UTC
19:29:29 KST

Courts in England and Wales have joined a number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in banning Meta glasses, amid a mounting backlash against what has been described as “spyware”.
Last month courts in New York announced a ban on the controversial glasses, which can record video footage while being worn.
Now His Majesty’s Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS), which is responsible for all criminal, civil and family courts in England and Wales, has made clear that Meta glasses will be confiscated from anyone entering its judicial buildings.
A spokesperson told the Guardian: “There are clear restrictions on taking images or videos within courts and tribunals which is why the use of Meta glasses is prohibited.”
Taking images or videos in court buildings is prohibited in the UK without official permission and can be prosecuted as contempt of court. While lawyers and members of the public are allowed to enter courts with smartphones, which can record both video and audio, the
HMCTS made clear that no such exception would be made for smart glasses.
A source said: “Users who bring Meta glasses into courts or tribunals will have them confiscated on entry and they will be returned when the owner leaves the building.”
They said smartphones were allowed on the condition they would not be used for recording court procedures.
Earlier this year, a claimant was accused by a judge of wearing smart glasses in the high court and getting “coaching” through them while giving evidence.
Laimonas Jakstys was told to remove the glasses during a case over the directorship of a property company. Raquel Agnello KC, sitting as a judge of the high court, said Jakstys had been “assisted or coached in his replies to questions put to him during cross examination”. Jakstys denied using the smart glasses to receive answers, and denied they were connected to his phone.
HMCTS does not hold figures on the number of incidents of smart glasses being used or taken into courts.
In February, members of the security team for Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, were seen wearing Meta glasses during a high-profile trial in California about social media addiction.
The judge, Carolyn B Kuhl, threatened the security guards with contempt of court if they had recorded any of the proceedings.
New York’s court system said it was banning smart glasses to ensure “individuals cannot surreptitiously record court proceedings”. It added: “No individual possessing smart glasses will be permitted to enter a UCS [unified court system] facility unless they voucher the smart glasses for safekeeping by uniformed personnel while the individual remains in the facility.”
Last year Meta sold 7m pairs of the glasses, which cost between £269 and £469.
Fears about Meta glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent has led to them being labelled “pervert glasses”. A number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in the UK, including Wetherspoons, have banned Meta glasses over privacy fears.
A spokesperson for Meta said the company did not want to comment on the court ban. They said when the glasses were recording a pulsing light was visible to people in the vicinity, and that frequently updated tamper detection technology is deployed to stop users covering this light during recordings.

Labour surges above Reform in polls once again as Nigel Farage’s woes continue
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Labour surges above Reform in polls once again as Nigel Farage’s woes continue
The latest survey is the fifth national poll Labour has topped since Andy Burnham entered Downing Street, ending the run that saw Nigel Farage’s party lead in the polls for more than a year
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Labour has overtaken Reform UK in yet another poll, as the party continues to see a surge in support after Andy Burnham entered Downing Street.
The latest YouGov survey put Labour on 24 points, two points ahead of Nigel Farage’s party on 22 per cent – the first time a YouGov poll has put Labour ahead of Reform in more than a year.
It is also Reform’s lowest score since March 2025, with the party losing ground to the Conservatives.
The latest survey is the fifth national poll Labour has topped since Mr Burnham became prime minister, ending the run that saw Mr Farage’s party lead in the polls for more than a year.
The polling put the Green Party on 12 per cent, down by one point compared to August 2-3, while the Liberal Democrats were also down by one point on 11 per cent.
The Tories were up two points, putting them on 21 per cent - just one point behind Reform.
The polling will come as another blow to Mr Farage’s party as they spend their final few days campaigning in a crucial by-election in Clacton.
The Reform leader dramatically quit as an MP earlier this summer – before Labour’s ‘Burnham bounce’ in the polls – and could find himself left without a seat in Parliament if he fails to win on Thursday.
When Sir Keir Starmer stood down in June, just 49 per cent of voters who backed the Labour Party at the last general election said they still backed the party. This has now risen to 60 per cent in the latest poll.
Meanwhile, the number of Labour voters who said they would lend their vote to the Greens has fallen from 9 per cent in June to just 8 per cent, the polling commissioned by The Times has found.
Anthony Wells, head of politics and elections for YouGov, told the newspaper that Mr Burnham has gone some way to reunite the left.
"What you see in the numbers is not only that Labour has increased its vote share but both the Greens and the Liberal Democrats have seen a substantial drop in their support, which had been boosted by Labour defectors,” he said.
“At the same time there are signs that, for the moment at least, Reform has peaked and is now losing some of the support it picked up from disaffected Tory voters who are now returning to Kemi Badenoch.
“However, more broadly the polls shows that the public are still deeply divided, with just three points separating the top three parties — which is within the margin or error.”
It comes just one day after an Ipsos poll put Mr Burnham’s party on 28 per cent, three points ahead of Reform on 25 per cent, Labour’s best position in an Ipsos poll for more than a year.
The survey also found Mr Burnham has a significant lead over his political rivals including Mr Farage, when asked who would make the best PM.
Some 36 per cent chose the Labour leader, more than double the 15 per cent who picked Mr Farage or the 13 per cent who selected Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch.
The YouGov polling spoke to 2,417 adults on August 9 and 10.

Solar eclipse warning after Britons suffered vision loss in 1999
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
11:25:52 BST
19:25:52 KST

Solar eclipse warning after Britons suffered vision loss in 1999
At least 70 cases of eclipse-related visual loss were reported following the total solar eclipse in 1999
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Britons planning to view the upcoming solar eclipse have been warned that even brief exposure to the sun can cause lasting vision damage.
The partial solar eclipse, which occurs when the moon passes directly between the sun and Earth, blocking most of the sun’s light, will be visible across the UK on 12 August.
Royal Museums Greenwich, which runs the Royal Observatory, said that it will be the most complete solar eclipse since August 1999.
Following the total solar eclipse in 1999, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists identified 70 patients with eclipse-related visual loss.
Most cases resulted from direct viewing of the eclipse without appropriate eye protection, and about 40 per cent had looked at it for less than a minute.
While some recovered useful vision, others were left with persistent visual deficits.
College President Mohamed Elalfy, a consultant ophthalmologist, says the “safest way” to view the eclipse is to “observe it indirectly, such as by watching a live broadcast”.
“Looking directly at the sun during a solar eclipse can cause damage to the retina, potentially damaging the cells responsible for sharp central vision. Crucially, the retina has no pain receptors, so people will not feel the damage as it happens,” he said.
“Symptoms may only become apparent several hours later and can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot, distorted vision, reduced colour perception and increased sensitivity to light. While some people recover over weeks or months, others can be left with permanent visual impairment.”
The advice is simple: never look directly at the sun without appropriate protection.
The college says ordinary sunglasses, binoculars, telescopes and cameras do not provide adequate protection, unless the equipment has an appropriate, professionally fitted solar filter.
Safe indirect methods of viewing a solar eclipse include pinhole projection, verified eclipse glasses that meet safety certification ‘ISO 12312-2' or ‘ISO 12312-2:2015’, or television and online broadcasts.
Even when only a small part of the sun remains visible during an eclipse, sufficient radiation can reach the retina to cause injury.
If you notice a change in your vision following the eclipse, seek advice from an eye-care professional.
What time is the eclipse?
The Royal Observatory will be livestreaming the solar eclipse on 12 August.
In person, it will be visible first to viewers in Scotland, with 'first contact' (when the moon first covers the disc of the sun) occurring at 6.08pm.
'First contact' in Manchester and Liverpool is 6.13pm, while in London, Bristol and Cardiff it's 6.17pm and in Cornwall it’s 6.18pm.
The peak of the eclipse will occur between 7.05pm and 7.16pm, depending on how far down the country viewers are.
The eclipse will end for all UK viewers by 8.10pm.
