Somalia malnutrition response hit by more than 80% funding drop as child hunger surges, MSF says
NAIROBI, Aug 11 - Funding to tackle acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80% this year, Médecins Sans Frontières said on Tuesday, even though one in every four children screened in displacement camps in the southwest is severely malnourished.
MSF Health Adviser Mitchell Sangma said the United States had cut its support to aid agencies in the country from $70 million last year to no funding this year, leaving aid groups struggling to respond as needs rise. Other Western donors have also cut funding.
"This year we have admitted 22,000 nutrition cases, more than 80% higher than last year. When we need this massive scale-up in intervention measures, we are seeing less interest from donor support," Sangma said.
A July survey by MSF of 888 households in 14 displacement sites in Baidoa, southwest Somalia, found that one in four children was severely malnourished. One third of families said they were surviving on one meal a day, while only 2% could afford three meals.
Somalia is facing a worsening hunger crisis after repeated failed rainy seasons devastated crops, killed livestock and depleted water supplies. Conflict and insecurity have compounded the crisis, disrupting livelihoods and limiting access to food, healthcare and aid.
In February, the Somali government and the United Nations said about 6.5 million people in the country faced acute hunger due to drought.
MSF said it had screened more than 21,000 children under five in Baidoa since the start of the year, finding acute malnutrition rates of about 50%. Acute malnutrition is less extreme than severe malnutrition but still involves sudden weight loss and is life-threatening.
According to the United Nations, more than half a million people were displaced in Somalia in the first three months of 2026, with drought driving most of the movement. Women and children accounted for about 85% of those displaced.
The crisis is reviving fears of a repeat of Somalia's 2022 near-famine, but aid agencies say the response is being constrained by severe funding shortfalls.
MSF says there is only about $300 million available for Somalia from donors, compared to $2.2 billion that was provided by donors in 2022 when a similar drought situation was experienced.
"The world cannot wait for a famine declaration before acting," said Allara Ali, MSF's project coordinator in Somalia. "Action is needed now to prevent loss of lives." REUTERS

Who is Atef Najib, former Syrian official sentenced to death with al-Assad?
Experts say this trial has been a test of Syria’s transitional justice.
Atef Najib, the former Syrian security official widely seen as the man who oversaw a regime of murder, torture and forced disappearances against Syrians during the country’s brutal 14-year civil war, has been sentenced to death by a court in Damascus.
On Tuesday, Najib was sentenced alongside ousted Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad and his younger brother, Maher al-Assad, who also received the death penalty in absentia for crimes including premeditated murder.
The Fourth Criminal Court found that crimes committed by al-Assad’s government in Deraa province in 2011 amounted to crimes against humanity.
Unlike al-Assad and members of his family who fled to Russia when the regime fell in December 2024, Najib has been in detention in Syria since January 2025. During his trial, he was charged with at least 10 crimes, including murder, torture and responsibility for massacres, as well as crimes against humanity linked to the 2011 Deraa crackdown on protesters.
We unpack who Najib is, what he is charged with and what we know about his trial and verdict.
Who is Atef Najib?
Najib, 66, is the first cousin of former President Bashar al-Assad and the former head of political security in southern Syria’s Deraa province.
Al-Assad was overthrown in early December 2024, when a coalition of armed opposition groups seized Damascus in a lightning advance and toppled his government. Since his ousting, al-Assad has lived in exile in Moscow under tight Russian supervision, far from any formal role in Syria’s new transitional authorities.
Al-Assad had been in power since 2000 until he fled. He took over after his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had been in power since 1970, died.
In the early 1980s, Najib joined the Military Academy in Homs after graduating from school. After completing his training at the academy, he became the head of political security in Deraa. The exact date he officially assumed his role is not documented in public state archives.
He remained in his role leading up to and during the initial outbreak of the Syrian uprising in March 2011. Accused of violently quashing this uprising, the al-Assad regime officially removed him from his post in April 2011.
Najib oversaw political security in Deraa when teenagers who scrawled antigovernment graffiti on a school wall were arrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for a broader uprising, which ultimately morphed into a bloody civil war.
The Ministry of Interior’s general security forces arrested Najib in January 2025 during a campaign targeting remnants of the former government in Latakia province. Najib had fled the country after al-Assad’s ousting, but then returned to Syria, Al Jazeera’s Obaida Hitto said, reporting from Damascus on Tuesday.
Najib’s arrest was considered one of the most significant detentions of former security officials because he held a sensitive security position in Deraa at the beginning of the Syrian uprising.
Najib’s sentence was issued by the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus on Tuesday, which oversaw the final review of his case and judgement. Closing arguments and his final statement had already been heard in the eighth session. The proceedings began on April 26.
What has the court decided?
Najib was sentenced to death, alongside al-Assad and his brother.
According to the court ruling, Najib was involved in the torture of a large number of detainees, including of children, and was responsible for the deaths of many of them during their detention.
This marks the first decision by a Syrian court against a senior al-Assad‑era figure under the current transitional authorities.
“This is a historic moment, here in Syria. Atef Najib is the only one of the codefendants who is actually standing trial here physically inside the country. The other codefendants are all being sentenced in absentia,” Al Jazeera’s Hitto said.
What was Najib accused of?
He was accused of overseeing a violent crackdown on antigovernment protesters in Deraa during the 2011 uprising, which led to the 14-year civil war.
Overall, he was charged with at least 10 crimes, including murder, torture and responsibility for the 2011 massacre in Deraa, which the court ruled was a crime against humanity.
According to an Al Jazeera Mubasher report, 75 plaintiffs filed cases against Najib and were understood to have provided testimony during the trial.
Why is this significant?
This trial was a test case for Syria’s transitional justice system and for the new government’s ability to hold al-Assad regime officials to account for abuses under his rule.
The government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa has faced criticism for delays in launching a promised transitional justice process following the war, in which an estimated half a million people were killed.
According to a 2025 report by the Syrian Network for Human Rights, more than 181,000 people were forcibly disappeared or arbitrarily detained during the war, 90 percent of them by the al-Assad regime.
“The legal issues that were discussed today are going to set the precedent for future legal actions taken against anyone that was involved in these crimes,” Hitto said.
The verdict is therefore being seen by many as a test of how far al-Sharaa’s government will go to mete out justice for past crimes.
“What is at stake in these proceedings is not confined to the question of whether Najib will be held to account for his actions … Rather, the true significance of this trial lies in the legal foundation of the judicial record that these proceedings will leave behind,” Fadel Abdulghany, the founder and head of the Syrian Network for Human Rights, wrote in an opinion piece for The New Arab last month.
Hitto reported that people had gathered around the court in Damascus when the verdict was announced, and they were “relieved that this is happening in this way”.
Syrians could be seen celebrating the verdicts in the streets outside.
“The country has been trying to reconcile more than five decades of dictatorship led by the al-Assad family over the last 18 months or so,” Hitto added.

The southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia was the hardest hit, with six people killed and 19 wounded, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“The city was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons, and guided aerial bombs,” Zelensky said. “It was a vicious attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage specifically on civilian infrastructure.”
Ukraine has not publicly provided evidence for the claim that North Korean missiles were used in the attack.
Seoul keeps weapons off the table
A senior South Korean foreign ministry official said Monday that Seoul’s defense exports remain subject to domestic law, signaling that Kyiv’s request for air defense systems and other military equipment has not prompted a policy shift.
“South Korea’s supply of defense materials to any country has always been carried out in accordance with domestic law,” the official told The Korea Times.
South Korea has provided Ukraine with humanitarian assistance and support for energy, infrastructure, healthcare and education, but has maintained a policy of withholding lethal weapons.
Zelensky: First Time, Russia Cannot Wage War Without North Korea
Zelensky warns of more North Korean troops
Zelensky has repeatedly warned that Moscow and Pyongyang are expanding their military partnership.
On Monday, he said Russia had received “additional ballistic missiles from North Korea.”
Over the weekend, he claimed that “a decision has been made for 30,000 to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on the territory of Russia.”
Kyiv has not explained how it obtained those figures or provided a timeframe for the potential deployment.
Zelensky said North Korea was gaining valuable battlefield experience through its cooperation with Russia and urged South Korea to provide Ukraine with air defense systems and other capabilities.
“They have a legal restriction under their Constitution. But we would like to have this cooperation and are counting on it. Our diplomats are in contact,” Zelensky wrote.
Seoul condemns Pyongyang-Moscow alliance
South Korea has not confirmed Zelensky’s claims about a new North Korean troop deployment or diplomatic discussions over weapons for Ukraine.
But Seoul has strongly condemned the growing military relationship between Moscow and Pyongyang.
“North Korea-Russia military cooperation is directly related to our security and violates United Nations resolutions,” the South Korean official said, according to The Korea Times.
“Our government’s position is that this cooperation should stop immediately,” the official added, saying Seoul was closely monitoring developments.
North Korea has become a key Russian war partner
Russia and North Korea signed a mutual defense pact in June 2024, deepening an alliance that has expanded rapidly since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Pyongyang has been accused by Ukraine, South Korea, and Western intelligence agencies of supplying Russia with large quantities of weapons and ammunition.
North Korea has also deployed thousands of troops to Russia, including forces sent to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the Kursk region.
The partnership gives Pyongyang access to modern battlefield experience while helping Russia replenish manpower and weapons for its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine faces growing ballistic missile threat
The latest attacks come as Russia has sharply increased its use of ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities.
The weapons are difficult to intercept, making advanced air defense systems such as the US-made Patriot critical to Ukraine’s ability to protect civilians and infrastructure.
Kyiv has repeatedly warned of shortages of Patriot interceptor missiles as Russia intensifies its missile campaign.
At the same time, Ukraine has expanded its own long-range drone strikes against Russian oil facilities, military-linked infrastructure and logistics hubs, saying the attacks are designed to disrupt Moscow’s war machine and revenue streams.

(도쿄=연합뉴스) 조성미 특파원 = 앤서니 앨버니지 호주 총리가 지난 5월 정상회담을 위해 호주를 방문한 다카이치 사나에 일본 총리로부터 받은 과일 선물을 성적 희화화의 대상으로 삼았다는 비판이 일고 있다.
 11일 아사히신문과 팟캐스트 영상에 따르면 앨버니지 총리는 지난달 초 공개된 코미디언 니키 오즈번의 팟캐스트 방송에서 다카이치 총리로부터 멜론을 선물로 받았다고 소개했다.
 팟캐스트 진행자 오즈번이 멜론을 양손으로 든 듯한 손짓을 하자 앨버니지 총리도 비슷한 손동작을 했고 "멜론이 아름다웠다"라고 발언했다.
 이에 야마가미 신고 전 주호주 일본대사가 지난 10일 호주 언론 '디 오스트레일리안'에 실은 기고를 통해 앨버니지 총리의 멜론과 관련한 발언이 무례한 성적 농담이라며 "모욕적이고 경솔하다"고 비판했다.
 호주 야당 지도부 등도 앨버니지 총리 발언이 부적절했다며 다카이치 총리에게 사과하라고 요구하고 나섰다.
 앨버니지 총리는 11일(현지시간) 호주 의회에서 해당 사안과 관련한 사과 의향을 묻자 "다카이치 씨는 호주의 친구이자 나의 친구다. 앞으로도 함께 협력해 나가는 데 주력하겠다"며 즉답을 피했다.
 한편, 앨버니지 총리와 같은 호주 노동당 소속 인사들은 야마가미 전 대사와 호주 언론 등이 그의 의도를 오해한 것이라고 옹호했다.
 앨버니지 총리는 지난달 호주의 유명 여가수와 잠자리를 원한다는 답변을 해 파문이 일자 결국 사과하기도 했다.
 그가 이 발언을 한 팟캐스트 역시 다카이치 총리에 대해 언급한 코미디언 오즈번의 팟캐스트였다.

IAEA to visit Syria after US-brokered deal to remove nuclear material from secret site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:01:21 UTC
19:01:21 KST

Syria’s Atomic Energy Commission said Tuesday that a delegation from the International Atomic Energy Agency will visit the country to announce “significant progress,” effectively confirming a report that the UN nuclear watchdog is preparing to remove nuclear material from a secret site in Syria.
The announcement follows a report by Axios that the IAEA is expected to begin removing the material after the Trump administration reached understandings with Syria and Israel.
According to Israeli and U.S. officials cited in the report, Washington and the IAEA worked together to secure a diplomatic arrangement that would remove the material and avert an escalation involving Israel, Syria and potentially Turkey over the sensitive site.
Behind the scenes, the report said, months of threats and intensive diplomacy preceded the agreement reached several weeks ago. Under former Syrian President Bashar Assad, Syria maintained a covert nuclear program centered on the secret reactor at al-Kibar.
Israel destroyed the reactor in a 2007 airstrike, largely dismantling Syria’s nuclear program. Several research, development and storage facilities, however, remained intact, though most were believed to have seen little significant activity.
After Assad’s regime fell, the IAEA reached an agreement with Syria’s new authorities allowing inspectors to visit the al-Kibar site and several other locations associated with Syria’s former nuclear activities.
One facility that Israel has closely monitored over the past two years is known as “Site 99.” Two Israeli officials cited by Axios said the Assad regime had stored nuclear material there that was connected to the al-Kibar reactor project. A U.S. official said the material included yellowcake, a uranium concentrate that can later be processed and enriched as part of the nuclear fuel cycle.
 The official said Site 99 also contained additional remnants and debris from the destroyed al-Kibar facility.
Although the material at the site could not itself be used to produce a nuclear weapon, officials said it could potentially be used in a “dirty bomb,” a conventional explosive designed to disperse radioactive material and contaminate an area rather than create a nuclear explosion.
Israeli officials said the IDF bombed the entrances to Site 99 shortly after Assad’s fall in an effort to prevent anyone from gaining access. A U.S. official said Israel and the United States had spent more than a year discussing the best way to deal with Site 99. White House National Security Council officials and their Israeli counterparts worked closely on the issue.
According to an Israeli official, Jerusalem made clear to the Trump administration that it would not accept the nuclear material remaining at the site. Israeli officials said Israel also threatened to strike the site again if the material was not removed or if there were signs that Syrian authorities were trying to access it.
A U.S. official, however, stressed that despite Israeli concerns, “they were never on the verge of bombing the site.” Washington and Jerusalem ultimately agreed, according to a U.S. official cited by Axios, that the best solution was to secure Syrian consent for the removal of the material. When the Trump administration raised the issue with officials in Damascus, the Syrians said they had not known nuclear material was stored there.
‘A good partner’
“Very few people in the U.S., Israel and Syria were aware of it,” the U.S. official said, adding that Washington had developed a productive working relationship with Damascus. “When we work with the Syrians on things, they are good partners,” the official said.
Several weeks ago, however, Israeli officials monitoring the site detected movement in the area that raised suspicions that Syrian authorities might be backing away from the understandings and attempting to reach the material.
According to the report, Israeli officials also feared Turkey might be helping Syria gain access to it. “The Israelis are always checking different possibilities to make sure everything looks right, and it’s good that they do,” a U.S. official said.
The Trump administration urged Israel not to act and brought the IAEA directly into the process. The result was an agreement signed around three weeks ago between the IAEA and Syria to remove the material from Site 99.
U.S. officials said work at the site is still underway and the material has not yet been removed. “But we think everyone is happy with the outcome,” one official said, expressing hope that the removal process could begin soon and be completed before the end of the year.

Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at risk | Stuart Russell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:57 UTC
19:00:57 KST

It is fashionable in certain circles to dismiss the catastrophic risks of AI. One often hears that “the real experts” who work on the technology every day are really not concerned at all; that only “doomers” and “Luddites” espouse a “fringe” view from a “position of ignorance”; that all talk of potential catastrophe is just “science fiction”.
Fortunately, an open letter has been published that lets us hear from the real experts who work on the technology every day, in their own words. And are they worried? Very.
The letter states: “There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” It asks the US government to support “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.
AI systems going “beyond our ability to understand or control” would mean that we no longer have a say in whether we exist. AI systems escaping their confines and breaking into other companies’ computers – something that has become an almost daily occurrence – are an early warning.
To “pace the frontier”, as the letter asks, is to ensure that more advanced systems are developed and released only when it is demonstrably safe to do so. This requires a licensing process with strong verification of safety; registration of AI systems and the ability to monitor and terminate them when necessary; and enforceable international agreements. All of this takes time and is impossible to put in place once a real emergency happens.
The concerns expressed in the letter about the rapid acceleration of AI capabilities have been bubbling up for some months under the heading of “recursive self-improvement” or RSI – that is, AI systems contributing to their own improvement, which then enables even greater contributions to their own improvement, and so on.
This was the subject of the “Recursive” conference in mid-May in San Francisco as well as Anthropic’s RSI warning, “When AI builds itself”, in early June. Broader concerns about the safety and societal impacts of AI have also motivated the formation of the Coalition of Concerned AI Staff, which links together employees of all the major AI companies.
The letter is signed by (at the time of writing) 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Deepmind. The list includes CEOs, co-founders, chief scientists, and hundreds of well-known AI researchers, including many of my former students. These are the people who are driving the AI revolution while trying to fashion brakes and steering wheels at the same time. If these are not the experts, then there are none.
What makes the letter so powerful is not just the first-person authority of the signers but the inclusion of personal statements from almost a hundred of them. The statements paint a much more detailed picture of what the experts really think. At least three major themes emerge.
The first is the need to coordinate to escape an arms race towards the edge of cliff. Earlier this year at Davos, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google Deepmind, both suggested they wanted to halt AI development if others would agree. “The world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion … To survive, we must coordinate to slow down the race,” said one signer.
Another wrote: “Once this becomes common knowledge – once all of us in China and the US and at the various labs see that all the rest of us also think we need to slow this down – that’s when coordination becomes possible.”
The second common theme in the remarks is, as one signer put it, “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling ‘superintelligent’ AI systems”. “These are the facts: The AI industry has the explicit goal of building things smarter than humans … None of us yet know how to make sure these things stay under human control … This is, objectively, an insane and suicidal thing to do,” wrote another.
Not surprisingly, these concerns lead to the third theme: real fear. “I currently feel quite afraid of all paths I see that don’t include a near-future negotiated slowdown.” “There is … a very dark future ahead of us if we don’t get this right.” And: “I want a world where my kids can have a full life not a world where they are wiped out.”
These are not greedy employees trying to hype their stock valuations. They say the same things in private conversations, closed-door meetings and off-the-record chat groups.
In the face of such real and well-founded fears, surely these trillion-dollar companies are devoting massive resources to ensure they don’t end our, and their own, existence? Wrong.
One researcher, quoted in a recent New Yorker article on the OpenAI systems that broke into Hugging Face, said: “If people actually knew what the safety culture looks like, even in the most safety-minded labs, then I think people would be genuinely much more freaked out.”
According to one senior safety researcher at Anthropic, their best bet for avoiding an irreversible loss of control works like this: as soon as the superintelligent machine comes into existence, but before it’s had a chance to take over the world, we ask it how we can stop it from taking over the world, and we do what it says.
This plan doesn’t fill me with confidence, and the Anthropic researcher gives it at best a 50% chance of working. It’s the same plan that IJ Good mentions in his famous 1965 paper on the intelligence explosion: “The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.” I rather think that Good meant this remark sarcastically.
The most powerful of all the personal signing statements is also the shortest: “Think of all we love.”
- 
  Stuart Russell is a distinguished professor of computer science at University of California, Berkeley, the president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence and a Guardian US columnist

Wisconsin considers democratic socialist for governor amid US wave of progressive wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:57 UTC
19:00:57 KST

Wisconsin voters will decide on Tuesday whether to nominate a democratic socialist for the state’s highest office in the latest test of an anti-establishment wave among Democratic primary voters.
Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist state lawmaker, emerged as the frontrunner in a four-way race to succeed Tony Evers, the Democratic governor who is not seeking another term.
Evers threw his support behind David Crowley, the Milwaukee country executive. Crowley previously left the race, before reentering it on 18 July.
Crowley and Evers toured the state in the last two weeks, centering his campaign around electability, saying Crowley was more poised to win a general election in a swing state like Wisconsin than Hong.
Eyes turned to the Wisconsin governor’s race after Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan last week in the most recent example of a progressive beating out a moderate. Next door, Minnesota voters have also been weighing a US Senate primary between a moderate and a progressive.
After a wave of wins of progressives and democratic socialists in solidly blue parts of the country, the midwest primaries centered more on electability concerns given the close nature of statewide races there.
While some saw Crowley’s reentry as evidence that the establishment was working to derail Hong’s campaign, Crowley balked at the idea that he was part of the establishment.
Hong, meanwhile, saw her past comments – including a tweet that said to cancel Thanksgiving, and previous support for defunding the police – scrutinized by journalists and attacked by Republicans, led by Donald Trump, as more national attention turned to Wisconsin’s primary.
Marquette University Law School surveyed the Democratic primary in late July, after Crowley reentered, and found Hong leading the pack, though a sizable chunk of voters were still undecided at that time.
The race had rearranged itself multiple times in the weeks leading up to 11 August, landing at four candidates: Hong, Crowley, the state senator Kelda Roys, and the former state administration department head Joel Brennan. A previous top contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities, after which Crowley reentered the race. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July.
Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, was first elected to the state assembly in 2020. She ran on a platform that included childcare for all, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on new datacenter construction. She said voters throughout the state have pushed back against the political establishment and want candidates who will advocate for changes that materially improve their lives.
“I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she previously told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.”
The winner will face Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. He voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost.
Tiffany’s role in the 2020 election highlighted the importance of keeping the governor’s office for Democrats. Democrats also hope to win both chambers of the state legislature to install a governing trifecta and enact their agenda.
Elsewhere in Wisconsin, voters in the western part of the state will decide which Democratic contender will face Republican Derrick Van Orden in the third congressional district, a key pickup opportunity for Democrats.
Rebecca Cooke, a “blue dog” Democrat who previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, has seen national support for her campaign against Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is most poised to win the district.

The return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.
Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.
“Today, we became witnesses of a truly historic event,” declared Yerlan Nysanbayev, Kazakhstan’s environment minister, after the release. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken.”
The caspian tiger was considered extinct in the 1970s after decades of fur hunting, habitat destruction and eradication campaigns. Its range once spanned from eastern Turkey to north-west China, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and swathes of central Asia, mostly in forest highlands and along the edges of lakes and rivers, particularly in Tugai forests that were widely destroyed for agriculture.
It was officially declared extinct in 2003, but a scientific breakthrough just six years later laid the foundation for the recent release. DNA analysis of the tiger’s genetic history revealed that the caspian tiger and the amur tiger found in eastern Siberia were almost identical, with populations probably intermingling until the early 1900s before they were isolated by hunting. What became known as the caspian tiger spread west from Siberia and were separated from the amur tiger by a single letter of genetic code.
“For all intents and purposes, this is the return of the caspian tiger, only this time they flew instead of walking,” said Dale Miquelle, an authority on Siberian tigers who heads Wildlife Conservation Society’s Russia programme. “The idea of bringing back a subspecies of tigers that has disappeared is very exciting. This is as close as we’re going to get to that process.”
Today, it would be practically impossible for the caspian tiger to re-establish its former range. A 2017 feasibility study identified two places in the region with enough suitable habitat to re-establish populations, both in Kazakhstan. The most promising was thought to be Ile-Balkhash, where Umit was released, which the Kazakh government made a nature reserve in 2018.
While this summer’s release is the first example of a cross-border tiger translocation, there have been several successful releases in the Russian far east as part of efforts to restore the amur tiger’s former range. One scheme involved rescuing orphaned cubs whose mothers had been shot by hunters in Siberia, and then releasing them into former ranges when they were strong enough. The project, which Miquelle worked on, was a huge success – especially because there was no human contact with the young big cats.
“The success rate was pretty close to 100% after the release. These animals adapt amazingly quickly. One young female killed a Himalayan black bear within 24 hours of being released and others have learned to hunt on their own in the wild really quickly,” he says.
But it is not all good news. Wild tigers have suffered a catastrophic century, with numbers falling from about 100,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 5,500 today. In many parts of Asia, they are still declining – and facing new threats from climate breakdown and disease. In recent years in Russia, African swine fever wiped out enormous numbers of wild boar, a tiger’s favourite prey, causing many to target human settlements. Ensuring there is enough food for the returning caspian tigers is key to their survival, says Miquelle.
“I am very hopeful this can work. In Russia, a number of translocations resulted in the recolonisation of tiger habitat. So there’s a blueprint that suggests that this can work as long as there is suitable habitat and sufficient prey,” he says.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

The Simple Trick That Can Help You Understand Your Emotions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Here’s the scene: You’re catching up with a friend over coffee when your elbow clips your cup, sending espresso all over her brand-new phone. You feel awful. You mop up the spill, apologize five times, and bolt—then avoid her for days, turning a ruined phone into a damaged friendship.
The problem isn’t that you feel awful. It’s that awful doesn’t give you much to work with. It tells you the situation feels bad, but not why—or what to do about it.
Katie Hoemann, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Kansas, uses a version of this scenario to explain emotional granularity: the ability to make precise distinctions among all the emotions you’re experiencing in a particular situation. Instead of stopping at “awful,” you might recognize guilt about damaging the phone, embarrassment about causing a scene, and anxiety that your ticked-off friend isn’t going to forgive you.
Those distinctions don’t just describe the moment. They point to different responses. Guilt might push you to offer to replace the phone, embarrassment might explain why you want to disappear, and anxiety might prompt you to ask your friend whether your relationship is OK. Distinguishing among them gives you access to what Hoemann calls “situated scripts”—a clearer sense of what to do and say next.
Lisa Feldman Barrett, a distinguished professor at Northeastern University, began documenting these differences in the 1990s. She compares emotional granularity to seeing color: One person might only notice red; another sees crimson, scarlet, burgundy, and maroon. Similarly, some people experience anger, sadness, and fear as different versions of bad, while others experience each one distinctly—and can make even finer distinctions among, say, anger, irritation, and frustration.
This isn’t simply a matter of collecting impressive new words. “The words are not the point,” Barrett says. It’s about developing a more precise understanding of what’s happening inside you, in this particular situation. The clearer that understanding becomes, she says, the better you can tailor your response.
Why getting specific can help
When all you know is that you feel bad, there are almost endless possible explanations: Maybe you’re lonely. Maybe you’re ashamed of something you said. Or maybe you’re disappointed that a friend let you down, resentful that your hard work is going unnoticed, or anxious about tomorrow’s doctor’s appointment. Each situation calls for something different.
“When there’s a precise cause, you can have a precise response,” says Eli Kraiem, a clinical psychologist in New York. If you’re lonely, you might call someone. If you’re resentful, you might need to have a difficult conversation. And if you’re anxious, you might make a plan, seek more information, or do something that helps calm your body. “Bad” leaves you with a giant, shapeless problem; specificity gives you somewhere to begin.
That doesn’t mean every feeling becomes a problem to solve. “Sometimes feelings don’t need solutions,” Kraiem says. “Sometimes they just need to be recognized.” Realizing that you’re not merely stressed but also grieving, for example, might not produce an obvious next step. But it can help you stop treating your sadness like a productivity problem—and give yourself permission to experience it.
Research has repeatedly linked higher emotional granularity with healthier ways of navigating difficult moments. In one study of young social drinkers, people who distinguished more precisely among their negative emotions consumed about 40% less alcohol when they were experiencing intense distress than those with lower granularity. Other daily-diary research found that people who differentiated among their emotions reported fewer aggressive tendencies when they were angry. A review of the literature has also linked higher granularity with more effective emotion regulation and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety.
Those findings don’t prove that pausing to name three feelings will produce all of those benefits. Much of the research is correlational: It tells us that people who habitually experience emotions with more precision tend to fare better, not that one labeling exercise will transform your mental health. Scientists are still working out exactly how to strengthen the skill—and how much practice it takes.
There is, however, some encouraging evidence that people can better develop their sense of emotional granularity. In a study co-authored by Hoemann, people were able to improve their emotional granularity over roughly two weeks of assessments, during which they responded to prompts about their emotions throughout the day and elaborated on those experiences in daily diary entries. A separate study found that people participating in a mindfulness-based intervention improved their ability to differentiate negative emotions, with the improvement still evident four months after the intervention ended—though it may have partly reflected the fact that they were feeling less negative overall.
Start with the words you already overuse
The next time you catch yourself saying you feel bad, stressed, or off, pause and try to name three specific emotions.
Start by paying attention to your emotional catchalls—the handful of words you use to describe almost everything. Bad, fine, and stressed are obvious candidates, but your favorite might be overwhelmed, annoyed, or tired.
When you catch yourself using one, don’t stop there. Ask: “What does stressed mean right now?” Maybe you’re anxious because you’re underprepared for a presentation, frustrated that your co-worker isn’t helping, or afraid you’ll disappoint your boss. Those emotions aren’t interchangeable, even though they’ve all been crammed into the same word.
If you draw a blank, Kraiem recommends opening the Hoffman Institute’s free online Feelings and Sensations list, which groups more than 100 options under broad headings like anger, fear, sadness, and stress. “It actually does the differentiation for you,” he says. Start with the category that comes closest to how you feel, then scan the words beneath it: stressed, for example, branches into anxious, frazzled, rattled, weary, and worn out.
Kraiem uses the list with patients, but he also pulls it up himself after a conflict with his wife or when work or parenting leaves him stressed. “There are times when I’m feeling stuck, and that’s when I pull out this list,” he says. With practice, you may need the list less often and eventually make those distinctions “on the fly.”
Once you have a few possibilities, make sure they capture genuinely different aspects of the situation. Then add a short explanation: “I feel anxious because I don’t know what will happen”; “I feel resentful because I’m carrying more than my share”; and “I feel embarrassed because I’m worried I’ll look incompetent.”
The explanation matters. If you write “angry,” “irritated,” and “annoyed” every time something goes wrong, you may simply be using three words for essentially the same feeling. Hoemann suggests asking not which word is objectively “correct,” but which emotions best explain what’s happening in this particular moment.
It’s also fine if only one precise word fits. Granularity doesn’t mean you have to conjure up three emotions because you’re stewing over the mile-long grocery-store line. The number is a nudge, not a rule.
Don’t wait until you’re furious
You can try to get specific in the heat of the moment, but that’s often the hardest time to learn. When your friend’s phone is dripping espresso, you’re probably not going to feel eager to conduct a nuanced emotional inventory.
Barrett recommends practicing when the stakes are lower. Think of it like strength training: You don’t wait until you need to lift something enormous and then pick up a weight for the first time. “You have to practice in advance,” she says.
At the end of the day, choose one emotionally charged moment and revisit it. What were you experiencing? What did each emotion mean in that context? What did it make you want to do? Hoemann says you can reflect immediately, later that evening, or even over the next few days; researchers don’t yet know which timing works best.
The goal isn’t to replay every unpleasant interaction until you’ve analyzed it to death. Hoemann cautions that more isn’t always better: Exhaustively labeling a negative experience can veer into rumination and may even make it harder to figure out what to do. Spend a few minutes teasing apart what you felt, then move on.
Learn emotions from other people
Your emotional vocabulary doesn’t have to come from a list. Barrett says we learn a lot about emotions from other people. Books, movies, plays, conversations, and travel expose you to experiences and perspectives you might not encounter in your own routine.
When you’re watching a movie or reading a novel, pause occasionally to consider what a character might be feeling—and why. Is she angry, or does she feel betrayed? Is he sad about losing the job, ashamed that he was fired, or afraid of what comes next? More than one interpretation may make sense. The point is to practice seeing different possibilities.
Talking to other people helps, too. Hoemann describes emotional granularity not as “insular internal tagging,” but as a dialogue with the world. Describe a difficult experience to a trusted friend and ask what emotions they hear in it. They may share something you hadn’t considered.
Don’t expect the words to make the feeling disappear
Naming an emotion might make it feel more vivid in the moment, not less. Paying closer attention to sadness can make you more aware of how sad you are. It can also be unsettling to realize that what you’ve been calling irritation is actually loneliness or shame.
“I hesitate to say that it’s like a magic spell—that you’re like, ‘Oh, I’m angry, and now everything’s better,’” Hoemann says.
Immediate relief isn’t the point. Each time you examine an experience closely, you build a more detailed understanding of your emotions—one you can draw on later. Over time, you may get better at understanding what’s happening as it happens, and choosing a response that fits.
Back in the coffee shop, you might still feel awful. But guilt, embarrassment, and anxiety give you something that “awful” doesn’t: a plan. Instead of fleeing and dodging your friend for the next week, you stay, offer to replace the phone, and then check in again the next day. The phone may be toast, but the friendship doesn’t have to be.

====================================================================================================

Taiwan’s Opposition Leader Says Talking to China Is the Island’s Best Defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Cheng Li-wun once called for the destruction of the party she now leads. Back in 1988, when she was still a teenager, Cheng took the dais at a farmers’ rally to condemn Taiwan’s Nationalist Party, or KMT, as “the most detestable ruling force,” urging her compatriots to “overthrow KMT tyranny and establish our own country.”
Today, Cheng runs the KMT from its Taipei headquarters, where her chairperson’s office boasts the eclectic talismans of her unconventional journey: a cuddly kangaroo, a model Xiaomi electric car, and a jade Buddha statue guarding her desk. “I’m a very devout Buddhist,” Cheng tells TIME.
Read more: Taiwan in the Shadow of War
Cheng’s stunning transformation from Taiwanese independence zealot to leader of the self-ruling island’s China-friendly opposition is illustrated by another office adornment: a framed copy of the China Daily newspaper documenting her April meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, under the headline “Xi calls for closer bonds across Strait.”
It was the first trip by a KMT leader to China in a decade and came against a backdrop of spiraling tensions, with near-daily Chinese combat aircraft, warships, and coast guard vessels rehearsing port blockades, precision strikes, and foreign-intervention denial. “Before the meeting [with Xi], nobody really had expectations of how it would go, and I think that they were very surprised by the goodwill that we received,” Cheng says.
For Xi, Taiwan is not merely unfinished business from the 1945–49 Chinese Civil War, after which the routed KMT fled to the now democratic island of 23 million. It is the keystone of a far grander project: the national rejuvenation of China as the world’s dominant technological, economic, and political power. The island’s very existence—a prosperous, democratic Chinese society integrated with the West—offers a stinging rebuke to the claim that authoritarian rule is uniquely suited to the Chinese people.
Cheng’s conversion encapsulates Taiwan’s own agonizing debate: whether security lies in distancing itself from the power threatening to take the island by force, or drawing closer to it. The ruling Beijing-skeptic Democratic Progressive Party, or DPP, sees Taiwan’s future as distinct from China’s and has prioritized building trade and other unofficial ties with Asian neighbors. In 2010, China accounted for 83.8% of Taiwan’s total outward investment; during the first five months of 2026, that figure had plunged to just 0.9%.
That decoupling has also seen Beijing squeeze Taiwan economically and diplomatically. Over the past decade of DPP rule, Beijing has restricted imports of Taiwanese goods and limited free-spending tourist arrivals, while poaching 10 of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies, so that only 12 remain.
Swelling anxiety increasingly shapes Taiwan’s domestic politics. Within the KMT, there is a strong belief that Washington cannot be relied upon indefinitely and that Taipei must engage Beijing from a position of weakness. The party’s implicit message is that Taiwan will not choose unification now—but nor will it formally choose another future.
Cheng’s emergence embodies that bargain. Despite her pro-independence past, Cheng has embraced Chinese identity, the so-called 1992 Consensus that both sides of the Strait belong to “One China,” and direct engagement with Beijing. Her meeting with Xi allowed Beijing to display its neglected carrots: economic incentives, restored exchanges, and the promise of stability. But Cheng’s limited electoral experience, thin Washington ties, and lackluster appeal to the KMT’s traditional base leave open the question of whether she can persuade Taiwan’s broader electorate.
“It’s not a good move for Taiwan,” Puma Shen, a DPP lawmaker and the party’s candidate for the upcoming Taipei mayoral election, says of Cheng’s meeting with Xi. “China is the country that wants to invade Taiwan … and they’re also pushing more and more gray-zone tactics.”
Yet that doesn’t necessarily mean Xi is racing toward war. He appears to regard history as moving inexorably in China’s favor and may believe he can afford to wait. The surest form of deterrence, then, may not be convincing Beijing that unification is impossible, but that patience remains the least costly path.
“I want to do away with the Cold War thinking,” says Cheng. “I do not want the first island chain to be thought of as the front line of military conflict. Rather, I would like it to be the front line of peace.”
The need to dial down the temperature is indisputable. A Taiwan contingency would decimate global supply chains in unprecedented ways, costing some $10 trillion, according to estimates by Bloomberg Economics. Opinion is split, however, on how best to prevent conflict.
While the DPP has formal independence for Taiwan written into its party charter, its recent leaders have pragmatically skirted that goal, aware that Beijing has vowed to meet secession with a military response. But such ambiguity has cut little ice with China’s leadership, which loathes President Lai Ching-te as a “provocateur and saboteur of peace.”
Cheng’s prescription is direct engagement and the revival of the KMT’s role as an intermediary between two governments that, under two-and-a-half DPP terms, only communicate through warplanes and naval exercises. But peace offered by a stronger adversary rarely comes without conditions—and Cheng’s task is to prove she understands the stakes.
“This is a really important time for Taiwan,” she says. “Are we going to go toward war or toward peace across the Strait? This is really why I decided to take the party chair.”
Standing 5 ft. 10 in., Cheng is an arresting presence with a reputation for chest-thumping speeches. Sure enough, during our interview, her answers betray a bombastic staccato honed on the stump. Behind the scenes, however, she is amiable and slightly introverted.
“I actually am a very, very quiet person,” she says. “I don’t like to see people, and I don’t like to talk to people. I like to keep to myself.”
It’s a surprising revelation given Cheng’s political journey under the spotlight, which in many ways reflects the complicated social dynamics of Taiwan, where political fault lines have historically been drawn between native islanders and mainland arrivals following the Civil War.
Cheng grew up in the southern city of Tainan, the daughter of a Taiwanese mother and a KMT soldier father from China’s southwestern Yunnan province, who fled to Taiwan in 1953 via Southeast Asia’s arcane Golden Triangle. “My father really hated politics, hated war, and hated the army,” Cheng says. “He hated the KMT. My father thought all politicians are assholes!”
How would he react to her current position? “I surprised my father quite a few times!” she laughs.
Indeed, Cheng was once a student leader in Taiwan’s Wild Lily democracy movement of the early 1990s, though her participation came as something of a shock to her parents. “One day when I was leaving my home, my father said, ‘Don’t go out today, it will be very dangerous,’” Cheng recalls. “He didn’t know I was the leader!”
After graduating in law at National Taiwan University and Philadelphia’s Temple University—she later earned a master’s degree in international relations at Cambridge—Cheng served as a DPP representative in the now-defunct National Assembly. As the daughter of a mainlander, she enjoyed a fast-tracked rise in a party desperate to broaden its appeal beyond its native Taiwanese base.
But Cheng resigned from the DPP after criticizing the party’s handling of sexual harassment allegations against a superior that were eventually dismissed, spurring disciplinary proceedings against her. Cheng insists her defection had nothing to do with sour grapes, but a Damascene realization.
“I became very disappointed because I realized that the DPP’s advocating for Taiwan independence was really a scam,” she says. “It’s something they pull out during elections in order to get votes.”
Cheng joined the KMT in 2005 and was elected as a lawmaker three years later, also serving as party spokesperson and hosting a TV talk show after briefly losing her seat. “I only did that for the money,” she laughs. After returning to the legislature, Cheng was then elected as KMT chairperson in October on a platform of reengagement with China. “Based on the 1992 Consensus, we want to create sustainable and institutionalized peaceful cross-Strait relations,” Cheng says.
Yet her rise was contentious. Cheng’s candidacy for the KMT leadership was supported by a social media blitzkrieg that critics allege was underwritten by Beijing. “That’s part of [China’s] information operations,” says Shen. “Tons of YouTube channels just emerged … to praise Cheng Li-wun. That’s one of the reasons why she got elected.”
Cheng vehemently denies she is a stooge of the Chinese Communist Party. “It’s a ridiculous joke,” she says. “This is a complete fabrication.”
It will be left to voters to decide. On one hand, Taiwan’s citizens have a dwindling affinity for the mainland; the proportion of Taiwanese who reject unification rose from 39% in 2005 to 61.7% this year. However, coercion and the constant specter of war have also fed disillusionment and conflict fatigue. A separate survey last year found that only 40.8% of respondents were willing to lay down their lives to protect the island—down four percentage points from two years earlier. Meanwhile, 58.3% favored resuming government-to-government talks with Beijing and easing people-to-people exchanges.
It is often quipped that Taiwanese want a “Goldilocks approach” to cross-Strait relations, says Ryan Hass, an expert in China-Taiwan relations at the Brookings Institution. “Not too hot, not too cold, just right.”
The problem is whether dialogue alone will be enough to satisfy Beijing. During the last KMT administration from 2008 to 2016, Xi pushed then President Ma Ying-jeou hard to enter talks toward closer political integration. Ma demurred, saying the time was not yet right. But by Taiwan’s next presidential election in 2028, 12 years will have passed since that strategy was last tested—and the gamble is whether Xi can still be strung along.
“Beijing is probably eager to pick things up and push them forward, maybe on a timeline that is a little bit more ambitious than what the KMT are hoping for,” says Hass. “This is the underappreciated risk of the KMT retaining power. Because unrealized expectations can fuel disappointment and actions that relate to it.”
Taiwan certainly has no appetite for Beijing’s standing offer of reunification under “one country, two systems,” the framework used in Hong Kong, where freedoms have drastically eroded. Cheng highlights that Xi did not raise “one country, two systems” in their April discussions and that they saw “a very friendly side” of the strongman. “He expressed real, authentic sentiment toward us and goodwill,” she says. “He treated us as members of the same family … and cherished the opportunity to show that he is not interested in war.”
Would she consider a referendum on reunification? “There is no rush to make any changes to the status quo,” Cheng says. “A referendum would count as a big change, and that would have to align with the interests and willingness of the Taiwanese people.”
Cheng’s words are carefully calibrated to reflect the tightrope she must walk. The KMT has long adhered to the mantra: “Endear ourselves to the U.S., befriend Japan, and pacify China.” But following three straight presidential election defeats and plummeting poll numbers, Cheng won the party leadership on the platform that a radical shake-up was needed. With anxiety growing over U.S. security guarantees under the capricious Donald Trump, Cheng’s pitch was that befriending Beijing was the party’s ace in the hole.
Cheng is now attempting to forge a controversial “Taiwanese KMT” narrative, delicately balancing local sentiment with an overarching Chinese identity. But it is an uneasy pivot: she cannot talk too much about shared democratic values lest she irk Beijing, and she cannot lean too heavily into blood bonds between Chinese across the Strait for fear of alienating Washington. What remains is a torrent of bromides without a clear plan for moving closer to China without salami-slicing away Taiwan’s cherished autonomy.
“I am not only seeking reconciliation across the Strait but also a better relationship between the U.S. and China,” Cheng says. “That not only helps create peace in East Asia but in the whole world.”
Above all else, securing U.S. commitment to Taiwan is paramount. While Washington officially switched recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1979, the U.S. is obliged by act of Congress to provide Taiwan with the weapons it needs for its own defense. However, the latest $14 billion package—the largest ever—has still not been signed off by Trump. The understanding in Washington is that the U.S. commander-in-chief does not want anything to derail Xi’s prospective state visit to the White House next month.
Cheng’s Beijing visit was also historic because she was the first KMT leader to visit China before the U.S.—which she eventually did in June. She denies this indicates that she is placing cross-Strait ties above those across the Pacific.
“The situation across the Strait is very tense and hostile, and we had to take the first step to show that we are interested in peace,” she says. “That’s the reason that I wanted to take that peace tour first—I had to confirm that there was this willingness to create peace in the Taiwan Strait before I went to the U.S.”
If that trip was intended to reassure the Beltway, it was not entirely successful. Cheng did not meet Trump and appeared to upbraid U.S. foreign policy when she told crowds in New York City that she did not want Taiwan to become the “next Strait of Hormuz.” She also attracted criticism for saying there is no reason ethnic Chinese cannot exert similar influence over American society as the Jewish community, prompting condemnation for seeming to parrot an antisemitic trope.
It was not her only questionable statement on the road. Cheng raised eyebrows while in China when she criticized the colonial legacy of Japan—one of Taipei’s staunchest backers. In November, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi even sparked a diplomatic spat with Beijing by saying that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a military response from Tokyo. Cheng, again, tries to walk the tightrope.
“The Japanese Prime Minister commented if there’s a problem in Taiwan, that’s a problem for Japan,” Cheng says. “I don’t want that to just be negative; I want it to be positive: if there are no issues in the Taiwan Strait, then there is no issue in the world.”
Taiwan’s future is a global quandary. For U.S. policymakers, above all hangs a semiconductor industry responsible for more than 90% of the world’s bleeding edge chips, which form the bedrock of the AI revolution and has propelled the tiny island’s bourse to become the fifth most valuable across the planet. Those advanced fabrication plants have long been dubbed a “silicon shield” that prohibitively raises the cost of conflict. Yet they are also a tantalizing prize, one which, if seized, could offer a commanding advantage in that transformative technology.
Cheng has campaigned against what she has called an “arms race” with Beijing and torpedoed the Lai government’s proposed NT$1.25 trillion, or $38 billion, special defense budget in the legislature. During meetings with U.S. lawmakers, Cheng said the KMT was not opposed to buying American weapons but wanted spending to follow due process, maintain fiscal discipline, and combat corruption. The final approved special budget was capped at NT$780 billion, or $24 billion.
“National defense is very important to us,” Cheng says. “If there are more details in the future for new amounts, then we would also put those to the [legislative] floor for review.”
Beijing’s pressure, meanwhile, is becoming subtler. Military intimidation continues, but China is also waging a battle over language, law, and international legitimacy. Its effort to reinterpret U.N. Resolution 2758—which switched the world body’s China representation from Taipei to Beijing—as recognition of Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan anticipates a future crisis in which diplomatic support could matter almost as much as battlefield success. A decisive U.N. vote for Beijing could portray China as the defender of the international order—and the U.S. as its reckless subverter.
Cheng says the KMT she once despised has the best vision for securing Taiwan’s future. In any case, local elections scheduled for November will provide a bellwether for whether her message has cut through with a Taiwanese electorate that craves neither confrontation nor political absorption. Cheng’s task is to persuade Taiwan that talking to China is not the same as yielding to it.
“To be honest, President Xi and I are strangers,” she says when asked whether she trusts China’s leader. “I’ve never met him before. Therefore, trust is something that we should build up on both sides. I also need Chinese people on the mainland to trust me, because this is something we need to create stability in the future.”

Press review: NATO boosts Northern Europe presence as Israel blocks Gaza peace efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, August 11. /TASS/. NATO seeks to strengthen its foothold in Northern Europe; Israel continues to hinder efforts to resolve the Gaza Strip conflict; and Moscow and Damascus reconfigure Russian military presence in Syria. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: NATO seeks to strengthen foothold in Northern Europe
Finland is rapidly becoming a NATO staging ground as the alliance works to establish multinational ground forces and regularly holds military exercises in the country. NATO’s growing military presence in Finland is a destabilizing factor in the region, an official at the Russian embassy in Helsinki told Izvestia.
Finland’s accession to NATO in 2023, followed by Sweden’s in 2024, gave the North Atlantic Alliance a free hand to substantially increase its forces in Northern Europe, turning the region into a key bridgehead for exerting pressure on Russia.
Analysts point out that the continued deployment of troops to Finland is moving NATO’s infrastructure closer to Russia’s strategically important facilities. Military expert Vasily Dandykin notes that by establishing a foothold in Finland, NATO strategists have gained the ability to control access to the Baltic Sea from St. Petersburg from both the Finnish and Estonian coasts. Moreover, the new ground troops stationed in Finland could operate in close coordination with naval forces. This creates the risk for Russia of the westernmost Kaliningrad Region becoming completely isolated and access to the world's oceans being cut off.
Military analyst Viktor Litovkin argues that Finland's infrastructure is already being modernized to meet the needs of the United States and NATO. Airfields across the country are being prepared to accommodate US fighter jets capable of carrying nuclear weapons, while Helsinki has in fact indicated its readiness to host such arms.
Russia has begun taking military and organizational measures in response to these threats. In particular, the Leningrad Military District has been reestablished, and new military units are being formed and deployed in the region, the analyst said. In addition, Russia also holds exercises involving the use of non-strategic nuclear weapons, which are intended to temper the aggressive zeal of NATO’s leadership.
The Finnish authorities’ belief that the country’s integration into NATO would automatically guarantee its security through allied support appears to have been mistaken. Instead, Finland now faces rising tensions as it becomes a potential zone of armed conflict.
Izvestia: Israel continues to hinder efforts to resolve Gaza Strip conflict
The United States has resumed diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict in the Gaza Strip, but Israel continues to hamper attempts to reach an effective settlement. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dismissed US President Donald Trump's proposal that Israeli troops withdraw from the enclave before Hamas fully gives up its arms, Izvestia writes.
The parties remain far apart in their positions, which is why the situation is at an impasse, Middle East expert Alexander Kargin said. According to him, Hamas is unlikely to agree to disarm because doing so would effectively spell the end of the group’s existence. While the Palestinian side continues to depend on US mediation, the White House is unlikely to resolve the deadlock.
Israel, in turn, will never give up its goal of preventing the establishment of a Palestinian state, political scientist Igor Pshenichnikov emphasized.
Meanwhile, Washington’s ambitious reconstruction plans for the region continue to draw strong criticism. The Guardian reports that the United States has no intention of restoring the enclave to its previous state. Journalists obtained the first construction contract signed by the Trump-led Board of Peace with US contractor Arkel International. Rather than financing the construction of homes, schools and hospitals, the first millions of dollars are allegedly set to be spent on a large fortified military base. Rights activists and Palestinian politicians accuse the US administration of lying when it says it is concerned about the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, arguing that its real focus is on militarization and strict security control.
As for the key domestic issue, Kargin points to divisions within Palestinian society stemming from the long-standing rivalry between Hamas and Fatah, the ruling party of the Palestinian Authority. The armed conflict between the two groups, which broke out back in 2006, remains unresolved. The persistent split between Fatah and Hamas is only deepening the situation, depriving Palestinians of unified leadership and reducing their prospects of achieving statehood anytime soon. As a result, the Palestinian people remain caught in a political stalemate, with the large-scale humanitarian disaster being pushed aside by the interests of external players.
Kommersant: Moscow, Damascus reconfigure Russian military presence in Syria
Russia and Syria have signed a memorandum of understanding on restructuring Moscow’s military presence in the Middle Eastern country. According to the document, Russian military bases established under former Syrian President Bashar Assad will be given the status of joint training centers. Experts say the bases have long altered how they operate and that the memorandum removes legal uncertainty surrounding the presence of Russian troops in Syria while retaining the possibility of using the bases as transit hubs on the route to Africa, Kommersant writes.
The Hmeimim facility will now serve as a training center for Syrian service members and will no longer function as a military base, a Syrian source familiar with the situation told the newspaper. According to the source, Hmeimim has effectively been converted into a military training center that Syrian and Russian officers will operate jointly. As for the Tartus facility, it will come fully under the control of the Syrian authorities.
The new agreements reached by Syria and Russia make it clear that both countries are willing to work together and strengthen mutually beneficial ties, the source stressed.
Russian International Affairs Council expert Anton Mardasov said that the bases used by Russian forces had already been partly transformed. "They have long ceased to perform military functions," he explained. "For Russia, the main objective is to continue using the Syrian airfield in Hmeimim as a transit facility on the route to Africa and maintain the conditions needed for a long-term presence," the analyst added.
Mardasov also noted that participating in the training of the new Syrian army would allow Russia "to stay informed about regional developments and offset Turkish influence," which is also in the interest of the government of Syria’s interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Vedomosti: Gold, silver prices climb as central banks boost purchases
Gold and silver prices have risen sharply in recent days. Gold prices increased following the release of US labor market data, as weaker figures lowered expectations of an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve, Vedomosti reports, citing Tsifra Broker.
A dramatic increase in gold purchases by central banks in the second quarter of the year is another factor pushing prices higher. According to the World Gold Council, central banks bought 289 metric tons of gold, five times as much as in the first quarter and the highest level for any second quarter. Record-high gold purchases by individuals, apparently seeking to hedge against risks, are another notable factor, said Dmitry Skryabin, portfolio manager at the Alpha Capital asset management company. Sales of gold bars and coins increased by 42% in the first quarter of 2026.
The rise in gold prices is likely to be a short-lived rather than sustained trend, Nikolay Maslikov, analyst at BCS World of Investments, believes. Macroeconomic factors suggest that gold prices are set to decline, as bond yields in developed countries have risen and interest rates are expected to increase. That said, investors are likely to prefer traditional assets over gold, the expert said.
In the short term, gold prices will largely depend on developments in the Middle East conflict, Skryabin said. If tensions subside, prices are likely to return to levels seen at the beginning of the year. US tariff policy will also play a significant role, he added.
As for silver, its price is highly dependent on global industrial trends, Vasily Danilov, leading analyst at Veles Capital, noted. Given the lower liquidity of the silver market, a rise in gold prices could trigger substantial fluctuations in silver’s value. Therefore, silver is likely to track the trend in gold in the short and medium term, the analyst said.
A supply deficit has persisted in the global silver market for a sixth consecutive year amid strong demand for bars and coins and tighter availability. Finam analyst Nikolay Dudchenko expects silver prices to continue rising under the baseline scenario.
Vedomosti: Russia’s Supreme Court excludes Yabloko party list from parliamentary elections
The electoral list of Russia’s Yabloko party, which has been participating in parliamentary elections since 1993, is apparently out of the race for seats in the ninth State Duma, the lower house of parliament, following a Supreme Court ruling on a claim filed by the Rodina party, Vedomosti reports.
Rodina’s claim was largely based on violations of intellectual property laws. A member of the Central Election Commission also pointed to alleged foreign funding received by Yabloko, citing data from the federal financial watchdog.
Meanwhile, the revocation of the federal electoral list’s registration does not mean that Yabloko’s single-mandate candidates will automatically be excluded from the elections, a party member told the newspaper. Indeed, Rodina’s claim concerned only Yabloko’s federal list and did not cover single-mandate candidates, electoral lawyer Garegin Mitin pointed out. Yabloko’s candidates will therefore continue campaigning, lawyer Maxim Sikach said.
If the Supreme Court’s ruling takes effect, Yabloko will miss out on a second consecutive nationwide election campaign, as the party did not nominate a candidate in the 2024 Russian presidential election. However, it will not face a formal threat of liquidation over non-participation in elections in the near future, lawyer Oleg Zakharov noted. Under the law, elections at any level, not just federal campaigns, are taken into account in this regard.
The last time Yabloko had a faction in the State Duma was in 1999-2003. The party has failed to pass the electoral threshold since then. The question now is how voters will respond. The first emotional reaction among those who planned to vote for Yabloko would be to stay away from the polls now that the party has been removed from the race, political scientist Konstantin Kalachev said. "Later, everything will depend on the New People party, which these voters may consider the second-best option. New People will either succeed in finding convincing arguments to attract them or fail to do so," the expert said.
Much will also depend on the position the party adopts. No specific decisions have been announced yet, as Yabloko plans to appeal the court ruling.

More Than One Third of U.S. Counties Are Maternity Care Deserts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In the last eight years, women living in counties in one-third of the country have faced an abysmal reality: they live in a maternity care desert, which means a place where there are no hospitals or birth centers or even any obstetric clinicians.
That reality has persisted: in its new 2026 report on women’s access to ob-gyn services, released on August 11, the March of Dimes found that 34.6% of U.S. counties are maternity care deserts, and that more than half of U.S. counties lack a hospital with labor and delivery services. That’s relatively unchanged since 2016, the report found.
But the situation is likely to soon get even worse, experts say.
H.R. 1, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed into law on July 4, 2025, is expected to dramatically cut payments to Medicaid as well as introduce burdens that make it more difficult for people to stay on Medicaid. Medicaid already reimburses hospitals at a lower rate than services cost; on average, Medicaid paid hospitals $8,732 less for childbirth services than did employer-sponsored health plans, one 2022 study found.
Meanwhile, the expiration of subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans have led to more uninsured patients visiting emergency rooms, challenging some hospitals’ financial status.
“It is going to be very challenging for rural hospitals to remain viable,” says Dr. Michael Warren, chief medical officer of the March of Dimes. “That is going to further exacerbate the patterns that we're already seeing, where these maternity care deserts tend to be concentrated in rural communities.”
Why maternity care deserts happen
A 2025 analysis from the National Partnership for Women and Families found that 131 rural hospitals across the country with labor and delivery units were at risk of closure or severe service cutbacks because of H.R. 1.
Maternity care deserts happen because of a few factors. Ob-gyn services often lose money for hospitals because they have to be staffed with medical providers, including anesthesiologists, around the clock. In rural areas with low birth rates, hospitals have to spend the money to keep obstetric units staffed and open, even when there are relatively few births generating revenue. And because rural areas have high shares of patients on Medicaid, the hospitals also don’t receive adequate reimbursement.
“It’s sort of a double whammy,” Warren says. “Their birth volume is low, so they have fewer folks coming through to make those payments, but also, when they do get those payments, it's likely to be lower because it's more likely to be Medicaid.”
Maternal care deserts aren’t just in rural areas. Some urban and suburban hospitals have also had to close their labor and delivery units because of cost or because they can’t find enough staff.
Those staffing shortages are also expected to increase. Today, the majority of rural counties—57.9%—lack a practicing obstetric clinician, the March of Dimes found. But by 2035, all but six states are projected to have an inadequate supply of obstetric clinicians, according to a recent study that used data from the Health Resources & Services Administration.
Maternity care deserts lead to worse outcomes for both mother and baby, Warren says. When women have to travel further to receive care, they often miss prenatal appointments, which means problems may not be diagnosed in time. They sometimes have to skip postpartum appointments, even though the majority of pregnancy-related deaths occur postpartum, he adds.
Having to drive farther to deliver a baby means that women with dangerous pregnancies may not get care until it’s too late. Some bleeding episodes in pregnancy have to be addressed quickly, says Dr. Lisa Bukovac, chief clinical officer at OB Hospitalist Group, which partners with hospitals to help deliver babies.
“In obstetrics and all specialties,” she says, “minutes count.”
