Congo’s Ebola outbreak surpasses 2,000 deaths as cases surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:07:24 UTC
18:07:24 KST

More than 2,000 people have died among confirmed cases in Congo’s Ebola outbreak, which is spreading at the fastest pace recorded in the country, according to government data released Tuesday.
The outbreak has recorded 4,381 confirmed cases and 2,011 deaths, while 704 patients are hospitalized or in isolation. The figures come less than three months after authorities declared the outbreak May 15.
The pace of deaths has accelerated sharply. It took about nine weeks for the outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths, but only about three additional weeks to record another 1,000, highlighting the difficulties health workers face reaching remote communities and containing transmission.
The outbreak is being caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a relatively rare species of ebolavirus for which there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said Monday that genomic and epidemiological evidence indicates the virus began circulating in February, months before authorities detected it.
The outbreak is centered largely in Ituri province, with cases also reported in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces.
Bundibugyo virus was first identified during an outbreak in western Uganda in 2007 and was later detected in Congo in 2012. The current outbreak is only the third known Bundibugyo outbreak and by far the largest.
Unlike the Zaire ebolavirus, which has caused most major Ebola outbreaks and is targeted by licensed vaccines and treatments, Bundibugyo has no approved vaccine or specific antiviral treatment.
Doctors therefore rely largely on supportive care, including managing dehydration, treating complications, isolating patients and preventing further transmission.
The fatality rate among confirmed cases has risen into the mid-40% range in some reports, reflecting delayed detection, late presentation for treatment and a significant number of people dying in their communities before receiving medical care.
Eastern Congo has endured decades of armed conflict, population displacement and weak health infrastructure, making the region particularly difficult for disease-control teams to reach.
Poor roads, insecurity and disruptions to supply routes have slowed the movement of health workers, medical supplies and laboratory samples. Some communities are also wary of health authorities and international responders because of past violence against health workers and mistrust surrounding previous Ebola campaigns.
Those concerns have complicated contact tracing, safe burials and efforts to persuade people with symptoms to seek treatment.
A significant proportion of new cases have been identified among people who were not previously listed as contacts of known patients, making transmission chains harder to track. Many patients have also died in their communities rather than treatment centers, reducing opportunities for early diagnosis and infection control.
Congolese authorities have expanded the response with support from the WHO, Africa CDC, Medecins Sans Frontieres and other partners.
Teams have increased laboratory testing, expanded treatment capacity, intensified contact tracing and strengthened infection prevention measures. Officials are also working to improve diagnostic systems capable of detecting different Ebola species and to expand testing closer to affected communities.
WHO and Africa CDC have called for faster delivery of funding and medical resources, while stressing that community involvement will be critical to controlling the outbreak.
Uganda also recorded a smaller outbreak linked to the situation in Congo, with about 20 confirmed cases and two deaths. Authorities declared it over in late July after 42 days without a new case, although border monitoring continues.
The current outbreak is Congo’s 17th since Ebola was first identified in 1976 near the Ebola River.
It has surpassed the country's previous largest outbreak, which struck North Kivu and Ituri between 2018 and 2020 and recorded about 3,470 cases and more than 2,200 deaths.
It is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded globally, behind the 2013-16 West Africa epidemic that caused more than 28,000 cases and over 11,000 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Scientists believe the current Bundibugyo outbreak represents a distinct zoonotic spillover event, underscoring the continuing risk of new Ebola strains emerging in areas where people have close contact with wildlife.
Despite the growing toll, health authorities say the risk of sustained international transmission remains low because Ebola is primarily spread through direct contact with infected bodily fluids rather than through the air.

Burnham vows to resolve ‘long-running injustice’ of indefinite prison sentences in boost for thousands of inmates
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:06:50 BST
18:06:50 KST

Burnham vows to resolve ‘long-running injustice’ of indefinite prison sentences in boost for thousands of inmates
Addressing the scandal of Imprisonment for Public Protection jail terms could free up thousands of prison spaces
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The prime minister has vowed to resolve the “long-running injustice” of indefinite jail terms as part of measures to ease prison overcrowding and stop PC Andrew Harper’s killers from being freed early.
Andy Burnham said he is “increasingly confident” that he can find a way to free up prison cells, which will allow him to curb the early release of some offenders such as the police officer’s killers.
Options being considered include the release of “lower risk” prisoners serving Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) jail terms, he said on Tuesday. The comments offer fresh hope for prisoners trapped on the open-ended sentences which were outlawed in 2012.
The Independent has long campaigned for the unjust jail terms - which have left thousands languishing without hope of release - to be reviewed.
In a statement issued on Facebook, he said he has asked justice secretary Alex Norris to fast-track a plan to create more headroom in the prison estate.
The plan will be based “on a range of options”, Mr Burnham said, including “increasing the rate of removal of foreign national offenders from the prison estate to their country of origin; finding an early resolution to the long-running injustice of IPP sentences, which could allow for the release of lower-risk prisoners; and making greater use of the entire prison estate including using the female estate for male offenders”.
He continued: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether.”
The development comes as the government faces legal action over the jail terms after the United Nations found Britain is unlawfully detaining a number of over-tariff IPP prisoners in a scathing legal opinion issued last month.
The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Britain to urgently act in relation to five men handed the jail terms, warning their imprisonment long beyond their original tariff amounts to arbitrary detention under international human rights law and they are entitled to compensation.
Separately, the UN special rapporteur on torture has accused the government of perpetuating human rights abuses and warned the jail term may amount to psychological torture.
Lawyers yesterday sent the justice secretary a letter before action as they prepare to submit a rare habeas corpus legal challenge to the High Court, which will force the government to justify the prisoners' continued incarceration to senior judges.
Human rights lawyer Karen Todner said UN’s findings have rendered the IPP jail term “indefensible”, adding: “It’s hugely significant and very damning for the UK government to receive such a condemnation of our justice system.”
The open-ended punishments were scrapped in 2012, but not retrospectively, leaving thousands languishing in prison without a release date for years beyond their tariff, including some for minor crimes. Once released, many find themselves trapped in a cycle of indefinite recall for minor breaches of strict licence conditions.
The architect of the flawed sentence, Lord David Blunkett, has since admitted that ushering in the draconian punishments under Tony Blair’s Labour government is his “biggest regret”.
In 2022, the cross-party justice committee inquiry found the sentences were “irredeemably flawed” and called for all IPP prisoners to be resentenced. Despite 96 people taking their own lives in custody after losing hope of release, successive governments have so far refused.
Four of the five cases condemned by the UN are still incarcerated, including Leroy Douglas, who has served almost 20 years without release for street robbery of a mobile phone; Abdullahi Suleman, who is still in custody 20 years after he was handed an IPP for a laptop robbery; Wayne Williams, who has spent more than 19 years in prison without release for a 23-month jail term for attempting to injure a police officer in a fight; and Shaun Lloyd, 39, who was recently hauled back to prison for the fifth time, having served more than 12 years for two street robberies.
Sadly, Joshua Mcrae, died in prison aged 34, having served more than 16 years for a four-year tariff for grievous bodily harm.
They are among almost 2,300 people still in prison on the controversial jail terms.
This week the chair of the Criminal Cases Review Commission, Dame Vera Baird, joined calls for the government to take “wholesale” action to address the scandal. Judges have recently quashed a string of indefinite sentences handed to children and young men and the CCRC is reviewing hundreds more.
Following Mr Burnham’s comments, Dame Vera, who is also a former victims’ commissioner, said debate around the early release scheme had brought an urgency to solving the problem.
“We are harming a lot of people with a leftover that international human rights institutions have condemned as torture,” she told The Independent.
“The CCRC is working as fast as possible to send cases to the Court of Appeal following some recent hopeful precedents from them, but, as multiple agencies have said, the way to grip the issue is to embark on a re-sentencing exercise. I imagine the complexities of working that through have played a role in deterring ministers.
“However, given the problems in the early release scheme, there are now two reasons to tackle IPP's, since many people are likely to be freed, creating much needed space in the prison system.”
Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti, the former director of Liberty, added: “It is extremely positive to see a prime minister personally trying to grip our long-term prison crisis. The scandal of IPP prisoners in particular- still taking up prison places long after they should have been released based on the seriousness of their offending, is one that should be urgently ended.”

Ukrainian firm tests mobile version of its acoustic drone detector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:05:02 UTC
18:05:02 KST

- Ukrainian company Zvook mounted its passive acoustic early warning sensors on a moving vehicle for the first time during NATO's BATT26 exercise in Latvia.
- The test, conducted with the Latvian National Armed Forces, moved beyond Zvook's standard deployment on fixed infrastructure like telecom towers.
A Ukrainian company that built its drone-detection network by listening for the sound of incoming Shahed attack drones has tried something its own engineers had never planned for, and it worked well enough to change how the technology might be deployed across NATO’s eastern flank.
Zvook, a Ukrainian defense and space manufacturing company headquartered in Lviv, announced that during NATO’s BATT26 exercise it mounted its passive acoustic early warning sensors on a moving vehicle for the first time, working alongside the Latvian National Armed Forces to test whether a detection system built for fixed installations like telecom towers could function just as well rolling down a road.
Zvook’s technology works by listening rather than transmitting, a passive detection method that identifies drones through the distinctive sound signatures their motors and propellers produce rather than emitting a radar signal that could reveal a defender’s position to an enemy equipped with anti-radiation weapons. That approach has made the system one of the more closely watched pieces of Ukraine’s homegrown air defense infrastructure since the company’s sensors first went operational on Ukrainian frontlines in 2022, and Zvook has continued refining the technology throughout the war, including a compact tactical version specifically tuned to detect fiber-optic FPV drones, the small, first-person-view attack aircraft that have become a defining weapon of the conflict and are notoriously difficult for radio-frequency detection methods to catch.
Company representatives described the BATT26 experiment as a case study in how real defense innovation actually happens, framing the challenge not as a failure to plan properly but as an opportunity created by unplanned circumstances during a multinational exercise where several different systems had to work together inside a shared operational environment.
“Innovation doesn’t always begin in a laboratory. Sometimes it begins in the field. During BATT26, one challenge reminded us what defence innovation is really about. Multiple systems were being integrated into a shared operational environment. As often happens during experimentation, not everything worked exactly as originally planned. Instead of waiting for the ‘perfect’ solution, engineers, military personnel, and partners gathered around one simple question: How do we accomplish the mission?” the company said.
The company was candid that the mobile deployment did not perform flawlessly on its first attempt, describing the outcome as promising rather than polished.
“Together with the Latvian National Armed Forces, our team explored a different approach. For the first time, Zvook’s passive acoustic early warning sensors were mounted on a moving vehicle, something beyond our standard deployment concept, where sensors are typically installed on fixed infrastructure such as telecom towers or other permanent locations. It wasn’t part of the original plan. That is exactly why experimentation exists. The result? It worked. Not perfectly, there were challenges, valuable lessons, and improvements to identify. But the concept proved itself under operational conditions, opening new possibilities for future mobile deployments,” the company said.
Zvook’s core network inside Ukraine relies on sensors mounted permanently on radio towers and similar infrastructure at heights of roughly 10 to 12 meters (33 to 39 feet), positioned strategically near entry points along Ukraine’s border with Russia to catch incoming Shahed drones, cruise missiles and low-flying aircraft before they reach populated areas or critical infrastructure. That fixed network reportedly feeds detections into Ukraine’s Delta situational awareness system within about 12 seconds, giving mobile anti-aircraft teams equipped with tablets enough warning to intercept threats while they are still at range. A vehicle-mounted version of that same detection capability would open up an entirely different category of use, allowing a military to extend acoustic drone detection to convoys, mobile command posts, or rapidly repositioned units in a way that permanently installed towers simply cannot support, a capability with obvious relevance for NATO forces operating along a border where drone incursions have become a persistent, evolving threat rather than an occasional nuisance.
The company previously demonstrated its passive acoustic system at the Dronetex launch event at Odense Airport in Denmark, where it joined a coalition of European and Ukrainian defense firms, including DefSecIntel Solutions, Weibel Scientific, TYTAN Technologies and Marduk Technologies, to showcase how multiple combat-tested detection and counter-drone systems could operate together as an integrated architecture rather than as isolated products competing separately for the same procurement budgets. That earlier demonstration, and this latest experiment in Latvia, both reflect a broader pattern of Ukrainian defense companies using NATO exercises and multinational trials as a proving ground, seeking to translate battlefield-tested technology developed under wartime pressure into systems allied militaries are willing to adopt during peacetime procurement cycles that typically move far slower than Ukraine’s own innovation pace has demanded.
Zvook credited the Latvian Armed Forces and the BATT26 organizers directly for making the unplanned experiment possible, closing its announcement with a broader argument about how the company believes defense innovation should actually work going forward.
“A sincere thank you to the Latvian Armed Forces, the BATT26 organizers, and all partners who showed what true collaboration looks like. Because the future of defence will not be built by individual companies. It will be built by people who trust each other, solve problems together, and are willing to test what has never been tested before,” the company said.

우크라이나가 국경에서 1천∼2천㎞ 떨어진 러시아 후방의 정유시설을 잇달아 타격하며 러시아 에너지 공급망을 겨냥한 공격을 이어가고 있다.
이 지역은 우크라이나 국경에서 약 2천200㎞ 떨어진 곳이다.
전날 우크라이나의 드론 공격을 받아 대규모 사상자가 발생한 타타르공화국 니즈네캄스크도 국경에서 1천200㎞ 떨어진 에너지 거점이다.
전체 내용을 이해하기 위해서는 기사 본문과 함께 읽어야 합니다.
송고 2026년08월11일 18시05분
구글 검색에서 연합뉴스 기사를 우선적으로 보여줍니다.
(로마·이스탄불=연합뉴스) 민경락 김동호 특파원 = 우크라이나가 국경에서 1천∼2천㎞ 떨어진 러시아 후방의 정유시설을 잇달아 타격하며 러시아 에너지 공급망을 겨냥한 공격을 이어가고 있다.
11일(현지시간) 현지 매체 키이우인디펜던트에 따르면 우크라이나군 총참모부는 전날 러시아 튜멘주 토볼스크의 석유 화학공장을 공격했다고 밝혔다.
전날 우크라이나의 드론 공격을 받아 대규모 사상자가 발생한 타타르공화국 니즈네캄스크도 국경에서 1천200㎞ 떨어진 에너지 거점이다. 이곳에는 정유공장 2곳과 석유화학 공장 등이 밀집한 것으로 전해졌다.
러시아 에너지 시설의 화재가 최근 극동 지역에서도 발생했다는 증언도 나왔다.
키이우인디펜던트는 이날 개인 텔레그램 채널을 인용해 우크라이나 국경에서 6천㎞ 이상 떨어진 극동 하바롭스크 지역의 콤소몰스크나아무레 정유공장에서 불이 났다고 보도했다. 국경에서 4천300㎞ 떨어진 이르쿠츠크 지역 안가르스크의 한 발전소에서도 화재가 발생한 것으로 전해졌다.
다만 이들 지역에서 발생한 화재가 우크라이나의 공격 때문인지는 확인되지 않았다. 국경과의 거리 등을 고려하면 단순 사고이거나 사보타주(파괴 공작) 가능성도 배제할 수 없다.
러시아는 우크라이나 도심을 겨냥한 공격을 계속했다.
우크라이나 지역 당국에 따르면 밤새 키이우, 자포리자, 드니프로페트로우스크 등이 공격받아 9명이 숨지고 22명이 다쳤다. 볼로디미르 젤렌스키 우크라이나 대통령은 러시아가 이날 북한산 미사일을 사용했다고 주장했다.

Kanyshai Butun
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) on Tuesday claimed the European Union plans to restrict funding for the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and other sports organizations that allow Russian athletes to compete, state-run Tass news agency reported.
“The European Union is prepared to do anything to prevent Russia’s return to international sport,” the SVR said in a statement.
The agency said European officials were “extremely concerned” about the IOC’s decision to lift sanctions against the Russian Olympic Committee and Russian athletes, particularly over the prospect of Russian athletes competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics under their national flag and anthem.
"In Brussels and the capitals of EU states, there are complaints that this move by the IOC effectively negates the West's long-standing efforts to 'isolate' our country from global sport," the statement said.
The IOC provisionally lifted the Russian Olympic Committee's (ROC) suspension on July 7, saying its Executive Board had determined that the committee no longer included regional sports organizations in territories under the jurisdiction of Ukraine’s National Olympic Committee.
Ukraine, in response, said that it had filed an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport challenging the IOC’s decision to provisionally lift the ROC’s suspension.
Ukraine's National Olympic Committee said the IOC acted prematurely and without properly verifying whether the violations that led to the ROC's suspension in 2023 had been resolved.
The IOC recommended that Belarusian and Russian athletes be barred from international competitions in late February 2022, days after the start of the Russia-Ukraine war.
It recommended in March 2023 that athletes from both countries enter international competitions as Individual Neutral Athletes, while stating that those "who actively support the war cannot compete."
On May 7, the IOC Executive Board said it no longer recommended restrictions on Belarusian athletes or teams in events governed by international federations and organizers, lifting its previous participation conditions.

Europe Runs Short of Patriot Missiles as Ukraine Braces for Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:01:48 UTC
18:01:48 KST

European countries are struggling to provide Ukraine with enough Patriot interceptors as Kyiv prepares for an expected Russian winter assault, with US supplies strained and new production unlikely to arrive before the attacks begin, Politico reported.
According to Politico on Tuesday, Ukraine is seeking hundreds of interceptors for its ballistic missile defenses, but several of its leading European supporters say they have limited stocks available, while also needing to protect their own territory and meet NATO commitments.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are literally fighting for every missile,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Ukraine relies heavily on US-made Patriot systems to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, one of the few weapons in its arsenal capable of countering the threat.
In July, Ukrainian air defenses intercepted just 29 of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, while another 40 reportedly failed to reach their targets, according to Ukraine’s defense ministry.
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Russia was firing more missiles at Ukraine each week than its partners were providing over several months.
Ukraine is also developing the domestically produced Freyja interceptor, but the system still requires investment, engineering work, and testing before it can provide a significant alternative to Patriot.
Most PAC-3 Patriot interceptors are manufactured in the US, making Washington central to Ukraine’s efforts to replenish its stocks.
US ‘Doing Its Homework’ On Risks of Ukraine Patriot Interceptor Production
US President Donald Trump previously raised hopes that Ukraine could eventually produce Patriot interceptors under license. But US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said a long-term production agreement would not be completed before winter, with manufacturing taking even longer.
Trump subsequently walked back the proposal.
“We have not agreed to that. We’re talking about it. But it’s a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology,” Trump said last week.
The situation has been further complicated by the war in Iran, which has strained US missile stocks as Washington works to replenish its own supplies.
Trump has also pushed back against calls for additional Patriot missiles for Ukraine.
“We want missiles too,” he said.
Germany has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine but is now facing pressure to preserve enough equipment to defend its own territory and fulfill NATO commitments.
“We are really reaching our limits here,” German Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl said. “We also have to ensure our own protection.”
Norway’s Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik said European countries need to contribute more but acknowledged that the current effort is difficult to sustain.
“I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Sandvik told Politico. “All the European countries have to step up.”
Poland, Spain, and Greece are now among the countries being pressed to examine whether they can provide additional Patriot interceptors.
Poland confirmed in July that it had transferred several PAC-3 interceptors following requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior US commanders. Polish outlet Defence24 reported that only five missiles were transferred.
Greece has not announced any Patriot transfers to Ukraine, although Greek media reported in July that Kyiv had requested as many as 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens.
Spain has previously confirmed sending Patriot missiles to Ukraine but has not disclosed how many or which variants were transferred.
Both countries are now facing questions over whether they can provide additional interceptors without weakening their own defenses.
Countries closer to Russia are particularly reluctant to give up existing Patriot stocks, with their militaries already considering air defenses insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat cited by Politico.
Ukraine continues to negotiate with European allies to find additional interceptors.
Fedorov recalled working with Rutte and European defense ministers to identify missiles that could be transferred to Ukraine.
Germany previously offered to provide additional interceptors if other European countries collectively contributed more.
But Ukrainian officials say the shortage remains severe.
“The American administration could have helped, but they don’t do this. And as the result it’s been hard with everyone else,” a senior Ukrainian official familiar with the talks told Politico.
With Russia expected to intensify its attacks during winter and demand for Patriot interceptors rising elsewhere, Ukraine faces an increasingly narrow window to replenish its defenses before the next major wave of Russian missile strikes.

Congo Ebola death toll tops 2,000 in fastest spreading outbreak on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

Congo Ebola death toll tops 2,000 as outbreak becomes fastest spreading on record
Bunia, Congo — At least 2,000 people have died among the confirmed cases in Congo's Ebola outbreak that is the fastest-spreading on record, according to the latest government data, as health authorities struggle to get help quickly to remote localities due to rebel conflict, bad roads and work stoppages over payment issues.
Data published overnight into Tuesday showed the outbreak has recorded a total of 4,381 confirmed cases, including 2,011 deaths.
The grim toll comes nearly three months since the outbreak was declared on May 15. While it took about nine weeks for the outbreak to record 1,000 deaths, it's taken just around three weeks to record the additional 1,000 deaths, showing how fast the health crisis is moving beyond the control of responders.
It's already the second-largest outbreak in history, only behind the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak that recorded more than 28,000 cases including over 11,000 deaths.
The World Health Organization has declared the outbreak, which has also led to cases in neighboring Uganda, a public health emergency of international concern.
Aid workers say the outbreak continues to outpace the response that's been expanding across the five provinces affected. Many health workers have gone on strike to protest not being paid for their work since the outbreak was declared. And most new cases are recorded outside of contacts that are being monitored.
The Ebola outbreak is unlike most previous ones because the rare Bundibugyo virus responsible for it has no approved vaccines or treatments. Clinical trials for those have begun in Ituri, the epicenter of the outbreak.
The WHO said on Monday that the outbreak likely started in February, long before authorities detected it in one of Congo's most remote and vulnerable areas. WHO said some cases early on were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid, and that early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola.
The WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, told a news conference that officials are "chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us."
The first Ebola virus to be identified was in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now Congo. The current outbreak is the 17th — and largest — the Central African nation has faced.

India deploys men pretending to be monkeys to protect Badminton World Championships venue
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:00:27 BST
18:00:27 KST

India deploys men pretending to be monkeys to protect Badminton World Championships venue
Delhi stadium brings in langur mimics to prevent repeat of macaque disruption at India Open earlier this year
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Indian organisers of the Badminton World Championships have hired three men trained to mimic langur calls to scare away monkeys in an attempt to secure the tournament against embarrassing disruptions.
The unusual measure was compelled by disruptions at the India Open earlier this year when a monkey was spotted in the stands and the practice hall at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in the capital Delhi. Players and spectators photographed and filmed the animal, embarrassing the organisers on the world stage. The India Open, an annual badminton event, was also disrupted by pigeons leaving droppings on the court and the practice areas.
The stadium, where the BWF World Championships 2026 begin on 17 August, has since been overhauled to keep animals and birds out. Its ventilator openings have been covered and broken windows sealed, and double doors have been installed at all the 16 entrances to the inner hall.
An anti-pest gel has been applied to air-conditioning pipes to stop pigeons from roosting, the Indian Express reported. A patented US-made device that emits sounds to deter and repel birds will also be deployed at the venue.
Alongside these measures, three men have been tasked with mimicking langur calls to scare away any monkeys.
“It’s not just me. There are two other guys with me,” one langur-mimic identified by the local media as Jabbar said on Monday.
“When we make these calls, monkeys just run away. We also ensure monkeys don’t run into people or cars, etc. We time the mimicking accordingly. This vocal method is quite effective.”
“Getting employment is not consistent, but we do keep getting work from time to time. There are many of us who do it,” he was quoted as saying by the Hindustan Times.
For years, trained grey langurs were used to deter monkeys in public spaces because rhesus macaques were known to fear them. The practice was discontinued after the species was listed under the Wildlife Protection Act, banning people from keeping them captive, owning them privately or hiring them for guard duties.
Langurs were deployed during the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi. At the G20 Summit in 2023, however, organisers used trained mimics to make langur calls and installed life-size langur cut-outs to deter macaques.
“Monkeys are absolutely terrified of langurs, which is why mimicking is so effective,” a second mimic, identified as Zafar, was quoted as saying by Reuters. “I have served in several government offices and the idea is not to harm the monkeys, but just to make sure they won’t come.”
Mr Jabbar told the Indian Express his mimicry skill had been passed down through generations in his family. “I learnt it from my father, but don’t want my son to do it,” he said.
Star Indian badminton player and former world champion PV Sindhu responded positively to the hiring of langur mimics. “You can laugh at the solution, but you have to love the effort,” she posted online.
“So many people are working behind the scenes to make sure India is ready to welcome the world. Our solutions may be uniquely Indian, but so are our warmth, our spirit and our hospitality,” she said.
Sanjay Mishra, general secretary of the Badminton Association of India, told Sportstar officials had also identified problems with the stadium lighting during the previous tournament and upgraded the system ahead of the World Championships.
The wider refurbishment includes renovation of 2,500 seats and 57 of the stadium complex’s 66 toilets, according to Ambar Pratap Singh, executive director of the Sports Authority of India.
India is hosting the World Championships for the second time. It previously organised the tournament in 2009 in Hyderabad’s Gachibowli Indoor Stadium. After the India Open faced criticism, the country’s ability to hold an event as prestigious as the BWF World Championships was under major scrutiny.
The tournament will see participation by top players such as Shi Yu Qi, Akane Yamaguchi, Kim Won Ho and Seo Seung Jae, Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning, and Chen Tang Jie and Toh Ee Wei. PV Sindhu, Lakshya Sen, and the doubles pair Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty are representing the host country.

MPs shouldn’t face abuse. Neither should their staff – but here’s what we deal with every day | Estelle Warhurst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:00:09 UTC
18:00:09 KST

Before most people have finished their morning coffee, an MP’s staffer might have already dealt with a suicidal caller, a victim of domestic abuse or a threat of violence. We’ve been yelled at, cried at and sometimes even physically attacked, all in the course of managing a heavy caseload of constituents’ most intractable problems. So, when I read the results of the latest survey by the wellness working group (WWG) I was not surprised to learn that half of us are experiencing clinical levels of psychological distress.
Psychological distress is a range of emotional or cognitive suffering, such as anxiety or depression, that impairs a person’s ability to cope with ordinary daily life and functioning. It makes you wonder why urgent action is not in place to support these staff members, who are holding together the day-to-day functioning of democracy as well as supporting constituents throughout the UK.
As the office manager for the Labour MP for Preston, and an executive committee member for the WWG, I encounter this distress every day. In an MP’s email inbox are images that no one should see. These include murdered children, flayed animals, nude images and graphic pictures of war zones, all sent by constituents to try to strengthen their points or illustrate the reality of the situations they face. While photos are often triggering, so is some written communication from constituents who urgently need their MP’s help. Vivid descriptions of child abuse, domestic violence, physical ill health or the thoughts of people who are severely mentally ill or suicidal take a huge toll. The reality is that usually it is not the MP who opens these communications but a member of staff in their constituency or parliamentary office – often an office manager, sometimes a junior colleague who has just left university and hasn’t received any training at all. These teams also receive the racist or sexist language and the rape and death threats that are levelled at some members of parliament.
Sometimes these communications are sent directly to the staff themselves, or staff are abused personally on social media. In my role at the WWG I speak weekly to colleagues who have been physically attacked, doxed (sharing someone’s person data online) and stalked. One told me how she lived in a small village, where a constituent found her address and knocked on her door to shout abuse at her. We all remember our colleague Andrew Pennington, who was killed in 2000 while protecting the MP he worked for from a constituent with a sword. This kind of abuse seems to be increasing, yet support and protection for staff has not kept pace. It’s little wonder that we are overwhelmed and at breaking point. A third of staff are considering leaving their jobs.
Staff members are now at their lowest psychological point since the WWG began the survey in 2000, including the year of the pandemic – and I think that’s because the nature of the work is changing. The pressure for MPs and their staff to be always on is increasing with the expectation by some constituents that we should respond immediately to their emails and posts on social media. What many people do not understand is that an MP is supported by a very small number of staff and that each year our casework is increasing, both in volume and complexity. This has resulted in some offices having hundreds of emails backlogged. Staff are fighting to reassure people for whom we are struggling to find solutions. Obviously to each constituent, theirs is the most important case, but offices have to triage. Is there an immediate threat of death, destitution or disaster? These cases must be brought to the fore, pushing others further back in the never-ending list of work to be done.
The survey too points to how many staff are working until late at night, logging on early in the morning and not taking lunch breaks, or their annual leave, to try to get on top of the workload. I know of staff who go into their offices at weekends to check the answerphone to see if their vulnerable constituent is still alive, and those who buy weekly shopping and deliver it to constituents who don’t receive any other support. Inappropriate? Most of us do this work because we care, we want to help people and we find it hard to see others in extreme distress.
Contrary to popular opinion, the vast majority of members of parliament are honest, decent people who come into public service because they also care and want to make the country a better place. They care about their constituents and hire people who want to help them. However, like any large group of people, there are always a few who don’t have the right intentions. Some of those few expect their staff to work all hours and a small percentage expect their staff to work in unsanitary conditions, without running water or even toilet roll.
In response to the annual survey the WWG provides a series of recommendations, and this year they are more urgent than ever. The House of Commons should mandate specific training for staff, taking the decision for this out of the hands of the individual MPs who employ us. This would equip them with the skills to help constituents, and to protect themselves mentally and physically. Similarly, the House should make its recommended safety measures mandatory in all MPs’ offices – these include providing alarms and security counters, and ensuring that all surgeries are by pre-booked appointment only. The House of Commons has a duty of care to the staff who work in MPs offices – it should ensure that basic security measures are provided as a standard minimum requirement away from the parliamentary estate.
If we expect MPs’ staff to absorb trauma, safeguard vulnerable people and keep constituency services functioning, then we also have a duty to equip and protect them. If we do not do this, the public ultimately feels the consequences, and we further erode faith in democracy.
- 
  Estelle Warhurst is the office manager for a Labour MP and an executive committee member for the parliamentary wellness working group

7 best coat stands and racks 2026, tested by an interiors editor
From traditional designs to modern takes on the classic, clothes racks are back in vogue

A great coat stand is more than just a place to hang your jacket – it’s a subtle yet essential piece that helps keep your home tidy and stylish. After all, your hallway is the first area you and your guests see, setting the tone for the rest of your space.
Whether you're aiming for sleek and modern or classic and functional, the right coat stand can transform your entrance from cluttered to curated. But with so many styles and materials to choose from, finding the perfect fit can be a challenge.
As an interiors expert, there are a few things I consider when investing in a coat stand. Do I want something slim and subtle – perfect for a tight hallway – or a more robust, statement-making piece? Perhaps you’ve got a minimalist look in mind, with clean lines and neutral tones, or maybe you’re after a bit of retro charm that leans into design nostalgia while still being practical. - Durability: To find the best coat stands, I assessed each piece for stability and durability, testing them with multiple coats, hats, and umbrellas. I looked for designs that would stand the test of time and hold strong under the weight of heavy items.

Ukrainian strikes kill 43 civilians, including four children, over past week — diplomat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:58:19 UTC
17:58:19 KST

LUGANSK, August 11. /TASS/. Almost 380 civilians, including 24 children, were injured in attacks launched by the Ukrainian army in the past week, while 43 people, including four children, died, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told TASS.
"Over the past week, attacks by Ukrainian Nazis affected 419 civilians – 376 people, including 24 minors, were wounded, and 43 more, with four children among them, were killed. <...> Most casualties among civilians have been reported in Kiev’s attacks on the Belgorod and Krasnodar Regions, the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), the Zaporozhye and Kherson Regions," he said.
Miroshnik added that 95% of those affected by strikes – 399 people – sustained injuries in Ukrainian combat drone attacks. The Ukrainian army fired almost 7,100 different rounds of ammunition at targets in Russia over the past week.
According to Miroshnik, the enemy carried out a series of attacks on medical facilities and vehicles in violation of international humanitarian law.
"Civilians were injured in a deliberate Ukrainian drone attack on City Clinical Hospital No. 7 in the Kievsky District of Donetsk. <...> A 78-year-old woman died after sustaining injuries. Another two patients were seriously wounded. <...> In the Novaya Mayachka settlement of the Alyoshki District of the Kherson Region, a Ukrainian FPV drone hit an ambulance that was heading to help a patient suffering from a heart attack. As a result of the explosion, a driver and a paramedic were injured, while the patient died as medical professionals could not reach him in time," he said.
Moreover, Ukrainian forces continued to remotely mine Russian regions. In the Troshino settlement of the Kursk Region, a 72-year-old pensioner died and a driver was wounded after their car struck a mine. Another man was injured in the Krasny Oktyabr village in the Belgorod Region. "In the Zaporozhye Region, the Ukrainian military regularly employs drones to mine roads leading to Energodar, as well as those used by staff of the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP). In the past week, as many as four ZNPP employees suffered injuries after triggering mines that had been laid remotely," the diplomat added.

Syrian court sentences Bashar Assad to death in absentia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:57:55 UTC
17:57:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Bashar Assad, eight others sentenced to death in landmark Syria trial
A Syrian court sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad, former security chief Atef Najib and seven other former officials to death on Tuesday over the violent suppression of protests in Daraa at the start of the 2011 uprising.
The Damascus Criminal Court convicted the nine men of offences including intentional killing, torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity.
Najib, who is in Syrian custody, was sentenced in person, while Assad and the remaining defendants were sentenced in absentia.
Those sentenced also included Assad’s brother Maher, former defence minister Fahd Jassem al-Freij, Mohammed Ayman Ayoush, Louay Ali al-Ali, Qusay Ibrahim Mahyoub, Wafiq Saleh Nasser and Talal Fares al-Issami.
The ruling marks the first conviction against Assad since his government was overthrown in December 2024, ending more than five decades of Assad family rule.
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said Assad’s role in the crimes was that of the “highest decision-maker”, accusing him of placing state institutions at the disposal of the crackdown.
The court found Assad guilty of the intentional killing of multiple people, including children, as well as torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity.
Najib, Assad’s maternal cousin and the former head of the Political Security Branch in Daraa, was convicted over his role in the crackdown on protesters in the southern province, where the uprising against Assad’s rule began in 2011.
The judge said investigations and witness testimony showed that Najib had been involved in interrogating detainees after the protests began and had led security operations against civilians in Daraa.
The court also said the Political Security Branch under Najib’s command took part in the storming of the Omari Mosque alongside other security agencies.
Najib was convicted of offences including intentional murder, the killing of children under the age of 15 and torture leading to death.
The court described the acts attributed to him as crimes against humanity and imposed the death penalty.
Najib stood inside a courtroom cage wearing a prison uniform as the sentence was read.
Tuesday’s ruling came during the ninth session of his trial, which began on 26 April before the Fourth Criminal Court at the Damascus Palace of Justice.
The proceedings were among the first public trials of senior figures from the former Assad government under Syria’s new authorities.
Najib’s case was heard in person, while the court formally recorded the absence of Assad and the other defendants who remain fugitives.
During previous hearings, prosecutors had called for the death penalty against Najib, while the court heard witness testimony and examined evidence related to abuses committed during the early stages of the uprising.
The final session was attended by Syria’s public prosecutor, Hassan al-Turba, the head of the National Commission for Transitional Justice, Abdul Basit Abdul Latif, members of the commission, representatives of international legal and humanitarian organisations and relatives of victims.
Najib served as head of the Political Security Branch in Daraa between 2008 and 2011 and became one of the most notorious security officials associated with the government’s response to the first anti-Assad demonstrations.
He was later detained after Assad’s fall, becoming one of the highest-ranking former officials to stand trial before a Syrian court.
Assad and Maher fled Syria after rebel forces entered Damascus in December 2024.
Bashar al-Assad had ruled Syria since 2000, succeeding his father Hafez al-Assad.
His government’s violent response to peaceful protests in 2011 helped trigger a conflict that lasted more than a decade and killed hundreds of thousands of people.

Israeli drone tested near tense Thai-Cambodian border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:57:34 UTC
17:57:34 KST

- Aero Sentinel demonstrated its surveillance drone technology to Thailand's Border Patrol Police near the Cambodian border, according to a social post from CMO Ofir Avram.
- The demonstration, led by chief pilot Or Shabat, tested the drone's performance in complex terrain under GPS-denied conditions.
An Israeli-made surveillance drone has proved it can keep working even when the satellite navigation system it normally relies on gets jammed, a capability that could matter enormously along a border where two neighboring militaries have spent the past year accusing each other of flying hundreds of unauthorized drones overhead.
Aero Sentinel, an Israeli manufacturer of low-observable tactical drones, demonstrated its surveillance technology to Thailand’s Border Patrol Police near the Cambodian border, according to a social post from the company’s chief marketing officer, Ofir Avram.
The demonstration, led by Aero Sentinel’s chief pilot Or Shabat, took place in what the company described as complex terrain under GPS-denied conditions, meaning the drone had to operate without reliable access to the satellite positioning system most aircraft depend on to navigate accurately. GPS-denied environments occur when a signal is deliberately jammed or spoofed by an adversary, or when terrain and infrastructure interfere with satellite reception, and the ability to fly and complete a mission without that signal has become one of the most sought-after capabilities among militaries watching drone warfare evolve in conflicts from Ukraine to the Middle East.
Avram framed the trial as a strong showing for the company’s technology.
“We recently demonstrated by our chief pilot Or Shabat our capabilities to the Thai Border Patrol Police near the Cambodian border, operating in highly complex terrain and under challenging GPS-denied conditions. The demonstration delivered outstanding results, exceeding all expectations and proving our system’s reliability and operational effectiveness where it matters most. Mission accomplished. On to the next destination,” said Avram.
Thailand’s Border Patrol Police, known locally as Tor Chor Dor, is a paramilitary law enforcement agency under the Royal Thai Police that has operated along Thailand’s borders since 1951, historically taking the lead on counterinsurgency, border security and intelligence gathering in remote frontier regions rather than conventional military combat. The agency has a long history of working alongside the Thai military in border security operations, and its personnel are often the first responders in areas where tension flares between Thailand and its neighbors.
That tension has been running hot along the Thai-Cambodian border for more than a year. Fighting between Thai and Cambodian forces killed dozens of people and displaced more than a million residents during clashes that began in mid-2025, rooted in a long-running territorial dispute over the colonial-era demarcation of the roughly 800-kilometer (500-mile) border the two countries share. Even after the countries agreed to a ceasefire, the Royal Thai Army accused Cambodia of violating that truce by flying more than 250 unmanned aerial vehicles over Thai border provinces in a single night, prompting Thailand to impose a temporary nationwide ban on civilian drone flights and step up nightly military patrols in the affected provinces. Thai officials have separately released footage showing their own forces striking what they described as a Cambodian drone control center, underscoring just how central unmanned aircraft have become to the standoff on both sides of the border.
Against that backdrop, a demonstration proving reliable drone performance in GPS-denied conditions carries obvious appeal for a border security force operating in an environment where jamming and interference, whether accidental or deliberate, have become a routine hazard rather than a rare complication. Aero Sentinel has built its commercial reputation specifically around this kind of resilience, and the company has said its systems saw earlier real-world use during Israel’s 2025 military campaign against Iranian targets, where the drones were reportedly employed for sensitive intelligence missions aimed at identifying high-value targets inside adversary territory.
This latest Thailand demonstration lands amid a period of rapid expansion for Aero Sentinel across multiple international markets. The company has signed an exclusive distribution agreement with the German firm 2LNK GmbH to supply its G2 and G3 drone systems into Kazakhstan’s security and defense market, according to prior reporting from The Defence Blog, and the company recently confirmed it is scaling up serial production in Israel, buying components well ahead of need and adding capabilities like visual navigation, a technology that lets a drone determine its position using onboard cameras rather than relying solely on GPS, directly relevant to the kind of contested, jammed environment the Thailand demonstration was designed to test.

Experts discuss whether Ted Lasso would be a good coach in real life

Amber heat-health alerts in force across England as drought reaches 71% of country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:56:25 UTC
17:56:25 KST

Aysu Bicer
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
Amber heat-health alerts are in force across most of England as temperatures begin to climb again, with forecasters warning of high and potentially extreme heat through the week.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said significant impacts are likely across health and social care, including a possible rise in deaths. The alerts remain in place until Friday evening.
Temperatures are expected to reach the low to mid-30s Celsius across much of England and Wales at the peak of the heat wave.
On Tuesday, the hottest conditions are expected around eastern Wales, the Midlands and central parts of southern England, where temperatures are forecast to reach 27C to 30C (81F to 86F).
The warnings come as drought conditions spread across England. The National Drought Group said Monday that 71.3% of England was now officially in drought, with the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs the latest areas to be affected.
About 45 million people are living in drought-hit areas, while more than 27 million are subject to water restrictions, according to the group.
The UK has experienced an unusually warm summer, with temperatures remaining above average for much of the season. Even cooler spells have generally only brought temperatures back toward the seasonal average.
Little or no rain is forecast across England and Wales for most of the week. The first significant rainfall for many areas in almost two months could arrive Sunday, when low pressure and rain-bearing fronts move in from the Atlantic across Wales and southern England.
The rain, however, is not currently expected to be particularly heavy or persistent.

Russia’s security services prevailed in fight over anti-war Yabloko party’s participation in elections, analyst says

The decision to remove the anti-war Yabloko party from Russia’s September parliamentary elections may been the result of a conflict between the civilian wing of the presidential administration, which was initially prepared to allow the party into the campaign, and the security services, which favored eliminating any political risks through outright bans and repression, political analyst Mikhail Komin told The Insider.
Komin is director of research at the Center for Advanced Governance, a Russian policy research organization.
In his view, the initial decision to register Yabloko may have been made by the presidential administration’s domestic policy department, which oversees Russian election campaigns. Komin said the Kremlin may first have studied closed-door polling and focus group results, including reactions to Yabloko’s main campaign slogan, “For Peace and Freedom.”
“I think that [the presidential administration] looked at some polling that they themselves commission and conduct, and that we do not see publicly,” Komin said. “They tested the slogans that Yabloko was planning to use in focus groups — ‘For Peace and Freedom.’ They looked at the results and understood that the polling showed a fairly small number of votes.”
According to Komin, the presidential administration may have assumed that Yabloko’s vote share could be kept below the 5% necessary for representation in the State Duma — and even below the 3% required to qualify for state funding — via a combination of propaganda, administrative mobilization, and vote-rigging. In that scenario, Yabloko’s participation in the election could itself have benefited the Kremlin, as a defeat for the only registered party with an anti-war platform would have allowed the authorities to present the results as evidence that calls for peace had little public support.
“They realized it would be better to let Yabloko in and make an example of it during the campaign, to show that a very limited number of people support the slogan ‘For Peace and Freedom,’ and that this social group is marginal,” Komin said. “It is a safe way to demonstrate that society is in fact consolidated around the idea of war.”
Komin said that, under that scenario, a strong result for the ruling United Russia party would take on additional significance. The authorities could use it as confirmation of public support for continuing the war, thereby giving the Kremlin extra political legitimacy to implement post-election decisions that would more directly affect the public.
Komin cited the possibility of a new wave of mobilization into the Russian army as one possible example.
“We know that the prospect of mobilization in one form or another is now being actively discussed: hidden mobilization, mobilization into [the] drone forces, mobilization in the form of rotation, or some other options,” he said. “Perhaps such broad legitimacy for the idea of the war is needed for other decisions as well — not only mobilization, but decisions that affect the population more directly and influence people’s social well-being.”
Komin said the initial plan may therefore have been to allow Yabloko to run, ensure its defeat, and then present the election results to Vladimir Putin as proof that society was consolidated around the continuation of the war. Such a course of events could have expanded the space for more radical decisions the Kremlin considers necessary to change the trajectory of events on the battlefield in Ukraine.
According to Komin, the civilian wing of the presidential administration, associated with Sergei Kiriyenko and the domestic policy department, initially approved of Yabloko taking part in the election. But the security wing, which Komin links primarily to the FSB’s Second Service and its head, Alexei Sedov, may have viewed the party’s presence on the ballot as too dangerous.
“Russia’s security structures favor cutting off risks through repression and bans,” Komin said. “The civilian administration more often takes the position that risks are better managed by creating a more complex picture and applying more complex solutions. And those protect against risks much better than blunt bans.”
Komin said Yabloko’s registration and then removal suggest that such a competition really did take place behind the scenes, likening it to the Kremlin’s decision to block Telegram. According to Komin, the civilian wing of the presidential administration opposed blocking the messaging service (or at least opposed making such a move before the election), while security officials took a harder line. Komin also attributes Telegram founder Pavel Durov’s addition to Russia’s list of extremists to developments in the internal Russian power struggle.
Komin sees the State Duma campaign of anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin, who was barred from running in Russia’s 2024 presidential election, as another similar episode. In his view, the civilian administration may have planned simply to deny Nadezhdin’s registration over problems with signatures, while security officials saw that scenario as too risky after lines of people seeking to support his nomination formed across the country.
“They saw those lines for Nadezhdin last time and did not want to create them under any circumstances,” Komin said. “So they opened the relevant cases against him, which prevented him from running and campaigning, and then pushed him out of the country.”
Nadezhin has fled Russia and now lives in France.
Komin stressed that these political developments do not represent a split inside the government so much as they signal the presence of competition between two approaches to controlling the political space. In his assessment, the advantage has increasingly gone to the security services.
“This is actually not a very good signal, because we see that in all these decisions, at least the ones we know about, the security services are winning,” Komin said. “That means repression as a tool will develop and expand.”
Komin said the presidential administration’s policy approach, which involved preserving a more complex and manageable political landscape rather than relying on direct bans, is clearly falling out of favor with the Kremlin as the full-scale war in Ukraine rages well into its fifth year.

Russian attacks kill 9 in Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Moscow is getting more North Korean missiles
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia attacked Ukrainian cities with missiles, drones and glide bombs Tuesday, killing at least nine civilians, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is getting new military help from North Korea for its more than 4-year-old invasion.
Zelenskyy said Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea in an overnight attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, where officials said six people were killed and 19 wounded.
Three more people, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said.
In addition to the ballistic missiles, North Korea is preparing to deploy more of its troops to Russia, Zelenskyy said late Monday.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2024, pledging mutual aid if either country faces aggression.
Kim has sent thousands of troops and huge supplies of weapons to support Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some experts say the engagement with Moscow is helping improve North Korea’s military capabilities, and Zelenskyy said the battlefield experience would help Pyongyang menace other countries in its region.
Ukraine says Russia is scaling up its production of ballistic missiles, aiming to exploit Kyiv’s critical shortage of Patriot air defense interceptors that can stop them, and claims Moscow is preparing to recruit more troops for a new push on the front line that stretches 1,250 kilometers (775 miles) along eastern and southern Ukraine.
“Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation,” Zelenskyy said on social media.
U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to stop the war have fizzled as Washington grew frustrated with the lack of progress and its attention turned to the Iran war.
“The Kremlin will not enter serious negotiations or make meaningful compromises on its demands as long as Putin believes that he has a viable military path to achieving his full objectives,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said in an analysis Monday.
“Ukraine’s Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war,” it said.
Russia hits the grounds of a Kyiv children’s hospital
Russian forces also struck parts of the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, overnight, according to officials. One strike hit the grounds of a children’s hospital, leaving two craters and shattering windows, the State Emergency Service said. Children and medical workers were in bomb shelters and nobody was hurt, it added.
At another location in Kyiv, a Russian strike started a fire in a warehouse that spread across about 1,200 square meters (nearly 13,000 square feet), according to emergency officials.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight struck “military industrial facilities and transport and logistics centers” in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with “ground-based precision weapons.”
It said in a statement that it hit civilian storage facilities housing drones in Kyiv and a metallurgical plant in Zaporizhzhia.
Russia targeted both cities with Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles, while launching 120 long-range strike drones across the country, Ukraine’s air force said.
Russia’s biggest e-commerce company hit again
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted nearly 400 Ukrainian drones over 14 regions and Crimea, the peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed from Kyiv in 2014.
Russia’s biggest online retailer, Wildberries, said in a statement its logistical facilities in the Voronezh region on the border with Ukraine came under attack and caught fire. It added that the fire was extinguished and goods stored there were “largely undamaged.”
Ukraine has repeatedly struck Wildberries warehouses and has also bombarded Russian oil facilities in what it says is a strategy to compel Putin to negotiate an end to the invasion.
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces struck an oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia’s Orenburg region near the border with Kazakhstan, about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, causing a fire.
The refinery, with an annual processing capacity of about 44 million barrels of crude oil, produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, among other products. The extent of the damage was being assessed, the military said.

Colombia busca a desaparecidos tras un fuerte terremoto que mató a más de 100 personas

Colombia busca a desaparecidos tras un fuerte terremoto que mató a más de 100 personas
BOGOTÁ (AP) — Las labores de búsqueda y rescate continuaban la madrugada del martes en decenas de ciudades y pueblos del oeste de Colombia después de que un potente terremoto sacudiera la región, matara al menos a 111 personas y dejara a muchas atrapadas bajo los escombros de edificios dañados y destruidos.
El terremoto del lunes, de magnitud 7,4, sacudió Cali, Quibdó, Pereira y muchas otras ciudades y pueblos. Se informó que alrededor de 1.600 edificios resultaron dañados o se derrumbaron. Soldados, personal de rescate y familias hurgaban entre los escombros, retirando y pasando a mano grandes trozos de concreto a lo largo de filas de voluntarios.
El presidente, Abelardo de la Espriella, dijo el lunes por la tarde que al menos 111 personas habían muerto.
Las familias publicaron información sobre seres queridos desaparecidos en sitios web administrados por ciudadanos. Para la noche del lunes se había reportado la desaparición de más de 2.700 personas.
Dana Carolina Zamora publicó una imagen de su tío desaparecido, Miguel Ángel Zamora, de 60 años, acunando a su perro. El agricultor vivía en una zona rural de El Cairo, no lejos del epicentro del sismo en San José del Palmar.
Las autoridades locales indicaron que el 80% de El Cairo, un pueblo de unos 7.000 habitantes, resultó dañado. Zamora dijo que estaba preocupada porque su tío vivía en una casa tradicional pero frágil, hecha de palos y barro.
“Tenemos miedo, esperemos que no sea así, que esté bien y que sólo sea falla de comunicación. Pero no hemos logrado saber nada más de él”, aseguró Zamora a la AP por teléfono desde Cali.
Chocó, la región que rodea el epicentro del sismo, es una de las zonas más pobres y desatendidas de Colombia, a menudo asediada por grupos armados enfrentados. A gran parte de Chocó solo se puede acceder en barco, a través de la selva o en avión. Se sabía poco sobre la magnitud de los daños allí.
De la Espriella viajó a la capital de Chocó, Quibdó, la noche del lunes para evaluar los daños y anunció que había movilizado “todo el aparato militar y policial” para responder, desplegando ingenieros, rescatistas y perros de búsqueda. Anunció subsidios de alquiler para quienes tengan viviendas dañadas mientras se realizan las reparaciones.
“El Chocó nunca más será la tierra del olvido”, afirmó el mandatario.
El terremoto representa la primera gran prueba para de la Espriella, quien juró el cargo el viernes. De la Espriella es una figura divisiva por su promesa de una ofensiva total contra los grupos criminales.
El Departamento de Estado de Estados Unidos anunció que proporcionaría 15,5 millones de dólares para refugios de emergencia, alimentos y otra ayuda. Gobiernos de toda América Latina también se dispusieron a ayudar.
El terremoto dejó a muchos en la nación andina inquietos después de que dos sismos consecutivos devastaran a la vecina Venezuela a finales de junio, destruyendo cientos de edificios y matando a más de 6.300 personas.
Muchos colombianos apenas comenzaban a asimilar las consecuencias a más largo plazo del desastre.
Mónica Sánchez es dueña de una pequeña empresa que fabrica uniformes de trabajo. Su ciudad, Pereira, fue una de las más golpeadas, y una pared dentro de la fábrica se derrumbó. Sánchez y sus 12 trabajadores lograron salir justo a tiempo.
“Fue impactante: la ciudad se vino abajo a nuestro alrededor”, relató.

Former Syrian President Assad sentenced to death in absentia

Former Syrian President Assad sentenced to death in absentia for war crimes
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — A Syrian court sentenced ousted Syrian President Bashar Assad along with his younger brother to death in absentia on Tuesday for crimes against humanity and war crimes during Syria’s 14-year conflict that left about half a million people dead.
The sentences at the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus are the first against Assad or members of his inner circle since the Assad family’s five decades in power came to an end 20 months ago.
“Bashar Assad used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity,” said judge Fakhareddine al-Aryan during a court session that was aired live on state TV.
Also sentenced to death was Assad’s maternal cousin Atef Najib, who was convicted of overseeing a crackdown in the southern province of Daraa that led to the uprising and later the civil war. Al-Aryan said Najib can appeal.
Under tight security, Najib stood inside a cage wearing a prisoner’s uniform as the judge read the sentence. A crowd gathered outside the courthouse in central Damascus to hear the verdict.
“Today is the day of justice for all the wounded, martyrs, detainees and Syrians who were forced to leave their country,” said attorney Adnan al-Masalmeh who represented families of Najib’s victims. “Today marks a victory of right against injustice, a victory of the Syrian people against the ousted regime.”
Assad and his brother Maher fled to Russia after the government’s fall in December 2024 and received political asylum. Syria’s new rulers have asked Russia to hand the Assads over.
Najib, who was sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury in April 2011, was later detained and is one of the highest-ranking security officials to be put on trial.
Najib is a former army brigadier general who was head of the Political Security Branch in Syria’s southern Daraa province under Assad in 2011.
During his tenure, more than a dozen teenagers who scrawled anti-government graffiti on a school wall in Daraa were arrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for mass protests against the repressive policies of Assad’s security forces.
The protests were met by a brutal government crackdown that spiraled into a 14-year civil war that ended with Assad’s ouster in a lightning rebel offensive.
Some of Najib’s victims were present at the courthouse including two who were teenagers in 2011 and expressed their opinions to The Associated Press.
“Today we reached a point where the blood was not wasted,” said Mouawiya Sayasneh, about those who died in the crackdown. Fifteen years later, “there is happiness that Atef Najib was sentenced to death,” he said.
Another man, Nayef Abazeid, who was detained at the age of 13 in 2011, expressed his satisfaction with the sentence, adding that “our biggest happiness will be when Bashar Assad is executed.”
Maher Assad was a former commander of the Syrian military’s 4th Armored Division — which opposition activists have accused of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, in addition to running its own detention centers.
“Today’s scenes outside the courthouse reflect 15 years of pain and a justice long denied. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all cases, including this one,” said Hiba Zayadin, Syria researcher at Human Rights Watch. “It’s cruel and irreversible, especially when a fair trial isn’t guaranteed.”
Zayadin added that Najib has the right to appeal, and that process “needs to meet fair trial standards too.” Real accountability for Assad-era crimes depends on Syria building a justice system that lasts, she said.

Associated Press writer Kareem Chehayeb contributed to this report from Beirut.

Colombia rescuers race against time as quake death toll tops 130
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:52:35 UTC
17:52:35 KST

More than 130 people have been killed after Colombia was struck by its strongest earthquake in decades, with the government declaring a state of emergency as rescue teams searched collapsed buildings for survivors.
At least 132 people died in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake, President Abelardo de la Espriella said during a crisis meeting Monday afternoon. Authorities warned that the death toll could rise as rescuers continue searching through the rubble, with many people feared trapped beneath collapsed structures.
The earthquake struck at about 7:34 a.m. local time (12:34 p.m. GMT), according to the Colombian Geological Service, known as the SGC. Its epicenter was near the town of San José del Palmar in western Colombia, at a depth of about 103 kilometers (64 miles).
The powerful tremor was followed by numerous aftershocks, further complicating rescue efforts and raising concerns about additional building collapses.
Emergency crews were deployed across affected areas as authorities assessed the scale of the destruction and worked to reach people trapped under the debris.
"The first priority is rescuing people buried under the rubble," de la Espriella said, adding that the government was mobilizing all available resources.
At a later news conference in Cali, south of the epicenter, de la Espriella said 188 people were missing in the city, while 35 had been killed and about 700 injured. He said three hospitals and about 40 buildings had collapsed entirely.
Another 400 soldiers were due to join the 600 already deployed to assist with search and rescue operations, the president said. Cali's airport was also operating on a limited basis because of damage.
More than 1,500 homes were severely damaged in several cities, including Pereira, Cali and Manizales.
Sixty people were killed in Pereira alone, according to the latest figures from city authorities. Eleven others were missing, the city said in a post on X.
The full extent of the disaster remained unclear.
In Cali, residents joined rescue workers in searching the rubble for survivors.
"We have a four-story building here that has completely collapsed. We have already managed to rescue three people alive," a fire service official in the La Alameda neighborhood told broadcaster Caracol.
Power supplies, telephone services and other communications links were disrupted.
Six airports were closed to commercial traffic because of damage to infrastructure, de la Espriella said. The cathedral in Manizales was also severely damaged.
Cars swayed in the streets, windows rattled and people fled their homes in panic.
"At first I thought it was something minor. But when it kept getting stronger and didn't stop, I thought we were going to die," a woman from Manizales told broadcaster La FM.
"Part of the roof of my house collapsed and the walls are cracked," Juan Bernal, a resident of Armenia, said.
The earthquake was also felt in Bogota, Medellin, Popayan and Armenia, as well as in neighboring Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama.
The quake comes after twin earthquakes struck neighboring Venezuela in late June, killing more than 6,000 people.
However, the Colombian Geological Service said there was no connection between the earthquakes. The Venezuelan quakes involved movement of the Caribbean Plate, while the Colombian earthquake was linked to the Nazca Plate off Colombia's Pacific coast.
The strongest previous earthquake occurred off the coast between Ecuador and Colombia in 1958 and had a magnitude of 7.6. Fifteen people were killed, according to the Geological Service.
In 1999, more than 1,000 people were killed when a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck Armenia and surrounding communities.

Syria court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death for crimes against humanity in absentia
A Syrian court sentenced ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia on Tuesday, along with his younger brother, for crimes against humanity and war crimes during Syria’s 14-year conflict that left about half a million people dead.
A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former ruler Bashar al-Assad to death after a trial in absentia, convicting him of atrocities committed during the country's nearly 14-year civil war.
It is the first such ruling under Syria's transitional leaders who ousted Assad in December 2024, vowing to provide justice and accountability for crimes committed under his rule.
Assad fled to Moscow as Islamist-led forces closed in on Damascus after a lightning offensive.
At a court in Damascus, Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan convicted Assad for crimes including "premeditated murder, the intentional killing of more than one person, the intentional killing of children under 15 years ... torture, torture leading to death, and deprivation of liberty on multiple occasions – classified as crimes against humanity and war crimes".
"He is therefore sentenced to death."
Read more Survivors of Assad's prisons speak out about rape and torture
Syria in April began proceedings against Assad and other officials accused in person and in absentia of atrocities during the country's civil war, which erupted with the former authorities' brutal repression of pro-democracy protesters.
More than half a million people were killed and millions displaced, while tens of thousands of people disappeared, many into the country's brutal prison system.
The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death including Assad's brother Maher, who ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled the country.
Those convicted included former defence minister Fahd al-Freij and Louay al-Ali, who headed military intelligence in Daraa province in 2011.
Torture
The court convicted the officials for crimes including murder, incitement to murder, torture leading to death and repeated deprivation of liberty, also considered "crimes against humanity" and "war crimes".
Former security official Atif Najib – the only one in the dock – was also sentenced to death for "crimes against humanity" committed when he was head of political security in Daraa province, the cradle of the country's 2011 uprising.
Najib, a cousin of Assad who was arrested in January last year, was convicted for crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15", and "torture leading to death".
The acts attributed to him are "crimes against humanity", the court said as it handed down "the harshest punishment against him, which is the death penalty".
Syria's uprising began in Daraa in March 2011, after 15 students were arrested for allegedly writing anti-government slogans on the city's walls.

Residents said the students were tortured, leading to a protest to demand their release that ended in bloodshed.
Security personnel suppressed peaceful demonstrations with force and fired live ammunition to disperse sit-ins at several locations.
Najib was dismissed after the crackdown, as the protests spread to other provinces.
Aryan said Najib had denied the charges against him and showed "no remorse".
Assad took the Syrian presidency in 2000 after the death of his father Hafez.

“The whole estate lost electricity, and there are fire engines, ambulances and police vehicles. One person had been carried downstairs, and there is some odour,” another wrote.
The user also said residents had to gather outside their homes with fans to fight the heat.
CLP Power, which supplies power to Kowloon and the New Territories, apologised to affected residents and said it would investigate the power failure. It said electricity supply to the area had gradually resumed after 10.45am.
