Source: Ukrainska Pravda article
Details: Less than a month after Poklad became acting head of the SSU, the Service's regional branches in eight oblasts and the Autonomous Republic of Crimea received new heads.
Brigadier General Oleh Fedoriv has formally taken charge of Special Group Alpha. According to a Ukrainska Pravda source in the security agencies, further personnel changes could soon take place at the SSU's central directorate, including possible replacements of the heads of the Logistics Department and the Operational Documentation Department.
Among the SSU head's four deputies, Ukrainska Pravda sources describe Andrii Tupikov and Yaroslav Merezhko as "Poklad's people".
Under former head Vasyl Maliuk, Tupikov headed the SSU's Counterintelligence Department. He now coordinates a number of areas, ranging from the Service's logistics to sanctions-related work. Merezhko previously headed one of the divisions within the Counterintelligence Department and is now responsible for military counterintelligence and the protection of critical infrastructure facilities.
Ukrainska Pravda sources describe Denys Kylymnyk as the only protégé of Yevhen Khmara among the deputy heads. Kylymnyk heads the SSU's Anti-Terrorist Centre and oversees Alpha's long-range operations.
Back in January and February, influential law enforcement officials told Ukrainska Pravda that they believed Poklad had a better chance of securing the top job at the SSU.
Quote from an Ukrainska Pravda source in the security agencies: "Poklad is a professional operative. He is prepared to use any methods to carry out the president's instructions – both legal methods and not entirely legal methods of 'achieving objectives'. Khmara is more cautious. He tries to act only within the law."
Details: Another Ukrainska Pravda source in law enforcement claims that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave Poklad tasks directly, some of which Khmara was not even aware of.
"Everything is very predictable. Oleksandr Poklad is building his own chain of command and rooting out pockets of resistance," an Ukrainska Pravda source in the leadership of the security establishment said.
Meanwhile, Poklad is described in parliament as "unconfirmable". As things stand, there are not enough votes to appoint him as head of the SSU, and it is unclear whether the leadership of the Servant of the People party will be able to secure the required 226 votes.
Previously: On 4 August, Zelenskyy said that he had approved new operations by the Security Service of Ukraine but did not disclose the results of the 40-day operation announced on 25 June, which was intended to push Russia towards ending the war.

Heathrow says need for expansion ‘clear’ as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:02:59 UTC
17:02:59 KST

Heathrow airport said “the case for expansion has never been clearer” after it was overtaken as Europe’s busiest airport by Istanbul.
Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.86 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s four terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.
Heathrow’s passenger numbers for July fell, while London Stansted and Manchester both had record traffic for the month.
Annual figures from the trade body Airports Council International show Heathrow was Europe’s busiest airport from 1996 to 2019.
The UK’s biggest airport, located west of central London, lost that position in 2020 amid coronavirus travel restrictions before regaining it in 2023 and holding the title since then.
Heathrow’s July passenger total was 1.5% down compared with the same month last year, while the Turkish hub recorded a 2.3% increase.
The US-Israel war on Iran has affected Heathrow’s passenger traffic. Numbers on Middle East routes were down 20.2% year on year in July.
Heathrow continues to operate its two runways at near full capacity, and is seeking government permission to build a third.
An expansion proposal by the airport’s owners would enable it to accommodate 150 million passengers a year - up from about 85 million in 2025.
The airport said: “Heathrow is operating at capacity. The case for expansion has never been clearer, as Heathrow was overtaken in July by Istanbul airport as the busiest hub in Europe.
“Our plans will ensure the country gets the infrastructure it needs to stay competitive and will deliver all-important economic growth.”
The comparison, however, may not fully bolster Heathrow’s case. The airport was only opened in late 2018 and built on a brand new site away from the city and residential neighbourhoods, gradually replacing the existing Ataturk airport as the main international hub. It has a vastly bigger footprint and is able to operate 24 hours a day.
The Turkish boom also owes much to its location near the Gulf, which has become the crossroads of international air travel.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, launched a consultation on the renamed Heathrow expansion national policy statement in June, setting out the conditions needed if the project is to be given the go-ahead.
The then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, said at the time she was determined to get “spades in the ground” for the third runway in the current parliament, and for it to be built by 2035.
Andy Burnham, who sacked Reeves, has previously expressed concerns over Heathrow expansion, stating the plans divert infrastructure investment “away from the north and traps it in London”.
Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said summer was “off to a flying start” but “we want to go further” by “growing our route network and passenger offering”.
“Expanding Heathrow will help ensure the UK remains home to Europe’s leading hub and continues to benefit from the trade, investment and tourism that increased connectivity will bring,” he said.
London Stansted said it had recorded the busiest month in the airport’s history in July, welcoming 3.1m passengers, a 6.3% increase year-on-year.
Manchester also had a record July, serving 3.4m passengers.

Former Moldovan Railways chief Oleg Tofilat estimated that the route could handle around 4.5 million metric tons of grain annually.
Ukrainian estimates suggest the corridor could eventually carry around 10% of the country’s exports. Moldova previously served as a transit route for Ukrainian grain in 2022-2023, after Russia’s full-scale invasion disrupted traditional Black Sea export routes.
Russian strikes threaten Ukraine’s grain lifeline
The push for an alternative comes as Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s southern ports and shipping infrastructure. Ukrainian grain exports have become increasingly vulnerable as Moscow targets facilities in the Odesa region, a critical hub for the country’s agricultural trade.
Russian Ballistic Missile Barrage Kills 9 Across Ukraine, Kyiv Warns of North Korean Missile Support
Ukraine ships more than 90% of its grain exports through seaports, making the attacks a direct threat to one of the country’s most important export industries.
Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi told Reuters on Monday that the government had cut its forecast for grain exports in the 2026-27 season to 38-40 million metric tons, down from an earlier estimate of 43 million tons.
Agricultural analysts at APK-Inform were also more pessimistic, lowering their forecast by 8.6% to 39.4 million tons because of export disruptions.
Moldova could also benefit financially from the expanded transit route. Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said Monday that Chisinau should seize the opportunity to earn millions of euros from Ukrainian grain shipments.
He also rejected concerns from Moldovan farmers that Ukrainian grain could undercut domestic produce.
“Let’s not look for enemies in places where there are none,” Tofan said on Moldovan television.

Trump's war fails to break Iran's resolve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:02:35 UTC
17:02:35 KST

The forty-day war that Donald Trump launched with the aim of changing Iran's behavior and imposing Washington's demands was supposed to end with a swift and decisive victory. Trump repeatedly spoke of Iran's "unconditional surrender" and imagined that military pressure could put Tehran in a position where it would have no choice but to accept America's terms. But the developments after the war paint a different picture—a picture that even American media outlets acknowledge.
CNN, in a report recalling Trump's stances on "Iran's unconditional surrender," wrote that Tehran has not only not surrendered, but has hardened its demands regarding the Strait of Hormuz. The American media outlet viewed Iran's positions on Hormuz as a sign that Tehran assesses it has greater bargaining power vis-à-vis Washington.
CNN also cited the depletion of American weapons stockpiles as one of the factors that could be influencing this calculation in Tehran—an issue that shows the prolongation of the war has not only imposed costs on Iran, and that America has also faced limitations in its military capacity.
The Goal That Was Not Achieved
Trump's initial calculation was built on a simple assumption: America's military superiority could force Iran to back down in a short period. In this view, the military strikes were not merely meant to cause destruction; rather, their main objective was to change Iran's political behavior.
But there is an important difference between inflicting military damage and achieving political victory. A country may be able to destroy targets, but if it cannot compel the other side to accept its political demands, it has not yet attained strategic victory.
What matters today is precisely this gap between goal and outcome. Trump began the war with the language of surrender, but Iran has not only not surrendered, it has adopted a tougher stance on one of the most critical regional issues, namely the Strait of Hormuz.
This development shows that Tehran has managed to transform part of the military pressure into a political and strategic issue. In other words, Iran has sought to raise the cost of continued pressure for the United States and to use available tools to strengthen its bargaining position.
Why Is Hormuz Important?
The Strait of Hormuz holds particular significance in this equation. This waterway is one of the world's most vital energy transit routes, and any instability there can affect the oil market and the global economy.
For this reason, Hormuz is not merely a shipping lane for the United States. A significant part of America's military presence in the Persian Gulf region over the past decades has been justified by the issues of energy security, freedom of navigation, and the protection of oil transit lines.
Now, if Iran can turn Hormuz into an effective lever in negotiations and bargaining, this not only signifies an increase in Tehran's power; it also raises questions about the efficacy of America's military presence in the region.
Washington began the war wanting to reduce Iran's ability to influence the regional environment. But if, after the war, Tehran can enter negotiations over Hormuz with a harder stance, this outcome would be exactly contrary to America's original objective.
That is why CNN's reference to the Strait of Hormuz is significant. The outlet is, in fact, speaking of a shift in Iran's bargaining position—a shift that shows Tehran does not see itself merely as a party under pressure, but still views itself as possessing levers it can use to increase America's costs.
Weapons Stockpiles and the Issue of a Protracted War
Another factor CNN mentioned is the depletion of American weapons stockpiles. This issue is of great importance from a strategic perspective.
America's military power is built upon a vast array of weapons, bases, defense systems, and military production capacity. Yet even such power faces the problem of consumption and replacement of equipment in a protracted war.
In a short war, technological superiority and high offensive volume can be decisive. But the longer the war drags on, the more important production and replacement capacity for weapons, the costs of war, and the ability to sustain military pressure become.
From this perspective, Iran's calculation is not shaped solely by the damage inflicted on the country. Tehran must see to what extent the United States is capable of maintaining its level of military pressure.
The depletion of weapons stockpiles, while not signifying American incapacity, can raise the cost of continuing the war. This very issue may alter the opposing side's calculations and allow Iran to emphasize its demands with greater confidence in any potential negotiations.
The Difference Between Military Victory and Strategic Victory
One of the most important lessons of the war is the difference between military success and strategic victory.
One side may inflict heavy blows on the battlefield, but if it cannot achieve its desired political outcome, one cannot speak of the full realization of the war's objectives.
Trump's declared goal was Iran's surrender. Therefore, the primary measure of Washington's success must be whether Tehran has, at the end of the war, agreed to accept America's core terms.
What CNN is now reporting about Iran's positions on Hormuz indicates that the answer to this question is, at the very least, not simple or clear-cut.
If Iran, after enduring the pressure of war, can maintain its positions and even escalate some of its demands, this means that the United States has been unable to extract the political outcome it expected from its military superiority.
Under such circumstances, the debate over which side has suffered greater damage gives way to a more important question: which side has managed to retain more bargaining power at the end of the war?
The Pressures That Rebound on America
The war has also imposed costs on the United States. The depletion of weapons stockpiles is only one of these costs. The financial costs of the war, the consumption of munitions and equipment, the strain on military production capacity, and the consequences for the energy market create a set of challenges for Washington.
This is the point at which Trump's initial calculation encounters a contradiction. Washington wanted to force Tehran into retreat by increasing costs for Iran; but the continuation of the war has simultaneously transferred costs to America itself.
On a global level as well, any increase in uncertainty in the Persian Gulf region can affect the energy market, oil prices, maritime transport, and the economies of various countries.
The outcome of the war is therefore not determined solely within the borders of Iran and the United States. The longer the war continues, the broader the scope of its costs will become, and more countries will be exposed to its consequences.
The Strait of Hormuz: A Symbol of the Shifting Equation
Under such circumstances, the Strait of Hormuz has become an important symbol of the shifting equation. The United States wanted to use military power to reduce Iran's ability to use regional levers. But Iran is now putting forward the Strait of Hormuz as one of the main axes of its demands.
This development should be seen within a larger framework. Iran is trying to show that the region's security cannot be defined solely through the presence of foreign powers, and that regional actors can still influence security and economic equations.
From this perspective, Hormuz is not merely an issue of oil or shipping; it is part of the contest over the future of the Persian Gulf's security order.
Conclusion
The forty-day war was supposed to bring Iran to the point of surrender, but now even American media outlets speak of a shift in Tehran's calculations and an increase in its bargaining power.
Iran has not surrendered, has adopted a tougher stance on Hormuz, and the depletion of American weapons stockpiles has been noted as one of the factors influencing Tehran's calculations.
This does not mean ignoring America's military power or the damage inflicted on Iran; rather, the issue concerns the political outcome of the war.
Trump began the war to change Iran's behavior, but if, at the end, Tehran is still capable of advancing its own terms and even hardening them, then one must acknowledge that a considerable gap has emerged between what Washington envisioned at the start of the war and what has occurred in the political arena after the war.
The calculation that was supposed to bring Iran to surrender has now become a test of America's ability to impose its will—and that, precisely, is the clearest sign that Trump's original equation has been inverted.

Most of England is now under amber heat health alerts – here’s what that means
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:00:59 BST
17:00:59 KST

Most of England is now under amber heat health alerts – here’s what that means
Health alerts have been issued across much of England from Tuesday until Friday
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The UK Health Security Agency has issued amber heat health alerts across much of England as Britons brace for the fifth heatwave of the year.
According to the Met Office, highs of 29C in Cardiff, 28C in Manchester and 25C in London are forecast for Tuesday, before the mercury climbs to the mid-30s in some regions on Thursday.
It comes as nearly three-quarters of England is in drought, with the National Drought Group warning that conditions will worsen should there not be "significant and sustained rainfall".
But what do these alerts mean and how can you stay safe?
What alerts are in place?
As of Tuesday at 9am, amber heat health alerts are in force for the following regions:
- North West
- Yorkshire and the Humber
- East Midlands
- West Midlands
- East of England
- London
- South East
- South West
Meanwhile, the North East is under a yellow heat health alert from 9am.
When are the heat alerts in place until?
The aforementioned alerts are in effect until 9pm on Friday, 14 August, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).
What do these alerts mean?
The alert system aims to provide an early warning to healthcare providers, the social care sector, voluntary organisations and Government departments that temperatures are likely to impact the health of the population.
The alerts – yellow, amber or red – depend on the level of impact expected.
Yellow alerts usually mean temperatures are unlikely to impact most people, but those who are particularly vulnerable may struggle to cope.
However, an amber alert would indicate the impact is expected to be felt across the whole of the health service, with the potential for the whole population to be at risk. In these circumstances, a co-ordinated response from services is required.
Which groups are particularly vulnerable in hot weather?
According to the NHS, the most vulnerable groups are older people, especially women over the age of 75, or those who live alone or in a care home.
People with long-term illnesses such as heart or lung conditions, diabetes, Parkinson’s and some mental health conditions are at a higher risk, as well as patients on multiple medicines.
Babies and very young children will also find it hard to keep cool, along with people dependent on alcohol or drugs or people with Alzheimer’s disease.
What are the main risks?
Not drinking enough water, which can cause dehydration, while overheating can make symptoms worse for people with heart or breathing problems.
Heat exhaustion can happen when the body overheats and loses too much water and salt.
Signs include tiredness, dizziness, headaches, feeling sick, excessive sweating and being very thirsty.
If people do not cool down within 30 minutes, heat exhaustion can lead to heatstroke, a life-threatening illness.
If you suspect someone has heat exhaustion, the NHS advises to move them to a cool place, remove all unnecessary clothing, giving them cool water or a sports drink, and cooling their skin by spraying cool water or fanning them.
How can vulnerable groups stay safe in a heatwave?
The NHS advises people to stay out of the sun where possible, especially between 11am and 3pm.
Wear sunscreen, a hat and light clothes, avoid exercise, alcohol, caffeine and hot drinks, and opt for cold food and drinks.
People can also keep their homes cool by closing windows during the day and opening them at night once the temperatures have fallen. Electric fans can also help if the temperature is below 35C, the NHS said.

US appeals court dismisses Meta, TikTok appeals in youth social media lawsuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:00:23 UTC
17:00:23 KST

Dilara Hamit
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
A US federal appeals court has dismissed appeals by Meta and TikTok challenging lower-court rulings that allowed claims in thousands of lawsuits alleging harm to young social media users to proceed.
A three-judge panel of the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that it lacked jurisdiction to review the lower court’s decisions at this stage of the litigation.
“Section 230 merely provides a defense to liability, not immunity from suit,” Judge Jacqueline Nguyen wrote for the panel.
The court consequently dismissed appeals brought by Meta Platforms and TikTok entities, along with conditional cross-appeals filed by groups of plaintiffs.
The decision allows the consolidated federal litigation to continue but does not determine whether the plaintiffs’ allegations are true or whether the technology companies will ultimately be held liable.
The multidistrict litigation includes lawsuits brought by individuals, state attorneys general, school districts and local governments.
Plaintiffs allege that social media platforms were designed in ways that encouraged addictive behavior among children and adolescents, failed to verify users’ ages, allowed young people to bypass parental controls and inadequately protected them from harmful content.
According to the US Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation, 3,137 cases were pending in the consolidated proceeding as of Aug. 3. A total of 3,312 cases have been included since the litigation began.
The cases are being managed by Chief US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in the Northern District of California.
Defendants named across the litigation include Meta, Google and YouTube parent Alphabet, TikTok owner ByteDance and Snapchat parent Snap.
 
Section 230 dispute
Meta sought to dismiss several categories of claims by invoking Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which generally prevents online services from being treated as the publishers or speakers of content created by third parties.
The District Court granted Meta’s motions in part but allowed other claims to proceed. It found that Section 230 barred some allegations involving platform features tied to the companies’ role as publishers of third-party content but did not require dismissal of all claims.
Meta argued that the partial rejection of its Section 230 defense could be appealed immediately because the law provided immunity from suit.
TikTok joined Meta’s arguments without separately briefing the issues, according to the appeals court’s opinion.
The 9th Circuit rejected the argument, finding that Section 230 protects companies from liability in qualifying circumstances but does not give them a right to avoid the litigation process altogether.
The court said Meta could challenge the District Court’s Section 230 rulings after a final judgment is issued.
It also noted that the lower court had allowed certain failure-to-warn claims to proceed “for now” because the litigation remained at an early stage and the relevant law was still developing.
The appeals court also denied as moot Meta’s emergency request to halt an upcoming trial while its appeal was being considered.
Jury selection in a multistate attorneys general case against Meta is scheduled to begin Wednesday in Oakland, California, with opening statements set for Aug. 18.
The case alleges that Meta violated federal and state laws, including the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, by designing and deploying features on Facebook and Instagram that allegedly harmed children and teenagers or encouraged compulsive use. Meta disputes the allegations.

Ukraine investigates MiG-29 fighter jet crash, searches wreckage for black box – photos
The State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) has opened a criminal investigation into the crash of a Ukrainian MiG-29 fighter jet, which occurred on the evening of 10 August in the Berezivka district, Odesa Oblast.
Source: State Bureau of Investigation
Details: Early reports indicate that the aircraft was carrying out a combat mission to destroy Russian drones.
However, during the active phase of the operation, an emergency occurred, causing the aircraft to catch fire and the pilot to lose control. He managed to eject, and his life is not in danger.
Immediately after the fighter jet crashed, an SBI investigative team arrived at the scene and worked there throughout the night. Bureau officers inspected the area, recovered and documented aircraft debris, collected the necessary evidence, and interviewed witnesses and military personnel.
The search for the flight recorder, or "black box", is currently ongoing. The Bureau stressed that its data will be important in establishing the circumstances surrounding the final minutes of the flight. Once the information has been obtained and analysed, investigators will be able to determine and announce early theories about the cause of the crash.
The investigation will also examine whether the rules governing flight preparation, the conduct of the flight and the operation of the aircraft were followed.
The case has been entered into the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations under Article 416.2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – violation of the rules governing flights or preparation for them, as well as the operation of aircraft, resulting in a crash.

Spain prepares for eclipse under shadow of wildfire risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:59:37 UTC
16:59:37 KST

Spain prepares for eclipse under shadow of wildfire risk
MADRID – Spain is rolling out a massive police operation and public safety campaign ahead of a rare total solar eclipse on Aug 12 that will coincide with one of the country’s highest-risk periods for wildfires.
Regional governments along the eclipse path across Spain – offering the best views of the solar event in mainland Europe – are seeking to corral an expected influx of six million people by designating 660 official viewing sites, along with parking and camping areas.
More than 35,000 officers will be deployed in a security operation to minimise the risks – such as fires caused by dropped cigarettes – linked to large gatherings in natural areas, Virginia Barcones, secretary-general for Civil Protection and Emergencies at Spain’s Interior Ministry, told Reuters.
“We’ve had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That's why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark,” Barcones said.
Temperatures set to reach 40 deg C
A control room in Madrid, seen by Reuters, is where the authorities will lead a surveillance operation in coordination with regional governments.
The full solar eclipse, visible in totality from only Spain and Iceland early on the evening of Aug 12, offers an example of how climate change will reshape the management of major public events.
Several Spanish regions are under alerts issued by weather agency Aemet for the day of the eclipse due to temperatures of up to 40 deg C and a “high” or “very high” wildfire risk.
Spain, along with France and Greece, has already battled heatwaves and severe wildfires this summer across an increasingly tinder-dry Europe.
By the evening of Aug 10, three major wildfires were burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. So far in 2026, fires have scorched about 200,000ha – six times more than by the same date in 2025, according to the Environment Ministry.
“This is a very bad time of year... It’s statistically the week when the most wildfires occur in Spain,” said Raul de la Calle, secretary-general of the Association of Forest Technical Engineers.
Rural crowds fuel fears
Some residents of small towns have launched their own public awareness campaigns urging visitors to avoid sensitive natural areas.
In Buitrago de Lozoya, a town of 2,000 residents north of Madrid, local group Monte en Pie (Keeping Woodlands Alive) staged a protest against events planned near forests.
The nearby town of Tres Cantos cancelled all eclipse-day events because of wildfire risks, though around 3,000 people – including Madrid’s regional leaders – are still expected at an observation site near Buitrago.
Monte en Pie argues that while the eclipse will last only a few minutes, the damage caused by a major wildfire could endure for decades.
“We are in a high wildfire-risk area. Barbecues and the use of machinery are prohibited because the countryside is extremely dry... The more people there are, the greater the danger,” said Ana Hernandez, the group’s leader.
The authorities estimate that around 1.5 million people could be on the roads during the day, travelling to rural north-western and central Spain, which is along the total eclipse’s path.
National and local authorities have launched public awareness campaigns, warning on local and social media and in visitors’ forums online against parking in unauthorised areas, littering, using barbecues or venturing into fire-prone countryside.
Fire risks do not, however, appear to be deterring astro-tourists. Travel platform Booking.com reported that foreign searches more than tripled in inland cities such as Burgos and Soria, while Amadeus travel data showed that bookings to the northern region of Asturias were up 292 per cent from a year earlier.
Around 70 per cent of Spain’s rental motorhomes, camper vans and caravans – around 500,000 vehicles – have already been booked for the eclipse period, industry association ASEICAR said. REUTERS

Fire breaks out after drone attack on major Libya gasoline tank
A major gasoline reservoir in Libya's Zawiya, west of Tripoli, caught fire and collapsed on Monday after what authorities said was an attack by unknown perpetrators.
The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said the tank contained about 4.5 million litres of gasoline.
The reservoir is located at the second-largest oil refinery in Libya, with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day.
"This evening, tank number 402-T, belonging to the Brega Oil Company and used for storing gasoline, was directly targeted, resulting in a severe fire before the tank completely collapsed," the NOC said in a statement.
Brega said in a statement that firefighters were working to contain the blaze, adding that "cooling operations are underway for adjacent tanks to prevent the fire from spreading".
The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone attacks on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant over the weekend.
Libya's emergency services agency said on Facebook that there had been "no serious casualties" and that most of the cases they were treating were of smoke inhalation.
The NOC declared a state of emergency and called for an investigation.
Separately, a Libyan parliamentary panel condemned the attack and called for stronger protection of oil installations.
"The House of Representatives' Energy and Natural Resources Committee condemns in the strongest terms the criminal attack targeting the Zawiya Refinery, one of the most vital facilities in the oil and gas sector that is a cornerstone of the national economy," it said in a statement.
Libya has the most abundant oil reserves in Africa but has been divided ever since it was plunged into war during the ouster in 2011 of former leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
In a statement, the Tripoli-based government said Dbeibah held a meeting earlier in the day with key officials, including the interior minister and the chiefs of some armed groups in the capital, "to follow up on the latest security developments".
Dbeibah "stressed the need to deal firmly with any transgressions or actions that threaten security or harm vital facilities and installations", the statement said.

Canton Vaud and city of Geneva reactivate heatwave plan
Owing to the return of a heatwave, the Swiss city of Geneva and canton Vaud reactivated their heatwave plan on Monday. The heatwave is expected to peak between Thursday and Saturday. It is more important than ever to remain vigilant, they said.
After a few days of respite, another spell of hot weather is set to continue until next weekend. The Lake Geneva region is already experiencing a level 3 heatwave, and a rise to level 4 cannot be ruled out over the coming days, the authorities noted. This spell of hot weather is expected to end between Sunday and Monday.
The recurrence of heatwaves should not lead people to underestimate their effects on health, they said. Particular attention must be paid to the elderly, the young, people with chronic illnesses, those who are dependent on others or living in isolation, and those who are particularly vulnerable to the heat.
More
Switzerland’s new energy challenge: keeping cool in a warming climate
Precautionary measures remain essential, they said: drink water regularly, eat enough, keep cool, keep your home as cool as possible, and carry out physical activity during the coolest hours of the day. In the event of heavy sweating, digestive problems or signs of dehydration, a drink containing electrolytes may be helpful; if in doubt, it is advisable to seek advice from a healthcare professional.
In the city of Geneva, people aged 65 and over can benefit from personalised support, including a daily phone call. People can register by calling the freephone number 0800 22 55 11.
To cool off, older people living within the municipality can also enjoy free entry in the mornings to the Vernets and Varembé swimming pools and, in the afternoons, to the Scala, Nord-Sud and City cinemas. During the first three activations of the heatwave plan, 7,432 people visited the cinemas and 1,144 visited the municipal swimming pools, according to the City of Geneva.

The Union of European Football Associations (UEFA), Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said in a joint open letter Monday that the plan amounted to a "fundamental breach of trust" with the institutions FIFA is meant to serve, warning that "when trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."
FIFA apologized last week for mistakes made in the plan, saying senior staff at a crisis meeting in Morocco "reaffirmed their full support" for Infantino's presidency.

Off sick for up to ten years: what lies behind Germany's teacher shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:57:47 UTC
16:57:47 KST

At the start of the new school year, many German schools face an acute staffing crisis, with teachers missing in several subjects and lengthy sick leave further tightening an already tense situation.
Germany’s schools are facing a structural staffing crisis. More teachers have been hired and the federal states are trying to counter this by creating additional posts, recruiting lateral entrants and offering financial incentives.
Yet in many places there are still not enough staff to cover all lessons in full.
There is a particularly chronic shortage of teachers in the STEM subjects – mathematics, computer science, physics and chemistry. There is also a continuing nationwide or regional need in special needs education as well as in art and music.
According to the latest projection by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK), there is a calculated shortfall of around 27,000 fully qualified teachers in Germany.
How dramatic the situation can become in individual regions is currently illustrated by Brandenburg. Education Minister Gordon Hoffmann (CDU) warned in June that the state would probably no longer be able to guarantee the standard timetable everywhere in the coming school year. The situation is particularly difficult in rural areas and in subjects such as biology and chemistry.
The situation also remains tense in North Rhine-Westphalia. Although the state now has more than 166,000 teaching posts, more than 7,770 positions were still unfilled most recently.
Berlin: Off sick for ten years
Berlin is an example of how sickness-related absences exacerbate the already strained staffing situation. According to the city’s education administration, 380 teachers have been on sick leave for at least a year. This emerges from a reply by the Senate to a parliamentary question from the MP Alexander King (BSW), first reported by the Berliner Morgenpost.
They include 225 civil servants and 155 salaried teachers. In total, Berlin employs around 35,000 teachers.
More specifically, 143 civil servant teachers have been absent for at least a year, and a further 50 for at least two years. According to the education administration, 18 teachers have even been on sick leave for at least ten years.
Primary schools are particularly hard hit, with 98 teachers out on long-term sick leave. Secondary schools are missing 54 teachers, grammar schools 34 and vocational schools 27.
There are also long-term absences among salaried teachers: five of them have been on sick leave for at least ten years, and 16 for at least five years.
The BSW MP Alexander King attributes this development, among other things, to the tight staffing situation: inadequate staffing levels increase the workload on those still in post and can in turn encourage further sickness-related absences.
North Rhine-Westphalia: sickness rate around 10 per cent
In Hesse, according to the Ministry of Education, around 225 of the approximately 67,000 teachers have been ill for at least a year, 16 of them for more than five years. Common causes cited include psychological strain and physical complaints.
In North Rhine-Westphalia, teachers in 2025 were on sick leave on average for 8.43 per cent of working days – more than in the state administration as a whole. Secondary modern schools (Hauptschulen) were particularly affected, with a sickness rate of 9.83 per cent.
In Saxony-Anhalt, around 8.6 per cent of lessons in the 2024/25 school year were cancelled because no cover could be provided.
It is impossible to say how many teachers nationwide have been off sick for at least a year. Why? The federal states collect and publish different sets of data. North Rhine-Westphalia, for example, distinguishes according to the duration of illness, while other states use other categories. The term "long-term illness" is also defined differently and in some states can apply to sick leave lasting more than 30 days.
Surveys in individual states nevertheless show that there are at least several hundred such cases.
The future: fewer teachers, more pupils
Many teachers are over 50. According to the Federal Statistical Office, in the 2024/25 school year exactly 35.4 per cent of teachers at general education schools were at least 50 years old. Some 25.4 per cent were between 50 and 59, and a further 10 per cent were 60 or older.
The German education system is therefore facing a major wave of retirements in the coming years. At the same time, it takes several years to train additional teachers.
Demand for teachers is likely to continue rising for the time being. According to the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education, there were just under 11.2 million pupils in Germany in 2024. By 2032 the number is set to rise to almost 11.8 million, an increase of around 5.3 per cent. After that it is expected to fall slightly again because of smaller birth cohorts. By 2040, however, around 11.3 million pupils are still expected.

Ukrainian prisoners say they were tortured and sexually abused in Russian detention
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:56:54 BST
16:56:54 KST

Ukrainian prisoners say they were tortured and sexually abused in Russian detention
Claims more than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed reported experiencing torture or ill-treatment
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Detainees from Ukraine have accused Russia of systematically torturing prisoners of war and civilian detainees, holding captives incommunicado and subjecting them to beatings, electric shocks and sexual abuse.
It comes as thousands of Ukrainians are still in captivity.
Russia rejected the allegations made at an informal U.N. Security Council meeting, with its Deputy U.N. Representative Maria Zabolotskaya calling it “a disinformation campaign” and alleging that Russian prisoners in Ukraine were subjected to “torture and degradation and moral and physical abuse.”
Khuan Alberto Levya Garsiya, still an active member of the Ukrainian military, said his Russian captors subjected him to every imaginable form of torture during 1,183 days in captivity.
"Yes ... I was tortured," he told reporters after the U.N. meeting. "Anything you can think of that can be done hurtful, humiliating to a man, unwillingly. Anything that comes to your mind, not only verbal, physical abuse, daily beatings, electrocution, excessive, excessive exercises in freezing cold when it's minus degrees ... sexual abuse. Everything that can be applied to a person into making a person break mentally. It was all applied to me and most of my comrades."
Garsiya said he was lucky to survive but two of his friends were beaten to death in detention centers in the Donetsk region. Prisoners were held in “overcrowded barracks without adequate conditions,” where “almost all POWs were ill with dysentery” and many were starving, he told the U.N. meeting.
A Ukrainian with a Cuban father, he said guards targeted him particularly because of his Latino name, accusing him of being "a mercenary and an American spy.”
Crimean Tatar activist Leniie Umerova, released in a prisoner exchange in 2024, said she was detained while trying to visit her seriously ill father in Crimea.
She described being moved through “seven detention facilities” in what she called “a carousel of repression” and accused Russia of using torture against Ukrainians in captivity. Oleg Gushin of the Ukrainian government's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said Ukrainian prisoners were “killed and tortured” in detention.
He said Kyiv had identified “more than 300 places of detention” in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territory and that while more than 9,000 Ukrainians had been returned through exchanges, “thousands” remained in Russian captivity.
Ukraine's Chargé d'Affaires Volodymyr Pavlichenko called for greater international pressure and accountability for Russia's treatment of prisoners.
U.N. Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio said U.N. monitoring showed that "widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees by the Russian Federation authorities continues,” including sexual violence.
Since February 2022, the U.N. Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights had documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the deaths of 48 in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention, she said.
She said more than 95% of Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed reported experiencing torture or ill-treatment.
She said more than half also reported sexual violence, including "rape, gang rape, beating while nude, beatings to the genitals, electric shocks to the genitals and nipples, and degrading treatment of a sexualized nature."
She said the U.N. had received "consistent accounts of severe beatings with objects such as batons, heavy belts, and wood, electric shocks, dog attacks, mock executions, and other forms of torture."
Fuentes Julio said the OHCHR had also documented torture and ill-treatment of Russian and third-country national prisoners of war held by Ukraine, but "on a fundamentally different scale.”
She said about half of Russian and third-country prisoners interviewed reported abuse during initial stages of captivity.

Powerball jackpot nears $1 billion in biggest prize of the year
The prize has increased by $70 million ahead of the next draw
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The Powerball jackpot has risen to nearly $1 billion after no winner matched all six numbers on Monday.
Ahead of the next draw, the mammoth prize stands at a staggering $975 million, with the winning numbers to be selected on Wednesday.
That means the value of the prize has rocketed by $70m since Monday, making it the biggest lottery prize of the year so far.
“This is the most exciting jackpot run we’ve seen all year, but it’s also important to remember that every $2 Powerball ticket purchased helps support public programs and services,” Stephen Durrell, Powerball Product Group Chair, said.
“Because a portion of each ticket sold stays where it was purchased, the benefits of Powerball are felt in communities across the country and around the world.”
In the previous draw, the prize stood at $905m with the winning numbers being 6, 37, 54, 55, 64. The Powerball number was 10. 
A potential winner has the choice to accept the prize as a lump-sum or over 30 graduated payments.
Powerball says that the lump-sum on Wednesday has an estimated cash value of $422.3m.
However, if the lump-sum is selected, a 24 percent federal withholding is applied to the winnings which would see Wednesday’s prize value drop to around $320m. 
A federal marginal rate could reduce the prize even further, dropping the value to $266m. Some states also apply additional taxes to lottery winnings.
The largest Powerball jackpot ever won was worth $2.04bn, after one lucky person purchased a ticket in California in 2022. 
Previously, the $2 tickets were sold in just 45 U.S. states, as well as Washington D.C., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. 
However, now, the Powerball draw is also available to British players after the game launched in the United Kingdom in July. 
Andy Carter, senior winners’ advisor at Allwyn, which runs the U.K’s National Lottery, said that it brings a “whole new level of possibility to U.K. players.” 
“It's a chance to win the biggest jackpot ever offered through The National Lottery and to dream bigger than ever before,” he said. 
A Powerball winner would have to overcome steep odds, though, to take home the massive prize. According to Powerball, the odds of winning the grand prize stand at just one in 292,201,338

PM asks justice secretary to find way to exclude PC Harper’s killers from early release scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:52:52 UTC
16:52:52 KST

Andy Burnham has said he is increasingly confident he can adapt the early release scheme for prisoners to exclude the killers of PC Andrew Harper and other serious offenders, saying he understood and shared the public’s concern about their potential release.
Writing on Facebook, the prime minister said on Tuesday he had asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to rapidly push through a series of measures to increase the number of prison places, requiring fewer people to be released early to free up room.
Downing Street said on Monday that there was no feasible way of exempting just a handful of prisoners from the scheme to block the release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for Harper’s manslaughter.
The pair were due to be freed in January under plans to release about 5,000 people early under an emergency plan to create more space in the prison estate in England and Wales.
Exemptions were made for those convicted of rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences, but not manslaughter, prompting pressure to block the release of Harper’s killers, including from police and his family.
No 10 had already changed stance, saying Burnham has asked Norris to “work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper”.
In his Facebook post, Burnham said the early release scheme could be mitigated by expanding prison places in three ways: removing foreign offenders more quickly; finding a way to release lower-risk prisoners stuck in jail on indeterminate sentences; and “making greater use of the entire prison estate including using the female estate for male offenders”.
He wrote: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether.
“In advance of the justice secretary’s proposals being presented to parliament, we will seek to engage other political parties in discussions with the aim of gaining the widest possible public and political consensus on the approach being taken.”
Burnham wrote that he understood “the depth of public concern about the potential early release of those involved with the killing of PC Andrew Harper – and I share it”.
“I fully appreciate the anguish of Andrew’s family and, more broadly, of all those victims and their families who may see those who caused them such harm not serve their full sentence. It is incumbent on me as prime minister to do everything within my power to minimise that possibility. And I am determined to do so.”
Speaking later during a visit in Derbyshire, Burnham said he would prefer to not release any prisoners early, and that he was aware of the public feeling over the issue.
“It’s my job to speak up for the public on this issue,” he said. “I take that duty very seriously indeed, and I’m confident that there’s more that can be done, and will be done to address public concern.”
He added that No 10 officials had been in touch with Harper’s family on Monday night, and Norris was “in regular touch as well”.
Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad-bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019.
Cole and Bowers, two of three men sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, having been convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.
Prison Service officials have warned Burnham that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so that those convicted of manslaughter, such as Cole and Bowers, remain in jail would mean further early releases would be needed within 18 months.
Governors told the Guardian the prime minister’s decision last week to exempt rapists and serious child sex offenders would force thousands of sentences to be recalculated in haste and could lead to the mistaken early release of some prisoners.
The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.
The third man jailed for the manslaughter of Harper – the vehicle driver, Henry Long – was given a longer jail term of 16 years. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme.
Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme on Tuesday the debate over the killers’ release had been a “rollercoaster” but that she had heard directly from Downing Street “so we’ve now got a little bit of hope”.
Speaking of others affected by the early release plans, she said: “We are not alone on this journey. It’s the world that we have been thrown into. You want what is right for your family member. They’ve lost their life through somebody else’s actions. You have to be their voice.
“We are not asking for a special case for Andrew here. We are not stupid, we know it needs to be done the right way.”

====================================================================================================

Study finds Finland’s economic forecasts consistently inaccurate
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
10:51:42 EEST
16:51:42 KST

Finland’s main economic forecasting institutions have repeatedly missed actual GDP growth by wide margins, according to a new study by the Kalevi Sorsa Foundation, which argues that fiscal policy should rely less heavily on forecasts and more on confirmed economic data.
The report examined forecasts from the Ministry of Finance, Bank of Finland, Etla, Pellervo Economic Research, Labore, Nordea and OP Pohjola.
It found that their spring forecasts for the following year’s economic growth differed from the eventual outcome by an average of 1.5 percentage points between 2016 and 2025.
That error exceeded Finland’s average annual economic growth of about 1.0 per cent over the same period.
The study also found little difference in forecasting accuracy between the institutions. Their estimates tended to move in the same direction and often missed turning points in the economy.
“All had roughly the same average error and tended to make mistakes in the same direction,” Lauri Finér, executive director of the Kalevi Sorsa Foundation and one of the report’s authors, said at a media briefing reported by Helsingin Sanomat.
The report examined forecasts over the period from 2011 to 2025 and combined statistical comparisons with interviews conducted at Finland’s main forecasting institutions and Statistics Finland.
One source of error identified by the researchers was the use of preliminary national accounts data.
According to the report, the first estimate of GDP growth published by Statistics Finland differed from the final confirmed figure by an average of 0.7 percentage points between 2011 and 2025.
Average GDP growth during the same period was also 0.7 per cent.
The study’s authors argue that institutions are therefore often trying to predict future economic development without having an accurate picture of the economy at the starting point.
“Forecasts are based on unconfirmed statistics that almost always turn out to be substantially wrong,” Jussi Systä, an economic policy specialist at the foundation and co-author of the study, said in the foundation’s release.
The report cites the latest revisions to GDP figures for 2024 and 2025 as examples. Preliminary data had suggested that the Finnish economy contracted in 2024, while later figures showed growth of close to one per cent.
The researchers also examined the methods used by forecasting bodies.
Institutions generally begin by reviewing earlier forecasts and adjusting assumptions according to changes in the international economy and economic policy. Separate forecasts are then produced for different parts of the economy before being combined into a broader model.
The report says forecasters themselves recognise the uncertainty in their estimates. It also argues that assumptions about the economy returning towards its historical average growth rate tend to produce estimates that are too optimistic.
The Ministry of Finance was examined over a longer period because its forecasts play a central role in government budgeting.
According to the study, the ministry’s spring forecasts made one year in advance projected average growth of 1.7 per cent between 2011 and 2025. Actual average growth was 0.7 per cent.
Finér said the ministry had therefore predicted growth at more than twice the realised rate on average over the period.
The researchers also reviewed Ministry of Finance forecasts for the public deficit.
Two-year forecasts for the deficit as a share of GDP differed from the eventual result by an average of 2.2 percentage points between 2011 and 2025, according to the study.
Converted into money at the projected size of Finland’s economy in 2031, an error of that scale would correspond to about €7.5 billion, the foundation said.
The findings matter because forecasts are built into several areas of Finnish economic policy.
Government budgets and programmes use Ministry of Finance forecasts as a basis for spending and revenue assumptions. Forecasts also affect research and development funding and annual inflation adjustments to income taxation.
The report notes that their role is set to increase under Finland’s new fiscal framework and planned debt brake.
A preliminary parliamentary agreement reached in February 2026 for €8 billion to €11 billion in public-finance adjustment measures was calculated using the Ministry of Finance’s forecast.
The authors argue that such decisions should not be tied too closely to estimates that have a history of large revisions.
“Forecasts are necessary because policy has to rely on some assessment of future economic development,” Systä said. “The problem arises if their uncertainty is not taken into account in decision-making.”
The report recommends making greater use of economic indicators that become available sooner and are less dependent on model assumptions.
These include real-time tax data and employment statistics, which the authors say might provide a more reliable picture of the current business cycle.

Would Ted Lasso be a good coach in real life? The research is in
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
08:50:03 BST
16:50:03 KST

Would Ted Lasso be a good coach in real life? The research is in
Ted’s approach resembles what researchers call ’autonomy-supportive’ coaching
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Ted Lasso is back: the hugely successful Apple TV series has returned for a fourth season.
The sports comedy-drama – which follows an American football coach with zero soccer experience who is hired to run a struggling English Premier League team – has become a cultural phenomenon. It has won 13 Emmy Awards and was the most-watched original streaming show in the United States in 2023.
In Season 4, Ted faces a new challenge: coaching a second-division women’s soccer team.
The show’s popularity raises an interesting question for anyone involved in sport: would Ted Lasso actually be a good coach in real life?
Goodbye, old school
Outwardly, Ted hardly fits the traditional image of a hard-nosed elite sports coach. He is relentlessly optimistic, talks about feelings and seems more interested in people than tactics.
For decades, successful coaching was often associated with authority, toughness and control.
But successful modern coaches such as Steve Kerr in the US National Basketball Association (NBA) and Chris Fagan in the Australian Football League (AFL) have challenged this model, speaking openly about vulnerability, empathy and genuine relationships with their players.
Their success suggests showing humanity is not a weakness in high-performance coaching.
What is Ted’s coaching style?
Ted’s approach resembles what researchers call “autonomy-supportive” coaching.
Despite the academic-sounding name, the idea is simple: rather than controlling every decision, coaches give athletes some ownership, listen to their views, explain why they are being asked to do something, and help them feel capable of doing it.
A meta-analysis of 131 studies involving almost 39,000 participants found autonomy-supportive coaching was associated with stronger motivation and wellbeing.
But does it improve performance?
One field experiment with 33 coaches and 64 athletes preparing for the 2012 Paralympic Games found autonomy-supportive coaching helped these athletes win more medals.
Research suggests the relationship between coach and athlete is crucial in elite sport.
Ted’s relationship with talented but tempestuous striker Jamie Tartt is a good example of this.
They begin with little trust or mutual understanding. Yet Ted continues to invest in him when things become difficult.
Gradually, Jamie begins to trust Ted, accept his coaching and put the needs of his teammates ahead of himself. Their relationship develops through trust, respect, cooperation and mutual understanding.
This reflects something Ted tells journalist Trent Crimm early in the series. For him, coaching is not ultimately about wins and losses – success is about helping his players become the best versions of themselves.
But Ted ends up influencing more than his players’ motivation and relationships. He also helps shape what they believe.
It’s not all warm and fuzzy
Coaches constantly communicate expectations through what they say and how they behave.
Over time, these messages can shape what athletes believe about themselves, their training and what they can achieve. A scoping review my colleagues and I recently published found that beliefs can be shaped not only by an intervention, but also by who delivers it and the relationship they have with the recipient.
Communication, confidence, empathy, enthusiasm and optimism can all play a role.
None of this means great coaching is simply about being nice. Athletes still need honest feedback, clear expectations and accountability.
Supporting autonomy does not mean allowing athletes to do whatever they want. Creating an environment where athletes can speak openly and make mistakes does not mean lowering standards.
Ted demonstrates the distinction when he confronts Jamie over his attitude to training.
Caring about an athlete and challenging them are not mutually exclusive. The best modern coaches combine high support with high expectations. They need technical and tactical expertise but they also need the ability to build relationships, communicate belief, listen and adapt.
The ‘Lasso Way’ works
Overall, modern coaches create environments in which athletes want to improve.
One exchange between Ted and Trent in Season 3 encapsulates this, when the journalist suddenly realises Ted’s coaching has transformed the squad from a bunch of individuals into a team capable of “total football”:
Trent: It’s going to work!
Ted: Great! What is?
Trent: Total football!
Ted: Ok…?
Trent: And I’ll tell you why.
Ted: Why?
Trent: The Lasso Way! You haven’t switched tactics in a week.
Ted: I haven’t?
Trent: No! You’ve done this over three seasons!
Ted: I have?
Trent: Yes! By slowly but surely building a club-wide culture of trust and support through thousands of imperceptible moments, all leading to their inevitable conclusion: total football.
Ted: Well, how about that!
Perhaps Trent was right: the “Lasso Way” was built through thousands of seemingly insignificant moments.
Modern coaching research suggests those moments may not be so insignificant after all.

Albanese shrugs off calls to apologize over Japanese PM ‘melon’ joke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:49:00 UTC
16:49:00 KST

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has rejected calls to apologize to Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi over crude remarks made during a podcast about a gift of premium Japanese melons, saying he rejects the suggestion that his comments were disrespectful.
The controversy erupted during a July appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, hosted by comedian Nikki Osborne, where Albanese discussed an unusual gift he received from Takaichi during her visit to Australia in May.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor on Tuesday demanded that Albanese personally apologize to Takaichi, describing the remarks as insulting and beneath the office of prime minister.
But Albanese dismissed the criticism during parliamentary question time.
“I reject the assertion in the question,” he said when asked whether he would apologize for what opposition lawmakers described as disrespectful behavior.
“Prime Minister Takaichi is a friend of Australia and a friend of mine,” Albanese said, adding that Australia and Japan have never been closer or more strategically aligned.
The comments concerned two Shizuoka Crown Melons presented to Albanese by Takaichi during a dinner in Canberra on May 4. Japan’s prime minister’s office confirmed that Takaichi presented Albanese with a Shizuoka-grown Crown Melon before the dinner, highlighting the significance of the gift as Australia had only recently lifted restrictions on imports of Japanese melons.
Crown Melons are among Japan’s most prestigious fruits. They are cultivated under highly controlled conditions using a system in which only one fruit is allowed to mature on each plant, making them a luxury gift in Japanese culture.
During the podcast, Osborne asked Albanese about the strangest gifts he had received while traveling or hosting foreign leaders. He mentioned the melons from Takaichi and joked about how they had made it through Australian customs.
“I got a couple of melons,” Albanese said.
Osborne then made a comparison involving Pamela Anderson. Albanese did not make that comparison, despite social media posts and some commentary attributing it to him, according to an AAP fact-check.
The episode also included a separate exchange in which Albanese was asked to choose among several celebrities in a “shag, marry or date” game. He selected singer Kylie Minogue for “all of the above,” comments for which he later apologized.
The melon remarks initially attracted less attention but resurfaced weeks later, prompting a political backlash and criticism from former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami.
Yamagami argued that Albanese's comments were inappropriate given the cultural and diplomatic significance of the gift. Australian opposition politicians subsequently seized on the issue, accusing the prime minister of using crude humor when discussing a female foreign leader and an important diplomatic partner.
The Australian government, however, has pushed back against the criticism.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Albanese had made clear that he did not intend the comments to be interpreted as an insult. Other government figures have also argued that the podcast was a comedic setting and that the remarks have been taken out of context.
More importantly, Japan itself has shown little appetite for escalating the controversy.
A Japanese diplomatic cable reportedly described the Australian media coverage as sensationalized and found no ill intention in Albanese's remarks. Japanese officials indicated that they did not intend to pursue the matter further, underscoring the government's preference to protect the broader bilateral relationship.
That relationship has expanded significantly in recent years.
During Takaichi's May visit, Australia and Japan announced agreements covering critical minerals, energy security and defense cooperation. The two countries have also strengthened their strategic partnership as they seek greater economic and security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific.
The Japanese prime minister's office said the May summit dinner was held in a relaxed atmosphere and that both leaders reaffirmed the importance of cooperation while deepening their personal relationship.
For Albanese, the controversy comes after an already damaging podcast appearance that forced him to apologize for the comments about Minogue.
But he has drawn a line between that apology and the separate controversy over the Japanese gift, refusing to offer another apology despite mounting pressure from the opposition.
As of Tuesday, there was no indication that Takaichi or the Japanese government had formally requested one.

Gangs using Airbnb-type rentals as drug stash houses, top Belgian official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:47:13 UTC
16:47:13 KST

Airbnb-type short-term rentals are being used as stash houses by criminal gangs for money, drugs, weapons and people, Belgium’s lead official in charge of countering drugs has said.
The booming e-commerce sector is helping “enormously” to facilitate organised crime, Belgium’s national drug commissioner, Ine Van Wymersch, said.
Authorities did not have a precise idea of the scale of the problem but criminals were taking advantage of the flexibility offered by short-term booking platforms, she told the Guardian.
“You need someone to pick up a cargo from the harbour. You don’t know exactly when the boat will arrive. Well, you can hire an Airbnb apartment or studio for three days. It’s very flexible. If the boat is not coming to Antwerp but going to Marseille, there is free cancellation.”
She said short-term rental companies had “a very good legal purpose” but needed to be more resilient to avoid abuse by criminals.
At the beginning of August, police seized 3.3kg of cocaine and €4,845 (£4,140) in cash from an apartment rented on Airbnb in central Brussels, which was believed to have been used for storing and packing drugs, the news agency Belga reported. In 2024 when 11 people were sentenced for their role in a vast drug trafficking operation between Belgium and the UK, it was revealed that drugs worth €21m were seized from an Airbnb rental in Staden, West Flanders.
A representative for Airbnb in Belgium declined to comment but directed the Guardian to recent remarks by Clément Eulry, Airbnb’s country manager for France and the Benelux.
He told De Staandard that such criminal bookings represented an extreme minority among the millions the company processes annually. He said every case was one too many and the company undertook various measures, including using artificial intelligence to identify suspicious bookings. He said reports of problematic renters were always notified to police and local authorities.
Short-term rentals are only one facet of the modern economy making life easier for organised crime.
Van Wymersch cited the ease of setting up anonymous email accounts, encrypted communications, cryptocurrency and the ubiquity of parcel delivery. “The fact that e-commerce is booming business is facilitating enormously organised crime.”
She said delivery firms were also “very at risk” of being instrumentalised by organised crime, because “it is not a suspicious situation any more when you see that there is a white van stopping at your neighbour’s house and … a small box handed over”.
Van Wymersch became Belgium’s first-ever national drug commissioner in 2023 after Antwerp was firmly established as one of Europe’s main gateways for cocaine.
Her appointment followed a wave of drug-fuelled violence and threats. In 2022 the then Belgian justice minister had to live under police protection after an alleged plot to kidnap him was uncovered. Antwerp endured a spate of grenade attacks and the fatal shooting of an 11-year old girl, the victim of a conflict between rival drug gangs.
Last year an anonymous investigative judge – who was forced to live in a safe house for four months – warned that Belgium risked becoming a narco state in an excoriating critique of the government’s response.
The narco state warning originated with Van Wymersch. She agreed, she said, with her earlier opinion that “if we don’t do anything, we are at risk to become a narco state … where you don’t know any more who are the good guys and who are the bad guys”.
Her priority is going after criminal money: “This multi-headed monster only has one heart and that’s the money.”
Her strategy means targeting small businesses – hairdressers, nail bars or night shops – used for laundering money. Her message to local authorities was that they needed to inspect and investigate “the dodgy shop” in their neighbourhood: “It matters because all these small businesses are one big network.”
She said criminal gangs had changed their modus operandi, exploiting small business, rather than using the “big money-laundering constructions” of the past.
Organised crime had morphed from top-down pyramid hierarchies bonded by trust into looser anonymous networks where criminals “don’t know to which network they are belonging any more”, she added.
Illicit activities are outsourced to different gangs, who specialise in money laundering, procuring or using weapons. “It is really crime as a service and it’s very opportunistic,” she said.
After a rapid rise through Belgium’s judicial system, Van Wymersch is known for articulating an “iceberg strategy” to combat organised drug crime.
The shootings and explosions are the visible part of the iceberg, she said, while below the waterline are harms not always linked to organised crime, from people killed by drivers under the influence, to victims of drug-fuelled domestic violence and sexual offences.
While stressing the importance of the police, she said society needed to guarantee young people a stake to prevent them being drawn into drug gangs – essentially melting the iceberg. “We need to invest in warming up the temperature of the water,” she said citing education, anti-poverty strategies, housing and adequate pay for delivery workers.
In Brussels, police recorded 101 shootings in 2025, reported by local media to be a record high, often resulting from turf wars between gangs. Van Wymersch sees a link between the increase in shootings and social problems, “because the people that are shooting are people without any perspective”.
In Brussels 12.8% of people aged 15-29 are not in education, employment or training – above the national average – although numbers have been on a downward trend since the millennium.
“It is naive to believe that a purely repressive approach will reduce the number of shootings,” Van Wymersch said. “We will see fewer shootings only when there are fewer vulnerable people. In fact, we need to strengthen the resilience of society as a whole.”
The European Holiday Home Association, which represents Airbnb and other platforms, said the companies were best placed to respond.
Van Wymersch said her team planned to be in touch with online booking platforms: “What we want to know now is what are the criteria for suspicious booking, what can we learn from that, how can we help you to be more resilient.”

- Emergency services are operating on site.
- According to the governor, falling UAV debris damaged three trucks and one passenger car.

- Rescuers are still battling a fire at the other facility.

- The company had evacuated workers at the facilities in advance.
- The RWB noted that it has suspended the acceptance of new supplies and rerouted them to other facilities.

With Ukraine short of Patriot interceptors, Russia sees no reason to enter real negotiations, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:42:38 UTC
16:42:38 KST

Russia has rebuilt its missile industry around the weapons most likely to pierce Ukraine's thinning air defenses. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) made that case on 10 August. Kyiv's Patriot interceptor shortage, it assessed, now hands Moscow no reason to negotiate. Because Kyiv can no longer reliably stop ballistic missiles, the Kremlin sees a clear military path to its maximalist aims.
Factories retooled around the missiles that get through
Since April 2026, Russian plants have prioritized ballistic and cruise missiles built to evade interception. HUR Deputy Head Major General Vadym Skibitskyi reported the shift. Monthly ballistic launches have more than tripled between April and July, he said. Meanwhile, output of key missile types runs 10 to 20% above plan. Moscow also met its full-year Zircon and Onyx targets by 3 August. To free capacity, it suspended the less accurate Kinzhal and Kh-32 lines. Skibitskyi flagged a newer twist, too: S-400 launchers now fire specially developed RM-48U rounds along a ballistic path. Russia is also striking Ukraine's defense plants, he warned, to choke off Kyiv's own ballistic-missile program.
Fired fresh, not from the stockpile
Crucially, these strikes draw on newly built missiles rather than war reserves. That approach lets Moscow sustain larger, more frequent salvos. Its stockpile stays intact for the occasional very large barrage. Unmanned Systems Forces commander Major Robert "Magyar" Brovdi put numbers on the trend. Russia can already loose a simultaneous salvo of 77 missiles, and it is pushing toward 200. He stressed that he meant weapons of all types, not ballistics alone. Kalibr cruise missiles, by contrast, are piling up unused. Moscow is shipping them to fleets beyond the Black Sea as Ukrainian crews down nearly all of them. Repeated strikes have meanwhile driven the Black Sea Fleet back to the port of Novorossiysk.
"The Patriot shortage hands Russia an opening to do serious damage over the winter — and a reason to keep meaningful talks at bay," - Institute for the Study of War assessed
Why the Patriot interceptor shortage stalls negotiations
This reprioritization feeds a winter strategy meant to break Ukraine's will to fight, ISW assessed. The Patriot is still the only system Kyiv fields that can down Russian ballistic missiles. And Kyiv has warned partners it cannot close the interceptor gap before the cold months. As a result, the Kremlin thinks it can hammer cities without paying a battlefield price. That calculation could drag the war into 2027, ISW noted. Putin's theory of victory still rests on outlasting Ukraine's defenses and Western resolve. On 9 August, Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin restated Moscow's line. Any "freeze" that ignores the war's "root causes" is unacceptable, he said — shorthand for the Kremlin's original demands.

Amber heat health alerts kick in across most of England ahead of fifth summer heatwave – latest news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
