Germany news: Rhine levels could cause production cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:39:00 UTC
15:39:00 KST

Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows
Published August 11, 2026last updated August 11, 2026
What you need to know
- Economic experts expect cuts to industrial production because of reduced cargo shipping on the Rhine river
- All shipping past the town of Kaub has now stopped due to record low levels
- Wildfires caused the temporary closure of a major autobahn in northern Germany
- The number of children involved in road accidents has increased
Join us as we cover these and other stories hitting the headlines in Germany on Tuesday, August 8.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Some shipping stops on Rhine as level keeps dropping
New record-low water levels have been measured on the Rhine, a vital transport waterway, with some cargo vessel owners stopping shipping on river sections in the south.
The inland navigation agency WSV reported that the gauge at Kaub, near Koblenz, had fallen to an all-time low of 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) on Tuesday, indicating that the river depth is about 115 centimeters at its deepest point .
A commodity trader told the Reuters news agency that it was "no longer to book cargo shipments on the Rhine past Kaub."
"Most sailings there have stopped," the trader said.
Traders said that sailings on northern sections of the river were continuing.
Germany, along with much of Europe, has experienced a series of heat waves and a long period without meaningful rainfall this summer, leading to low water levels in several rivers.
The situation is having not only an environmental but also an economic impact, with companies that are reliant on goods normally transported via water suffering supply shortfalls.
The ships that are still sailing are carrying much lighter loads than usual and at higher prices.
In pictures: Rhine water levels hit historic low
Endurance athlete to swim 200 kilometers from Frankfurt to Cologne for child water safety
The 31-year-old endurance swimmer Nathalie Pohl took to the water in the Main River in Frankfurt on Tuesday at the start of a planned 200-kilometer (125-mile) swim to Cologne.
Pohl intends to swim via the Main and Rhine rivers to her destination over four days in a feat aimed at drawing attention to the importance of safe swimming, particularly for children.
According to figures from the German Livesaving Association (DLRG), at least 261 people have died by drowning this year up to the end of July.
The action is intended to raise money for swimming projects and education.
Swim not without risks
She is being accompanied by other swimmers who will put in one-hour sessions between her two-hour stints in the water.
Ahead of the start, Pohl showed herself unfazed by the possibility that low water levels in the Rhine could mean a weaker current at her and her team's back.
"Enough water is there and it shouldn't be a problem," she told the German DPA news agency, saying, however, that she hoped the algae that thrive in low water would not affect her health.
Pohl received a special permit for her action, with German authorities fundamentally warning against swimming in large rivers.
"Ultimately, something can always happen," she said, while stressing that she and her team had a comprehensive safety concept.
What you need to know about low river water levels
Water levels in several rivers in Germany, including the Rhine, have hit record lows that are well below normal for this time of year, causing severe disruptions to river traffic, with ships cutting their loads by about 80%.
The water shortage comes during a prolonged dry period in Germany, accompanied by frequent heat waves, both of which are attributed by scientists partly to the effects of human-induced climate change.
But why is the situation so serious for Germany, and what are the key terms in connection with low water levels?
The Rhine: A vital transport waterway
The Rhine has been used as a transport corridor for much of western Europe since Roman times.
It is the most important waterway in Europe, connecting industrial regions in Germany, Switzerland and other countries with big North Sea ports, including Rotterdam in the Netherlands.
Although only one in 10 tons of freight in Germany is transported via rivers such as the Rhine, they are much used for certain goods, including ore, oil, chemical products and coal.
As a result, industries that depend on these for their production are likely to be forced to cut their output, as not only is supply reduced in the current situation, but transport prices have also gone up massively.
What are river gauge measurements?
The depth of water in German rivers is measured by gauges (Pegel) situated at strategic points on their course.
These gauges, which are mostly located near the banks of a river, measure the depth of the river over an arbitrarily selected baseline.
This means the measurements are only an indication of the actual navigable depth, which can be much more.
For instance, although the gauge at the town of Kaub currently measures 16 cm (6.3 inches), the depth of the river in the channel used by shipping there is around 129 cm.
Why is the gauge at Kaub so important?
Kaub is situated on the Middle Rhine between St. Goar and Budenheim.
This section of river is seen as a chokepoint for shipping on the Rhine, as the navigable channel is not as well developed as in other places.
It has also long been used since 1856 as a key location to measure low water levels in the Rhine.
The previous lowest measurement in Kaub was 25 cm (9.8 inches) on October 22, 2018.
The present measurement of 16 cm is thus already a historic low — and it is expected to sink to single figures in the next few days.
Child road accidents rising steadily
More children were killed or injured in road accidents in 2025 than in in the previous year. That represents a renewed rise in road deaths and injuries affecting children since a decline during the coronavirus pandemic, statistics show.
Altogether 29,270 children under the age of 15 were injured in traffic accidents in Germany last year, a 7% increase over 2024, the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Monday.
The number of children killed in such accidents also rose from 53 in 2024 to 74 in 2025.
Of those fatalities, 30 were children under 6, well up on the number of children in that age group that were killed in 2024 (18).
The largest increase in deaths was seen in children travelling in cars (21 to 31).
The number of children killed on their bicycles in 2025 rose to 13 from 8 the previous year, while 4 were killed riding e-scooters, compared with none in 2024.
Most of the children involved in road traffic accidents in 2025 were riding a bicycle (34%). Altogether 31% were in a car, 20% were on foot and 8% were travelling on an e-scooter when the accidents occurred
"On average, a child was injured or killed in a road traffic accident every 18 minutes in 2025," Destatis said.
Germany needs planned intelligence agency reforms, top politician says
The chairman of the parliamentary panel overseeing Germany's secret services, Marc Henrichmann, has defended the new powers planned for intelligence agencies.
"The latest security incident at the Leipzig freight airport has shown once again that we are dealing with a new quality of hybrid threats," Henrichmann told the daily Rheinische Post.
An explosives-laden unmanned aerial vehicle was flown into the airport last week.
Henrichmannsaid that cyber attacks, sabotage and unauthorized drone overflights were "now part of a reality for which we have to be better prepared."
For this reason, he said, both the foreign intelligence agency (BND) and the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) needed the "necessary legal and technical options" to detect threats early on and identify their sources.
The reform plans have met with criticism from civil liberty activists.
The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) has voiced fears that they could lead to a "massive increase in power for intelligence agencies.
"The BND and BfV are to be allowed to intervene profoundly in basic rights with expanded use of government spyware, AI analyses practically without protective measures, access to private video cameras and even hack-backs although the legal hurdles often remain vague and too low," the organization's Kai Dittmann said.
He called for the draft bill to be thoroughly revised, calling it "unconstitutional in many parts."
The draft reform bill is set to be approved by the German Cabinet on Wednesday.
Autobahn reopens after closure because of wildfire
A highway in the northern state of Lower Saxony has reopened after being closed for over 12 hours as wildfire smoke dangerously reduced visibility.
Police closed the A7 autobahn to traffic between Göttingen and Kassel on Monday afternoon after thick smoke from the fire near Hannoversch Münden engulfed the road.
A police spokeswoman said some clean-up operations on a section of the motorway went on until the early hours of Tuesday morning but that both sides could now be used.
Low water in Rhine will cause production cuts — IW research institute
The reduction in cargo being shipped via the Rhine because of low water levels will lead companies to cut production, a leading economic research institute reports.
"Transport routes south of Kaub are now threatening to become completely severed, meaning the Rhine is cut in two," Thomas Puls, the transport expert from the German Economic Institute (IW) told the daily Rheinische Post.
"Because neither road nor rail are able to take the goods needed, the most likely reaction of primary industries will be to reduce production," he said.
This assessment appeared to be confirmed by a spokesman for the chemical company Covestro, who told the paper that the shortfalls in supply caused by the disruption to Rhine shipping was already affecting production.
The spokesman said that the current lifting of a ban on trucks using the motorway on Sundays would be of only temporary benefit.
"Ship transport via the Rhine can barely be compensated on the road, as a cargo vessel that can carry 1,500 tons is the equivalent of around 60 trucks," he said. "So ship transport cannot be completely shifted to roads."
The record low water levels on the Rhine caused by a prolonged shortage of rainfall in Germany mean that ships are currently able to carry only around a fifth of the load they usually transport.
Welcome to our coverage
A warm guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!
And, as has so often been the case recently, that very river is at the focus of our reporting from Germany as low water levels cause major disruption to cargo shipping and thus potentially to the industries that depend on it.
Another main topic is the threat to national security from hybrid forms of warfare, as reflected in recent drone incidents at sensitive sites.
The government is moving to give intelligence agencies new powers to combat this threat, something that some see as a danger to civil liberties.
And we also take a look at statistics showing that road accidents involving children are on the rise again after a reduction during the coronavirus pandemic.

Barack Obama launches new podcast about books that have shaped him. How many have you read?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Barack Obama launches new podcast about books that have shaped him. How many have you read?
The list includes works by Toni Morrison, James Baldwin, and John le Carré
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Barack Obama is set to host a new podcast about six books that he says have shaped his worldview, including works by Toni Morrison, James Baldwin, and British spy novelist John le Carré.
A Great Book with Barack Obama will launch exclusively on Audible on 24 September, with the former US president discussing one of his chosen titles in each of the six episodes alongside a guest.
The guests are yet to be announced.
The series is a collaboration between Audible and Higher Ground, the media company founded by Obama and his wife Michelle.
The books Obama has chosen are The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Song of Solomon by Toni Morrison, All the Pretty Horses by Cormac McCarthy, Gilead by Marilynne Robinson, All the King’s Men by Robert Penn Warren, and Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy by John le Carré.
The Fire Next Time examines race and religion in America, while Song of Solomon follows a young Black man trying to understand his family history and his place in the world.
In All the Pretty Horses, a young Texan heads to Mexico in search of a new life while Gilead follows an ageing minister reflecting on his life, faith, and family.
All the King’s Men explores the rise and corruption of a powerful politician. Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy follows retired British intelligence officer George Smiley as he hunts for a Soviet mole.
“At a time when fewer people are able to sit down with a book, it’s important to remember the joy and power that can come from reading. And some books don’t just tell a story – they change the way we see the world,” Obama wrote in an Instagram post announcing the podcast.
“Great books have always helped me figure out who I am and what I believe. The six books featured in this series have stayed with me throughout my life, and each one has something to teach us about the human experience.”
Gilead, published in 2004, is the only book on Obama’s list that was written in the 21st century, with the other five dating from the 20th century. Obama’s connection with its author, Marilynne Robinson, goes back to his presidency when he invited the novelist to the White House for dinner and awarded her the National Humanities Medal in 2012.
Two years later, the pair met in Des Moines for a conversation published by the New York Review of Books, discussing Robinson’s views on Christianity and democracy, the role of fear in US politics and the influence of novels on Obama’s own understanding of citizenship.
Last month, Obama released his annual summer reading list, which saw books by Tayari Jones, George Saunders, Elizabeth Strout, Ben Lerner, and Colson Whitehead among his selections, alongside several other writers.
A Great Book with Barack Obama is the latest podcast collaboration between Higher Ground and Audible after projects like Michelle Obama: The Light Podcast, The Wonder of Stevie, and Fela Kuti: Fear No Man. The two companies entered into an exclusive first-look deal in 2022, under which Audible became the home for Higher Ground’s podcast projects.
Audible’s chief content officer, Rachel Ghiazza, said Obama had a “remarkable ability to connect books to the questions of who we are and how we see the world”, according to Variety. She said the podcast would feature “deeply personal conversations about books that have shaped not only a president but also a person and citizen”.
Dan Fierman, head of audio at Higher Ground, said Obama had “always been a champion of reading” and that the series would explore how books can “challenge us, comfort us, and change us”.
He also said the conversations would reflect Obama’s “genuine passion for literature”.
A Great Book with Barack Obama will debut exclusively on Audible on 24 September.

Explosive drone at Leipzig airport: whose DNA trail is it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:38:32 UTC
15:38:32 KST

Following the discovery of an explosive drone beside Ukrainian Antonov aircraft, investigators in Leipzig have found DNA traces. According to several media outlets, there are indications of a link to a case from 2024.
On the night of 5 August 2026, Leipzig/Halle Airport came close to disaster when a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator appeared near a cargo aircraft operated by Ukrainian Antonov Airlines. Ammunition destined for Ukraine is reported to have been on board.
According to new findings, reported by the weekly Die Zeit, CCTV footage shows that at around 7.30 pm the drone deliberately flew towards the Ukrainian cargo aircraft and slammed into its wing. The device packed with Semtex did not explode on impact, however, but bounced off the Antonov and fell to the ground. The explosives appear to have become detached from the drone. According to Bild, the drone struck the Antonov close to the aircraft's fuel tank.
The drone was not picked up by any security system later that evening; instead, according to the report, an airport bus driver noticed the dangerous device four hours after the collision. He stepped on the drone with his foot. The explosives were apparently lying some distance away.
DNA trace on the drone apparently leads to Lithuania
Five days after the incident at Leipzig Airport, Bild and Die Zeit report that investigators have secured DNA traces on the drone that failed to explode. No individual has yet been identified, but, according to Bild, there has been a match in the European DNA database and the trail apparently leads to Lithuania.
In addition, the DNA now secured is said to match that from an arson attack on 20 July 2024 on the DHL logistics centre at Leipzig Airport. The parcel bomb exploded on the ground rather than in the air on board the aircraft only because the DHL cargo plane was delayed.
Several suspects have been on trial in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius since the spring over the 2024 parcel bomb in Leipzig. The charge is "terrorism and sabotage on behalf of a foreign power". The Lithuanian prosecutor's office stated that the offences involving improvised explosive devices had been "organised and coordinated by citizens of the Russian Federation who are linked to the military intelligence services of the Russian Federation".
The defendants are alleged to have sent parcel bombs across Europe via freight services such as DHL and DDP. According to the Lithuanian authorities, the intended targets were Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. The EU judicial agency Eurojust in The Hague also believes Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, was behind the 2024 wave of attacks.
Following the discovery of the drone in Leipzig, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office is investigating on suspicion of attempted detonation of an explosive device and of endangering air traffic. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has so far avoided any hint that Russia might be responsible for the drone incident. During a visit to Leipzig, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke only of the possible involvement of "foreign powers".
The Kremlin denies any involvement by Russia in the drone attack on Leipzig. On Telegram, the Russian embassy in Berlin described it as a "provocation directed against Moscow" and warned of "a new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany".

Trump returns to an old weapon: Behind US's decision to economically choke Iran - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:38:09 UTC
15:38:09 KST

After months of war, strikes, threats, and negotiations that have so far failed to end the ongoing conflict, US President Donald Trump is returning to one of the oldest tools in the United States' arsenal against Iran: choking it economically.
According to a Wall Street Journal report, Trump has for now adopted a "wait and see" strategy, giving financial sanctions and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports more time to deepen the damage to the Islamic Republic’s economy instead of launching another broad round of strikes.
According to the report, the shift followed persuasion efforts within the administration. Trump’s aides presented him with data intended to show the extent to which existing sanctions have already hurt Iran.
Senior administration and White House officials have recommended tightening the current sanctions further and imposing new ones, based on the assessment that economic pressure could be the most effective way to force the Iranian regime to back down. Trump, at least for now, was persuaded and told his advisers that he would prefer not to order additional strikes.
Trump publicly announced the return to this approach on Monday, telling reporters that Iran has "no money," adding, "Iran is broke, completely broke."
Iranian economy in 'free fall'
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month that the administration’s economic policy had sent the Iranian currency into "free fall" and pushed inflation into triple-digit rates.
The decision to pursue the economic sanctions route comes as Trump currently has reservations about the two other options available to him. He is reluctant to return to an all-out war, but he is also wary of another round of negotiations with Tehran.
In recent days, talks surrounding the Strait of Hormuz have once again become complicated after Iran presented far-reaching demands in exchange for fully reopening the shipping route, including billions of dollars in US payments, the lifting of the blockade, and the withdrawal of US forces from the region.
From the White House’s perspective, the sanctions strategy offers another advantage: It allows Washington to maintain heavy pressure on Tehran without immediately entering a new military round that could drive up energy prices and trigger an Iranian response against infrastructure in the Gulf.
Risk of economic pressure
Former senior officials described this as the "optimal space" for the US, provided that increasing amounts of oil can continue to reach the market despite the threats. According to one, a bad agreement could effectively subsidize Iran’s reconstruction, while a major military escalation could shock the oil market if the regime survives the strikes and retaliates against energy infrastructure in the Gulf.
Economic pressure, however, also comes with risks. Experts who served in previous US administrations warned that an American blockade could further worsen Iran’s already difficult economic situation, and that this could make a response from Tehran more likely, as "no one should expect Iran to simply sit idly by while this is happening."
That is also the main vulnerability of the renewed strategy. It rests on the assumption that economic pain will force Tehran to yield before it chooses to escalate militarily.
US officials stressed that Trump could still change his mind, particularly in the event of a severe Iranian response. For now, however, the president is choosing to give time, sanctions, and the blockade a chance to do the work instead of aircraft and bombs.

'Evil incarnate': Hunter Biden, Tucker Carlson bond over criticism of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu

Tucker Carlson, one of the most prominent and provocative voices on the American right, and Hunter Biden, the son of former Democratic president Joe Biden, who for years was himself one of the right's favorite targets, bonded over a common enemy in an interview Carlson conducted with Biden on Tuesday: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and to a large extent Israel as well.
Biden is continuing an unusual round of media interviews. Last Friday, in an interview with the BBC, he spoke about his father's condition and said that the cancer affecting the former president had spread to his bones.
In the interview with Carlson, however, the discussion focused at length on the controversies surrounding Hunter himself, his drug addiction, the laptop that became a political weapon against the Biden family, and, at one point, Israel.
During the conversation, Carlson claimed that at the time of the Hunter Biden laptop affair, Israeli figures or figures with ties to Israel were the ones who pushed claims to him that material showing the abuse of minors had been found on the computer. It is important to emphasize that Carlson did not present public evidence for this claim during the segment, but described it based on what was referred to as his personal experience.
"The claim that there was material involving the abuse of minors on the computer came from the Israelis," he said. "I'm just telling you that they came to me with it, and that's how I know it."
Carlson rejects Russian involvement in Hunter Biden laptop
Carlson went on to claim that at the time, he sent one of his producers to meet with a person who, he said, had ties to Netanyahu. According to Carlson, this particularly angered him when former senior US intelligence officials instead pointed to Russia in connection with the affair.
"They were behind it," Carlson claimed. "I felt like everybody in Washington knew it, but there was so much pressure not to criticize Israel in any way that they just said, 'It's the Russians, it's the Russians.'"
Carlson also acknowledged that while he was working at Fox News, he did not say this publicly. "I admit it. I didn't say it. I was part of the problem too, but I knew."
It was precisely at this point that a symbiotic connection emerged between the two participants in the interview. Hunter Biden, who explained how deeply the serious allegations against him had affected him, moved on to discuss the criticism now directed at Carlson himself and rejected claims that Carlson is antisemitic.
"I'm supposed to hate Tucker Carlson because he's antisemitic and all of that stuff," Biden said to Carlson, adding, "I know you're not. You're not antisemitic. I know 100 percent you're not antisemitic."

I don't know what to tell people anymore," he said. "All you have to do is open your eyes. Literally, open your eyes, open your heart for one second and understand."
Carlson responded that, in his view, the claim that such criticism is antisemitic is "such an obvious lie," and effectively asked who else feels threatened by such an accusation.
Criticism of Israel spreading across US party lines
In doing so, two people who for years belonged to almost entirely opposing political camps found themselves agreeing on an issue that in recent years has become one of the deepest fault lines in American politics: attitudes toward Israel and Netanyahu.
Harsh criticism of Israel no longer comes only from the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, but has also gained a foothold in parts of the populist right and the "America First" movement, in which Carlson is one of the most influential figures. Biden and Carlson are not political partners, and their agreement does not turn the two camps into one.
But the moment in which the son of a former Democratic president and a star of the American right agree that Netanyahu is a legitimate target for the harshest criticism, and jointly reject the claim that such criticism is necessarily antisemitic, once again illustrates the extent to which negative attitudes toward Israel today cross the old dividing lines of American politics.

                    MINSK, 11 August (BelTA) – Forest access has been completely banned in 30 districts of Belarus, BelTA reports, citing data from the interactive map of the Forestry Ministry of Belarus.
In Brest Oblast, the ban applies to Stolin District. In Minsk Oblast, it affects Borisov, Lyuban, Slutsk, and Soligorsk. In Mogilev Oblast, bans are in place for Klimovichi, Kostyukovichi, Krasnopolye, Krichev, Mstislavl, Slavgorod, Khotimsk, and Cherikov. In Gomel Oblast, most forests are marked in red, meaning a complete ban on entry, while less severe restrictions remain in effect for Bragin, Lelchitsy, Loyev, and Khoiniki.
Restrictions on visiting forests are in effect across all other districts of the country. Verkhnedvinsk District is the only area where forest access remains fully permitted.
The Ministry of Forestry’s interactive map of forest bans and restrictions is constantly updated, providing real-time data on the situation in forests across the country’s districts and the introduction of restrictive measures. Information can also be confirmed through local district executive committees and forestries.

Russia sanctions bill introduced in US House of Representatives
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
09:36:44 EEST
15:36:44 KST

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has introduced a bill on sanctions against Russia in the House of Representatives, which the Senate passed earlier this month.
"Today I introduced the Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026 in the House, together with Steny Hoyer and 16 colleagues," Republican Representative Michael McCaul wrote on social media.
The Hill reported that the text of the bill is identical to the Senate version, which passed by an overwhelming majority of 86 to 11.
The publication estimated that a House vote on the bill will take place in the fall.
The House is currently on recess, meaning consideration of the bill cannot begin there until September.
The bill provides for maintaining sanctions in the future against Russian officials and major businessmen. The measures would also apply to state-owned enterprises and foreign companies that support Russia's military-industrial complex.
The document allows for tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil and gas, including goods from China and India. The exact tariff rate is to be determined by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
The Senate also held a vote on an amendment that would have stripped the administration of the ability to impose tariffs against buyers of Russian oil and gas, but senators did not support it.
At the same time, media have noted that, unlike senators, many members of the House have objections to the bill. In particular, many Democrats see it not so much as an attempt to pressure Russia as an effort by the White House to obtain a legal tool for imposing large tariffs against a number of countries. As a result, debate on the bill is expected to drag on, with numerous amendments likely to be introduced. There is as yet no certainty that Congress will ultimately pass the bill, according to reports.

The number of air conditioners in households and the electricity they consume are expected to double over the next decade, according to experts at the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry.
The ministry said rising temperatures during summer months and more frequent heat waves driven by climate change are increasing the use of air conditioners every year.
Research conducted by ministry experts projects a significant rise in household air conditioner ownership. According to the study, there were approximately 11 million air conditioning units in households in 2025. Projections indicate that this figure is expected to increase by 100 percent over the next 10 years.
In line with the growth in air conditioner numbers, total electricity consumption for heating and cooling purposes in households is also expected to rise. The study forecasts that electricity use from household air conditioners could increase from 6,000 gigawatt-hours in 2025 to more than 12,000 gigawatt-hours by 2035.
Türkiye has seen a notable increase in air conditioner sales in recent years, while electricity consumption for cooling during the summer has become one of the major components of overall power demand.

Five years on, Taliban broadens diplomatic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:32:53 UTC
15:32:53 KST

Nearly five years after returning to power, Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities have expanded working relations with regional and European governments, although Russia remains the only country to formally recognize their rule.
Formal recognition remains limited by concerns over the rights of women and girls. Trade, security and migration, however, have drawn a growing number of governments into direct contact with Kabul.
Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the government “seeks relations with all countries,” with neighboring states taking priority because Afghanistan’s economic interests are closely tied to the region.
Kabul has hosted envoys from China, Japan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Britain. Officials from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan also met in the Afghan capital in April as Central Asian governments pursued trade routes through Afghanistan to ports farther south.
Erica Gaston of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research said regional governments had long been “more pragmatic” in their dealings with the Taliban, largely accepting engagement as inevitable.
Taliban officials have promoted cross-border infrastructure and mining projects as the country struggles with cuts in international aid. Chinese and other foreign companies have shown interest in Afghanistan’s natural resources, although sanctions and the lack of wider recognition continue to deter investment.
Contacts with European governments have also increased. In June, a Taliban delegation held talks in Brussels with European Union officials and representatives of 15 member states, mainly on the return of Afghans without a legal right to remain in Europe.
Germany deported 31 Afghan men in July, including one without a criminal record — the first such case since the Taliban returned to power in August 2021.
Deeper ties remain constrained by the Taliban’s restrictions on women and girls. Girls are barred from secondary and higher education, while Afghan female staff have been prevented from entering United Nations premises since September 2025.
The International Criminal Court last year issued arrest warrants for Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani over allegations of the crime against humanity of gender-based persecution.
India has also strengthened its contacts with Kabul. In June, its U.N. envoy, Parvathaneni Harish, called for a reassessment of international sanctions on Taliban officials.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current U.N. sanctions regime must take that into account,” he said.

Nvidia links with Wall Street firms for $500bn AI financing deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:32:13 UTC
15:32:13 KST

Nvidia has struck a deal with six large Wall Street firms to raise more than $500bn (£370bn) to fund the datacentres, chip factories and power stations needed to fuel the artificial intelligence boom.
The Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, said on X that it marked “a major milestone for Nvidia and the AI industry”, as he posted a photo of himself smiling and giving a thumbs up alongside finance bosses involved in the deal, including the head of Goldman Sachs, David Solomon.
He confirmed that Nvidia, which has a market value of $5.3tn, had signed memorandums of understanding with Goldman, Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield and KKR to offer funding for what the industry calls “compute”, referring to hardware such as datacentres and chips that are used to run train and build AI.
“Many great AI companies, enterprises and AI clouds have demand for compute but do not yet have access to financing at the scale or cost required to build quickly,” Huang said, adding that the funding “will make AI factories more accessible to the companies, industries and nations building the future”.
The move highlights how rising demand for AI computing capacity is drawing institutional investors, as governments, companies and startups race to build out datacentres. Big tech companies have signalled that spending on AI was likely to surpass $730bn this year. However, there have been concerns over the link between high valuations of tech companies and the need for vast investments to support their ambitions.
Last month, the Bank of England warned that AI developments could pose a risk to financial stability, particularly if the companies who take on debt end fail to deliver sustainable profits, or face big disruptions.
“The pace of investment is unprecedented historically,” the Bank of England said in its financial stability report in July, noting that AI companies were increasingly taking on debt “to support investment in infrastructure”.
“If the scale of AI debt financing grows as expected over the coming years, an adverse shock to AI companies that results in losses or affects their ability to service debt could more materially affect global financing conditions,” it said, suggesting that it could lead to a credit crunch in which it would be harder and more expensive for businesses and households to secure loans.
The Bank also warned banks and private credit firms to consider they may not be getting the full picture about the risks they were taking in relation to the AI industry. “Given the different funding sources from which AI companies are drawing, and different levels of transparency in those arrangements, it may be difficult for financial firms to be aware of the full extent of their direct and indirect exposures to the AI ecosystem and AI companies,” policymakers said. “This could increase the risk that exposures to developments in AI are greater than anticipated, or not fully reflected in firms’ risk management.”
Nvidia said the funding arrangements would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates” for its customers. The company did not disclose the financial terms, investment commitments by individual firms or a timetable for deploying the planned $500bn.
“Every industrial revolution has been built on infrastructure: electricity, transportation, communications and computing, with every build-out enabled by external financing,” Huang said. “AI factories are the infrastructure of the intelligence era.”

10 books, 9 films and 8 songs about eclipses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:30:55 UTC
15:30:55 KST

With the 12 August total solar eclipse in sight, remember this cosmic event has long shaped culture, as spectacle and storytelling tool. Here is a cultural selection inspired by it.
Since Antiquity, eclipses have been interpreted as omens, as punishment or as romantic metaphors, and that fascination has left its mark on literature, cinema and music. In fact, the phenomenon has been depicted in numerous paintings, but how have eclipses influenced the most popular artistic creations?
Here is a look at 10 books, nine films and eight songs that, in one way or another, revolve around an eclipse.
10 books marked by an eclipse
1. 'The Odyssey' (Homer, 8th century BC) In Book 20 of the poem, the seer Theoclymenus interprets a sudden darkening of the sky as heralding the imminent death of Penelope's suitors, shortly before Odysseus confronts them.
A study published in 2008 linked that passage to a real eclipse observed in the Ionian Islands in 1178 BC. The work is currently on everyone's lips because of Christopher Nolan's film, although that episode is not mentioned in the movie.
2. The 'Song of Roland' (anonymous, 11th century) This medieval epic poem, which tells of the defeat of Roland and his army at Roncesvalles at the hands of the Saracens, describes a sudden darkening of the sky, storms and an earthquake as signs of a possible end of the world. It is a classic example of how medieval literature associated eclipses with ill omens.
3. 'A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court' (Mark Twain, 1889) Hank Morgan, a mechanic from Connecticut, travels back in time to 6th-century England and is sentenced to death by burning at the stake. He then remembers that a solar eclipse is approaching and threatens to plunge the world into darkness if his life is not spared, which allows him to escape and earn a reputation as a sorcerer at King Arthur's court.
4. 'King Solomon's Mines' (H. Rider Haggard, 1885) A few years before Twain, Haggard had already resorted to a very similar device: an explorer who knows the date of an imminent eclipse persuades the Kukuana tribe that he can hide the Sun with his powers, and in exchange demands that the people obey his orders.
5. Diaries (Virginia Woolf) The author of 'Mrs Dalloway' travelled in 1927 to the north of England to witness the first total eclipse visible in the country in almost 200 years. In her diaries she describes how the light disappeared completely for a few seconds and then returned all at once, which she herself noted as the most astonishing moment of the experience.
6. 'Dolores Claiborne' (Stephen King, 1992) The protagonist plans her husband's death, a violent, alcoholic man, taking advantage of the real solar eclipse that could be seen in the United States in 1963. Years later, during a police interrogation over another death, she recalls that episode to the investigators.
7. 'Gerald's Game' (Stephen King, 1992) Published in the same year as 'Dolores Claiborne', this novel also assigns a key role to the 1963 eclipse, which King used as the backdrop for two different stories told in very different tones.
8. 'Nightfall' (Isaac Asimov, 1941) On the planet Lagash, permanently lit by six suns, its inhabitants have no concept of darkness. When astronomers announce that a total eclipse will leave the planet without light for the first time in 2,000 years, society is confronted with something for which it is utterly unprepared. It is regarded as one of the best science-fiction short stories of the last century.
9. 'The Eclipse' (Augusto Monterroso, 1959) In this very short Guatemalan story, a Spanish friar lost in the jungle tries to save himself from being sacrificed by a group of Maya by warning them that, thanks to his knowledge, he is capable of darkening the Sun. The ironic ending turns his expectations completely on their head.
10. 'Total Eclipse' (Annie Dillard, 1982) This essay, included in the book "Teaching a Stone to Talk", recounts the author's journey to the Yakima Valley in Washington State to observe a total eclipse in 1979. Dillard describes the experience as something that completely transforms one's perception of reality, far more unsettling than she herself had expected.
Eclipse inspiration on screen
1. 'Barabbas' (Richard Fleischer, 1961) To film the crucifixion scene in this epic production, the crew timed the shoot to coincide with a real solar eclipse that took place in Italy on 15 February 1961, and deployed more than 40 cameras across Tuscany to capture the phenomenon's strange light.
2. 'Eclipse' (Michelangelo Antonioni, 1962) That same Italian eclipse of 1961 inspired Antonioni to choose the title of this film, starring Alain Delon and Monica Vitti, one of the classics of European cinema of the 1970s.
3. 'Ladyhawke' (Richard Donner, 1985) The two protagonists of this medieval fantasy, played by Michelle Pfeiffer and Rutger Hauer, are under a curse that turns her into a hawk during the day and him into a wolf at night. Only a solar eclipse, a day without night and a night without day, allows them to recover their human form at the same time.
4. 'Apocalypto' (Mel Gibson, 2006) Set on the Yucatán peninsula in the early 16th century, the film shows its protagonist about to be sacrificed atop a Maya pyramid when a solar eclipse, interpreted by the priests as a sign from the Sun god, allows him to save his life.
5. 'Dolores Claiborne' (Taylor Hackford, 1995) A film adaptation of Stephen King's 'Dolores Claiborne', starring Kathy Bates and Jennifer Jason Leigh, which retains the central role of the 1963 eclipse in the plot.
6. 'Gerald's Game' (Mike Flanagan, 2017) Netflix's version of Stephen King's novel of the same name, starring Carla Gugino, which also brings back the 1963 eclipse as a central narrative element.
7. 'Darkness' (Jaume Balagueró, 2002) In this horror thriller, a family moves into a house near Barcelona where, 40 years earlier, six children had been sacrificed in a ritual that coincided with a solar eclipse.
8. 'Venus' (Jaume Balagueró, 2022) The director of 'Darkness' once again turned to the motif of the eclipse in this film, in which a demonic entity tries to possess the protagonist, played by Ester Expósito, during the phenomenon.
9. 'Verónica' (Paco Plaza, 2017) Set during the 1991 solar eclipse in Madrid, the protagonist holds a seance with a ouija board in the middle of the phenomenon, with consequences that shape the rest of the film.
Eclipse in music
1. 'Total Eclipse of the Heart', Bonnie Tyler (1983) Written and produced by Jim Steinman, it became the biggest hit of the Welsh singer's career and a classic that gets played every time there is an eclipse anywhere in the world. Tyler died last July at the age of 75, just a few weeks before this eclipse, which her song has ended up turning into the phenomenon's unofficial anthem. Link:
2. 'Eclipse', Pink Floyd (1973) The track closes the album 'The Dark Side of the Moon' with a melody that builds to a climax and ends with the same heartbeat that opens the record, thus completing the circle of the whole album. Link:
3. 'You're So Vain', Carly Simon (1972) In one of its most memorable verses, the singer tells how the song's protagonist flies by private jet to Nova Scotia, in Canada, to witness a total solar eclipse, one of pop's most frequently cited references to this phenomenon. Link:
4. 'Eclipse Total del Amor', Lissette (1984) A Spanish-language version of 'Total Eclipse of the Heart', recorded by Cuban singer Lissette for her album 'Caricatura', with its own lyrics that depart in part from the original and that became a hit in Spanish-speaking countries. Link:
5. 'Eclipse' (feat. Los Macorinos), Natalia Lafourcade (2018) Included on 'Musas, Vol. 2', the album in which the Mexican singer pays tribute to Latin American folk music together with guitar duo Los Macorinos, this song uses the image of a lunar eclipse to describe the sadness of heartbreak. Link:
6. 'Eclipse de Luna', Luciano Pereyra (2000) A track from the Argentine singer's album 'Recordándote' that uses the image of a lunar eclipse as a metaphor for a night of passion. Link:
7. 'Total Eclipse', Klaus Nomi (1981) The German singer and countertenor, one of the most singular figures of New York post-punk, turned the eclipse into a metaphor for a nuclear catastrophe in this song, one of the most memorable tracks of his career, which he first performed at the festival "Urgh! A Music War" in 1980. Link:
8. 'Bad Moon Rising', Creedence Clearwater Revival (1969) Written by John Fogerty, it does not speak of an eclipse in the strict sense, but its lyrics about earthquakes, storms and dire omens under a menacing moon have made it a regular feature of playlists devoted to astronomical phenomena and dark portents. Link:
Bonus track
'Eclipse', Delta Goodrem (2026) The Australian singer represented her country at Eurovision 2026 with this track, written together with Jonas Myrin, Ferras Alqaisi and Michael Fatkin, which uses the image of an eclipse as a metaphor for a love that aligns two different worlds in a perfect instant.
The video, shot on the dunes of Newcastle, stages that crossing between light and shadow. The song reached the final of the festival, held in Vienna, where it finished in fourth place. Link:
At Euronews we will be offering live coverage of the eclipse, so if you cannot get to the eclipse path in Spain, or if you are outside Spain, we invite you to join us to experience the total solar eclipse, a rare event that has not occurred in the Iberian Peninsula for more than 100 years.

Colombia rescue efforts press on after quake with death toll expected to rise
- A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia's coffee region, killing at least 164 people and causing severe damage in cities like Cali and Pereira.
- Rescue teams, including volunteers and security forces, are searching through rubble for survivors, with hundreds injured and some trapped in collapsed buildings.
- The government deployed 1,000 security personnel to Cali to prevent looting and maintain order, imposing curfews amid fears the death toll may rise further.
AI generated
BOGOTA - Rescue efforts across western Colombia carried into a second day on Aug 11 as emergency workers dug through collapsed buildings and flattened homes, amid expectations that the death toll from the country’s most powerful earthquake in decades could rise.
The 7.4-magnitude earthquake tore through Colombia’s coffee-growing heartland early on Aug 10, killing at least 164 people.
The quake reduced multi-storey buildings to rubble in cities such as Pereira and Cali, and cracked apart one of the towers of a historic cathedral in the city of Manizales.
Emergency teams aided by the police, soldiers and volunteers worked through the night with excavators and, at times, their bare hands, hunting for survivors beneath debris.
In Cali, home to about 2.2 million people, at least 85 people were killed. Dozens of buildings were left leaning precariously or destroyed outright, forcing residents into the streets.
Several of the top floors of one of the city’s hospitals – some dedicated to paediatric care – collapsed upon themselves, leaving some patients trapped and forcing some 600 others to be tended to on a street strewn with rubble, hospital director Irne Torres Castro told Caracol television.
Carmen Yasmin Garcia, 43, a Cali resident volunteering with rescue teams, said on the afternoon of Aug 10 that her group had freed seven people from a collapsed building, but four others and a dog remained trapped.
“A moment ago, there was scratching but now we can’t hear anything. We still have faith that the dog is alive and we can get these people out,” Garcia said. “We need people with sticks and spades, the more people lending a hand, the better.”
In Pereira, capital of the hard-hit state of Risaralda, the authorities reported 66 dead.
The city also bore some of the most visible destruction, with entire residential blocks reduced to piles of concrete and twisted steel.
Video posted on social media and verified by Reuters showed the city’s airport violently swaying during the quake, with large chunks of the ceiling collapsing as people sheltered.
Another 13 people died in Choco, the rural province closest to the quake’s epicenter.
Security forces headed to Cali
Colombia’s President Abelardo De La Espriella, who assumed power just days ago, said 35 people died in Cali alone, while 188 were missing.
He said 1,000 members of the security forces would be deployed to the city by dawn, following reports of looting. Cali, as well as Pereira, implemented curfews on the night of Aug 10.
“Our intention is to cooperate in any way necessary. Here, there are no distinctions or ideological divisions when it comes to defending our people or showing solidarity,” De La Espriella told journalists on the evening of Aug 10.
The disaster has drawn comparisons to a deadly 1999 earthquake that devastated the same coffee-growing region, killing more than 1,000 people, as well as to catastrophic quakes that killed more than 6,300 in neighbouring Venezuela in June. REUTERS

Trump hid in catering cart during secret Turkey escape from Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:29:40 UTC
15:29:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump hid in catering cart in secret Turkey escape over alleged Iran threat
US President Donald Trump was secretly moved off Air Force One in an airport catering truck before leaving Turkey aboard a smaller military plane last month, part of an elaborate security ruse prompted by an alleged Iranian threat to assassinate him or attack his aircraft.
Trump had boarded the presidential Boeing 747 in full view of television cameras after attending a NATO summit in Ankara on 8 July, appearing to begin his journey to Britain aboard Air Force One.
But minutes later, he and several aides were concealed inside a catering truck of the kind normally used to load meals and supplies onto aircraft and driven across the airport to an Air Force C-32A, according to The Washington Post.
The smaller aircraft then secretly flew Trump to RAF Mildenhall in Britain, while the Boeing 747 departed Ankara separately carrying journalists and White House staff who believed the president was travelling with them.
The deceptive operation was reportedly triggered by intelligence pointing to an alleged Iranian threat against Trump or his aircraft, the Post reported.
Trump’s real location was concealed not only from journalists but also from some White House staff and senior officials, who reportedly believed for hours that he was aboard the presidential plane.
Reporters travelling on the decoy aircraft were instructed to keep their window shades closed before departure.
When they later asked Trump why, he told them they had been “probably on a dangerous flight”.
“But if I go, you go,” Trump added.
The operation took place a day after US forces renewed strikes on Iran on Trump’s orders following the collapse of negotiations aimed at ending the months-long war between Washington and Tehran.
The New York Times and CBS News had reported last month that US intelligence agencies had reportedly detected a specific threat of an attack against Trump or his aircraft, prompting heightened security precautions.
The episode initially raised questions over whether the new Boeing 747-8 gifted to the United States by Qatar and converted for presidential use was sufficiently secure.
Trump had flown to Turkey aboard the Qatari-gifted aircraft on its first international presidential trip, but announced before leaving Ankara that he would travel to Britain aboard the older Air Force One “for old time’s sake”.
The White House said at the time that the new aircraft would fly separately to RAF Mildenhall so US service members stationed there could tour it.
But Trump was not aboard either of the two Boeing 747s during the first leg of his journey.
After boarding the older Air Force One in front of cameras, Trump was moved into a catering truck positioned at a door on the opposite side of the aircraft, away from view. The truck was then lowered and transported him and several aides to the waiting C-32A.
Flight-tracking data and other material reviewed by the Post showed that the Qatari-gifted aircraft departed Ankara first for Britain using the call sign “SAM 33”.
The older Air Force One, carrying journalists and White House staff but not Trump, later used the presidential call sign “AF1” during the flight.
Trump’s C-32A, meanwhile, flew under the call sign “RCH18”, or “Reach 18”, which is generally used for military transport missions. Systems that would have allowed the aircraft to be publicly tracked were switched off, according to the report.
The three aircraft arrived at RAF Mildenhall within minutes of one another.
Trump was subsequently seen descending the stairs of the older Air Force One, indicating that he had been quietly transferred back onto the aircraft after arriving in Britain.
He then greeted US service members before boarding the Qatari-gifted presidential jet for the final leg of his journey to Washington.
The White House had publicly maintained that Trump left Turkey aboard the older Air Force One, while his actual whereabouts remained secret during the operation.
Asked about the revelations, White House communications director Steven Cheung did not directly address the deception but defended the security of the Qatari-gifted aircraft.
Cheung said the plane had been fitted with “high-level security protocols” and added that the United States had “many enemies” targeting Trump.
“We use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” he said.
Using a presidential aircraft as a decoy is not unprecedented. Bill Clinton employed a similar tactic during a visit to Pakistan in 2000, travelling aboard an unmarked executive jet while another aircraft served as a decoy.
Agencies contributed to this report.

우간다 청년들도 결혼비용에 부담…"지참금 소 15마리"

(서울=연합뉴스) 박성진 기자 = 한국 청년들이 결혼식 비용에 큰 부담을 느끼는 것과 마찬가지로 아프리카 우간다에서도 치솟는 결혼식 관련 비용이 사회적 문제가 되고 있다.
11일 우간다 인터넷 매체인 나일 포스트에 따르면 요웨리 무세베니 우간다 대통령은 늘어난 결혼 지참금과 호화로운 결혼식을 비판하며, 이런 커진 경제적 부담 때문에 많은 우간다 젊은이가 결혼을 포기하고 있다고 지적했다.
무세베니 대통령은 최근 고위 관료 딸 결혼식에 참석해 "(우간다 서남부) 바냔콜레 부족 사람들은 신랑이 신부 측에 주는 지참금으로 주민들에게 해를 끼치고 있다"며 "왜 소 15마리와 수백만 실링(100만 실링=약 38만원)을 요구하는가. 왜 당신들의 자녀를 파는가"라고 말했다.
그러면서 "당신들은 젊은이들이 결혼식을 두려워하게 만든다. 안타깝게도 일부는 빚을 진 채 결혼 생활을 시작하게 된다"며 각 지역 사회가 결혼의 본래 가치로 돌아가 검소하게 예식을 치를 것을 촉구했다.
국제통화기금(IMF)에 따르면 올해 우간다 1인당 국내총생산(GDP)은 1천480달러(약 210만원)로 국민소득 세계 하위권에 속한다.
무세베니 대통령은 자기 경험을 예로 들며 "나는 손주가 15명이다. 나는 8명의 하객만 초대해 점심 식사를 하며 결혼식을 올렸다"며 "호화로운 결혼식은 사람들에게 불편함을 주기 때문에 종교 지도자들이 설교를 통해 이 문제를 다뤄주기를 촉구한다"고 밝혔다.
무세베니 대통령은 1986년 쿠데타로 집권한 아프리카의 대표적인 장기 집권 지도자로 올해 81세다.
1996년 최초의 직선 대통령으로 선출된 뒤 헌법을 두 차례에 걸쳐 개정해 임기 제한과 입후보자 75세 연령 제한을 없애고 올해 40년 연속 집권 중이다.
나일 포스트는 무세베니 대통령의 발언이 지참금 관습과 점점 비싸지는 결혼식의 적정성에 대한 전국적인 논쟁에 불을 붙였다고 소개했다.

Why part of your brain stays awake when you sleep in an unfamiliar bed
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:27:44 BST
15:27:44 KST

Why part of your brain stays awake when you sleep in an unfamiliar bed
Most people have trouble sleeping for the first time in a new place
- Bookmark
Whenever Robinson Leoni spends his initial night somewhere new, the pattern remains identical: drifting off takes longer, nighttime awakenings occur far more frequently, and his total rest suffers.
At home, he averages seven hours. Spending an evening elsewhere—regardless of earplugs or mattress quality—drops his smartwatch total to roughly five hours.
"I feel normal, you know, no stress, nothing, but it’s just I notice I wake up continuously," said Leoni, a sales director for a tech company who travels once or twice a month for work.
He is experiencing what sleep specialists call the first-night effect. The phenomenon has been confirmed by dozens of studies and is believed to have evolutionary roots, according to Anna Wick, a senior sleep researcher at the University of Freiburg in Switzerland.
"It’s assumed to be an adaptation response that the sleeping brain remains vigilant in this unfamiliar environment," Wick said.
Ahmad Mayeli, a psychiatry professor and sleep researcher at the University of Pittsburgh, noted that most people experience it, and even those who do not notice it likely do on a minor level.
On average, individuals sleep about 20 to 30 minutes less in a new environment. His research found that the frontal lobe, an area linked to the deepest sleep stage, was more active, indicating a sense of alertness. Consequently, people sleep less overall and less deeply.
"They are saying that, like in dolphins, part of the brain is awake when you are sleeping," Mayeli said. "It’s not exactly like dolphins, but still, studies show part of the brain is sleeping less."
He noted that age makes a difference. The effect is more pronounced in children, adolescents, and older adults, and it typically worsens with age. Individuals in their 20s are the least affected.
"Maybe it’s the sweet spot," he said.
Mayeli suspects that the human brain may be wired to be wary of new places because, historically, unaccustomed surroundings were the most dangerous during rest.
"It doesn’t matter if it’s a Marriott hotel or it’s the savannah," he said. "Your brain hasn’t gotten the memo that this place is completely safe."
Wick said evidence suggests the effect fades after the first night.
Lisa Strauss, a psychologist specializing in cognitive behavioral treatment of sleep disorders, noted that several factors can impact sleep in a new setting beyond evolutionary vigilance.
Travel itself can have a negative effect, even within the same time zone. Environmental factors may get in the way, like a flashing smoke alarm light in a hotel room. Relational tension, perhaps while visiting distant relatives, could also contribute.
Strauss observed that some people may sleep better the first night if they are exhausted after a long day of travel or if the new location provides a sense of detachment from daily stressors. People who have trouble sleeping at home might also fare better because they do not associate the new environment with a history of restless nights.
While anyone can experience the first-night effect, Strauss said those who are more anxious at baseline are especially vulnerable. It becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy—the worry about whether they can sleep is what keeps them awake. Leoni acknowledged there are times he enters the first night contemplating how he will sleep.
"Sometimes the thoughts come automatically," he said. "You talk with your colleague, and you say, 'I’m going back to the room, but I’m not going to sleep anyway.’"
Strauss recommends general sleep hygiene practices such as going to sleep in a cool, dark room at the same time every night, following a nighttime routine, and turning off screens well before bed. These steps are particularly helpful if started or resumed in the days or weeks prior to an important trip.
She suggested people try to make the environment their own by spending a little extra time in the new bed. They could read or engage in another peaceful, familiar activity to make the experience less novel, or bring familiar objects, like a favorite pillow or blanket.
For someone who is particularly anxious, Strauss recommended visualizing themselves in a safe, familiar environment, such as on a favorite hike or beach.
They should notice the anxiety they are feeling, then repeat positive phrases to help lower feelings of hypervigilance: "May you know that you are safe. May you know that you are loved. May you be at peace."
Mayeli said the first-night effect is not really anything to worry about, and people can easily make up for missing an hour or two of sleep for one night. However, he recommends arriving a day early to acclimate before an important meeting or event.
"If tomorrow matters, get there a night early," he said, "so you’ll sleep like yourself when it counts."

日나가사키 원폭 추모식 좌석 배치 놓고 중·대만 '국격' 공방
South Korea
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:27:15 KST
15:27:15 KST

대만 "국격 훼손" 불참…中 "대만은 국가 아냐"
 
 (베이징=연합뉴스) 한종구 특파원 = 일본 나가사키 원자폭탄 투하 희생자 추모식의 좌석 배치를 둘러싸고 중국과 대만이 '국격' 공방을 벌였다.
 11일 대만 자유시보 등에 따르면 나가사키시는 지난 9일 열린 원폭 투하 81주년 평화 기념식에서 대만 대표단의 좌석을 외교사절단 구역 밖에 배치했다.
 이에 주일 대만대사 격인 리이양 타이베이 주일경제문화대표처 대표는 " 나가사키시가 의도적으로 대만의 국격과 지위를 낮췄다"며 행사에 참석하지 않았다. 
 대신 후쿠오카분처 관계자가 대만을 대표해 행사에 참석했다.
 리 대표는 "나가사키시가 중국의 의지에 굴복해 대만의 국격을 낮추고 존엄을 훼손했다"며 엄중히 항의하고 규탄한다고 밝혔다.
 중국은 즉각 반발했다.
 주일 중국대사관 대변인은 전날 홈페이지에 올린 입장문에서 "대만은 국가가 아니기 때문에 국격이라는 말이 존재하지 않는다"고 주장했다.
 이어 리 대표를 겨냥해 "분수를 모르고 곳곳에서 존재감을 과시해야 결국 스스로 망신만 자초할 뿐"이라고 비판했다.
 또 "세계에는 오직 하나의 중국만 있으며 대만은 중국 영토에서 분리할 수 없는 일부"라며 "중화인민공화국 정부가 중국 전체를 대표하는 유일한 합법 정부"라는 기존 입장을 거듭 강조했다.
 리 대표는 중국 측 비판이 나온 뒤 자신의 페이스북을 통해 이번 좌석 배치를 중국의 대만 압박과 연계하며 재차 반발했다. 
 그는 "대만이 외교사절에 준하는 대우를 받지 못한 것을 그대로 받아들이면 중국은 나가사키 사례를 근거로 히로시마 등 다른 일본 지방정부에도 같은 대우를 요구할 수 있다"고 주장했다. 
 그러면서 "대만이 이를 묵묵히 받아들이면 그 결과가 도미노 효과로 이어질 수 있다"며 "이런 선례가 한번 만들어지면 중국은 일본 각 지역에서 우리가 어렵게 구축해 온 대만과 일본이 구축해 온 관계를 훼손할 것"이라고 말했다.

Skywell ET5 fire incidents in Türkiye rise to eight in six months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:26:23 UTC
15:26:23 KST

A new fire involving a Skywell ET5 electric SUV in Istanbul on Aug. 10 has increased the number of reported fire incidents involving the model in Türkiye to eight over the past six months.
The Skywell ET5, an electric SUV imported from China, has recorded more than 3,000 sales in the Turkish market.
Ulu Motor, the Turkish distributor of Skywell, stated that investigations into previous incidents revealed that four of the affected vehicles had sustained significant underbody damage to their main battery packs before the fires occurred. In another case, the company said bodywork, repair, and paint operations had been carried out without removing the main battery and in a location deemed unsuitable for such procedures.
The distributor also reported that five vehicles involved in fire incidents were found to be operating with software that was not considered suitable for Turkish market conditions. Regarding the most recent fire, company officials said the possibility of unauthorized software modifications is being evaluated.
Some Skywell ET5 owners, however, dispute the distributor’s explanation. They argue that customer support has been inadequate since Türkiye introduced new requirements for imported Chinese electric vehicles, which led to the suspension of new sales of the model in the country.
One owner whose vehicle was recently damaged by fire said the car had never been serviced outside the authorized network and had undergone routine maintenance before a vacation trip. According to the owner, no unauthorized software had been installed and there was no known prior damage to the vehicle.
The owner also claimed that customers had been promised regular software updates when purchasing the vehicle but that several software-related issues remained unresolved. Some users have sought alternative solutions because they believe their concerns have not been adequately addressed, the owner added.
Under current Turkish legislation, products may be recalled by manufacturers or importers, either voluntarily or at the request of a competent authority, if other measures are considered insufficient to eliminate a safety risk.
As a result, attention is now focused on whether a broader technical investigation covering all Skywell ET5 vehicles in Türkiye will be conducted and whether a formal recall process may be considered.

Russia has lost around 1,460,400 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces reported on Aug. 11.
The figure includes 1,190 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day, according to the General Staff.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,259 tanks, 25,120 armored combat vehicles, 132,543 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,713 artillery systems, 2,020 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,560 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters 2,190 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Heathrow overtaken by Istanbul as Europe’s busiest airport
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:17:58 BST
15:17:58 KST

The busiest airports in the world, revealed
One UK aviation hub retained a spot in the top 10
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A new report has revealed the busiest airports in the world for 2025, with one UK aviation hub retaining a spot in the top 10.
Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International, in the US, was the busiest airport in the world last year in terms of total passenger traffic, according to the Airports Council International (ACI) annual rankings.
The Georgia airport retained the top spot after more than 106 million passengers travelled through it last year.
It had the title of the world's busiest airport for 22 consecutive years up until 2020, when Covid restrictions saw passenger numbers drop.
In 2021, Atlanta airport returned to the top of the list and has remained there since.
However, in 2025, overall passenger traffic fell by 1.6 per cent year on year. More than 108 million passengers travelled through the airport in 2024.
In second place on the list is, Dubai International airport, which recorded more than 95 million passengers in 2025 – a 3.1 per cent increase from the previous year.
The hub’s large numbers can be attributed to its role as a gateway to the UAE and its large number of connecting flights.
The airport may fall down the rankings next year, however, after passenger numbers plunged by more than half due to flight restrictions caused by the Iran-US war. Some 18.6 million passengers were reported in the first quarter of 2026, down 20.6 per cent year on year.
In third place for 2025 is Tokyo Haneda, which rose an impressive 6.7 per cent in passenger traffic to more than 91 million.
London Heathrow is the busiest airport by passenger traffic in Europe and the seventh busiest in the world, with 84 million passengers.
This is closely followed by the transcontinental city Istanbul, which recorded just 44,000 fewer passengers than Heathrow.
Other European airports, Paris (72m), Amsterdam (68m) and Madrid (68m) made it into the top 20.
Overall, global air travel reached 9.8 billion in 2025 across the 2,817 airports in more than 180 countries and territories according to the ACI dataset.
The world’s 20 busiest airports handled 1.59 billion passengers, representing 16 per cent of all air travellers globally.
The 10 busiest airports in the world in 2025, based on passenger traffic
- Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International, Georgia, US: 106,302,208 passengers
- Dubai International, UAE: 95,192,160 passengers
- Tokyo Haneda, Japan: 91,679,814 passengers
- Dallas Fort Worth International, Texas, US: 85,660,127 passengers
- Shanghai Pudong International, China: 84,994,548 passengers
- O'Hare International, Chicago, US: 84,856,018 passengers
- London Heathrow, UK: 84,482,126 passengers
- Istanbul airport, Turkey: 84,437,710 passengers
- Guangzhou Baiyun International, China: 83,582,952 passengers
- Denver International, Colorado, US: 82,427,962 passengers
According to the Airports Council International (ACI) annual rankings.

Mecca pact: How the Middle East is building a new order
After more than a year of talks, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a landmark defence pact last week in Mecca.
Bringing together Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim country, Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters and custodian of Islam’s holiest sites, and Turkey, NATO’s second-largest military, the agreement marks a significant shift in the regional security architecture.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack against one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all, echoing NATO’s Article 5. It also builds on the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) signed by Riyadh and Islamabad last September. Unlike that bilateral accord, however, the new arrangement could be expanded to include other countries.

오픈AI 윤리책임자, 1년 안돼 퇴사
South Korea
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
15:17:04 KST
15:17:04 KST

(서울=연합뉴스) 설원태 기자 = 오픈AI의 윤리책임자 클로이 바칼라르가 회사에 합류한 지 1년도 안 돼 회사를 떠났다고 파이낸셜타임스(FT)가 10일(현지시간) 보도했다. 
 오픈AI 대변인은 바칼라르의 퇴직을 확인하면서 "AI 윤리는 오픈AI 내 특정 개인이나 단일팀의 업무가 아니다. 윤리적 고려는 여러 팀이 주도하는 모델 구축 과정에 깊이 반영돼 있다"고 밝혔다. 
 6년간 메타플랫폼의 윤리책임자로서 인스타그램과 페이스북 등에 윤리 원칙을 반영하는 업무를 맡아온 그는 지난해 8월 오픈AI의 AI 윤리책임자로 이직했다. 
 바칼라르의 퇴사는 요하네스 하이데케 안전시스템 책임자, 미션 조율 책임자겸 미래학자인 조슈아 아키엄을 비롯해 오픈AI 고위직들이 최근 몇 주 새 퇴사한 가운데 나왔다.
 바칼라르는 최근 한 AI 콘퍼런스에서 "우리는 비행하면서 동시에 비행기를 만들어가고 있다"고 말했다. 
 바칼라르는 오픈AI에서 모델 개발에 대한 윤리적 접근법, 인간과 AI의 상호작용, 기계의 의식 여부를 둘러싼 논쟁 등을 주로 다뤘다. 그는 오픈AI의 유일한 전담윤리학자였으며 현재 그를 대체할 인물은 없는 것으로 알려졌다.
 기술기업들은 기술이 이용자와 사회에 미치는 영향을 다루기 위해 윤리학자를 영입했다. 이들의 역할은 제품 개발과 규제 대응으로 확대되는 경우가 많았다.
