====================================================================================================

Russian theater’s exiles and the artists who stayed have almost nowhere left to see each other’s work. Once a year, in Yerevan, they do.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:23:02 UTC
14:23:02 KST

Russian theater’s exiles and the artists who stayed have almost nowhere left to see each other’s work. Once a year, in Yerevan, they do.
After 2022, Russia’s theater community was left fractured: many directors, actors, and playwrights had to emigrate, parting ways with longtime collaborators. Entire institutions closed under pressure from the authorities: the Gogol Center, the Meyerhold Center, the NET festival, and the magazine Teatr (“Theater”). Almost no venues remain where Russians who left and Russians who stayed can follow one another’s work — with one exception: Chronofest, a festival organized in St. Petersburg by the theater company Khronotop and later moved to Yerevan. The independent journalists’ cooperative Bereg published a piece by the theater critic Alla Shenderova on the main events of the latest Chronofest, held in late spring and early summer 2026. Meduza is translating it in full.
Migrants dreamed up Chronofest and migrants run it: the director Ilya Moshchitsky, who moved from St. Petersburg to Yerevan, and Artyom Arsenyan, formerly the producer of two important theater festivals — St. Petersburg’s Tochka Dostupa (“Access Point”) and Moscow’s NET.
In 2020, Moshchitsky founded the theater company Khronotop in St. Petersburg; until recently, it called itself “temporary.” Chronofest became one of its projects. The first festival was held in St. Petersburg, at the very start of 2022. After moving to Armenia, Moshchitsky and Arsenyan revived Chronofest in Yerevan just a few months later.
From the start, what was expected of the project was not so much free artistic statements about what was happening — that, after all, would have required some distance in time. It drew people who no longer had any way to see theater in Europe and people hoping to see friends and family who had left to escape criminal prosecution.
That is how one of Chronofest’s most important roles today came about: it became a meeting place for theater artists from the East, the West, and Russia. Here, people from different countries — sometimes countries at war with one another — freely show each other and the public what they are making now, as everything changes fast and irreversibly.
Unlike many émigré theater ventures from the war’s first year, the festival did not shut down. It paused. The same team held the second Chronofest in spring 2025, and its influence was felt for a whole season afterward. One of the most notable events at another émigré festival, Voices. Berlin, was Alexander Plotnikov’s one-man show Alpha Centauri, based on the director’s debut book about cosmonauts who never made it into space. It had premiered at Chronofest in Yerevan.
The third “international festival of contemporary theater and performance” — as the Khronotop company describes what it does — ran in Yerevan from May 28 to June 7. Around the same time, incidentally, Khronotop stopped calling itself a “temporary association.” And rightly so: it would be good if this project were here for the long haul.
The Belgrade festival BITEF could be called Chronofest’s older relative and historical counterpart. It came into being in 1967 and quickly took its place among the world’s leading theater showcases.
The reason lies in more than the talent of its organizers, the playwright and director Mira Trailović and the poet and critic Jovan Ćirilov. Belgrade was then the capital of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where, for a variety of reasons, there were more rights and freedoms than in other countries of the socialist bloc. Ćirilov and Trailović managed to bring East and West, socialism and capitalism, together in a single lineup.
BITEF’s 1976 program, for instance, placed Yuri Lyubimov’s Hamlet, with Vysotsky in the role of the prince, alongside Robert Wilson‘s postdramatic Einstein on the Beach, which had neither a linear plot nor dramatic roles in the usual sense. That was where the festival’s main value lay: audiences and the casts of both productions saw radically different kinds of theater, and it noticeably broadened their sense of art in general. Wilson himself, many years later, in 1999, insisted at the Taganka Theater’s anniversary celebration that Lyubimov had influenced his own directing. In short, BITEF was theater’s breach in the Iron Curtain.
Chronofest has taken on a similar role: it is introducing Yerevan — a city with a strong theatrical tradition but almost no contemporary theater — to recent trends. Performers throw themselves into every master class with real relish: Armenians, relocated artists, and the visiting Germans who turned up for some of this year’s projects. That speaks to real demand.
The Chronofest 2026 lineup featured productions by directors from all over the world, predominantly Armenian and Russian but not exclusively. Even so, it was hard to say of most of the festival’s projects whether they were Russian, Armenian, or something else entirely. A good example is the work of the Russian émigré Alexander Plotnikov. His ethnographic performance The Book of Sorrow is the director’s personal account of a trip to present-day Turkey and the site of an ancient Armenian city; Love Radio, more traditional in form, is about a radio station that came into being in Soviet Armenia and broadcast in Kurdish.
This year’s program — or at least its first half — had a clear running theme. It may not have been formulated in advance. But from one production to the next, audiences watched different ways of working with memories: personal and archetypal, traumatic, repressed, recovered anew, and spoken aloud before our eyes.
The audiences at the performances and master classes were international. Every show carried English, Armenian, and Russian subtitles. You could watch Russian artists who hadn’t seen each other since February 24, 2022, meeting again — among them the longtime collaborators Dmitry Volkostrelov, a director who lives in Russia, and Ksenia Peretrukhina, an artist who moved to Finland. Chronofest’s format, with two or three events a day on the schedule, left little room for excess sentimentality — but meetings like these made a convincing case that the theater community torn apart by the war could still be glued back together.
Which Chronofest shows didn't make it into this piece?
The author wasn’t able to see the productions in the second half of the program. Among them was Birch Sap, by Anton Gusakovsky, a dancer and performer from Belarus, who describes his military service from a choreographer’s perspective. There was also Given Circumstances, in which the Khronotop company, Ilya Moshchitsky, and actors from the hosq contemporary theater workshop build their own dialogue with the Stanislavski system (the performance itself took place at the theater named for the system’s founder). And there was a production dedicated to the memory of the director Yuri Butusov: audiences were shown archival video of Butusov reading Mama, a play by Esther Bol (previously known as Asya Voloshina) — that footage reached Esther only after Butusov’s death.
Alexander Plotnikov, Love Radio
Alexander Plotnikov’s two productions are also an attempt, if not to “glue it all back together,” then at least to work out where the crack runs. His Love Radio is built on a startling fact: in 1955, Radio Yerevan began broadcasting in Kurdish. It was an unprecedented act of forgiveness and mercy toward Kurds who had once taken part in the Armenian genocide and were afterward scattered across Turkey, Syria, Iran, and Iraq, going a long time without even national autonomy.
Plotnikov named his production by analogy with Hate Radio, the Swiss director Milo Rau’s famous staging about the Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, where cheerful DJs told the people who went on to kill Tutsis in Rwanda exactly where to find them. In the story Love Radio tells, everything at first looks like the opposite.
Plotnikov separates the tiny audience area from the playing space with the glass of a radio booth, where two hosts, Arshi and Archi (Maral Kasbaryan and Manvel Sargsyan), literally radiate love — for their listeners and for each other. Their live broadcasts, and Arshi’s stories about what the Kurdish-language programming meant to her family, are full of tenderness. The ending, though, is thoroughly bloody. The director poses the question of boundaries: where does the recovery of national identity end and the nationalism that leads to massacre begin? And why, whatever kind of radio you set up — “Love” or “Hate” — do the consequences turn out terrible all the same?
Alexander Plotnikov, The Book of Sorrow
In this ethnographic performance, the director recounts his trip to the once-Armenian Lake Van and to the ruins of Narekavank, the monastery where the poet and theologian Grigor Narekatsi, author of the Book of Lamentations, lived 1,100 years ago. The good news: the author of many productions built on sorrowful pages of history shows some self-irony in this one. At the start, he tells the audience: “I’m not going to talk about the genocide. Even though there’s nothing I love more than talking about the genocide.” Then he wrestles with his own talkativeness: his prerecorded monologue is in Armenian, though Plotnikov admits his Armenian is still “terrible.”
Russian subtitles run over footage shot during the trip and over old photographs. Here is the late 19th century: “the pearl of Anatolia, the city of Van, which never once fell silent.” And here is the present: the remains of a wall from the ancient state of Urartu, where teenagers stash drugs between the stones.
A disgruntled driver suggests swapping the trip to the ruins (“There’s nothing there!”) for an ATV ride. Poor Kurdish neighborhoods in Turkey flash past. In voiceover, Plotnikov describes asking the driver to translate a question for the locals: “What stood here before the mosque?” There’s a pause. No one knows. At last a community elder shouts that there has only ever been a mosque there. And nothing else.
Here, at last, is what’s left of Narekavank’s thousand-year-old wall. As the director’s voiceover describes gathering old stones, twigs, and sand near the church, Plotnikov moves silently across the stage, arranging it all in a particular order — like scattered islands of antiquity. In another voiceover, he describes the particular “religious” silence inside the ruins of the ancient church, its dome full of holes. Then, with the composer Shahen Khandkaryan, he lets us hear a symphony of objects: stones, twigs, sand, and water knock and creak as Plotnikov joins them all into a single “continent” — metaphorically rebuilding everything that was destroyed.
Boris Nikitin, Magda Toffler, or an Essay on Silence
Silence of an entirely different kind was the subject of a production by Boris Nikitin, a Swiss director with Slovak, French, Ukrainian, and Jewish roots. His Magda Toffler is made very simply, in the same style as his Essay on Dying — a piece shown years ago in Moscow at the NET festival: Nikitin himself, in a white T-shirt, sits on a chair and reads his text from a sheet of paper. But this is a case where a formally simple staging is almost impossible to replicate. Nikitin has calculated every movement, every beam of light and intonation. By moving his chair closer to or farther from the audience, the performer signals different parts of the show.
Magda was Nikitin’s grandmother, who survived the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia. Even facing death, she never revealed the “terrible” secret to her children: that she was Jewish, and so were they. Nikitin never learned why. Her private story is framed by a larger one — the account of how, in October 1943, Himmler gathered 43 Gauleiters in occupied Poland and delivered a speech about the regime’s decision to exterminate Europe’s Jewish population completely. The SS chief spoke onstage in front of two phonographs, which recorded his speech and the scratchy silence in the hall: not one of the 43 made a sound. That silence, captured on two records, became evidence of fear, submission, and mutual complicity. Evidence that, as Nikitin puts it, “nothing will ever be normal again.”
That silence — and Magda’s own, since she never reclaimed her history or her identity — echoes in the protagonist’s halting attempt to answer a chance seatmate’s question on a flight to Israel. “So you’re Jewish?” “No. I mean, yes. I mean, no.” The words catch in his throat.
Ilya Moshchitsky, Michael Craig-Martin’s Oak
The 20th century accumulated so many unspoken traumas that they have today spilled into the conflicts tearing humanity apart. But how do we put them into words without manipulating one another?
Michael Craig-Martin’s Oak, by Ilya Moshchitsky, is partly about that. The director himself plays a driver who accidentally hits a little girl on the highway. The role of her father goes to a more or less randomly chosen audience member, who is expected, as the action unfolds, to agree to help the unwitting killer cope with the trauma. Before the full-scale war, the performance ran at Moscow’s Meyerhold Center. Whether Moshchitsky has since honed it to full virtuosity or the war has sharply changed how audiences perceive it, this story about the manipulative nature of theater — about how relative perception is, and how easily an audience’s feelings can be controlled — is staggering today.
Dmitry Volkostrelov, Gorky/Tolstoy
Volkostrelov is engaged in an ironic re-creation of memory: taking as his basis the recollections Gorky set down, he casts as the show’s characters the objects that supposedly came into contact with Tolstoy and hold their own memory of him. Volkostrelov is elegant, as always: he stands at the console himself, carefully laying out on a white sheet objects whose photographs are then projected onto a screen, along with captions such as: “The socks quote his words about science …” “The sand on the path remembers his footsteps …” Dry leaves and branches in the garden “comment on” Tolstoy quotations too. The audience greets each slide with delighted laughter, as if it were an old acquaintance.
But Gorky/Tolstoy is really about more than ”the memory of the noosphere” — and about more than Tolstoy and Gorky. Quotations from the writers’ conversations are voiced by the people the director worked with before the war at Teatr Post, a small theater that is probably Russia’s most unusual. Alyona Starostina, Ivan Nikolaev, and Ksenia Volkova have now all scattered, but thanks to Volkostrelov’s production, their voices are heard together again.
Hadas Neuman, 100 Men
The project by Neuman, who is Israeli, is another attempt to work through past trauma. One morning Hadas got up, took a camera, and walked down the street, filming and interviewing men she didn’t know: only older ones, roughly the age of the father who left the family when she and her brother were very small. We see Hadas’s interlocutors on screen; the performer herself is on a darkened stage. Like her camera, she is in motion for the entire show, walking on a treadmill. The metaphor of “running in place” has nothing to do with it here: over the course of the story, the narrator covers considerable ground. The climax comes in a park: one of the men she interviewed says he saw a man in a wheelchair who, by the description, resembled her father. The footage shakes as Hadas chases after the stranger — but the park is empty.
This bitter and, at bottom, very youthful performance is steeped in an acceptance of life all the same: at 40, the performer still finds the strength to see the situation from the outside. A broken childhood can’t be fixed, but the experience can be shared.
Alexey Kiselev and Siniy Karandash, This Is a Performance
“Do what you want today, because tomorrow may not come” — that piece of advice is probably worth taking as Chronofest’s slogan. It was spoken in the festival’s least classifiable show, called This Is a Performance. The critic and editor Alexey Kiselev and the artist Siniy Karandash made their medium chat roulette — a site that pairs you at random with strangers, fashionable in the early 2000s and suddenly back in circulation now. Users joined the video chat live during the performance, their faces appearing on screen, while Siniy Karandash wrote his own remarks beside them in his distinctive blue script. (Many people remember that script from the well-known Yekaterinburg art action “Get Lost,” which cost the artist his anonymity and forced him to leave in a hurry for Yerevan.)
The audience laughed with delight at the grimaces the faces on screen froze into whenever the connection glitched. At the same time, the room proved as friendly and open as it could be. When one of the strangers on the video chat, an English-speaking Muslim, invited the room to join him in a song with the words “Allahu akbar,” the audience readily sang along.
The random strangers’ remarks complemented the festival’s main themes beautifully. One man said almost immediately that he had spent his whole life searching for his parents, to ask them why they had abandoned him as an infant on the doorstep of a maternity hospital: his few minutes on screen felt like a prologue to Hadas Neuman’s 100 Men. Another, a smiling blond man in a carefully pressed suit, turned out to be a Spanish pathologist, the son of a Russian mother, who was glad to practice his Russian. Remarkably upbeat, he reminded everyone that death is the only thing in life that can’t be undone, and advised against putting life off until later.
Chronofest itself, which came into being at a time ill-suited to theater, follows that advice: here and now, it lets people meet and see the art that, in the new reality, is out of reach for many.

Mystery solved: story of Wehrmacht motorbike found in the Danube
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:20:51 UTC
14:20:51 KST

Record low water on the Danube has revealed in Budapest a perfectly preserved Wehrmacht DKW NZ 350-1 motorbike from WWII. Euronews investigates its role, its factory origins, when it may have sunk, and whether the dead nearby were its riders.
The water level in the Danube has never been this low. The low water level is exposing what lay hidden on the riverbed for decades, including a Wehrmacht motorcycle of the DKW NZ 350-1 type from the Second World War. DKW is short for "Dampfkraftwagen", a former German car and motorcycle brand from the Saxon motor city of Zschopau that was later taken over by Auto Union.
The motorcycle was found on the riverbed in the centre of Hungary's capital Budapest, level with the Hungarian Parliament building. For staff at the local Institute and Museum of Military History it is a real once-in-a-century discovery. According to the institute, the vehicle is almost completely intact. It was effectively preserved in the Danube's mud.
The motorcycle found is a model developed specifically for wartime use and produced from 1944 onwards. It was powered by a single-cylinder two-stroke engine delivering 11.5 hp. Thanks to their robustness and reliability, these so-called Kräder, or military motorcycles, were popular with the troops. One of the key identifying features of the DKW 350-1 is the metal side pannier, also found on the machine recovered from the Danube.
Around 12,000 units were built by the end of the war in 1945. The predecessor model, the DKW (source in German) NZ 350, reached a top speed of 105 km/h, according to the ADAC. In the Wehrmacht, motorcycles were usually used as dispatch, reconnaissance or courier machines, carrying orders, reports and information materials such as maps.
The motorcycle was manufactured by Auto Union AG, a car and motorcycle producer founded in 1932 that was then the second-largest German manufacturer after Opel. Auto Union AG was created through the merger of several brands, including Audi.
On earlier models from the company, the frame components were still bolted together; on the NZ series they were welded. Because welding required a high power supply, this work could only be carried out at night, when the electricity grid was not under strain from other uses.
German Tellermine 35 anti-tank mines, remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells have also been found on the Danube riverbed. This stretch of the Danube may have been used as a "war debris dump", according to the Hungarian Institute of Military History.
From March 1944 German troops occupied Budapest. Between October 1944 and February 1945 the Battle of Budapest was fought between the Soviet Red Army and German and Hungarian forces. Around 30,000 German, more than 17,000 Hungarian and some 80,000 Soviet and Romanian soldiers were killed. On 13 February 1945 the remaining German units surrendered.
After the war the DKW production facilities were dismantled and transferred to the Soviet Union as part of war reparations. In Moscow and other locations they were used to build, in large numbers until 1951, the largely identical ISCH-350.
Human remains were found beneath the motorcycle. The Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge, the German War Graves Commission, took charge of the recovery and said the remains belong to two Wehrmacht soldiers. Were they the motorcycle's crew? Their identity tags are well preserved, so they should be able to be identified. The two dead men are to be buried at the German war cemetery in Budaörs, west of Budapest. More than 16,000 German soldiers are buried there.
The Volksbund is a non-profit association which, on behalf of the German federal government, searches for, recovers and buries war dead abroad. In 2025 alone it dealt with more than 5,500 cases.

Trump secretly left Türkiye on smaller jet amid Iran threat: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:20:37 UTC
14:20:37 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump secretly flew out of Türkiye last month on a smaller plane than previously known due to an assassination threat from Iran, the Washington Post reported on Aug. 11.
Trump boarded an Air Force One jet in Ankara on July 8, but then moved into a catering container attached to the plane, the report said.
The container then ferried him to a smaller C-32A aircraft that flew him to Britain, while media and some officials were led to believe Trump was still on the bigger jet.
The Iranian threat had previously been reported by U.S. media as the reason that Trump did not fly out of Türkiye aboard the new Boeing 747-8, gifted to the United States by Qatar, which he had used to fly into the country.
Trump, who was in Ankara for a NATO summit, said at the time he would be taking the older Boeing 747 so that members of the U.S. military at an airbase in Britain could tour the new plane.
However, several U.S. media outlets reported that a threat from Iranian proxy forces had prompted the switch.
Journalists on the old plane out of Ankara were also told to keep their window blinds down, a step normally reserved for war zones, furthering suspicions of security concerns.
The plane swap prompted renewed scrutiny of the Qatar-gifted jet, which the Times reported did not have the same security features as the older jet, including anti-missile defenses.
Video in the Washington Post’s report showed a catering truck lowering from the older Air Force One jet, minutes after Trump walked up stairs into the plane.
The catering vehicle can then be seen transiting in the distance to the smaller C-32A aircraft.

Australia v the world: Why our official interest rate stands out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:20:31 UTC
14:20:31 KST

in brief
- The RBA has kept interest rates on hold at 4.35 per cent in August.
- Australia's cash rate target and inflation is higher than some other comparable economies.
Australia's cash rate remains higher than those of several comparable economies after the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) left it unchanged at 4.35 per cent on Tuesday.
The decision underscores a key difference between Australia and many of its peers: inflation has proved more persistent, prompting the central bank to take a more cautious approach to cutting rates.
In its statement of monetary policy, the board explained its widely-anticipated decision was affected by global uncertainty and high inflation in 2026.
"The board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded," it said in its board statement announcing the decision to leave the cash rate on hold.
"While the impact of the Middle East conflict on inflation has so far been less than expected, headline inflation is still too high."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It said trimmed mean inflation — which strips out volatile items — also remained elevated and was "little changed form the March quarter".
The latest inflation data showed signs of cooling but it is still running about the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band, and the ongoing global uncertainty is likely to give the central bank "reason to pause", according to AMP chief economist Shane Oliver.
Oliver described interest rates as a "blunt instrument" for central banks around the world to reduce households' spending on discretionary items and tackle inflation.
So how do Australia's interest rates compare globally?
How Australia compares globally
Oliver explained that, historically, levers reserve banks can pull have been the best way to tackle inflation.
Relying on governments alone to help doesn't work as well, he said, because governments can be incentivised to spend more to win votes, even when inflation is high.
Cash rate targets differ around the world but share the unifying goal of keeping inflation down and promoting a high-employment economy.
Australia's cash rate target of 4.35 per cent is higher than those of other countries, such as the United States at 3.5-3.75 per cent, the UK at 3.75 per cent, and Canada at 2.25 per cent.
Australia also has higher core inflation, a measure stripping out economic volatility, than these other economies.
Professor and economist Warwick McKibbin from the Australian National University said that trends such as oil supply shocks can impact inflation globally.
Domestic factors, such as economic structure and openness to trade, can also play a part.
Different countries also have different goals for inflation, he said.
"The US has an inflation target of 2 per cent, that's the Federal Reserve's goal," McKibbin said.
"And so, historically, inflation generally doesn't rise significantly above that, although it actually has since COVID-19."
Meanwhile, Australia's inflation target is between 2 and 3 per cent, which can also lead to marginally higher inflation.
"What drives actual inflation is both expectations of inflation as well as what's happening in the economy," McKibbin said.
"So you'd expect our inflation rate's probably going to have a higher number than the US because our expectations will be leveraged somewhere between two and three, and that matters as well."
Aside from its inflation target, the RBA's other mandate is to support full employment, meaning as many Australians as possible in work without creating excessive inflation.
While Australia has higher inflation and a higher cash rate target than some other countries, it also has a healthy unemployment rate of 4.4 per cent, lower than the UK, Canada and New Zealand.
What's ahead?
Oliver said that the Australian economy has become more inflation-prone than that of some other countries over the last two years.
"And that is a concern, and something that the Reserve Bank has to be aware of and a reason why they need to be more cautious," he said.
"The RBA will likely retain a tightening bias as it does whatever is necessary to bring inflation down to target."
Australia's 'big four' banks — the Commonwealth Bank, NAB, Westpac and ANZ — don't expect any further movement this year.
But they all anticipate a cut in 2027.
- ANZ expects a 0.25 percentage point cut in September and December, lowering the cash rate to 3.85 per cent by the end of 2027
- Commonwealth expects cuts in May and August, bringing the rate to 3.85 per cent by the third quarter
- NAB forecasts three cuts — in June, September and December — taking the cash rate to 3.60 per cent
- Westpac expects cuts in August and December, taking the rate to 3.85 per cent
But Oliver said the RBA wouldn’t hesitate to lift rates in 2026 if needed.

'물 부족' 중앙아 국가들, 시르다리야강 계측 시스템 구축 합의
South Korea
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:20:06 KST
14:20:06 KST

갈등 대신 '협력' 선택…수자원 외교 중대 진전 이뤄내
 
 (서울=연합뉴스) 유창엽 기자 = 만성적인 물 부족에 시달리는 중앙아시아 국가들이 역내를 관통하는 시르다리야강을 효율적으로 이용하기 위해 자동 수량계측 시스템 구축에 합의했다.
 11일 타임스오브센트럴아시아(TCA)에 따르면 우즈베키스탄과 카자흐스탄, 키르기스스탄, 타지키스탄, 투르크메니스탄 등 5개국 대표들은 최근 카자흐스탄 남부 투르키스탄주에서 만나 이같이 합의했다.
 시스템 구축을 위한 실무진은 다음달 말까지 구성될 전망이다.
 합의는 옛소련 시절 구성된 중앙아시아 5개국 협의체인 '국가간수자원조정위원회'(ICWC) 회의에서 이뤄졌는데, 기후 변화로 시르다리야강 수량 부족이 심해지는 상황에서 관련국들이 갈등 대신 협력을 선택함으로써 수자원 외교의 중요한 진전을 이룬 것으로 평가된다.
 길이 2천200여㎞인 시르다리야강은 나린강과 카라 다리야강의 합류 지점인 페르가나 계곡에서 형성돼 우즈베키스탄과 타지키스탄, 카자흐스탄을 지나 북아랄해에 유입된다. 
 나린강은 키르기스스탄에서 발원하기 때문에 이들 4개국이 시르다리야강 관리를 맡고 있다.
 시르다리야강 수량은 주로 농업지역에 공급되고 일부는 수력발전에 쓰인다.
 강물 이용과 관련해 공유국들 간 이해관계가 늘 일치하지는 않았다. 강물은 상류지역에선 수력발전, 하류지역에서는 여름철 농작물 재배에 이용되면서 의견 조율이 되지 않은 경우가 많았다.
 따라서 정확한 수량 계측과 시의적절한 자료 공유는 강물의 효율적 이용에 큰 도움이 된다.
 시르다리야강과 함께 대표적인 중앙아시아 강인 아무다리야강을 비효율적으로 이용함으로써 관련국들은 그동안 큰 경제적 손실을 봤다. 
 세계은행은 경제적 손실이 연간 45억달러(약 6조4천억원) 이상에 달하는 것으로 추산한 바 있다.
 이런 점을 고려해 카자흐스탄과 우즈베키스탄은 각각 국내 시르다리야강 유역에 자동수량계측소를 5개씩 구축하고 있다. 
 이번 투르키스탄주 회의에서 양국은 계측소 구축을 위한 무상원조 자금 확보를 위해 함께 노력하고 이 시스템을 유역의 다른 지역으로 확대하는 방안을 검토하기로 합의했다.
 앞서 카자흐스탄과 타지키스탄, 우즈베키스탄은 타지키스탄의 바흐리 토지크 저수지에 대한 여름철 운영 일정에 합의한 바 있다. 
 상류국가 타지키스탄이 여름에 저수를 방류해야 하류국가인 우즈베키스탄과 카자흐스탄은 가뭄을 겪지 않고 목화 등 농작물 재배를 안정적으로 할 수 있다.
 중앙아시아에선 양대 젖줄인 사르다리야강과 아무다리야강이 톈산산맥과 파미르고원의 빙하 융해수에 전적으로 의존하는데, 빙하가 옛 소련 시절에 비해 약 36% 소멸한 것으로 알려졌다. 
 이 때문에 물 부족 현상은 단순한 환경문제를 넘어 국가의 안보와 에너지, 식량, 경제구조를 뒤흔드는 최대 위기로 부상한 상태다.

France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:20:00 UTC

France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
Segolene Le Stradic
PARIS – In France, incessant cold calls advertising solar panels, roofs, heat pumps and other items will stop on Aug 11, when a ban on unsolicited telemarketing calls goes into effect.
Companies will no longer be allowed to advertise goods and services through such calls unless consumers previously gave their consent or if the calls are about a pre-existing contract.
The ban is unlikely to be met with any opposition in a country where 97 per cent of the population say they are annoyed by daily telemarketing calls, which have been steadily increasing in recent years, according to a parliamentary report.
A leading consumer advocacy group, Que Choisir Ensemble, called the ban a “historic measure” that “should finally put an end to the daily harassment that the French have endured for far too long”.
“Peace and quiet is a right,” the group’s president, Marie-Amandine Stevenin, said in a statement. “This observation holds true both online and on the street, where we are inundated with calls to consume.”
Frederic Billon, head of Federation de la Vente Directe, a business organisation, said that the law would add administrative burdens for all local businesses that used to call their customers without giving it much thought.
“Today, that ‘without giving it much thought’ approach no longer exists,” he said. “You’ll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you’ll also have to keep proof of that consent.”
Billon also said he was worried about unfair competition from unethical companies operating within and outside France.
In Morocco, where France represents a major market for telemarketing companies, the ban could lead to the disappearance of up to 50,000 jobs in the country, according to a government official quoted by Le Matin, a daily Moroccan newspaper.
Delphine Batho, a French lawmaker, said in a broadcast interview on Aug 10 that calls from abroad “will be illegal” and that “necessary steps must be taken, including with telecom operators, to ensure that these calls, which are scams, are technically blocked”.
The new legislation, which Parliament adopted in May 2025, is a significant shift from having French people consent by default to receiving telemarketing calls. Previously, consumers could be contacted at random unless they signed up on “Bloctel”, a free government registry to avoid getting such calls.
Though phone numbers listed on “Bloctel” nearly doubled between 2021 and 2024 and more than 38 million calls a day were being blocked, the service was deemed inefficient because companies often failed to take it into account, according to the parliamentary report.
Under earlier legislation that aimed to tackle the issue, some companies in specific industries like home renovations for older people or for people with disabilities were already forbidden to make unsolicited telemarketing calls.
Now, individuals face a fine of up to €75,000 (S$110,000) and companies can be fined €375,000 if they fail to comply with the new law. For calls targeting vulnerable individuals, the sentence could be as much as five years in prison and a fine of €500,000.
“From a legislative standpoint, we couldn’t do any better,” Pierre-Jean Verzelen, the French senator behind the initial bill, said in a broadcast interview at the time the new ban was adopted in 2025.
“The government will have to act immediately, hitting companies that don’t play by the rules hard and fast,” he said. “That’s the price we’ll have to pay to get results.”
In a July decree specifying the application of the law, the government said that even if consumers agreed to receive cold calls, they could change their mind at any point and businesses would have to seek consent again within a year. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Student police officer, 23, charged with rape and kidnap of woman
Mohammad Hassan, 23, serving with Greater Manchester Police (GMP), has been charged with multiple offences
- Bookmark
A 23-year-old student police officer has been charged with the rape and kidnapping of a woman in Manchester.
Mohammad Hassan has been charged with multiple offences after reports were made to the force on Saturday evening, which ended in a pursuit on the M62 in West Yorkshire.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) previously said that a 999 call had been received shortly before 10.20pm in which a woman could be heard in distress in a vehicle in the Manchester area.
Hassan has been charged with oral rape, kidnap, strangulation, sexual assault, theft of a mobile phone and dangerous driving.
He has been suspended by the force and will appear at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday.
Assistant Chief Constable Mark Dexter said: “GMP detectives and staff have been working on this investigation throughout the last 48 hours to ensure charges are brought in this case.
“The victim is our priority, and we are ensuring she continues to receive specialist support. Criminal proceedings must now take its course without interference.
“I understand and share the feeling among the public and our thousands of hard-working, decent staff who will have seen this news.
“Proceedings are under way, and necessary action will be decisively taken within the regulations.”
A woman was safeguarded at the scene and continues to be supported by specialist officers and support services, the force said.

Battlefield sees 212 clashes over past day, 26 of them on Kostiantynivka front – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 212 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day, with the Russians conducting the heaviest attacks on the Kostiantynivka (26 assaults) and Pokrovsk (25 assaults) fronts.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 11 August
Details: In total, 212 combat clashes were recorded on the front line over the past 24 hours.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, four combat clashes occurred. The Russians launched one airstrike, dropping one guided bomb, and conducted 62 strikes on Ukrainian positions and settlements.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, the Russians conducted 12 attacks on Ukrainian positions near the settlements of Starytsia and Lyman and towards Volokhivka.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians conducted one attack towards the village of Novoplatonivka.
On the Lyman front, the Russians conducted 10 attacks, trying to break through Ukrainian defences near the settlements of Lyman and Dibrova and towards Novoselivka and Karpivka.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted 15 assaults near the settlements of Zakitne and Kryva Luka and towards Dronivka and Rai-Oleksandrivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians conducted two attacks near Chasiv Yar and towards Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, the Russians conducted 26 attacks near the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Illinivka and Ivanopillia and towards Novoselivka, Torske and Mykolaipillia.
On the Pokrovsk front, Ukraine's defence forces stopped 25 Russian assaults near the settlements of Bilytske, Novooleksandrivka, Kotlyne and Serhiivka and towards Kucheriv Yar, Toretske, Vilne, Novyi Donbas, Svitle, Vasylivka, Udachne, Novomykolaivka, Molodetske and Novoplatonivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians conducted four attacks towards the settlements of Kalynivske, Danylivka, Yehorivka and Rybne.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russians conducted eight attacks near Hirke and towards the settlements of Vozdvyzhivka, Rivne and Charivne.
On the Orikhiv front, Ukrainian defenders repelled seven Russian attempts to advance towards Novoselivka, Zarichne, Novoiakovlivka, Novodanylivka and Pavlivka.
On the Prydniprovske front, the Russians did not conduct any offensive operations over the past day.
On the Volyn and Polissia fronts, there is no evidence of any offensive Russian groups being formed in the area.

Hong Kong considers lowering heat-stress warning thresholds amid criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:14:21 UTC
14:14:21 KST

Hong Kong considers lowering heat-stress warning thresholds amid criticism
Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui says thresholds could be adjusted after the heat-stress warning failed to rise during city’s hottest day on record
Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui Chark-shum said on Tuesday that the warning system was currently more responsive to “muggy weather” than conditions of purely high temperature and strong solar radiation, but the government would seek to improve its sensitivity during periods of extreme heat.
Hui explained that the heat stress at work warning system took into account factors such as air temperature, humidity, wind speed and solar radiation, but that their weighting was “localised” to suit Hong Kong’s climate.
“In Hong Kong, the heat stress does not always track actual temperature change. When the humidity is high and the wind speed is slow, our cooling efficiency will drop sharply even if the temperature is not that high, and the associated health risk could be higher than in a well-ventilated open space with a higher temperature,” he said.
“Our system is more sensitive to this muggy situation, and the weighting of direct solar radiation is relatively smaller.”
The Labour Department recently came under criticism after its Heat Stress at Work Warning System remained at the lowest level while the city’s forecaster recorded a scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius (103 Fahrenheit) on Sunday afternoon – the highest temperature since records began in 1884.

美래퍼 투팍 피살 30년 만에 재판…갱단 두목 회고록이 실마리
South Korea
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:12:36 KST
14:12:36 KST

자서전서 "조카 복수하려 투팍 찾아가 총격"…이제와서 "거짓말이었다" 주장
(로스앤젤레스=연합뉴스) 김경윤 특파원 = 1990년대 미국 힙합계 전설적인 가수였던 투팍(2Pac·투팍 샤쿠르)의 피살 사건을 놓고 사후 30년 만에 관련 재판이 진행된다.
AP 통신과 로이터 통신 등은 등은 10일(현지시간) 네바다주(州) 클라크카운티 1심 법원 재판부가 투팍 살인 공모 혐의를 받는 드웨인 케피 디 데이비스가 출석한 가운데 배심원 후보 검증 작업을 시작했다고 보도했다.
투팍은 솔로 앨범 판매량만 500만장에 이르는 힙합계 영향력 있던 가수였으나 1996년 9월 7일 라스베이거스 도로를 달리던 중 피격 사망했다.
불과 25세였던 투팍의 갑작스러운 죽음은 대중에게 큰 충격을 안겼지만, 그간 총격범과 사망 배경 등은 확인되지 않았다.
이 가운데 데이비스가 2019년 자서전 '콤프턴 스트리트 레전드'를 출간했고, 이 책을 통해 자신이 투팍 살인을 지시하고 총기를 제공했다고 주장했다.
자서전에는 당시 상황이 상세히 기술됐다.
로스앤젤레스(LA) 지역 갱단 사우스 사이드 콤프턴 크립스의 두목이었다고 밝힌 데이비스는 자기 조카 올랜도 베이비 래인 앤더슨이 폭행당해 이에 보복하고자 투팍을 쫓았다고 설명했다.
투팍은 차량 선루프를 통해 몸을 내밀고 있던 가운데 데이비스가 캐딜락을 타고 접근했고, 뒷자리 남성 두 명 중 하나에게 총기를 건넸다.
다만, 직접적으로 누가 투팍을 죽였는지는 밝히지 않았다. 당시 차에 타고 있던 조카 앤더슨은 사건 2년 뒤 총격전으로 사망했고, 디안드레 프리키 스미스, 테리 버블업 브라운 등 동승자도 세상을 떠났다.
또 데이비스는 자서전에서 힙합계 거물이자 현재 성매매 강요 등의 혐의로 복역 중인 숀 디디 콤스가 투팍 살인 대가를 돈을 주겠다고 한 적이 있다고 언급하기도 했다.
경찰은 2023년 9월 데이비스의 공개 발언을 바탕으로 그를 체포했으며, 이번에 검찰이 살인 또는 살인 공모 혐의로 재판에 넘기게 됐다.
네바다 주 법은 직접 방아쇠를 당기지 않았더라도 범행에 참여했다면 살인 혐의로 기소할 수 있도록 하고 있다.
데이비스는 자서전 내용이 거짓이라고 해명했다.
그는 사건 당일 자신이 라스베이거스에 없었다고 강조하는가 하면 자서전은 대필 작가가 썼으며 허위 정보를 끼워 넣었다고 주장 중이다.

Zuckerberg spokesperson says his yacht did not hear distress call in time to assist skiff that ran out of fuel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:09:06 BST
14:09:06 KST

Meta spokesperson says Zuckerberg’s yacht did not hear distress call in time to assist skiff
The skiff ran out of fuel off the coast of Alaska when it made the call
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A spokesperson for Mark Zuckerberg said the crew of a yacht owned by the Meta CEO didn't respond to a call for help from a skiff that ran out of fuel because it did not hear their radio call and by the time it did, another nearby ship had already rendered assistance.
The skiff ran out of fuel off the coast of Alaska. The 3 Aug incident gained attention in recent days after a passenger on the cruise ship posted on social media that the captain had said Mr Zuckerberg’s yacht “refused” to respond.
The US Coast Guard said the 21ft Hewescraft vessel first hailed it for assistance at approximately 9.32pm, using a radio frequency all boats are expected to monitor. About 25 minutes later, the Coast Guard determined the vessel was not in distress and issued an assistance request.
The skiff was able to make it safely to Farragut Bay after the Wilderness Legacy cruise ship towed it there, and helped it refuel.
A maritime law expert said on Monday the crew may not have been obligated to after the Coast Guard determined the boat wasn't in distress.
When another ship is in distress, everyone in the area is obligated to respond as long as doing so doesn't put their own ship at risk. But maritime law expert Ian Ralby said this situation appears different, and the crew of Mr Zuckerberg's yacht wouldn't face that legal obligation.
“It’s the difference between calling AAA and 911. You need an ambulance on site, that’s a distress call. You need somebody to give you a jump or to tow your car, you call AAA,” said Mr Ralby, who is president of the nonprofit Auxilium Worldwide that focuses on promoting sustainable development and ocean governance, among other goals. It is a big difference in terms of the emergency type, he said.
"Both concerning, both needing assistance, but the legal obligations to respond are very different.”
Mr Zuckerberg and his family were not on the 387ft Launchpad yacht when this happened, according to his spokesperson, who didn't specify what the yacht was doing at the time.
“As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe," Mr Zuckerberg's spokesperson, Brian Baker, said.
Retired Coast Guard Captain Aaron C Davenport, who spent three decades with the branch of the military responsible for rescues on the water, said running out of gas simply isn't considered an emergency, and the Launchpad wasn't obligated to help.
“If Zuckerberg’s ship is there and this vessel just ran out of fuel, they’re under no obligation whatsoever to assist them. Zero,” said Mr Davenport, who led rescues in the Bering Sea during his career.
“Is it that common courtesy to help other mariners out? Yes, because someday you’re going to need assistance.”
The Coast Guard also isn't going to automatically deploy ships when a ship runs out of gas, but Mr Davenport said that in the harsh environment of Alaska a ship that ran out of gas could become an emergency if it drifts into some rocks or a storm is brewing. The fact that this cruise ship responded saved the Coast Guard a trip.
“Alaska is a remote place so it could easily go from non-emergency to emergency and very quickly,” said Mr Davenport, who worked as a consultant on security and maritime issues for several years before retiring.
The Alaska Beacon first reported on what happened after Michael Love, who said he was a passenger on the Wilderness Legacy cruise ship, posted on Bluesky on 5 Aug.
“Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this),” he said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement that they determined within half an hour of when the skiff radioed in that the small ship wasn't in distress. A marine assistance request was broadcast on their behalf, and the Wilderness Legacy responded, reaching the 21ft vessel about an hour later.
Mr Ralby said it's a little unusual that the Launchpad crew missed the call for help because it is common practice for ships to always be monitoring channel 16 on their radios and keep it as the default frequency to hear any distress calls or emergency notices.
But typically the Coast Guard tries to keep channel 16 as free as possible so they might announce an emergency on that channel and ask anyone who can help to switch to a different channel to hear the details.
“The situation was resolved without any harm to life," said Mr Ralby, who is a maritime lawyer with experience in more than 100 countries.
"It does not seem that there was any immediate issue in terms of threat to life of mariners or concerns for the marine environment, which are the two main things that lead to that urgent distress call where all mariners no matter who they are legally obligated to try and respond.”

Cortnee Vine back in A-League Women for Melbourne City, Tameka Yallop joins Wellington Phoenix
In short:
Triple ALW premiership winner and Matildas star Cortnee Vine is heading back to Australia to spearhead Melbourne City's title tilt.
Vine is leaving NWSL side North Carolina Courage to join City, while Brisbane veteran Tameka Yallop is leaving the Roar to link up with grand finalists Wellington Phoenix.
What's next?
The new ALW season begins on Friday October 16.
Cortnee Vine has returned to A-League Women with champions Melbourne City in a move that could help the Matildas' penalty shootout hero push for a second Women's World Cup berth.
Elsewhere, Matildas great and Brisbane captain Tameka Yallop has joined Wellington in a huge recruiting coup for the grand finalists.
Vine, 28, starred for Sydney FC as an explosive and tricky winger, winning three premierships and two championships.
Vine catapulted to stardom when she scored the winning spot-kick in the Matildas' famous penalty shootout against France that secured a maiden Women's World Cup semi-final berth in 2023.
The winger joined North Carolina Courage in 2024 but made just 23 appearances in two years, scoring twice, while also taking time away from football to prioritise her mental health.
With golden boot winner Holly McNamara leaving City for Super League club Everton, Vine is instantly the club's biggest name.
"I'm really excited to be coming home and joining Melbourne City," Vine said in a statement.
"I've watched what City has achieved over the last few seasons and the standards this group continues to set, so the opportunity to come into that environment and be part of a team competing for trophies was really exciting to me.
"My time in the NWSL has helped me grow both as a player and a person, and I'm looking forward to bringing those experiences back to Australia."
Vine will have the opportunity to impress and push for three trophies across the ALW and the Women's Asian Champions League.
Attacking midfielder Yallop looms as the missing piece for Bev Priestman's Phoenix.
Yallop's wife Kirsty Yallop is a former New Zealand international and the move allows the couple and their two young daughters to be closer to family.
The 35-year-old, who missed this year's Asian Cup through injury, can also press her Women's World Cup case with the ambitious Phoenix.
"I'm chasing that trophy and so is Wellington, so we're aligned," Yallop said.
"Getting the opportunity to work under Bev was a massive drawcard, not to mention the facilities at NZCIS. They're second to none.
"It's a high performance environment in Wellington and that's something that I love being a part of.
"And the Phoenix have shown they're dedicated to their women's program. That was a major pull for me too."
Brisbane is retiring the former Julie Dolan Medallist's number 13 jersey — the first time the club has done so for a men's or women's player.
Yallop, who has attended four World Cups and three Olympics and played overseas in several top leagues, spent the majority of her decorated A-League Women career at the Roar, bar a one-season stint at City in 2018-19.
An inaugural Queensland Roar player at the age of 17 in 2008, Yallop won three premierships at Brisbane and scored in two grand final wins.
Yallop scored 66 goals in 158 games in three separate stints at the Roar.
The new season is due to start on Friday October 16.

US judge rules Meta hid evidence in Australian tycoon fake ad case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:05:00 UTC
14:05:00 KST

US judge rules Meta hid evidence in Australian tycoon fake ad case
- A US judge ruled that Meta destroyed evidence in a case where Australian billionaire Andrew Forrest accused the company of allowing fake ads using his image for scams.
- The judge called Meta's actions "gross negligence" and rejected Meta's claim it needed two years to find the data, though no intent to harm was found.
- The case challenges Meta's immunity under Section 230, with allegations that Meta's AI tools actively shaped fraudulent ads, making it responsible for scam content.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A federal judge in California ruled against Meta on Aug 10 for destroying evidence in a case brought by Australian billionaire Andrew Forrest over scam advertisements using his likeness without permission.
The mining tycoon has accused the social media giant of allowing ads using his image to promote bogus cryptocurrency investments, and said Meta actively modifies the ads it distributes and profits from them.
That behaviour makes it liable for the fraudulent content, Forrest’s lawyers said.
In his ruling, seen by AFP, Judge P. Casey Pitts found that Meta did destroy or allow essential data to be erased, causing harm to the plaintiff.
Meta argued it needed two years to discover the existence of the data in its own systems, a claim the judge called “simply not credible”.
“It is not reasonable to assert that Meta itself needed two years to learn about its own data,” Pitts said.
The judge did not, however, find intent to cause harm, instead calling Meta’s conduct “gross negligence”.
Meta has said it is protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 1996 law that spares internet firms from being accountable for content posted by users on its platform.
The destroyed data is central to Forrest’s legal strategy as it would purportedly show how Meta’s own tools reshaped the ads, thus forfeiting the company’s immunity claims.
The case is still in its preliminary hearing phase, and Meta is expected to seek to have the case thrown out on immunity grounds at a hearing before Pitts expected by the end of 2026.
Since 2019, thousands of deceptive ads on Facebook have used the likeness of the highly prominent figure in Australia to promote scams, racking up thousands of victims, according to the suit.
The billionaire’s legal team argues that Meta’s artificial intelligence tools optimised and personalised fraudulent ads before distributing them, thereby making Meta an active participant, rather than a mere intermediary.
The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court has already ruled that Section 230 does not protect Meta from the state’s lawsuit concerning Instagram’s design being addictive to children.
That represents a legal setback for the Facebook and Instagram owner, which has also been found liable for harming minors on its platforms by juries in Los Angeles and Santa Fe, New Mexico in 2026. AFP

Australia to vaccinate vulnerable bird species against H5 flu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:02:29 UTC
14:02:29 KST

Australia will begin targeted vaccinations for bird species considered especially vulnerable to the highly contagious H5 bird flu virus, authorities said on Tuesday.
Environment Minister Murray Watt said the programme would cover both captive and wild birds, although vaccinating wild species presents logistical challenges.
"It is difficult to vaccinate birds in the wild -- it does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds," Watt said.
"It is difficult to catch wild birds once, let alone twice," he added, saying captive birds would be the priority while authorities would vaccinate wild birds where possible.
Australia was for years the only continental landmass free of the H5 strain, which has caused severe disease and deaths among poultry and wild birds worldwide.
Mass bird deaths expected
Australia recorded its first H5 case in a migratory seabird in June, while the government reported the country's first mass wildlife mortality event last week.
Agriculture Minister Julie Collins warned that more mass bird deaths were likely as the virus spreads.
"This will continue to spread across the country," she said.
Waterfowl, shorebirds, seabirds and birds of prey are among the wild species most affected by the H5 strain.
As of Monday, authorities had recorded 231 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia.
No cases have been detected in poultry or Australia's agricultural production, authorities said.
Almost half of Australia's wild bird species and 83 percent of its mammals are found nowhere else in the world, making the spread of the virus a particular concern for wildlife conservation.
Australian scientists said in June that H5 bird flu had killed more than 13,000 elephant seal pups after infecting a breeding colony on the remote Heard and McDonald Islands.

House prices drop in six councils in three months
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The price of homes fell in six Dutch councils in the second quarter of 2026, up from just one three months earlier, a sign that the housing market is levelling off.
Figures from national statistics agency CBS and the Land Registry showed the biggest drop was in Noord-Beveland, in Zeeland, where prices were 5.1% lower than a year earlier.
Prices also fell in Ouder-Amstel (-2.8%), Hillegom (-2.5%), Valkenswaard, Veldhoven and IJsselstein. In the first quarter, only Gulpen-Wittem in Limburg had seen a fall.
Nationally, prices were still 4.2% higher than a year earlier – the tenth quarter in a row of increases, though the pace has slowed.
The sharpest rises were in the rural east and north. Prices in Oost Gelre, in Gelderland, jumped 20.9%, followed by Voorst (19.4%) and Pekela (16.2%).
Among the four biggest cities, prices in Amsterdam rose 0.1%.

Kazakhstan offers crypto amnesty as it seeks to bring billions in digital assets home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

Astana has introduced tax incentives and regulatory reforms to encourage crypto investors to move their digital assets onto domestic licensed platforms, hoping to revive an industry that largely left after a post-mining-boom halt.
When Kazakhstan became one of the world's largest crypto mining hubs five years ago, the boom strained the country’s power grid, and the government’s response resulted in most miners either leaving the country or going underground.
Now the Kazakh government is looking to bring it all back home by offering tax breaks and legal certainty.
The Kazakh government signed a decree designed to encourage citizens to declare cryptocurrency holdings, move them onto regulated domestic platforms and integrate digital assets into the country's economy.
The authorities are offering private investors a tax break on personal income from digital asset transactions for three years, provided the assets were not connected to fraud, money laundering or linked to unlicensed crypto services.
The decision has opened the door to making it easier for miners to operate in the country — and for everyone to profit.
Crypto boom cut short
Cryptocurrency mining uses powerful computers to solve complex mathematical problems in order to verify and add transactions to a blockchain — the ledger on which a cryptocurrency's transaction history is recorded.
Miners who successfully complete them are rewarded with cryptocurrency deposited directly to their personal crypto wallets, which in some cases like Bitcoin can bring in significant profits.
The downside is that the process consumes a large amount of power because the computations require sustained processing.
After China banned Bitcoin mining in 2021, many miners began looking for new locations with low-cost energy.
At that point Kazakhstan rapidly became the second-largest Bitcoin mining location after the US. Many tried to get in on the profits, with people even putting mining equipment on their balconies.
Some went so far as to masquerade the mining farms as vegetable storage facilities, greenhouses or AI data centres at abandoned Soviet-era industrial sites to conceal their massive electricity consumption.
The country did not get to enjoy the crypto bloom for too long. The rapid influx of miners placed an enormous burden on the country’s ageing electricity grid.
In October 2021, surging electricity demand contributed to outages at three power plants in northeastern Kazakhstan, while rolling blackouts affected several regions. At peak, cryptocurrency miners were consuming an estimated 8% of Kazakhstan's total electricity output.
Authorities responded by repeatedly tightening regulations on electricity consumption and digital asset legalisation, leading to miners' departure abroad and the proliferation of illegal operations.
Kazakhstan never outright banned crypto mining, keeping its options open to potentially harness its potential in the future.
According to Kazakhstan's financial regulator, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakh citizens own approximately 1 million crypto wallets.
The AIFC, modelled on Dubai's DIFC financial free zone, has functioned as Kazakhstan's sandbox for financial innovation and serves as the regulatory home for digital asset companies operating in the country.
This figure is nearly four times the number of users registered on authorised local exchanges, which in March reached 256,900.
Bringing crypto assets back onshore
Attracting crypto owners back to their home countries with incentives and simplified legal frameworks has turned into a global trend in recent years, experts say.
The UAE, Hong Kong and Singapore have implemented similar tax measures alongside clear licensing, regulations and access to banking services, bringing in additional revenue.
The decree also addresses the energy question that triggered Kazakhstan's earlier mining crisis.
Under the plan, associated gas from oil fields not required for state use can be used to generate electricity for mining operations, broadening miners' options beyond the main national grid.
General Manager of Binance Kazakhstan Nurkhat Kushimov believes the tax incentive is the most important measure in the decree.
“This is a strong incentive for users to choose regulated jurisdictions and platforms operating within them," Kushimov told Euronews.
"This approach makes working in a licensed environment more attractive, fosters trust in the market and creates the conditions for its further development,” he said.
Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Association of Fintech, AI and Crypto Industry Bakhytzhan Kenzhebayev believes that the tax incentive removes one of the main uncertainties for the private investor, namely the question of when and on what basis the obligation arises. But the measure in itself is not sufficient.
“Users choose a platform not based on the tax rate, but on a combination of factors: how easy it is to deposit and withdraw (the local currency), the liquidity, and how clear the rules are,” Kenzhebayev told Euronews.
"For a licensed participant, the predictability of the rule is more valuable than the benefit itself."
President of Kazakhstan’s Blockchain and Digital Mining Association Daniyar Mubarakov told Euronews that any government support is welcome, but wonders how long this measure will work.
“For certain categories of entrepreneurs preferential tax regimes mean not only a reduction in taxes in the current period, but also a possible several-fold increase in taxes in the future due to increased volumes,” Mubarakov said.
Vice Minister of AI and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov said that his department is working on a proposal for a simplified tax regime following the expiration of the exemption in three years' time.
He added that the department is also working on cancelling tax audits for private investors covering the previous three years.
Beyond tax incentives
Experts say that Kazakh private investors' return to domestic platforms will depend on their competitiveness.
“For most users, convenience of service, liquidity, availability of instruments, speed of transactions, and the ability to seamlessly interact with the banking system remain the key factors,” Kushimov said.
According to Kenzhebayev, the main risks now lie in the legal definitions and terminology used. If the exemption is defined too broadly, it could create space to abuse the system and avoid paying taxes on other assets unrelated to crypto.
“This creates the risk of a reversal of the norm in a year or two, and that causes more damage to the market than an initially high but stable rate,” Kenzhebayev explained.
He also warned that the same digital asset can be treated as two different things depending on whether it falls under the AIFC or Kazakhstan's national rules, which would in turn mean companies would have to comply with two separate legal structures at once.
"The difficulty arises at the intersection. As a result, the participant builds two parallel infrastructures for one business, which reflects on the costs," he said.
Kenzhebayev said tax breaks alone would not be enough to draw users to licensed Kazakh platforms.
What would make the difference, he said, is reliable access to banking, clear rules for converting crypto into the local currency, straightforward requirements for keeping client assets safe, and a regulatory environment that does not put licensed operators at a disadvantage.

Dog-friendly beaches in Spain 2026: Where to swim with your pet this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:21 UTC
14:00:21 KST

Spain has more than 100 dog-friendly beaches. Before travelling with your pet, check which stretches of sand allow dogs and the local rules in each area.
More and more people are choosing to travel with their dog on holiday. However, not all Spanish beaches allow pets, especially in high season. To avoid fines or other problems, it is advisable to check in advance which beaches are dog-friendly and to find out about the specific rules in each municipality.
Spain currently has more than 100 dog beaches spread along its coastline, according to the specialist website Patitas&Co.
The Valencian Community, Catalonia, Andalusia and Murcia have the highest concentration of these areas, although there are also options in Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, the Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands.
The regions with the most options
The Valencian Community is one of the regions with the highest number of dog-friendly beaches. Some of the best known include Agua Amarga, in Alicante; Caleta dels Gossets, in Santa Pola; Punta del Riu, in El Campello; and Pinedo beach, in Valencia. Catalonia also offers plenty of alternatives, such as La Rubina, in Castelló d'Empúries; Rec del Molí, in L'Escala; or Els Griells, in L'Estartit.
In Andalusia, designated beaches in the provinces of Málaga, Almería and Cádiz stand out, while Murcia has several specific areas for pets. Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, the Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands also offer spaces where dogs are allowed in the water all year round or at certain times of the year.
Always check the local regulations
Although the number of options grows every summer, most Spanish beaches still ban dogs during the summer season. Restrictions are set by each local council, so it is essential to check the rules before you travel.
Some beaches require animals to be kept under control at all times, while others insist on having up-to-date health documentation or restrict access to certain times of day.
Advice for going to the beach with your dog
If you are planning a day at the beach with your pet, vets recommend avoiding the hottest hours, taking enough water to keep your dog hydrated and making sure there are shaded areas available.
It is also important to always pick up your dog's waste, respect other beachgoers and keep an eye on their paw pads, as the sand can reach very high temperatures in summer.

Matilda in pieces: what one mother’s suicide reveals about the carers broken by the system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:05 UTC
14:00:05 KST

Two days before she died, Matilda Davis issued a plea on Facebook. Sharing a study that found more than 40% of parent-carers had considered suicide, she called for “greater awareness, action and change” in Britain’s broken social care system. “This speaks the words I can’t,” she wrote.
Matilda, known as Tilly to her family and friends, had spent years battling for support in a regime that close observers and those who rely on it often say is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate.
Her seven-year-old son, Jude – not his real name – has significant disabilities. She was, her friends said, an “absolutely inspirational” mother, juggling care for Jude’s five-year-old sister Lilly – also a pseudonym – alongside his appointments at therapy, physio, hospital and two schools, as well as the significant financial and administrative burden.
She cherished every moment with her children. “Tilly cared more than anyone I know,” said her sister Georgina Davis, 35. “It was what she lived for.”
On 3 October last year, Matilda, 36, was found dead in the bathroom of their home in Stratford-upon-Avon in the West Midlands.
She had killed herself a day after saying she felt “completely exhausted” by her responsibilities, and “paralysed with anxiety” about the prospect of her looming divorce from her estranged husband, who the Guardian has chosen not to name.
After Andy Burnham promised the biggest reforms to social care in a generation, experts said Matilda’s death showed how carers were being “pushed to breaking point” by a broken system.
“Health and social care services in England are failing disabled children and their parents are being left to pick up the pieces,” said Dr Siobhan O’Dwyer, one of Britain’s leading experts on family carers.
“In his speech, the prime minister acknowledged that without support unpaid carers can break. But what does it mean to break? For Matilda it meant death by suicide, it meant dying alone and in pain because services failed to fully appreciate the impact of the caring role and the troubled marriage, and it meant leaving behind the children she loved more than anything else in the world.
“That is a break that can never be healed, but it was entirely preventable. If the government really wants to stop other carers breaking, it’s going to need more than a heartfelt speech. It’s going to need real action.”
‘I won’t be here much longer’
Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest earlier this year, including GP records and disclosures to professionals, showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life.
Last August, she told her GP she was worried about her “ability to cope emotionally with the daily demands as a parent-carer living with a home environment, which is becoming increasingly stressful, full of anxiety and worry … My absolute focus is to ensure [Jude and Lilly] are spared the turmoil of the unrest and upset in the house.”
Matilda had struggled with her mental health since Jude became critically unwell shortly after his birth. But two days before she died, she was in the “slight depths of ruin”, she told a friend in a voice note.
“I’m just in pieces and I’m trying to hold it together with the children, but it’s so physically taxing and emotional with what I’m dealing with [Jude] alone,” she said. “I’m just breaking really. I’m just completely broken. I haven’t really got any physical strength in me.”
Matilda had given up work as an art teacher to care for Jude full time. Social workers had not carried out a family care assessment, where professionals assess what support they might need, for almost four years by the time she died. They were due to visit the following week to carry out an updated plan.
On 2 October, Matilda told her divorce solicitor the worry was “overwhelming”. “My capacity to earn is basically nothing and will be long term,” she said.
Her day-to-day life was packed with “appointments, rehabilitation, admin, emails, phone calls, transporting/commuting”, she said, which would become more complex over the coming years with Jude’s schooling and health needs.
With her marriage coming to an end, Matilda said she was “desperately fearful” about the future of the family home, as she had sacrificed years of earnings to care for Jude full time. “The estate agents will not accept me as a non-earning single occupant and I have absolutely no where else suitable to go,” she said the day before she died, the inquest heard. She said she felt “financially trapped” and that it was “both physically and emotionally relentless at times”.
That morning, her husband called social services to say he was concerned about Matilda’s mental health. He said she had expressed suicidal thoughts that morning by saying: “I won’t be here much longer and then you will all have to look after yourselves.”
Social workers are obliged to act on welfare concerns within 24 hours and visited Matilda at home at 2pm the following day, a Friday.
A note of the meeting, shared at the inquest, detailed how Matilda was “visibly upset and tearful” when they arrived and “expressed significant anxiety” about the visit.
The coroner, Deborah Sewell, noted that Matilda spoke of the “emotional and psychological strain arising from relationship conflict, financial pressures, and the ongoing divorce proceedings”. Matilda told the social workers she had hit her head on the door in front of the children that morning “as a manifestation of emotional frustration”.
Before they left the meeting, social workers suggested her husband look after the children that weekend and that Matilda stayed with her parents. She was reluctant to leave, having already expressed concern about how Jude would manage without her.
When the social workers left at 2.30pm, Matilda “appeared calm” and there was “no indication of any suicidal ideation”, the note of the meeting recorded. Minutes later, she was dead.
At the inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask Matilda whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress. Nor was she directed to crisis organisations.
Neither social worker who visited her that day had undertaken suicide prevention training. When told it is best practice to ask someone directly whether they have plans to kill themselves if they have expressed suicidal thoughts, one said: “Well, I’ve not done the training.”
Asked whether they were concerned that Matilda had said a day earlier she “won’t be here much longer”, which they were told by her husband was a suicidal thought, the social worker added: “Obviously it is concerning she said that but she wasn’t using the word ‘suicide’.”
Sewell issued a rare prevention of future deaths report in April to direct Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff.
The council said: “We extend our deepest sympathies to the family and all those affected by this tragic loss. Following Matilda’s death and the subsequent coroner’s inquest, we have implemented enhanced suicide prevention training for all social workers to equip staff with skills to identify when parents and carers need additional support and to help them to access it.
“In addition, all agencies involved with this case will participate in a review to look closely at all the circumstances leading up to Matilda’s death. The purpose of the review will be to make recommendations for improving services and support.”
‘Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure’
In research published in 2024 – and shared by Matilda two days before her death – the University of Birmingham found 42% of parent-carers had thought about suicide, many times higher than the general population.
Those caring for significantly disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress that are “compounded by other factors like poverty, domestic abuse, or social isolation”, said O’Dwyer, who led the research.
She said social workers often had an “excess of professional optimism” about parents’ ability to cope with the pressures of caring for children with complex needs, particularly when they saw a devoted, loving mother – and it was often women who took on primary care responsibilities – and would think she would never act on thoughts of self-harm because she loved her children so much.
“But it is possible to love your children and be pushed to the point of suicide,” O’Dwyer said. “Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure of caring for a disabled child in a broken system.”
Contact, a charity for families with disabled children, said parents often reach crisis point before help was available and had to “fight for basic support”. Anna Bird, its chief executive, said parent-carers were being “squeezed from every direction: by the cost of living crisis, reduced services; and a support system that is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate”.
In the garden of Jude’s primary school in Birmingham, two apple trees and a rose bush have been planted in Matilda’s memory. Twenty miles away in Stratford, her friends at a family club have raised money for a bench engraved with her name and a number for the Samaritans suicide helpline.
Her sister Georgina described Matilda as “the most incredibly devoted mother”, draining her savings and driving hundreds of miles a week to get Jude the support he needed.
“She would tell me how she had to really fight to get what she wanted and needed for [Jude],” she said. “[Often talking about] how exhausting it is having to continually have to battle to get the provision he so needs.”
Matilda’s friend Francesca Roberts, a nursery manager, said she was constantly in awe of her ability to go “far beyond what any parent should have to do simply to access proper care and support”.
“She absolutely adored her children and dedicated every part of herself to them,” she said. Matilda was “one of the most caring, devoted, and selfless people I have ever known,” she added. “She was the village that everybody dreams of having around them.”
