They cannot even flush their toilets: life in east London blocks where taps often run dry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:05 UTC
14:00:05 KST

Christmas Day in east London. Beatrice Asante empties a bag of potatoes into her kitchen sink and turns on the tap. Nothing. She turns it off and on again. Still nothing. What now?
Asante rushes out to the only shop that is open, the local Nisa convenience store. She buys several big plastic bottles of water. Enough, she thinks, to make dinner and to last until the taps start running again.
Seven months later and as parts of the country brace for a fifth heatwave, Asante still cannot rely on tap water. She is one of hundreds of householders in housing association flats on the Devons Road estate in Tower Hamlets who have been left for up to a year without a reliable supply. Only now, after months of delay, is the landlord mobilising to have the problem repaired.
It is difficult to understand just how much we rely on running water – until it is taken away. Residents of the nine blocks affected have been left unable to properly wash themselves, clean their homes or cook. For long stretches each day, they cannot even flush their toilets.
“You can’t put a price on it,” Asante says. “Water is essential. Even if you haven’t got food, [if] you can drink water or have a very nice bath, you are OK.”
Rajia Begum and Jasmine Begum are two mothers living and raising their families in east London. Both have been without a reliable supply of water this year.
Like others with whom the Guardian spoke, they often only get running water in the middle of the night. “Everything [we] do is after 1 o’clock at night,” Rajia says. “We can’t sleep. [Instead] we do cooking, washing toilet, everything.”
In July, she went three days without any water at all. Her landlord, Poplar Harca, sent the family three five-litre bottles. But when one toilet flush requires five litres, 15 litres is insufficient to keep a household going. “We can’t clean,” she says. “It’s a messy house. Because without water how can it be possible?”
Trying to raise children without a reliable supply of water presents particular problems. Rajia says her two daughters refuse to use the toilet at home because it is unclear when it can be flushed. As a result, they have become unwell.
In this deprived part of east London, many residents of these estates are in poverty, or are affected by disability. For many, English is their second, or even third language. They are among the most marginalised people in the capital. But it seems remarkable that so many can have gone without water for so long without action being taken.
The first time Poplar Harca came to deliver water to Razna Begum’s home after she made a number of attempts to get through to their phone line, the landlord came to check her taps turned on. “We are not lying, what would we do for our taps to turn on? We’ve had no water for the last eight months,” she says.
The 64-year-old lives on the Devons estate with her youngest son, who has severe eczema, and her husband, Abdul Hai, who had a stroke in June and is now mostly bedbound.
Razna believes her husband can no longer use his right side because of the stress from being without water for more than eight months. His visiting carers have advised that he should stay hydrated in the current heatwave. “Sometimes I think my husband could have a heatstroke because there’s no water,” she says.
 “We have emailed our Tower Hamlets mayor but no one has replied. They have stayed silent,” she adds. “This is a first-world country but there is no water.”
A Poplar Harca spokesperson said: “We recognise the disruption and frustration that intermittent low water pressure has caused residents, and we understand the impact this has had on day-to-day activities such as washing, cleaning and cooking. Residents continue to receive water, although pressure levels can fluctuate and, at times, may be insufficient for some households’ needs.
“As soon as we became aware of the issue in December, we worked with Thames Water to investigate the cause, who confirmed that pressure to the affected buildings remains above the minimum level required under Ofwat’s guaranteed standards scheme.”
The landlord said it did not need to pursue an emergency route to fit the pumps to fix the problem and therefore had to follow a statutory consultation process with leaseholders before major works could proceed.
“Our focus has been on maintaining support for affected residents – including supplying bottled water on request as quickly as possible, providing alternative washing facilities and offering additional assistance to residents with support needs – while progressing the permanent solution as quickly as the statutory process and technical works allow.”
A spokesperson for Tower Hamlets council said: “We recognise the significant disruption and inconvenience that water supply issues have caused for affected residents and understand the concerns that have been raised.
“Although the delivery and maintenance of water services within these buildings is a matter for the landlord, Poplar Harca, the council and the mayor’s office are working with them throughout to escalate residents’ concerns, seek updates on remedial works, and ensure appropriate support arrangements are in place, including provisions for vulnerable residents and access to bottled water where required.”

Hundreds in London flats left without regular running water since last year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

Hundreds of residents in blocks of flats in east London have been left without regular running water for more than seven months after development in the area may have left it without an adequate supply.
Taps have been running dry in nine blocks in Tower Hamlets, where residents have been forced to use bottled water while their landlord, the housing association Poplar Harca, delayed works to solve the problem.
In the meantime, hundreds of families have been unable to properly cook, clean, wash or even flush their toilets. Residents, who are bracing for a fifth heatwave this week, say they are still in the dark about why their water suddenly stopped – although some suspect it is because of new housing developments built nearby.
“I’m appalled at the situation my constituents find themselves in,” said Uma Kumaran, the area’s Labour MP. “Access to water is a basic right, yet residents of Devons Road estate have been denied that right for far too long. It’s a gross failure of one of the most fundamental duties a landlord owes to their tenants – especially during record-breaking heatwaves.
“I have repeatedly pushed Poplar Harca to take urgent action, full accountability, and set out a clear and swift timetable for repairs, for all buildings. Residents deserve nothing less than an urgent and permanent fix.”
Poplar Harca acknowledges “pressure levels can fluctuate” but denies the water supply has ever stopped completely.
Residents who spoke to the Guardian said they first began experiencing water shortages last summer. By December, the problems had become widespread, with at least nine blocks affected.
In correspondence with residents, seen by the Guardian, Poplar Harca initially claimed the problem lay with the water supplier. The housing association claimed Thames Water was supplying “lower flow pressures than in previous years”.
But at the same time, Poplar Harca was also telling other residents that their flats needed “extensive works” to create a new pump room in their block to increase water pressure. The landlord said these works could not begin until a formal process – called section 20 – was carried out to determine what share of the cost should be borne by leaseholders.
In common with social housing blocks around the UK, some flats have been purchased by their residents under the right to buy. Those homeowners must share the costs of the blocks’ upkeep. When major works are planned the freeholder must carry out a consultation to determine how much leaseholders should contribute.
Poplar Harca suggested there was no need for emergency action from a judge but a property solicitor the Guardian spoke to said that may not be the case.
Clair Phillips, a senior associate at the law firm Moore Barlow, said: “In circumstances where works are urgent, such as a prolonged loss of water supply, one would ordinarily expect the landlord to undertake the necessary works without delay and then apply to the first-tier tribunal for [urgent] dispensation from the section 20 consultation requirements.”
In the meantime, Poplar Harca told residents – including families and those classed as vulnerable – to access public shower facilities at Poplar Baths and by expensing day passes at Mile End leisure centre. Residents, many of whom are parents with young children, or are elderly or disabled, said this was not an acceptable solution.
As a landlord, Poplar Harca was obliged to provide water to its tenants whose taps had run dry. Residents said they often ended up waiting on the housing association’s phone line for more than an hour at a time, often not getting through at all on weekends or during July’s unprecedented heatwaves.
When they did get through, deliveries were limited to 15 litres per household, regardless of how many people lived there. Some residents said they only received their first delivery last week – more than eight months after the shortages began.
Residents suspect their water has been diverted to new developments in their neighbourhood. Water shortages began for many last autumn, around the time of the completion of Stroudley Walk, a Poplar Harca commercial housing development.
Water engineers were divided on the cause. Paul Kent of Kent Group Services said: “As a boom in construction has emerged over the past few decades, [Thames Water’s] infrastructure is still decades and centuries old, with lots of leaks on the systems due to the number of new housing developments in east London. Thames Water has had to lower water pressure to be able to supply everyone.”
Dale Joseph, a gas and plumbing engineer with Under Pressure Plumbing London, visited some of the affected blocks with the Guardian. He said that given Thames Water said it was meeting its responsibility to provide adequate pressure to the properties, it was up to the landlord to ensure each flat had enough to keep the taps flowing.
Towards the end of last month, Poplar Harca told some residents they could expect the issue to be fixed in six affected blocks between 5 August and 8 September. Work at three blocks is not due to begin until 27 August. That means some residents will have been left without adequate water for up to a year.
A Thames Water spokesperson said that after investigating a number of complaints, the company believed the low pressure was “due to extensive new development in the area, as well as some problems related to customers’ internal plumbing.
“We are looking into remodelling the wider area, which could raise the water pressure to take account for increased localised development. This requires extensive testing and any plans are at a very early stage.”
Sadaf Moosvi, an organiser with the community organisation Acorn, who helped some residents to come together to make a complaint, said: “There are genuinely no words to describe the scale of this scandal. I’ve been organising communities for several years and have seen a great deal, but never anything like this.”
A Poplar Harca spokesperson said: “Residents continue to receive water, although pressure levels can fluctuate and, at times, may be insufficient for some households’ needs. As soon as we became aware of the issue in December, we worked with Thames Water to investigate the cause who confirmed that pressure to the affected buildings remains above the minimum level required under Ofwat’s guaranteed standards scheme.
“The permanent solution requires the installation of new pump systems within the affected buildings. While we were keen to move forward as quickly as possible, because the water supply has remained available, albeit with temporary interruptions, we did not need to pursue an emergency route to fit the pumps. As a result, we’ve followed the statutory section 20 consultation process with leaseholders before major works can proceed.”
The spokesperson added: “We appreciate that residents would have liked a faster resolution. Our focus has been on maintaining support for affected residents – including supplying bottled water on request as quickly as possible, providing alternative washing facilities and offering additional assistance to residents with support needs – while progressing the permanent solution as quickly as the statutory process and technical works allow. We have kept residents updated throughout by text message, online, drop-in sessions, door-knocking and regular written updates.”

Could you predict which children will be Neets? No – and it’s unfair to ask that of teachers | Daisy Christodoulou
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

When you go to the dentist, what do you expect? That they will check your teeth, see if you need any fillings, give you some advice on oral hygiene? You probably don’t expect that they will teach your child to read, tackle youth unemployment or solve poverty.
But when it comes to education, politicians are remarkably relaxed about loading wider social responsibilities on to schools. The suggestion from Alan Milburn, a former minister and now a senior government adviser, is that primary schools – that is, schools that educate children aged four to 11 – should identify children who might not be in education, employment or training at the age of 16. “The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,” he said. “So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”
Laudable in theory, but we need a bit of realism about what it is fair to make schools responsible for, and if making them responsible for so many things is going to cause more problems than it solves.
Defenders of this approach will argue that big problems have many causes, so we need a holistic response that breaks down institutional silos. I’d argue that by making people responsible for outcomes they have very little control over, you risk demoralising them and distracting them from what they can control.
Of course, it is true that primaries, and secondaries as well, have some influence over students’ later career prospects. There are numerous studies showing the importance of numeracy and literacy to economic outcomes. Getting GCSE English and maths means a student will be much less likely to be Neet. In fact, if a primary did want to create a “Neet risk register”, the simplest thing to do would be to list the pupils struggling to read.
But that just shows the futility of this kind of policy. The main way a primary school can contribute to a pupil’s future work success is by teaching them maths and English. Requiring a separate Neet strategy would add another layer of bureaucracy to a system that is already too full of them. A boy who is struggling to read shouldn’t need a “potentially unemployed in 2034” database tag before a school can act.
We also need to recognise that while schools have influence over students’ later success, they are just one small part of a wider system. Having better basic skills and more qualifications will help individuals succeed in the labour market. But if there are persistent structural problems with the labour market, improving individuals’ skills will not necessarily create more or better opportunities overall.
Our new government disagrees. They see rising youth unemployment rates as largely education’s problem. It isn’t just Milburn: the new education secretary, Lucy Powell, has suggested a causal link between schools policy and Neet rates, and this analysis is being used to justify radical reform, or as she puts it “rewiring the entire education system to give young people from all backgrounds the chance to thrive”. But is that link true? Neet rates have risen in England and Wales, despite them having very different education systems. The tax and regulatory burden of employing young people has increased in the past few years, and this may have contributed to the sudden rise in Neets over and above what goes on in schools.
More broadly, we need to look at systemic issues with the British economy. A recent analysis by John Burn-Murdoch in the Financial Times showed that US workers who are functionally illiterate earn as much as the average British worker. “The same proportion of US workers who score stunningly low on literacy earn an average of almost $30 per hour, and two-thirds of them are in work,” he said. “Their British counterparts make the equivalent of $20 and fewer than half are employed.”
Schools can make sure students have the skills they need to thrive in a modern economy, but the economy has to be set up to take advantage of those skills. Increasingly, ours is not. We need to look at all the factors other than skills that might be contributing to this: housing, energy, transport, tax, regulation, health.
And we need to be careful: if we keep improving skills without increasing opportunities, we risk creating a generation of smart but disillusioned young people, youngsters who worked hard at school and university but still ended up with worse living standards than their parents and their peers in other countries.
Over the past 20 years, the UK has barely seen any per capita GDP growth, or any growth in median wages. In the same period, primary schools in England have risen up the rankings on international tests: according to the most recent rankings in 2021, England is one of the best-performing countries in the west on Pirls, a test of primary literacy. Primaries are a rare example of an English public policy success. We risk undermining that success by making them compensate for state failures elsewhere.
More broadly, why is it that a holistic approach to a social problem generally requires schools to take on extra responsibilities? “Joined-up government” always seems to involve schools helping the Treasury and Home Office achieve their objectives, not Treasury officials and police officers teaching eight-year-olds to read and count.
Schools are already doing a good job. Some other parts of the British state need to get better at doing theirs.
- 
  Daisy Christodoulou is an education writer and director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startup

José Pizarro’s recipe for peach and moscatel granita
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

For me, the best desserts are often the simplest. In Spain, we often finish a meal with something light, something that refreshes rather than fills you up. This is exactly that. It has a lovely texture that sits somewhere between a drink and something you eat, and is perfect at the end of a long meal. It feels relaxed but still special, the kind of thing you enjoy on a warm day, when all you want is something fresh and uplifting.
Peach and moscatel granita
Prep 5 min
 Cook 40 min, plus chilling
Freeze 3 hr+
Serves 6
500ml moscatel wine
  125g caster sugar
5-6 lemon thyme sprigs
Pared zest of 1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemon
6 ripe peaches or nectarines
Put the wine and sugar in a pan with the lemon thyme and lemon zest, then heat gently until the sugar dissolves. Add 500ml water and bring to a simmer.
Lower the peaches into the liquid and poach for four to five minutes, until tender. Lift out the peaches with a slotted spoon, transfer to a plate or tray and leave to cool. Once cool enough to handle, remove the skins from the peaches and add these to the pan of poaching liquid. Put the peeled peaches in the fridge to chill.
Bring the poaching liquid to a boil, then simmer for 15-20 minutes, until it reduces slightly and turns a lovely pink colour. Strain into a jug, pressing the juice from the skins, then stir in the lemon juice: you should have about 700ml syrup. Leave this to cool, then chill in the fridge until cold.
Pour the chilled syrup into a shallow tray and put in the freezer for 30 minutes. Stir with a fork then repeat, stirring every half an hour or so. You will need to do this five or six times, until you have a lovely granita.
Serve scoops of the granita with a whole poached peach, or cut the fruit in half and remove the stones.

The ‘real’ Mourinho is nowhere to be found in this Netflix documentary
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:00:00 BST
14:00:00 KST

Mourinho falls foul of Netflix’s A-list documentary curse
The pugnacious football manager is the perfect subject for a documentary, writes Louis Chilton. But this one comes up short
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The Special One is some special s***,” says Jose Mourinho, near the start of Netflix’s new three-part career documentary. The self-aggrandising sobriquet that’s trailed him since his early days at Chelsea was, he claims, the contrivance of “some guys in England”. It is then revealed that Mourinho is making this claim while standing in front of a huge mural of himself, inside his own home.
It is obvious from the beginning of Mourinho that the Portuguese tactician – a man who has spent the past 25 years magnetised to both silverware and scandals – is the perfect candidate for a documentary. Much like Netflix’s slick, hagiographic David Beckham doc (2023’s Beckham), Mourinho has a subject with an interesting, controversy-filled arc, full of rises and falls and fights against the world; unlike Beckham, it has a subject with a sharp sense of conversational showmanship. Mourinho, aware of the preposterousness of his own ego but never shy to indulge it, revels in his reputation. “What does it feel like to win?” he is asked at one point. “Normality,” he says. “That’s what I did my whole life… You don’t do a documentary with a guy that wins nothing.” Hatchets are left defiantly unburied: he shows no remorse when it comes to his feud with Spanish goalkeeper Iker Casillas and the “spoiled” Real Madrid galacticos he inherited in 2010. Or his bitter war of words with ex-Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, whom he claims was “as much as I am if not more guilty” of what he nostalgically describes as “that beautiful fight”.
And yet, for all the bluster on show, for all Mourinho’s (in a way, admirable) willingness to play the villain, Mourinho is not the documentary it should be. Three episodes, it turns out, is not really enough to cover his whole career in detail. His first stint at Chelsea – that paradigm-shifting, double Premier League/League Cup-winning stint from 2004 to 2007 – is given ample shrift (taking up the bulk of the first episode), likewise his historic treble-winning time at Inter Milan, the fractious spell at Real, and his return to Stamford Bridge in 2013. But much of what followed, the less gilded decade spent drifting around Manchester United, Tottenham, Roma, Fenerbahçe and Benfica, is sped through. You emerge from watching the series with only a partial sense of Mourinho’s actual career history, almost no insight into the tactical innovations that made him so successful, and – most frustrating of all – no real grasp of who he is, underneath the flashy facade.
It may be that documentaries like these are simply not equipped for the sort of deep-dive scrutiny that would make them truly worthwhile. Mourinho isn’t a puff piece in the traditional sense – he is presented as an egotist with (as one person says) something of a “god complex”, a man who seems to delight in pissing people off. (“I enjoy the negativity,” he says at one point – referring to the hostile atmosphere of big away games, but an admission that really applies to his whole life.) But his own active participation in the series allows him to dictate the conversation, and there are key areas that seem conveniently elided.
An interesting counterpoint might be something like Asif Kapadia’s 2019 documentary film Diego Maradona, which adopted a similar kind of propulsive, accessible approach, but dove more greedily into its subject’s personal life and dark side. It’s curious just how little time is spent discussing Mourinho’s life before Chelsea, and indeed any part of his life that doesn’t involve football. He does not discuss his political views – he never does – views that The Times claimed decades ago were “believed to be strongly right wing”. His background too, as the child of wealth, is breezed over; these things not part of the established Mourinho Myth, that of the self-made outsider. When he then makes pugnacious statements like, “Football belongs to people like me… the others are intruders, they don’t belong,” they pass by uninterrogated.
There is an inherent, unavoidable unfinishedness to this narrative: where Beckham followed its subject from his debut to retirement, Mourinho’s story is still ongoing. The documentary comes as the manager begins his second tenure at Real Madrid, the world’s biggest football club; it is an appointment that came as a shock to many, a return to the big leagues after years spent – with all due respect to Tottenham, Roma, Fenerbahçe and Benfica – slumming it with teams unable to compete at the very highest level of European football. It seemed, until recently at least, that the world had moved on from Mourinho’s antics, and from his brand of football: he was a tactical dinosaur with a meteor looming. But in Mourinho, this is left as postscript. While the fortunes of his comeback are still yet to play out, it would have been useful to dive into his decade-long nadir with even the same surface enthusiasm Mourinho applies to his spiky heyday. Has football left Jose Mourinho behind? I’m not sure. But this documentary doesn’t even consider it.
‘Mourinho’ is available to stream on Netflix

As the world burns, what does it take to make people laugh in 2026?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
06:00:00 BST
14:00:00 KST

Knitting, Tom Cruise and sex: What it takes to make people laugh at the Fringe today
The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is back for its 49th visit to the Scottish capital, even though finding the funny can prove difficult with the world in turmoil. Four comedians tell Lauren Morris how they plan on procuring giggles this year
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
One of the biggest arts festivals on the planet, the Edinburgh Fringe is still hitting audiences’ funny bones almost 50 years on – even though, in 2026, they might seem harder to find than ever.
From international conflicts to climate change and threats of a British recession, it feels like we’re slapped with a barrage of bad news on a daily basis. However, the depressing state of the world won’t stop the comics at this year’s Fringe from looking for laughs.
“If anything, I feel like people want to laugh and go out and have a good time,” says Ania Magliano, who is performing her show Peach Fuzz at the Fringe. “I haven’t felt any more resistance.” The Saturday Night Live UK star is getting personal on stage, tackling everything from sex and boundaries to how “a lot of us are quite disconnected from our bodies”.
“Society can feel more isolated, with us spending a lot of time on our phones and feeling quite separate,” she continues. “It’s a good sign that there’s still a need for collective experience. You can obviously watch stand-up on your own at home now or on your phone, but if that were to replace live comedy, it would be a real loss. There’s something about being in the room with other people and enjoying something together that I think is really magical.”
Some comedians are quite literally knitting their audience members together, with Tom Towelling making his stand-up debut at the Fringe with his alternative take on community. The Brummie comic and teacher is drawing on his academic day job with Tom Towelling Teaches You To Knit – “sending up the idea of how, over an hour, we can build connections with each other” through song, dance and balls of wool.
“The main similarity between teaching and comedy is they are both about meeting crowds, audiences, and classes halfway,” he says. “I think people really like comedy shows when they feel drawn in and get involved.”
Plus, thanks to the rise of social media, audiences are ready to laugh – with fans flocking to the Fringe to see their favourite comics after being served their stand-up by TikTok and Instagram algorithms.
“Audiences are much more comedy savvy,” says Olga Koch, who has performed at the Fringe for a decade. Her current show, Fat Tom Cruise, sees her turn a hilarious dinner party anecdote into an hour of stand-up on an unrequited crush, fraternity hazing and gender equality.
“There’s the ubiquity of the YouTube special or a TikTok clip, but also more people know about comedy as a thing. They can actively go to see it and not just on TV, so I do think there is a huge and wonderful democratising force. You don’t have to be a comedy nerd to go see comedy anymore and it’s all over social media now.”
For Magliano, social media has also been a game-changer. “It’s been massively helpful because you can put your clips online,” she says. “And while the algorithm is obviously evil, it will send your clips to the exact target demographic who will enjoy them.”
While Magliano admits that sometimes the algorithm will send clips to demographics who “will comment hateful stuff and get really wound up” by a particular comic’s content, the social media grind is worth it just to find an audience that’s right for you. “When I was newer, it would send my clips to young women my age who related to the stuff I was talking about,” she continues. “It’s a good way to find them.”
So, are we all looking to comedy, now more than ever, for an escape in these uncertain times? Fringe veteran Pierre Novellie thinks it’s not that simple.
“People would say that back in 2016 with Brexit and Trump,” says the comic, whose show Okay, One More Then Bedtime, examines his “workaholic” tendencies and why he keeps returning to the Fringe. “By the time they’re in a comedy audience, they’re already halfway to not thinking about the outside world, which is useful for us.”
It’s also not always guaranteed that audiences want to completely disengage from the crumbling state of the world, with a number of shows tackling big issues like gender identity politics (Dee Allum: Raumdeuter), the Russia-Ukraine war (Sasha Nezlobin: I’m Fine) and artificial intelligence (Garrett Millerick: We Tried it Your Way).
“I’m a very avid comedy audience member and my two domains are either silly and nonsensical or something that’s really head-on, difficult and knotty,” Koch says. “I’m looking for extremes and I do think that’s reflective of all audiences who either want to completely smooth-brain it and have a giggly old time or talk about it.”
Ultimately, the Edinburgh Fringe is still a buzzing hub for all things live comedy – and only becoming more important with the artform starting to disappear from TV. Live at the Apollo, which launched the careers of Michael McIntyre, Mo Gilligan and Katherine Ryan among other comedians, was axed by the BBC last month after 22 years.
“That means there’s no stand-up on mainstream TV anymore,” Novellie says. “Yet, it’s the cheapest thing to film. You just need a camera, the stage and the audience. I don’t really understand what’s so incredibly complicated about it.”
“It’s a heartbreaking thing,” Koch adds, “when any sort of comedy platform disappears. It makes the world smaller.”
Magliano says that the comedy industry needs “big-scale funding” to be pumped into it for it to continue thriving – much like South Korea has invested in its flourishing K-pop market.
“British comedy is such an export and loved worldwide. You still need big portions of money going into it because it can open doors with what can be created – I love Nathan Fielding’s [American docu-comedy] The Rehearsal and it just shows that if you have a big budget, it really makes a difference for comedy and art,” she says.
The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is running in venues across the city until 31 August

A 600-year-old mystery: Will Lithuania finally find the remains of Vytautas the Great?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

A nearly century-old empty sarcophagus in Vilnius Cathedral is waiting for the remains of one of Lithuania’s most revered rulers. This autumn, archaeologists will begin a new search for the remains of Grand Duke Vytautas the Great (c. 1350–1430), as part of a much broader effort to uncover the secrets of the cathedral’s past.
The Lithuanian government approved a plan in early July for scientific research aimed at investigating possible locations of Vytautas’ remains. It also approved a wider program of research into Vilnius Cathedral, including archaeological excavations, architectural studies, historical research and the examination of human remains.
The work is expected to create a database of people buried in the cathedral over different periods and a comprehensive bioarchive of samples taken from the remains.
Historians and archaeologists broadly agree that the research will significantly expand knowledge of the cathedral, where systematic investigations have never been carried out on this scale. But they are divided over whether the long-standing search for Vytautas’ remains will succeed.
The stone sarcophagus in the cathedral’s Chapter Crypt was made nearly 100 years ago and remains empty. Its inscription bears the date October 27, 1930, when Lithuania marked the 500th anniversary of Vytautas’ death.
Vytautas, who ruled the Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1392 until his death in 1430, never became king, although he sought a royal crown. He remains one of the most important figures in Lithuanian history.
A search that began a century ago
The first serious professional archaeological investigations of the cathedral’s underground crypts began around the 1930 anniversary, when researchers hoped they might find Vytautas’ intact remains, perhaps alongside his insignia or regalia.
Instead, they encountered problems from the get-go.
“The reality turned out to be much more complicated because of the dampness of the underground spaces, the high groundwater level and flooding in the city,” said Alina Pavasarytė, a historian at the Church Heritage Museum. “The underground spaces are, obviously, underground, and this is the deepest place in the Old Town.”
Wooden coffins buried there had largely decomposed, leaving human remains mixed together, she said.
The search intensified in recent years as Lithuania approaches the 600th anniversary of Vytautas’ death.
It also gained momentum after historical researcher Saulius Poderis, who has been convicted of illegal archaeology, published his theory about where Vytautas’ remains might have been hidden.
“I am a supporter of the theory that Vytautas was found during the interwar period,” Poderis said, arguing that systematic excavations at the cathedral at the time uncovered his remains.
He points to a letter by 18th-century historian Franciszek Ksawery Bohusz, which he says indicated that Vytautas was buried near Grand Duke Alexander Jagiellon in the cathedral’s crypt.
According to the official historical account, the remains of three rulers – Alexander Jagiellon, Barbara Radziwiłł and Elisabeth of Austria – were discovered in the cathedral in 1931. All three are now buried in the royal crypt.
Poderis argues that the remains of Vytautas may also have been discovered but deliberately concealed because Vilnius was then under Polish control and relations between Poland and Lithuania were deeply strained.
“It was a political decision. It was made on the same day the crypt was discovered,” Poderis said.
A ruler turned into a national symbol
Vytautas’ remains have long carried significance beyond archaeology.
The 500th anniversary of his death in 1930 was one of the most important state events in interwar Lithuania. The country was still building its national identity after declaring independence in 1918, and Vytautas was embraced as a symbol of a powerful and independent Lithuania.
With Vilnius under Polish control at the time, his legacy also came to symbolise Lithuania’s historical claim to its capital.
“Vytautas is remembered in Lithuanian consciousness and memory as one of the most prominent and successful rulers, a defender of independence and a symbol of Lithuania in the 14th and 15th centuries,” said Antanas Petrilionis, a lecturer at Vilnius University’s Faculty of History.
“That image of Vytautas and his remains becomes important because people need a symbol they can see, not just hear about,” he said.
Poderis said he has spent 17 years investigating the mystery and remains convinced that Vytautas’ remains were secretly reburied during the interwar period.
One of the locations he considers most likely is the western wall of the royal mausoleum. Archaeologists from the Lithuanian Institute of History plan to investigate the site this autumn.
The method will be deliberately limited.
“This will be an invasive investigation to check the location indicated by Poderis,” said archaeologist Rytis Jonaitis. “A hole will be drilled through the wall, a probe with a camera will be inserted and we will look at what is inside.”
Poderis has identified several other possible locations. But Jonaitis said archaeologists cannot simply drill into every one.
“If we drilled into every place, we would turn the cathedral into a sieve,” he said.
Ground-penetrating scans and other technologies can reveal whether there is an empty space behind a wall, Jonaitis said, but they cannot determine what is inside it.
A much bigger investigation
The search for Vytautas is only one part of the government-backed research program.
The government has allocated about 7.5 million euros for a comprehensive investigation of Vilnius Cathedral. Researchers will examine the cathedral’s history and historical documents, study its structure and masonry, conduct archaeological excavations, assess artworks and their value, and analyse human remains.
Researchers believe about 800 sets of human remains have already been identified in the cathedral.
But identifying Vytautas would require more than finding remains in a plausible location. Scientists would need a reliable genetic reference for comparison.
“We all know that there are about 800 sets of remains that have been discovered,” said Darius Jakavičius, chairman of the Lithuanian parliament’s Commission for Historical Memory. “To begin studying them, we need what you could call a reference gene or code that we can use as a basis for comparison.”
Potential DNA reference samples could come from the graves of Vytautas’ close relatives in Ukraine or the Czech Republic. Seeking a sample from Russia, where Vytautas’ only daughter, Sophia, is buried, is not currently being considered.
Jakavičius said he had visited Prague and spoken with representatives of St Vitus Cathedral, where he was told there would be no obstacles to obtaining material needed for the research. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry is also working on the issue, he said.
Ukraine could provide another potential source of genetic material. The Pechersk Lavra in Kyiv contains the remains of prominent historical figures connected with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Gediminid dynasty, Jakavičius said.
Scepticism and hope
Despite the excitement surrounding the renewed search, scientists remain cautious.
Asked whether he would bet on archaeologists finding Vytautas’ remains, Jonaitis said he would not.
“In science, I am an extreme sceptic,” he said. “In my personal opinion, it is more likely that we will not find them.”
Jakavičius is more optimistic.
“A year ago, there was more pessimism. Now I see more reasons for optimism,” he said.
Petrilionis also expressed confidence.
“I am optimistic. I think he is hiding somewhere there,” he said.
Poderis, whose theory has driven much of the renewed search, stopped short of claiming certainty.
“I am not saying 100%,” he said. “My intuition has not deceived me in life. I think it won’t be empty there.”
The investigation is expected to produce answers by 2030, when Lithuania will mark the 600th anniversary of Vytautas’ death.
If his remains are found, the cathedral could become home to a pantheon of Lithuanian rulers.
If they are not, historians say the broader investigation will still be a major success, providing a much more detailed understanding of the history of Vilnius Cathedral and the people buried beneath it.

인니 중앙은행 총재 후보로 수석부총재 단수 지명…여성 최초
South Korea
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
13:58:05 KST
13:58:05 KST

임기를 2년이나 남겨둔 중앙은행 총재가 최근 돌연 사임한 인도네시아에서 처음으로 여성 중앙은행 총재가 나올 전망이다.
그러나 이번에는 프라보워 대통령이 데스트리 부총재만 후보로 지명하면서 이변이 없는 한 그가 인도네시아에서는 처음으로 여성 BI 총재가 될 전망이다.
2008년 이후 인도네시아 의회가 대통령이 지명한 BI 총재 후보를 거부한 사례는 지금까지 없었다.
전체 내용을 이해하기 위해서는 기사 본문과 함께 읽어야 합니다.
송고 2026년08월11일 13시58분
구글 검색에서 연합뉴스 기사를 우선적으로 보여줍니다.
(자카르타=연합뉴스) 손현규 특파원 = 임기를 2년이나 남겨둔 중앙은행(BI) 총재가 최근 돌연 사임한 인도네시아에서 처음으로 여성 중앙은행 총재가 나올 전망이다.
11일(현지시간) 로이터·블룸버그 통신 등에 따르면 전날 프라세티요 하디 인도네시아 국가비서실 장관(국무장관)은 프라보워 수비안토 대통령이 현재 BI 총재 대행을 맡고 있는 데스트리 다마얀티(62) 수석 부총재를 차기 총재 후보로 지명했다고 밝혔다.
다만 신임 BI 총재가 페리 와르지요 전 총재의 잔여 임기 2년을 채울지, 아니면 새로 5년 임기를 시작하는지는 설명하지 않았다.
2019년부터 수석 부총재를 맡은 데스트리 부총재는 지난달 25일 페리 전 총재가 임기를 2년이나 남겨놓고 갑자기 사임한 뒤 총재 대행을 맡았다.
인도네시아에서는 대통령이 여러 명의 BI 총재 후보자를 지명하면 의회 심사를 거쳐 이들 중 한 명만 승인받아 총재로 임명된다.
앞서 프라보워 대통령은 최근 데스트리 부총재와 함께 참석한 중부자바주 행사에서 "그가 현재 총재 대행인데 어떻게 생각하느냐"고 청중들에게 물었다. 그러면서 "괜찮지 않느냐"며 "의회에 맡기겠다"고 덧붙였다.
경제학자 출신인 데스트리 부총재는 과거에 씨티은행과 인도네시아 국영은행인 만디리 은행 등지에서 근무했으며 BI에 합류하기 전인 2015∼2019년에는 인도네시아 예금보험공사 이사회에서 위원을 역임했다.
전문가들은 그가 금융 분야에서 많은 경험을 갖고 있으며 올해 인도네시아 루피아화의 가치가 급락한 상황에서 통화 정책을 안정시킬 수 있는 인물이라고 평가했다.
싱가포르 DBS 은행 소속 경제학자인 라디카 라오는 "데스트리 부총재가 BI와 국내 금융시장에서 쌓아온 풍부한 경험을 고려하면 그의 지명은 시장에서 호의적으로 받아들여질 가능성이 높다"고 예상했다.
그러면서 "그는 통화를 안정시켜야 할 필요성을 분명하게 강조해왔다"며 "정책도 연속적으로 이어갈 수 있을 것"이라고 덧붙였다.
인도네시아 트리메가 증권 소속 수석 이코노미스트인 파크룰 풀비안은 "(데스트리 수석 부총재는) 실용적이고 안정 지향적"이라면서도 "성장 지향적 인상도 가진 정책 입안자"라고 평가했다.
다만 페리 전 총재가 정책 의견 차이 등으로 프라보워 대통령과 대립한 뒤 돌연 사퇴하면서 그는 BI의 독립성에 관한 우려를 해소해야 하는 숙제도 안고 있다.
앞서 소식통들은 프라보워 대통령이 공격적인 경제 성장을 원했지만, 페리 전 총재는 통화와 금융 정책을 안정적으로 유지하는 데 주력했다고 전했다.

South Korea aims to criminalise fictional AI pornography after man’s acquittal
Lawmakers move to close a legal loophole by proposing a bill criminalising virtual porn of fictional characters
The move by lawmakers came after a court in Goyang, Gyeonggi province, acquitted a man accused of distributing deepfake images of nude women in a Telegram chat room.
Despite prosecutors presenting the evidence under a law carrying up to seven years in prison or a maximum fine of 50 million won (US$35,341), a judge last August ruled that the victims were virtual, not human.
“There is no material confirming the origin or synthesis method of the image, making it difficult to conclude that a real person was depicted,” Lee Jung-hoon of the Uijeongbu District Court said in the case, as reported by the Dong-A Ilbo.
That verdict prompted representative Huh Young and nine other lawmakers of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea to propose a bill criminalising the creation, distribution and possession of sexually explicit material made using artificial intelligence, even when it does not depict a real person.
“Rapid advances in AI have made it easy for anyone to create images of virtual people that are difficult to distinguish from real individuals,” the legislators said in the proposal referred to detailed review by the subcommittee of the National Assembly’s Legislation and Judiciary Committee, according to The Korea Times.
“However, the technology has also been misused to produce and distribute manipulated sexual content that causes sexual humiliation or disgust, which is emerging as a serious social problem.”

Extreme heat is reshaping Italy’s sparkling wine industry with early harvests and nighttime picking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
04:53:02 UTC
13:53:02 KST

Extreme heat is reshaping Italy’s sparkling wine industry with early harvests and nighttime picking
CORTE FRANCA, Italy (AP) — Workers fan out before dawn to clip clusters of grapes destined to be transformed into Italy’s prized Franciacorta sparkling wine a full 10 days earlier than anticipated, as scorching temperatures brought the fruit to maturation earlier than ever.
Climate change is narrowing the window for harvesting wine grapes, forcing winemakers to make quick decisions when even a few days can mean the difference between a good vintage and a bad one.
“These are delicate, frantic moments, and everything has to work perfectly,’’ said Berlucchi CEO Arturo Ziliani, whose father, Franco, and estate owner Guido Berlucchi became the first winemakers in the northern Italian region of Franciacorta to produce sparkling wine using the “classic” method famously employed by France’s Champagne makers.
“We did not expect such an early harvest or such an acceleration in ripening,” Ziliani said.
Heat forces predawn picking under floodlights
Weeks of temperatures reaching highs between 37 and 38 degrees Celsius (99 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit), combined with below-average rainfall, have pushed some winemakers in Franciacorta to record the earliest start on record — 10 days earlier than last year and about a month earlier than three decades ago.
Berlucchi, the oldest producer of Franciacorta, which is made using the traditional method of secondary fermentation in the bottle, began harvesting Aug. 2 as part of an industrywide effort to preserve grape quality in the face of increasingly extreme weather.
Experts say several factors combined to push Franciacorta’s harvest so early this year. A relatively mild winter meant the vines produced buds earlier, while hailstorms damaged some of the yield, lightening the fruit and bringing it to earlier maturation.
Even in late July, Berlucchi was targeting an Aug. 10 harvest date, but it quickly became clear that Pinot Nero used for sparkling blends and rosé was ready to be picked, signaled by rapidly rising sugar levels. Within two days, workers were mustered and the presses were readied.
The midday heat has been so extreme that workers are forced by regional labor rules to stop between 12:30 p.m. and 4 p.m., but winemakers say it has been too hot for the afternoon shift. To gain time and bring grapes to the presses before they are overheated, Berlucchi last week started the harvest at 4 a.m., with workers picking under the blaze of floodlights.
“The grapes are perfectly healthy,” said Ferdinando Dell’aquila, an oenologist who is Berlucchi’s technical director. “We just have to work as quickly as possible, harvest them and preserve their acidity.”
Sparkling wine requires complex calculations
It is not just Franciacorta that is starting early. Sicily began the wine harvest for still wines in late July. Small parts of Tuscany also started picking, as well as most sparkling wine regions.
The calculation is most complex for the makers of Champagne-style sparkling wines, which require a delicate balance of much higher fixed acidity, much lower pH and lower sugars than for still reds and whites.
“Early-ripening varieties such as Chardonnay require great care, because a delay of just a couple of days can leave you with grapes unsuitable for sparkling wine. Sugar rises too quickly and acidity falls too quickly,’' said Attilio Scienza, a professor emeritus at the University of Milan.
High outdoor temperatures require the grapes to be cooled before being gently pressed in stainless steel machines to extract the highest quality free-run juice, a crucial step in sparkling wine production that cannot be rushed. Berlucchi operates up to 24 presses a day, often late into the night, to process the unusually early harvest.
Berlucchi remains Franciacorta’s largest producer, making about 4 million bottles annually, about 20% of the Franciacorta consortium’s total production of about 20 million bottles. About 90% are sold in Italy, with the remainder exported to markets including Germany, Switzerland, the United States and Japan.
Winemakers adapt to a new harvest calendar
“Climate change and the African weather systems settling over Europe are bringing extraordinary temperatures and forcing early picking, not only in Italy, but also in France and Germany,” said Paolo Castelletti, secretary general of the Italian Wine Union trade organization.
With earlier harvests becoming a trend, winemakers say they will have to begin monitoring the fields even earlier to make sure they don’t miss the best harvesting moment.
“A good oenologist can manage situations like this. I can say with confidence that wine quality is not compromised. It simply requires a different organization of work than in past years,” Castelletti said.

Colombia searches for its missing after a powerful earthquake kills more than 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
04:53:02 UTC
13:53:02 KST

Colombia searches for its missing after a powerful earthquake kills more than 100
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Search and rescue efforts were underway early Tuesday in dozens of cities and towns in western Colombia after a powerful earthquake struck the region, killing at least 111 people and leaving many trapped under the debris of damaged and destroyed buildings.
Monday’s 7.4 magnitude earthquake rattled Cali, Quibdo, Pereira and numerous other cities and towns. Around 1,600 buildings were reported damaged or collapsed. Soldiers, rescue personnel and families picked through the rubble, removing and passing large pieces of concrete by hand down lines of volunteers.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Monday afternoon at least 111 people had died.
Families posted information about missing loved ones on citizen-run websites. By Monday night, more than 2,700 people had been reported missing.
Dana Carolina Zamora posted an image of her missing 60-year-old uncle, Miguel Ángel Zamora, cradling his dog. The farmer was living in a rural area of El Cairo, not far from the epicenter of the quake in San Jose Del Palmar.
Local authorities said 80% of El Cairo, a town of about 7,000 people, was damaged. Zamora said she worried because her uncle lived in a traditional but fragile house made of sticks and mud.
“We are afraid. We hope that is not the case, that he is all right and that it is only a communication failure. But we haven’t heard anything from him,” Zamora said.
Choco, the region surrounding the quake’s epicenter, is one of the poorest and most neglected regions of Colombia, often beset by warring armed groups. Much of Choco is accessible only by boat, through the jungle or by airplane. Little was known about the extent of the damage there.
De la Espriella traveled to Choco’s capital, Quibdo, on Monday night to assess the damage and announced he had mobilized “the entire military and police apparatus” to respond, deploying engineers, rescue workers and search dogs. He announced rental subsidies for those whose homes were damaged while they undergo repairs.
“Choco will never again be the ‘land of the forgotten,’” he said.
The earthquake presents the first major test for de la Espriella, who was sworn in as Colombia’s leader on Friday. De la Espriella is a divisive figure because of his pledge of an all-out crackdown on criminal groups.
The U.S. State Department announced it would provide $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food and other aid. Governments across Latin America also lined up to help.
The earthquake left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighboring Venezuela in late June, destroying hundreds of buildings and killing more than 6,300 people.
Many Colombians were only beginning to grapple with the disaster’s longer-term consequences.
Mónica Sánchez owns a small company that makes work uniforms. Her home city, Pereira, was one of the worst hit, and a wall inside the factory collapsed. Sánchez and her 12 workers were able to get outside just in time.
“It was shocking — the city fell down around us,” she said.

Janetsky reported from Mexico City.

Unknown Publisher

Beijing is expected to hit by more than one-third of its annual rainfall over a 24 hour period starting late Tuesday, as Typhoon Dolphin moves deeper inland prompting the closure of tourist areas and suspension of construction projects.
From Tuesday evening through to Thursday, most areas in Beijing will experience heavy downpours with a cumulative rainfall of more than 150mm in 24 hours, the city’s meteorological service has forecast. That compares with Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm, the bulk of which normally falls between June and September.
Four districts on Beijing’s outskirts activated level one emergency flood responses. In the mountainous district of Mentougou in western Beijing, authorities issued the highest level of flood emergency alert on Tuesday and advised people to stay indoors unless necessary, and avoid travelling to mountainous areas and rivers.
The strongest typhoon to hit China this year, Dolphin has proved an unusually resilient storm system, travelling nearly 6,000km (3,728 miles) before making landfall over the weekend, drenching China’s eastern coast and bringing with it a sprawling cloud field.
More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China over the weekend, amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.
Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved.
In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening.
Early on Tuesday Dolphin moved over the central Chinese province of Hubei, a major auto and hi-tech electronics manufacturing hub and home to more than 58 million people.
On Tuesday, the National Meteorological Center renewed an orange alert for heavy rain, the second-highest warning level, with north-western Hubei expected to receive up to 250mm in a 24-hour period. Hubei authorities have issued a yellow warning for cities including Xiangyang, Huanggang and Suizhou, citing a heightened risk of flooding and landslides.
Scenic areas across the province have announced temporary closures, including the popular Three Gorges Dam tourist area in Yichang. Of 107 major highway and waterway construction projects under way in the province, 26 projects deemed high-risk have been suspended.
In neighbouring Henan province, authorities issued a flash-flood alert as the storm continues to channel moisture northward.
Japan is also preparing for landslides, flooding and strong winds after the Japan Meteorological Agency said Typhoon Chan-hom, could move across Japan’s mainland later on Tuesday.

Parliament passes key law in ‘terror-free Türkiye’ process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
04:49:42 UTC
13:49:42 KST

The Turkish parliament has approved a 12-article framework law to ensure the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK terrorist organization with the votes of more than two thirds of the lawmakers, increasing hopes for the smooth continuation of the process.
Some 468 lawmakers voted in favor of, and only 88 against the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration on late Aug. 10 after almost 10 hours-long discussions. All the political parties, except for the İYİ (Good) Party, supported the bill with few defections.
“We will all together build a new era. Türkiye has enough ability to resolve its most difficult problem. The process will run afterwards in a smooth way,” Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş told the reporters after the vote.
“This is not just the success of a certain political party but the entire Türkiye. We’ll now carefully follow the next steps,” he added.
Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz also hailed the vote, stressing that the overwhelming support to the framework law demonstrates the existence of political consensus and people’s ownership for the resolve of the terror problem.
Ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) parliamentary group leader Abdullah Güler thanked to all the lawmakers who approved the bill, saying “We want to open new horizons for Türkiye. We’ll accomplish all together this no matter what the cost is. Our objective is to silence the weapons permanently.”
The law will take effect after being signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and published in the Official Gazette.
The legislation sets out judicial and administrative procedures linked to the dissolution and disarmament of the PKK, which is listed as a terrorist organization by Türkiye, the United States and the European Union.
The measures can be applied only after security agencies verify that the PKK/KCK and affiliated formations no longer maintain an operational presence and have surrendered all weapons and ammunition.
The National Security Council must endorse that finding in a decision published in the Official Gazette.
Eligible applicants will have six months to apply. Depending on the offense and sentence, investigations, trials and the execution of sentences may be postponed for five or 10 years. Intentional killings committed as part of the organization’s activities and certain offenses committed before June 1, 2005, carrying life or aggravated life sentences are excluded.
The law also establishes an eight-member board chaired by the vice president to oversee implementation, along with a parliamentary commission that will monitor the process.
Dubbed the terror-free Türkiye project, the process begun in late 2024 after a historic call by Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) Chairman Devlet Bahçeli. PKK’s jailed leader Abdullah Öcalan released a call on the PKK in February 2025 to give an end to its armed conflict and dissolve itself.
In line with this call, the PKK declared that it decided to drop the weapons and dissolve itself in June 2025. A month later the first batch of PKK members burned their weapons in a symbolic event in northern Iraq.

Trump secretly switched planes to leave Turkey due to Iran assassination threat

Trump hid in catering cart in secret Air Force One swap to fend off Iran assassination threat
White House staffers and journalists on Air Force One were unaware of the dramatic switch and were left on board to become unwitting decoys to the threat, according to a report
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
President Donald Trump was secretly transported away from Turkey in an extraordinary plan triggered by an assassination threat from Iran, according to a report.
Air Force One, a catering truck and a secondary military plane were all part of an elaborate “deception operation” to safeguard the commander-in-chief when he departed last month’s Nato summit in Ankara, The Washington Post has revealed.
Several White House staffers and journalists remained on Air Force One as unwitting decoys to the threat while Trump was quietly smuggled off the plane and boarded onto a different flight, according to the Post.
The newspaper based its account on reviewed documentation, a U.S. official aware of the operation and another individual familiar with the president’s travel arrangements.
Trump had originally arrived in Turkey on a newly retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet presented as a gift from Qatar. Prior to leaving, however, he announced he would complete the first leg of his journey home on an older, baby-blue Air Force One aircraft.
At the time, the president explained that the luxury aircraft was departing Ankara early so that military personnel stationed in eastern England could view the updated Air Force One.
Trump was filmed by television crews boarding the older jumbo jet in Ankara before it set off for the Mildenhall Royal Air Force base in Suffolk.
But shortly after stepping onto the legacy Air Force One, he was transferred to a smaller Air Force C-32A plane. He was moved using a catering truck usually employed for loading inflight meals, before flying to Mildenhall in the smaller aircraft.
The White House did not directly address enquiries about the clandestine operation to transfer Trump onto a third plane or the scheme designed to make it look as though he remained aboard the baby-blue Air Force One bound for Mildenhall.
“As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a statement.
The Secret Service declined to comment while the Air Force, which operates the executive transport fleet, directed enquiries to the White House.
During Trump’s stay in Turkey, the U.S. military carried out significant strikes inside Iran following attacks on commercial shipping in the surrounding region.
Intelligence officials had previously warned of a possible attack targeting the president or his aircraft, as reported last month by The New York Times and CBS News. Those concerns prompted heightened security measures and the decision not to fly the newly-gifted Qatari jet for the initial leg of Trump’s return from Ankara.
The switch raised doubts concerning the safety of the new plane, which the president later noted would undergo further security enhancements.
On Monday, Cheung insisted that the Qatari plane remained “a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.”
The revelations regarding Trump’s covert transfer to a third plane highlight the severity with which U.S. security officials view potential threats against him amid conflict with Iran.
Paul Eckloff, a former Secret Service agent, remarked that such a tactic could indicate specific intelligence or extreme caution amid regional instability involving conflicts in Iran and Ukraine.
“I would not say unprecedented, but it is an unusual occurrence,” Eckloff said.
To leave the aircraft unnoticed, Trump and a small group of aides boarded the hydraulic catering vehicle, which had been raised to a door on the far side of Air Force One, according to the Post.
The traveling press corps, unaware of the manoeuvre, was asked to pull down its window blinds prior to departure.
Upon landing at Mildenhall, photographers captured Trump disembarking the primary presidential plane, indicating he had re-boarded Air Force One away from the reporters.
Connecticut Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal demanded a congressional inquiry into the matter.
“It is unprecedented and it’s surreal,” he stated on CNN Monday, describing the event as “downright scary.”
Following the short stop at the British airbase, Trump boarded the newly-gifted Air Force One jet to complete his journey to Washington.
Speaking to reporters on board, Trump was asked directly whether there were credible Iranian threats against Air Force One.
“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list before you,” he replied.
He then told the accompanying press: “But if I go, you go.”

Breaking: Reserve Bank keeps interest rate at 4.35pc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
04:48:33 UTC
13:48:33 KST

Interest rates on hold but RBA governor keeps door open to hikes
In short:
The RBA has kept interest rates at 4.35 per cent.
Headline inflation cooled a bit in June, and property prices have declined by a little more than anticipated, but underlying inflation pressures remain elevated.
What's next?
The monetary policy board's next interest rate meeting will be held on September 28-29.
The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold at 4.35 per cent, in a unanimous decision.
The move comes after headline inflation cooled a bit in June, and property prices declined by a little more than anticipated in recent months.
It also comes after economists have been warning that underlying inflation is still too high, with some saying that they expect interest rates to have to rise again, at some point, to squeeze inflation out of the economy.
But the RBA's latest forecasts, also released today, show a more upbeat picture than the bank's last forecasts published in May.
They suggest inflation may have peaked a lot lower than the RBA previously feared.
However, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock used her press conference to highlight that the risks to inflation remain to the upside, including the Middle East conflict.
Asked if the board considered cutting rates, Ms Bullock said it only considered the options of hiking interest rates or holding them steady, eventually deciding unanimously on the latter.
"There was a diversity of views [on the board] about how strongly people felt they were worried about inflation, but everyone was at least a little bit worried about what those inflationary risks may be and what they may imply," she said.
"We're staying put, but staying put with a very clear focus on watching how the data come in, and whether or not the next interest rate move, we may need to increase again, if it looks like we're not on track to get inflation back down."
RBA lowers inflation forecasts
In the central bank's new forecasts, headline inflation, while still well above the bank's 2-3 per cent target range, has come in nearly a full percentage point lower than its previous forecast.
Its preferred more stable measure of "trimmed mean" inflation is 0.2 per cent below the last forecast.
The bank is now forecasting inflation to have a slower, steadier trajectory down from current levels to be back at the 2.5 per cent midpoint of its target by early 2028.
Following today's decision, the official cash rate target will remain at 4.35 per cent for the next seven weeks, until the RBA Board's next meeting in late September.
Loading...
Its latest forecasts are based on an assumption that the cash rate stays around current levels at 4.35 per cent in December 2028, versus the previous forecasts which had the cash rate peaking around 4.7 per cent over the next year.
That does not mean that the Reserve Bank itself expects rates to be on hold at current levels for the next two years or more; it is based on what traders are betting on in financial markets.
But the fact that both headline and "core" inflation are still expected to get back to the mid-point of the RBA's 2-3 per cent target range by early 2028, despite one less rate cut than the May forecasts, is evidence of the lower-than-feared inflation trajectory and suggests that the RBA may be done with rate hikes, if its forecasts prove accurate.
Competition takes edge off mortgage borrowers
The bank's new forecasts show that many borrowers have also had the edge taken off recent interest rate rises by competition between the banks for mortgages.
"Spreads between lending rates and the cash rate also remain low by historical standards, reflecting low risk premia, favourable funding conditions and strong competition in lending markets," the RBA noted.
Despite this, the RBA has noted that scheduled mortgage repayments relative to household disposable income have increased to be close to their 2024 peak.
It says Australian households are spending about 12 per cent of their disposable income servicing debt, including consumer credit repayments. That overall number includes the millions of households that have little or no debt.
As in 2024, Australia is now approaching the overall debt payment burden households faced just before the global financial crisis in 2008, when the RBA's cash rate was 7.25 per cent, but mortgage debts were generally much smaller.
However, the RBA has noted that the previous period of low interest rates had seen most mortgage borrowers stash extra cash into their offset accounts or get ahead on their loan repayments and build large redraw buffers, with the typical borrower now having the buffer of around a year's worth of scheduled repayments in these savings.

'시즌 9호' 이정후, 개인 한 시즌 최다 홈런…타율 3할 복귀
South Korea
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
13:45:53 KST
13:45:53 KST

3경기 만에 선발 출전한 송성문, 2타수 무안타에 희생번트 1개
밀워키 배지환·애틀랜타 김하성은 결장
(서울=연합뉴스) 김동한 기자 = 이정후(27·샌프란시스코 자이언츠)가 시즌 9호 홈런을 터뜨려 빅리그 개인 한 시즌 최다 홈런 기록을 새로 쓰고 타율 3할에 복귀했다.
이정후는 11일(한국시간) 미국 캘리포니아주 샌프란시스코 오라클 파크에서 열린 2026 미국프로야구 메이저리그(MLB) 정규시즌 휴스턴 애스트로스와 홈 경기에 1번 타자 우익수로 선발 출전해 5타수 2안타(1홈런), 1득점, 1타점을 기록했다.
이날 시즌 9호 홈런을 친 이정후는 빅리그 데뷔 후 개인 한 시즌 최다 홈런 기록을 세웠다.
이정후는 빅리그 데뷔 시즌인 2024년 홈런 2개를 쳤고, 2025년에는 8개를 기록했다.
홈런 1개를 보태면 MLB 진출 후 처음으로 한 시즌 두 자릿수 홈런을 달성한다.
시즌 타율은 0.298에서 0.300(414타수 124안타)으로 올라 다시 3할 고지를 밟았다.
이정후는 휴스턴 선발 오른팔 투수 헤이든 웨스네스키를 맞아 고전했다.
첫 타석 1회말에선 유격수 뜬공, 3회말 1사 1루에선 유격수 병살타로 물러났다.
그러나 1-1로 맞선 5회말 2사에서 홈런을 쳤다.
웨스네스키의 2구째 시속 148.8㎞ 몸쪽 포심 패스트볼을 잡아당겨 오른쪽 담장을 넘기는 비거리 116ｍ짜리 솔로 홈런을 터뜨렸다.
3-2로 앞선 8회말엔 선두 타자로 나서 상대 바뀐 투수 스티븐 오커트의 바깥쪽 슬라이더에 방망이를 살짝 갖다 대 좌전 안타로 연결했다.
이 안타로 이정후는 올 시즌 35번째 멀티히트를 완성했다.
3-6으로 뒤진 연장 10회말 2사 2루에선 유격수 땅볼로 물러나면서 경기가 끝났다.
샌프란시스코는 9회초 동점을 허용한 뒤 10회초 연장 승부치기에서 3점을 내줘 3-6 역전패를 당했다.
3연패에 빠진 샌프란시스코는 49승 70패, 승률 0.412로 내셔널리그(NL) 서부지구 4위를 유지했다.
3경기 만에 선발 출전한 송성문(샌디에이고 파드리스)은 캘리포니아주 샌디에이고 펫코 파크에서 열린 밀워키 브루어스와의 홈 경기에 9번 타자 유격수로 나와 2타수 무안타 희생번트 1개를 기록했다.
시즌 타율은 0.213에서 0.209(110타수 23안타)로 하락했다.
송성문은 1-2로 뒤진 3회말 무사 2루에서 희생번트로 주자를 3루에 보냈지만, 후속 타자들이 범타로 물러나 점수로 이어지지 않았다.
6회말과 7회말엔 각각 좌익수 뜬공과 1루수 땅볼에 그치며 아쉬움을 삼켰다.
전날 밀워키 데뷔전이자 빅리그 복귀전에서 번트 안타와 희생번트를 기록한 배지환은 이날 결장해 '코리안 더비'는 성사되지 않았다.
3-2로 승리한 샌디에이고는 63승 57패, 승률 0.525로 NL 서부지구 3위를 유지했다.
전날 연장 10회 승부치기 상황에서 대주자로 나와 결승 득점을 올린 김하성(애틀랜타 브레이브스)은 조지아주 애틀랜타의 트루이스트 파크에서 열린 뉴욕 메츠와 홈 경기에서 벤치를 지켰다. 애틀랜타는 5-8로 패했으나 71승 48패, 승률 0.597로 NL 동부지구 1위를 지켰다.

Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
04:39:10 UTC
13:39:10 KST

Days after a massive fireball flashed through New Zealand’s skies last month, Steve Wyn-Harris spotted a small, black stone on the bare ground. The citizen astronomer was on the hunt for debris from the meteor that had flown over the North Island. He bagged the rock but wasn’t too confident, as he says most finds turn out to be “meteor-wrongs”.
But when he held the thumb-sized rock next to a fridge magnet, to detect iron and nickel in meteorites, it clicked. Wyn-Harris did the test on a video call with other citizen scientists and geologists and after the click “we were all yelling”.
“I went from doubting Thomas to a convert,” says Wyn-Harris.
His discovery marks the 11th confirmed meteorite to be found in New Zealand. Meteorites are the leftover rock that hits the ground after the meteor has burned up entering Earth’s atmosphere. Finding the debris in New Zealand can be difficult, a consequence of the country’s sparsely populated, rugged terrain.
Wyn-Harris is the director of Fireballs Aotearoa, an alliance of astronomers, geologists and citizen scientists that now has a network of 200 cameras set up around the country designed to help document meteor showers and recover meteorites.
On 28 July, the group and their cameras had tracked a meteor over the North Island, and people had rushed online to describe the dazzling display and a “huge boom”.
Footage indicated there was an exciting possibility of many fragments from the meteor on the ground. After crunching data, including wind speed and flight path projections, the group zeroed in on an area where they calculated meteorites could be strewn. They kept the location a secret, worried a public appeal for help could trigger a “meteor rush” – a martian meteorite found in Niger sold for more than $5m last year – though New Zealand law prohibits such sales.
Wyn-Harris says he found the meteorite near a riverbank while scouting farmland a day before he and the group were due to search the area.
“I wasn’t so excited when I first spotted and bagged it because I’d only been looking around … for 40 minutes,” he says.
But on the video call later that night a geologist looked at the rock and noted its crust had a meteorite quality. The next day, a team of 11 people carried out a wider search of the area.
Two days after Wyn-Harris’s discovery, which weighed eight grams, Liam McGovern, a geology PhD student, found a second fragment, weighing 39 grams. Over 10 days, the search party discovered four pieces, weighing 75g in total, including a fragment that had crashed on to the driveway of a house.
Wyn-Harris says the meteor’s trajectory before it entered the atmosphere indicated it came from the asteroid belt, making it an “ordinary chondrite”. The name is “unfortunate, because they’re not ordinary,” he says.
All four fragments will now be analysed further by Dr Marshall Palmer, a geologist who is part of Fireballs Aotearoa. Palmer will give the meteorites an official name and, together, they will become New Zealand’s 11th documented meteorite.
Prof James Scott, a geoscientist and the founder of Fireballs Aotearoa, says the pieces are “100%” meteorite, and he believes they likely share origins with New Zealand’s first meteorite discovered in 1863 nearby in Masterton.
“Both likely come from the same parent body, which was an asteroid from near the start of the solar system. That blows my mind. We have two rocks, formed elsewhere in space from a smallish asteroid … that has been catastrophically destroyed, and yet they land within 10km of each other.”

“The company’s board of directors also confirms that if these attacks continue, it will have to declare a state of force majeure and suspend operations at the refinery,” it warned.

The attacks highlight the continuing security challenges in Libya, where rival administrations and armed groups have retained influence despite a 2020 ceasefire that halted major warfare. The country split in 2014 after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Two governments are currently vying for power: the United Nations-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
In a statement, the Tripoli-based government said Dbeibah held a meeting earlier in the day with key officials, including the interior minister and the chiefs of some armed groups in the capital, “to follow up on the latest security developments”.
Dbeibah “stressed the need to deal firmly with any transgressions or actions that threaten security or harm vital facilities and installations”, the statement said.
Separately, a Libyan parliamentary panel condemned the attack and called for stronger protection of oil installations.
“The House of Representatives’ Energy and Natural Resources Committee condemns in the strongest terms the criminal attack targeting the Zawiya Refinery, one of the most vital facilities in the oil and gas sector that is a cornerstone of the national economy,” it said in a statement.

Chinese satellite-carrying rocket explodes seconds after launch
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
05:35:06 BST
13:35:06 KST

Chinese rocket launch explodes into dramatic fireball
‘Rockets are insanely hard,’ writes SpaceX founder Elon Musk, commenting on post about failed launch
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
China said a Long March 7A rocket carrying the ChinaSat-4B satellite failed after an in-flight anomaly following liftoff from the Wenchang space launch site in the southern island province of Hainan on Monday.
The rocket blasted off at 8.02pm Beijing time (1202GMT), state news agency Xinhua said, adding that the mission was unsuccessful and the cause was under analysis and investigation.
A report by China National Radio, later removed from a page hosted by the Baidu search engine, identified the payload as Zhongxing-4B, or ChinaSat-4B, and the launcher as the Long March 7 modified rocket, another name for the Long March 7A.
The failure could trigger checks of other Chinese launches if investigators identify a problem involving shared components, manufacturing or Wenchang launch operations.
It will use a Long March 5, a larger rocket that is different from the Long March 7A.
China's National Space Administration did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, commenting on a post about the failed launch on X, wrote "rockets are insanely hard".
Many private and state-owned Chinese firms are racing to close the gap with SpaceX.
"I hope they have a speedy recovery," he added.
Jonathan McDowell, an honorary professor at Durham University and a member of the Center for Space Environmentalism, said launch video showed the rocket was completely destroyed at relatively low altitude and velocity, meaning neither the payload nor debris reached orbit.
Monday's failure was the Long March 7A's first since its maiden flight in March 2020, when an in-flight malfunction caused the mission to fail.The rocket returned to flight successfully a year later and completed over a dozen successful flights before Monday's mission, based on Chinese launch records.
The satellite is part of the same series as ChinaSat-4A, launched in 2024, according to an assessment by Reuters of the available evidence.
China described that satellite as providing voice, data, radio and television transmission services. Such high-orbit communications satellites can relay broadcast programming and telecommunications over large areas, including remote locations beyond the reach of terrestrial networks, but it was not immediately clear whether ChinaSat-4B had the same role, customers or capabilities.
The Long March 7A is a medium-lift rocket designed for high-orbit missions.
China is preparing for the Chang'e-7 lunar mission at Wenchang. Chinese authorities have officially said Chang’e-7 is planned for launch in the second half of 2026, but launch observers have identified a possible window late this month. The mission's Long March 5 rocket and spacecraft are at the site. Chang'e-7 will explore the Moon's south pole, including permanently shadowed craters that may contain water ice.

Estonian foreign minister backs Helsinki-Tallinn tunnel plans
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
07:34:30 EEST
13:34:30 KST

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna has called for Estonia to advance plans for a tunnel connecting Helsinki and Tallinn.
Writing in a guest column for Helsingin Sanomat, Tsahkna said that while Estonia's most significant infrastructure project, Rail Baltica, remains a priority, "attention should also turn north."
Rail Baltica is a major planned railway that will connect Tallinn with the rest of Europe. The roughly 1,000-kilometre route will run through Latvia and Lithuania to Warsaw, opening a new rail connection between the Baltics and Central Europe.
Tsahkna said no significant environmental or geological obstacles have been identified that would rule out a fixed link between Estonia and Finland.
He argued that Estonia should therefore begin preparing a special state plan for the project.
According to Tsahkna, stronger transport links are needed to deepen business, security and cultural ties between the Nordic and Baltic countries through the NB8 cooperation framework.
"The first step in renewed Nordic-Baltic infrastructure cooperation could be to advance the Helsinki–Tallinn tunnel," Tsahkna wrote.
He said the tunnel could also help accelerate other strategic infrastructure projects across the region.
A Helsinki–Tallinn tunnel has been discussed for years, but the project has faced questions over its cost, financing and feasibility.
