Where did the ivory trade go after China banned elephant tusks? North, into the Russian permafrost — where an estimated 10M frozen mammoths lie waiting, and a kilogram of tusk fetches up to $1,900.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:49:39 UTC
08:49:39 KST

Where did the ivory trade go after China banned elephant tusks? North, into the Russian permafrost — where an estimated 10M frozen mammoths lie waiting, and a kilogram of tusk fetches up to $1,900.
Mammoth tusks came to be known as “ethical ivory” after China banned imports of elephant tusks in 2017, closing the market that elephants were being slaughtered to supply. China and Hong Kong are home to the world’s most developed tusk-carving industry, in which a single piece can sell for as much as billions of rubles (tens of millions of dollars). Meeting that demand fell to Yakutia‘s tusk hunters, who dig the frozen ivory out of the permafrost. The independent Siberian outlet People of Baikal describes how this punishing trade works — and what the hunters may be costing science and themselves. Meduza has translated the story in full.
Some names were changed at the request of the people involved.
A mammoth tusk fresh out of the ground smells like a wet dog. It has lain in the permafrost for tens of thousands of years, barely changing. But once it’s hauled out into the sun, the countdown runs in weeks, and even in days, before it dries out and cracks. Hunters race to sell it before it loses value.
Yuri trudges along the sticky shoreline with a probe — a long metal rod. He looks about 50, dressed in khaki, with thigh-high rubber waders and a rifle slung across his back. “It should sound like tysh-tysh. When the probe hits bone, it makes a ringing sound. But when the sharp tip goes into wood, it gets stuck and makes a dull sound instead: tuk-tuk,” Yuri says.
A mammoth tusk is easy to mistake for a piece of wood. Locals sometimes call tusks “horns,” though they’re actually the incisors of an animal that died out 4,000 years ago. The permafrost has held the remains ever since, like a freezer. Researchers estimate the ice may hold around 10 million mammoth carcasses. Stocks of tusks still in the ground may reach half a million metric tons.
Mammoth remains surface when permafrost thaws or erodes. Tusk hunters spend whole days walking the ocean shore, following the ravines and tapping the ground with their probes, dreaming of the treasure that might lie beyond the next hill. The simplest method — searching “by eye,” as locals call it — requires nothing more than a metal probe.
Yuri found his biggest tusk by eye as well — about 85 kilograms (187 pounds), near a mountain river. He won’t say what he sold it for, only that an intact, crack-free tusk weighing 100 kilograms (220 pounds) or more goes for around 3 million rubles (about $36,000).
A kilogram of pervach, the top grade, can bring a hunter 40,000 rubles (about $485), and the price climbs higher when both tusks from the same mammoth turn up together. Second grade — intact tusks that have already sat in the sun and cracked — sells for about 15,000 rubles (about $180) a kilogram. The lowest grade, shchepa, or splinters, means tusks that have crumbled into fragments; it brings only about 5,000 rubles (about $60) a kilogram, and hunters usually leave it where it lies, since the fuel would cost more than the haul.
‘Ethical ivory’
Yuri remembers when a whole mammoth tusk could be had from reindeer herders for a few bottles of vodka. In Soviet times, his father ran a carving club at a local school and ordered craft materials from people he knew. His father died 10 years ago; Yuri keeps a red suitcase in his father’s memory.
Yuri unfolds a piece of velvet and lays out several dozen figurines his father carved with his students: a polar bear and a dog the size of a matchbox, an ancient warrior with a spear and shield, a reindeer herder saddling his mount. One piece, carved from a chunk of tusk, shows a battle scene: revolutionaries rising up.
“There used to be a lot of them lying around,” Yuri says. Tusks turned up right underfoot. People made them into souvenirs, knife handles, boxes, and jewelry, and decades ago tusks even went into small parts for airplanes and radios, prized for not conducting electricity. Once plastics and composites came along, manufacturers dropped them.
Mammoth tusk prices jumped after China banned the import and sale of elephant ivory at the end of 2017. Until then, Chinese bone-carving factories had been buying elephant ivory. In Europe and North America, ivory went into piano keys, billiard balls, jewelry, and even medicine — a trade that killed roughly 75,000 elephants a year.
By the end of the 1980s, the African elephant population had been cut in half, to around 600,000 animals. Countries party to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, or CITES, responded by banning the ivory trade, and the United States, France, and China — the biggest markets — gradually adopted domestic bans of their own.
Ivory sellers and manufacturers sought a substitute, and top-grade mammoth tusk proved the perfect fit. Its creamy white color earned it the nickname “ice,” or “ice ivory,” and it works almost exactly like elephant ivory. The only way experts can tell the two apart is by their Schreger lines, the barcode-like pattern on a tusk’s cross-section.
But most important of all: no one has to kill anything to get mammoth tusks. The animals died on their own long ago, traders reasoned, so mammoth ivory fell outside the CITES ban and could be traded legally. Sellers began marketing it as “legal,” “ethical,” and “not linked to killing animals.” Northern Yakutia — the banks of the Yana, Indigirka, and Kolyma rivers, plus the New Siberian Islands — supplies 80 percent of the mammoth tusks on the world market. The remaining 20 percent is found in other regions of Russia — Chukotka, the Magadan region, and Taymyr — and in North America, in Alaska and Canada.
Up to 97 percent of tusks from Russia are shipped to China and Hong Kong, where a kilogram can bring up to $1,900 — several times what it fetched coming out of the Arctic.
The curse of the earth rat
“You should never search for or dig up tusks! In the old days, that was a grave sin!” Vera Rozhina, an elder of the Yukaghir people, exclaims, then cuts the conversation short. Born and raised in the village of Yukagir, she now lives in Kazachye. Old-timers here forbid not just searching for mammoths but talking about them at all. The animal’s name in the Yukaghir language is made up of two roots: “kholg,” meaning mammoth, and “ol,” meaning death. Legends passed down through generations warn that anyone who disturbs the sacred giant’s thousand-year sleep will be cursed and die soon after. Certain death awaits not that person alone but the whole settlement.
For most northern peoples, the mammoth is tied to evil spirits and the underworld of death. Only shamans could take its bones — for use in rituals for traveling to the Lower World, for example. The Yakuts call the mammoth the Water Bull (Uu ogusa). The Nenets describe it as a giant rat afraid of light, tunneling through the depths with its huge tusk-horns.
As long as the mammoth stays underground, it is alive; the moment it surfaces, breathes air, or sees sunlight, it dies instantly. That is how Yakutia‘s Indigenous legends explain why people find only carcasses and bones, often jutting out of the ground along riverbank bluffs.
For Indigenous peoples, the mammoth is a magical creature that literally shaped the land. Evenki and Even legends say that when nothing existed but water, the giant pulled lumps of clay and earth from the bottom to create dry land. According to a Sakha legend, the mammoth grew so heavy that it gouged the Earth with its tusks and the world nearly tipped over under its weight — for which a supreme deity punished it by turning it to stone, or, in another version, driving it underground.
Over time, the biblical story of the Great Flood worked its way into local mammoth legends. Ethnographers have recorded several versions among the Sakha people, including one in which the mammoth tried to board Noah’s Ark and nearly capsized it. To keep the ark and the other animals from sinking, Noah pushed the mammoth away, and it drowned.
The Russian authors of Giants of the Ice Age recount the story of Khristofor Struchkov, a hunter from the village of Suturuokha. His luck was extraordinary: he handed 30 top-grade tusks to the state and reported two valuable finds to scientists — the Tirekhtyakh mammoth, discovered in 1970, and the mummified remains of the Mylakhchin bison, found in 1971. Struchkov became famous, and in the summer of 1971, journalists from national newspapers, paleontologists, and writers flew out to his hunting cabin.
Soon after, Struchkov — energetic and to all appearances healthy — fell ill and died. The story went that his children had returned a 700-ruble bonus the authorities had given their father, hoping the illness wouldn’t pass to them. In fact, no one returned anything: Struchkov’s story had simply become another folk myth about the mammoth’s curse. What actually killed him is unknown.
The Yakuts used to sacrifice and bury an entire reindeer to pay the spirits for a large tusk. For a small one, they buried money or scraps of fabric. Modern tusk hunters have adapted this ritual, known as sir belege, “gift to the earth.” Ahead of a hunt, they order strings of colorful Chinese plastic beads from an online marketplace, break them apart, and scatter the beads into a river or ravine.
“Do you need some kind of spell or prayer for the ritual?” we ask Yuri.
“We’re northern people; we don’t speak loudly. We commune with the spirits silently, inside ourselves. We thank the spirits and the earth for giving us their material.”
Into the tundra with your own toilet
At any given time, 100 to 200 crews are out searching for mammoth tusks in Yakutia‘s Arctic districts. The season runs from June to October. With no roads across the tundra, hunters travel by boat, working the few months when the rivers — the region’s main transport routes — are free of ice.
The Laptev Sea coast, where most of the searching happens, is divided into zones among local Indigenous communities. Even so, people from Yakutia and other Russian regions turn up to hunt every year, along with groups from Belarus, Kazakhstan, and sometimes farther afield. Hoping to find enough tusks to get rich, some take out loans and sell their apartments.
“I don’t understand people who take out loans and use that money to go after tusks. Nobody buys lottery tickets on credit! Searching for tusks is very hard, hard psychologically. It’s a lottery. You can spend the money, make the investment, and find nothing. You can end up not just earning nothing but going into the red,” Yuri says.
Preparations for an expedition begin months in advance. Men form crews of three to five. Equipment, fuel, and food are hauled in ahead of time along a winter road from Yakutsk, 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) away. If something turns out to be missing once the expedition is underway, there’s nowhere to buy it.
A crew needs about 1 million rubles (about $12,000) to get through the season. “Just count it up: you need half a metric ton (about 1,100 pounds) of gasoline with you and enough food for several months. The boat needs a good motor, imported, preferably Japanese. And all of that cargo has to come from Yakutsk,” Yuri says.
Expedition members live in tents, and the earnings are usually split evenly. When the season ends, the crews go back to their regular lives: Yuri teaches computer science; most locals hunt, fish, or herd reindeer.
Outsiders usually work alongside locals, because without someone who knows the tundra, it’s easy to get lost or run into trouble in the Arctic. Yuri recounts, smiling, how one inexperienced newcomer shipped a portable toilet up the winter road along with the necessary cargo, saying he wasn’t used to living without amenities. When the season opened that summer, the crew used the toilet a few times and then left it behind in the tundra.
Finding tusks takes some “luck,” Yuri says, but locals know quite specific places where parts of a mammoth can be found: the ravines and fissures along the sea coast. With good fortune and sensible planning, a hunter can come out of a single season with enough to buy an apartment.
Yuri’s older son, 23, already knows how to search for tusks. The younger one is training to be a pilot, and his daughter is still in school. Yuri says he’d like his sons to do what he does but has no intention of pushing them: “Let them decide for themselves. It’s their fate.”
The money from tusks lets Yuri live the way he wants. When his younger son finished school, Yuri surprised the whole family with tickets to Sochi, which he had bought well in advance.
His younger son will remember that trip for the rest of his life: at an amusement park, he made his first bungee jump. “Before that, he was afraid of heights. Good for him — he beat the fear,” Yuri says proudly. But after a couple of weeks away, Yuri starts missing home. “Nature,” he says.
A deep blue tusk
Searching for tusks isn’t just expensive — it’s dangerous, and locals say so constantly. Out at sea, a boat can capsize or break down. The hunters here are called bivnists, from bivni, the Russian word for tusks, and they risk running into polar bears. Crews clash over territory, sometimes to the point of gunfire and knife fights. Within a single crew, fights break out when it’s time to split the earnings.
“Our territories are huge. People go missing; it happens,” says Sergei, a local resident. He recalls an incident from several years ago: two friends went out after tusks, and only one came back. At home, he said his companion had gone off somewhere in the boat and that he had never seen him again. What really happened to the missing man, no one knows.
On one of his first tusk-hunting trips, 20 years ago, Yuri traveled more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) with his companions. They landed on one of the New Siberian Islands in northern Yakutia, known for its mammoth graveyards, and while they searched the shore, waves carried their boat off and smashed it. “Remember Robinson [Crusoe] from the book? That’s what we were, Robinsons. A real storm blew in, the waves tore loose the rope we’d tied the boat with, and it got thrown into a ravine. We were beginners then; we didn’t know you’re supposed to leave someone with the boat and the supplies,” Yuri says.
They found the wrecked boat below the ravine about 5 kilometers (3 miles) from where they’d landed. Only the canned meat and the pasta survived — the meat sealed in tins, the pasta in a plastic bag in the glove compartment. The ammunition got wet.
“The bread was covered in sand. We’d scrape the edge off with a knife and eat it. You could feel the grains crunching between your teeth,” Yuri says. They pitched a tent for the night, and the next morning, as Yuri was taking it down, he noticed something beside it that looked like a piece of wood sticking out of the ground. It was a large tusk, weighing 65 kilograms (143 pounds).
All that remained was getting off the uninhabited island. They spent several days there, climbing a hill to watch for a passing boat. When a motorboat finally appeared on the horizon, the “Robinsons” started shouting and waving their arms. “Our shouting sounded like the noises Arctic foxes make. It was autumn, and that’s exactly when Arctic foxes bark and howl. ‘Listen to those foxes carrying on!’ we joked at the time,” Yuri says with a satisfied smile.
The motorboat slowed, and the helmsman switched off the engine to listen. Once the hunters were sure they’d been heard, they fired several shots into the air. These were the last of the ammunition they’d brought with the rifle.
“They picked us up. We were overjoyed!” Yuri says.
“And what about the tusk? Did it wait for you?”
“Ah, the tusk. Of course it waited. It can’t run, after all,” Yuri says, still joking. And again he dodges the question of what he sold the find for, adding only that the tusk was a rare color — a deep, deep blue. Scientists explain that over thousands of years in the permafrost, a tusk soaks up minerals, chiefly vivianite. The more unusual a tusk’s natural pattern and shade, the more it is worth; blue tusks are considered the most valuable of all.
After that adventure, Yuri prepared more carefully for his trips: he watched the forecast and the wind direction, and he stopped leaving the boat on the shore.
Moving underground through sticky slurry
Hills sliced in half, riddled with gaping holes: that is what a place worked by tusk hunters looks like. It is as if unknown creatures really had tried to claw their way out of the underworld, boring multilevel tunnels through the icy hills. Against those unearthly surroundings, a person looks like a grain of sand. Amos Chapple, who spent three weeks in Yakutia with the hunters, photographed the work.
Armed with fire hoses, the hunters wash the ice away centimeter by centimeter. The tunnels run dozens of meters (100 feet or more) deep. They move underground in waterproof suits, coated head to toe in sticky slurry, while outside, gasoline pumps rattle and spit clouds of smoke, drawing water from the river and forcing it through the hoses under pressure. The runoff — dirty water mixed with icy slush — goes back into the river.
Yuri describes another method that appeared a little over a decade ago: diving for tusks with scuba gear. One or two members of a crew put on the gear, go down into a river or lake, and work the slopes and the bottom with their probes.
It’s the most expensive method. A single wetsuit can run 150,000 rubles (about $1,800) or more; a tank starts at 50,000 (about $600); and crews also need spare tanks, compressors, and other equipment. Putting an expedition like that together takes even more money, Yuri says — around 2 million rubles (about $24,000) for gear, spare parts, fuel, and a season’s food. But there’s less competition.
Yuri and his crew are self-taught, having learned in local lakes. They usually search river bends or spots where the bank has washed out, going down as deep as 9 meters (30 feet). Each dive lasts about an hour, as long as the tank holds out. A diver can manage five dives in a day at most; doctors advise no more than three or four.
At least one crew member always stays in the boat to watch the dive and pull the divers out in time. In recent years, crews have turned more often to underwater drones with cameras: someone in the boat pilots the drone and looks for tusks, and the divers go down only to bring a find up.
A recovered tusk is cleaned of dirt, wiped dry, and “stabilized” — sealed in a vacuum bag. Because a tusk has only days before it starts to spoil, hunters line up buyers in advance. When the boats come in, a box-bodied UAZ van is waiting right at the water’s edge. The hunters unload the goods and take the money. What becomes of the tusks after that doesn’t interest them.
A bulldozer in a skirt
Buyers pay more when hunters dig up not a single tusk but a matched pair from one mammoth. Hunters usually take only the tusks and leave the carcass lying in the ground or on the surface.
When hunters come across a carcass, they may feed the meat to their dogs. In Soviet times, when the republic employed Arctic fox trappers — state farm workers who harvested the then-valuable fur on state orders — mammoth meat was used as bait. Today, besides tusks, collectors and dealers occasionally order teeth, bones, or other parts of a carcass.
Yuri once saw the remains of a whole mammoth inside a crack on Soplivaya Mountain, about 130 kilometers (81 miles) up the Yana River from Kazachye. In summer the icy mountain thaws and a mix of earth and water runs down it — hence the name, Soplivaya, or “Snotty.” “The water washes the carcass and the bones come through to the surface. A mammoth is easy to recognize once you’ve hunted tusks a lot and seen a lot of remains. Big bones, long fur… how could you not know it!” Yuri says.
People from Moscow once contacted him and asked him to collect three sacks of mammoth fur. It was an unusual order. “I said no. Think about it — how am I supposed to get that fur? One guy collected some, knitted a hat out of it, and sold it for $10,000,” Yuri says.
The story sounds like a tall tale, but it checks out. Media outlets reported on Vladimir Ammosov, a construction worker from Yakutsk, and published photos of the hat. He got a certificate of authenticity from the mammoth museum in Yakutsk, and the museum’s director, Semyon Grigoriev, confirmed the hat really was made of mammoth fur. “It’s the scratchiest hat I’ve ever put on. It has no smell at all,” Ammosov told reporters. In the photo, the hat is dark brown.
Illustrations usually depict mammoths as reddish-brown. But modern research suggests their coats ranged from dark brown to cream. Genetic studies confirm that at least some animals were light-colored.
Long fur over a thick undercoat covered the mammoth’s whole body. On the flanks and belly, the strands reached a meter (3 feet) in length, forming a warm “skirt.” On the neck and withers sat a fatty hump, like a camel’s. Mammoths stored nutrients in summer and spent them through the hungry winter.
Tusks — greatly enlarged upper incisors — grew throughout a mammoth’s life and curled inward like a corkscrew. In adult males, they reached 4.5 meters (15 feet) in length and weighed up to 140 kilograms (about 310 pounds). The animals used them like bulldozers, shoving snow aside to get at food. Calves were born with milk tusks a few centimeters long, which later fell out and were replaced by permanent ones.
Like modern elephants, mammoths probably lived in family herds of 8 to 20 animals, led by an adult female, while adult males kept to themselves.
The animals traveled long distances in search of food, trampling wide paths that early humans later followed. Adult mammoths stood up to 3.5 meters (11.5 feet) tall and weighed as much as eight metric tons (about 17,600 pounds). The giants were long-lived, reaching 75 or 80 years.
Modern research doesn’t support the familiar image of early humans as mammoth hunters. More often, people were scavengers: they ate the meat of mammoths that had already died and finished off the weak and the wounded.
During the last ice age, mammoths lived from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Their traces turn up in Spain, France, Germany, Poland, Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, China, Alaska, and Canada. But nowhere are they preserved as well as in the permafrost of Yakutia.
How scientists tried to ‘resurrect the mammoth’ and turn it into a meatball
In May 2013, Semyon Grigoriev, the mammoth museum director from Yakutsk, set out for the Arctic with his assistants on snowmobiles and all-terrain vehicles.
“I had an overwhelming urge to taste it,” Grigoriev says, scraping fur and dust off pieces of meat with a knife. The slices are pink, with ice crystals inside — a sign the mammoth froze immediately after it died.
“The meat’s a bit tough,” Grigoriev says, studying two pieces on a white napkin in front of him. He sniffs one, then takes a small bite. “I’m probably the only person in the world who has tasted raw mammoth meat,” he says solemnly to the camera.
Mammoth meat tastes like slightly rancid dried reindeer meat, one resident of the village of Yukagir tells People of Baikal. He found a mammoth carcass while searching for tusks and cut off a piece to try. Not exactly a delicacy, but not disgusting either.
The mammoth Grigoriev tasted had lain in the ground on Maly Lyakhovsky Island for some 30,000 years, preserved in the permafrost as if in a good freezer. A hunting crew took its tusks. One of the hunters was Grigoriev’s brother, Pyotr, who reported the find to researchers at the university in Yakutsk and agreed to hand over the tusks. Tusk hunters don’t usually do that. Hunting sites are strewn with the skulls and bones of mammoths and other animals: the tusks are taken and the rest is mostly discarded, with rare exceptions.
As the carcass was being chipped out of the permafrost, a dark red liquid suddenly began to flow from it. “I hit it once with a pickaxe under the belly. Pfft — something started flowing out, something like blood,” Pyotr says. “It was astonishing! Nobody had ever seen anything like it. How can mammoth blood be liquid, and in that kind of cold!” his brother Semyon says, unable to contain his excitement.
The carcass was pulled out of the ground piece by piece and delivered to a laboratory, where scientists determined it was a female about 55 years old. Among the tissue recovered were the nipples of an adult female. Layers inside her tusks showed she had borne at least 11 calves. That is a lot. Mammoth pregnancies lasted about 22 months, with several years between births, and over a lifetime a female could carry up to 10 calves.
Once the female was out of the ground, the expedition members performed a ritual called “putting the mammoth’s spirit to death.” “We didn’t dig you up for money. This is all for science,” Grigoriev recited as a kind of “prayer.” They lit a fire at the bottom of the pit and “fed” it a few pancakes. Then the members of the expedition took turns walking up to the fire and throwing colored beads into it.
“That’s the best gift for the spirits. We did it to appease the mammoth’s spirit, so it wouldn’t be angry at us for pulling it out after 30,000 years,” Grigoriev says. He concedes that asking spirits not to punish the people who disturbed a sacred creature’s rest is superstition. ”[But] sometimes you think: there really is some kind of connection,” Grigoriev says.
The find from Maly Lyakhovsky Island became a worldwide sensation. In the laboratory, scientists found that the liquid from the carcass contained blood cells with traces of hemoglobin. Foreign researchers started coming to Yakutia.
The South Korean specialists at Sooam Biotech, a lab that did commercial dog cloning, were especially interested. They tried to find living mammoth cells, extract their nuclei, and transplant them into Asian elephant eggs to produce a live embryo. It didn’t work out. No living cells had survived in the liquid, and the scientists never found an undamaged cell nucleus to clone from.
How mammoth cells from Yuka were transplanted into mice
In 2019, scientists from Russia and Japan conducted an experiment with cells from a woolly mammoth named Yuka, another female preserved in the permafrost of Yakutia. She was about eight years old when she died, and she lay frozen for some 28,000 years. Using a technique roughly similar to that developed for cloning, the international team transplanted mammoth cells into mouse egg cells to see whether the cells retained any biological activity.
The researchers observed that some processes in the transplanted cells still began: proteins began to gather around the nuclei, structures associated with cell division took shape, and the cell itself tried to “recognize” the ancient genetic material. But no full cell division occurred. The mammoth’s DNA had been damaged too badly by thousands of years in the permafrost.
The scientists concluded that cloning a mammoth with current technology is impossible. Their other finding was that traces of biological activity within cellular structures can persist for tens of thousands of years in permafrost. For the researchers, that was an important step — not toward “resurrecting the mammoth,” but toward understanding how long DNA can hold onto its properties.
In 2021, the American company Colossal Biosciences announced that it wanted to “bring the mammoth back” through genetic engineering: altering the cells of an Asian elephant so that calves would be born with mammoth traits — thick fur, a layer of fat, and the ability to live in the cold. The scientists spoke less of “resurrecting” the mammoth than of creating an elephant-mammoth hybrid, a mammophant. Among the people behind the project is the well-known Harvard geneticist George Church.
The project is still going. In 2025, the researchers presented a “woolly mouse” carrying mammoth genes, with long, golden, wavy fur. They expect to have the first “mammoth” elephant around 2028.
In 2023, the Australian company Vow unveiled a “mammoth meatball” at the Nemo science museum in Amsterdam — a grapefruit-sized ball grown not from real tissue of the ancient animal but from synthetic protein. Scientists took the published mammoth DNA sequence, filled in the missing fragments with African elephant genes, and inserted the resulting sequence into sheep cells. Nobody ate the meatball; its creators worried the protein might not be especially good for people.
No one has managed to clone a mammoth. The research continues, but without Grigoriev. He died suddenly seven years after the expedition, in May 2020. Grigoriev was 46. His colleagues said his death might have been linked to poisoning. Locals believe the spirits punished him: he didn’t just pull a mammoth out of the permafrost, he ate its meat. And what especially outraged the old-timers was that he filmed it.
The path to a mammoth begins with an application to the Federal Security Service
Russian law permits collecting only tusks that lie on the surface; nothing may be dug up and no ground may be washed out. Violators face fines starting at 2,000 rubles (about $25). Using motor pumps brings a penalty under Article 7.6 of Russia’s Administrative Offenses Code for “unauthorized occupation of a body of water or use of one in violation of established conditions.” If the work is also done in a specially protected natural area, Article 8.39 of the code applies, with fines of up to 500,000 rubles (about $6,000) for companies and organizations.
There are places where the penalties for illegal digging are far harsher than in Russia. In the Canadian province of Alberta, anyone who finds the bone of an ancient animal or another fossil is required to leave it where it is and report it to scientists. Digging it up yourself can bring a fine of up to 50,000 Canadian dollars and up to a year in prison — both at once.
In Russia, traveling to one of the main tusk-hunting areas — the New Siberian Islands — requires obtaining a permit from the Federal Security Service’s border service, because the islands lie in a border zone with special rules for visitors. The hunters themselves say that in practice many work without one: there are no permanent border posts out there, and inspections are rare.
Tusk hunters are also required to carry a license for collecting mammoth fauna. It costs 7,500 rubles (about $90) and grants the right to collect up to 150 kilograms (331 pounds) of remains — tusks, bones, and other fragments. A person or an organization has to register the plot where the collecting will happen and file paperwork naming who will do the searching and describing how the work will be done. Licensees are also required to keep records and document what they find. Crews usually go out “wild,” as locals say — filing no paperwork, or only part of it.
The hunters get into their boats, head out to sea, and reach the islands, where they roll out kilometers of fire hose and start up gasoline generators. “Poachers wash away the permafrost with directed jets of water. This does irreparable damage to the tundra, turns whole areas into swamp, and accelerates permafrost degradation,” said Sakhamin Afanasyev, Yakutia‘s former environment minister and now a senator, in remarks published by the Arctic Russia portal.
Officers of the Federal Security Service, the prosecutor’s office, and Rosprirodnadzor, Russia’s environmental watchdog, rarely appear in these places. “Bivnists aren’t afraid of inspectors. First of all, how would they even get here? If a boat’s coming up the river, you can hear the motor from several kilometers away. If a helicopter’s flying in, you can hear that from far off too. You can hide, and nobody will find you,” a local resident says.
Even when inspectors — environmental prosecutors or border guards — do reach a dig, the bivnists usually scatter in all directions, abandoning their haul. In December 2025, for instance, news outlets reported that inspectors on the bank of the Yana River in Yakutia found seven fragments of mammoth tusk weighing 20.7 kilograms (46 pounds). The fragments were declared ownerless and became state property.
Environmental prosecutors documented that the bank’s destruction had killed crustaceans, benthic organisms, and zooplankton living in the river. The damage to the ecosystem was put at 404,000 rubles (about $4,900). A criminal case was opened under Article 257 of Russia’s Criminal Code for violating the rules protecting aquatic biological resources, but no one was identified to be charged, and the culprits were never found. Fines are rare here as well, because catching a violator in the act across the tundra’s vast expanses is next to impossible.
On the way out of the tundra, a hunter can say he found the tusk lying on the ground. Selling it and shipping it out, though, is not so simple. Formally, a found object belongs to whoever collected it. But the finder must submit the tusk for examination by the Academy of Sciences, and if the experts determine that the specimen is unique, it goes to the state. Science values tusks that carry information about a mammoth’s life and were found without destroying the site. Museums prize rarities: unusually large tusks, intact ones, or ones with beautiful natural coloring.
The examination can take anywhere from several weeks to several months. Hunters don’t have that kind of time. Tusks that stayed intact for thousands of years can spoil in a few weeks.
Judging by the licenses issued, about 150 metric tons of mammoth remains are extracted in Russia every year, 96 percent of that tusks. There is no public information on how many experts examine the finds, or how much of that mass has stayed in museums and institutes after being deemed valuable. Research suggests that another 50 to 75 metric tons may be illegally extracted in addition to the licensed 150.
‘Let something remain for our descendants’
Wang Zhongbang, a master craftsman from Nanjing, in the Chinese province of Jiangsu, is in no hurry to cut. He studies the tusk for a long time, judging the grain direction and examining the color. From the outside, a block can look nearly perfect and still hide cracks and voids. The first cut, Wang says, is the most nerve-racking part of the job: a mistake of a few centimeters can cost him the best — that is, the most intact — section of the tusk, and nothing can replace it.
The tusk is sawed into large blocks, with cracks and damaged sections cut away. Only then is it clear how much carvable material is left. The craftsman starts working out a composition: a long, well-preserved curve becomes a dragon or a boat; a wide, massive piece becomes a mountain landscape or a multi-figure scene. Wang talks about the tusk as a living material he has to adapt to.
Wang says the switch from elephant ivory to mammoth was hard. Mammoth tusk demands more care. But it has something elephant ivory doesn’t: natural color. Over its time in the permafrost, a tusk can take on honey, amber, brown, bluish, and near-black tones, depending on the soil it lay in. Some carvers deliberately leave the colored sections untouched and work them into the composition. Cut away too thick a layer and the pigment is gone.
Carvers say mammoth tusks saved their craft. Chinese bone carving is considered one of the oldest artistic traditions in the world; it dates to the second century B.C. Without mammoth raw material, the traditional trade might simply have died out. The best examples of the art sell at auction and on online marketplaces for tens and hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Most of the tusks dug up in Yakutia go to China, where an entire industry has grown up around mammoth ivory. In Russia, by contrast, the work remains a traditional craft — the domain of small workshops and individual carvers.
A tusk carved with figures of sages and musicians sold for nearly $550,000. Some mammoth ivory pieces make their way back to Russia, where online stores present them as luxury gifts for loved ones. A multi-tiered composition called Zheng He’s Sea Voyages, for instance, is listed for sale at a cool 2 billion rubles — about $24 million.
With small objects — pendants, figurines, beads — even connoisseurs have trouble telling mammoth tusk from elephant ivory. And small objects are most of what’s on the market. Scientists obtained 79 uncarved blanks from craftsmen in Hong Kong and China; 44 turned out to be elephant tusk, the rest mammoth.
Researchers at the University of Hong Kong write that traders can use mammoth tusks to “launder” material. Elephant tusks are still smuggled into China and passed off as “ethical” mammoth ivory. Scientists estimate that 24,000 elephants a year are killed worldwide for their tusks. Mammoths, then, have become cover for the illegal trade in elephant ivory. Some U.S. states have already banned trade in mammoth tusks for that reason.
Russian scientists estimate the damage from the illegal tusk trade at billions of rubles a year. But the loss of information matters far more. The permafrost is an enormous archive. It holds a record of processes that unfolded tens of thousands of years ago: human campsites, what people did, and how they lived alongside animals.
Innokenty Pavlov, a research engineer in the mammoth fauna department of the Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia), tells People of Baikal that tusk hunters often hand over finds — bones bearing the marks of ancient tools, for example. The researchers are grateful for these gifts: they can’t always get out to a site themselves, even when locals report a find.
Scientific expeditions to the Arctic cost millions of rubles, and the places where mammoth remains turn up are often hundreds of kilometers from the nearest settlement. The only ways in are by helicopter, along winter roads, or by boat during the short navigation season.
But every bone that falls out of the permafrost or is washed out by water is already a find that has lost part of its scientific value. What matters to paleontologists is not only the remains but how they lay in the ground: the position the animal was in, why it died, and which plants, insects, and microorganisms survived beside it. That context makes it possible to reconstruct, quite literally, a mammoth’s last days and the ancient ecosystem around it.
Excavations in permafrost can take weeks; each layer of soil is carefully cleared and documented. Unlike tusk hunters, paleontologists don’t use motor pumps, which can erode entire slopes in a few hours. That method reaches the tusks fast, but it destroys everything around them. As a result, many unique specimens are either lost to science for good or reach researchers only after the site has been wrecked.
“Research in the permafrost is going on. Slowly, you could say. But it matters for all of humanity, however grandiose that sounds. Eternity is ahead of us. Let something remain for our descendants,” says paleontologist Sergei Leshchinsky.
Yuri the tusk hunter doesn’t dwell on eternity. He walks along the endless shore, wet clay squelching underfoot. He stops every few meters and drives a metal rod into the ground: tuk-tuk.
“Maybe it’s lying right here,” Yuri says, and taps the probe again. The answer comes back dull: tuk-tuk.

Trump says will demand 'conflict compensation' from Iran
US President Donald Trump said Monday he would seek conflict compensation from Iran as part of any peace negotiations, citing attacks stretching back decades allegedly backed or perpetrated by Tehran.
Negotiations on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz have stalled, and his new demands risk putting a quick agreement further out of reach.
Trump's announcement was a direct response to Iran's insistence that US payment of war reparations are a pre-condition to any resolution of the ongoing hostilities.
"I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran," he said, noting that his demand included not only damages arising from the current war, but also Iranian attacks on US targets going back more than two decades as well as payments to the families of Iranian protestors killed by authorities over the past 50 years.
In a later post, Trump also said that Iran should be responsible for deaths and damage it caused in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza.
In what has become a regular pattern, Trump last week threatened to hit Iran "very hard", potentially with attacks against civilian infrastructure, only to pull back, hinting a peace deal was near.
Trump this weekend said he was "low-keying" his approach to the conflict, suggesting that he was prepared to let economic pressure mount in place of further military strikes.
Digital media outlet Axios said that the US president did not express any frustration with Iran's delaying an agreement to open the Strait of Hormuz in their interview with him published Sunday.
Tehran has demanded that the US first end its blockade of Iranian ports and lift sanctions on its oil industry.
As negotiations have floundered, the strait's blockage by Iran has sent fuel prices soaring and rattled the world economy, putting pressure on Trump ahead of midterm elections in November.
In his post, Trump referenced the bombing of the USS Cole in 2000, which he has previously said Iran was "probably involved" in. The attck was however carried out by Al-Qaeda, a group opposed to Iran.
On Monday he said his various demands for compensations would be put "firmly into any, and all, future negotiations" with Iran.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is set to remove nuclear material from a clandestine Syrian site following an agreement made by the US, Syria, and Israel, Axios initially reported on Monday, citing Israeli and US officials.
Syria's government corroborated the report on Tuesday morning, confirming that it had cooperated with the IAEA, the US, and "friendly countries" on this matter.
The Trump administration and IAEA scrambled to reach the agreement that would secure the material and prevent a potential escalation between Israel, Syria, and Turkey, said Axios, adding that the site in question is sensitive.

Effort was kept secret
An exchange of threats and diplomatic correspondence occured throughout months until a resolution was reached a few weeks ago, said Axios. The efforts had since been kept secret and unreported.
According to Axios, the regime of former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad had developed the secret nuclear program around the al-Kibar reactor, a plutonium production facility built with the help of North Korea in the Deir Ezzor region of northeastern Syria.
Following Assad’s fall, the IAEA signed an agreement with the country’s newly installed government to visit the reactor and several other nuclear sites, the report said.
Axios said Israel has been closely monitoring Syria’s nuclear facilities, particularly a site called “Site 99,” which US officials claim held residue from al-Kibar.
Discussions underway for over a year
The US and Israel have been discussing for more than a year the best way to deal with the site, Axios cited a US official as saying.
An Israeli official said that Jerusalem made it clear it wouldn’t allow nuclear material to remain at the site, with Israel even threatening to bomb the facility again if the material was not removed or if Syria showed signs it was trying to access it.
The US and Israel eventually agreed that the best approach would be to “buy in” from the Syrian government to remove the material, said Axios. However, Syrian officials denied having knowledge of nuclear material at the site, sources said.
A US official said that “very few people in the US, Israel, and Syria were aware of this” and added that the new Syrian government was a “good partner” in the newly established relationship, the report said.

Canadians made overnight drive to safety as fire spread
WEST KELOWNA, Canada – After being ordered to evacuate their homes at 3am local time because of a fast-spreading Canadian wildfire, Larry and Mora Goodman formed a convoy with their neighbours, driving as a group towards safety.
“Many of our residents are elderly, and afraid to drive in the night,” Mora Goodman told AFP in West Kelowna, British Columbia, one of the communities hosting those displaced by the Bald Range wildfire.
The fire in the interior of the western Canadian province began on Aug 7 and spread with terrifying speed over the weekend.
More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes and officials have warned that the situation could worsen due to drought-like conditions in the region more than 400km north-west of Vancouver.
An 80-year-old woman died while fleeing her home and the provincial government has declared a state of emergency.
The Goodmans live in Peachland, one of the communities under direct threat from the Bald Range Fire.
Mora Goodman said that after ensuring everyone was properly packed, Larry put a light on the hood of his car to improve visibility as the convoy set out towards West Kelowna, about 20km away.
“We all caravaned down the highway, in the middle of the night,” she said.
Larry Goodman said he considered himself among the “lucky ones”, with no indication yet that his community had been destroyed.
“We’re eating far more food than we ever would at home,” Mora added, citing the local restaurants and civil society groups around West Kelowna that have mobilised support.
‘Uncertain’
Canada is extremely vulnerable to intense, extensive wildfires and experts say emergency evacuations in the summer months are set to persist.
Canada is home to about a quarter of Earth’s boreal forest area and average annual temperatures in the country are increasing roughly twice as fast as the global average.
There are also growing communities scattered across the vast country in areas highly susceptible to fires.
Ottawa is trying to adapt, procuring more water bombers and backing proactive forest management strategies, but those tactics have limits.
More than 4 million ha have burned so far in 2026, an area roughly the size of Switzerland.
Tens of thousands of people have been forced from their homes and major population centres like Toronto endured some of the worst air quality in the world in July.
In West Kelowna, Salvation Army officer Rob Henson said a wide range of people had been impacted by the Bald Range blaze.
“There are migrant workers that we’re supporting here that have had to come off the farm where they would normally work, and now they’re here without any clothing or anything.”
“People are just uncertain,” he added. “They want to go back to where they were, and that’s tough.” AFP

July marked warmest month on record for contiguous US: NOAA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:34:56 UTC
08:34:56 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
July was the warmest month ever recorded in the contiguous United States, surpassing previous record-setting temperatures from 1936 and 2012, a federal agency announced Monday.
"July 2026 averaged 76.9F (24.9C), the warmest month on record (1895–present) for the contiguous United States (CONUS),” the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said.
Temperatures across the lower 48 states and the District of Columbia averaged 1.8C (3.3F) above the 20th-century mean, with every state ranking in the warmest third of their historical records.
Nighttime provided little relief, as average low temperatures reached 17.9C (64.2F), making it the warmest month for average minimums.
While the country was generally dry, ranking in the driest third of the 132-year record with 6.5 centimeters (2.55 inches) of rainfall, extreme weather events persisted.
Major flash flooding struck the Texas Hill Country and eastern New York during the month.
In contrast, Alaska recorded its coldest July since 2008, while Hawaii maintained its wettest year-to-date on record with nearly 1.5 meters (59 inches) of rain since January, 173.9% of normal.
Drought conditions covered 48.5% of the contiguous US, an increase of 0.7% since June.
In Puerto Rico, more than one-third of the island faced severe drought or worse.
The agency warned that wildland fire potential remains above normal for August across the Northwest, Great Basin, central Rockies, the Lower Mississippi Valley, southern Florida and Puerto Rico.
Forecasters expect above-average heat to persist through August across the central and southern US.

At another location, a strike caused a fire and structural damage to a warehouse. The fire, which spread over an area of 1,200 sq m, has been contained.
Rescue workers and other emergency services continue to work at the sites of the Russian strikes.
Background:
- At around 00:30, an air-raid warning was issued in Kyiv and several Ukrainian oblasts due to the threat of Russia using ballistic weapons.
- In addition to Kyiv, Russian forces launched ballistic missile and aerial bomb attacks on Pavlohrad and Zaporizhzhia. There are also reports of injuries and damage in those areas.

Caitlin Clark was nearly out Tuesday. A quick reversal sets up Liberty-Fever at full strength
NEW YORK (AP) — The surging New York Liberty will face Indiana on Tuesday night in a marquee WNBA matchup that will see the Fever at full strength after the league rescinded a technical foul against Caitlin Clark that would have kept her out.
Clark picked up her eighth technical of the season on Saturday, the number that triggers a one-game suspension, but league officials quickly rescinded it.
New York has won four straight games and seven of its last eight thanks to strong play from its top three players Breanna Stewart, Jonquel Jones and Sabrina Ionescu. The trio has been taking turns leading the Liberty during the recent hot streak that’s bumped them up to seventh place in the standings — but just two games behind third-place Las Vegas.
The Liberty are coming off a 40-point win over the defending champion Aces on Sunday. The Aces rested stars A’ja Wilson, Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young as it was the second half of a brutal back-to-back for Las Vegas.
“It doesn’t matter who’s playing on the other side, we understand we needed to win,” Ionescu said. “It doesn’t matter, we wanted to go out. We wanted to execute, we wanted to play our brand of basketball, knowing every game is important and this game isn’t going to have an asterisk by it because those players didn’t play. It’s going to show up as a win or a loss.”
New York lost by 20 to Indiana just before its current hot streak, so the Liberty would love to get some revenge.
Power poll rankings
Minnesota held onto the top spot in the power poll this week, although the Lynx weren’t unanimous. No. 2 Golden State received two votes and third-ranked Washington got one. Las Vegas, Indiana and New York were next. Atlanta, Dallas and Chicago followed the Liberty. Portland was 10th and Los Angeles 11th. Phoenix, Connecticut, Toronto and Seattle rounded out the poll.
Taskforce meeting
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent a memo to all the teams that there will be a meeting this week to continue discussions around transgender athletes in women’s basketball. The memo, sent Friday afternoon, said the topic will be discussed further by a task force of team presidents and general managers at a previously scheduled meeting next week.
Record shooting performance
Kayla McBride had a record-setting game Sunday, scoring a career-high 43 points and hitting a league-best 10 3-pointers in a win over Dallas. McBride made 10 of 14 shots from behind the arc.
“Minneapolis has become home for me and I want to give my best,” she said. “Whether the ball goes in or doesn’t, I just feel so much love. I think that’s why I can come out here and do my thing. I feel so loved and appreciated for who I am and I just love the game. I want to win. So I’m grateful for these fans, this organization. I’m just overcome with joy, and when I have opportunities like that I want to give it back.”
Player of the week
Shakira Austin of Washington was the AP player of the week for the second consecutive week. The forward averaged 22.3 points, 11.7 rebounds and 2.3 blocks to help the Mystics win all three of their games last week. Other players receiving votes included Breanna Stewart of New York, Bridget Carleton of Portland, Kelsey Mitchell of Indiana and Kayla McBride of Minnesota.
Game of the week
Washington at Las Vegas, Tuesday and Thursday. The Mystics will try to extend a seven-game winning streak when they visit the Aces for a pair of games. A win Tuesday would tie the franchise record of eight consecutive victories by Washington, matching the 2018 team.

The pull of a home Olympics: Why US medalists are coming back for Los Angeles 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:23:02 UTC
08:23:02 KST

The pull of a home Olympics: Why US medalists are coming back for Los Angeles 2028
PHOENIX (AP) — For those who have competed — or nearly competed — under the Olympic rings, the fear of missing out the next time the Games beckon is real. Regardless of the venue. Regardless of the sport.
Athletes who try to run it back following a lengthy sabbatical (and in some cases, a lengthy retirement) is hardly new. The list is filled with household names, from Mark Spitz to Michael Phelps. From Lindsey Vonn to Simone Biles. And on and on and on.
Still, the steady drip figures to be more of a deluge as Los Angeles 2028 approaches. The inherent pull of the Games combined with the chance to compete at home on the world stage under the white-hot spotlight only the Olympics provide is already proving too tempting to ignore for a generation of American stars who have racked up medal after medal on seemingly every other continent but their own.
Track icon Allyson Felix is mounting a return in her early 40s. Six-time Olympic medalist and 2020 Olympic gymnastics all-around champion Suni Lee (with documentary crew in tow) announced last month she’s started training for a shot at her third Games. Two-time Olympic gold medalist Jade Carey is already back, winning the vault and finishing fifth in the all-around at the U.S. championships over the weekend.
Asked how much of a factor the chance to do her thing on American soil played into her decision as she enters her late 20s, Carey just smiled.
“I probably would have gone for it regardless,” said Carey, who will be 28 when the flame is lit at the Coliseum in Los Angeles. “But it does make it a little extra special that it’s in the U.S.”
Or maybe a lot more special. Oh, and conceivably a lot more lucrative too.
Olympic success at home can be life-changing
The media landscape has shifted dramatically since the 1996 Games in Atlanta. The rise of social media allows athletes to easily tell their stories directly to new audiences, and the ability to create and curate their own brand opens sponsorship opportunities that didn’t exist a generation ago.
Finding your way onto the medal stand at the Olympics anywhere in the world can make you a hero. Doing it in the States, however, can turn you into a legend. Mary Lou Retton, Mike Eruzione and Kerri Strug know how that goes.
Longtime agent Sheryl Shade, whose list of clients over the last 30 years has included a “who’s who” of Olympians, from gymnasts Nastia Liukin and Shawn Johnson to soccer pioneer Mia Hamm and figure skater Tara Lipinski, called the opportunities for athletes to capitalize on success in Los Angeles “exponentially” greater than any Games that have come before.
“It’s going to be long-range too,” Shade said. “Because now it doesn’t end at the Olympic Games. That’s why LA is so important. This is about legacy.”
Look no further than “The Magnificent Seven” for proof. Three decades ago, the members of the 1996 U.S. women’s Olympic gymnastics team walked onto the floor of the Georgia Dome for the team final as underdogs. They walked off it with gold medals around their necks, their lives forever altered.
“I mean, we all knew that was going to be special,” team captain Amanda Borden said.
Even if they had no idea how special at the time. While the group, all teenagers that summer, eventually retired and went on with their lives, to this day they get stopped by fans who remember where they were that memorable July night when the injured Strug gingerly stuck her vault landing to secure gold for the Americans.
They’ve lived the dream. In some ways, they’re still living it. So no, they’re not surprised that so many who’ve “already been there, done that” want to give it another shot.
“I can promise (for) every athlete that makes the team, this Olympics will be one of the greatest moments of their careers,” seven-time Olympic medalist Shannon Miller said.
Her advice to anyone considering it: go for it, even if things don’t work out exactly as you planned.
Miller decided less than a year before the 2000 Games in Sydney to give it one final shot at age 23 — considered ancient for a gymnast at the time, though not so much anymore. An injury at the Olympic trials ended that dream. Miller has no regrets, and a quarter century later it’s considered largely a footnote for the most-decorated American women’s gymnast not named Biles.
The quest for Olympic immortality can come at a potentially high cost
Still, the attempt comes with considerable risk to both your mental and physical health. For every athlete that makes it, there will be countless others that don’t. And for those that do, the burden to succeed will be ratcheted up to a level they’ve likely never experienced.
Dominique Moceanu, the youngest member of the Magnificent Seven, described it as a “double-edged sword.”
“You have to understand that it will be probably the biggest moment of your life,” Moceanu said. “Whether it’s because you put it on yourself or you feel the enormity of the weight of the country and the expectations. That does something to people, right?”
It does. Biles brought the discussion around mental health to the forefront of the Games in Tokyo when she removed herself from multiple nights of competition to protect herself while dealing with “the twisties.”
She took some time off before returning in 2023, capping the perhaps final chapter of her career — Biles remains noncommittal about her future — by winning a second all-around gold in Paris a year later.
Skye Blakely watched Biles’ triumph from afar after her bid to make the 2024 Olympic team ended when she tore her right Achilles while training at the Olympic trials, three years after her outside shot at making the 2021 squad ended with an elbow injury at the same meet.
While she’s just 21, Blakely is also an old soul in many ways, one who has grown more acquainted with disappointment than she ever imagined. She’s well-versed in what it costs to make it, and what happens on the other side when you don’t.
That has not stopped her from throwing herself into the mix once again. When describing why she continues to press on, and Blakely sounds like so many American athletes across the spectrum — regardless of their resume — who feel the Games’ unique gravitational pull.
“Having a dream is always a risk if you’re going to go after it,” she said before finishing seventh in the all-around at the U.S. championships, her first elite all-around meet in two years. “And I feel like the want for that dream has to be more than being afraid of that risk. And for me it is.”

Ex-fraternity member pleads guilty to hazing an Arizona university pledge to death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:23:02 UTC

Ex-fraternity member pleads guilty to hazing an Arizona university pledge to death
A former leader of a Northern Arizona University fraternity pleaded guilty Monday to hazing and causing a pledge’s death by making him drink excessively at an off-campus rush event.
Carter Eslick, 20, entered the plea to a felony hazing charge involving the death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, in Coconino County Superior Court in Flagstaff.
Under an agreement with prosecutors, Eslick would serve no more than four years of probation. A judge will determine the length and could also impose up to a year in jail at a Sept. 30 sentencing hearing.
Martinez, who was pledging to the now-defunct Delta Tau Delta fraternity chapter at NAU, was found unresponsive Jan. 31. An autopsy found his blood-alcohol level was 0.425%, which is considered life-threatening.
Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said the plea doesn’t diminish the “profound harm caused or the sorrow of Colin’s death.”
The Associated Press left an email and voicemail for Eslick’s attorney, Burges McCowan, requesting comment on Monday. The AP also left a phone message with the attorney for Martinez’s family.
Eslick was serving as the fraternity’s pledge master at the time, responsible for welcoming new members. He’s no longer a student at NAU. Martinez was among four men pledging to Delta Tau Delta who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez’s sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said.
The university suspended the Delta Tau Delta fraternity after Martinez’s death, and the national organization closed the NAU chapter.

Welcome to the Fire Pit: Portland embraces its reborn WNBA team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:23:02 UTC
08:23:02 KST

Welcome to the Fire Pit: Portland embraces its reborn WNBA team
The fact Portland has shown up for its new WNBA team is, in many ways, unsurprising given the city’s long history of embracing women’s sports.
The expansion Fire rank fourth in the league with an average attendance of about 14,500 fans per game. The only teams drawing more are the Golden State Valkyries, the New York Liberty and the Caitlin Clark-led Indiana Fever.
The Fire have dubbed the Moda Center the “Fire Pit” on game days and the team leans into the motif with pyrotechnics in game introductions.
“I think we’ve just been so fortunate, to be honest, all year to have such an amazing atmosphere here at the Fire Pit,” Fire coach Alex Sarama said. “So that’s on the fan base, that’s because of this local community and just turning up and supporting the team as they do.”
Portland has long supported women’s sports. For many years, the University of Portland’s soccer team had the top attendance in college soccer, spurred by national championships in 2002 and 2005 and star players like Christine Sinclair and Megan Rapinoe.
The Portland Thorns were among the founding teams of the National Women’s Soccer League in 2013 and have regularly been one of the top drawing clubs in the league.
And then there’s the Sports Bra, the nation’s first women’s sports bar, which opened in 2022.
“We have some of the loudest fans in the WNBA,” center Megan DiLeo said. “And they’re really like our sixth man, to be honest.”
This is the second iteration of the Fire. Portland’s first WNBA team started its short run as an expansion team in 2000. Portland Trail Blazers owner Paul Allen, the co-founder of Microsoft who died in 2018, was the Fire’s chairman.
Among the Fire’s original players were Jackie Stiles and Vanessa Nygaard. The team averaged some 8,600 fans per game in 2001.
So when the team folded in 2002, it was not for lack of fan support. That year the NBA, which had owned the league’s teams, sold them to affiliated NBA teams or independent owners. Allen declined to buy the Fire and the team folded.
In 2024, the Bhathal family bought the NWSL’s Thorns for $63 million. Later that year, Lisa Bhathal Merage and brother Alex Bhathal, under the banner Raj Sports, were awarded a WNBA expansion team.
The Bhathals invested in a joint basketball-soccer training facility, the first of its kind in women’s sports, which will formally open this month.
The team leaned heavily into the “Fire Reignited” theme and has so far put on a respectable performance for an expansion franchise, ranking ninth overall in the league with a 13-19 record.
“They’ve done a really nice job of recognizing the past while also bringing in new fans,” said fan Laura Belfour. “There’s a welcoming atmosphere and it’s cool to see so many families with kids.”
Guard Carla Leite is averaging 15.5 points and 6.2 assists a game and Bridget Carleton is averaging 14.6 points and 4.4 rebounds. Carleton was the team’s first pick in the WNBA expansion draft. But the team has been stung by the recent loss of guard Sarah Ashlee Barker to a season-ending ACL injury.
DiLeo and her corgi Pancake, who has her own Instagram following, have become local celebrities. Formerly Megan Gustafson before her recent marriage, DiLeo has written a children’s book “Pancake’s Passport” about the beloved pet’s travels.
“I always heard things here and there about Portland and the women’s sports fandom that is here,” Carleton said after the team’s home opener. “But never knew too much about it, especially never really being on the West Coast. But even this past week, feeling it on social media, feeling it in the city — going on a walk and people recognized me already, and I hadn’t even played a game yet. It’s just incredible.”
Sarama is the team’s inaugural coach after serving as an assistant for the Cleveland Cavaliers. He practices an innovative coaching method called the Constraints-Led Approach, or CLA, which eschews repetitive drills in favor of putting players into situations that require creative problem-solving.
“I think we’re excited because I think there is a really good foundation here,” Sarama said. “I think the good thing is we overachieved, but we haven’t done that at the cost of development and playing our young players. So I think what that will do is put us in a very strong position in two years and three years as we kind of add to this core group that we have.”

The Trump Administration Has Revoked More Than 175,000 Visas. Here's Who's Included in the Crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:23:01 UTC
08:23:01 KST

The State Department announced on Monday that it has revoked over 175,000 visas since President Donald Trump returned to office last January.
The department stated that the revocations targeted foreign nationals who had “violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against U.S. citizens, defrauded Americans, abused our immigration system, or endangered national security.” According to the department, the “majority” of the visas were revoked due to “criminal activity.”
Trump has launched an aggressive crackdown on both legal and illegal immigration in his second term, vowing to deport the “worst of the worst” from the U.S.
Data have shown, however, that the majority of the people who have been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement during the second Trump Administration have had no criminal convictions. The Administration’s immigration enforcement tactics, meanwhile, have drawn widespread outcry and official pushback, with courts striking down a number of its moves as violating longstanding laws and protests breaking out around the country following the killings of multiple U.S. citizens.
The department offered multiple examples of people whose visas have been revoked and the reasons why in its Monday release, though it did not provide any evidence or identifying information about the cases it referenced.
“The Trump Administration is protecting our nation and its citizens by upholding the highest standards of national security and public safety through our visa process,” a State Department spokesperson tells TIME in a statement, saying that the Secretary of State has “broad discretionary authority to revoke visas.”
Here are some of the groups of people who have been included in the Trump Administration’s sweeping visa cancellations, according to federal officials.
People accused of “criminal activity”
Most of the visas were revoked as a result of “law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity,” the State Department said.
It listed “assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug crimes” as the “leading causes,” while noting that a “significant share” of the cancellations were also due to “reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud and embezzlement, and other crimes.”
The department listed among its individual examples foreign nationals who it said were charged with violent and sexual offenses including instances of “rape and sexual battery – including of a victim who was mentally disabled”; kidnapping and human trafficking; domestic violence; and “sodomy of a child.”
Multiple other people whose visas were revoked, it said, were involved in fraud schemes—which Trump has made it a major focus of his second term agenda to c. One person “built a company on lies,” the department alleged, “faking revenue and fooling investors to swindle millions of dollars from clients.” In another of the examples it offered, the department said the visa holder “helped orchestrate a massive Medicaid scam – billing for over $5 million of fake services.”
Trump has made cracking down on fraud a major focus of his second term agenda. And foreign nationals have in multiple instances been targeted in the Administration’s anti-fraud campaign.
In one notable instance, the President accused Somalis in Minnesota of being involved in a welfare fraud scandal in Minnesota amid his immigration crackdown in the state, marking just the latest instance in which Trump has gone after the state’s sizable Somali community. “Somali gangs are terrorizing the people of that great State, and BILLIONS of Dollars are missing,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Democrats have condemned Trump’s targeting of the community.
In still another alleged instance cited by the State Department in its Monday release, someone had their visa revoked after they were arrested “for driving with heroin and a blood alcohol level more than 3x the legal limit.”
People who “celebrated” Charlie Kirk’s death
The State Department said that it had revoked the visas of "multiple foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk,” including one who allegedly said of the conservative commentator, “when fascists die, democrats don’t complain,” and another who said Kirk “died too late.”
Kirk, the founder of the conservative youth activist group Turning Point USA and a friend of Trump’s, was shot and killed while he was hosting an event at Utah Valley University in September. Tyler Robinson, the suspect in Kirk’s killing, was arrested after a 33-hour manhunt.
In the aftermath of Kirk’s death, some on the right, including Trump, blamed the left for his killing and the broader rise in political violence around the country—despite data contradicting that portrayal—and called for a crackdown. The President asserted in an address at the time that “radical left” rhetoric comparing “wonderful Americans like Charlie to Nazis and the world’s worst mass murderers and criminals” was “directly responsible for the terrorism that we’re seeing in our country today.”
The State Department indicated at the time that it may withhold—or revoke—visas from non-citizens who made social media posts making light of Kirk’s shooting.
“In light of yesterday’s horrific assassination of a leading political figure, I want to underscore that foreigners who glorify violence and hatred are not welcome visitors to our country. I have been disgusted to see some on social media praising, rationalizing, or making light of the event, and have directed our consular officials to undertake appropriate action,” Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in a post on X . He called for people to make him aware of such remarks and said that he would “direct consular officials to monitor the comments to this post.”
A State Department spokesperson said in a statement to news outlets when asked for comment on Landau’s post that "this Administration does not believe that the United States should grant visas to persons whose presence in our country does not align with U.S. national security interests."
The department in October said that it had revoked the visas of six foreign nationals over comments they made online about Kirk’s assassination, saying in posts on X that it had “no obligation to host foreigners who wish death on Americans.”
“Aliens who take advantage of America’s hospitality while celebrating the assassination of our citizens will be removed,” the department wrote.
People deemed deportable on ‘foreign policy grounds’
The State Department credited Secretary of State Marco Rubio with identifying “numerous” foreign nationals who it characterized as “deportable on foreign policy grounds.”
These people, according to the department, included a Cuban national “connected to a Cuban communist regime influence operation” and Iranian nationals “with connections to the Iranian regime.”
The Trump Administration has reportedly been moving to remove Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel, and the President has suggested that he would turn his attention to the country after the war in Iran has been resolved. In February, the U.S. and Israel forced a different regime change when they launched their initial wave strikes against Iran, in which the Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic, Ali Khamenei, was killed.
The department also cited as examples of those whose visas were revoked for foreign policy reasons “a Laotian child sex offender” who it said was pardoned by Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, and “a Kuwaiti national who wished for violence against the President of the United States and called Americans his ‘enemy.’”
“Wishing violence upon the President of the United States and characterizing Americans as one's enemy are not protected activities that entitle a foreign national to remain in the United States,” the department spokesperson says to TIME.
‘Birth tourists’
The department said that a U.S. embassy in North Africa revoked the visas of over 100 “birth tourist” parents, who intentionally give birth in the U.S. so that their children receive citizenship status.
Trump has sought to severely restrict birthright citizenship, which was established in the Fourteenth Amendment in the 19th century. Under the amendment, almost all of those born on U.S. soil automatically become citizens.
Trump attempted to take executive action to limit those privileges significantly, but the Supreme Court deemed the move unconstitutional and struck it down. Since that ruling, however, the Trump Administration has continued his efforts to restrict the law. The Department of Justice, the same day as the Supreme Court decision, said that it would “prioritize the investigation and prosecution of birth tourism schemes.” And last week Trump signed two new executive orders targeting birthright citizenship.
International students
Though the State Department did not include any mention of it in its Monday release, the Trump Administration has also revoked thousands of student visas.
The Administration has targeted student activists on college campuses; expanded social media screenings for certain visa holders’ accounts; targeted visas from Chinese students, citing security concerns; and limited the amount of time that students and foreign journalists can stay in the country, among a number of moves impacting foreign-born students.
Rubio said in August, roughly seven months after Trump returned to office, that more than 6,000 student visas had been revoked in that time.

At least 111 dead after 7.4-magnitude earthquake hits Colombia
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
02:19:44 EEST
08:19:44 KST

At least 111 people have died and 87 have been injured after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, bringing down buildings across several cities and leaving people trapped beneath rubble.
The earthquake struck at 07:34 local time, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in the Chocó region, according to the US Geological Survey.
The USGS placed the quake at a depth of about 107 kilometres. Tremors were felt across Colombia and in Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama.
Colombia’s geological service said the earthquake was the strongest recorded in the country this century. It reported at least 21 aftershocks by late Monday and said further tremors were expected.
President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on 7 August, declared a national emergency and ordered state resources towards rescue and recovery operations.
“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” de la Espriella said in a national address.
Authorities reported deaths across several regions, with Risaralda among the areas reporting the highest toll. The Guardian reported that at least 40 people had died in Pereira, citing the city’s mayor.
Damage extended across Colombia’s coffee-growing region and into Cali, the country’s third-largest city.
Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder told the BBC that 32 buildings had collapsed in the city and emergency teams had rescued 38 people.
In Pereira, local authorities declared an emergency and imposed restrictions intended to clear roads for emergency vehicles. Schools were closed, while damage affected medical facilities and the city’s airport.
Flights were also suspended at airports serving Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.
The earthquake caused damage in Manizales, where part of a cathedral tower collapsed. Residents in several cities reported power cuts, damaged homes and streets blocked by rubble.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU had activated its Copernicus satellite service to support rescue work and stood ready to provide further assistance.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was monitoring the situation and was prepared to support Colombia. France, Spain, Mexico, Brazil, Ecuador and other countries also offered assistance.
Colombia experiences frequent seismic activity, though earthquakes above magnitude 6 are less common. A magnitude 6.2 earthquake in the country’s coffee region in 1999 killed more than 1,000 people.
