Netanyahu pushes to have 3 senior ministers bypass Likud primaries amid battle over slate control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:19:17 UTC
08:19:17 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced overnight Monday that he intends to seek approval from the Likud Secretariat for guaranteed places on the party’s Knesset slate for Defense Minister Israel Katz, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Minister Haim Katz.
The announcement came late at night as Likud ministers and lawmakers are locked in an increasingly fierce battle over their positions on the party’s slate ahead of the next Knesset election.
Netanyahu has already been granted eight reserved slots on the Likud list, at positions 3, 5, 9, 11, 15, 18, 26 and 29.
The central question now occupying senior party figures is whether the three ministers will be placed within those eight slots or whether Netanyahu is seeking three additional guaranteed positions beyond the quota already approved for him.
According to the scenario being discussed within Likud, Netanyahu intends to seek the three positions in addition to the eight slots he has already received.
Such a move is expected to trigger opposition and anger among Likud ministers and lawmakers because every additional reserved place further reduces the number of realistic positions available to candidates competing in the party primaries.
Likud’s official statement said: “The Likud Secretariat will be asked to approve, alongside the prime minister’s reserved slots, the placement of Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, Defense Minister Israel Katz and Likud Central Committee chairman Minister Haim Katz on the Likud slate, in addition to the new reserved candidates the prime minister is expected to bring.”
The party said Israel Katz would be given a guaranteed place following a ruling last week by the Likud tribunal, which determined that reserving a position for the defense minister would allow him to focus on Israel’s security needs rather than engage in internal political campaigning.
Sa’ar, meanwhile, is to receive a spot under the agreement merging his party with Likud, while Haim Katz is to be placed on the slate because of his role as chairman of the Likud Central Committee.
The wording of the Likud statement, particularly its reference to the three ministers being placed “alongside the prime minister’s reserved slots” and “in addition to the new reserved candidates the prime minister is expected to bring,” strengthens the possibility that their positions will not come out of Netanyahu’s existing quota of eight.
Still, the exact placement has not yet been finalized, and the ultimate number of slots on the Likud slate that will not be determined in the primaries remains unclear.
Israel Katz reservation draws surprise
The most surprising of the three moves is the decision to reserve a place for Defense Minister Israel Katz.
The plan had not been known in advance to Likud ministers and lawmakers and was not included among the eight positions previously approved for Netanyahu.
Last week, the Likud tribunal ruled that Katz should be allowed a reserved position, arguing that doing so would enable him to concentrate on security matters rather than the political battle surrounding the primaries.
Katz is already regarded as one of Likud’s most senior figures and had been expected to compete for a place near the top of the party slate.
Sa’ar’s placement, by contrast, had been expected because it stems from the merger agreement between his party and Likud.
The intention to reserve a spot for Haim Katz is also not new and was first reported by ynet about a month ago.
The three moves are now being brought together for approval alongside the broad quota of reserved positions already available to Netanyahu.
The decision is expected to intensify tensions within Likud because it could further reduce the number of realistic Knesset slots left for party members competing in the primaries.
Senior Likud figures have been fighting in recent days over every position on the slate, and the possibility that three additional candidates could receive guaranteed places beyond Netanyahu’s existing eight is likely to sharpen the internal struggle even further.

Trump order pushes for overhaul of childhood vaccine schedule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:15:00 UTC
08:15:00 KST

Trump order pushes for overhaul of childhood vaccine schedule
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Aug 10 pushing for a rethink of school vaccine mandates and repeating calls for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to be separated into three individual shots.
Many medical experts cast the push as scientifically baseless and potentially damaging to public health.
Curbing vaccines has been a key priority for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, who founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit and has long promoted a disproven link between immunisation and autism.
The federal government does not have direct control over several areas covered by the order. States, for example, have the authority to require vaccinations for students to attend school.
On these points Trump’s move is more of a suggestion than an order.
“States and territories are advised to review” the Trump administration’s recommendations on “immunisation requirements for contexts such as school enrolment and attendance”, the order states.
In another section, it says the US Health and Human Services department will form a task force to offer the MMR shot as individual vaccines “by working with the private sector and other countries as appropriate, while guaranteeing continued availability of combination vaccines and those vaccines recommended for shared clinical decision-making”.
New York City’s health commissioner, Alister Martin, said the order was based “in politics and conspiracy theories”.
“Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be,” Martin said in a statement.
“Cities and states can set their own recommendations and requirements, and many, including New York City, have moved away from the federal government’s recommendations as they’ve become politicised and unscientific.”
Years of clinical evidence support the safety of a combined MMR vaccine.
Public health experts have long advised that the combined shot offers children more protection faster, and also decreases the logistical hurdles for parents who may struggle to make multiple appointments.
Yet during the Oval Office signing, Trump made a series of incendiary and unsupported statements countering that advice.
In a call with reporters, Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Paediatrics (AAP), estimated it would take more than a decade to develop approved separated vaccines in the US.
“We’re advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data,” added Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.
Worst measles outbreak in decades
Senator Bill Cassidy, a doctor whose deciding vote confirmed Kennedy’s controversial appointment as health chief, posted on social media platform X that the president’s initiative would only serve to “increase hesitancy and make children less safe”.
“This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism,” Cassidy said.
The Trump administration’s push to overhaul vaccine policy comes as its efforts to implement major changes were blocked by a federal court earlier in 2026, pending further court proceedings.
The judge’s stay preventing the overhaul sided with major medical organisations, which asserted that the Trump administration’s actions to push the changes through were unlawful.
The president’s latest order arrives just as children across the country are readying to return to school, and as the US suffers its worst measles outbreak in 35 years.
Trump’s health secretary Kennedy is accused of contributing significantly to the crisis by spreading anti-vaccine sentiment and fuelling fears of well-studied and proven immunisations.
Polling indicates that most Americans still support vaccination, and in recent months both Kennedy and Trump had backed off anti-vaccination rhetoric which could spell negative repercussions in November’s midterm vote.
But the efforts on Aug 10 show the issue remains a core component of their health policy agenda, as both men remain committed to the false notion that vaccines can cause autism.
Such a potential link has been debunked by years of research. AFP

Colombia recognizes Israeli claim over the Golan Heights
Colombia's newly appointed hard-right government on Monday recognized Israel's claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which it captured from Syria in 1967.
The United States was until now the only country to recognize Israel's annexation of the territory in 1981.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella took power on Friday, following a bombastic campaign during which he promised tight relations with the US and Israel as a way to combat armed groups in his own country.

"The Government of Colombia recognizes Israeli sovereignty over this territory, as well as that State's right to protect itself against external threats," read a statement published on X.
"Colombia recognizes that maintaining Israel's control and sovereignty over the Golan Heights is an essential component of its national defense," it added.
The United Nations and nearly all its member countries recognise that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation.
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar thanked his "good friend" De la Espriella for the recognition.
The pair had agreed on the move in the Colombian city of Barranquilla, he said, one day before De la Espriella's inauguration.
Last month, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres reiterated that the Golan Heights were part of Syria, describing Israeli occupation as "totally unacceptable."
De la Espriella's leftist predecessor Gustavo Petro had ardently criticized Israel's genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, severing diplomatic relations and halting Israeli arms imports into Colombia.
The US-backed millionaire now in office has promised to restore ties.

'Evidence is clear': Players association says brutal schedule behind injuries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:11:45 UTC
08:11:45 KST

The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals for this year's Canadian Open is more evidence the tennis season is too long.
Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic are all out of the men's draw, while Victoria Mboko, Karolina Muchova and Emma Raducanu are among the missing names on the women's side.
Tournament organisers believe recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events have become a wider issue for the sport.
The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals from the Canadian Open underscore concerns that professional tennis's lengthy calendar and expanded top-level events are increasing injury risks.
The players' advocacy group said it was saddened but not surprised by the absences from the tournament, arguing that reduced recovery time between tournaments was contributing to injuries occurring earlier in the season and becoming more serious.
The Canadian Open men's event in Montreal was hit by the withdrawals of world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, while Carlos Alcaraz was also sidelined with a wrist injury. Hometown favourite Felix Auger-Aliassime also pulled out due to a back injury before his opening match.
On the women's side, defending champion Victoria Mboko, Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova, Emma Raducanu and Jasmine Paolini are also missing the tournament with injuries.
The first quarterfinal matches of the tournament begin later on Tuesday AEST.
Tournament organisers said last month that recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events had become a wider issue for the sport.
PTPA says 'evidence is clear'
The PTPA said it had collected and analysed injury data from more than 30,000 professional matches across all levels of the game over the past eight years in a project launched three years ago with its medical director, Dr Robby Sikka.
"The evidence is clear: the season is too long, recovery time is shrinking, and injuries are occurring earlier and becoming more severe," the PTPA said in a statement posted on social media.
The group said upper-body injuries were up 42 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to its analysis. Arm injuries were up 112 per cent this year compared with the 2025 average, it added.
The ATP expanded seven of its nine Masters 1000 tournaments to 12-day events under its OneVision strategic plan, with 2025 the first season in which the longer format was used across those events.
The PTPA said the change had cut into the time players have to rest, train and travel between tournaments, despite players having voiced concerns about the demands of the schedule for years.
"Short-term commercial interests cannot come at the expense of player health," the association said. "Protecting players isn't just about today's competitors, it is about protecting the future of tennis."
Schedule the players' choice
The ATP has previously said players retain choices over their schedules and that it is working to create incentives for an appropriate number of matches to be played during the season.
Spokespeople for the ATP and WTA Tours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The PTPA called for the sport to take a player-health and data-driven approach to restructuring the calendar.
It said players should have a meaningful role in shaping the schedule, while mandatory tournament commitments should be reduced to allow adequate recovery.
It also urged the ATP to consider reversing the 12-day Masters 1000 format.

Palestinian church affairs committee warns of continued Israeli violence, displacement

Mohammad Sio
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
The Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine warned Monday of continued Israeli violence, forced displacement and persecution targeting Palestinians..  
In a letter addressed to church leaders and heads of churches around the world, the committee expressed grave concern over the situation faced by Palestinians -- particularly Palestinian Christians -- across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip.  
The letter, issued by Ramzi Khouri, a member of the Palestine Liberation Organization Executive Committee and head of the committee, warned that attacks against Palestinian Christians can no longer be viewed as isolated incidents.
“They form part of an ongoing and systematic pattern that includes settler violence, land confiscation and settlement expansion, restrictions on freedom of worship and access to Christian and Muslim holy sites, and attacks against clergy, nuns, churches, monasteries and church properties and institutions,” it said.
The committee also expressed concern over attempts to undermine the historic and legal status quo governing holy sites in Jerusalem.
It said the policies were placing growing pressure on Palestinian Christian communities and threatening their “historic and deeply rooted presence” in their homeland.
The committee singled out Taybeh village in the West Bank, described as Palestine's last entirely Christian town, “which is experiencing a painful decline in its population.”
It said increasing numbers of Christian families have been compelled to leave Palestine since 2023 “amid deteriorating economic conditions, escalating attacks and restrictions, and the absence of any credible political horizon.”
The letter also highlighted the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip, saying the suffering endured by Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, “is part of an ongoing reality affecting the Palestinian people as a whole.”
“The Christian presence cannot be separated from the broader Palestinian cause,” the committee said, adding that “protecting the Christian presence in Palestine means protecting the Palestinian people, their rights, dignity and freedom.”
The committee urged church leaders worldwide to listen to Palestinian churches, clergy and theologians and to visit Palestine to witness conditions firsthand.
It called on them to meet with church leaders and Christian communities and visit churches, monasteries and holy sites, saying firsthand witness can contribute “to developing stronger and more effective positions and actions.”
The committee welcomed expressions of solidarity from churches around the world but called for such solidarity to translate into more effective positions and concrete action.
It urged churches to act according to their respective roles, capacities and ecclesial and humanitarian responsibilities in defense of justice, dignity and accountability and to protect holy sites and the Palestinian Christian presence.
The committee said it had attached a report documenting violations against Palestinian Christians, their churches and holy sites from the beginning of 2026 through August.
It said the current situation requires a shift from expressions of concern and sympathy to “witness, principled positions, and action.”
The committee concluded its message with a call to church leaders around the world to “See. Listen. Speak. And let what you see and hear lead to action.”
Alongside settlement expansion, Israeli forces and occupiers have intensified attacks in the West Bank, including damaging and demolishing homes and other structures, burning mosques and vehicles, bulldozing agricultural land and preventing farmers from reaching their fields.
In Gaza, a ceasefire agreement was reached in October last year to halt Israel's genocide, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 174,000 since October 2023. The war has caused extensive destruction, affecting 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure, with reconstruction costs estimated by the UN at about $70 billion.

'Dreams disappear' as Gaza students await evacuation to Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

Breadcrumb
'Dreams disappear' as Gaza students await evacuation to Italy
Dozens of Gaza students who won scholarships to universities in Italy are still waiting to be evacuated due to bureaucratic red tape, leaving qualified students in a deadly conflict zone, AFP has found.
Although more than 200 Palestinian students have been successfully enrolled in Italian colleges through a government university corridor project started in 2025, others have been left behind.
About 50 students are still awaiting clearance to leave devastated territory where most higher education institutions have been destroyed by Israel's genocidal war -- despite having met the same requirements of previous Gazan students now in Italy, non-governmental organisations say.
Between September 2025 and June, 246 scholarship recipients from Gaza were flown to Italy and San Marino in a series of evacuations through Italy's "IUPALS" program for Palestinian students, according to the foreign ministry.
But there have been no evacuations since June 1, said Anna Giada Altomare, founder of the Fiori dai Cannoni charity that helps the accepted students, who cited conflicting rules and a lack of transparency within the program.
One male student still waiting in Gaza -- who requested that his name not be used -- described to AFP a "long waiting period, the uncertainty about the travel date, and the fear of losing an educational opportunity obtained after great effort".
"The Italian government could resolve this situation very quickly," Altomare said, adding: "It is the state that should accelerate the process."
Neither the foreign ministry nor the ministry for universities and research responded to a question from AFP about the evacuation delays.
Contacted by AFP, the Israeli foreign ministry also did not immediately respond for comment.
Universities destroyed
Nada Abunada and Mohamed Arafat are among the lucky ones. They began their studies in economics at Rome's Sapienza University in November 2025, having graduated high school in Gaza with scores above 99 percent.
"I couldn't enrol in university (in Gaza) because the war started. Everything that I had been planning for disappeared," Abunada told AFP in Rome, adding that "most universities were destroyed".
Arafat was studying business administration at Gaza's Al-Azhar University before Israel's war forced him to stop. "We were focused on surviving," he said.
They were alerted to their evacuation just the day before by Italy's consulate in Jerusalem.
"I didn't tell anyone until the very last day because I wasn't sure it would happen... I didn't have much time to say goodbye," said Arafat.
Students left behind say they are facing bureaucratic problems, including confusing evacuation criteria.
The young man still in Gaza - who was awarded a scholarship to study computer engineering in October 2025 - wonders whether his score on an Italian proficiency exam may have played a role in delaying his evacuation.
"I tried to answer as much as I could since I had been learning Italian despite all the difficult circumstances, including internet outages, fear, and the pressure of daily life during the war," he said.
In July, Italy's university and research ministry called for greater flexibility in applying the language requirement to students from conflict zones.
But that hasn't helped the students still waiting in Gaza.
Disappearing dreams
Other Palestinian students hoping to study in Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium face similar unexplained delays, the student said.
A pre-med graduate, who also asked not to be named, told AFP she was accepted to an Italian master's program in June 2025 without asking for a scholarship.
She was later told by the Italian consulate that those without scholarships would not be evacuated.
Altomare said students with private Italian sponsors are also not being evacuated, questioning the rationale for rejecting such applicants.
Beyond administrative hurdles, students face difficult personal choices, such as family separation and mothers unable to evacuate with their children.
"I find it absurd that a woman should be forced to choose between continuing her education and leaving her child behind in Gaza," said Altomare.
Student Arafat worries whether his family will be forced to leave their home, where they hear nightly strikes from nearby Israeli forces.
He is trying to help his younger brothers study in Italy, but said they face even greater challenges than he did.
They have been asked to provide an equivalency assessment of their grades - one they cannot possibly meet because, he said, "there are no functioning ministries or institutions" in Gaza.
Back in Gaza, the computer engineering student expressed the frustration felt by many.
"We are not just files or numbers," he told AFP.
"All we ask is to be given the opportunity we have already earned, and not to let our dreams disappear while we wait."

Labour ‘spitting in faces of police’ by failing to halt release of PC Harper’s killers, says ex-colleague
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
00:01:00 BST
08:01:00 KST

Government ‘spitting in faces of police’ by failing to halt release of PC Harper’s killers, says ex-colleague
‘Andy did his duty that night. The least they can do is show him some respect’, says a first responder at fatal scene – as No 10 claims it can’t keep killers behind bars
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A first responder has accused Andy Burnham’s government of “spitting in the faces of police officers” after Downing Street claimed it cannot stop the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.
Former officer Chris Bushnell, who met with PC Harper on the day he died while responding to a quad bike theft in Berkshire in 2019, said he finds the possibility of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers being released early “absolutely outrageous”.
Downing Street faces immense backlash over the situation, with more than 880,000 people signing a petition calling for the pair to remain in jail, while Thames Valley Police Federation is weighing legal action to prevent their release.
On Monday night, PC Harper’s “really angry” mother Debbie Adlam told ITV News she had not heard from the prime minister: “My message is that you want to tour the country, you want to meet the people. You haven’t even got in touch with me. How about coming to see me?”
Newlywed PC Harper, 28, was caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary. Mr Bushnell, then a police constable, was waiting in a lay-by for the suspects’ vehicle when he saw it dragging his colleague’s body behind.
The officer pursued but was ordered to stop through the radio. Minutes later, he was told PC Harper had been killed.
In a statement issued through the Thames Valley Police Federation (TVPF), Mr Bushnell said: “I will never get over it. The guilt. That feeling of ‘what if?’ Today, I feel pretty much how I felt the day after it happened.
“This news about the sentencing – and the offenders being released early – has brought it all back again.”
Cole and Bowers were convicted of manslaughter in 2020. But under current early release plans, they remain eligible to be freed in January – halfway through their 13-year sentences. The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and would not be eligible for early release.
Some 5,000 inmates are expected to be released early under sentencing changes, down from 6,000 after the exemptions announced as part of an urgent review of the scheme.
Despite growing pressure, Downing Street said yesterday it is “not possible” to exempt “one or two offenders” convicted of manslaughter from early release.
No 10 insisted Mr Burnham is “far from accepting the situation” but played down the prospect of a carve-out to keep Cole and Bowers behind bars.
“He understands the public wants him to go further, and he wanted to go further, but on the wider issue that prisons would have run out of space, police would stop making arrests, it would be impossible to lock up convicted offenders and that would put public safety at untold risk,” the prime minister’s spokesperson said.
But late on Monday night Sky News reported, via a spokesperson at No 10, that Mr Burnham has asked justice secretary Alex Norris to “work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper”, conflicting with Downing Street’s position throughout the day.
Mr Bushnell, who was serving in the West Berkshire dog unit when PC Harper was killed, said: “I’ve seen people die before. I’ve seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful.”
Recounting the court hearings he had to attend, Mr Bushnell said: “They were mocking it. The second time they were in the cells, but we heard they weren’t even paying attention.
“There was no remorse at all. It was almost a joke to them. Nothing serious. If you have an accident, if you kill someone, you show remorse. I just can’t comprehend it.
“And for all this to be coming up again now is unbelievable. It stirs up all those emotions once more.”
Mr Bushnell, who retired from Thames Valley Police in 2022, added: “We can’t change the verdict. They got their sentences, which were pretty pitiful, to be fair.
“When I first heard a couple of weeks ago there was a chance they could be let out early, I was shaking. It brought everything back.
“To think they could be released early is absolutely outrageous. I’m angry with them, but I’m also angry with the government. They’re spitting in the face of police officers.”
“They have got to serve their full sentence. Andy did his duty that night. The least they can do is show him some respect.”
The national chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, Mark Fairhurst, said he is “positive we could free up additional space and block anybody convicted of manslaughter from early release”.
He added: “You only have to look at the remand population. We’re knocking on to some 17,000 people on remand. I’m sure we could get a couple of thousands of them bailed or tagged with the GPS tag to monitor them electronically. That’s an easy win for this government and I can’t understand why they don’t consider it.”
It comes despite Mr Burnham earlier this week saying he had “pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do without risking the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing” by excluding sentences for “rape, serious child sex offences and other grooming offences” from eligibility.
Reforms in the Sentencing Act came after prisons came close to running out of space entirely last year, risking the “total breakdown of law and order”, which would leave police unable to make arrests and courts unable to send offenders to custody, the then justice secretary Shabana Mahmood said.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The death of PC Andrew Harper was a horrific crime. Our thoughts are with his family and friends, and we share the anger from the police community that we are in this position.
“Thanks to tireless campaigning by Andrew’s family, Harper’s Law means that anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime now gets a mandatory life sentence. This government has gone further by introducing a presumption that anyone convicted of murdering a police, prison or probation officer is handed a whole-life order.
“We have been clear that we wanted to go further and block more offenders from getting out sooner into their sentence but could not do so without risking prisons reaching capacity and collapsing.
“If that happened, police could not make arrests, courts could not remand offenders and there would be unchecked criminality on our streets.”

Used EV sales jump 67% as Britain’s second-hand car market gets its spark back
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
00:01:00 BST
08:01:00 KST

Used EV sales jump 67% as Britain’s second-hand car market gets its spark back
Electric cars claim a record share as the wider used market tops two million sales for the first spring quarter since 2021
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Britain’s used car market has returned to growth, with electric cars providing much of the extra spark as used EV sales jumped by 67 per cent.
More than two million used cars changed hands between April and June, according to new figures from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). The total of 2,009,318 transactions was up 0.7 per cent on the same period last year.
It was the first time since 2021 that second-quarter sales had passed the two million mark, leaving the market just 1.2 per cent below its pre-pandemic level. That small rise helped to make up for a slight fall during the first three months of the year. In total across the first half of 2026, 4,025,550 used cars found new homes, an increase of 0.2 per cent.
The biggest movement came from fully-electric cars. A total of 110,761 used EVs changed hands during the quarter, up 67 per cent and representing the strongest quarterly growth since the start of 2024. Electric cars also took a record 5.5 per cent share of the used market. That means more than one in every 18 second-hand car buyers chose an EV, compared with around one in 30 during the same period last year, when their share stood at 3.3 per cent.
It’s still a relatively small slice of Britain’s enormous used car market, but the direction of travel is clear: more electric models are reaching the second-hand market as cars originally bought or leased new are traded in, giving used buyers a broader range of ages, sizes and prices to choose from.
Growth was especially strong during April, when used EV transactions more than doubled with a 110.9 per cent rise. They increased by 57.6 per cent in May and 37.8 per cent in June. SMMT said the sharp rises in April and May coincided with higher fuel prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The figures were also compared with a weaker period last year, when changes to vehicle excise duty came into force.
Regular hybrids had a busy quarter too. Sales rose by 31.2 per cent to 130,825, lifting their share of the market from 5 per cent to 6.5 per cent. Plug-in hybrids didn’t join the growth, however. Transactions fell by 6.8 per cent to 22,856, leaving them with 1.1 per cent of all used car sales, down slightly from 1.2 per cent a year earlier.
Despite the rapid rise in electric and hybrid sales, petrol and diesel cars remain comfortably dominant. Together, they accounted for 86.7 per cent of all transactions during the quarter, or almost nine out of every 10 used cars sold. Petrol was still the country’s favourite fuel type, with 1,121,243 cars changing hands, although that figure was down by 1.2 per cent. Diesel transactions dropped by 7.2 per cent to 620,045, reflecting the falling number of new diesel cars feeding into the used market.
Mike Hawes, SMMT chief executive, said: “A return to growth is good news for motorists and the wider automotive sector, with sales of used EVs rising particularly strongly as more choice reaches more buyers. As the used market is where most people buy their cars, plentiful and affordable supply is vital, however, increasingly unrealistic targets in the new car market risk constraining that supply and pushing up costs. Urgent regulatory reform is needed to deliver a transition that works for every driver.”
Smaller cars continued to rule the used market. Superminis accounted for 31.7 per cent of all transactions, with sales edging up by 0.2 per cent. Lower-medium cars, another familiar source of everyday hatchbacks and family models, followed with a 26.6 per cent share and the same 0.2 per cent rise. Dual-purpose cars including SUVs recorded the strongest growth, climbing by 7.4 per cent to take 17.7 per cent of the market.
Used car buyers weren’t feeling especially adventurous when it came to colour. More than 1.1 million of the cars sold during the quarter were black, grey or white, with the three shades accounting for 56.5 per cent of the market. Sales of black cars rose by 0.7 per cent, grey increased by 4.1 per cent and white was up by 4.7 per cent. Blue remained the fourth most popular colour despite a 1.1 per cent decline, while silver held on to fifth place even as sales fell by 6.4 per cent.

England ‘on the cusp’ of eliminating hepatitis C, health officials say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
00:01:00 BST
08:01:00 KST

England ‘on the cusp’ of eliminating hepatitis C, health officials say
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
England is “on the cusp” of becoming one of the first countries globally to eradicate hepatitis C, health officials have said.
Efforts such as A&E blood tests, GP registration testing, and free home test kits have helped identify individuals who were previously undiagnosed.
Global health leaders have set out plans aimed at eliminating viral hepatitis across the world by 2030.
NHS England stated that the nation is among a small number of countries worldwide to have already beaten the World Health Organisation benchmark of treating 80% of all known cases.
It added that deaths associated with the virus have fallen by 36% over the past 10 years.
Hepatitis C is transmitted via contact with infected blood.
Many people have no symptoms but if it is not treated it can cause serious, and potentially life-threatening, liver damage.
A treatment course of antiviral drugs for eight to 12 weeks cures more than 95% of cases.
NHS England said that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, often referred to as hep C.
Professor Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, said: “Hepatitis C can cause serious harm, including liver failure and cancer, yet many people live with it for years without knowing or having any symptoms at all until it’s too late.
“That’s why the NHS has worked hard alongside public health teams and charities to find and treat hidden cases, and it’s really encouraging that over 100,000 people have now received potentially life-saving treatment in just a decade.
“England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO’s 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.
“With hepatitis C curable in more than nine out of 10 cases, we are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online.”
Rachel Halford, chief executive of The Hepatitis C Trust said: “We are on the cusp of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country’s history. To sustain this momentum, continued commitment and long-term investment are essential.”
Health officials have urged people at risk of undiagnosed hepatitis C – including people who have had a tattoo abroad, people who have moved to England from certain eastern European countries or those who use or have previously used injectable drugs – to order a confidential home-testing kit.
Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as many could have been potentially infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.
Paul Eatwell, 65, tested positive for the virus after routine liver function tests flagged an abnormality.
The grandfather from Blackburn, Lancashire, said: “My first reaction was disbelief. I remember saying: ‘Are you sure? Surely there’s been some mistake’.
“I didn’t feel ill. I kept wondering how I could possibly have caught it.
“The support from the specialist team made a huge difference. Their message was simple: ‘Don’t spend your time worrying about how you got it – focus on getting rid of it’.”
While it has not been established how Mr Eatwell caught the virus, it has been suggested that surgery in South Africa decades ago is a potential risk factor.
He added: “If you think you may be at risk, why wouldn’t you have the test? It gives you peace of mind.
“Treatment today isn’t life-changing in the way people might imagine – it’s one tablet a day for 12 weeks and a few blood tests.
“The alternative is to ignore it, potentially develop serious liver disease, or unknowingly pass the virus on to someone else.”
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: “We are leading the world in wiping out this disease for good.
“This is exactly the kind of preventative, forward-looking healthcare that we want the NHS to deliver across the board – catching illness earlier, easing pressure on hospitals, and giving people the chance to live longer, healthier lives.”
Dr Sema Mandal, from the UK Health Security Agency, said: “We are making significant progress towards eliminating hepatitis C as a public health threat.
“The sharp fall in cases since 2015 shows the impact of expanded testing and sustained access to modern curative treatments, and the commitment of health services and community partners across England.
“Treating over 100,000 people in just 10 years is a remarkable achievement and brings England closer than ever to becoming one of the first countries in the world to eliminate this disease as a public health threat.”
It comes just after the closure of the Infected Blood Inquiry.
The probe examined what has been dubbed the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS.
The inquiry concluded the scandal “could largely have been avoided” and there was a “pervasive” cover-up to hide the truth.
More than 30,000 people in the UK were infected with HIV and hepatitis C after they were given contaminated blood and blood products between the 1970s and early 1990s.
More than 3,000 people have died as a result while survivors are living with lifelong health implications.

The "Thousand Martyrs' Cup" will kick off simultaneously across three locations as a transitional league, ahead of a classified league next season.

The initial group stage will operate by region and branch. The association will provide a uniform grant to every qualifying club to assist with equipment and transportation costs.

Three physical trophy editions are being crafted for the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and Lebanon, each bearing the names of 1,014 athlete martyrs.
Financial strain

Rajoub urged FIFA and the international community to safeguard the rights of Palestinian athletes, reiterating calls to enforce regulations equally and uphold international sporting charters.

An analysis by the RAC revealed that an average of 721 people were killed or injured in drink-drive collisions during August between 2014 and 2024.
That total sits ahead of July, which saw an average of 704 casualties over the 11-year period.
By comparison, December, typically linked with drink-driving, recorded a lower average of 663 casualties.

“Warmer weather, longer evenings as well as holidays, festivals and barbecues all create more opportunities and temptation for people to drink and then get behind the wheel.”
“Enforcement of the drink-drive law at this time of year is therefore extremely important in keeping everyone safe.”
Mr Williams called for stronger measures to tackle the “genuine problem” of repeat drink-driving, such as introducing court-ordered alcolocks.
These are devices preventing a vehicle from being driven without a breath test for alcohol.
Drivers would “strongly support” their use in the UK, Mr Williams added.
The DfT is analysing feedback on a consultation on proposed changes to penalties for motoring offences, which include the use of alcolocks.
A previous investigation by the Press Association found nearly 28,000 British motorists were convicted of drink-driving multiple times in the 11 years to July 20 2024.
The DfT was approached for a comment.
Statistics revealed last year showed that almost 100 motorists a day were caught drink-driving in Britain across the past three years.
Road safety charity IAM RoadSmart, which obtained the figures, highlighted an urgent need for "a shift in mindset" among drivers.
A total of 108,000 drivers received drink-drive licence endorsements from 2022 to 2024, an average of 99 per day.
These statistics were acquired from the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) via a Freedom of Information request.
The data shows drivers aged 25-39 were the most frequent offenders, with 48,000 caught. This was followed by the 40-65 age group (40,000) and younger drivers aged 17-24 (15,000).

Putin’s Political Longevity – A Framework of Considerations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Putin’s Political Longevity – A Framework of Considerations
Historic economic and social conditions point to a change of leadership in Russia, but a triggering event is still on the horizon for Putin.
In October 2025, your author published a paper with RUSI concluding that Putin had the resources to continue and even expand the war in Europe. Since then, things have got worse economically, militarily and socially. In April 2026, Thomas Nilsson the head of Sweden’s Military Intelligence and Security argued that that Russia’s economy was much weaker than official figures report and that Moscow was ‘living on borrowed time’. How weak is Russia? How much of a threat are current conditions to Putin’s reign?
This article develops a framework intended to identify when an authoritarian leadership enters a historically significant zone of vulnerability.
The purpose is not to predict regime collapse. That would be foolish. The aim is to produce a historical framework of conditions that coincided with leadership (not regime) change in an array of dictatorships (including Russia) in the past.
The Logic of the Framework
Historical experience suggests that economic weakness alone rarely determines political outcomes. Venezuela demonstrated that severe economic stress could coexist with regime survival. Egypt demonstrated that a leader can be removed without state collapse. Russia in 1998 experienced crisis and leadership transition while the state endured.
The overall score of Russia today puts it in the High Stress and Increased Vulnerability Category
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 combined:
- Economic stress - years of economic stagnation, consumer shortages and a fiscal crisis).
- Elite fragmentation - hard liners versus reformers, KGB & Military uncertainty, institutional decay and contestation by Yeltsin, exiting member states.
- A powerful trigger event (The August 1991 Coup Attempt).
The Framework therefore assumes economic stress creates pressure, elite fragmentation creates vulnerability and trigger events determine timing.
The weight (score) attached to each variable is derived from the historical precedents of dictatorship that fell.
A recurring challenge in political-risk analysis is converting qualitative observations into structured assessments. The Leadership Vulnerability Framework addresses this by assigning scores to Economic System Stress (ESS), Elite Fragmentation Risk (EFR) and Trigger Index (TI) on a ten-point scale. Scores are not intended to represent precise measurements. Rather, they provide a disciplined method of comparing historical and contemporary cases.
The scoring system is:
Economic Stress
Economic stress is measured by the divergence between government reported economic performance and measurable reality. The reason to use this measure and not humdrum economic reports is because the government will only lie when things are bad and when it is afraid of the effect on the public.
Some of the measures used here are measured inconsistences between:
- Declared inflation and central bank interest rates.
- Fiscal arithmetic and military expenditure.
- Stable banking conditions and evidence of monetization of the cost of war - as well as corporate indebtedness and debt service arrears.
- Real wages, wage arrears and inflation.
- War, the labour market and coming conscription.
ESS combines household stress, financial stress and fiscal stress. Household stress includes inflation, real wages and wage arrears. Financial stress includes credit distortions, regional financial strain and the Financial Reality Gap. Fiscal stress includes budget deficits, defence burdens and resource dependence; dislocation of labour markets by war casualties and recruitment. Under current assumptions ESS is estimated at approximately 7.8, placing Russia in the framework’s high-stress category.
The Financial Reality Gap is a specific attempt to measure divergence between reported banking health and observable financial strain. A system reporting low non-performing loans and strong profitability should not normally exhibit rapidly rising forbearance, hidden support mechanisms, increasing wage arrears and widespread corporate distress. Historically, major banking and financial crises have often been preceded by such divergences. The FRG is therefore treated as a core component of Financial Stress.
The final ESS score represents a synthesized assessment of these pressures.
Elite Fragmentation Risk
EFR checks whether the elite backs the leadership. It evaluates succession uncertainty, patronage compression, security competition, regional fiscal stress and military sustainability. Authoritarian systems can endure economic stress while elite cohesion remains intact. They become more vulnerable when competition for resources increases or when uncertainty develops regarding future leadership arrangements.
EFR is intended to capture pressures acting upon the cohesion of the ruling coalition rather than popular dissatisfaction.
In the past nine months one important measure of emerging Elite Fragmentation has been the increasingly vocal media condemnation of domestic oppression and the ‘Stalin Cult’; the internet blackout and the emergence of the war in Ukraine as the cause of economic difficulties for ordinarily people. The fact that these issues can be articulated publicly indicates that not all the elite is onboard with the polices behind them.
Trigger Index
The TI captures catalytic events capable of converting latent pressure into political action. Military setbacks, financial accidents and banking instability, succession crises, elite defections, succession disputes and social unrest and major protest movements all fall within this category. Current trigger pressure remains materially below the levels associated with major historical transitions.
Upcoming potential Triggers include:
- Conscription.
- Economic collapse (particularly food inflation and energy scarcity);
- Military defeat.
- The loss of Crimea.
- Bad results in the forthcoming presidential and Duma elections.
For the TI, scores are derived from the probability and severity of catalytic events capable of converting latent stress into political action.
Historical Validation
The Framework was tested against Venezuela 2014, Egypt 2011, Russia 1998, Romania 1989 and the Soviet Union in 1991. The Framework scored well both statistically and in terms of qualitative ratings and outcomes:
The overall score of Russia today puts it in the High Stress and Increased Vulnerability Category.
A System Moving in the Wrong Direction
One of the principal advantages of the Framework is that it can be applied retrospectively. This allows one to see the direction of travel.
Over the past year ESS has increased materially, rising from approximately 6.5 to 7.8. EFR has followed a similar trajectory, increasing from 5.8 to 6.9. Trigger pressure has increased only modestly from 3.0 to 3.5.
This pattern is important because it suggests deterioration is occurring primarily within the underlying structural variables rather than through the emergence of a single catalytic event.
Conclusion
Vladimir Putin’s leadership appears to be entering a grey zone of increasing vulnerability. Economic stress is high, elite pressures are rising and discrepancies between official military, economic and social narratives and observable realities continue to widen.
However, Russia has not entered a collapse zone, and the Framework does not imply imminent leadership change. However, it has entered a historically significant leadership-vulnerability zone in which increasing fragility and increasing propensity for risk-taking may coexist.
In plain text, this is a cornered Putin. A Putin who has nothing to offer his people except more of the same except worse: a draining economy; a war longer than the First World War and more murderous than the Soviet war in Afghanistan with no tangible benefits to show for it. ‘Worse’ because the increasing cost of war in economic and human terms cannot be achieved by market means. It will take increasing repression to allocate resources to the task.
And now looms the threat of conscription to continue fighting it. Russia’s losses are running at 1300 – 1,400 per day killed and wounded. Recruitment is hovering around 1000 per day. The policy goal is to recruit 409,000 people in 2026. Conscription would violate Putin’s social contract not to let his ‘Special Operation’ hurt the urban elite. The economic effects of the war are already doing so. But conscription could be a flash point.
It is comforting to think that a leader in this predicament is weakened and therefore enjoys less power. But weakness is likely to make Putin more isolated. His perceptions may become even more divorced from reality. His feeling of insecurity is likely to increase. That would make Putin more unpredictable and dangerous. Dying fish flap hardest!
The temptation for Putin is to extend the war in the form of a step change in Grayzone escalation to Europe in the hope that this will undermine European support for Ukraine but not trigger NATO Article 5 type military action against Russia.
In a nutshell, as the Ukraine war becomes more economically unsustainable and Putin’s regime weakens, this may mark the moment when Putin will escalate his European war out of desperation. Failure of this policy would increase the likelihood that Putin will be replaced. But by what?
A military putsch is unlikely. A popular revolt even less so. And a Kremlin elite coup is as likely to be more extremist than less so. Furthermore, in the background, the threat of nuclear weapons will always be lurking.

Trump signs order to revamp childhood vaccines, against medical groups’ guidance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:59:06 UTC
07:59:06 KST

Trump signs order to revamp childhood vaccines, against medical groups’ guidance
The order advocates separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different single-disease shots
US President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held but discredited theory that childhood vaccines should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
The order advocates separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different single-disease shots and administering all childhood immunisations at separate appointments whenever possible.
It also directs the nation’s health department to improve research on vaccines, which are already extensively studied, and present a plan to offer separate measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines for children, since that is not currently an option in the United States.
The renewed focus on vaccines marks a departure from the Trump administration’s recent efforts to emphasise less controversial health policies related to healthy eating, drug price negotiations and medical fraud crackdowns ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.
Childhood vaccines – and how and when to give them in combination – go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.

Zuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta drops open-source model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:57:57 UTC
07:57:57 KST

Mark Zuckerberg published a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views on artificial intelligence and announced several plans for how Meta would develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-source AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer.
Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled “The Future is for Everyone,” Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian vision of AI as a personalized “superintelligence” – using the word 60 times.
“Some argue that superintelligence itself or a small set of experts who control it should decide what is best for humanity. We disagree,” Zuckerberg wrote.
Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – like the kind Meta develops – and a lack of government regulation of artificial intelligence. Zuckerberg’s stance sets him and Meta apart from industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued that open-source AI is dangerous. The two frontier labs have released proprietary AI products and argued that cutting-edge models should remain tightly controlled by the companies that build them.
Zuckerberg’s post comes as Silicon Valley is engaged in a heated debate over how to regulate AI development, which has involved the creation of a secret White House framework for testing new models and an ongoing debate over whether to restrict the use of Chinese-made open-source AI. As Anthropic and OpenAI have surged ahead in the AI industry, competitors such as Meta have also grown wary of their dominance and sought to position their open models as alternatives.
Zuckerberg framed Meta’s pursuit of open-weight AI as a more democratic version of the technology and one that will create a “balance of power” between users, whether that involves states, companies or individuals. His plans also called for letting users decide what “values” an AI model should have, as opposed to a company encoding it with rigid guardrails and beliefs.
“If the power of superintelligence is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or AI itself, then that will naturally lead to outcomes that are less favorable for everyone else,” Zuckerberg wrote.
Tech leaders have made a cottage industry out of releasing broad, vaguely philosophical treatises on artificial intelligence, which tend to double as marketing materials for their own companies and products. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Palantir’s Alex Karp and the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have all written long manifestos on the virtues and dangers of the technology.
In addition to weighing in on open source models, Zuckerberg also called for accelerating the buildout of AI infrastructure such as datacenters. The massive development of resource-hungry datacenters has become a divisive issue in the US, with rapidly growing public opposition and calls from politicians to issue moratoriums on their construction. Zuckerberg wrote in the essay that Meta would create a fund to invest more in local communities near datacenters, as well as cited an example from Louisiana where some teachers received a $50,000 bonus check as a result of increased sales tax revenue from the company’s infrastructure investment.
On government testing of AI models for cybersecurity risks, a tangible concern after rogue models have hacked outside organizations in recent months, Zuckerberg agreed that companies should share “intermediate training checkpoints and technical staff” but provided few details. He broadly warned that regulation would cause China to overtake the US in the AI race, where he claimed it already has an advantage in terms of building infrastructure.
“Any policy that slows American model releases – even by a month – could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg.
Many of Zuckerberg’s policy plans in his essay lacked detail or reiterated previous claims about the abundant wealth and prosperity that AI would create, such as touting that everyone would have “invention superpowers” to create new businesses. His version of the future also is inherently tied to Meta products, such as the company’s AI-enabled smart glasses.
“Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said. “You’ll be able to interact with your agent through any device, including your glasses to keep you present in the moment with the people you care about.”
On thornier issues such as loss of jobs from AI, autonomous weapons and government surveillance, Zuckerberg mostly brushed them aside. Law enforcement and the military already possess greater intelligence-gathering powers than the average person, Zuckerberg argued, and this would continue with access to AI. Companies may shrink in size due to AI, he conceded, but the technology would create new economic opportunities.
“People will have to adapt, and this will be challenging,” Zuckerberg said about labor disruption from new technology. “But the more that everyone has a personal agent that is superintelligent at teaching us new skills and helping us adapt to change, the smoother this will be.”

Canada joins Ukraine, EU, and Switzerland in sanctioning UAE arms maker whose vehicles equip Russia’s National Guard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:54:52 UTC
07:54:52 KST

Canada has moved against a Gulf company arming Russia. Ottawa has imposed sanctions on Streit Group, a UAE-based weapons manufacturer that supplies military equipment to Russia, Canada's Foreign Ministry announced.
The move closes a gap in an international net that has been years in the making. Ukraine sanctioned Streit Group in 2023, and the EU and Switzerland followed in 2025. Canada's action now aligns with those measures, part of a Western effort that has, since 2014, seen Canada alone sanction more than 3,500 individuals and entities complicit in violating Ukraine's sovereignty.
The company's vehicles are used by Russia's forces
Canada acted on evidence tying the firm to the war. Streit Group is a defense company that produces armored vehicles and other military equipment. Canada imposed the sanctions after receiving credible information that its armored vehicles are used by Russia's National Guard, which takes part in Russia's war against Ukraine, the diplomats announced.
"...Streit Group continues to feed Russia’s war machine and the Putin regime’s unprovoked and unjustifiable war against Ukraine," Canadian Foreign Ministry said.
The sanctions target the supply of military technology
Canada framed the measure as degrading Russia's ability to wage war.
"The sanctions announced today will reduce Russia’s military capabilities in its war against Ukraine," the Canadian Foreign Ministry stressed.
One node in a coordinated campaign
The value of the Canadian action lies in the coordination behind it. By joining Ukraine, the EU, and Switzerland in sanctioning the same company, Canada closes another jurisdiction to Streit Group and signals to other would-be suppliers that arming Russia carries widening consequences.
Sanctions on a single manufacturer rarely stop a determined supplier on their own, but a company sanctioned across four jurisdictions faces shrinking room to operate, banking, and legitimacy. The measure is one strand of the years-long Western effort to make supplying Russia's war costly enough to deter, tightening around the networks that keep Russian forces equipped.

The 28-year-old Carrington played for Stanford for four years before spending her final season of college ball at Baylor.

Trump media company announces a massive loss and new turnaround effort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:53:01 UTC
07:53:01 KST

Trump media company announces a massive loss and new turnaround effort
NEW YORK (AP) — The president’s media company posted a massive loss in the second quarter and announced plans to ditch new business lines and refocus as a forum for users to post their views.
Trump Media & Technology, the company behind the Truth Social platform, said Monday that it lost $238 million in the three months through June as it branched into businesses unrelated to media, including crypto. That was more than 10 times the loss from a year earlier. The per-share loss widened to 86 cents from 8 cents.
In a conference call after the earnings release, the new chief executive, Kevin McGurn, said a yearlong effort to expand by branching into several new industries including online betting and crypto would now be largely abandoned as he refocuses the business on its social media mission.
“We made the disciplined choice to pivot in order to invest more time and resources in our most important initiatives,” McGurn said. “We will say no to things or change course as warranted.”
Trump Media stock fell slightly in after-hours trading following the earnings report. The stock had fallen 8% in regular trading.
Key to McGurn’s plan is a service called Truth API that offers early access to Wall Street trading firms to top posters on the Truth Social platform. That includes the user with most followers, President Donald Trump, who often moves markets by breaking major U.S policy shifts on the site.
Trump Media has been attacked by good government watchdogs from the start of Trump’s second term as a vehicle for him to profit off the presidency. The new service has only heightened those concerns, with Democrats vowing to investigate the paid service if they get control of Congress in the midterms.
McGurn has dismissed such concerns, noting that other companies sell special, fast access to traders.
“Providing licensed real-time public data through commercial APIs is a well-established business practice across the technology, financial information and media industries,” he said. “This is no different.”
One previously announced new venture, nuclear fusion, will continue. McGurn said Trump Media hopes to close a previously announced merger with energy company TAE Technologies by the end of the year.
“We continue to believe it’s the single most important driver of long-term value for this company,” McGurn said of the fusion business.
Much of the damage last quarter was due to unrealized paper losses from the falling values of Trump Media’s holdings of bitcoin and a crypto token called Cronos.
Excluding those paper losses as well as taxes, interest and other items, so-called operating losses still increased, but much less than the unadjusted results — a $164 million loss from a $44 million loss a year earlier.
The new Truth API service is charging $60,000 to $100,000 a month, McGurn said, adding that Trump Media has already signed up 10 customers, mostly so-called high frequency trading firms that buy and sell in milliseconds.
“We’re in the early innings,” said McGurn, noting that the potential market was much bigger than traders, including data center companies, news organizations and developers of large language models.
Ten customers translates into a big new revenue source for Trump Media, possibly bringing in between $7 million to $12 million a year, or roughly two to three times the company’s entire revenue last year.
In the second quarter, Trump Media posted $1.7 million in revenue, more than double from a year earlier.
The company has $1 billion in debt from special convertible notes that don’t come due until 2028, but the lenders have an option to demand they be cashed out in November, a possible hit to finances though the company appeared to have ample cash.
At the end of the quarter, Trump Media had more than $400 million in cash and short term investments. It also had $1.2 billion in bitcoin and bitcoin-related assets.
——
This story corrects that Trump Media took in $1.7 million in revenue last quarter, not $1.7 billion.

The Board of Peace has dropped clauses from the Gaza agreement that explicitly stipulated that Hamas would not possess weapons, sources familiar with the negotiations have told The New York Times. The final agreement commits the organization to "decommission and store" heavy weapons as part of a process to be led by a group of Palestinian technocrats supported by the United States. However, the timetable for handing over weapons and the manner of Israel's withdrawal have not yet been determined.
Additionally, three sources told the newspaper that said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the IDF to stop strikes in the Gaza Strip following pressure exerted on him by the Board of Peace. The following day, Netanyahu met with senior Board of Peace officials, including the board's high representative, Nickolay Mladenov. Since that evening, Israel has not attacked the Strip, according to Mahmoud Basal, a senior official in Gaza civil defense.
At the same time, a senior Board of Peace official told Reuters that talks with Israel are continuing. He said Israel is not being asked to take irreversible steps before "verified actions on the ground" take place. The official added that the plan for the Strip is still operative.
On Sunday, Netanyahu said that "Israel does not accept the 15-point document" of the Board of Peace. At the cabinet meeting the prime minister added that Israel will not withdraw from the Gaza Strip before Hamas is disarmed.
"When I say disarming Hamas, that means heavy weapons, less heavy weapons, all weapons. And we are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," he said. "We are talking with the Americans about this issue. They have ideas, some of them are acceptable to us and some of them are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up against these things."
Netanyahu added that "as long as I am prime minister, a Palestinian state will not be established, either in Gaza or in the West Bank."
Hamas responded to Netanyahu's statement by saying it "adheres to what was agreed with the mediators and the Board of Peace regarding the roadmap." The organization's statement said it is committed to acting seriously and responsibly to implement the agreements included in the 15 clauses and to formulate a timetable for their implementation.
Hamas stressed that at the current stage, priority must be given to ensuring the implementation of the agreement in all its stages and the commitments included in it, in a manner that will lead to a full cease-fire.

The Toto Cup preseason tournament group stage came to an end, with the semifinals now set as Maccabi Netanya hosts Maccabi Tel Aviv and Ironi Kiryat Shmona welcomes Hapoel Tel Aviv this coming Sunday night.

Hapoel Jerusalem finishes group stage with victory
Petah Tikva will face Bnei Sakhnin, while Jerusalem will play Maccabi Haifa in Toto Cup placement games next weekend.
Jerusalem Head Coach Lior Zada spoke about the win: “I felt the exhaustion of the players in the second half, but the final quarter hour was great, and the guys did what they needed to do to win the game. I’m happy that Israel Dappa was able to score, although he had a rough time when he first came in, but he did what he needed to. We have one more game against Maccabi Haifa at Sammy Ofer Stadium, which will be a good test for us ahead of the season.”

Petah Tikva knows how to keep the ball, and I’m happy with how we handled it and that we were able to eventually win. It’s not my first time in Israel, so I’m used to playing, and the club has done everything to make me feel comfortable since I’ve arrived.”
Up north, Maccabi Haifa blanked Bnei Sakhnin 1-0 as Silva Kani put the ball in off Cedric Don’s shot, which had hit the post, to give the Greens the Toto Cup victory.

“This was a better game. It wasn’t great, but it was definitely one that was more aggressive,” Haifa Head Coach Barak Bachar began after the win. “We didn’t concede, and they didn’t create chances as easily as they have in recent games. We’re working and putting the pieces together. We’re trying to establish a core of players who can play together, and we’re working and will continue to work. I saw improvement, and I expect to see further improvement going forward.”
Yossi Abukasis summed up the loss: “We’re playing without a natural striker at all; everyone is a midfielder. The only striker in the squad is suspended after receiving a red card, and we’re waiting for a foreign striker to arrive. Our attacking play isn’t good because we don’t have a natural striker. We haven’t been worse than our opponents in these games.”
Kiryat Shmona clinches Toto Cup semifinal berth

Shai Sabag polished off the victory during second-half injury time as he scored into a wide-open goal to secure the win and a place in the semifinals.
Goal scorer Ariel Sheratzky spoke about the match: “We really wanted to reach the semifinals. We wanted it badly, and we appreciate the situation we’re in. We need to continue working hard so that we can be even more prepared for the league, because that’s the real money time. We’ll try to be as prepared as possible and win the next game, but for now, the entire team looks good and is giving everything, so I’m happy about that.”
Hapoel Haifa Head Coach Haim Silvas summed up the loss.
“First of all, credit goes to Kiryat Shmona, who reached the semifinals after recording four wins. We had an excellent first half, and we gave Kiryat Shmona no chances. But the second half is something that has characterized us somewhat so far. Our response to the penalty wasn’t good enough, and we’ll have to learn from that; it’s an excellent lesson. The fact that we conceded a goal immediately after the penalty is something I don’t like. We got ourselves into trouble with the ball in the second half.”
Maccabi Petah Tikva closes group stage with win
Also, Maccabi Petah Tikva slipped by Hapoel Ramat Gan 2-1 in the final game of the Toto Cup group stage. After a goalless first half, Samuel Owusu scored a screamer off the bar to give Petah Tikva the lead, while Liran Hazan doubled the advantage when he headed home the ball in the 74th minute.
Amit scored soon thereafter to cut the lead, but that’s as close as Ramat Gan would get as Ziv Arie’s team wrapped up the win. Petah Tikva will now visit Ironi Tiberias, while Ramat Gan will host Beitar Jerusalem in placement games next week.

Return of Syrian Kurds to Ras al-Ain suspended after violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:49:27 UTC
07:49:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Return of displaced Syrian Kurds to Ras al-Ain suspended after violence
The return of displaced Syrian Kurds to their northeastern hometown of Ras al-Ain was suspended on Monday after a first group of returnees was attacked, a local security official said.
Hundreds of people had gone back to the town on Monday, months after a January agreement with the Syrian government on merging Kurdish forces and civil institutions into the state that included provisions for the return of displaced Kurds.
Jawan Isso, from a committee representing displaced people from Ras al-Ain, told AFP that a "first batch" of around 2,500 people were headed home but were later attacked by "armed groups".
Mahmud Khalil Ali, deputy head of security forces in Syria's Hasakeh province, said several of those involved in the attacks were arrested, but return trips were "temporarily suspended as a precautionary measure to ensure the safety of residents".
"These trips will resume as soon as the situation stabilises and full protection is provided for the returnees."
A second batch of Kurds was supposed to head to the town in the coming days, according to Isso.
Tens of thousands of Kurds were uprooted when Turkey and allied Syrian fighters seized an Arab-majority strip of territory along the Turkish border, including Ras al-Ain, from Kurdish control in 2019 during Syria's civil war.
The attacks on Monday sparked a demonstration in nearby Kurdish-majority Qamishli, where an AFP correspondent saw angry protesters try to break into the security forces' headquarters, with Syrian officers pushing them back.
"We condemn the assault to which the displaced Kurdish families were subjected during their return," Mazloum Abdi, leader of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces who signed the January deal with Damascus, said on X.
"We understand the angry reactions in the Kurdish street in response to this assault, and at the same time, we call on our people to exercise self-restraint, refrain from being drawn into any irresponsible acts, and preserve our civil and security institutions," he added.
Abdi said he was working with the relevant authorities "to ensure the protection of the returning displaced civilians".
'Waiting for this moment'
Earlier in the day, an AFP correspondent saw dozens of trucks loaded with furniture and other belongings waiting to set off from near the city of Hasakeh, with men, women and children eager to depart.
"I've been waiting for this moment... It's like a dream for a person to return to their home," said returnee Nora Khodor, 37.
Isso said that around 100,000 people from the Ras al-Ain area had applied to return.
Human rights groups say residents' homes and belongings there were seized or looted after the offensive.
Some of the fighters subsequently settled in the area with their families, with some reportedly still living in the formerly ethnically-mixed region, known as Sari Kani in Kurdish.
Turkey launched successive cross-border offensives against Kurdish-led forces in the country's north before Syrian rebels ousted longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Since then, Syria's new authorities have been extending central government control across the country, including formerly Kurdish-held areas.
"We are very happy about returning," said Rawda Mohammed, 39, before the violence erupted.
"I asked about my home. They told me it is totally destroyed, but we did not get pessimistic because we're happy to return, and when we get there we'll see what we can do."
Some 5.5 million people remain internally displaced in Syria following the more than 13-year civil war, according to the United Nations.
