Speedboat operator charged after mom and baby die following boat capsizing in New York Harbor
Twelve other individuals were rescued and remain in stable condition
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A speedboat operator has been charged in federal court with misconduct and neglect after a vessel capsized near the Statue of Liberty, killing a 27-year-old mother and her infant daughter.
Manuel Hernandez, 46, of Manville, New Jersey, wiped away tears during his initial appearance in Manhattan federal court on Monday, where he appeared in ankle shackles. He was released on $50,000 bail without entering a plea.
Sara Sanchez and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, died after the 22-foot Yamaha AR210 speedboat overturned in New York Harbor late Saturday.
Authorities attributed the disaster to an overcrowded boat, improper decision-making by Hernandez, a lack of required commercial licenses, and the failure to secure a life jacket on the infant. Twelve other individuals were rescued and remain in stable condition.
Following the hearing, court-appointed attorney Amy Gallicchio guided Hernandez to a waiting vehicle, with both declining to offer comment.
The vessel was retrieved from the water and transported to the New York Police Department’s harbor unit facility on Randall’s Island.
Although state charges were initially lodged over the weekend, prosecutors announced Monday that Hernandez will face trial in federal court. He was transferred into federal custody on Sunday.
A federal criminal complaint levels two charges against Hernandez, alleging that as the operator, his negligent actions and omissions led to the capsizing and fatalities. Prosecutors noted the boat carried 14 people, exceeding its maximum limit of 10.
Officials further stated that he knowingly operated the boat with an infant aboard despite being aware that no infant- or child-sized life jackets were present.
The evening charter began at 7 p.m. Saturday and was more than three hours underway when Hernandez steered the boat toward the Statue of Liberty and executed a U-turn into a swell, likely created by the wake of a larger passing vessel, according to court documents.
In an attempt to maneuver past the swell, Hernandez accelerated, causing water to swamp the bow and immediately capsize the vessel, prosecutors wrote.
Hernandez informed investigators that he had worked for the charter firm on a freelance or contract basis since last year, starting out as a limousine driver.
He acknowledged using his personal boat, a slightly larger Yamaha AR250, twice recently for tours organized through Zeus Luxury Rentals Inc., according to the filing.
On Saturday, however, he borrowed a friend’s boat because his own was undergoing repairs, omitting to tell the owner that he intended to use it for a commercial tour, court records state.
Hernandez admitted to investigators that he had never obtained the required licensing, claiming he was unaware it was needed.
He also acknowledged proceeding with the excursion involving the 5-month-old infant despite knowing the vessel lacked child-sized life vests.
Police Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch said the "tragedy could have been prevented, and now a family is left to grieve the unimaginable loss of a mother and her 5-month-old daughter because of his negligence."
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald stated in a press release that Hernandez disregarded federal regulations and maritime safety standards by carrying paying passengers on a commercial trip without the necessary licenses.
"We mourn the tragic drowning deaths of the infant and her mother and urge would-be tour operators and the public to observe all safety protocols for commercial vessels," he added.
Capt. Doreen McCarthy, the Coast Guard Sector New York commander, credited the rescue of the surviving passengers to "heroic, swift actions" by multi-agency responders and a good Samaritan vessel.
Meanwhile, an online fundraiser established Sunday to help partner Andres Garcia pay for funeral and living costs for Sanchez and their daughter had surpassed $25,000 by Tuesday afternoon.
Garcia was also aboard the vessel when it overturned.
Antonio Russo, general manager at Il Punto Ristorante, called Garcia an "amazing guy" who worked extensive hours weekly as a driver, waiter, and food-runner to support his family in New York and Colombia.
Diego Naranjo, a Queens neighbor of Sanchez, recalled first meeting her last spring when her young son accidentally threw a ball into his yard, leading to an invitation for him to play on a trampoline with Naranjo's children.
"They were really nice people. You can see when a person is noble," Naranjo said, adding that he was deeply shocked after having just seen Sanchez bringing groceries home last Tuesday.

Trump mocked over apparent zone-out during Oval Office vaccine announcement

- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
President Donald Trump appeared to zone out during an Oval Office announcement on vaccines, prompting a fresh round of mockery online.
On Monday, Trump signed an executive order that calls for reducing the number of vaccines recommended for children and splitting the MMR shot — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — into three individual vaccines.
The order is the latest step in the administration’s campaign to remake the childhood vaccination schedule, led by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long questioned vaccine safety.
During the ceremony, the 80-year-old president appeared to repeatedly close his eyes while seated behind the Resolute Desk — including as Kennedy and National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya spoke beside him.
Videos of the moments quickly circulated on social media.
“I love how he pops out of it for a few seconds then closes his eyes again and he's right back in dream land. This is getting ridiculous,” wrote one X user. Another chimed in: “Why doesn't the assembled media speak out about this...they all see it.”
“What a loser,” a third user wrote. “After years of listening to those ‘sleepy joe’ comments…” The remark referred to Trump’s longtime nickname for former President Joe Biden, whom he repeatedly accused of being mentally and physically unfit for office.
Some commenters, however, were more supportive of the president. “In Trump's defense, good Lord, the speaker is boring,” one wrote.
The White House defended Trump, saying: “President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people. President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible President in American history who is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises.”
Trump, the oldest person ever inaugurated as president, has faced persistent scrutiny over his health since returning to the White House, including over moments during official events in which he has appeared to close his eyes for extended periods. One such moment came during Lindsey Graham’s funeral last month.
“The president has severe daytime somnolence,” CNN medical analyst Dr. Jonathan Reiner said in May. “He falls asleep very often. He’s fallen asleep in the Oval Office on multiple occasions with people talking to him, in the cabinet room,” he said. “And chronic insomnia is a severe illness. It can result in an increase in risk of dementia, a decrease in cognitive effects in older people.”
Trump, for his part, has repeatedly insisted that he is in excellent health. After a physical at Walter Reed in May, the president wrote on Truth Social that “everything” had “checked out PERFECTLY.”
In a YouGov survey conducted last year, 78 percent of respondents said they believed Trump had not been transparent about his physical health.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Burnham to give councils more powers to block vape and betting shops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Councils are to be given powers to stop betting and vape shops taking over their high streets under new plans announced by Andy Burnham.
Local authorities will be able to reject new betting shops and adult gaming centres, while vape shops will be subject to planning permission under plans Downing Street said could be in place from the start of next year.
Burnham is promising to scrap the “aim to permit” rule in the Gambling Act 2005, which in effect requires councils to allow new gambling premises where applications meet licensing requirements.
This could mark a big shift from changes introduced by Keir Starmer in April that gave councils more scope to consider the number of gambling premises already in an area but stopped short of scrapping the “aim to permit rule”.
As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called on Starmer to abolish the rule in January, alongside almost 300 other politicians and campaigners.
Burnham said communities should have much more control over their high streets, where traditional shops, pubs and other services have disappeared while vape and gambling shops have expanded.
Burnham is attempting to make the first weeks of his prime ministership about tangible changes people can see in their everyday lives.
A No 10 source said the government was determined to crack down on vape and betting shops because they were two of the most visible signs of decline on high streets, and local people were genuinely concerned. A fast-tracked consultation on the new measures would take six weeks, with the aim of having the measures in place by the start of 2027.
“Local people will actually have more of an input into whether or not those shops should open in the first place, giving them a proper say about how their high streets should look,” they said.
The move comes after research suggested Labour would be “washed away in a tide of discontent” at the next general election unless it tackled the decline of Britain’s high streets.
Prof Will Jennings, who led the University of Southampton research, said Burnham’s targeting of vape and betting shops was “an important first step”. With nearly one in three retail sales in the UK now online, it was clear that the policy would “not solve everything”, he said. “But it is speaking to some real area of concern that impacts how people view their local area.”
Vape shops currently fall into the same planning category as shops, cafes and banks, meaning they can open without needing a new planning application. Ministers will consult on putting them into their own planning category so councils will be able to consider each new vape shop application individually and reject those they deem not appropriate for the area.
The government is also looking at tightening the definition of what a vape shop is, to prevent people saying they were opening a convenience store that had the primary function of selling vapes. It will also make provisions to stop them opening near schools. Angela Rayner said the move addressed problems that had built up over decades. “That’s why we’re giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn’t belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves,” the communities secretary said.
Jennings said the government also needed to tackle opaque ownership structures of high street property, which allows some landowners “who aren’t necessarily that motivated to have shops in their property”.
The growth of vape shops is not evenly spread. Research from Health Equity North found that the most deprived communities had three times as many as the most affluent areas.
Burnham said high streets had become “unrecognisable” after decades of decline. “The rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services and community spaces that people are crying out for.
“That’s not on. I said we would improve Britain’s high streets, and that’s exactly what we are starting to do.”
The measures are seen as a “first step” on a wider beautification of Britain’s high streets, with Westminster setting clearer expectations for the design and appearance of high street shopfronts.
Local leaders will be encouraged to look at blueprints for ideal high streets, and given examples of what works best and how they can improve the look of their own main shopping areas.
Dawn Butler, the MP for Brent East, who has campaigned on the issue, said: “It was a real shock to me to discover, during a previous visit to a high street with the Guardian, just how much money gambling machines can generate.
“Government analysis of Gambling Commission data found that B3 machines generated an average of £35,000 in gross gambling yield per machine each year. That figure really brought home to me the scale of the gambling industry’s presence on our high streets and why they would want multiple shops on the high street to maximise their profits.
“To put it in perspective, the national living wage for someone aged 21 or over works out at around £26,400 a year for someone working 40 hours a week. And in Brent the average wage is less than £35k. That experience underlined for me why urgent action was needed.”

Crackdown on vape shops and bookies as Burnham gives councils power to choose what is on their high streets
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

Crackdown on vape shops and bookies as Burnham gives councils power to choose what is on their high streets
New prime minister Burnham to tackle Britain’s ‘hollowed-out high streets’ by scrapping Blair’s Aim to Permit directive
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Councils will be given greater powers to block betting shops and vape stores under government plans to revitalise Britain’s "hollowed-out high streets".
Andy Burnham plans to abolish the so-called "aim to permit" rule, first introduced by Sir Tony Blair, which limits the ability of town halls to refuse licences to gambling premises and venues with round-the-clock slot machines.
Vape shops will also face tighter controls, with new stores required to see planning approval from next year. The legal definition of a vape store will also be tightened to prevent retailers trying to bypass regulations by describing themselves as a "convenience store”.
Similarly, centres which operate 24-hour slot and fruit machines will also require planning consent under the changes.
The measures are part of a package designed to halt the decline of Britain’s high streets - and even make them look better. New expectations on the design of shop fronts will tackle “garish neon signs” and oversized logos, while there will be “practical guidance” for councils on how to make towns more attractive.
Police will be able to shut “dodgy” barbers, vape shops and nail salons for twice as long - up to a year - to allow officers more time to investigate links to organised crime, under proposals first announced by Sir Keir Starmer’s government.
Mr Burnham said the changes would help put local communities “back in control” and bring town centres back to life.
He said: “For many people, the high streets they grew up with have been hollowed out and become unrecognisable over decades of decline.
“The rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for.
“That’s not on. I said we would improve Britain’s high streets, and that’s exactly what we are starting to do.”
He added: “High streets are the beating heart of local communities, but for too long Westminster has stood by while they have been in decline. This government is committed to restoring our high streets and bringing back hope across Britain.”
The “aim to permit” policy was introduced when the Blair government, in which Mr Burnham was a minister, liberalised gambling laws in 2005.
The prime minister, who has returned from a holiday a little over a fortnight into the job, will spend much of August travelling the UK asking people how the government can improve their lives.
He will have a focus on reviving high streets and tackling the cost of living, while officials say he will be in “listening mode”.
The Centre for Social Justice think tank, which has found that Britain has lost nearly 1,800 pubs and bars while vape and tobacco shops have increased in number to almost 2,200 since 2016, welcomed the plans.
Joshua Nicholson, head of housing and communities at the think tank, said: “The government is right to give councils new powers to say no to these dodgy shops. High street renewal is vital to restoring security within our communities.”
But Sir James Cleverly, the shadow local government secretary, said: “Everyone can see what has happened to our high streets, with once-treasured shops being replaced by a smattering of rogue operators, many of which have links to organised crime and fraud.
“Labour’s business rates hikes have hollowed out our high streets, driving out the shops people want and leaving empty units for whoever is left standing to fill. Conservatives would cut business rates for high street firms and back the small businesses that give a town centre its character.
“Unless the government takes steps to support the high streets and hard-working businesses, Labour’s increases in planning regulation will just mean more empty and boarded up shops.”

Europe braces for another heatwave after record-breaking temperatures

Europe braces for another heatwave after record-breaking temperatures
Extreme heat warnings issued in Britain and France with temperatures forecast to reach mid-30s Celsius this week.
Many parts of Europe are bracing for another heatwave after record-breaking temperatures in June and July sparked wildfires, dried out rivers and contributed to thousands of deaths.
Parts of Britain and France on Monday were already under extreme heat warnings with forecasts of temperatures around the mid-30 degrees Celsius (mid-90 degrees Fahrenheit).
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3As Spain grieves, recurrent heatwaves stir fears of further wildfires
- list 2 of 3Central Europe sees record temperatures as heatwave continues
- list 3 of 3June and July hottest on record in Western Europe, monitor says
“We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment,” said the British Environment Agency’s Director of Sustainable Business and Development Tony Grayling.
The British government has imposed irrigation restrictions on farmers and introduced a hosepipe ban in some regions, with more than 27 million people living under water-use restrictions as Britain prepares for its fifth consecutive heatwave this year.
Meanwhile in France, water-use restrictions have been applied on 70 percent of the country as drought conditions worsen amid successive heatwaves, the government said Monday.
Restrictions apply to activities such as watering gardens and green spaces, filling swimming pools, washing cars and irrigating crops.
Spain’s national weather agency AEMET said on Monday Spain recorded the joint-hottest July since records began in 1961, after scorching temperatures fuelled the country’s biggest wildfire in recent history.
Last month was also mainland Spain’s driest July on record as 4.3 millimetres of rain fell, which represented just 26 percent of the normal precipitation for the time of year.
The parched conditions are fuelling wildfires in Greece and Spain, including in Andalusia where firefighters are struggling to put out blazes.
Andalusia’s emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, told reporters that extinguishing fires around the medieval town of Niebla was akin to a “long-distance obstacle race” and was expected to last several days.
Sanz said nearly 500 people have been evacuated from the area.
Meanwhile, the BDB association, an inland shipping group, warned that vessels will soon not be able to navigate parts of the Rhine river in Germany as water levels drop further due to soaring summer temperatures and low rainfall.
“With water levels this low, commercial shipping will no longer be able to transport goods in the region,” the group’s managing director Jens Schwanen told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
“In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer continuously navigable and thus divided in two.”
Europe is the fastest-warming continent on the planet due to climate change.Soaring temperatures are also forecast in Switzerland, Austria and Hungary.

WHO warns it is ‘chasing’ Ebola as death toll surpasses 1,900: ‘The virus is ahead of us’
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:24:42 BST
06:24:42 KST

WHO warns it is ‘chasing’ Ebola as death toll surpasses 1,900: ‘The virus is ahead of us’
Confirmed cases of Ebola in this outbreak have reached 4,200, including over 1,900 deaths, according to the latest government figures
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The most rapidly spreading Ebola outbreak ever recorded actually began in February, several months prior to its official declaration in mid-May, according to the World Health Organization, as responders in eastern Congo attempt to catch up.
Confirmed cases of Ebola during this outbreak have now reached 4,200, resulting in more than 1,900 deaths, according to recent government figures.
Speaking at a news conference, the WHO regional director for Africa Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi explained that genetic sequencing revealed the earlier start.
He noted that initial cases were mistakenly diagnosed as other illnesses, including malaria and typhoid.
"So we are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," Janabi said.
Dr Thierno Balde, WHO's incident manager for the Ebola response, stated that the genetic sequencing was carried out under the leadership of Dr Steve Ahuka, head of the virology department at Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research.
The WHO assesses the worldwide risk of spread as low because Ebola is not airborne, making it far harder to transmit than respiratory viruses.
Cases identified outside the affected region have so far been promptly caught and contained without causing sustained transmission, the agency said.
The outbreak declared on May 15 is unlike most previous ones for Ebola because the rare Bundibugyo virus responsible for it has no approved vaccines or treatments. Early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola, contributing to delays.
The outbreak is unfolding in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, with strikes by some unpaid health workers, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatized communities and misinformation asserting that Ebola isn’t real. Health teams travel remote, unpaved roads and have reported shortages of protective gear, while a vast population of displaced people struggles to find reliable water sources for washing hands.
This Ebola outbreak has killed more people at a quicker rate than any other, including the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa that is considered the worst on record with over 11,000 deaths out of at least 28,000 cases. That one took about eight months to reach 1,000 deaths.
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Last week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesu said Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to fight it. New cases are doubling in some hot spots, Tedros said on X after meeting with officials in the capital, Kinshasa.
Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside of contacts being monitored, and that the outbreak is spreading at an “alarming” rate.
Access to healthcare in the region already had been challenged by years of rebel conflict in one of Congo’s most remote and vulnerable areas, near the borders of South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda. Now some pregnant women and others are avoiding health centers for fear of the virus, at risk to their lives.
Several past Ebola outbreaks have also been declared weeks or months late, including the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. That outbreak was declared in March 2014, although the first human case later was found to have occurred in December 2013.

Russia’s playbook for taking Ukrainian cities needs more troops than Russia has
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:24:22 UTC
06:24:22 KST

- Russian forces use the same strategy over and over to capture Ukrainian cities
- Surround on the flanks, infiltrate in the middle
- But that strategy requires doing both at once, and Russia lacks the infantry
- Around Kramatorsk, every Ukrainian unit that holds forces a shuffle that stalls something else
Russian troops are slowly marching toward and around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, the last two big free cities in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast.
The Russians have a standard playbook for taking a Ukrainian city, and running it means doing two things at the same time. Along the nearly 100-km Kramatorsk front, they don't have the infantry to do both at once. Every time a Ukrainian brigade holds somewhere, the Russians have to move men to cover it—and something stalls somewhere else.
That strategy is simple in concept but difficult in practice. The idea is for Russian forces to advance along a city's under-protected flanks in order to put pressure on the main supply lines of the city's garrison. As the flank attacks squeeze the garrison's logistics, Russian infiltrators slip into the city, hoping to create a lodgement for follow-on forces.
The final assault through that lodgement comes late in the campaign, after the Ukrainians are already weakened by a lack of supplies.
The strategy only works when the troops on the flanks and those in the middle work together. The former squeezes. The latter infiltrates. The problem for the Russian Center Group of Forces on the Kramatorsk front is that it's not squeezing and infiltrating at the same time. That delays the overall Russian advance and buys time for Ukrainian forces to dig in, reinforce, and hope for a miracle.
"Russian offensive planning at the operational level remains disciplined," mapper and analyst Vitaly explained. But only "on paper," Vitaly added. "Groupings are sequenced, axes are assigned, objectives are staggered."
"What the discipline is not is well-manned," the mapper wrote.
Vitaly reads one recent Russian adaptation as evidence of the shortfall rather than of cleverness. "I read the shift to two- and three-man infiltration teams on motorcycles and ATVs as less a sign of tactical innovation than of a manpower deficit that organization is straining to hide," he wrote.
Manpower shortages
Ukraine's manpower problems are well-known. Fewer observers appreciate that Russia struggles, too. Yes, the Russians still recruit around 30,000 fresh troops every month. In theory, that's enough new manpower to replace monthly losses.
But replacing casualties is not the same as resourcing a strategy. Ukraine's commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi put the Russian force in Ukraine at 721,300 at the end of June—a gain of only around 11,000 since late 2025, against Russian losses he estimated at 30,000 to 35,000 a month. Contract recruitment collapsed in the spring, falling by a third year on year, and Ukraine's foreign intelligence service counted 195,000 contract recruits by early July against an annual target of 409,000.
A Russian general, speaking anonymously to the investigative outlet IStories, put the requirement more starkly. To capture the rest of the Ukrainian-held Donbas, he said Russia would need to replace at least 55,000 to 60,000 casualties every month—roughly double what it recruits. That figure rests on a single unnamed source and should be weighed accordingly. But it describes the same gap Vitaly sees on the map.
When a Ukrainian brigade defeats one attack anywhere along the Kramatorsk front, it may compel Russian regiments to shuffle troops between units in order to quickly replace the losses. The shuffle may sap the combat power of a flanking or infiltration unit working along some other section of the front.
Trending Now
A weak flanking unit may not be able to keep up the pressure on enemy supply lines, perhaps imperiling the adjacent infiltration unit as it probes for the gaps in Ukrainian defenses that the flankers were supposed to help create. By the same token, weak infiltrators may find gaps in Ukrainian defenses, but fail to secure a lodgement—effectively wasting the efforts of the adjacent flankers.
Russia is assaulting the gateway to Sloviansk. Ukraine’s 81st Brigade is holding it nearly alone
"That gap keeps producing the same effect," Vitaly explained. The Ukrainian armed forces' "ability to hold separate sections of the front independently forces Russian formations to compensate for each other's failures, and that compensation creates new stalls."
Vitaly gave a name to the effect, and was careful about what he was not claiming. "I call it structural deterrence—not deterrence in the conventional sense, and not a doctrine, but the byproduct of asking an undermanned army to keep a sequenced plan on schedule."
A byproduct is not a defense, and it holds only as long as the Ukrainians can keep producing it. That requires synchronization of their own. Supplies and reinforcements must arrive when and where they're most badly needed. Air and artillery support should shift from sector to sector depending on the urgency of the local garrisons' needs.
All that is to say, the lack of synchronization that has slowed the Russians' march on Kramatorsk could eventually speed up the Russians' march—if and when the Ukrainians are the ones struggling to synchronize.
It's worth noting that the Russians aren't advancing fast toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, but they are advancing—especially from the northeast.
The Russians may not be perfectly synchronized. But they're clearly synchronized enough to grind toward the last free cities in Donetsk. Just very, very slowly.

The Fed didn't respond to a request for comment.

Otherwise, Trump has put extreme pressure on the Fed. Last week, he revived an effort to fire Governor Lisa Cook, who is serving a 14-year term on the Fed's Board. It wasn't clear if the Trump-Warsh conversation came before or after that call.
Trump has said Warsh should lower interest rates while insisting that the Fed chairman has the latitude to do otherwise.
"If it was up to him, it would be different, but he's got a board," Trump said Monday.
"But they made it sound like I live and breathe — you know, I speak to Kevin all the time, every time. I spoke to him one time," Trump said.
Congress gave the Fed the power to set interest rates independently of political considerations. In the 1970s, a too-close relationship between Fed Chairman Arthur Burns and President Richard Nixon preceded a sharp bout of inflation.
Warsh's calendar for June showed that he met three times with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, continuing a longstanding custom of the two officials meeting regularly for breakfast.

Indian billionaire Gautam Adani has fraud and bribery charges dropped by US judge
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:22:25 BST
06:22:25 KST

Indian billionaire Gautam Adani has fraud and bribery charges dropped by US judge
The Adani Group has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Criminal fraud and bribery charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani were dismissed by a U.S. judge on Monday, following a decision by the Justice Department to drop the prosecution.
Brooklyn-based U.S. District Judge Nicholas Garaufis granted the rare request by federal prosecutors after questioning the reasoning behind the move, which included directly asking Adani if any promises were made in return for tossing out the case.
In November 2024, before the unsealing of the indictment, Adani committed to investing $10 billion in the United States.
The charges brought in 2024 alleged that Adani agreed to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of the Adani Group could secure approval to build a solar energy plant.
Prosecutors contended that he subsequently misled U.S. investors by offering false assurances about the company's anti-corruption policies.
The Adani Group has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. Adani has not appeared in a U.S. court to answer the charges.
The Justice Department announced on May 18 that it would no longer pursue the matter.
The decision represents the latest instance of federal prosecutors seeking to drop a high-profile white-collar prosecution during Republican President Donald Trump's second term in office.
Legal experts note that U.S. judges have little authority to force prosecutors to continue criminal cases they prefer to abandon, though charges cannot be formally dismissed without a judge's sign-off.
Garaufis had asked the Justice Department to justify dropping the case, writing that its initial "bland and conclusory" announcement provided insufficient detail.
In a court filing on July 4, Trent McCotter, a senior Justice Department official, explained that the matter was primarily foreign, difficult to prove, and misaligned with the agency's current priorities.
McCotter also refuted media reports as false after they suggested he sought to throw out the case partly due to Adani's commitment to invest funds within the United States.
In response, Garaufis asked Adani directly whether he was "aware of any agreement exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment."
In a sworn declaration submitted on July 15, Adani stated that he was not aware of any such arrangement.
He recognized his prior pledge to invest $10 billion in the U.S. and noted his lawyers had told the Justice Department during meetings that the commitment "might be part of a resolution of these matters."
Robert Giuffra, an attorney representing Adani, stated in a court filing on July 15 that the Justice Department informed him it would not consider the Adani Group's willingness to invest in the U.S. as part of any resolution.

One in six Russian diplomats in Austria may be tied to intelligence agencies, RuPEP data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:20:06 UTC
06:20:06 KST

At least 20 of the 117 employees of Russian diplomatic missions in Austria are likely tied to the SVR, GRU, or FSB, according to a report by the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo, which made use of information from the RuPEP public figures database and the foreign diplomatic staff list published by Austria’s Foreign Ministry.
The count covers only the officially published staff of the Russian Embassy and Russian missions to international organizations. Administrative and technical staff were not included. Some of the identified links are confirmed by previous places of service or employment, while others are based on registered addresses, information about relatives, and other indirect indicators.
Of the 48 employees of the Russian Embassy, at least eight showed signs of links to intelligence agencies. Counselor Evgenii Ambrosii is registered at an SVR departmental building on Vilniusskaya Street in Moscow. Attaché Aleksandr Sobolev received income from military unit 21247, which corresponds to the Foreign Intelligence Academy. Alexander Paloyan received income from SVR military unit 33949.
First Secretary Alexander Golovashkin, military attaché Alexey Fokin, and attaché Stanislav Aleksandridi are linked to GRU addresses and units (Aleksandridi listed the military intelligence headquarters on Khoroshevskoye Highway in Moscow, while Fokin was registered on the grounds of the Senezh Special Purpose Center). Attaché Dmitrii Kramarev worked in the 2000s at the Atlas Scientific and Technical Center, which at the time was under the FSB.
Ambrosii and Golovashkin had already appeared in The Insider’s previous investigation into Russian intelligence activity in Austria. Ambrosii supervised the SVR’s Vienna station on the political intelligence track, while Golovashkin served at the GRU’s Moscow Intelligence Center before arriving in Vienna. In March 2024, a source in Austria’s Foreign Ministry told The Insider that both had been added to the list of personae non gratae. The Insider found that they still appear among embassy staff in the Austrian Foreign Ministry directory updated in August 2026.
Of the 22 employees of Russia’s mission to the OSCE, links to intelligence agencies are suspected in seven cases. Four figures — Counselors Anton Momatyuk and Vitaly Kozlov, First Secretary Sergei Kildyashov, and Second Secretary Alexei Silantyev — used addresses of facilities linked to the GRU and military education. Three other employees previously worked at Defense Ministry institutions or listed addresses belonging to the General Staff, military academies, and military units.
Among 47 employees of Russian missions to other international organizations, signs of links to intelligence agencies were found in five cases. Three of them work at the IAEA. In particular, Sergei Berezin was registered on the grounds of the GRU’s Central Special Communications Hub, while Grigory Krivenchenko received income from military unit 52025, a nuclear weapons arsenal in Mozhaysk. Two other diplomats with possible links to military intelligence represent Russia at U.N. institutions.
Vienna remains one of the most important centers of Russian intelligence activity in Europe. The Financial Times previously reported that Russian diplomatic facilities in the city have become Moscow’s largest signals intelligence platform in the West. According to Austria’s intelligence service, Russian diplomatic missions in Vienna employ around 500 individuals when staff members (who are not included in public lists) are counted. Up to one-third of these nominally lower-level figures may also be involved in espionage.
In May 2026, Austria expelled three Russian diplomats, accusing them of intelligence activity. Austrian authorities did not disclose their names.

Ukraine’s new AI platform trains weapons on five million frames of drone footage. Partner countries can use it too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:16:56 UTC
06:16:56 KST

Ukraine is turning millions of hours of battlefield footage into fuel for its defense industry's AI. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has announced that it has opened Avengers Labs, a platform for training artificial intelligence models, to Ukrainian defense companies.
The platform is a new piece of the defense-tech ecosystem Ukraine has built around its war. Alongside the Brave1 cluster that funds and codifies weapons and the Test in Ukraine framework that trials them in combat, Avengers Labs supplies the raw material for AI, a vast, curated dataset of Russian military targets that a single private company could never assemble on its own.
The data comes from the battlefield
Avengers Labs was developed by the Center for Innovation and Development of Defense Technologies, the team behind the DELTA battle-management system, and most of its data comes from DELTA and is constantly expanded.
The dataset captures the enemy in detail. It contains images of tanks, artillery, air-defense systems, infantry, and aerial targets, including Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, a labeled library of what Russian forces look like from a drone's camera. According to the ministry, the system can significantly speed up the development of AI solutions for unmanned systems.
The AI already works in combat
A system trained on Avengers data is already in the field, analyzing over 100,000 drone video streams a month and detecting about 70% of enemy targets in real time, day and night.
The models enable more autonomous drones. Trained on Avengers data, they support automatic trajectory correction after an operator marks a target, and independent target detection by a drone in a defined area according to set mission logic, steps toward drones that find and strike targets with less human input, according to the ministry.
Partner-country firms can join too
Access extends beyond Ukraine, under vetting. The first Ukrainian defense companies have signed licensing agreements to use Avengers Labs, and companies from Ukraine's partner countries can also join, per the ministry.
The screening guards against leakage to the enemy. To gain access, companies must pass checks confirming no ties to the aggressor state, no business in Russia, no sanctions, and no activity in occupied territories.

Trump administration reaches secret deals with Syria and Israel to remove nuclear materials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:16:15 UTC
06:16:15 KST

ALBAWABA- The administration of US President Donald Trump has reached secret understandings with the Syrian government and Israel to remove nuclear materials stored at a covert site in Syria, according to US and Israeli officials cited by Al-Arabiya, which reported on an investigation by Axios.
The operation is being coordinated with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and is intended to secure the materials and prevent a potential confrontation between Israel and Syria. US officials said the arrangement reflects Washington’s close working relationship with Syria’s new government and its efforts to contain security risks stemming from the country’s former nuclear program.
The materials are linked to the nuclear program developed under former President Bashar al-Assad, which centred on the clandestine Al-Kibar reactor. Israel destroyed the reactor in a 2007 airstrike, but several associated research, development and storage facilities remained, most of them inactive.
Following the fall of the Assad government, the IAEA reached an agreement with Syria’s new authorities allowing inspectors to visit Al-Kibar and other sites associated with the former nuclear program. One such location, referred to as “the site,” has reportedly been under Israeli surveillance for about two years.
According to US officials, materials stored there include yellowcake, a uranium-processing product, as well as residues and other material left over from the Al-Kibar project. Although the material is not considered suitable for producing a nuclear weapon, US officials said it could potentially be used in a radiological “dirty bomb.”
Israeli forces reportedly bombed the entrances to the site shortly after the Assad government fell, seeking to prevent access to the materials. For more than a year, US and Israeli officials discussed how the materials could be secured and removed. Israel reportedly warned Washington that it would strike the site again if the materials were not removed or if Syria attempted to access them.
The issue became more urgent several weeks ago after Israeli surveillance detected activity near the site that raised concerns that Syrian authorities might be attempting to gain access to the materials. Israeli officials also reportedly suspected that Turkey could be assisting Syria in accessing the site.
Washington urged Israel not to launch another strike and instead brought the IAEA into the effort. The talks resulted in an agreement signed about three weeks ago between the IAEA and the Syrian government to remove the nuclear materials.
The removal process, however, has not yet been completed. US officials said the materials remain at the site while arrangements between Syria and the IAEA are finalized. Washington and Israel continue to monitor the situation. US officials said the parties are satisfied with the agreement and hope the transfer will begin soon and be completed before the end of 2026.

Russian investigators said they had opened a criminal case into what they described as a terrorist attack, alleging that Ukraine had struck residential areas and that a child was among the dead.
Tatarstan declared a day of mourning. Additional medical teams were deployed to Nizhnekamsk from the nearby city of Naberezhnye Chelny.
The independent Russian outlet Astra conducted an open source intelligence (OSINT) analysis of one of the published videos and concluded that the Nizhnekamskneftekhim plant was likely attacked. The site of the strike had not been officially confirmed at the time Astra released its analysis.

The General Staff also clarified the results of previous attacks. It said an AVT-6 crude distillation unit was damaged at the Ilsky refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Region on Aug. 8, while on Aug. 3 nine aviation fuel tanks were destroyed and two aircraft hangars damaged at the Hvardiiske airfield in annexed Crimea.
Last night’s attack extended beyond Tatarstan. Russia’s Defense Ministry said 456 drones were intercepted over 16 Russian regions and annexed Crimea. The ministry did not say how many drones were intercepted over Tatarstan itself.
Ukraine has intensified strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent months, contributing to severe fuel shortages across many parts of Russia and Russian-occupied Ukraine, though authorities claim that most early disruptions have been resolved.
Kyiv says the campaign is intended to make ordinary Russians feel the cost of Moscow’s war. Russia has turned to fuel imports from countries like Belarus and South Korea to shore up supplies.
Nizhnekamskneftekhim, one of Europe’s largest petrochemical plants, is part of the Sibur holding company. It produces rubber, plastics, ethylene, and other petrochemical products. It ranks among the world’s 10 largest producers of synthetic rubber.
The Nizhnekamsk industrial zone, which also contains the TANECO and TAIF-NK oil refineries, has been attacked by Ukraine several times. In June, Ukraine’s General Staff said it had struck both refineries, and The Insider detected a fire in the industrial zone using data from the satellite-based fire monitoring system NASA FIRMS. In early July, Astra speculated that a drone captured on video had crashed on the grounds of TAIF-NK.

Wildfires burn across Indonesia as officials cite El Nino as a cause
Hundreds of firefighters and helicopters battle a growing wildfire at Indonesia’s Mount Bromo.
Close to 50,000 firefighters and disaster personnel, backed by dozens of helicopters, are battling wildfires in several parts of Indonesia after an unusually dry season in the sprawling archipelago.
Increased El Nino conditions have raised the risk of more forest and land fires during the peak dry season, said Indonesia’s Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs, Djamari Chaniago, on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Powerful El Nino to intensify heat on ‘a planet already on fire’: UN
- list 2 of 3India’s severe monsoon season causes more than 100 deaths since July

Authorities in East Java say the largest blaze is in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, where about 743 hectares (1,836 acres) of land have been scorched. The park is closed to visitors until further notice.
“This closure is a crucial step to maintain the safety of visitors, staff and people in the surrounding areas,” the park’s operator said on its Instagram page.
The fire has burned large areas of dry grassland, vegetation and protected Edelweiss flowers. Flames have spread to the Penanjakan area, a popular viewpoint for tourists visiting the volcanic landscape of Mount Bromo, one of Indonesia’s best-known attractions. No injuries or building evacuations have been reported.
Almost 6,000 firefighters have been deployed to battle wildfires in Jambi province. Officials said deep peat soil, limited water supplies, difficult access and strong winds have complicated efforts, even with help from three firefighting helicopters.
El Nino increases fire risk
Dry weather and strengthening El Nino conditions have raised the risk of fires during the peak dry season, according to Indonesia’s forestry ministry. Indonesia’s BMKG weather agency has warned that the 2026 dry season will be more intense and prolonged than usual, with a higher risk of wildfires and drought due in part to El Nino.
The naturally occurring climate phenomenon brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns and typically causes drier conditions in India and Southeast Asia. The last El Nino helped make 2023 and 2024 the two hottest years on record globally.
Indonesia’s forestry ministry says more than 107,000 hectares of land caught fire nationwide between January and June this year – double the area burned in all of 2023. Indonesia’s meteorological agency warned that August and September are expected to be the most critical months for fire risk.
Weather-modification, or cloud-seeding, operations are considered one of the most effective ways to help firefighters combat wildfires by inducing rainfall through the dispersal of salt particles into suitable clouds.
However, the effort would be difficult to carry out because scientific monitoring “found no rain-bearing clouds suitable for weather-modification operations,” government minister Chaniago said.
With cloud-seeding ruled out because of unfavourable weather conditions, “we are relying solely on water bombing and ground firefighting teams,” said Forestry Minister, Raja Juli Antoni, while visiting Mount Bromo on Sunday. He urged the public to avoid activities that could spark new blazes, including discarding cigarette butts and clearing land by burning.
Wildfires have been reported in several of Indonesia’s most fire-prone regions, including 48,890 hectares of peatland ablaze in the provinces of Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra on Sumatra island, as well as Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan on Borneo island. The emergency has forced regional authorities to deploy over 48,000 firefighters and disaster personnel, the National Disaster Management Agency said.

US court rules Meta, other tech firms must face thousands of lawsuits over social media addiction

US court rules Meta, other tech firms must face thousands of lawsuits over social media addiction
- A US appeals court ruled that Meta, TikTok, and other tech firms must face over 3,000 lawsuits claiming their platforms are addictive to young users.
- The court denied Meta's attempt to delay a multistate trial accusing it of illegally collecting children's data and misleading users about safety.
- Previous trials found Meta negligent and ordered large fines, highlighting ongoing legal battles over social media’s impact on youth mental health.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A US appeals court on Aug 10 allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet’s Google, ByteDance’s TikTok and Snap Inc’s Snapchat over claims they designed their products to be addictive to young users.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an appeal by Meta and TikTok seeking to overturn a lower court ruling requiring them to face more than 3,000 lawsuits filed in federal court, saying the companies had appealed too early.
The companies had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 – which generally shields online companies from claims over content posted by their users – also bars lawsuits claiming they failed to warn the public about the addictive nature of their platforms.
Most appeals come after a case has concluded with a ruling or a verdict.
The companies contended that they should not have to wait until the litigation ends to challenge the lower court’s rejection of their immunity defence.
But the 9th Circuit said Section 230 provides a defence to liability, not immunity from lawsuits, so the appeal was premature.
Meta loses bid to delay multi-state trial
The court also denied Meta’s bid to postpone a trial beginning on Aug 12 in a lawsuit brought by 29 state attorneys-general alleging that the company illegally collected and used children’s data, designed its social media platforms to keep young users hooked and misled consumers about their safety.
The company had argued that the trial could not go forward while the appeal had been outstanding.
The news comes days after a New Mexico judge found Meta had created a public nuisance in the state and ordered it to pay US$567 million (S$726 million) into a teen mental health fund and implement youth-safety measures.
A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment.
Representatives for TikTok did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Aug 10 ruling.
Lexi Hazam and Previn Warren, attorneys representing thousands of school districts and individuals suing Meta and other companies in the litigation over the claims in federal court, said in a statement the ruling would allow the states’ trial to move forward, as well as a trial over claims brought by school districts scheduled for February.
“A trial is how the public finds out what Meta knew about its products’ impact on children, when it knew it, and what it chose to do with that knowledge,” Hazam said. “Meta has fought to keep that evidence from the public.”
Thousands of lawsuits
Filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals, the lawsuits allege that social media companies intentionally addicted young users, contributing to rising rates of depression, anxiety and body-image issues and a broader mental health crisis among American youth in recent years.
Parents, school districts, states and other plaintiffs had argued that the trial court’s ruling was not final and therefore could not be appealed.
But they also objected to the companies’ arguments about Section 230, saying it does not cover claims related to how they operate and design their products.
The cases, which have been centralised before US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, seek damages, penalties and restitution from the companies.
The companies appealed against Rogers’ orders in 2023 and 2024 that largely allowed the litigation to move forward.
The companies are facing hundreds of additional lawsuits over similar claims in state courts, with approximately 3,300 of them in a consolidated proceeding in California state court.
In the first lawsuit to go to trial in the California litigation – a closely watched test of how juries might respond to similar claims – a Los Angeles jury in March found Meta and Google negligent for designing social media platforms that harm young people.
The jury awarded US$6 million to a young woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.
The New Mexico public nuisance ruling against Meta followed an earlier phase in the trial, in which a jury in March ordered it to pay US$375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms.
Both Meta and Google, which have denied the claims in those cases, said they would appeal. REUTERS

Turkiye approves pardon-like bill for thousands of PKK fighters
The text envisages a return to civilian life for some of the PKK fighters who lay down their weapons.
Turkish lawmakers have approved legislation offering a conditional pardon for thousands of members of the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a major step towards ending decades of deadly violence.
The text – which passed on Monday with a vote of 468 in favour and 88 against, with six abstentions – envisages a return to civilian life for some of the PKK fighters who lay down their weapons without granting a total amnesty.

The law is Turkiye‘s first legislative step towards ending the conflict and comes 18 months after Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK’s jailed founder, urged his followers to disarm.
The PKK, designated a “terrorist” organisation by Turkiye, the United States and the European Union, launched its rebellion in 1984. The conflict has killed more than 40,000 people, imposed a heavy economic burden on mainly Kurdish southeast Turkiye, and fuelled decades of political and social division.
Backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party) and the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the bill suspends prosecutions and prison sentences for some offences for between five and 10 years.
The move is expected to involve the release of around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees in an initial phase, lawmakers said – around a third of the number held in Turkish prisons.

Trump administration extends limited shipping waiver to keep oil flowing amid Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:13:17 UTC
06:13:17 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
US President Donald Trump’s administration extended a limited waiver of the Jones Act for another 90 days on Monday to support domestic fuel supplies amid disruptions caused by the Iran war, according to a White House spokesperson.
The extension allows foreign-flagged vessels to transport certain energy resources between US ports, easing restrictions imposed under the century-old shipping law.
Unlike the previous blanket waiver, the new extension will be applied on a voyage-by-voyage basis. The Pentagon will consult the US Maritime Administration to determine whether individual shipments qualify, according to White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers.
She said the waiver was extended to ensure that the US military and key industries maintain uninterrupted access to critical resources.
“Data shows the waiver has driven a significant increase in domestic deliveries of essential products such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel,” Rogers wrote on the US social media firm X.
The latest extension is expected to remain in effect until mid-November. Trump initially issued a 60-day waiver on March 17 before extending it for another 90 days in May.
The administration narrowed the scope of the latest measure following concerns raised by the US maritime industry that a broader waiver could undermine domestic shipbuilders and shipping companies.
The Jones Act, formally part of the Merchant Marine Act of 1920, generally requires goods transported between US ports to be carried aboard vessels built, owned and operated by Americans.
Since the initial waiver was introduced, around 210 voyages that would otherwise have been prohibited have been completed, according to US Maritime Administration data. Most of the vessels transported gasoline or crude oil.
The extension comes as restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continues to disrupt global energy supplies and place upward pressure on oil prices.
US Strategic Petroleum Reserve holdings also fell by about 6.1 million barrels last week to 298.7 million barrels, their lowest level since 1983.

Israel has seized 550 acres of land belonging to the Palestinian town of Marda in the northern occupied West Bank's Salfit province, citing "military purposes," the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission said.
The government body said in a statement that Israeli authorities issued a new military order "to seize 2,224 dunams (550 acres) of land belonging to Marda."
The order targets land in the areas of Wadi Qasim and Kafif al-Abhar and "explicitly provides for taking control of the specified area and transferring its possession to the Israeli military commander through the relevant official at Israel's Defense Ministry," it said.

The site has strategic importance because of its position overlooking and controlling a key transportation route in the area, the commission said. It added that the stated purpose of the seizure is "to establish a tower or communications facility."
Expanding land confiscation orders
The commission said the order comes amid an expanding use by Israeli authorities of "seizure for military purposes" orders to temporarily take control of Palestinian land and reshape control over routes, corridors and areas surrounding illegal settlements.
Israeli authorities issued 33 military orders in July, including 31 new seizure orders targeting 205,324 acres of Palestinian land, according to a commission statement issued August 3.
About 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 outposts across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, and carry out attacks under Israeli military protection with the aim of forcibly displacing Palestinians.

Russian anti-war opposition had a 5-day run
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:07:58 UTC
06:07:58 KST

Russian anti-war opposition had a 5-day run
Russia's liberal Yabloko party leader Nikolai Rybakov talks to the media outside the Supreme Court in Moscow on Aug. 10, 2026. (Igor Ivanko / AFP via Getty Images)
Russia's Supreme Court, on Aug. 10, barred the country's only anti-war party from taking part in parliamentary elections scheduled for September. The liberal Yabloko party had been approved to take part in the vote and was assigned a spot on the ballot five days prior.
Between the two dates, a few notable events took place — the largely obscure party received wide-ranging support from anti-war activists and the country's exiled opposition, and pro-Kremlin political projects went after it as a result.
The accusations, spearheaded by the nationalist pro-war Rodina party, circled around Yabloko's anti-war stance, which they viewed as a "support for extremism" and compared to calls for Russia to cede its sovereign territory.
"Part of Russia's territories are occupied by a neo-Nazi regime," a Rodina representative told the court, as cited by Russian news outlet Meduza, referring to Ukrainian territories that Russia views as theirs and has inscribed their ownership into its own constitution.
"Calls for an immediate ceasefire agreement constitute calls to stop the liberation of the occupied territories or to abandon their liberation."
A few other accusations were brought up against Yabloko, among them not asking OpenAI for permission to use an image generated by ChatGPT and violating campaign financing laws, Russian media outlets reported.
Russia's Central Election Committee, which greenlit Yabloko's place in the election days earlier, told the court that they had uncovered foreign sources of funding for Yabloko candidates.
Yabloko denied all of the charges. "(Young voters) support us simply because they want to live in Russia and do not want to be killed. I do not know how to explain this to the plaintiffs," Yabloko chairman Nikolai Rybakov told the court. The party said they would appeal the decision.
Grigory Yavlinsky, Yabloko's co-founder and the chair of its political committee, said that the move exposed "the true nature" of Russia's political system.
"This decision speaks volumes about the importance of our platform — far more than any official election results could. It is evident that the public demand for peace and freedom today has proven far stronger than the authorities anticipated."
read also
A safety valve for dissent
Yabloko is the only officially registered political party in Russia to promote a pro-peace platform.
Short and delicately worded, its manifesto calls for "a ceasefire agreement, diplomacy, and the achievement of peace." It does not directly reference Ukraine.
The text — which, in Russian, reaches just 43 words — shows the difficult line that Yabloko has chosen to walk in order to survive in Russia's increasingly repressive public sphere.
Several of Yabloko's leading members have been jailed for sharing information about Russia's war against Ukraine. Maxim Kruglov, one of the party's deputy chairs and a former member of the Moscow city council, was sentenced to seven years in prison in June after sharing information on Russia's killing of civilians in Bucha and Mariupol. Another deputy co-chair, Lev Shlosberg, is currently facing similar charges.
More high-ranking members have been legally designated as "foreign agents," or found guilty of "displaying extremist symbols" — a designation that in Russia can include images of late opposition leader Alexei Navalny or Facebook and Instagram logos — meaning they are unable to run for office.
But so far, the party itself has been allowed to survive.
For the Kremlin, Yabloko's place on the ballot paper helped to preserve the image of a competitive vote, says David Szakonyi, an associate professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University.
Founded in 1993, the party itself is a stalwart of Russia's political scene. In 1995, it had 45 representatives in Russia's lower house of parliament, the State Duma. Members of the party also held several regional offices.
Yet the party also isn't a real threat to United Russia's power. Yabloko hasn't reached the 7% and later 5% vote threshold needed to gain parliamentary seats for more than two decades. In Russia's last parliamentary elections in 2021, the party saw a 1.34% result.
In the meantime, parties such as Yabloko can be used to control the risk of protest votes.
"In general, there have always been some liberal opposition party that's been presented to voters and used as a safety valve," Szakonyi says.
"(It's) a way of channeling the angriest votes towards one body that is never going to be able to accumulate enough across the country to surpass the electoral threshold and actually take seats."
read also
Plummeting ratings
The Supreme Court case shows that something may have shifted in these calculations. Yabloko's pro-peace message has resonated, particularly on social media.
Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin has also been forced to contend with growing public discontent. Increasing Ukrainian drone strikes, intermittent internet blackouts, chronic fuel shortages, and growing taxes on small businesses to fund Moscow's invasion have all added to the burden.
Even Putin's government-sanctioned approval ratings dipped sharply over the past few months.
There's a greater chance that Yabloko can not only win the vote of dissenting, anti-war citizens, but also those unhappy with the country at large, says Mikhail Turchenko, a political scientist at Northwestern University in Illinois.
He points to the other parties on the ballot, who are opposition parties in name, but largely support the Kremlin on all major points. Yabloko's anti-war position differentiates it from the main field and attracts anyone who may be dissatisfied with the status quo, he says.
"Yabloko has this unique position inside the Russian political system, this anti-war position," says Turchenko. "I would speculate that this time, Yabloko will be able to get pretty solid popular support from the people."
Yabloko's potential has also been noticed elsewhere. Several of Russia's leading opposition figures, now in exile abroad, had urged their followers last week to vote for the party in protest.
In one video message, Yuliya Navalnaya, the widow of late opposition leader Alexei Navalny, said that Russians "must view the upcoming elections, no matter how unfair they may be, as the only legal and safe opportunity in many years to express our dissent with the government."
"This can be done by voting for a party that takes an anti-war stance," she said.
Such statements of support, however, were a double-edged sword, and Yabloko has sought to distance itself from these calls in an attempt to avoid repercussions from the state.
Writing on social media, Yabloko chairman Rybakov stressed that the party has "absolutely no foreign sources of funding, maintains no ties with organizations designated as 'undesirable' in Russia, and does not consider statements, appeals, or events organized by anyone abroad to be part of its election campaign."
Despite Rybakov's appeal, Yabloko's disappearance from the ballot will be seen as a swipe at opposition both inside and outside the country.

US judge dismisses criminal case against Indian billionaire Adani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:04:59 UTC
06:04:59 KST

US judge dismisses criminal case against Indian billionaire Adani
Move comes after the Justice Department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case in which Adani Group has denied wrongdoing
A US judge on Monday dismissed criminal charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, after the Justice Department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case.
Brooklyn-based US District Judge Nicholas Garaufis’ decision to grant federal prosecutors’ rare bid to toss the case came after he inquired into their reasons for doing so, including by asking Adani whether anything was promised in exchange for the dropping of the case.
In November 2024, before the charges were unsealed, Adani had promised to invest US$10 billion in the United States.
Adani was charged in 2024 with agreeing to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of his Adani Group could win approval to develop a solar energy plant, then misleading US investors by providing reassuring information about his company’s anti-corruption practices.
Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing. Adani himself has not appeared in court in the US to respond to the charges.
On May 18, the Justice Department announced it would no longer pursue the case. That marked the latest instance in which federal prosecutors had sought to drop a high-profile white-collar criminal prosecution during Republican President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House.
Legal experts say US judges have little discretion to compel prosecutors to continue with criminal cases they no longer wish to pursue but the charges cannot be formally dismissed without a judge’s approval.

Russia and Syria have signed a memorandum of understanding on the organization of Russia’s presence on the Syrian coast. Syria’s state news agency SANA, citing the Syrian Foreign Ministry, reported that the document provides for converting the Russian military bases at Hmeimim and Tartus into joint training centers.
The ministry said the agreement was the result of negotiations that lasted 18 months. Under the document, Syria will take over management of civilian facilities, including Hmeimim airport and the commercial vessel pier at the port of Tartus, in order to gradually integrate them into the country’s civilian infrastructure.
The memorandum provides for a three-month transition period, after which the new arrangements will take effect.
Russia’s Hmeimim air base, along with the Tartus naval facility, are located in Syria’s Latakia province on the Mediterranean coast. After the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Russia began withdrawing its forces and equipment from Syria. In late 2024 and early 2025, significant amounts of weapons and military hardware were removed from the naval base in Tartus.
In January, Reuters reported that Russia had also begun withdrawing troops from the Qamishli air base in northeastern Syria. According to the agency, some personnel and equipment were being transferred to Hmeimim, while others were returning to Russia.
Reuters also reported that Moscow was trying to repurpose Tartus for commercial use, writing that the Syrian company Rus Line, together with its Russian partners, is preparing to create a logistics hub at the port of Tartus for transshipping Russian cargo, including grain, coal, timber, and steel.

Family of former Palestinian ambassador urge Lebanon to not extradite him
The family of former Palestinian ambassador to Lebanon Ashraf Dabbour urged Lebanese authorities on Monday to not extradite him after authorities in Ramallah requested his transfer over corruption allegations.
Lebanon's public prosecutor ordered the arrest of Dabbour, ambassador from 2012 to 2025, last week after questioning him based on a warrant from the Palestinian Authority over corruption and embezzlement during his tenure, a judicial official told AFP at the time.
The judiciary then recommended in a letter to the justice ministry that Dabbour be extradited as his case involves "Palestinian funds", another official said on Monday, on condition of anonymity.
The request must be signed by the justice minister, president and prime minister before security forces can hand him over.
"We are not asking for his protection from the judiciary, nor are we asking for charges to be dropped," Dabbour's daughter Israa said in a press conference in Beirut.
"Why should our father be moved from the country where he lived, and from the place where the alleged crimes took place, in order to be tried somewhere else?" she said, calling on the Lebanese judiciary to look into the case instead of sending him to Ramallah.
Dabbour has a "critical health condition and is in intensive care", according to his daughter, who appealed to Lebanon to "provide him with the necessary care".
In April, Lebanese authorities detained Dabbour over the same case before releasing him with a travel ban.
He has repeatedly denied the accusations on social media, accusing Yasser Abbas, son of Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, of leading a campaign against him.
Israa Dabbour said "the file includes political accusations seeking to settle personal scores" without elaborating.
Lebanon's National Human Rights Commission asked the cabinet last week to "refrain from approving the extradition" due to "reliable information that raises serious reasons to believe that (Dabbour) is at risk of being subjected to torture, ill-treatment or arbitrary detention".
The organisation also pointed to legal loopholes that could prevent the handover due to the lack of "an effective treaty between Lebanon and the State of Palestine that regulates extradition".

Allison Janney reveals the two roles she’d love to play
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
22:02:30 BST
06:02:30 KST

Allison Janney reveals the two roles she’d love to play
Emmy-winning actor has earned a reputation for playing a woman in power
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Allison Janney has an impressive range of projects under her belt, from TV to indie films to Broadway, but there are some roles that she has yet to conquer.
In a recent interview with Variety, the Oscar-winning actor admitted that there are two types of characters that she would like to play in the future — the first of which being a superhero.
Janney, 66, said that she has wanted to portray a character with superpowers ever since she spent her childhood watching the classic Sixties sitcom Bewitched.
“I was determined that if I twitched the right body parts, I too could be magic,” the seven-time Emmy winner explained to the publication.
Secondly, although she portrayed the comic relief part of the veterinarian boss in the 2019 cult classic Ma, Janney said she is ready to take on another scary movie.
“I’ve never done a horror film before,” she told the outlet. “That would be really fun.”
A superhero and/or a final girl role for Janney would be a drastic change from the reputation she has earned for playing strong women in Washington, D.C.
After making a name for herself in the theater world — and earning her first Tony nomination in 1997 — Janney broke into Hollywood by playing White House Press Secretary C.J. Cregg on the beloved drama The West Wing from 1999 to 2006.
Over on The Diplomat, the Netflix political thriller created by Debora Cahn, Janney plays Grace Penn, who ascended from the vice president role to the commander in chief.
However, the Ohio native insists that her personality is much different than the characters she winds up playing.
“I love playing strong women with huge flaws or huge secrets,” she told Variety. “But in real life, I am not that at all. I am shy. I do not like to speak in front of people.
“I am not these characters at all, and all my friends will tell you that too,” she said.
Her presidential role in The Diplomat landed Janney a nomination at this year’s Emmy Awards for best supporting drama actress, with the drama series receiving seven nominations total ahead of the September 14 ceremony. If she wins, Janney will tie Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus as the most awarded female performers in the history of the Emmys.
While season four of the Netflix show is set to be released later this year, Janney will also be returning to Broadway this fall in the first revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s drama Other Desert Cities.

US appeals court says social media addiction lawsuits can proceed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
21:02:06 UTC
06:02:06 KST

US appeals court says social media addiction lawsuits can proceed
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals rejected tech companies’ bid to stop more than 3,000 lawsuits over addictive platform design
A federal appeals court in the United States has permitted thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta, Google, TikTok, Snapchat and other social media companies for allegedly designing addictive products that harm children, rejecting the companies’ initial bids to stop litigation before trial.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the appeal came too early – most appeals are only filed after a case concludes with a ruling or verdict. The companies had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act which generally shields online platforms from liability over user-generated and user-posted content, also protected them from claims that they failed to warn the public about the addictive design of their platforms.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Social media platforms swamped with fake news on the Israel-Hamas war
- list 2 of 3What’s behind Israel’s Arabic social media accounts?
- list 3 of 3New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harm to youths
The court disagreed, finding that Section 230 offers a defence to liability rather than blanket immunity from being sued, rendering the appeal premature.
The panel also denied Meta’s request to delay the trial set to begin on Wednesday, brought by 29 state attorneys general who allege the company illegally collected and used children’s data, and engineered its platforms to keep young users hooked, ultimately misleading the public about their safety.
The ruling comes as several countries are penalising social media platforms’ allegedly harmful design that can directly impact children’s and teenagers’ health, including self-harm and eating disorders, according to The Guardian. France plans to ban under-15s from social media sites and prohibit mobile phones in high schools from next month. Australia has also imposed a ban and Britain plans one next year.
The legal moves reflect rising public concern over online harms to minors. President Emmanuel Macron has pointed to social media as a factor in youth violence and has signalled he wants France to follow Australia’s world-first ban on social media for children under 16. The law obliges major social media platforms to block under-16s, with companies that fail to comply facing penalties of up to 49.5 million Australian dollars ($35 million).
In late May, Britain’s then Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, vowed to take “decisive” action to tackle the impact of social media on British youngsters. That was after families, who insist their children died as a result of social media, and campaigners rallied outside Downing Street to hold tech giants accountable.
The US lawsuits, filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individual families, allege that the companies knowingly built addictive products that have fuelled the surge in depression, anxiety and broader youth mental health crises. The cases are centralised before US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, where plaintiffs are seeking damages, penalties and restitution.
A jury in Los Angeles has already found Meta and Google negligent in the first such case to reach trial, awarding $6m to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child, according to Reuters.
Meta separately lost both phases of a New Mexico lawsuit, with a jury ordering $375m in damages over misleading safety claims and a judge later imposing an additional $567m penalty after finding the company had created a public nuisance.
Meta and Google have denied wrongdoing and said they plan to appeal.
