Donald Trump has signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that would require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to be broken into three separate shots, once it becomes available in the US.
The order recommends that all shots be given at separate medical visits, a frequent point Trump has made despite the safety, ease and lower costs of giving vaccines together.
The move is an attempt to undermine and override the changes made earlier this year to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) vaccination recommendations, which were halted by a federal judge. The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House.
On a press call, a White House official said the order draws on a Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) scientific assessment published in January 2026, which examined “comparisons of the US to other peer-developed nations” and looked at “where there is consensus amongst our peers on recommendations for immunizations for children”.
The official said the number of recommended childhood immunizations would drop “down to 11 diseases”, compared with 18 at the end of 2024.
Only six of the 17 vaccines currently routinely recommended for all children in the US would continue to have full recommendations: measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DTaP), polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV and varicella.
“Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” Trump said of the MMR vaccine at the signing of the order on Monday.
Five other shots would be recommended only for those at high risk: monoclonal antibodies to protect against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as well as vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal ACWY, which is recommended for teens and high-risk infants. Dengue and meningococcal B vaccines are also on this list, but dengue was already recommended only for those at risk and meningococcal B was shared clinical decision-making.
And six shots would be pushed to shared clinical decision-making: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and Covid-19.
This is a previously obscure category that means a provider would be required to weigh the risks and benefits, despite strong evidence for the safety and efficacy of these vaccines.
On the call, the White House official said vaccines moved into this category “still are a recommendation, and so we assume that that means they’ll still be covered by insurance” and remain “available to parents that want them”, adding: “The president is interested in getting parents more choice and flexibility.”
The executive order would also require the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots, which is not currently possible in the US as there are no separately licensed vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella and the licensing process takes years.
The order also states that, “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits”. This would put a financial and logistical strain on families and medical providers by creating several additional visits.
The US attorney general would also be tasked with challenging state laws that conflict with the executive order. The US has no vaccination mandates. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state and local level.
Both Trump and Robert F Kennedy, the health secretary, made repeated mentions of autism throughout the order signing, emphasizing a scientifically unproven link between vaccines and the condition. Dozens of studies show no link between the two.
“Today we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s gold standard childhood vaccination recommendations. That has to do with many subjects including autism in particular,” Trump said at the beginning of the order signing.
“I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination where it looks like the size of a bottle of soda, poured into a little child’s body and bad things happen in too many cases,” Trump later said on breaking up each shot into an individual medical visit, before adding: “This is an explosion, it’s an epidemic,” in an apparent reference to autism.
Kennedy claimed at one point: “Something happened in the mid-90s that changed our children, and it has to be an environmental exposure.”
On the call, officials were pressed on why Kennedy has not yet delivered the finding on the cause of autism he had promised by the previous September, and why the US president continued to suggest a vaccine-autism link without new supporting evidence from HHS. An official declined to engage directly, asking to keep the discussion “germane to today’s executive order” rather than address the broader autism-research timeline.
Asked about criticism from the American Academy of Pediatrics that the administration invoked autism repeatedly during the signing without offering any concrete support for families already raising children with autism, an official pointed instead to a toolkit the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service released on applied behavior analysis services, framing it as guidance to help states serve autistic patients and curb fraud in relevant programs.
Rebuking these claims and ties to autism, Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana senator, tweeted in response to the order that it “is so wrong”.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy wrote.
Executive orders are meant as guidance to federal agencies; they are not laws passed by Congress, and thus they have no legal effect on the public.
The White House official estimated that 28 states “have implemented their own vaccine recommendations or diverged from the federal guidance”. The order is intended to ensure the remaining states “are aware of this information as they go into … their legislative sessions”, they said, and weigh “what vaccine requirements they want to implement as law in their state, particularly … school attendance and entry requirements”.
“This should have no direct operational effects,” says Dorit Reiss, a vaccines expert at UC Law San Francisco. Twenty-nine states and the District of Columbia have decoupled their vaccination requirements from the CDC, and insurance continues to cover the shots.
However, “Trump has influence,” Reiss said, and the order may intensify “political pressure on states” to change school requirements.

British defense officials have disabled connectivity on Royal Navy surveillance drones after cameras containing Chinese-made components were found transmitting signals to an IP address in China, according to a media report Monday.
The drones, manufactured by Kraken Technology Group and purchased by the Royal Navy in March, were equipped with cameras that suppliers had reportedly assured were secure, The Telegraph reported.
An investigation later found that the cameras were sending what were described as “heartbeat” signals to an IP address in China, prompting the Ministry of Defence (MoD) to remove their connectivity.
The drones have been used by British special forces and are expected to be deployed to the Strait of Hormuz as part of Britain’s efforts to help protect the strategically important waterway.
The MoD said there was no evidence that sensitive information had been compromised and that the identified vulnerabilities had since been addressed.
Defense sources cited by the newspaper, however, described the incident as a major security failure, raising questions over the use of foreign-made components in sensitive military equipment.
The discovery comes amid heightened scrutiny in Britain and other Western countries over potential security risks linked to Chinese-made technology used in critical infrastructure and defense systems.

Where does your superannuation go when you die?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
19:03:06 UTC
04:03:06 KST

Where does your superannuation go when you die? How can you make a binding death benefit nomination?
Where your superannuation savings go when you die is not always straightforward, but there are ways to increase the chance the money will go where you want it to with minimal delays.
As ABC News reported on Monday, it is estimated 15.5 million Australians may not have made a binding death benefit nomination, so it is worth exploring how to set up one to ensure your super money (and any insurance payout) goes to whom you wish to receive it.
A binding nomination means the fund will pay to one or more of your dependants and/or your legal personal representative (executor of your estate).
If you have made a non-binding nomination or did not make a nomination, the trustee of the fund may use their discretion to decide which dependant or dependants is paid the death benefit.
According to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), a dependent can include:
- their spouse or de facto spouse
- a child of the deceased (any age)
- a person in an interdependency relationship with the deceased
- a person substantially financially dependent on the deceased
An interdependency relationship exists between two people if all the following conditions are met:
- they have a close personal relationship
- they live together
- one or both provides the other with financial support
- one or both provides the other with domestic support and personal care
What happens if you don't have a dependent? How can you nominate who gets your super?
Superannuation does not automatically form part of your estate or get distributed by your will because it is held in a trust by your super fund.
Scott Forster, special counsel at Queensland Estate Lawyers, says a member cannot simply nominate anyone they choose.
"For example, a neighbour, grandchild or sibling cannot generally be nominated unless they meet the definition of dependent for super purposes," he said.
"Because the definition of a dependant can be complex, it's important to seek legal advice if you are uncertain if someone qualifies."
If you want to leave your super to someone who does not qualify as a legal dependant under superannuation law (such as adult children, siblings or friends), it must go through your estate via your will.
Loading...
To leave your superannuation as part of your estate, you must formally nominate your legal personal representative (the executor of your will) as the beneficiary with your super fund. That will ensure the super money, and any insurance, is paid out according to the instructions in your will.
You can log in to your member online portal or request a death benefit nomination form. Then on the nomination form, name your legal personal representative.
Some super funds do not allow binding nominations to be made digitally and require it on paper with two wet signatures. Check with your super fund what the process is.
You will also need to update your will to ensure it outlines how you want the super fund money distributed once it is paid into your estate.
Bear in mind that depending on what super fund you are with, binding nominations typically lapse after three years, so it would be worth checking with your fund about renewing them regularly to keep them valid.
Louise du Pre-Alba, a consultant to the super industry, says the reason super funds are required to pay out to dependents over others is simple.
"If someone has to go on a government age pension while $2 million is going into an estate to be distributed in a different way, as a taxpayer, I would say, why am I subsidising that system?" she said.
"Of course, if someone is single, if someone doesn't have children and doesn't have financial dependents, things should be made easier and more straightforward for them so that they can leave money in accordance with their wishes and their will."
Loading...
What are the tax implications on super death benefit payouts?
Most people do not realise that super death benefits can be taxed. That is because super is concessionally taxed on the way in.
You pay a discounted tax rate on super contributions on the way in, as well as on super earnings.
The rationale behind the top-up taxes on super passed on through inheritance is that the previous tax discounts were intended to help fund one's retirement, not to subsidise an inheritance for someone else.
How payouts get taxed depends on who receives the money and whether it is paid as a lump sum or a regular income stream.
Tax dependents — for example, a spouse or a child aged under 18 — pay zero tax.
Non-dependents — for example, independent adult children — can face up to 32 per cent tax on the taxable parts of the payout.
Mr Forster says whether a superannuation death benefit is taxed depends on tax law rather than superannuation law.
The tax treatment will depend largely on who receives the benefit and the components of the superannuation account.
There are circumstances where a child aged over 18 is still studying and financially dependent on their parents can qualify as a dependant, Mr Forster says.
"A child with certain disabilities may also qualify.
"These tax rules apply whether the superannuation benefit is paid directly from the super fund or it is paid to the deceased's estate."
For someone who is not a tax dependant, such as adult children who do not meet the tax criteria of dependency, tax will be payable on the benefit paid.
"What tax is payable will depend on the tax components of the benefit being paid," Mr Forster said.
"A superannuation death benefit can contain tax-free, taxed and untaxed components."
The tax-free component is not subject to tax.
The taxed component consists of amounts that have already been taxed within the superannuation system and will usually attract further tax "in the order of 15 per cent" (17 per cent including Medicare).
The untaxed component is where no tax has yet been paid on this part of your superannuation, and the tax payable on this will be in the order of 32 per cent including the Medicare levy.
The exact tax outcome varies depending on the recipient, their dependency status and the components of the superannuation benefit being paid.
KPMG partner and superannuation expert Ross Stephens says the tax rates for death benefits also depend on whether the amounts are being paid as lump sums or income streams (pensions), and whether the benefit includes an insured component, and if so, whether the fund had claimed a deduction for the insurance premiums on the policy.
Some people gift super before they die
Mr Stephens notes that many industry commentators believe the tax settings discriminate between members who have dependants and those who don't.
"For example, a person that knows they are dying may be able to withdraw all of the monies in their superannuation fund prior to death and, say, gift these monies to their adult children, and the taxes and death benefits would not be payable," he said.
"Whereas if the same person dies unexpectedly and has no dependants at the time of death, death benefits paid to non-dependants would be subject to these taxes."
While in many cases death is unexpected, Scott Girdlestone, a William Buck partner in wealth advisory, says for people who do have time to get their affairs in order, "it may be appropriate to consider a lump sum payout" to an intended recipient before a person's passing.
"This is only available if the individual satisfies a condition of release, but two relevant conditions are terminal illness and total and permanent disablement, which can be used where it is beneficial to do so.
"Under these circumstances, the tax treatment is often more favourable and can reduce the tax that beneficiaries of an estate may pay."
This is not intended as legal or financial advice and people should speak to a lawyer and or tax adviser about their individual circumstances.

Parents beware your kid’s favorite squish toy might be a danger
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
20:03:01 BST
04:03:01 KST

Parents beware: your kid’s favorite squish toy might be a danger
Viral videos show these popular toys being heated up in the microwave to expand — but parents are being warned that this trend may be dangerous for their kids
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Parents are being warned that fake or counterfeit versions of their children’s favorite toys may put them in danger.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission warned in an August 5 notice against fake or counterfeit squishy toys — and cautioned against a viral social media trend that encourages children and teens to microwave them.
These toys, which can resemble popular characters, animals or food, are sold online, on social media and at discount stores and other retailers.
Viral videos show these toys expanding, changing texture or even bursting when they are heated up.
However, the commission warns that these trends are “dangerous and should never be attempted or imitated.”
In January, a 9-year-old boy in Plainfield, Illinois, suffered burns to his face and hands when he microwaved a NeeDoh toy, which exploded, covering him in scalding goo, reported the New York Times. The youngster was taken to the emergency room and later transferred to a burn center where he was treated for second-degree burns .
Some versions of them do not comply with federal safety requirements for children’s toys. Some squishy toys contain water beads, gels, liquids, powders or sand. If the toys burst, children may be exposed to the contents.
“Water beads can expand after being swallowed and cause intestinal blockages, choking, aspiration, or injuries when inserted into the nose or ear. Other unknown filling materials may present chemical exposure, inhalation, or ingestion hazards,” the CPSC warned.
The CPSC also warned that some fake toys may break or tear during use, releasing hazardous materials or contain excessive amounts of lead, prohibited phthalates or other chemicals.
Some also fail to comply with federal requirements governing water beads, lack required warnings, age grading, tracking information or manufacturer identification. They may also be sold without testing and certification required for children’s products.
The commission has identified 55 shipments of these dangerous toys at U.S. ports, and worked with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to prevent 355,683 units from entering the country.
The CPSC recommends that parents and caregivers purchase toys from reputable retailers, be cautious of unusually low prices, check packaging for misspelled words or missing manufacturer information or safety warnings and keep damaged toys away from children.
The commission says that if a burn should occur as a result of the toys, the affected area should immediately be placed under cool running water for at least 20 minutes.
Gently washing the area with mild soap and water also helps to remove any remaining material.
Medical attention should be sought for a severe burn, a burn involving a young child, or if there are signs of an infection after the burn.

What happens if you do not complete your census form?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
19:02:24 UTC
04:02:24 KST

When is census night? What happens if you do not complete the form?
Have you checked your mail recently?
You might have received an envelope with census written on it.
It's not junk mail or a scam letter; it contains important details to help you complete the census tonight.
What is the census?
It's something the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) does every five years to count every person and every household in Australia.
Technically called the Census of Population and Housing, it gives the ABS a snapshot of Australia on a particular night.
This year, census night is Tuesday, August 11.
The ABS is our official national statistical agency tasked with gathering information about the people and economy of Australia.
Outside the census, the ABS is responsible for data about things such as inflation, unemployment and how many people got married last year.
Information collected via the census helps the government make decisions about things including health care, transport, schools and infrastructure.
How safe is it?
The ABS is an independent statutory authority and an official organisation trusted by 90 per cent of the general community, according to an ABS survey last year.
And the personal information you give on your census form is confidential and protected by law.
It is not shared with anyone else.
This means government agencies such as the Department of Home Affairs, the Australian Taxation Office and Centrelink cannot see what you have written on your census form.
"We have a range of processes and protections that make sure information on census forms stays confidential," an ABS spokesperson said.
"For example, we use the strongest encryption technology available to make sure information from the online census form is secure.
"People should be reassured that organisations [other government departments and marketing companies] can't access any personal information you include on your census form."
The legislation around the census also imposes strict secrecy obligations on all ABS employees.
How does it work?
You have to participate in the census wherever you are staying on census night.
Each household has to fill out a census form.
Typically, there will only be one form per household.
However, people can complete their census separately from their household if they want.
They will need to call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227 to get a special number to complete their census online or request a paper form to be sent by mail.
What if I haven't received my census instructions?
It doesn't matter if you haven't received a census letter with instructions or have mislaid it.
You can call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227 to request another paper form to be sent out to you.
And the other option is going online to do it.
Is completing the census online easy to do?
Yes.
You simply go to the ABS Census website.
Your home should have received a letter from the ABS containing a census number and a temporary password; you will need to enter these details on the website to complete the census online.
If you don't have a census number, you can go to this website, where you'll be prompted to enter your mobile phone number so the ABS can text you a one-time PIN and your census number.
This takes just a matter of seconds.
For help over the phone, you can call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.
Where do I get my census form?
You'll be able to find the form online at the ABS website.
The ABS may have sent you a paper form.
The paper form has enough spaces for six people, but you can request an extra form or complete the census online if there will be more than six people at your place tonight.
If you want a paper form and haven't received one, you can request one via this online portal or by calling the 24/7 automated paper form request service on 1800 130 250.
An additional paper form may take up to 10 days to arrive, but the ABS says you will still have time to complete it.
Do I have to do the census?
Yes.
Participating in the census is compulsory.
Even if I'm not a citizen?
Yes, non-citizens must complete the census.
Almost everyone in Australia on census night needs to be counted.
That includes people on visas, international students and people visiting from overseas.
However, foreign diplomats and their families living in Australia are not included.
What if I'm not at home on Tuesday night?
Here are some of the most common reasons for being away:
- If you're spending the night at someone else's place, you should be included on the form for the household you're staying at.
- If you're doing shiftwork on census night and will return the following day, you should ask someone else in the household to count you on the household form.
- If you end up staying at work because of multiple shifts, the ABS says you should complete a census form at your workplace.
- If you're spending the night in accommodation like a hotel, hospital or staff quarters, you'll need to fill out a personal form (as opposed to a household form) or complete the census online. The same goes if you'll be in transit within Australia on census night.
If no-one will be at your household on census night, you should let the ABS know by either filling out this online form or calling the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.
If you're not sure what to do in your specific situation, you can call the Census Contact Centre for advice.
What if I'm out of the country?
You do not have to complete a census form if you're out of the country on census night.
What about children?
Children and babies must be counted.
If your child is staying at someone else's place on census night, they should be included on the census form for the household they're staying at.
- If they're away at a school camp, the ABS says you should include your child on the census form as if they were at home.
- If they're at boarding school and they live there less than six months of the year, include them in your household census form.
- If they're at boarding school and live there for more than six months of the year, they'll be counted at their boarding school, and you should mark them as "away" on your form.
If you have shared custody of your child, they should be included on the form for whatever household they're staying at on census night.
Put down the address they spend most of their time at under the "usual address" question.
Does every person have to fill out a form?
No, not if someone else they live with or are staying with has included them and their details on the household form.
Some households might elect one person to fill out the form on everyone else's behalf.
Others might pass the census around and complete their own details.
It's up to you and your household to decide.
How many people have done the census early?
By Thursday, August 6, more than 1.2 million household census forms — online and paper — had already been completed.
And as of 10am on Tuesday, the ABS had received more than 5 million forms.
At the last census, about 3 million households completed their forms early, so it appears Australians have been more proactive this time around.
What happens if I forget?
You are able to submit your form late, the ABS spokesperson said.
"There is still time to complete your form after census night," they said.
But make sure you fill it out.
"While we aim to get everyone to participate in the census voluntarily, penalties can apply if someone refuses to complete the census," the spokesperson said.
However, the ABS website says it will contact people to encourage participation as a first port of call.
But if they don't respond to this, the ABS will send a formal legal instruction to complete the census.
Failing to comply with this direction could lead to prosecution.
Is there a fine for not completing the census?
Yes.
"If a person does not complete the census, they could be fined up to $364 a day," the spokesperson said.
"It is also an offence to knowingly provide false or misleading statements or information."
People found to have lied on their census form could face a fine of up to $3,640.
Wait, when is census night again?
Census night is Tuesday, August 11.
That's tonight.

Tupac Shakur murder trial begins 30 years after rapper's death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
19:00:07 UTC
04:00:07 KST

The trial of a former gang leader accused of orchestrating the murder of rapper Tupac Shakur has finally begun, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unresolved killings.
Monday’s proceedings, expected to last a month, will likely not make clear who fired the shots that killed the California hip-hop star on the night of September 7, 1996, while he was in Las Vegas to see a Mike Tyson boxing match.
But prosecutors aim to show that the defendant, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, onetime leader of the South Side Compton Crips, ordered the killing and provided the gun used to kill Shakur in a drive-by shooting.
The trial began with jury selection, a process expected to last through the week.
Davis, 63, appeared in court wearing a light-blue shirt and blue tie. He faces life in prison without parole if convicted.
The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, is one of America's most celebrated cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it and why.
The rapper, who died at age 25, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the East Coast against the West Coast.
Revenge
Known for hits like "California Love" and "All Eyez on Me," Shakur — the son of a Black Panther — was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but quickly became the epitome of a California bad boy when he signed with Los-Angeles based Death Row Records.
The trial will revisit the battle between Death Row, founded by Marion "Suge" Knight, and Bad Boy Records, the East Coast label created by Sean "Diddy" Combs and starring Christopher "The Notorious B.I.G." Wallace (murdered in March 1997).
Prosecutors say Death Row Records was protected by Mob Piru, a Los Angeles gang that was part of the wider Bloods alliance. Knight was affiliated with the group.
Bad Boy Records had hired the rival group South Side Compton Crips, led by Davis, as bodyguards.
After the Tyson fight at the MGM Grand casino, Knight and Shakur beat up Davis's nephew, Crips member Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, in retribution over an alleged assault of a Death Row employee.
Davis was out for revenge, the prosecution says.
Later that night, a white Cadillac carrying Davis, Anderson and others pulled up beside Shakur's car in Las Vegas. Shots were fired from the Cadillac, and Shakur was fatally wounded.
Compromising memoirs
The investigation sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the cold case was revived with the publication in 2019 of Davis's memoirs.
In that book, Davis recounted that he was in the front seat of the Cadillac and that he handed a pistol to those in the back seat. But he does not say who opened fire on Shakur. Everyone else who was in the Cadillac that night has since died.
These compromising revelations were consistent with remarks Davis had made previously to reporters. But this time, they came back to haunt him and he was arrested in September 2023.
Davis has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty.
"I'm innocent. I ain't killed nobody. Never did ever kill nobody," Davis said in March 2025 in an interview from prison with ABC News. "They don't have no evidence against me. They can't even put me in Las Vegas."
Davis now says he was in Los Angeles the night of the Shakur killing and that he has never even read his own memoirs. He asserted that these were inflated by his co-author to generate book sales.
"I just gave him details of my life," Davis said. "And he went and did his little investigation and wrote the book on his own."
In the run-up to the trial, Davis's lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008 as a witness to the killing.
Whatever the verdict is, it is unlikely to satisfy those close to Shakur.
In May, the rapper's stepbrother Maurice Shakur filed a wrongful death lawsuit in civil court.
"There remain individuals who were involved in Tupac's murder who, for 30 years, have not been held accountable for their crimes," his complaint says.
The suit cites a recent TV documentary mini-series entitled "Sean Combs: The Reckoning," in which Davis says in an interview with police that Combs, now in prison himself, offered him $1 million to kill Shakur.

Mehreen Faruqi feels her Australianness is conditional on 'keeping my head down and my mouth shut'
Ask Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi what she was like as a child and you'll catch a revealing glimpse of her as an adult.
Growing up in Lahore, Pakistan, she would often watch her two older brothers play street cricket.
"I wanted to be like them," the deputy leader of the Greens told Annabel Crabb on ABC iview's Kitchen Cabinet.
"I wanted to do everything my two older brothers would do. And there were restrictions on what boys could do and what girls could do.
"You could do anything else but not cricket on the street … that's the only thing that I wanted to do."
After arguing for her right to play, Senator Faruqi soon found herself on the makeshift pitch.
"My mum said I was very stubborn," she said.
Life in Lahore
Senator Faruqi describes her hometown of Lahore as the "best city in Pakistan". But growing up in an environment beset with violence, due to numerous conflicts between India and Pakistan, was never easy.
She recalled sitting on her mother's lap in a trench as a two-year-old, a pencil between her teeth to stop them from shattering each time a bomb went off.
"It is scary as a kid to see planes being shot in the air, hearing bombs blast around you, hearing sirens every evening,"
"People who had been friends for centuries suddenly became enemies. It was horrendous."
Senator Faruqi was 25 and working as an engineer in Pakistan when she met her husband, a fellow engineer called Omar.
"The first day I started my job I actually saw him — I remember very, very clearly — in the lobby. That was it for me and that was it for him as well. I think it was really lucky," she said.
Senator Faruqi said their marriage was arranged but not forced.
"I've had clickbait headlines in newspapers in Australia, saying 'Exclusive: Feminist Greens MP condones arranged marriage'! [There's] no understanding of what that means. It's not like a forced marriage."
A family followed, but "corruption was setting in in Pakistan" by then and the decision was made to find a new home.
"We were like, 'I don't think we want our kid to have to deal with this, to fight a system'," she said.
So, with a young child and two suitcases, the senator and her husband moved to Australia in 1992.
Building a home in Australia
Senator Faruqi first glimpsed her future home through photos her father had taken when he had studied in Sydney under the Colombo Scheme in the 1950s.
"My dad, once he had been to Sydney, came back and he thinks Sydney is one of the most beautiful cities in the world," said Senator Faruqi.
So, it was in this city that they settled, enticed by the promise of work.
But the hustle of full-time work while raising children would eventually prove too much and the family moved to Port Macquarie, hoping for a slower life.
In a happy coincidence, they both found work as engineers with the same local council, and Senator Faruqi also became involved in community work in both land care and refugee support.
It was during this time she began to consider a career in politics.
"I thought, 'OK, maybe it's time to put my heart and soul into a political movement'," she said.
First Muslim woman in Australian parliament
Port Macquarie was a safe National seat, yet it didn't dissuade Senator Faruqi from joining the Greens and running for a spot in the NSW state parliament.
She described herself as having a "passion for equity" and "standing up for marginalised communities".
After unsuccessful runs in 2011 and 2012, she joined NSW's state parliament in 2013, becoming the first Muslim woman to sit in an Australian parliament.
In 2018, she made the jump to federal parliament and became Australia's first Muslim senator.
But according to Senator Faruqi, becoming the first Muslim woman inside the New South Wales parliament was not a consideration.
"You don't think about those things. I was running to use my experience and my skills to make this country a better place for everyone," she said.
The senator believes politics should be secular and is "annoyed" that some people have a stereotypical view of Muslims, particularly when it comes to a Muslim woman's agency.
"The first question that I was asked when I was elected to New South Wales parliament was, 'Would I compromise my religion for Greens policy?'" she said.
"I introduced the first ever bill in New South Wales history to decriminalise abortion.
"If you break that mould, people just get confused. They don't know what to do with you anymore."
For Senator Faruqi, nowhere has this been more prevalent for her than in parliament.
"There are people, your colleagues in your workplace, saying 'Ban Muslims from coming into this country' or denigrating your religion or telling you to pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan,"
"In which other workplace would even a skerrick of this be tolerated?
"[Parliament] is a tough place at the moment, I must say. And that has changed for the worse, I think, in the last few years."
Senator Faruqi said her Australianness was conditional on "keeping my head down and my mouth shut".
"My experience has been, as soon as you raise your head — disagree, express your opinions loudly and proudly as you should be able to do in a liberal democracy — that's when all hell breaks loose.
"It's like, 'Who are you? You're not even from here. Who are you to say what we should do?'"
There is 'no room for racism' against anyone
Senator Faruqi defended her protest of the government's decision to light up Canberra's parliament house with the colours of the Israeli flag shortly after October 7, calling the gesture "distressing".
"Of course, [October 7] was atrocious what happened. Killing any civilian, anywhere in the world is completely unacceptable and is completely wrong," she said.
"It was a government that I was criticising, both the Israeli government and the Australian government. And I think it's pretty important to say that we shouldn't be conflating criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism."
Senator Faruqi said Jewish people should "never be made to feel hate against them".
She added there was "no room for racism anywhere, against anyone", and said that Jewish people were experiencing anti-Semitism in Australia.
"And we must tackle that as we must tackle any other form of racism. Absolutely," she said.
But according to Senator Faruqi, not all political issues are "black and white", and nuance can be lost when talking to media.
"I'm a people's person. I grew up in a city of 15 million people, and I love people. And I would love for people to love me as well," she said.
"But I am there to represent some issues, some policies, that I went into politics for. And if it does alienate some people, it is what it is."
"I would like to have those conversations with people to change hearts and minds or even have my mind changed. You can't expect others to change if you're not open to that change yourself.
"Alienating people is something, obviously, that I don't want to do. And every opportunity I have, I will have difficult conversations with people."

Traffic to Trump’s Truth Social suffers double-digit decline over summer as rival sites see numbers climb

Traffic to Trump’s Truth Social suffers double-digit decline over summer as rival sites see numbers climb
Howard Polskin of TheRighting, a website that tracks conservative media, says he’s ‘really struck by the steepness of the plunge’
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
President Donald Trump's social media website has a bad case of the summertime blues — and the controversial offer of early access to his posts doesn't appear to be the cure.
Online traffic to Trump's Truth Social platform plummeted about 36 percent last month, even as larger rivals saw their numbers of users grow, according to a report Monday.
The site also suffered a slightly larger dip in users during June, The New York Times said, citing figures compiled by the Similarweb digital data company.
Howard Polskin, founder of TheRighting, which covers conservative media, told the Times he'd been tracking Truth Social's traffic numbers "for years" and was "really struck by the steepness of the plunge."
“When you think of how much Trump uses Truth Social as a megaphone you would think the numbers would be skyrocketing,” Polskin said.
Despite the situation at Truth Social, competitors including X, owned by Trump supporter and world's richest person Elon Musk, and Threads, owned by Facebook parent company Meta, have experienced increased traffic this summer, according to the Times.
The White House referred an inquiry from The Independent to Truth Social's publicly traded parent company, Trump Media & Technology Group, which didn't immediately respond.
The Times said a Truth Social spokesperson declined to comment on the site's traffic numbers.
The sharp drop in traffic to Truth Social comes as Trump Media has been selling subscriptions to Truth API — which provides near-instantaneous alerts to Trump's social media posts — at a cost of up to $100,000 a month.
Critics, including Democratic lawmakers, allege that the subscriptions enable insider trading because Trump's posts on subjects including tariffs and his Iran war can move markets.
“If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time,” Irene Aldridge, head of the Able Alpha Trading investment company, told The Associated Press earlier this month. "We have a President of the United States who has the front seat to all the action, who makes all the decisions, and he’s disclosing this ahead of time to a select group.”
The Truth Social spokesperson told the Times that congressional Democrats “continue to mischaracterize” the subscriptions “either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.”
Trump is the biggest shareholder in Trump Media, but he doesn't hold a formal position with the company. His eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., sits on its board and oversees a trust that controls his dad's nearly 115 million shares.
The president's stake is valued at about $1.1 billion, although its stock price has fallen about 80 percent since the company went public in March 2024, according to the Times.
The struggling company has also reported steep operating losses every quarter since then, including a net loss of $406 million against $871,000 in revenue, mostly from ads on Truth Social, during this year's first quarter, the Times said.
In April, it ousted CEO Devin Nunes, formerly a Republican House member from California, replacing him with former Hulu executive Kevin McGurn as it seeks to merge with nuclear fusion power company TAE Technologies in an all-stock deal valued at more than $6 billion.

11 weekend fires in Canada send new round of smoke to blanket the US

- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Canadian wildfire smoke is pouring over the U.S. border again as 11 new fires burn across British Columbia.
A state of emergency was declared in British Columbia Saturday, forcing thousands living around the Summerland area to evacuate their homes.
The largest of the regional fires has been dubbed the Bald Range Fire, and it had burned more than 33,000 acres by Sunday, according to The Washington Post.
As it did earlier this summer, fires from the Canadian wildfires have produced toxic smoke that is now billowing over the border and south into the U.S.
NOAA imaging shows wildfire smoke coverage in eastern Washington, Idaho, parts of Montana, Wyoming, northern Utah, northern Nevada, eastern Oregon, and northeastern California.
The impacted areas will see the smoke until midweek, forecasters say.
Air quality in the affected portion of the northwestern U.S. ranged from "unhealthy for sensitive groups" in Wyoming and southern Montana to hazardous in northeastern Washington, including Spokane.
The toxic clouds gave the region a hazy, orange hue over the last few days.
Nadège Dubuisson, a public health program supervisor with Multnomah County, told the New York Times that the wildfire haze is likely going to become a new normal for the region's summers.
“This is a good reminder that our summers are changing,” she said. “This is probably going to be our new reality, and we need to kind of be helping everybody get smoke-ready and wildfire-prepared.”
The smoke has already forced a number of cancellations in Spokane. The Spokane Indians canceled their scheduled Northwest League baseball games against the Eugene Emeralds, citing the air quality, according to The Spokesman-Review.
Country star Luke Bryan, who was also scheduled to play on Friday and Saturday, canceled both of the outdoor shows due to the poor air quality. He explained in a video that he had been "really, really" struggling during a show he played in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday due to the wildfire smoke.
According to IQAir, the poor air quality in Spokane will remain at either unhealthy for sensitive groups or unhealthy for the remainder of the week.
The smoke coverage comes just under a month after the Midwest and the East Coast were similarly blanketed with a toxic haze from Canadian wildfires.
Between July 18 and 20, smoke from fires in central and eastern Canada covered a stretch of the U.S. ranging from Illinois and Michigan in the Midwest to New York and Virginia in the East.
The coverage prompted an angry letter from Michigan Republicans accusing Canada of failing to do enough to prevent wildfires and mitigate smoke migration that affects their constituents. President Donald Trump has also threatened Canada over the wildfire smoke.

AI TikTok videos of violent vegetables could ‘radicalise’ young people, researchers warn
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
19:58:44 BST
03:58:44 KST

AI TikTok videos of violent vegetables could ‘radicalise’ young people, researchers warn
Such clips are circumventing the social media platform’s moderation policies that prohibit extreme violent material, GNET said
- Bookmark
AI-generated videos depicting fruits and vegetables committing gory acts of violence are spreading extremist agendas on TikTok and presenting a "radicalising potential" for young people, researchers have warned.
The Global Network on Extremism and Technology (GNET) said such clips bypass the social media platform’s moderation policies designed to strictly ban extreme violent content.
Disguised by a "cute" and "Pixar-like" visual style, some of these videos convey messages from extremist organisations including extreme right "accelerationism", "nihilistic violence extremism", and the so-called Islamic State (IS) group, GNET detailed in a Monday report.
These violent scenes form part of a broader trend of artificial intelligence clips showing humanlike food acting out melodramatic romance, betrayal and scandal storylines.
Experts from GNET, a research initiative backed by the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism (GIFCT), said: “Violence-based AI slops (low-quality, mass-produced digital content) reinforce a fascination with violence for violence’s sake, thereby allowing the so-called online ‘ode to violence’ to progressively gain ground among young people within the digital space.
“More concerning, however, is the escalation from absurdist AI-generated drama into explicitly graphic content.
“The radicalising potential of this content does not necessarily lie in ideological messaging alone, but in the normalisation of cruelty, emotional numbness and algorithmically amplified shock culture.
“In this sense, the transition from harmless surreal humour to graphic AI gore reflects a broader dynamic of online radicalisation: the gradual erosion of emotional boundaries through constant exposure to increasingly violent and dehumanising imagery.”
Animated foods use guns and axes to kill their enemies in some videos, while other videos are linked to specific criminal groups.
One example appears to replicate content from official IS videos with a carrot that makes a potato “explode”, the study found.
Another features a “Carrot Khalifah” telling his army “the Carrot State will rise again”, which experts said evokes an infamous slogan used by IS.
Two IS posts included hashtags often used by the terrorist group’s supporters to disseminate propaganda.
The report also highlighted an account that shares violent fruit and vegetable AI content and also references neo-Nazi terrorist organisation Atomwaffen Division, as well as the nihilistic violence subculture No Lives Matter.
Comments on the content include statements of extreme right-wing ideology, researchers said, with the message “potato supremacy” referring to white supremacy.
One post included in the report shows an AI image of a tomato that says: “No vegetables matter.”
The researchers said: “It is clear that AI-generative platforms are a crucial tool for creating viral content online, including violent and extremist content, as in the aforementioned cases.
“Food violence-based material empowered by AI is easily accessible, putting minors and youth at risk of inadvertently consuming graphic or disturbing content.
“Scenes with AI fruit and vegetables are simple and highly repetitive. They require no cognitive effort, provide constant rewards through unexpected scenes, and are perfect for endless scrolling.
“They are specifically designed for the algorithm, extremely quick to produce, and optimised for engagement. Hence, they act as attention traps.”
The team raised fears that users may “stumble” on the terror material and approach membership into the online ecosystems.
The comments could function as “communication hubs” where users provide extra details, GNET added.
“This type of content can lay the basis for the consumption of further violence-based audiovisual material, making young users fall into the trap of online radicalisation and audiovisual violence consumption.”
The authors called on TikTok to develop “countermeasures” to effectively limit such AI-generated content.
TikTok has been approached for comment.

A $20,000 “welcome bonus” that was never paid: how a Colombia-registered recruiter sent Peruvians into Russia’s war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
18:58:40 UTC
03:58:40 KST

On 9 August, Peru's foreign ministry officially reported that 459 Peruvians had been recruited into the Russian army. Of these soldiers, 11 have been killed, 114 are missing, and three have been captured by the Ukrainian army. Another 31 Peruvians were evacuated: three of them chose to stay in Europe, and the rest returned home.
As of 29 April 2026, Russia had drawn in at least 27,000 foreign nationals from more than 130 countries to take part in its war against Ukraine, the International Federation of Human Rights reports. The Peru case is part of Russia's systematic recruitment of foreigners into its military, often through deception. Some men were offered civilian jobs or roles far from the front, only to end up in the thick of the fighting.
Relatives of the recruited men held demonstrations in Peru
On 29 April 2026, relatives of men recruited into the Russian army demonstrated outside Peru's foreign ministry in Lima, urging the authorities to help bring their family members home, according to SwissInfo.
On 30 April, the Russian embassy in Peru responded that it agreed some Peruvian men were taking part in the war on Russia's side, but said this was their own voluntary choice. La República, however, reports that before leaving for Russia, the men were made to sign papers in Russian.
On arrival, their documents were taken, after which they underwent brief military training and were ultimately sent to the front. According to media reports, most were former military and police personnel lured by promises of jobs as security guards or civilian specialists, with salaries of $2,600–4,000 a month and bonuses of up to $20,000.
A “rear position” — until it isn’t
First, recruiters promise foreigners high salaries, signing bonuses, and “rear” or civilian positions. Debt traps and threats of deportation are also used. They lure people even through video games and chats. Once in Russia, recruits are forced to sign contracts, after which their documents are confiscated to keep them at the front. The contracts are often written in Russian, a language the foreign recruit does not understand.
Instead of the promised “rear positions,” recruits are thrown into infantry “meat assaults” after just a few days or a week of training. Mercenaries are killed while carrying out missions, while the wounded are often left on the battlefield without evacuation. Some men go missing or flee. Russia treats foreign mercenaries as “expendable labor,” according to leaked recordings cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
This is not an isolated case
Facing losses that now outpace its own mobilization, Russia has turned to citizens of other countries to keep its ranks filled in its war against Ukraine.
Kenya has become one of the largest sources of people recruited through deception. At first, Nairobi believed the number was only a few hundred, but the scale proved much larger. Nairobi thought Russia had recruited around 200 Kenyan citizens, but a new report says the figure is over 1,000. The scheme relied on fake job and education offers, after which recruits had their documents confiscated to keep them on the front line. The European Parliament found that Russia confiscates African recruits' documents and sends them to the front line in Ukraine.
In Cuba, recruiters promised people lucrative jobs, only to lure them into a trap. A Cuban captured near Kupiansk said he joined Russia's war effort under threat of deportation. The scale of the recruitment has been enormous. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that around 20,000 Cuban mercenaries have fought on Russia's side against Ukraine.
The Philippines case shows what awaits the recruited at the end of this pipeline. Ukrainian military intelligence identified a Filipino named John Patrick among Russian soldiers killed in Donetsk Oblast. He was sent into a "meat assault" after just one week of training. He did not speak Russian and carried only a piece of paper with his unit number and his commander's name. After he was wounded, he was left to die in a tree line without evacuation, and Ukrainian intelligence warned that any work in Russia now carries a real risk of forced deployment into an assault unit. The deception relied on promises of high salaries, non-combat positions in the rear, and fast-tracked Russian citizenship, after which recruits were sent into infantry assaults.

Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
18:58:00 UTC
03:58:00 KST

Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026
A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.
Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.
Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.
The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.
The government has declared a state of emergency.
What is the latest?
Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.
He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.
"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.
"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."
What's happening on the ground?
The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.
"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."
Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.
Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.
The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.
And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.
Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.
"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.
What do we know about the quake's size and location?
The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.
The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.
The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.
The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.
The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.
Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.
USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.
The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

RFK Jr takes aim at ‘unvetted’ ingredients in US food supply with new FDA proposal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
19:56:10 BST
03:56:10 KST

RFK Jr takes aim at ‘unvetted’ ingredients in US food supply with new FDA proposal
Neither of Monday's announcements are likely to immediately impact American diets, which are blamed for a host of chronic diseases such as obesity, diabetes and heart disease
- Bookmark
U.S. health officials have proposed a rule change that would require food producers to inform authorities prior to introducing new ingredients or additives into packaged and processed goods.
This measure seeks to alter a long-standing policy criticized by advocates as a regulatory loophole that has permitted thousands of unvetted substances to enter the nation's food supply.
Under the Food and Drug Administration's draft regulation, businesses would be required to document and present written safety justifications for new ingredients, allowing officials to examine potential hazards. Currently, manufacturers independently determine whether an ingredient qualifies as "generally recognized as safe," or GRAS, without any obligation to report or submit evidence to the agency, though a subset of companies does so voluntarily.
"Shifting to a mandatory notification system closes a decades-old information gap, giving the FDA the comprehensive visibility needed to enhance postmarket safety," acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas told reporters on Monday.
A 120-day public comment window has been opened by the agency to gather feedback on the plan.
Susan Mayne, former director of FDA's food program, observed that while the rule would provide the agency with improved oversight of the wide array of market additives, only a minor fraction would face formal evaluation.
"This is a reasonable first step towards a more complete inventory, but most self-affirmed GRAS ingredients will still not be reviewed for safety by the FDA, with food ingredient safety continuing to be risk-based," said Mayne, who is now a public health expert at Yale University.
Additionally, the FDA intends to make public a directory of submissions provided by manufacturers. Mayne emphasized that consumers must recognize that "inclusion on the list would not mean FDA thinks the ingredient is safe."
Scrutiny of ultraprocessed food continues, but with few details
In a related step, the agency announced it has finalized the federal government's initial formal definition for ultraprocessed foods, though specific wording and details remain undisclosed. The draft definition has been forwarded to the White House for further evaluation.
Public health proponents view a standardized definition as a critical milestone toward examining products linked to widespread chronic illnesses in the population. A formal baseline could facilitate expanded federal research and lay the groundwork for potential future restrictions or mandatory warning labels.
Neither measure is anticipated to instantly alter consumer eating habits, which remain heavy in sugar, sodium, and fats that contribute to conditions including heart disease, diabetes, and obesity. Nevertheless, these efforts align with the central agenda of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who assumed office with a pledge to target synthetic dyes, additives, and related compounds.
"These two actions will change how the federal government oversees what’s in our food and how we understand the foods that Americans eat," Kennedy said at an event Monday at HHS headquarters.
Ultraprocessed items undergo industrial manufacturing processes involving additives, colorings, preservatives, and other elements absent from home cooking. Common examples comprise soft drinks, sweetened breakfast cereals, snack chips, frozen pizzas, and processed grocery goods.
Researchers have spent more than ten years trying to establish standardized classifications for processed foods. However, broad criteria present challenges, as they may capture items such as whole wheat bread, granola, and yogurt—foods that undergo substantial processing yet maintain nutritional value. Recent classification frameworks have incorporated specific exemptions for items fulfilling established dietary standards regardless of their processing level.
FDA proposal would bring new insights on additives used by food companies
Approximately 10,000 chemical additives, including thickeners, preservatives, and packaging substances, are currently permitted across the domestic food supply.
Advocacy groups have maintained for years that many of these compounds lack rigorous safety evaluations due to the FDA practice allowing companies to self-certify additives under the "generally recognized as safe," or GRAS, designation.
Diamantas clarified on Monday that the proposed adjustments would not force every new ingredient to undergo a full agency evaluation, noting that mandatory pre-market approvals would require legislative action from Congress.
"What we’re doing is requiring companies that utilize the pathway to notify us of their conclusions so that we have greater visibility," Diamantas said.
Framework guidelines specify a 180-day window for the agency to review filings. Should health officials identify potential safety issues, they could seek supplementary data or request that the manufacturer postpone launching the ingredient.
Reform advocates argue that mere notification does not go far enough.
"It must also include strong, science-based safety standards and thorough, independent FDA review before chemicals are allowed in our food," said Melanie Benesh of the nonprofit Environmental Working Group.
Kennedy indicated that the Trump administration intends to petition Congress to grant the FDA expanded authority over food additives.
"Congress needs to give FDA the additional tools it needs to keep pace with the changing food supply and protect the American people," Kennedy said.
A rule change in the 1990s created what advocates call a loophole
In principle, any intentional food additive requires formal agency authorization unless deemed inherently safe. Since the late 1950s, federal oversight has acknowledged that staple items like vinegar and spices are widely consumed and traditionally regarded as harmless.
Although the agency originally evaluated GRAS exemptions directly, the process proved resource-intensive. Beginning in 1997, the FDA authorized food producers to independently decide whether a new substance was safe based on published research and expert consensus.
Over time, the inventory of self-certified GRAS substances expanded to encompass numerous natural and synthetic additives, which entered commercial distribution without external government evaluation.
Health advocacy organizations, including the Center for Science in the Public Interest, contend this framework created a "secret GRAS loophole."
Industry representatives maintain that corporate safety evaluations are every bit as comprehensive as formal regulatory reviews.

Police Scotland is assessing a series of posts published on a large Scottish tourism Instagram account claiming that explosive devices had been planted in shopping centres and universities across the country, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The posts appeared on the account 100scotland, which has around 140,000 followers and normally publishes photography of Scottish landmarks. The material was first reported by the Edinburgh Evening News.
We understand that Police Scotland has said it is aware of the posts and is assessing them to establish the source.
We have seen the screenshots. One of them is included below.
The posts claim to come from a group styling itself WF, which the account described as a terrorist organisation, and state that the group had decided to use the page to publicise what it called pranks. One post claimed that bombs had been planted in shopping centres, universities and other places where people gather in Scotland, ending with the line “Good luck finding our bombs”. A further post carried the words “Scotland will be dead”.
The posts directed readers to a Telegram channel and tagged a second Instagram account, inviting direct contact. The UK Defence Journal is not reproducing those handles. The tagged account has been linked to a SoundCloud profile whose listed location is given as Russia, though that detail is self-declared and carries no verification.
Timestamps on the posts indicate they were published within hours of each other, appearing alongside the account’s routine content, which included an image of the Kelpies at Grangemouth.
Claims of this kind circulated through social media accounts are common and are very rarely followed by any device being found. A wave of hoax bomb threats sent by email and social media has affected schools, hospitals and public buildings across the United Kingdom and elsewhere in Europe over the past several years, many of them traced to individuals operating from outside the country and some routed through Telegram channels advertising the service. Scottish schools and public buildings have been among those targeted in previous rounds, with evacuations ordered as a precaution and nothing subsequently located.
That does not make them costless, of course, as each threat has to be assessed, and where the assessment cannot immediately rule out a risk, buildings are cleared and police resources committed, which is generally the point of making the threat in the first place.
Making a hoax bomb threat is a criminal offence in Scotland, prosecuted under the Criminal Law (Consolidation) (Scotland) Act 1995, and carries a maximum sentence of seven years on indictment. Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or social media account is separately an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

Trump extends Jones Act waiver 90 days for foreign ships moving energy, fertilizers
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday extended a waiver for 90 days for foreign ships to transport goods, including oil, fertilizers and other fossil fuel products, among U.S. ports.
The president first waived the Jones Act on March 17 so that it would be easier to transport oil and refined fuels among ports, reducing price pressures after the start of the war with Iran.
The latest extension will take effect on August 17 and suggests that the U.S. might be preparing for continued price pressures as the Strait of Hormuz, a primary waterway for shipping oil and natural gas, remains effectively closed because of the war.
Unlike previous extensions, the Pentagon will consult with the Maritime Administration to decide which voyages are exempt from the 1920 law containing the Jones Act. The new waiver will only apply to cargo that are sources of energy and commodities related to agriculture such as fertilizers and soybean oil.
Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said the administration extended the waiver “to ensure our military and key industries maintain uninterrupted access to critical resources.” Rogers added that the waiver has increased domestic deliveries of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.

FBI teams with the NCAA to help athletes avoid sexual exploitation
INDIANAPOLIS (AP) — The FBI is teaming with the NCAA to start a program to combat sexual exploitation of college athletes whose private images are increasingly found and targeted online in an era when they use their name, image and likeness to enhance their own marketability.
The FBI, which unveiled the collaboration Monday, said bad actors typically target athletes through phishing, and also by password and PIN targeting and by portraying themselves as social media customer service representatives with urgent requests to reset passwords.
“Athletes have large social media followings, expended further by NIL activities that not only increases the exposure for targeting, it increases the leverage vendors believe they hold to exposure them,” said Shohini Sinha, assistant director of the FBI Victim Services Division. “There is a pressure to protect the clean image of their school, team and themselves.”
The FBI said hackers can steal images, then post or sell them, which can lead to sextortion, in which athletes can be harassed, stalked or even have the content that’s stolen from them posted on their own social media pages.
Neither the NCAA nor the FBI had specific numbers of athletes who were victimized by sextortion plots. Their partnership will go toward educating athletes.
“If we can play even a small role in preventing these crimes or getting justice or appropriate support for the people impacted by them, we will do everything we can to help,” NCAA Vice President of Enforcement Jon Duncan said.

Trump to sign executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

Trump signs order calling for spacing out childhood vaccines, against medical groups’ guidance
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held but discredited theory that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
The order advocates separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different single-disease shots and administering all childhood immunizations at separate appointments whenever possible. It also directs the nation’s health department to improve research on vaccines, which are already extensively studied, and present a plan to offer separate measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines for children, since that is not currently an option in the United States.
The renewed focus on vaccines marks a departure from the Trump administration’s recent efforts to emphasize less controversial health policies related to healthy eating, drug price negotiations and medical fraud crackdowns ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. Childhood vaccines — and how and when to give them in combination — go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Trump called the announcement a “major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science.”
Speaking about the order at the Oval Office on Monday, Trump repeatedly suggested the number or timing of vaccines could play a role in rising rates of autism spectrum disorder, even as scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link. The order also includes several changes to the childhood vaccine schedule that his health department has already attempted, but that have been blocked by a federal judge. A White House official who insisted on anonymity to brief reporters said Trump was within his right to provide his own recommendation through the executive order and said the lawsuit blocking the health department’s schedule was a separate issue.
Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said the announcement spreads uncertainty, fear and confusion where “there doesn’t need to be any of that.” He disputed Trump’s recommendations and said previous ones should stand.
“Science about vaccines and their efficacy has not changed,” he said. “The distribution of viruses and other pathogens in our environment has not changed. Children in this country have not changed in the last 48 hours.”
Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, slammed the executive order in a social media post, saying vaccines are safe and do not cause autism.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong,” the Louisiana senator wrote. “The President does not have the expertise to make these changes.”
Who is in charge of vaccine policy?
Even as the order calls for revised vaccine recommendations, states, not the federal government, have the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren. The order advises states with school vaccine mandates to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration’s preferred schedule, according to a White House fact sheet.
Last December, Trump ordered the Department of Health and Human Services to review how peer nations approach vaccine recommendations and consider revising U.S. guidance accordingly. The department responded by cutting the number of vaccines it recommends for every child, a move that has since been blocked in court.
Changes to federal childhood vaccine recommendations customarily require approval from the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The newly Senate-confirmed CDC director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, oversaw policies promoting vaccination of service members while in a leadership position at the U.S. Coast Guard.
However, public health law expert Lawrence Gostin at Georgetown University said the Supreme Court’s interpretation of Trump’s power may allow him to supersede Schwartz if she does not agree to new recommendations.
“This is clearly the first test for Dr. Erica Schwartz,” Gostin said in an email. “The President is placing her in an untenable position.”
Asked on a call with reporters why the president was advocating splitting MMR into three single-disease vaccines, the White House official did not provide any studies supporting the decision. They said that was Trump’s long-held view and that some countries provide individual measles vaccines in certain circumstances.
Kush Desai, a Trump spokesperson, told The Associated Press that the president is “one of countless parents who have voiced questions and concerns about the combined MMR vaccine” and said the plan to develop single-disease vaccines would “give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children,” ultimately increasing vaccine uptake.
Studies of babies and toddlers in the U.S. have shown that the use of combination shots for childhood vaccines, rather than single ones, increased the likelihood of completing all recommended vaccinations by the age of 2.
Announcement follows other Trump administration vaccine actions
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an anti-vaccine activist before he entered politics, set out to overhaul immunization guidance at DHS in the first year of Trump’s term. He fired an entire 17-member vaccine advisory committee, installing replacements who made far more restrictive recommendations that have since been halted by a federal judge. He also personally directed the CDC to abandon its position that vaccines do not cause autism, without supplying any new evidence to support the change.
Throughout his second term, Trump has been fixated on connecting autism to vaccines. He has recently ramped up pressure on Kennedy to identify the cause of autism, something Kennedy had pledged to do with new research unveiled last year. Trump publicly prodded the health secretary for an update on autism research in a Cabinet meeting last month.
“How are you doing on the autism research?” Trump asked.
“We will have an answer for you,” Kennedy said.
Scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between childhood vaccines and autism. Racine reiterated that point on Monday, noting that the potential link had been studied in “over 40 methodologically well-designed studies in over seven countries involving over 5 million children.”
“I’m not sure that there is anything that has been as thoroughly looked at as this question,” he said. “And the answer is unequivocally no.”
In the Oval Office, Kennedy repeated his assertion that he believes an unknown environmental factor is to blame for rising autism diagnoses and said that his department will deliver research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
Monday’s order comes as students are returning to classrooms around the country and the nation contends with a measles outbreak that experts say could result in the U.S. losing its measles elimination status.
Doctors have raised concerns that Trump’s falsehoods on vaccines could stoke vaccine hesitancy. Federal data shows U.S. kindergarten vaccination rates have been dropping, with the share of children with exemptions rising to an all-time high in the 2024-25 school year.

Associated Press writers Laura Ungar and Mike Stobbe contributed to this report. Swenson reported from New York.
