Drought declared in ‘almost three-quarters’ of England
- Almost 71.3% of England is in drought after the driest July on record and a fifth heatwave, causing parched lands and low river levels.
- The UK government has imposed water-use restrictions, including hosepipe bans, affecting over 27 million people to manage scarce water resources.
- Experts warn climate change is increasing extreme weather, with long-lasting impacts on farming and the environment across England and Wales.
AI generated
LONDON - Some 71.3 per cent of England is in drought, the UK government said on Aug 10, after the nation experienced its driest July on record, with a fifth heatwave and scant rain forecast for the week ahead.
Parks and fields that are usually green at this point in the year were parched and yellow, according to AFP photos, as river levels dwindled and farmers battling low crop yields warned of possible food shortages.
“Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought as conditions worsen following a dry start to August,” the environment department said, as parts of the central Midlands and north-east England joined other areas of the country experiencing prolonged dry weather.
“All regions of the country are experiencing pressure on their water resources,” the department said, with “nowhere” in the UK having a “normal” status.
The Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) said most of England is experiencing a “flash drought”, which develops quickly and is the result of very low rainfall and high temperatures.
It is the third drought Britain – usually known for its unpredictable wet weather – has experienced in five years.
More than 50 per cent of England was declared to be in drought at the end of July.
Britain is also facing its fifth heatwave of a 2026 summer that has seen multiple temperature records being broken.
As much of Europe braces for another heatwave and prolonged dry conditions, scientists warn climate change is making extreme weather events more intense and frequent.
England and Wales both experienced the driest July on records, the UK’s Met Office weather agency announced earlier, with England recording just 10 per cent of its usual long-term average rainfall.
“There are warnings of more dry weather and another heatwave on the way, with temperatures tipped to reach the mid-30s in some places,” DEFRA said.
The government has imposed irrigation restrictions on farmers and introduced a hosepipe ban in some regions, with more than 27 million people living under water-use restrictions.
There are now 45 million people living in a drought area, according to official figures.
The total population of the United Kingdom is estimated at 69.3 million.
“We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment,” said the Environment Agency’s Tony Grayling, who heads the National Drought Group. AFP

TEHRAN – Thirteen Iranian students aged below 12 have showcased their scientific, technical capabilities, and creativity ranking second and third in different leagues of the RobotChallenge 2026 which was held in Beijing, China.

The scientific competition aimed to promote knowledge, foster international networking, and establish scientific authority in AI and programming.
Enhancing algorithmic thinking, problem-solving skills, teamwork, developing innovative ideas, starting new businesses, and expanding AI engineering and programming were among the other objectives of the contest.

Ukraine confirms the strike
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) confirmed the strike in a Telegram post hours later, specifying that the attack hit the plant’s central gas fractionation unit (CGFU).
“The plant produces raw materials that are critically important to Russia’s military-industrial complex,” the General Staff said, adding that the strike is conducted as part of broader efforts to reduce the military-economic potential of Russia’s war machine.
No casualties were confirmed at the site, and neither the General Staff nor regional governor Moor disclosed the number of drones involved in the attack.
Zelensky praises the strike’s reach
President Volodymyr Zelensky hailed the strike as a significant achievement in his statement on Telegram, noting that Tobolsk is now within Ukraine’s reach.
He added that even deeper strikes would follow, “which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary.” 
Russia’s Supreme Court Bars Yabloko, Only Pro-Peace Party, From Upcoming Elections
Citing Russia’s own internal polling data, Zelensky said that a growing number of Russians want the war to end.
“This is the first time in Russia’s history that they no longer have a secure strategic rear,” he continued, adding that “for the first time, they cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea.
His remarks come as Russia’s Supreme Court removed on Monday, Aug. 10 the only registered liberal and openly pro-peace party Yabloko from the upcoming State Duma elections in September.
North Korea has become one of Russia’s most critical wartime partners. Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) estimated that North Korea supplies between 25% and 40% of Russia’s artillery shells.
Moscow signed a defense pact with Pyongyang on June 19, 2024, with both countries officially recognizing North Korean troop deployments in April 2025.
Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 additional North Korean troops and more ballistic missile launchers, according to Zelensky on July 29.
Among Russia’s largest plants
The damaged unit processes about 6.6 million tons (around 14.5 billion pounds) of feedstock annually, and forms a key part of the production complex at one of the largest petrochemical enterprises in both Russia and Europe.
According to the General Staff, the facility produces butadiene, isobutylene, maleic anhydride, and MTBE, a high-octane oxygenate additive – all used in the manufacturing process of rocket fuel components, aviation fuel, and composite materials for drones.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces will continue to systematically carry out measures aimed at ending the armed aggression of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff said.
As both sides continue to exchange strikes, this latest attack adds to a broader series of Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s critical oil and energy infrastructure, as well as military-industrial sites deep inside Russian territory.
On Aug. 8, Ukrainian attack drones struck two major Russian oil refineries, sparking large fires at the Syzran and Ilsky facilities as part of an overnight barrage across multiple Russian regions.
The coordinated refinery strikes follow another deep-strike operation on Aug. 7, targeting Russia’s vulnerable civilian logistics network.
On the same day, Ukrainian drone struck a Wildberries warehouse in Yekaterinburg, over 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the Ukrainian border, as part of a sustained, effective campaign against Wildberries, Russia’s largest e-commerce retailer.
Meanwhile, Russia has focused its attacks on Ukraine’s defense industry, logistics, ports, railways, and energy facilities supporting critical infrastructure.

Russian court bars from parliamentary ballot the only party opposing the conflict in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:53:02 UTC

Russian court bars from parliamentary ballot the only party opposing the conflict in Ukraine
MOSCOW (AP) — Russia’s highest court on Monday ordered the only party opposing the Kremlin’s military action in Ukraine to be removed from the ballot in next month’s parliamentary election.
The Supreme Court annulled the registration of Yabloko — which is Russian for “apple” — after an appeal from a pro-Kremlin party. Last month, the Central Election Commission had initially allowed Yabloko on the ballot along with 10 other parties.
Once a leading liberal voice in parliament and often critical of the government, Yabloko later lost its bloc of seats in the State Duma as the Kremlin tightened its grip on Russian politics.
In recent years, Yabloko was the only registered opposition party that opposed sending troops into Ukraine.
Its campaign slogans included “For a ceasefire agreement, diplomacy and peace!” “Our goal is to prevent nuclear war!” and “For a Russia free from fear and political repressions!”
Veteran liberal politician Grigory Yavlinsky, who co-founded Yabloko in the 1990s and chairs its political committee, deplored the ruling and said the party would appeal it.
“Barring Yabloko from the election means a refusal to engage in dialogue with those who ask questions that make the authorities uncomfortable,” Yavlinsky said in an online statement. “We hope the authorities will heed the public demand for peace, freedom, and life without fear, and change their policy.”
Yabloko’s platform draws strong support
Many Russian opposition figures in exile had urged voters to back Yabloko, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny, and politicians Ilya Yashin and Vladimir Kara-Murza.
“I believe it’s morally and politically right to support the Yabloko party,” Navalnaya said in an Aug. 6 statement on Telegram, noting the party’s anti-war stance.
Yabloko chairman Nikolai Rybakov, who was in the courtroom Monday, sought to distance the party from what he described as unwarranted support from Navalnaya and other Kremlin foes living abroad in an apparent attempt to prevent its removal from the ballot.
In the meantime, social media buzzed with videos supporting Yabloko. Many didn’t contain political slogans but instead showed young men and women holding apples when asked their voting preference for the Sept. 18-20 election or dancing to Russian songs that referenced apples.
Rybakov told the court the party wasn’t paying for the videos, saying that people who posted it were backing Yabloko “simply because they want to live in Russia and don’t want to get killed.”
The authorities likely initially allowed Yabloko on the ballot to give Russians an outlet for their discontent while also showing, through the party’s traditionally low vote count, that few people support its stand on Ukraine, said Nikolay Petrov, senior research fellow at the NEST Centre, founded by exiled Russian tycoon and opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
But Yabloko’s campaign for peace struck a chord and upended the Kremlin’s calculations.
Now “the Kremlin is facing a rather difficult task, to come out of the situation with minimal losses,” Petrov said, because kicking the party off the ballot is effectively “demonstrating that they’re afraid of what Yabloko stands for.”
Yavlinsky said the court’s ruling “speaks volumes about the importance of our platform — far more than any official election results ever could.”
He added that “the public demand for peace and freedom today has proven far stronger than the authorities anticipated.”
Kremlin-aligned parties bash Yabloko
Several Kremlin-aligned parties have assailed Yabloko for its stance on Ukraine, and some even urged authorities to investigate it.
Sergei Mironov, head of A Just Russia Party, called on the Prosecutor General’s Office and the Justice Ministry to “look closely” at Yabloko and “give a legal assessment to their actions.”
“A party that openly opposes the special military operation, promises a shameful peace, and supports foreign agents is running for the State Duma,” Mironov said, using the Kremlin’s term to describe the 4-year-old conflict.
Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said Yabloko is not supporting President Vladimir Putin’s policies and has not helped “those suffering, those fighting on the front line.”
The Motherland Party filed the lawsuit with the Supreme Court demanding Yabloko’s removal from the ballot. It accused Yabloko of copyright infringement and exceeding campaign spending limits. The party also viewed Yabloko’s stance on Ukraine as unlawful and tantamount to calling for the violation of Russia’s territorial integrity.
Rybakov and lawyers representing the party in the Supreme Court on Monday rejected the accusations.
A crowd of supporters greeted Rybakov and other Yabloko representatives with applause as they entered the courthouse in central Moscow.
Yabloko members faced a Kremlin crackdown
Yabloko has faced increased pressure in recent years as the Kremlin ramped up its crackdown on dissent to levels unseen since the Soviet era.
Several prominent Yabloko members were jailed or designated as “foreign agents” — a label that brings additional government scrutiny and aims to discredit the recipient. As a result, its most prominent members were not on the ticket.
Maxim Kruglov, a deputy chairman and former member of the Moscow city council, was convicted in June of spreading false information about the Russian army and sentenced to seven years in prison.
Another senior member of the party, Lev Shlosberg, is on trial for similar charges in his native city of Pskov, facing up to 10 years in prison if convicted. It’s the third criminal case brought against Shlosberg in the last two years. He has also been designated a “foreign agent.”
That designation was also slapped on Boris Vishnevsky, another Yabloko deputy chairman, in 2024. The designation forced Vishnevsky to step down from the St. Petersburg city council after legislation was adopted later that year, barring “foreign agents” from participating in elections or holding public office.

Contiguous US breaks its record for hottest month ever, NOAA says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:53:02 UTC

Contiguous US breaks its record for hottest month ever, NOAA says
The contiguous United States sizzled to its hottest month ever last month, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. July averaged 76.89 degrees Fahrenheit (24.94 degrees Celsius) across the Lower 48 states, eclipsing the Dust Bowl’s July 1936 by an eighth of a degree.
KENSINGTON, Maryland (AP) — The contiguous United States sizzled to its hottest month ever last month, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
July averaged 76.89 degrees Fahrenheit (24.94 degrees Celsius) across the Lower 48 states, eclipsing the Dust Bowl’s July 1936 by an eighth of a degree. Records go back to 1895.
“It’s not good when you’re breaking records from the Dust Bowl, which we are in this case,” said meteorologist Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections. “And that was a crazy sort of situation where you put tens of millions of people in motion. You had this great migration because of the drought and the heat that hit the center of the U.S. — just a cataclysmic event in U. S. history. If we’re exceeding records from The Dust Bowl, that says that we’re in deep trouble.”
Although it was unusually cool in Alaska, hotter-than-normal conditions blanketed the Lower 48, with the most excessive heat in the Mountain West, Southwest, Northern Plains and Southeast. The heat was so widespread that every one of the Lower 48 states was at least 1 degree Fahrenheit (nearly 0.6 degrees Celsius) warmer than the 20th century average, said Russ Vose, chief of monitoring at NOAA’s National Center for Environmental Information.
The heat in the Dust Bowl years was more concentrated in parts of the Midwest and was aggravated by agricultural practices at the time, Vose said.
What’s happening now is due to the burning of coal, oil and gas, scientists said.
“Extremely high temperatures across the continental U.S. this summer, along with intense drought and fire conditions, are absolutely consistent with the climate change signal,’ said Katharine Jacobs, a climate scientist at the University of Arizona.
The biggest driver of the record heat was nighttime lows that smashed the old mark for hottest minimums by 0.7 degrees, NOAA said. Hotter nights are a classic sign of human-caused climate change, according to scientists and several studies in peer-reviewed literature. NOAA’s calculation is based on averaging 24 hours of temperature, not just highs or lows.
“If you’re talking heat waves, that nighttime low is incredibly important for determining total heat stress,” Masters said. “So if it doesn’t cool off at night, your body doesn’t have time to readjust to all the heat.”
As nighttime temperatures increase, more people die and lose sleep, studies show.
The years 2021 and 1936 tie for America’s hottest summer, which is June through August. Through July, 2026 is a shade cooler than 2021, which was powered by record heat in June.
Because of climate change, Masters said, “this may be one of the coolest years we’re gonna experience for the rest of our lives.”
What’s needed, Masters said, is “to stop burning so many fossil fuels. We also need to be spending money to adapt to the new climate that we’ve put in place.”

Russia's monthly production of key missiles is running 10–20% above target, while output of some models is even higher, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine, published on Aug. 10.
According to Skibitskyi, Russia produced 87 Kh-101 cruise missiles in July, reaching 140% of its planned monthly output. Moscow had set a target of 72 Kh-101 missiles for both July and August.
A similar pattern can be seen with the Kalibr cruise missile: Russia planned to produce 26 in each month but manufactured 29 in July, exceeding its target by 11%. The largest overperformance was recorded in Kh-35 production, which reached 200% of the planned monthly output, the official added, without specifying the exact number of missiles produced.
Skibitskyi added that, as of Aug. 3, Russia had already fulfilled its annual production targets for the Zircon and Oniks missiles, with 33 and 60 units manufactured in the first seven months, respectively.
Skibitskyi said Moscow has significantly increased ballistic missile production partly because Russian defense plants are now operating under a "simplified system of technical controls" for missile production.
"However, there is another explanation here — the Russians have also been able to increase ballistic missile production because they have now stopped producing Kinzhal missiles. Accordingly, the rocket fuel is no longer going to the Kinzhal, but to other ballistic missiles," Skibitskyi said.
"In addition, they have suspended the production and use of Kh-32 missiles, so the funds and components allocated for them have been redirected to other types of missiles, which are considered more effective."

Over 95 earthquakes hit Iran in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 96 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from August 1st to 7th, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 78 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, 13 earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and four earthquakes with a magnitude between 4 and 5 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, two had a magnitude of 4.1 on the Richter scale, which occurred on August 4th in Hormozgan and Kerman provinces.
Among the provinces of the country, Semnan experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 17, followed by North Khorasan with 11, Yazd and Kerman each with seven earthquakes.
During the same period, no earthquakes were recorded in Tehran, Isfahan, Alborz, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Kurdistan, Gilan, andMarkazi provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Russia bars only anti-war party 'Yabloko' from September parliamentary elections
Russia's Supreme Court on Monday barred the country's only anti-war party, Yabloko (Apple), from running in September's parliamentary elections. About a hundred protesters gathered outside the courthouse chanting, "Shame! Shame!" after the ruling was delivered.
The court thereby upheld a suit brought by a pro-Kremlin nationalist party, stripping voters opposed to the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine of their last option on the ballot.
"The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted," judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said.
About a hundred supporters, mostly young people, gathered outside the courthouse, chanting "Shame! Shame!" after the ruling was delivered.
Addressing them after the hearing, Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov said the party would appeal the decision.
"We have a long way ahead and we have a big and important task: to stop deaths and bring the peace back," he said.
"Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added.
Putin opponents jailed, exiled or dead
Russia opened a criminal case in 2024 against Yabloko's Lev Shlosberg, one of the few remaining anti-war Kremlin critics still in the country. He was charged again in 2025 for allegedly spreading false information about Russia's army, a new charge announced three days before he was to be released from house arrest.
With most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents jailed, exiled or dead, Yabloko is the only liberal party still operating in Russia.
Read moreThe mysterious fates met by Putin critics
The party has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.
Both are listed as "extremists" in Russia.
A poll conducted earlier this year showed Yabloko ("apple" in Russian) at just 3 percent support – short of the 5-percent threshold needed to enter Russia's lower house.
With the Kremlin tightening its control over elections, Yabloko has failed to win seats in the State Duma since 2003.
Since then, every parliamentary vote has been won by the ruling United Russia party, which backs Putin.
Efforts to end the Ukraine war through diplomacy have so far failed, with Putin pushing hardline territorial demands to end the fighting and ruling out talks with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Independent polls show most Russians favour peace negotiations with Kyiv.

02:47:44 KST

At the end of July, Donald Trump announced that a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it was reported that another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe.
Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitly rejected the sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.”
In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazen violation of the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle.
Formal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largely destroyed and the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first building contract issued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievous miscalculation in which Israel’s prime minister also played his part.
In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue a scorched earth project of revenge following the Hamas massacre of October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruption charges first laid more than five years ago.
Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point.
Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recent polling suggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza.

Tensions in the Arctic: Greenland issues sharp rebuke to Trump-linked oil company
Greenland’s government issued a “strong warning” last week after a new Texas oil company linked to US President Donald Trump moved equipment intended for exploratory drilling ashore without the required approval. Nuuk’s authorities must now walk a tightrope between stabilising relations with the US and resisting Trump’s territorial ambitions.
A Texas oil company that wants to extract what could amount to billions of barrels of oil from East Greenland’s Arctic basin has crossed a red line before even starting to drill.
In a statement issued on July 30, Greenland’s mineral resources authority said it had become aware that Greenland Energy – a Texas oil company founded last year – had transferred drilling equipment ashore on a remote stretch of the island’s eastern coast.
“All future logistical matters must be advised and approved by the mineral resources authority – before they are carried out,” the government said.
Greenland Energy has claimed that $1 trillion in crude oil may lie beneath the Jameson Land region. The firm thus announced plans to spend $60 million drilling two exploratory wells to find out.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Greenland Energy’s chairman and a significant shareholder, Larry Swets, "appears to enjoy access to Trump’s circle", The Guardian reported. Swets has said the oil project is “not related to American annexation”. Carol Craig, a US navy veteran involved with Trump's Golden Dome missile-defence plan for Greenland, reportedly sits on the company's board.
Read moreDoes the US need to ‘own’ Greenland to build Trump's Golden Dome missile shield?
“The exploration for oil by Greenland Energy is relatively unproblematic,” said Lukas Wahden, an associate fellow of the Russia programme at George Washington University, in an interview on FRANCE 24. “The issue that caused political controversy last week is that the US company Greenland Energy didn’t coordinate with the relevant Greenlandic authorities in its disembarking of equipment for the exploration that is planned in East Greenland.”
The move by the US firm “stepped on a number of toes” given the delicate political context, according to Wahden. Trump flummoxed his NATO allies in January when he announced he must “have” Greenland – even by force, if necessary.
He also threatened tariffs against European countries opposing his conquest of the mineral-rich Arctic territory, an autonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark.
The shock announcement triggered the biggest crisis in transatlantic relations in decades. European NATO members deployed troops in Greenland for a military exercise designed to show the world – and the United States – that they were prepared to defend Danish sovereignty.
To defuse the crisis, Denmark, Greenland and the United States established a working group early this year to find a framework for the future of Greenlandic and US relations.
Greenland’s authorities must now “walk a tightrope”, said Wahden. The main question is whether the behaviour of a private US company will be raised within the negotiation group, “about which we know relatively little”.
Read moreTaking over Greenland, a long-standing US obsession
Delicate diplomatic context
If Trump sides with Greenland Energy, it would disrupt “this very sensitive and very important diplomatic process and undermine some of the gains that the Greenlandic authorities in particular have been making in trying to stabilise the relations with the United States over the last couple of months”, said the expert.
At the height of the transatlantic crisis he sparked in January, Trump suddenly pivoted from military intervention to a NATO-brokered compromise.
The US president announced after a meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Davos that he had found “a solution” to Greenland, adding that he was rescinding the tariffs scheduled to go into effect in February.
But Trump’s appetite for Greenland has not subsided after the dramatic climbdown in January, said Mikaa Blugeon-Mered, a Greenland specialist, on FRANCE 24.
Read moreAcquire territory, export culture wars: How to make sense of Trump’s ‘new imperialism’
He cited the US president’s July interview with the right-wing Real America’s Voice News host Steve Gruber, during which the president predicted that Greenland would come under US control before the end of his presidential term.
For Blugeon-Mered, the unauthorised movement of equipment by Greenland Energy, which stopped short of actual drilling, could lead to a stand-off between Trump and Greenland’s authorities.
“If Greenland doesn’t give the company permission to drill between now and October, the question that will arise is whether or not Trump [will] send in the army or employ security methods that will allow this company – with collaborators close to him – to go forward,” said Blugeon-Mered.
For the moment, the power struggle remains between the US firm and Greenland’s government. “We have a company that claims to be ready [to drill] after engaging costs and transferring its material. On the other hand, we have a government that responds by saying, ‘You don’t have authorisation to launch the drilling.’”
“It’s a free-for-all situation with political, economic and technical implications,” said Blugeon-Mered.

The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:47:18 UTC
02:47:18 KST

It is not yet clear to what extent Meta’s new smart glasses will live up to the nickname of “pervert glasses” – bestowed in recognition of the obvious appeal of wearable cameras to voyeurs. The past week has seen rising criticism of the devices, which in the UK have been banned by the pub chain Wetherspoons and the theatre group ATG, as well as restaurants, schools and members’ clubs. These organisations deserve praise for standing up for privacy. By contrast, regulators appear once again to be on the back foot.
There have, inevitably, already been reports of women being mistreated. Earlier this year the BBC spoke to several who had been filmed without their consent, with footage subsequently uploaded to social media. In one case, the content creator demanded a fee to remove it. In the year to March 2025, image-based sexual abuse and cyberflashing were responsible for more than half of an 11% increase in reported sexual offences in England and Wales. Normalisation of smart glasses would, clearly, make such offences easier to commit.
Worrying as this is, it is not the only reason to be concerned. Privacy has much wider significance and most people, as the businesses banning smart glasses from their premises have recognised, do not want to be filmed as they go about their lives. While videoing in public is not illegal, this does not give smart glasses wearers the right to place others under involuntary surveillance. An LED light that blinks when the camera is in use, and cannot be disabled, is not an adequate safeguard, whatever Meta might think. Pubs, parks, beaches and workplaces are not film sets.
Having invested $80bn in its latest product, Mark Zuckerberg’s company is unlikely to give up easily on its ambition to make the glasses, which have been likened to face-mounted smartphones, as ubiquitous as the handheld kind. More than a decade after the first smart glasses, made by Google, flopped, Meta has bet heavily on making its latest version more stylish, functional and affordable – with UK prices starting at £269. The choice of Kylie Jenner to front this summer’s advertising campaign, and the slogan “Never miss a moment”, aimed at parents of young children, appear calculated to dispel fears about how the glasses will be used by sexually predatory men.
Like most digital devices, these ones can be helpful as well as harmful. As aids for people who are blind or visually impaired, smart glasses that can read text or describe images have been described as life-changing. Any restrictions, in the UK or elsewhere, should be crafted so as to enable such uses to continue – just as guide dogs are exempted from rules about pets. But while the benefits that smart glasses offer to groups of people with specific needs should be recognised, this must not be allowed to distract from their potential to cause harm.
Tech regulation is difficult. But given the UK government’s recent moves towards restricting smartphone use among young people, and the public outcry regarding sexualised AI imagery, it is disappointing that ministers have so far had almost nothing to say about the rollout of wearable hidden cameras. While the tech companies market their products as tools to be used, one of the key lessons of the last two decades is that users are rarely, if ever, as in control as they would like to be. Ministers and regulators should be active, not passive, as Meta intentionally blurs the line between looking and filming.

The largest amount, UAH 174.6 million, consisted of so-called "combat allowances" paid to those who did not actually perform combat duties. Another UAH 22.8 million was paid based on forged documents, and UAH 4.7 million was lost due to official negligence.

In 82 criminal cases, 131 individuals have been notified of suspicion. A total of 148 indictments have been filed with the court.
Fictitious medical exemptions, illegal deferrals, and aiding in evasion of military service. "Behind every such "service" lies not only a bribe but also a direct blow to the state's mobilization capacity. Approximately 23 million hryvnias in illicit gains have been documented. Payments were made not only in cash but also in the form of cars and fuel vouchers," Kravchenko said. In 126 criminal cases, 52 officials have been notified of suspicion. The chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council said that the government will no longer allow the Houthis to monopolise decisions on war and peace, following a recent escalation that included a Houthi attack on the port of Mokha in southwestern Yemen.
Speaking at a meeting with ambassadors of countries sponsoring Yemen's political process, Rashad al-Alimi said on Monday that the Yemeni state did not initiate the latest escalation but would not allow its commitment to peace to give the Houthis the freedom to decide when and where to attack, according to a statement by his office.

He said the government has prioritised peace and exercised restraint, facilitating air and port traffic and the flow of goods while cooperating with UN, regional and international efforts.
‘Illegitimate gains’
Al-Alimi said the latest developments showed that the political and military equation had changed and warned that “the period of Houthi attacks without consequences has ended.”
“The state will no longer allow the (Houthis) militias to monopolise the decision to start the confrontation, its timing, location and scale, and then also monopolise the decision on when it should stop,” he said.
He called on the international community to protect civilians, civilian facilities, and commercial ports, respect state sovereignty, and reject the use of missiles and drones to obtain “illegitimate gains.”
The ambassadors strongly condemned the latest Houthi attacks on government forces, civilian sites, and economic facilities, including the port, as well as attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels, according to the statement.
On Sunday, at least seven civilians and military personnel were killed and around 35 others injured in the Houthi attack on the port near the Bab al Mandeb Strait and nearby residential areas, according to official Yemeni sources.
Fighting has periodically intensified along several Yemeni fronts since last month, leaving dozens of people dead and wounded on both sides.
Yemen had been under a relative lull since April 2022 after nearly 12 years of war between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Iranian-backed Houthis, who seized control of the capital Sanaa and large parts of the country in 2014.

Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect? | Nils Pratley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:44:09 UTC
02:44:09 KST

Anybody who followed the supposed “clampdown” on bankers’ bonuses after the great financial crash in 2008 knew what to expect when water company bosses became a similar target for a bash in the bonus department. We would see the waterbed principle in action: when you push down in one area of remuneration, such as the performance-related stuff, another tends to go up.
Back in the day, banks invented “role-based allowances” – salary top-ups – to “compensate”, as they put it, their top earners for being subject to EU caps on bonuses. No executive was seriously inconvenienced by forgoing the chance of an astronomical (but not guaranteed) bonus and getting a smaller (but still hefty) increase in fixed pay instead. Some even preferred greater certainty over what they would take home.
In water-land, the Labour government arrived in 2024 promising to “ban the payment of bonuses to polluting water bosses until they have cleaned up their filth”, which generated a few pleasing headlines. But the flaw in the resulting Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 was obvious. While the regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, was given powers to block performance-related bonuses at the worst environmental and financial miscreants, it could do nothing formally about other payments.
Thus – surprise, surprise – salary increases, allowance awards and, most of all, retention payments have proliferated. After the English and Welsh companies published their annual reports last month, this newspaper found that overall reported pay packets rose by 1.5% to £25.3m for chief executives and chief financial officers for the year. It was the second year in a row that a bonus ban had resulted in higher overall pay across the sector.
One can usually rely on Thames Water to muddy things further, and its post-annual report contribution was the news that the chief financial officer, Steve Buck, who was paid £591,000 in the financial year to March, got a delayed £1m signing fee at the end of July. As for retention payments for other executives that were “paused” after a political kerfuffle a year ago, the company has “entered into 14 agreements” to “resolve its liability for any potential claims”.
The government is shocked, or pretends to be. “It is unacceptable that one of the worst-performing water companies is handing out huge payments to its executives when it should be focusing on improving performance and rebuilding public trust,” a spokesperson for the environment department said.
Again, though, one must ask: what did ministers think would happen? It’s easy to agree that executives of underperforming monopolies are grossly overpaid but it was fantastically naive on the part of politicians to think a ban on bonuses would not result in alternative wheezes. It was predictable.
Water companies in general have deployed the retention manoeuvre in less-than-transparent – or just shameless – ways, it should be added. Helen Campbell, the interim executive director of Ofwat, was clearly correct last month when she complained that customers’ trust is harmed when remuneration committees make decisions that “give the appearance of circumventing the rule” or aren’t explained.
The point, though, is that the government left the door wide open to such behaviour. If ministers were relying on remuneration committees to obey the “spirit” of their reforms, they were born yesterday. Restricting bonuses is not the same as restricting overall pay. And Ofwat can use only the powers it was given by parliament.
The dance now moves to the regulator’s review, due in the autumn, of whether the rules should be strengthened. Maybe it will yield something different in the prime minister Andy Burnham’s undefined era of “greater public control”. On past experience, however, believe it when you see it.

Iran’s Supreme Leader appoints six top military commanders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:40:10 UTC
02:40:10 KST

ALBAWABA- Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei formally appointed six senior military commanders, consolidating wartime leadership structures amid ongoing US-Iran tensions, stalled efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and a recent meeting between the Iranian president and the supreme leader.
The decrees replace or formalize roles left vacant or interim after the killings of several top officers in the US-Israeli strikes that began the conflict on 28 February 2026.
According to decrees published by the supreme leader’s office and reported by Iranian state media and international outlets, Major General Ali Abdollahi was appointed Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces, succeeding Lieutenant General Abdolrahim Mousavi, who was killed in the initial strikes. Abdollahi previously commanded the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters.
The decree directs him to enhance the capabilities and readiness of the Armed Forces and Basij, ensure effective responses to conventional, modern, cognitive and hybrid threats, and complete the integration of the General Staff with the Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters. Brigadier General Kioumars Heydari was named his deputy.
Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi was promoted to major general and appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, succeeding Lieutenant General Mohammad Pakpour, also killed early in the war. Vahidi, a longtime hardliner, previously headed the Quds Force, served as defence minister from 2009 to 2013 and interior minister from 2021 to 2024, and had held senior interim IRGC roles. He is under US sanctions and subject to an Interpol notice linked to the 1994 AMIA bombing in Argentina. Major General Mostafa Izadi was appointed deputy commander-in-chief of the IRGC.
Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei was appointed commander of the IRGC Navy, succeeding Alireza Tangsiri, who was killed in an Israeli strike in March 2026. Ozmaei had long commanded the IRGC Navy’s Fifth Naval Region responsible for approaches to the Strait of Hormuz and had already been functioning in the top role; the decree formalizes the appointment. Hossein Taeb, former head of the IRGC Intelligence Organization, was named head of the Basij Organization, marking a notable return after earlier setbacks.
Khamenei’s decrees emphasize strengthening defence capabilities, revolutionary readiness, deterrence and responses to threats against the Islamic Republic. Some positions, notably those of Vahidi and Ozmaei, had already been filled on an interim basis; the formal decrees place the supreme leader’s clear authority on the structure.
The appointments followed reports of a rare seven-hour meeting between President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
Pezeshkian said the discussion covered livelihoods, markets, employment, housing, the impact of sanctions, national resilience, unity, the repercussions of the war, military affairs, resource management, foreign exchange and energy issues, and economic ties with foreign partners.
According to the president, the supreme leader’s overriding message was the need to preserve internal unity amid external pressures. Mojtaba Khamenei has maintained a very low public profile since succeeding his father, who was killed in the 28 February strikes that also reportedly injured him. Communication with him has been described as difficult, and public footage has not yet been released, though officials have promised it.
The military reshuffle takes place against the backdrop of the prolonged conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes in late February 2026. Iran closed or heavily restricted the Strait of Hormuz in response. Limited traffic has been permitted under strict conditions, including permits from Iranian authorities and alternative routes due to mine risks, but normal commercial flow has not resumed. Iran and Oman have been negotiating new shipping lanes, with an agreement described as near final stages, yet Tehran has repeatedly insisted that full reopening depends on the United States meeting broader conditions.
Iranian officials have listed demands that include ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting sanctions especially on oil, releasing frozen Iranian assets, paying compensation for war damage caused by US and Israeli attacks, and ending further military threats and aggression against Iran and its regional allies. Compensation and an end to sanctions and the blockade form the consistent core of these conditions. Iran has stressed that the strait will not return to its pre-war status and that management will involve coordination with Oman.
On the same day, US President Donald Trump responded on Truth Social to Iran’s compensation demands. He noted that Tehran was seeking reparations for damage from the five-month conflict, which he attributed to Iran’s nuclear ambitions, even though the issue had not featured in prior talks.
Calling the idea interesting, Trump announced that he was now demanding compensation from Iran for Americans killed or wounded by Iranian-linked roadside bombs and conflicts, including victims of the USS Cole bombing and thousands of others, as well as for the families of protesters Iran has killed over decades and in recent months.
He said he had instructed US negotiators to include the demand in all future talks. The reciprocal claim further complicates already strained indirect negotiations, currently limited to messages through intermediaries, over ending hostilities, sanctions, assets and access to the strategic waterway.

Iraq sets up military command to curb attacks on Saudi Arabia
Iraq has established a new military operations command to strengthen security near its southern borders following a spate of attacks by Iran-aligned militia against Saudi Arabia, Iraqi sources told The New Arab.
The sources said the formation of the Al-Badiya Operations Command covers its southern desert region and is part of a security response aimed at preventing Iraqi territory being used to attack neighbouring countries.
It also seeks to prevent any external retaliation for such attacks from turning into strikes inside Iraqi territory, which could exacerbate the country's dire security situation, they said.
Iraq's porous southern border runs through the vast expanses of the remote Al-Muthanna desert. Controlling the area requires advanced reconnaissance and surveillance capabilities and a continuous security presence to detect illegal activity in remote areas and along desert roads.
Monitoring these areas is not a new measure for Iraq’s security agencies. Iraqi forces have previously conducted operations aimed at preventing the use of desert areas for infiltration, smuggling, or armed movements.
Closing security gaps
Military sources told The New Arab that Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s directive came after intelligence reports indicated security gaps that armed groups had exploited to evade security agencies.
They said that groups have been able to transport drones and launchers to the area and use it to stage cross-border attacks.
These measures gained additional importance in late July, when Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes against targets in Iraq that Riyadh said had attacked Saudi oil facilities.
The announcement of the command comes just a few days after al-Zaidi pledged to clamp down on the attacks during discussions with Saudi general intelligence chief Khaled al-Humaidan.
The military sources said Al-Badiya's establishment is consistent with al-Zaidi's move to disarm non-state groups, especially the network of powerful Iran-linked Shiite militia known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq.
Several factions, including Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, have rejected calls to surrender their weapons ahead of the prime minister's 30 September deadline.

Europe braces for another heat wave as drought hits UK, France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:36:00 UTC
02:36:00 KST

Much of Europe is set to face yet another intense heat wave this week, following periods of record drought that have driven water levels at major rivers to historic lows, ignited historic forest fires and contributed to thousands of deaths.
Swathes of Britain and France on Monday were already under extreme heat warnings with forecasts of temperatures around the mid-30s Celsius (90-95 Fahrenheit), while parched conditions saw new fires erupt in Greece and Spain.
Unusually high temperatures were also forecast in the coming days across a number of countries not accustomed to the heat, such as Switzerland, Austria and Hungary.
The heat wave comes after mainland France and Switzerland saw their widest-ranging droughts for the month of July on record, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP) data released by Europe's Copernicus climate observatory on Monday.
Europe's weather warning system, MeteoAlarm, on Monday, also said that scorching temperatures are already being felt across much of Italy and coastal areas of Croatia.
Here's what to know as temperatures soar again across the continent, the fastest-warming on the planet due to human-caused climate change.
The U.K.'s Met Office warned at the weekend that the summer's fifth hot spell was about to take hold in a country whose infrastructure was built for a more temperate, cooler climate.
Nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales is already officially in drought, with more than 27 million people under water-use restrictions, and with the environment department warning on Monday that "all regions of the country are experiencing pressure on their water resources."
Next to no rain was forecast for the affected areas this week.
In France, the national weather agency Meteo-France warned on Monday that the southeast would see temperatures as high as 35 degrees Celsius, spreading further across the country as the week progresses.
The agency also warned that due to climate change, "future summers will generally be hotter than those experienced to date."
The country's environment ministry said on Monday that "nearly 70% of French territory is subject to restrictions on water use," with the liquid reserved for priority uses such as health care, sanitation and drinking water in the areas most at risk.
Both France and the U.K. have seen thousands of excess deaths during previous heatwaves this year.
Greece reported its second fire this season near the capital, Athens, on Monday, despatching hundreds of crew and equipment.
Already, more than 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) of pine forests were blackened by a blaze that broke out 10 days ago northwest of the capital.
Firefighters were also struggling to contain a rapidly expanding blaze in southwestern Spain that had forced the evacuation of some 800 people and counting.
The weather was offering "no respite," local officials said.
France and Spain have already seen historic wildfires so far this summer, with record levels of drought causing tinder-dry conditions.
Some 95% of mainland France and 99% of Switzerland saw drought conditions in July, both record figures since the European Drought Observatory began collecting such data in 2012, according to an AFP analysis on Monday.
Heat and drought are also driving rivers across Europe to record lows. The Rhine in Germany could drop so much it becomes unnavigable, industry groups warned on Monday.
And Polish officials announced that the Vistula, the country's longest river, had matched its record low in Warsaw on Monday, a record set only on Friday.
Low levels along the Danube River have already seen Hungary and Romania forced to consider shutting down their nuclear plants, which rely on the water for cooling, in late July, although both managed to avoid doing so for now.
Nearly 120 million Europeans live in regions where July 2026 was the hottest ever recorded, according to an AFP analysis of national weather agencies and Copernicus climate data.
The records were concentrated in southern Britain, western France, and northern and eastern Spain.
At least 12,000 excess deaths were recorded across nine European countries during one heatwave in June, an AFP analysis of national statistics found last month, a toll that could rise as more data is released.
A solar eclipse that will be visible across parts of the European continent on Wednesday is expected to attract skygazers despite the unwelcoming weather.
The European Space Agency's observatory in Teruel, Spain, will host a day of activities up to the main event with the eclipse beginning at 7:33 p.m. CEST (5:33 p.m. GMT) and reaching totality at 8:23 p.m.
The area saw temperatures breach 30 degrees Celsius on Monday and the eclipse will cross over areas that were hit by the devastating Spanish fires last month.

Loneliness before the Digital Age: How Ancient Rome invented the architecture of alienation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:32:31 UTC
02:32:31 KST

For our ancestors, separation from the tribe often carried fatal consequences. A lone individual faced constant threats from predators, starvation, and exposure to the elements. Through natural selection, loneliness evolved as a vital internal alarm, a biological warning that social bonds were weakening and survival was at risk. Like hunger or thirst, loneliness was nature's way of driving us back toward the safety of the group and for millennia, human societies were structured to answer that call.
From hunter-gatherer bands to agrarian villages, life was anchored in daily interdependence. Within these small communities, anonymity was nonexistent. Everyone knew one another – their families, histories, and roles.
Relentless proximity came at the cost of privacy, but it also provided a powerful psychological anchor. Everyone had their place within the group, and no one disappeared unnoticed.
Over time, however, these small-group dynamics began to collapse under the weight of rapid urbanization.
That man who talks in the bath
Nowhere was this shift more dramatic than in ancient Rome. As the Republic expanded from a city into a vast empire, the very fabric of the human community underwent radical transformation.
Rome itself became the Western world's first cosmopolis, drawing hundreds of thousands into its densely packed capital. Displaced farmers, provincials seeking economic opportunities, and freedmen poured into the Eternal City, creating an unprecedented urban crush.
At its peak in the 1st and 2nd centuries C.E., Rome is estimated to have had around a million inhabitants. For many, the sudden influx was likely psychologically disorienting. Amid a sea of strangers, Romans both new and original became the first in the West to experience anonymity amidst the crowd – stripped of traditional kinship networks, and left profoundly isolated in the ancient world's first brush with modern alienation.
The city's architecture only deepened this sense of detachment.
Rome was built less on a human scale than as a visual projection of imperial authority and expansionist ambition. Monumental structures loomed over narrow, choking alleyways, a deliberate design that reinforced the immensity of the Roman Empire and the insignificance of the individual. While wealthy elites could retreat to spacious, quiet domus, most Romans lived in cramped high-rise buildings called insulae.
These apartment blocks could reach up to 70 feet in height, the maximum allowed by Augustus' decree. Forced to live alongside strangers from across the empire in cramped and overcrowded conditions, residents may have regarded those around them less as neighbors with whom they shared a community and more as part of the city's incessant background noise.
Seneca vividly captured this experience while living directly above a public bathhouse, where the sounds of strangers penetrated the privacy of his flat: "Imagine now every kind of sound that can make one hate one's ears: I hear their groans, and then the sharp hissing whenever they let out the breath they have held. Or again, I may notice some lazy fellow content with a cheap and ordinary massage, and hear the smacking of a hand on his shoulders… Add to this the quarrelsome man, the thief caught in the act, the man who likes to hear his own voice in the bath."
Seneca's story illustrates how the close physical proximity of Rome's inhabitants could erode the boundaries between private and public life.
Juvenal presents a similar problem, yet on a much greater scale. He portrays Rome as a sleepless city, where constant movement made tranquility almost impossible. The crowded urban environment was particularly oppressive at night, when the noise of traffic and passing crowds kept residents from sleeping: "Here many a sick man dies from lack of sleep. For what rented rooms admit sleep? Sleep in Rome costs a fortune."
The overpopulation of Rome produced a constant sensory presence from which individuals could scarcely escape. In this sense, physical proximity did not necessarily translate into social connection. The same density that brought hundreds of people into close contact could also make them feel intrusive, and even hostile to one another.
Furthermore, the extreme concentration of people facilitated the rapid spread of disease, making Rome perpetually vulnerable to epidemic outbreaks.
In his "Satires," Juvenal offers a grim portrayal of these living conditions, describing the perpetual fear that haunted the urban poor: the threat of their homes collapsing on them or of perishing in a fire while trapped inside. When a building burned down or crumbled, hundreds would instantly become homeless.
To preserve their sanity, Romans learned to tune out the noise. Faces blurred into the background, and emotional detachment became a form of survival.
In the end, the very structures designed to pack humanity together ended up forcing it apart, transforming close physical proximity into profound emotional distance. This withdrawal was not merely a Roman coping mechanism; it anticipated the emotional landscape of the modern metropolis. Beyond the physical architecture of the city, the social landscape offered little relief. Even for those who attained status within the capital, genuine human connection remained elusive.
Rome was, above all, a city sustained by relentless transactional networking. The elite cultivated elaborate daily rituals such as the salutatio, wherein crowds of citizens from almost all levels of Roman society gathered at a patron's doorstep each morning to offer him their services in return for his protection and help. Unsurprisingly, such bonds proved exceptionally fragile: when an individual's fortune or influence dried up, their entourage was gone overnight.
Philosophical refuge
Recognizing the hollow nature of urban noise and transactional social ties, ancient thinkers turned to philosophy, distinguishing between unwanted isolation and the deliberate withdrawal that could restore the mind and cultivate the soul. The intellectual elite, in particular, drew a clear line between solitudo and otium.
Solitudo referred to involuntary physical or social isolation, a condition Romans often regarded with suspicion as a possible sign of deviance or madness. Otium, by contrast, denoted purposeful and elevated leisure: a conscious retreat from the turbulence of the city to read, write, reflect, and pursue intellectual cultivation.
Stoic thinkers such as Seneca wrote extensively on the value of turning inward. The philosopher argued that life amid a crowd offered no guarantee of genuine human connection, urging his readers instead to: "Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual."
Decades later, Emperor Marcus Aurelius embodied this same ideal. While composing his Meditations during prolonged military campaigns along the Danube frontier, he reflected that one could always find a place of quiet retreat within the soul.
For the Stoics, intentional solitude was not a withdrawal from civic responsibility but a disciplined practice of self-examination that restored the mind and strengthened one's capacity to re-engage with the world.
Yet, while philosophers could choose to turn inward, voluntary otium was a luxury of the elite. In the Greco-Roman world, an individual's identity was not an internal, self-contained project; it was a communal construct derived entirely from active participation in the Greek polis or the Roman res publica. To be separated from this collective fabric was to suffer social death. Consequently, for those forcibly cast out, whether through legal action, civic punishment, or forced migration, loneliness ceased to be a quiet background ache and became a profound personal tragedy.
Lost in translation
While neither ancient Greek nor Latin possessed a specific word for "loneliness" that conveys today's precise psychological weight, the experience of forced isolation was a terrifying reality.
The Greeks spoke of eremia, a term spanning desertion, wilderness, and desolation, which captured the eerie void of existing beyond the city walls. Classical Athens formalized this systemic expulsion through ostracism. Once a year, citizens gathered in the Agora to scratch onto broken pottery shards (ostraca) the name of any figure deemed too dominant or dangerous. A successful vote meant immediate expulsion: ten years of exile beyond the city's borders.
Rome inherited this practice of social banishment, elevating it into a formal judicial sentence, known as exilium. Among the gravest punishments short of execution, it inflicted a devastating psychological blow, forcibly severing individuals from the culture, politics, and sense of self that defined them.
The poet Ovid embodied this devastation when Emperor Augustus banished him to Tomis, a remote outpost on the Black Sea. In his Tristia, Ovid lamented the crushing isolation he explicitly equated to a living death. Marooned in a harsh climate among people whose language he could not understand, he was stripped of the intellectual world he once dominated. Surrounded by crowds yet entirely alone, Ovid famously observed that he had become the "barbarian" to the locals simply because they could not find a common language. The writer was lost in translation.
His experience exposes a distinction that remains relevant today: solitude is not simply the absence of people but the absence of meaningful human connection. One may be surrounded by others and yet remain profoundly alone when deprived of a shared language, common customs, and mutual understanding.
Ovid's exile demonstrates that true belonging depends not merely on being among others but on participating in a community where one is recognized and able to share one's identity and thoughts.
Yet his banishment, for all its suffering, remained the tragedy of a privileged Roman citizen whose grievance was immortalized in literature. Countless millions across the Empire suffered a far colder exile, without status or legacy. For many, displacement was not a solitary decree but a desperate, forced flight in search of work opportunities in foreign cities. Many were pushed to the margins by economic collapse, fleeing wars, ruinous taxation, or simply enslavement. Stripped of their ancestral soil, cultural roots, and legal protections, these nameless exiles experienced the same profound alienation Ovid described, but without the luxury of artistic expression or the hope of imperial pardon.
Long before algorithms and screens, Romans were already dealing with the anonymity of crowded cities, the challenges of cultural assimilation, and relationships that could feel increasingly transactional. Looking back at the first apartment blocks or at Ovid's lonely exile, we are not simply studying the ancient world, we are looking into a mirror. Technology has changed, but the human condition has not. Rome reminds us that belonging has never been guaranteed by proximity, visibility, or constant interaction. Human connection requires more than simply living alongside others. Two thousand years separate us from ancient Rome, and yet we suffer from the same condition – the absence of belonging.

Ukraine strikes Russia’s Tatarstan oil hub, killing 13, injuring 78

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:31:00 UTC
02:31:00 KST

A Ukrainian attack on the major petroleum hub of Nizhnekamsk in Russia’s Tatarstan region killed at least 13 people and wounded 78 others Monday, local authorities said, marking one of the deadliest strikes inside Russia since the war began.
The Ukrainian military said it hit an oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, which is about 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) east of the Ukrainian border and has a population of about 240,000.
Russian officials didn't say what the drones targeted, but the city is home to two refineries and a petrochemical plant. Ukraine has targeted Russian oil facilities with long-range drones almost daily in recent months. The campaign has caused fuel shortages in Russia, eaten into its refining capacity and unsettled the population.
Previous Ukrainian attacks on Russian soil with high death tolls have come in the border region of Belgorod. In December 2023, Ukrainian shelling of the region’s capital, also called Belgorod, killed 25 people and wounded over 100, local officials said. Five months later, a Belgorod apartment building partially collapsed after shelling, killing at least 13, according to Russian authorities.
Also on Monday, several Ukrainian drones sparked a fire at an industrial facility in the Tyumen region of western Siberia, said Gov. Alexander Moor, without offering any details.
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces damaged part of a petrochemical complex in Tobolsk, in the Tyumen region. The plant produces rocket fuel components, aviation fuel, composite materials for drones and high-octane gasoline, it said in a Telegram post.
Last month, Ukrainian drones hit a refinery in Tyumen, more than 2,400 kilometers (about 1,500 miles) east of the border with Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his country is trying to force Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table and stop his full-scale invasion, launched in 2022. Russia is one of the world’s biggest energy producers.
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces struck a Taneco oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, starting a fire.
The city came under a "massive” drone attack targeting industrial and civilian facilities, according to the press service of Tatarstan’s head, Rustam Minnikhanov.
One of the drones hit a hostel, killing nine of the 13 victims, including citizens of Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, officials said. Uzbekistan’s consular office in Tatarstan said seven of its nationals were killed.
A child was among the dead, along with the 75 injured, the press service said, adding that Monday was declared a day of mourning in Tatarstan.
It was not possible to independently verify either side’s claims.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry urged foreign governments and international organizations to condemn Ukraine for the attacks.
Russia has also regularly battered Ukraine from the air using missiles, powerful glide bombs and drones, hitting civilian areas and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations. In the first six months of this year, 1,396 civilians were killed and 7,978 injured in Ukraine, the U.N. office in Kyiv said last week. That was a 37% increase from the same period last year, it said.
A Russian glide bomb struck the city of Zaporizhzhia in southern Ukraine, injuring 24 people, authorities said Monday. The city is the capital of a region of the same name that is partly occupied by Russian forces.
The World Health Organization’s European office said that one of its warehouses in the central Dnipro region of Ukraine was hit twice in less than 24 hours. The attacks destroyed emergency supplies worth an estimated $500,000 that were intended for front-line health facilities, it said in a statement. No casualties were reported.
Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones have flown increasing distances deep inside Russia, with some now reaching Siberia, around 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) from the border.
"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home -- in Russia,” Zelenskyy said late Sunday on social media.
"The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war.”
As part of a parallel campaign to disrupt Russian military supply lines leading to the front line in eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's forces struck road, rail and pontoon bridges in six regions last month, the Defense Ministry said Monday.
By repeatedly striking routes for fuel, ammunition and reinforcements, Ukrainian commanders say they have made Russian logistics slower, costlier and hard to organize. That has helped stall Russian advances and enabled Ukrainian counterattacks, they say.
Repairing the stricken refineries also is complicated for Russia. Ukraine’s attacks have damaged specialized equipment that is often imported, making repairs time-consuming and expensive as workarounds or replacements are sought by evading international sanctions.

Colombia: Dozens killed after large earthquake rocks region

Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026
A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.
Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.
Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.
The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.
The government has declared a state of emergency.
What is the latest?
Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.
He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.
"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.
"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."
What's happening on the ground?
The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.
"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."
Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.
Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.
The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.
And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.
Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.
"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.
What do we know about the quake's size and location?
The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.
The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.
The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.
The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.
The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.
Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.
USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.
The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.
