Ukraine's military intelligence reveals Russian missile production figures 'exceeding monthly targets'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:30:46 UTC
02:30:46 KST

Ukraine's military intelligence reveals Russian missile production figures 'exceeding monthly targets'
Russia's monthly production of key missiles is running 10–20% above target, while output of some models is even higher, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine, published on Aug. 10.
The statement comes as Ukraine faces a significant shortage of air defense capabilities needed to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. While Ukrainian forces have maintained high interception rates against other missile types, Russia's growing production is putting further strain on Ukraine's air defenses.
According to Skibitskyi, Russia produced 87 Kh-101 cruise missiles in July, reaching 140% of its planned monthly output. Moscow had set a target of 72 Kh-101 missiles for both July and August.
A similar pattern can be seen with the Kalibr cruise missile: Russia planned to produce 26 in each month but manufactured 29 in July, exceeding its target by 11%. The largest overperformance was recorded in Kh-35 production, which reached 200% of the planned monthly output, the official added, without specifying the exact number of missiles produced.
Skibitskyi added that, as of Aug. 3, Russia had already fulfilled its annual production targets for the Zircon and Oniks missiles, with 33 and 60 units manufactured in the first seven months, respectively.
Both were originally developed as anti-ship weapons but are now also used to strike ground targets. While the Oniks follows a conventional cruise missile trajectory, the Zircon is essentially a quasi-ballistic weapon, although Moscow has described it as a hypersonic cruise missile.
Ballistic missiles are among the most dangerous threats to Ukraine, as the U.S.-made Patriot is currently the only air defense system in the country's arsenal capable of intercepting them, and Ukrainian forces face a critical shortage of Patriot missiles. Russia launched nearly 70 ballistic missiles at Ukraine in the first 10 days of August, with only one intercepted, according to Ukraine's Air Force.
Skibitskyi said Moscow has significantly increased ballistic missile production partly because Russian defense plants are now operating under a "simplified system of technical controls" for missile production.
"However, there is another explanation here — the Russians have also been able to increase ballistic missile production because they have now stopped producing Kinzhal missiles. Accordingly, the rocket fuel is no longer going to the Kinzhal, but to other ballistic missiles," Skibitskyi said.
"In addition, they have suspended the production and use of Kh-32 missiles, so the funds and components allocated for them have been redirected to other types of missiles, which are considered more effective."
The official clarified that Russia stopped producing the Kinzhal, an air-launched aeroballistic missile carried by MiG-31 aircraft, in April. He also cited the weapon's "low precision" as another reason for the halt in production.
"For an effective missile, the deviation from the target should not exceed 5–7 meters, while theirs is 30 meters or more," Skibitskyi said.
Although production of some types has been put on hold, the overall trend points to an increase in their use during Russian attacks. According to Ukraine's military intelligence, July saw the second-highest number of Kh-101, Kalibr, and Kh-32 cruise missiles launched at Ukraine since the start of the year. Russia launched 157 such missiles in February and 153 in July.
The trend is even more pronounced with ballistic weapons. Russian forces launched 198 ballistic missiles at Ukraine in July, including 9M723 missiles from the Iskander-M system, RM-48U missiles from the S-400, and Zircon missiles — the highest monthly figure so far in 2026, Skibitskyi said.

Palestinian club football to restart in September after Gaza war suspension
Palestinian sports leagues, including professional football, were halted due to Israel’s genocidal war on Palestinians.
The Palestinian Football Association has announced that it will resume activity in September after a nearly three-year pause due to Israel’s genocidal war on Palestinians in Gaza.
“We announce the resumption of sports activities and the football association’s league beginning September 4,” association President Jibril Rajoub said at a Ramallah news conference on Monday.
Palestinian sports leagues, including professional football, came to a halt after the war began on October 7, 2023.
The association has named the first tournament back the “Thousand Martyrs’ Cup”, to honour the 1,014 Palestinian athletes killed by Israel during the war, according to the association’s data.
More than 200 clubs will compete in the tournament, including 146 from the Israeli-occupied West Bank, 44 from Gaza, and 36 from Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon.
The tournament will kick off simultaneously in the three locations.
Rajoub said the war “created difficult conditions for all Palestinians that led to the suspension of our competitions and activities”.
“But we have not lost our Palestinian national will, nor have we lost our belief that sport will remain a symbol of hope and life,” he said.
Rajoub noted that the association and Palestinian clubs faced tough financial circumstances.
During the news conference, he called on FIFA and other federations to stand by Palestinian sports and to protect the rights of players, clubs and children to enjoy sports in “freedom and dignity”.
The association previously issued a statement regarding FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s now-withdrawn plan to open tournaments to private investors, saying “many today are questioning FIFA’s commercial direction”.
“But for Palestine, the issue is more fundamental … Our question is whether FIFA still has the courage to apply its regulations to everyone equally … without succumbing to political pressures,” Rajoub said.
The association has called on FIFA to impose sanctions on Israeli clubs that operate in occupied West Bank settlements and to suspend Israel’s FIFA membership over the country’s conduct in Gaza.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.
“We are not asking for privileges; we are demanding legitimate rights guaranteed by international sporting laws and charters,” Rajoub said.

It concluded with the adoption of the BRICS Education Ministers’ Declaration, reaffirming education as a key pillar of BRICS cooperation and outlining a shared roadmap across five priority areas under India’s 2026 BRICS Chairship.

BRICS Action Plan for Innovation 2025-2030 is a document that outlines the roadmap of cooperation among member states in the digital economy, technology transfer, support for knowledge-based companies, and the development of an innovation ecosystem.
Iran’s engagement in the plan can pave the way for the exchange of technical knowledge, enhancement of industrial cooperation, and entry of Iranian knowledge-based companies in new markets.
The report also shows that human capital and innovation are among the top priorities of BRICS; the 10th Young Scientists Forum, 8th BRICS Young Innovator Prize, and the first BRICS Startup Forum are among the main events held in this sector.
Iran’s membership in BRICS can bring about numerous advantages, such as greater access to international scientific and research networks, collaboration in joint research projects, enhancement of technological and industrial cooperation, utilizing the capacity of the technology transfer network, developing a market for knowledge-based companies, and attracting investment in technology and innovation sectors.
The report highlights AI, biotechnology, nanotechnology, quantum technologies, digital economy, and space technologies as the most important axes for future cooperation between Iran and BRICS member states.

====================================================================================================

No escape from the Russian terror playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:28:26 UTC
02:28:26 KST

No escape from the Russian terror playbook
Russian police officers guard the entrance to Penal Colony No. 2 in Pokrov, Russia, on April 6, 2021. (Kirill Kudryavtsev / AFP / Getty Images)
Nina L. Khrushcheva
Professor of international affairs at The New School
In the early 1950s, a group of prominent, mostly Jewish doctors from Moscow was accused of plotting to assassinate Soviet leaders on orders from the West. The accused were fired from their jobs, arrested, and tortured.
But after Joseph Stalin died in 1953, Lavrenty Beria — one of Stalin's longest-serving secret police chiefs, who oversaw the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs (NKVD) in 1938–45 and spent decades filling the Gulags — called off the investigation. As it turned out, the security services had made the whole thing up.
Today, the Kremlin is following the same playbook. While the 2012 foreign-agent law was initially applied to organizations receiving international funding, its reach has expanded dramatically since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with the "foreign agent" label slapped on anyone deemed inconvenient.
This label carries a range of penalties, from a ban on holding public office or performing publicly funded work (such as teaching) to disclaimers on social-media accounts.
In July 2026, the Duma approved measures to strip key citizenship rights — including access to bank accounts and consular services (such as passport renewals) — from Russians living abroad who face prosecution at home over political "offenses," such as failing to comply with foreign-agent legislation.
Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin derided those affected as "degenerates and traitors to the motherland." His choice of words was telling: not dissidents, but "degenerates."
Around the same time, the Justice Ministry added a new section to its website tracing a long series of supposed anti-state plots, from the 1500s through today, thereby presenting all of Russian history as one long siege by foreign enemies. The 1,200-plus people currently designated as foreign agents are listed, along with a portrait and description of their offenses (here is my entry).
In doing so, the Kremlin has left no doubt about the message it wants the foreign-agent designation to send.
The foreign-agent label is just one way Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime silences dissent. More than 5,600 people (probably many more) are currently facing politically motivated prosecutions in Russia, compared with fewer than 5,000 following Stalin's death. (This figure continued falling after Nikita Khrushchev delivered his "Secret Speech" denouncing Stalin's cult of personality.)
Putin's campaign of repression is starting to resemble the Great Terror of 1937.
To be sure, there is a lot about Stalinism that Putin has not quite replicated, beginning with the scale of the Gulag system. But in one respect, Putinism is worse. However distorted Vladimir Lenin's vision of a workers' paradise became under Stalin, it remained fundamental to the Soviet system. Today, there is no ideology, no grand project. There is just one man and his security apparatus working out how to safeguard their own power indefinitely.
The Russian author Vladimir Sorokin saw this coming. In his 2006 novel Day of the Oprichnik, Sorokin describes the brazen, violent, and debauched behavior of a state enforcer within a new tsarist-totalitarian Russia of the kind envisioned by nationalists like the political philosopher Aleksandr Dugin.
Two decades later — with Putin's security services having dusted off the playbook of the NKVD (not the KGB, which after Stalin's death was mild by comparison) — it reads more like nonfiction than satire.
An older work offers further insight into modern Russia. In Mikhail Bulgakov's The Heart of a Dog, written in 1925, the brilliant surgeon Filipp Filippovich Preobrazhensky turns a stray dog into a crude, aggressive proletarian named Sharikov. Russia has since produced plenty of educated, capable professionals like Preobrazhensky. But nowadays, they are increasingly choosing to behave more like Sharikov.
Dmitry Medvedev, who once served as Russia's somewhat liberal president (2008–12), praises the Kremlin and spews vulgar insults against its "enemies" on social media.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, who once displayed unwavering professionalism, now discusses diplomatic relations like mafia deals, using colloquial expressions like "patsan skazal— patsan sdelal" ("the guy said, the guy did"). Gulag culture—in which the "guards" are pitted against the "guarded," and anyone who challenges the norm is silenced, humiliated, and punished — encourages this kind of race to the bottom.
One should not assume that all of Russian society is submitting to Putinism. For starters, Putin's approval ratings are dropping.
While there is a limit to how low these ratings can tumble — the Kremlin-controlled Public Opinion Foundation published a 66% rating early last month, but obediently pushed it back up to 70% the following week—the signal is clear. Even the Levada Center reports that the share of Russians who approve of Putin's activities has declined from 84% to 74% this year.
Moreover, evidence of covert protest is everywhere. A shopkeeper displays balloons in the yellow and blue of the Ukrainian flag, as if part of an unrelated product promotion. A bookstore sells tote bags emblazoned with 1984, as if it were simply a literary novelty item. A theater stages anti-Stalinist plays, such as Evgeny Schwartz's The Dragon.
True, there is no mass mobilization against the Ukraine war, even as Ukrainian drones reach targets deep inside Russia, let alone against Putin's regime. But Russians have endured enough tyranny to know what it means to be at the mercy of security forces that will stop at nothing to maintain control.
Even subtle resistance to the Kremlin's demand for total surrender is enough to enrage its occupants — and bring intensifying repression.
Ultimately, the only exit from Putinism may well be the same as the exit from Stalinism: the leader's demise. Many Russians hope that, at that point, a Khrushchev-like figure will emerge to denounce the worst of what came before. But Russia might also get a Beria, who was directly responsible for many of the regime's atrocities.
In such a scenario, Russians must ensure that the limits of totalitarian control are undeniable.
Only then will the new leader be motivated to dismantle the systems of repression that are now in place, just as Beria, in the brief period between Stalin's death and his own downfall, began dismantling the Gulag system he had spent his career building.

Benjamin Netanyahu’s rejection of US deal for Gaza is risky move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:27:54 UTC
02:27:54 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier.
The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.
The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory.
Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs.
With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail.
On Sunday, he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.
The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported.
“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”
The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.
Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.
He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television.
Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.
But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”
In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.
For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes.
Last week, Netanyahu scaled back Israeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”.
Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand.
Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October.
Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes.
Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspaper noted.
It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said.
The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”.
Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction.
Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure.
The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security experts have warned.
Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.

Why the Houthis' new offensive could reverberate beyond Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:27:49 UTC
02:27:49 KST

Breadcrumb
Why the Houthis' new offensive could reverberate beyond Yemen
The past week has seen a dramatic and worrying escalation in the Yemen conflict, with the Iran-backed Houthis launching simultaneous attacks against the internationally recognised Yemeni government and its backer, Saudi Arabia.
The return of large-scale fighting risks bringing a violent end to the 2022 ceasefire and inflicting additional chaos on a wider region already reeling from the Iran war.
In the latest indication that internal escalation in Yemen won’t remain confined to the country’s borders, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree announced Sunday the group targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery in the kingdom’s southwestern city of Jazan.
Additionally, the group said it fired missiles and drones at Yemen’s Mocha port, one of the main ports still controlled by the internationally recognized government that was using it as an alternative to the major Houthi-held Hodeidah port.
The cross-border strikes followed two separate Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Najran border province last week, injuring 11. The group also resumed attacks on commercial ships passing through the Red Sea, sinking an Indian-flagged vessel.
On Thursday, they escalated inside Yemen, launching attacks against government forces in Hadhramaut and Marib provinces, killing an estimated 38 to 58 troops.
Over the weekend, Yemen’s army announced the launch of a military operation in response to these attacks and accused the group of dragging the country into regional conflicts.
Yemen on the brink
“We are on the brink of another escalation, but it's unclear to what scale this will take shape,” Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, told The New Arab.
“It’s clear the Houthis are now pushing on the Marib front line,” he said. “But what is less clear is whether or not the Saudis are going to escalate to responses beyond that geography or towards other cities throughout Houthi-controlled territory like Taiz or Hodeidah.”
The RANE analyst assesses this latest attack as significant since they suggest the Houthi offensive will consist of ground offensives against Saudi Arabia’s coalition allies in Yemen.
“This suggested that the Houthi campaign is not merely about harassing Saudi Arabia’s economic model,” Bohl said. “But also taking and holding ground within Yemen over long-disputed territory.”
Emergent alliances
A Saudi official said late last week that the kingdom was bracing for “multiple coordinated attacks” against it by both the Houthis and the Iran-backed Iraqi militias.
Citing “multiple intelligence reports,” the official said Iran-backed Iraqi militias plan on attacking Saudi Arabia “in coordination with the Houthis” and guided by Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps paramilitary.
In a first in late July, Saudi Arabia and the United States executed joint airstrikes targeting IRGC-backed Iraqi militias across Iraq after these groups after the kingdom came under fire from Iraq in tandem with Houthi attacks.
Reuters subsequently reported that the Houthis had attacked Saudi Arabia from Iraqi territory in addition to Yemen in coordination with the Iraqi groups.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey signed a new defence agreement in Mecca titled the “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement” on Friday. In a joint statement, the three countries affirmed that the agreement means that an armed attack against any one of these countries would be seen as an attack on all three.
“I think it’s too early to say whether or not the tripartite pact will actually have an impact on Saudi Arabia’s security environment,” said RANE’s Bohl.
“Turkey is very unlikely to intervene against militias in Iraq or the Houthis, and for that matter it doesn't look like Pakistan will either,” he added. “But the alliance isn’t designed for that sort of tripwire deterrence. Instead, it may shape perceptions of risk and escalation.”
For now, the RANE analyst believes it’s hard to assess how much political will Saudi Arabia has to escalate against the Houthis.
“I tend to see that the immediate outlook is that they will focus on using their Yemeni proxies to reduce Houthi capabilities and pressure them along the front lines,” Bohl told The New Arab.
“But if the Houthis continue to escalate against them, I think that they might consider more significant ground operations starting with major pushes around disputed cities,” he added.
“However, if there is an offensive, it could exacerbate the already dire humanitarian situation in Houthi-controlled territory.”
New threshold
Fatima Abo Alasrar, author of the Ideology Machine, a publication on authoritarian information systems, says that the attacks inside Yemen mark a new “threshold” in the conflict with regional ramifications extending beyond that country.
She strongly underlined that these latest developments in Yemen aren’t merely tied to a perceived threat to the Houthis from Saudi Arabia.
“The Houthis are an arm of Tehran and cannot be seen any other way,” Alasrar told The New Arab.
“They’re moving to solidify their grip on Yemen and protect themselves from any backlash precisely because Iran is interested in the Bab al-Mandab and through them it implements this policy,” she added.
“So, they’re moving to make sure they don’t incur any losses.”
The timing of the Houthis latest moves inside Yemen undoubtedly benefits Tehran in its current negotiations, as the Bab al-Mandab is important for the IRGC.
Iran is presently negotiating over the Strait of Hormuz with Oman and the United States, making severalsteep demands for any reopening on Sunday.
Having the Houthis positioned to close Bab al-Mandab alongside Hormuz simultaneously gives Tehran greater leverage against its adversaries and the capability to disrupt and escalate far beyond its borders and impact global trade.
The Iran-backed group already declared a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia in July after Riyadh opposed Tehran resuming flights to Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital city Sanaa.
The past week’s events, Alasrar noted, mark the deadliest escalation between the Houthis and the government in years. The Houthis’ renewed and ferocious attacks in Yemen are aimed at shoring up their position and undermining the government’s power ahead of any movement against the vast swathes of strategic Yemeni infrastructure and territory it controls.
The group currently controls about one third of Yemen’s landmass, in which at least 70 percent of the population lives.
Alasrar recalled that the previous Saudi-led intervention against the Houthis from 2015 until 2022 prevented the Iran-backed group from capturing even more vital territory in Yemen, such as Marib but also Hadramawt and Aden.
The latter critical port city is where the UN-recognised government, the Presidential Leadership Council, has operated since the Houthis captured Sanaa in 2014.
“The direct challenge by the Saudi-led coalition quickly saw the Houthis pushed back from these strategic areas,” Alasrar said. “That was significant since the Houthis main objective was and remains land conquest, unilaterally controlling Yemen, and guaranteeing a permanent foothold there for Iran.”
“The Houthis seemed to show restraint at the start of the regional Iran war earlier this year, but in reality, they were preparing precisely for this present moment,” she added.
“As I wrote in early March, they had already spent months turning the civilian infrastructure they control into a conscription apparatus for a war no one, but them, was planning for yet.”
Now it seems that war may have just begun.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in the Middle East who writes extensively about the region's affairs, conflicts, and politics

Taylor Farms recalls jalapeno products sold in two dozen states over salmonella concerns
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
18:26:38 BST
02:26:38 KST

Taylor Farms recalls jalapeno products sold in two dozen states over salmonella concerns
The products were shipped to several major retail stores, including Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Taylor Fresh Foods, parent company of Taylor Farms, has issued another recall, this time for some items containing jalapeños amid concerns over potential salmonella contamination.
The decision comes on the heels of another major Taylor Farms recall for iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico which was linked to a nationwide cyclospora outbreak that sickened people across the US.
Taylor Farms announced the jalapeño-related recall after Coast Citrus Distributors said it was recalling fresh jalapeños over salmonella concerns. Taylor Farms foods covered by the new recall include guacamole, pico de gallo, and taco dip, according to the FDA notice about the recall.
Distributed by Taylor Farms across dozens of states, the recalled items have "Best If Used By" dates through Aug. 16, 2026. They were sold at major retailers including Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s, and Walmart.
Taylor Farms distributed peppers covered by the recall to Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Wisconsin and West Virginia.
Salmonella outbreak
The FDA and CDC are working with state and local partners to investigate a multistate salmonella outbreak tied to fresh jalapeños from Coast Citrus Distributors. A total of 345 cases have been reported across 27 states, and 36 people were hospitalized as a result of the outbreak.
A grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, supplying Coast Citrus Distributors, was identified as the source, according to the CDC.
Taylor Fresh Foods said it is no longer sourcing from the farmer and will fill orders using alternative suppliers. The company added that it is currently unaware of any reported illnesses linked to its jalapeño products.
Consumers who have any recalled product are advised to throw it away immediately and avoid eating it. Refunds can be claimed at the original place of purchase.
Chipotle and Qdoba both previously stopped serving the affected peppers.
The jalapeño recall comes as the FDA released a new report about the explosive diarrhea-causing cyclospora outbreak, the clearest picture yet of the health crisis that escalated over the summer.
The report, released this weekend, details the full scope of the recall connected to the nationwide outbreak, naming major restaurant chains and retail brands that pulled nearly 240,000 cases of lettuce.
In total, 236,192 cases of iceberg and romaine lettuce — some mixed with carrots and red cabbage — were removed from distribution across Mexico and 27 U.S. states.

Zyuganov praises farming culture in Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:25:00 UTC
02:25:00 KST

SMOLEVICHI DISTRICT, 10 August (BelTA) - Belarus has one of the best farming cultures, and there is much to learn from it, Gennady Zyuganov, Chairman of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF) and head of the CPRF faction in the State Duma, said during a visit to Minsk Oblast on 10 August, BelTA has learned.
Gennady Zyuganov was briefed on the progress of the harvesting campaign at Shipyany-ASK. The enterprise is of particular importance to the country as it is engaged in seed production jointly with the National Scientific and Practical Center for Agriculture of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus. The guest was shown a number of seed varieties, the crops in the fields of Smolevichi District, and the experience accumulated over the years. Gennady Zyuganov stressed that the agricultural and industrial sector had always been one of Belarus’ priorities. “We learned from you and, I must say, we continue to learn. The roadside strips are cultivated, the fields are clean, and the corn is standing tall,” he said. 
He also spoke about the Zyuganovka winter wheat variety, which is grown in Russia and Brest Oblast. Gennady Zyuganov stressed that the variety produces a record yield in his home country. “Farming here is also a model in many respects. The Lenin State Farm is one of the best in Moscow. We buy seeds from you, as well as strawberry planting material,” he said. 
 
 
He noted that food security had become particularly important in today’s world. Belarus had shown everyone how a country could produce more food than its population needed. 
Director of the agricultural enterprise Vadim Kostenevich said that 55% of the grain crops had been harvested so far. The average yield was 6 tonnes per hectare. The rapeseed harvest had been completed, with an average yield of 4 tonnes per hectare. “It will take about seven or eight more days to finish, and we will complete the entire harvest campaign,” he added. 
The high results were driven by both favorable weather conditions and compliance with all technological requirements. “At our farm, 97% of the seeds are Belarusian-bred varieties. We are fully ready to supply seeds to one-third of the republic. Our seeds have high yield potential and good quality characteristics,” Vadim Kostenevich stressed. 
Sergei Kravtsov, Director General of the Scientific and Practical Center for Agriculture of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus, spoke about the achievements of Belarusian breeding. “Here we are presenting the breeding work of the National Scientific and Practical Center. The center is responsible for 36 types of agricultural crops. These include cereals, legumes, groats crops, industrial crops, oilseeds and forage crops. All domestically bred seeds and varieties supplied to the Republic of Belarus fall within the remit of our scientific and practical center for arable farming. This year, 26 varieties of domestic breeding have been approved for cultivation across all agricultural crops,” he said. 
“We cooperate closely with the Russian Federation in all areas. It is gratifying to note that in 2026, seven Belarusian varieties were approved for cultivation in Russia, including varieties of wheat, legumes and barley,” Sergei Kravtsov said. The cooperation covers plant breeding, seed production and joint research and development.

Italian businessman is mastermind behind journalist bomb attack, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:24:21 UTC
02:24:21 KST

Italy police say businessman with ties to Berlusconi is mastermind behind journalist bomb attack
A businessman who had ties to former Italian premier Silvio Berlusconi is the alleged mastermind behind an October bomb attack against one of the country's leading investigative journalists, police said on Monday.
Rome's Carabinieri police said they arrested Valter Lavitola for allegedly ordering the attack outside journalist Sigfrido Ranucci's house last year. The two men are said to be friends.
The blast in a residential neighborhood of Pomezia, about 12 miles south of Rome, destroyed two cars belonging to Ranucci, known for investigations into corruption and the mafia. Ranucci had just returned home at the time, and his daughter had walked by a half-hour before, his employer said at the time.
Video shot by Ranucci, who has been under police protection since 2021 because of his hard-hitting investigations, showed the mangled remains of the cars and the gate.
Lavitola is accused of instructing a second man, Tavares Gomes Clesio, to recruit four men to place the bomb in front of Ranucci's home, police said. The four men were arrested near Naples in June for carrying out the attack.
Police are still looking for Gomes.
According to police, Lavitola and Gomes took part in an "initial exploratory inspection" outside of Ranucci's home in September.
Lavitola thought the bombing would raise Ranucci's profile ahead of a possible career in politics, authorities wrote in the arrest warrant, according to local media.
Ranucci, the popular star of the weekly investigative show "Report" on state broadcaster Rai, is not accused of any wrongdoing and detectives believe he was unaware of Lavitola's plans.
Ranucci has taken on sensitive topics such as Italy's mafia and political corruption in past investigations, and has lived under police protection for years. He told the ANSA news agency the day after the attack that he had received "an endless list of threats."
The journalist, who once described Lavitola as a "true friend," was not injured in the attack.
Lavitola, a former journalist and import-export businessman who owns a restaurant in Rome, is well known in Italy, having been close to Berlusconi, who died in 2023.
In 2015, a lower court convicted the former prime minister of having bribed a senator, handing him a three-year sentence. The same sentence was given to Lavitola, whom prosecutors accused of having handed the cash to the lawmaker.
The explosion targeting Ranucci occurred on the eighth anniversary of the car bomb slaying of Maltese investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, who wrote extensively about suspected corruption in political and business circles.

Trump demands reparations from Iran for ‘all the people they have killed’
Demand comes as Tehran takes a hard line on compensation for war Trump started on February 28
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
President Donald Trump is demanding that Iran pay compensation to American victims of Iranian-backed attacks as he responds to Tehran's own demand for war reparations.
In a Monday post on Truth Social, Trump said he had "instructed my representatives to put this firmly into any, and all, future negotiations" — casting Iran's compensation demand as a novel idea he was happy to borrow.
"I see that Representatives of the Islamic Republic of Iran are asking for compensation for the damage done to them during the last five month Military Conflict (started because, THEY WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON), even though it was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings!" he wrote.
He then called Tehran’s demand for compensation “an interesting idea” and said he was in turn demanding the same “for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous” as well as “thousands of others killed in combat” in addition to the nearly 40 killed in the 2000 bombing of the U.S.S. Cole even though that attack was carried out by al-Qaeda, not anyone affiliated with Iran.
Trump also claimed that Iran should pay some recompense to families of "the hundreds of thousands of innocent protestors that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months."
It’s unclear how the president came to the idea that there’ve been 52,000 killed in the five-month-old war he started, as official American and Israeli estimates have placed the actual number of casualties at somewhere just north of 6,000.
Trump’s latest social media missive comes amid a delicate stretch of negotiations to bring an end to the conflict as the U.S. continues to grapple with a munitions shortage with the war nearing the half-year mark.
On Saturday, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, published a list of six conditions Tehran says the United States must meet before the Strait of Hormuz reopens: an end to US threats and to what he called insults to Iran's national and religious values; a permanent halt to attacks on Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq; the lifting of the US naval blockade and withdrawal of American naval and air forces from the region; compensation for damage from what he described as two "imposed wars"; an end to sanctions; and the unconditional release of frozen Iranian assets.
Iranian officials also said over the weekend they were close to a separate agreement with Oman on control of the waterway, but that no deal would actually reopen it to traffic unless Washington met the six conditions first.
Both sanctions relief and some form of reparations were supposed to be handled in talks pursuant to the interim memorandum of understanding signed by American and Iranian representatives at the start of what was supposed to be a 60-day ceasefire period starting in June.
That two-month period ends in just over a week, and it’s unclear whether there will be any extension.

China fails to launch a rocket carrying a coms satellite, state news agency says
BEIJING (AP) — China ‘s launch of a rocket carrying a communications satellite on Monday evening was not successful, state media reported, adding that the cause of the failed launch was under investigation.
The ChinaSat 4B satellite aboard a Long March 7A rocket was launched from the country’s southern island of Hainan, which is home to the Wenchang Spacecraft Launch Site, part of China’s space program. The ChinaSat 4B is a comms satellite.
“The rocket experienced an anomaly during the flight and the launch mission failed,” the Xinhua news agency said.
It was the first reported Long March 7A failure since its maiden flight in March 2020, when the rocket malfunctioned after launching from Wenchang, according to Xinhua. China has launched hundreds of missions using Long March carrier rockets delivering internet and communication satellites into a pre-set orbit.
Hainan Island is a popular beach destination off the country’s southern coast.

Pentagon official asks Asian allies to invest more in defense to deter aggression

Pentagon official asks Asian allies to invest more in defense to deter aggression
MANILA, Philippines (AP) — A Pentagon official on Monday asked allies in Asia to invest more in their defense and help deter aggression in the region and said the United States remains committed to do the same with “partners, not protectorates.”
Elbridge Colby, an undersecretary of defense, made the remarks at a forum in the Philippines, his first stop in Southeast Asia, where he will also visit Indonesia, Thailand and Cambodia. He renewed Washington’s assurances that the U.S. is not backing away from Asia despite its current preoccupation with the Iran war and the Middle East.
“America is definitely not disengaging from Asia — to the contrary. Our vital national interests dictate our enduring presence here,” Colby told an audience that included foreign diplomats, generals, business executives and journalists.
“We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in, to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most,” the Pentagon’s top policy adviser said. “We see Asia as of paramount importance.”
Colby stayed away from the usual U.S. tirade against China’s growing aggression in the region, including in the disputed South China Sea. Washington has often expressed alarm over Beijing’s increasingly hostile actions against Philippine coast guard and naval forces in recent years.
Washington has repeatedly warned that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines, its oldest treaty ally in Asia, if Filipino forces, ships or aircraft come under armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
China and the Philippines, along with Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan, have been locked in territorial standoffs in the disputed waters, a key global trade route, for decades. Beijing virtually claims the entire waterway and has rejected a 2016 ruling in an arbitration case initiated by the Philippines that invalidated its expansive claims.
Colby repeated a vow by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a speech at the Shangri-La defense conference in Singapore in May that the U.S. will build and sustain a strong defense in the Western Pacific “that ensures aggression is infeasible, escalation unattractive and war deemed irrational.”
Colby said the U.S. is committed to ensuring “we can sustain combat-credible power where it matters most. Yet this defense architecture cannot rest on American shoulders alone. It must be upheld by a network of highly capable, sovereign nations that have modernized their own forces and stepped up to secure their own territory — transforming our relationships into true partnerships of equals.”
He added: “When we ask our allies and partners to step up, to invest more in their own defense and to take responsibility for their own sovereign security, we are not signaling abandonment. We are looking for partners, not protectorates.”
Colby praised efforts by the Philippines, which holds large-scale combat exercises with U.S. forces each year, to strengthen its defense capabilities and cited similar efforts by Thailand, Indonesia and other security allies in Southeast Asia.

How Russia's shadow fleet forced Europe back to sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:19:41 UTC
02:19:41 KST

How Russia's shadow fleet forced Europe back to sea
A tanker passes a border security vessel and the detained Smyrtos shadow fleet tanker outside the harbour in Portland, UK on June 15, 2026. (Finnbarr Webster / Getty Images)
Europe's campaign to choke off Russia's ability to finance its war in Ukraine through oil revenues began with sanctions, legislation, and price caps. But as hundreds of ships helped Moscow evade those restrictions, Western governments increasingly backed those measures with aggressive maritime enforcement — deploying naval power and pirate-like tactics to disrupt the shadow fleet.
As of May 2026, a Ukrainian government register has identified 1,404 vessels belonging to Russia's so-called shadow fleet. Those ships are almost always dangerously old, uninsured, and registered in third countries where there are fewer laws to follow, so-called flags of convenience.
Moscow coordinates them to carry mostly oil, but also other sanctioned products like grain illegally taken from occupied territory in southern Ukraine, in a way that allows Russia to evade sanctions.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the EU banned Russian ships from accessing the bloc's ports as early as April and introduced its first price cap on Russian oil in December 2022.
Those two moves together led Moscow to seek alternative means to keep selling oil and keep the money flowing into state coffers.
However, it was only in June 2024 that the EU first issued sanctions directly against the shadow fleet: 27 tankers, "part of Putin's dark fleet," read an EU press release at the time.
Since then, the EU has added new ship listings in every subsequent sanctions package and quickly shifted its language from "dark fleet" to "shadow fleet," the more commonly used term for ships that aim to deceive and disregard the law.
read also
By the time the EU adopted its 21st sanctions package in July 2026, 692 ships were on the EU's list, along with a range of individuals and companies involved in servicing shadow fleet ships and enabling the deception.
Those listings have been complemented by separate lists of sanctioned ships drawn up elsewhere.
The U.K.'s latest sanctions package against the shadow fleet on Aug. 6 brought the total number of ships listed to 659. The U.S has sanctioned 453 vessels, while Canada and Australia have sanctioned 731 and 262, respectively.
"The community is more confident in their legal position when they act."
And there are moves to increase cross-border coordination in adding ships to sanctions lists.
For example, a draft Shadow Fleet Sanctions Act has been introduced in the U.S. Senate that includes a chapter intended to align U.S. listings with those of the EU and the U.K. at least twice per year.
But listings alone do not stop Russia's shadow fleet from sailing. Countries need to enforce those sanctions.
"Coordination among European countries that border the Baltic and North Seas has been intense on shadow fleet monitoring over the past two years," said Tom Keatinge, director of the Center for Finance and Security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank.
Several multilateral organizations, including the G7, the Nordic-Baltic Eight, and the Joint Expeditionary Force, discussed the issue more often, but also shifted "from understanding the problem to action," Keatinge said.
"The result is that the community is more confident in their legal position when they act," he added.
Days before an October 2025 summit of European leaders in Denmark, Copenhagen was threatened with Russian drone incursions, suspected to have been launched from a shadow fleet vessel.
European countries dispatched naval and air support to Denmark, French President Emmanuel Macron called for the Coalition of the Willing to double down on restrictions against the shadow fleet, and Paris boarded the ship suspected of being used to dispatch drones into Danish airspace.
But it was only in 2026 that boarding suspect ships became a more regular occurrence.
In March, Sweden began intercepting Russian shadow fleet vessels, and had already intervened against five ships by the beginning of May.
The first ship to be seized, the Caffa, was carrying grain taken illegally from Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.
Courts in Stockholm have since agreed that the vessel and its cargo should be given to Kyiv.
"Since March 1 2026, the Swedish Coast Guard has, through several different legislative amendments, been given increased opportunities to conduct effective intelligence work, which makes it easier to make decisions to intervene against vessels on Swedish territory," a coast guard spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
"If Swedish law is violated and the conditions for intervention in accordance with international regulations are met, we will intervene," they added.
Also in March, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave the green light for the British military to board shadow fleet vessels entering the country's waters.
London intercepted its first shadow fleet vessel, the Smyrtos, in June.
France also stopped a shadow fleet boat in the Mediterranean in June.
And Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken announced on March 1 that his country had seized a ship belonging to the Russian shadow fleet for the first time.
In addition to greater coordination among European countries, Keatinge highlights that the respective postures of Moscow and Washington have also facilitated the newly assertive approach.
The U.S seized a Russian-flagged oil tanker in the Atlantic Ocean on Jan. 7 for the first time in recent history, even after Moscow had reportedly dispatched a submarine to protect it.
"There is no doubt that this (the U.S. posture) has also encouraged European countries to act as they can anticipate non-objection from the U.S," Keatinge said.
Likewise, Keatinge noted that "Russia is not retaliating in any sort of meaningful way," leaving Europeans confident they can "take action without repercussions."
Russia threatened Europe in February, saying it would deploy its navy if Europe seized shadow fleet vessels, but that threat did not materialize.
Ukraine has also stepped up its campaign against the shadow fleet, announcing on July 1 that it would be treated as military targets, before carrying out attacks on at least seven different nights that month, striking no fewer than 78 ships in the Black Sea.
That same month, the EU agreed its Atalanta naval operation in the Indian Ocean could start intercepting ships suspected of belonging to Russia's shadow fleet. On Aug. 2, its operation IRINI boarded a sanctioned tanker in the Mediterranean.
On July 24, the bloc also agreed on its 21st sanctions package, which introduced a provision allowing member states to confiscate the assets of any shadow fleet vessels that they board.
"It sends a clear and unmistakable signal: the European Union is serious about countering the shadow fleet and closing every loophole Russia seeks to exploit to finance its war of aggression against Ukraine," a European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
"Shadow fleet vessels are a threat to the environment and neglect safety rules. We are showing now that such tactics will not go unanswered," they added.
But whether Europe's more assertive stance is having any effect on Russia remains to be seen.
Keatinge said the impact is "difficult to measure, particularly in an environment where the oil markets are highly volatile due to the U.S. war in the Middle East."
Instead, he pointed to the impact of Ukraine's attacks on Russia's energy production capacity, which have already led to sales restrictions and export curbs.

Yair Golan unveils NIS 1b. plan to fight crime in Arab society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:17:32 UTC
02:17:32 KST

A national state of emergency, a special task force, and an annual budget of NIS 1 billion are at the center of a plan unveiled Monday by the Democrats Party leader, Yair Golan, to combat organized crime in Arab society.
Golan presented the plan, which he described as a "root treatment," at a press conference in Nazareth.
Under the proposal, Golan pledged that within the first week after the formation of a government led by him or including his party, a national state of emergency would be declared and a dedicated task force would be established to bring together the country's law enforcement agencies.
Golan outlined several key elements of the plan, including shortening judicial proceedings with the goal of moving from arrest to imprisonment within nine months, establishing dedicated courts for serious crimes, and launching a broad economic campaign to cut off criminal organizations' sources of funding and bar companies linked to them from public tenders.
Golan also announced the establishment of "Team 49," an interministerial body that would bring together the education, welfare, law enforcement, and rehabilitation systems to identify and rescue at-risk youth from the grip of criminal organizations. The body is named for the 49 children and minors who have been murdered in recent years.
Golan speaks to Israel's Arab citizens
During the press conference, held alongside a display of weapons seized in the field, including rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs), automatic rifles, and handguns, Golan directly addressed Arab citizens and bereaved families and asked for their forgiveness.
"Sorry that the government abandoned you and gave up on its most basic duty, to protect the lives of its citizens," he said. "Instead of fighting the criminal organizations, it allowed them to grow stronger and become the de facto rulers of entire streets."
Golan also sharply criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, stressing that the rise in crime was neither inevitable nor a cultural issue.
"This is an ongoing failure of the government. A country that knows how to reach every terrorist organization in the world and expose nuclear facilities in Iran knows how to reach every criminal organization and locate illegal weapons anywhere in Israel. When there is a decision and a will, there is also the ability."
Golan said crime in Arab society should not be viewed as a problem affecting only one sector, but as a threat to Israeli society as a whole.
"When a criminal organization takes control of an Arab locality, it does not stay there, it reaches the roads, the cities, businesses, and all of our lives. No one will be safe until all of us are safe,"
Golan concluded, pledging: "Our first demand will be to receive the National Security Ministry portfolio. We have one test, the test of results."
MK Naama Lazimi presented a firm position on the role of Arab society in Israel's political and social future.
Drawing on childhood memories from the Migdal HaEmek, Yafia, and Nazareth area, Lazimi described how the shared life she once took for granted had eroded as a result of what she described as discriminatory government policies.
Lazimi stressed that "democracy is measured not only by the inclusion of the minority but by the treatment of it," and said Arab society must be an integral part of rebuilding a cohesive and democratic Israel.
She sharply criticized the current government, saying that approximately 700 citizens had been murdered since it took office and describing the failure to provide security as abandonment rather than governance.
Lazimi also addressed potential partners in a future coalition, calling on them to abandon cynical political calculations and stop rejecting partnership out of fear.
She made clear that "those who ignore the existing situation give power to the elements seeking to destroy shared life in this country."
MK Gilad Kariv accused Netanyahu's governments of abandoning Arab society for years, which he said had contributed to the spread of weapons and deadly crime.
Kariv argued that Netanyahu and his political partners had turned Arab citizens into enemies for political reasons. He stressed that combating crime requires Jewish-Arab partnership.
According to Kariv, his party would not be drawn into Netanyahu's "disqualification campaign" and would work to ensure that Arab citizens are included as equal partners.
Parents of crime victims speak out
Parents whose children had been murdered also addressed the conference. Among them was Dr. Ashraf Sapia, a well-known and respected dentist and the father of 15-year-old Nabil, a gifted student who was shot dead while walking on a street in Kafr Yasif.
"For those who don't know, I am Nabil's father. A gifted child who studied all day for his biology exam, and with permission from his father and mother, went out for a walk after a full day of studies. At seven thirty, after the visit from his father and mother, at eight o'clock he came back in a coffin. Now, Nabil, like every boy, every girl... We in Arab society have been abandoned. For 70 years we lived in this country; there were no people killed. We were young, we were children, we were little, and we didn't have this. 75,000 weapons circulating.”
"My duty is to protect my son, teach him, and educate him. But who guarantees me... Now my youngest son, two groups in Kafr Yasif want him for soccer, I work at a hospital, work at my clinic... Who guarantees me that he finishes soccer practice in Kafr Yasif and that from the game he will come home and no one will come near him? No one can guarantee that. And the one who deals with this is the top of the pyramid and downward. Whoever abandoned us, then he has to move himself aside and bring us people who will look us in the eyes.”
"I thank you very much, and with God's help I see light at the end of the tunnel. I really see light. We will succeed because God does not accept this chaos. There needs to be order. I fulfill my obligations, and the entire sector fulfills its obligations, but we are asking the leadership to protect us. Simple. That's all."

Drought declared in ‘almost three-quarters’ of England, government says
England and Wales both experienced the driest July on record, the UK’s Met Office said, with a fifth heatwave forecast for the week ahead
Some 71.3 per cent of England is in drought, the UK government said on Monday, after the nation experienced its driest July on record, with a fifth heatwave and scant rain forecast for the week ahead.
Parks and fields that are usually green at this point in the year were parched and yellow, according to Agence France-Presse photos, as river levels dwindled and farmers battling low crop yields warned of possible food shortages.
“Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought as conditions worsen following a dry start to August,” the environment department said, as parts of the central Midlands and northeast England joined other areas of the country experiencing prolonged dry weather.
“All regions of the country are experiencing pressure on their water resources,” the department said, with “nowhere” in the UK having a “normal” status.
The Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said most of England is experiencing a “flash drought”, which develops quickly and is the result of very low rainfall and high temperatures.
It is the third drought Britain – usually known for its unpredictable wet weather – has experienced in five years. More than 50 per cent of England was declared to be in drought at the end of July.

Indian police use force to disperse youth protesters calling for exam overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:16:28 UTC
02:16:28 KST

Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.
Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.
The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.
Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.
“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.
The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.
They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.
Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.
Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.
The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.
The Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.
The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.
The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.
Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.

Ukraine avoids power shortage during heatwave thanks to thermal reserves, optimised nuclear maintenance – ex-energy minister
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
20:15:30 EEST
02:15:30 KST

Ukraine managed to avoid an electricity shortage that could have led to power restrictions during the heat wave thanks to several thermal power units held in reserve, the optimization of maintenance schedules at nuclear power units, and a reduction in consumption since the beginning of 2026, former Energy Minister Olha Buslavets has said.
"When the heatwave hit, Ukraine had a surplus of electricity generation, thanks in part to having, as a rule, two or three thermal power units in reserve that could not be used to export electricity due to the SWAM environmental tax," she told Interfax-Ukraine.
In addition, since late July, JSC Energoatom has postponed the scheduled maintenance shutdown of another nuclear power unit, which had been operating at reduced capacity for some time while awaiting the return from maintenance of a counterpart unit.
"This was the right decision: the maintenance schedule was optimized to ensure there would be enough fuel for the extended period, with the aim of waiting for the compensating capacity of the other unit to come online," Buslavets said.
According to her, another factor contributing to the absence of an electricity shortage was the overall decline in consumption since the beginning of 2026, particularly due to businesses building generation capacity for their own use, and the shutdown of certain industrial enterprises ahead of the heatwave due to Russian attacks on port infrastructure and vessels. In particular, the Southern GOK and enterprises of the Ferrexpo Group suspended operations.
According to the former minister, in the first six months of this year, total electricity consumption in Ukraine's integrated power grid decreased by 6% compared to the same period last year, with industrial consumption falling by 13%.
Currently, seven out of nine nuclear power plant units located in unoccupied territories are operating in Ukraine's power grid; last week, one unit completed repairs while another unit entered scheduled maintenance.
As previously reported, First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal stated in late July that Ukraine's power grid was being prepared for peak August loads resulting from hot weather and a 1 GW increase in electricity consumption.

74 killed as 7.4-magnitude earthquake devastates western Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:14:36 UTC
02:14:36 KST

ALBAWABA- A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 74 people and injuring dozens, with the death toll expected to rise as rescue teams continue searching damaged and collapsed buildings.
The earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time (12:34 UTC), with its epicenter near San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, about 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of Bogotá. The quake occurred at an estimated depth of 96–110 kilometers (60–69 miles) and was felt across much of Colombia, as well as in Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. A magnitude-5.0 aftershock followed about 45 minutes later.
The earthquake was an intermediate-depth strike-slip event associated with the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate, producing intense shaking that reportedly lasted nearly two minutes. No tsunami warning was issued.
The hardest-hit areas include Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Caldas and Chocó, with fatalities reported in Pereira, Cali, Manizales, Quibdó, Buenaventura and surrounding areas.
Buildings and other structures have collapsed or sustained major damage in several cities. In Cali, authorities reported dozens of affected structures, with some people trapped under rubble. A tower of a cathedral in Manizales also collapsed, while homes and other buildings were heavily damaged in smaller communities.
Several airports were damaged or temporarily closed, disrupting flights in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura. Damage was also reported at Matecaña International Airport in Pereira.
Emergency teams are conducting search-and-rescue operations, while authorities warn of further aftershocks. Colombia's national disaster-management authorities have activated emergency response mechanisms, with international assistance also being offered. The 74-death toll remains preliminary and could rise as rescue teams reach remote and heavily damaged areas.
