Poll-rigging bots and AI robocalls: The dark tech running Israel's election campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:12:27 UTC
02:12:27 KST

A month after Israel's last general election in November 2022, ChatGPT was launched. In the four years since, though Benjamin Netanyahu's government has remained in power, political campaigns and the available technology have changed dramatically.
A Haaretz investigation has found a slew of new campaign and influence tools, among them bots that try to rig online polls in favor of a party's candidates. The new tools, experts say, show how the laws designed to safeguard election integrity are woefully obsolete.
Drawn up in the 1950s, these laws were updated recently to address new threats including deepfakes and other AI-generated campaigning ploys. But sources across the parties' campaigns and senior figures at the tech companies serving them have exposed the new toolbox of Israel's election industry, a full range of unregulated technologies.
These are the parties' instruments for identifying and persuading voters, including bots and avatars, advanced intelligence tools and efforts to engineer public opinion through AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT. Some of these tools are illegal, and none are subject to any election oversight.
Polling bots
Bots is a much overused term that just means software performing actions usually done by humans; it does this automatically and at scale. Bots have long been used in digital marketing to inflate view counts and boost content's standing on sites like Google. Campaign managers say bots are also widespread in politics. Parties buy them to inflate view counts across social media, or to comment on and share content to boost the party's apparent "organic" reach.
But ahead of the October 27 election, a new service is being offered: a fleet of bots that vote in online polls and skew the results of unregulated surveys. Alongside polls by respected institutes for media outlets, social media platforms and the wider web are flooded with open polls that let any user vote.
One right-leaning popular Instagram news account recently published a poll asking who is more suited to be prime minister, Naftali Bennett or Gadi Eisenkot. It drew 312,000 views and over 140,000 votes. An unregulated poll like this is relatively easy to manipulate – and that's exactly the service now being offered.
The bots that are sold to campaigns scan social media and the wider internet, identify open polls and systematically vote for their candidate. Also, some of the more advanced avatars – digital personas that seem to be real people – have real phone numbers and can vote in polls distributed via text messaging or in large WhatsApp and Telegram groups. Industry sources say the use of such bots in the current election cycle is massive.
Although such polls have no statistical credibility, they matter. They can be amplified online, generate momentum for a party or damage a rival's image. A party near Israel's 3.25 percent electoral threshold might use them to falsely reassure hesitant voters that the party faces no danger in qualifying for the Knesset.
The Israeli authorities have long been concerned by the impact on voters of polls, which are forbidden in the last few days before an election. This month, the Central Elections Committee took this caution much further: It told media outlets to submit data on every published poll within 24 hours.
But the directive applies only to polls using recognized statistical methods, not to open internet polls. The law requires anyone publishing a nonstatistically significant poll to state clearly that its results do not reflect public opinion. But a Haaretz review found that this is not yet being done.
Agents for hire
Bad actors in the current election campaign are also using fake accounts more sophisticated than bots – avatars that pose as real users and function as influence agents. Haaretz has found that at least two avatar networks have been set up ahead of the vote, serving the campaigns of candidates across the political spectrum.
Avatars post and share content, comment on articles and other posts, and amplify campaign messages. Unlike a bot, which is fully automated, an avatar is usually partially maintained by a human and is designed to look indistinguishable from a real person. Some of these services also offer avatars for identifying closed groups of potential voters, infiltrating them and only then plying targeted influence.
"This isn't something you can build overnight – there's a process. Building a network like this requires real infrastructure," says a senior figure at a company working with one of the campaigns.
A 2023 Haaretz-TheMarker investigation revealed that an Israeli firm sold software for creating such accounts at scale and also maintained a roster of tens of thousands of fake identities as part of election interference and a disinformation service it offered. This was the first time such disinformation software was exposed, but it's far from the only one out there.
In 2024, Haaretz revealed that in the wake of the digital backlash that followed October 7, Israel bought a mass-avatar influence system developed by another contractor and deployed by it, which was used to troll the pages of U.S. lawmakers. But it was caught by Meta, which took the campaign down, causing embarrassment in Israel.
Since then, more Israeli companies offering similar technologies have emerged, and though these products are usually exported as part of campaigns run in other countries, many times by Israeli contractors, they are now targeting Israelis.
Volunteer armies
Alongside the fictitious digital activity, campaigns recruit real users for organized online influence. "Imagine a setup where about 6,000 supporters receive a daily briefing with messages, images and videos they're expected to amplify, and links they're asked to comment on," says a political consultant for one of the campaigns.
Parties build up volunteer armies through mass text messaging and promotion campaigns. They deploy these digital conscripts to shape a discourse that seems organic but is dictated from above.
Here, too, artificial intelligence plays a role. AI agents scan the internet for discussion hubs that volunteers are directed to engage with, and AI tools draft the messages and comments that these innocent users post. Such technologies were launched after October 7, initially developed as part of ad hoc Israel PR initiatives by volunteers. These apps and capabilities are now being turned inward toward Israeli hearts and minds.
ADINT
At the heart of the election operation are basic software systems that allow parties to collect and manage vast databases of voter information – to locate committed supporters and wavering former voters, and even identify a rival's base to suppress its turnout.
These are benign programs – or at least they began that way. The foundation is the voter registry, provided by the Interior Ministry ahead of every election. Using AI, parties enrich each person's record with contact details and political indicators, cross-referencing massive commercial databases to match voter names with phone numbers or email addresses. Though campaigns have always worked this way, with the help of AI, bigger and more diverse datasets can be integrated, including new types of data that have emerged in recent years to serve the mobile advertising market.
To profile voters, some parties use campaign apps like Elector, where supporters tag each of their contacts' political leanings.
Parties also use advertising intelligence, ADINT, a technology used by intelligence agencies and exposed in a number of Haaretz investigations as leaking to the private market. With ADINT, data collected from apps and smartphones and sold to advertisers for marketing purposes is turned into geolocation data that allows tracking and targeting.
We may not realize it, but each of us has a unique digital ad identifier, which supposedly is anonymous. But as Haaretz has revealed, companies have developed de-anonymization capabilities linking these identifiers to phone numbers – capabilities once reserved for espionage such as tracking nuclear scientists in Iran. Now such capabilities and the data behind them are sold to commercial clients that, thanks to AI, can process data at a scale once considered too big for marketers or campaigns.
However, according to the sources in Israeli campaigns and at tech companies, political campaigns are deploying this know-how alongside their VRM (Voter Relations Management) systems and get-out-the-vote apps like Elector.
ADINT can identify anyone who follows a party on Facebook or joins a group related to a party; some companies even conduct polls whose real purpose is to collect data on the respondents. To obtain this intelligence, parties buy databases; some of the means for this are more legal than others. "There's a lot less than three months left, and the race to obtain voter data is at its peak," a campaign operative says.
At the center of the data effort are VRM systems. Two companies dominate the market, but during this election cycle, parties have also decided to build their own systems using Anthropic's Claude and other AI models that can code and build software.
These systems are also used on Election Day. Observers report which targeted voters have voted, and headquarters sends operatives to those who have not.
But this week, the head of the Central Elections Committee, Justice Noam Sohlberg, barred observers from reporting to their parties in real time on who has voted, which he said "constitutes a violation of privacy." The ruling riled the ultra-Orthodox parties and Likud, the main users of these systems.
Ramped-up robocalls
Once the relevant voters have been identified, parties target them through paid ads, social media and phone calls, as well as SMS and WhatsApp messages. Companies specializing in mass WhatsApp campaigns have emerged despite Meta's policy of blocking such efforts.
The biggest technological change involves the oldest tool – phone calls. Robocalls have existed since the '90s but have evolved beyond recognition. Industry sources describe AI systems that tailor each call to its recipient, like "Hello Omer, this is Benjamin Netanyahu," and respond to questions and responses using answers drawn from a preprepared set. It all sounds real, an example of how AI is upgrading old election technologies.
Parties are also investing in AI as actual influence channels. In the past, the focus was billboards and posters, then search engine optimization, SEO; for example, getting a party's message high on a Google search. Now anyone looking to reach a wide audience concentrates on penetrating AI-based chatbots – also called GEO, with the "G" standing for GPT.
Campaigns build online content so that AI engines reflect it in their answers, absorbing positive information about a candidate and negative information about rivals.
A Haaretz test found that chatbots avoid direct answers to questions like "Who is the most suitable candidate for prime minister?" But the more specific the question, the less cautious they become.
When we asked which candidate is most likely to rehabilitate Israel's standing around the world, ChatGPT omitted one prominent candidate, Avigdor Lieberman, citing "[Yair] Lapid, Bennett or Eisenkot as having potential for this." But it qualified: "There is no professional or public consensus that any one candidate is clearly the most suitable."
Is any of this legal?
The gap between privacy laws and election laws leaves campaign managers significant room to maneuver, especially given that no government body is responsible for regulating the election tech and capabilities described in this article.
"Elections are a mass casualty event for privacy," said attorney and activist Shahar Ben Meir, who petitioned the Central Elections Committee to ban parties from using dedicated campaign apps. Political campaigns, he said, "engage in a range of actions that significantly violate privacy, and there is considerable doubt regarding their legality."
According to Ben Meir, "In any normal country, an expert committee is appointed to set guidelines for protecting voter privacy in the age of Big Data, and these are implemented through legislation and regulation."
Ben Meir believes that Israel's shortfall is no accident. "This failure has direct culprits – Prime Minister Netanyahu and the party he leads, who prefer to operate in an environment of outdated laws," Ben Meir says. "Ofer Golan, the former head of Likud's campaign headquarters, made this clear when he said in an interview in 2019: 'We have no red lines. The goal is to win – we'll do damage control later.'"
The hardest test may come after the polls close, warns Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler, head of the Democracy in the Information Age program at the Israel Democracy Institute. "These tools can be used not only to promote a candidate, harm a rival or influence turnout, but to generate a real-time stolen-election narrative and undermine public trust in the elections committee and the results," she says.
"In such a scenario, all existing tools would need to be deployed swiftly, decisively and with a deliberate interpretation of the law, because public trust lost in the hours after the polls close will be very hard to restore by a legal ruling issued days later."

Your Dog Really Can Tell When You're Happy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:12:14 UTC
02:12:14 KST

If you’ve ever suspected your dog can read your mind—sussing out through some canine intuition when you’re happy, sad, scared, or cross—you’re half right. Many dogs can do exactly that, but it’s not mind-reading that’s involved: it’s face-reading. That’s the word from a new study in the journal iScience, in which researchers not only established dogs’ ability to discern human moods by examining our facial expressions, but also pinpointed the spots in the brain where that processing takes place. They did this by scanning canine brains with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
Figuring out how dogs read human emotions
“This ability to perceive emotions in humans is really hard to find in other species,” says Rául Hernández Pérez, professor of psychology at the University of Vienna and first author of the study. “Chimpanzees have a harder time than dogs. Wolves can also do it, but not at the same level as dogs can.”
Getting a dog to tolerate an MRI scanner is no small matter. The same things that so often freak people out about the MRI experience—the confined space and the infernal noise—can have a similar effect on a dog. That was an impediment to the kind of study the researchers planned to conduct. In order for a brain scan of the proper fidelity to be produced, the dogs must spend a minimum of six minutes in the machine, moving less than three millimeters in any direction. “If they move more than three millimeters, we can’t use the data,” says Laura Cuaya, professor of biological psychology at the University of Vienna and a co-author of the study.
Looking for dogs who could perform that feat, she and Hernández Pérez recruited 14 cooperative canines, consisting of 11 border collies—a highly trainable breed—two golden retrievers, and one Labrador, the last three of which were already working as service animals.
The animals then went through a series of at least 20 training sessions—the first involving just introducing them to the researchers and building a sense of trust. Next, the dogs were taught to lie still for just five seconds in the position they would have to maintain in the MRI scanner. “We reward them with treats, though some dogs prefer to play as a reward,” says Cuaya.
Over the course of several days, that brief five seconds was steadily extended to 10 full minutes. The dogs were then introduced to the headphones they would have to wear while in the machine to protect their hearing. “The headphones are not uncomfortable, but they’re weird,” says Cuaya. Finally, the dogs practiced holding their pose in a mock MRI scanner, and only then were they ready for the real, clanking, buzzing, banging machine.
In the study, the dogs were positioned in the machine and shown pictures of a human face wearing either a happy or neutral expression. All the while the fMRI churned on, peering through the dogs’ skulls into the brain below and looking for the areas that lit up as a result of the visual stimuli. When the dogs saw pictures of happy people, their temporal cortex and caudate nucleus became active. In humans, the temporal lobe plays a role in forming memories, mastering language, responding to visual cues such as familiar faces, and processing emotions. The caudate nucleus processes rewards and motivation and manages learning and memory. The neutral face did not elicit the same response in either region.
Next, the dogs were once again shown images of happy and neutral faces, but along with those they were also shown angry, frightened, and sad ones. The researchers were trying to determine whether the dogs processed human faces in a binary way—registering the positive, happy face in one part of the brain and the three negative ones together in one other part, or if each negative emotion had its own discrete brain region.
“This would mean that the dog brain is not only categorizing emotions between positive and negative," says Cuaya. “We were using this [stage of the experiment] as a demonstration that there is more detailed processing.”
What dogs’ brains reveal about the dog-human bond
That was the result they got. Sadness and fear, for example, lit up the right rostral supra sylvian gyrus—which, in humans, contributes to the processing of visual information. Anger and fear were processed in the right ectosylvian gyrus and the left splenal gyrus—the former integrating visual, auditory, and other sensory information, and the latter managing visual perception, spatial orientation, and episodic memory.
“We found that the dog brain is not only categorizing emotions as positive or negative, but instead can exhibit more detailed processing, responding in different ways to emotions,” says Hernández Pérez.
This isn’t the first study to find that dogs respond in unique ways to human faces. Other research has shown that when a human face is happy, for example, dogs look more at the eyes than the mouth. They examine emotional faces longer than they examine neutral ones. And they have more difficulty reading the faces of people who are of a different gender from their principal caregiver.
There are benefits to the study—beyond the simple matter of adding to the body of knowledge on how dog brains operate. Hernández Pérez and Cuaya believe their work can also help improve the already deep ties dogs and humans share.
“Humans are not so good at perceiving the emotions of our dogs,” says Cuaya. “We are confused by them. Maybe this work can be an invitation to try to be more aware of the emotions of our dogs and how they are expressing [them].”
That understanding can also pay dividends when we are training our dogs. “When you are teaching something to your dog, you can have treats on hand, and you can give the treats when they are appropriate. But you can also show your emotion. You can say to the dog, ‘Very good!’ The dogs in our MRI machine were already reacting to the faces of strangers. Think about how much more activation there is with a familiar face expressing, ‘I love you so much. I am happy with you.’”
The dog-human love story—which has been going on for some 14,000 years now—has been a long and tender one. The more we understand the canine contribution to that bond, the more we can improve our own.

Ukraine’s cardboard protests look like democracy working. In a war, that’s also the risk.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:10:57 UTC
02:10:57 KST

On 16 July 2026, protesters took to the squares in Ukrainian cities with cardboard signs bearing the same demand in various forms: to reinstate Ukraine’s Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The following day, protesters added a new demand: to dismiss Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Oleksandr Syrskyi. A few days later, Zelenskyy met the second demand—but not the first, which the protesters are still waiting on.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine has been under martial law, which necessarily restricts democracy in order to centralize governance. The country is not holding elections, citizens’ rights are restricted, and the military has become one of the country’s key institutions. Under these circumstances, the President dismissed one of the most important figures in the military at the demand of street protesters.
These centralizing tendencies of wartime rule could lead either to “strengthening democracy” or to “strengthening authoritarianism,” political science professor Anatolii Romaniuk told Euromaidan Press—and this year's protests, he argues, show that society is reaching for more democracy. Ukrainians recognize the cardboard-sign protests as an expression of democracy while also worrying about what such developments mean for a country at war.
What the protests for Fedorov achieved
- On 14 July, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine backed the resignation of Prime Minister Yuliia Svyrydenko and the Cabinet of Ministers;
- On 15 July, Fedorov confirmed that he was leaving the position of Defense Minister;
- On 16 July, the first demonstrators gathered on Ivan Franko Square in Kyiv holding handwritten cardboard signs calling for Fedorov’s return. Similar protests soon spread to other Ukrainian cities;
- On 20 July, Major General Yevhenii Khmara, acting head of the SBU, became acting defense minister—the post the protesters want returned to Fedorov.
- On 21 July, President Zelenskyy announced that the commander-in-chief would be replaced. The following day, Syrskyi was officially dismissed, with Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi appointed as his successor;
- On 24 July, protesters declared the rallies open-ended until Zelenskyy reinstates Fedorov as Defense Minister.
“The fact that the authorities took the protesters’ demand into account is good,” Romaniuk says. He considers this an important element of political culture.
More than three weeks on, the protests continue—smaller than at their July peak but daily, from Lviv to frontline Dnipro, now under a broader call for "dialogue and reforms" in the defense sector. Fedorov himself has declined to lead them: he told the New York Times he will not go into opposition during the war or be "artificially dragged" into politics, and has turned down every post the president has offered except the one he lost.
We stood, we stand, and we will stand
Not every protester can fully explain every aspect of the issue, but they all recognize a sense of injustice and feel compelled to speak out against it, Ukrainian photojournalist Stas Kozliuk says.
Romaniuk sees these handwritten, highly individual signs as evidence of personal agency.
“This is a form of self-expression—of a person's identity, views, and position. To me, the cardboard sign itself is a powerful marker. Not a professionally printed slogan, because once perfectly designed placards start appearing at protests, it usually means someone has commissioned them,” Romaniuk says.
Do we know who the people holding cardboard signs at the protests are? Probably not. According to Ukrainian analyst Vadym Denysenko, no one really knows who these protesters are. He argues that no comprehensive sociological research has been done on either last year's protests or the current wave.
“Who are these people? Do they have a political program? What is their vision of the future? Ultimately, do they see themselves entering politics? These are basic questions. The answers would cost a few tens of thousands of dollars, yet no political force has been willing to spend that money,” Denysenko wrote on Facebook.
Twenty-two-year-old Dariia, who came to the rally in Lviv on 24 July, believes that the protests will not simply disappear.
“I think people will stay for as long as it takes, until Fedorov is restored to a position where he can genuinely influence the current situation,” she says.
Among the protesters at the 24 July rally in Lviv was also a woman holding a cardboard sign that read: “Swap the POWs, not Fedorov.” She came there with her husband and child.
“I am originally from Kharkiv. My father is missing, so first of all I was against Syrskyi. Now I am already satisfied. But now we need Fedorov, because he is ‘technology, not people,’” the woman said.
Ukraine’s Gen Z protested for their anti-corruption agencies last year. Now they’re protesting for one man
Strength and risk at the same time
Russia has sought to exploit the protests for its own purposes. It seizes on the fact that Ukrainians hold different views on the protests, amplifies divisions in public opinion, and presents them as evidence that the country is becoming ungovernable.
Writing for Ukrainska Pravda, media expert Oksana Moroz argues that the Kremlin has attempted to weaponize public discontent through coordinated information campaigns.
According to Moroz, Russia relied not only on artificially generated TikTok videos spreading narratives harmful to Ukrainian society but also on Telegram. There, she says, “a classic network of Russian or pro-Russian bloggers” circulated posts aimed, among other things, at discrediting the demonstrations. These bloggers promoted claims that the protests were orchestrated and that participants were being paid to attend.
Some demonstrators have responded to those accusations with humor. Protesters voluntarily bring candy, cookies, pastries, and other snacks to share with anyone attending, joking that this is the “salary” they supposedly receive for protesting.
Military Ombudsperson Olha Reshetylova argues that “a sense of injustice in society cannot be bought, fabricated, or created overnight through a social media post. It is the result of accumulated and unresolved problems.”
Where the line has to be drawn
Opinions within the military are divided. Some servicemembers have openly supported the protests despite pressure from their commanders. Others believe demonstrations of this kind are inappropriate and harmful under wartime conditions, says Reshetylova.
“Many people around me today — including combat officers — see the cardboard-sign protests as infantile, detached from reality, and unacceptable while the country is fighting a war. Although I disagree with some of the protesters' demands, I do not share that view,” she says.
Personnel changes in the military should be made in consultation with the officers responsible for the country’s defense, says MP and member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on National Security, Defense, and Intelligence Oleksandr Fedienko. He emphasizes that this reduces the risk of weakening the country’s defense capabilities due to inappropriate personnel changes.
Despite his positive view of the protests, Romaniuk warns that such pressure is dangerous in a country at war.
“During wartime, changing the military because of protests rather than professional assessments carries obvious risks. In this case, things ended well. But as a mechanism, it is dangerous. Someone could organize demonstrations demanding the dismissal of any official. That is where the line has to be drawn.”
Dariia, back at the Lviv rally, voiced her own doubt about whether President Zelenskyy would meet the demand:
“The pessimistic question arises: are they feeding us these little crumbs so that we calm down and forget about it? Many older people, for example, my parents, think that they will feed us a crumb of honey now, and then start stealing the budget again.”

More than 70 dead after powerful earthquake strikes western Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:10:54 UTC
02:10:54 KST

More than 100 people died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.
The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June.
The quake killed at least 132 people and more than 570 were injured as of Monday afternoon, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a group coordinating cities across the country.
“The national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed,” Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in a national address at about 1pm local time upon declaring a national state of emergency. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”
Western Colombia appeared to have suffered the most serious damage. Authorities reported 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas.
The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed.
In a video post, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet. I know this isn’t easy but stay outside for a little while at least because there could be an aftershock.”
Social media videos showed people searching for victims in the wreckage of a four-storey hotel in Cali and a woman sprinting from a building as it collapsed in Manizales.
One video showed part of San José church in Pereira collapsing as palm trees around it shook. Another video published by the newspaper El Tiempo captured the moment a building gave way in Manizales.
The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said at least 20 buildings collapsed in his city and people were trapped inside.
“Right now, we are trying to map out what has happened, firstly to protect lives and secondly to be able to push ahead with any kind of rescue that might be necessary,” he said, urging citizens to stay calm.
He told residents to check their buildings for structural damage. “If you do not feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please leave the building.”
In an interview, the mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims thought to be trapped in at least 15 of them. Five of the city’s hospitals were reportedly inundated with the injured.
Raúl Andrés Buitrago, the head of customer service at a business in Pereira, said he was leaving for work when the seismic alert on his watch went off.
“There are often little tremors here,” he said. “But I’d never felt an earthquake like this. It started softly, softly, softly, then it felt like it was getting stronger every second.”
He spoke of “horrible” scenes as he fled outside on to the street in the city centre, which is home to many old buildings. “The roofs started to fall in. The buildings collapsed in on themselves. The panic was terrible. They were the four longest minutes of my life.”
The governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba, said people had been injured and buildings severely damaged in the department’s capital, Quibdó.
De la Espriella, who took office on Friday, said he would lead the government response. “Colombia has a president whose heart aches for his people and who will do everything in his power to help them in the most difficult moments,” he said in a video post.
De La Espriella visited Quibdo where he promised rent subsidies for those who had lost homes, and then travelled to Cali. Authorities in Cali, Armenia and Manizales announced curfews, with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets. De La Espriella promised 1,000 additional security personnel for the city.
Aviation authorities said the airports were damaged in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Cartago, Armenia and Buenaventura.
Neighbouring Venezuela was struck on 24 June by twin earthquakes that devastated the country’s northern coast, killing more than 6,000 people.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration – which has thrown its weight behind Colombia’s new rightwing president – would provide $15.5m in emergency aid.

Russian attacks have destroyed nearly 1.2m school textbooks in Ukraine
Large-scale Russian attacks on Ukrainian printing companies and logistics warehouses have destroyed nearly 1.2 million school textbooks. The biggest losses have affected textbook print runs for students in Years 4 and 9 (aged approximately 9-10 and 14-15 respectively).
Source: Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian Parliament), citing Serhii Babak, Chairman of the Committee on Education, Science and Innovation
Details: Babak said a total of 1,166,874 copies have been destroyed, accounting for 8.6% of the total number of textbooks printed for the 2026-2027 academic year.
The biggest losses were among books for Year 9: more than 850,000 copies were destroyed, equivalent to 9.5% of the print run. More than 271,000 copies for Year 4 were lost, accounting for 7% of the print run. Almost 45,000 textbooks for pupils in Years 6 and 7 were also destroyed, representing 6% of their print run.
The books destroyed in the attacks had been prepared for dispatch. Some print runs were also still being produced at the time of the attacks.
Significant losses were incurred by some Ukrainian publishers – Ranok, Hramota, Lingvist, Akademiia, Osvita, Litera, Aston and Shkoliar.
The committee has now identified which textbooks need to be reprinted as a priority. The government is looking for additional printing capacity to ensure that Ukrainian schoolchildren receive all the books they need by 1 September, when the new school year begins in Ukraine.
The authorities have also decided to improve logistics and establish safer storage facilities for new print runs.
"There are two equally important goals for us today. The first is to do everything possible to ensure that Ukrainian schoolchildren receive the textbooks they need by 1 September. The second is not to leave Ukrainian publishers to deal with the aftermath of Russian strikes on their own. This is only the beginning of our joint work," Babak said.
Background:
- In early July, Russian missiles struck the central warehouse of the BookChefpublishing house's logistics partner, destroying around 800,000 books.
- A partner printing house of the publishers Ranok was also affected. A Russian strike damaged a warehouse belonging to the Nash Format publisher and online store.
- During a strike on Kyiv on 19 July, Russian forces destroyed a warehouse belonging to the knigolove publishing house where 250,000 books were stored.
- The premises of the Mison publishing house's editorial office were completely burned down in the same attack. The Konvi printing and polygraphy company, which produces materials for Ranok, Laboratoriia, ArtBooks, BookChef and many other publishers, was also affected.
- Overall, Russian attacks destroyed more than 1.5 million copies of Ukrainian books in July alone. Tetiana Berezhna, Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture, said publishers have lost hundreds of millions of hryvnias due to relentless Russian attacks.

70 ballistic missiles and 12 launchers: Ukraine lines up deep-strike refill from an unlikely supplier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:01:03 UTC
02:01:03 KST

Ukraine has agreed to buy a batch of American-made ballistic missiles and rocket launchers from Türkiye, according to Militarnyi. The weapons sit in Turkish stockpiles and still need to clear a routine US review before they ship.
Ukraine's deep strikes run on a scarce, politically gated supply of Western missiles, which it burns through faster than allies' resupply.
What Ukraine is buying
US government paperwork lists 70 M39 ATACMS (Army Tactical Missile System) missiles and 12 M270 rocket launchers, plus tens of thousands of cluster munitions. The M270 is a tracked launcher that fires guided rockets and ATACMS, the heavier sibling of the wheeled HIMARS.
The cluster load adds 2,524 M26 rockets for the M270 launchers and 47,000 M509A1 shells for Ukraine's 2S7 Pion and M110 guns. Both scatter bomblets over a wide area. The deal surfaced in US State Department notifications in the US Congressional Record for 6 August 2026. Türkiye wants to shed older weapons and fund newer systems, the filings say. The shipment moves through Turkish, Bulgarian, and American exporters.
How the sale clears Washington
Frontline report: ATACMS returns to battlefield as Ukraine destroys Russian training facility in Voronezh
Because these are US-origin weapons, Washington must sign off first. The filings note that US law forces the State Department to notify Congress once major equipment tops $14 million, or other articles and services top $50 million. There is no approval vote: if neither chamber blocks the sale within 15 days, US consent takes effect automatically. Both chambers sit in recess past that deadline — the House until 31 August 2026, the Senate until 14 September 2026.
What the M39 ATACMS is
The M39 is the original production model of ATACMS, flying about 165 kilometers, or roughly 103 miles—shorter than later versions Ukraine has fired. It steers by laser gyroscopes with no GPS correction, which makes it less precise. Instead, it carries a 560-kilogram cluster warhead of 950 M74 submunitions built to hit troops, unarmored vehicles, and air defenses.
Ukraine marks invasion anniversary with ATACMS strikes on Russian command and supply lines (MAP)
How Ukraine uses ATACMS
Ukraine has fired ATACMS at Russian command posts, ammunition depots, and air defenses across occupied land and inside Russia. Even occasional launches force Russia to shift air defenses back from the front, easing pressure on Ukrainian troops. That firepower had gone quiet. Ukraine ran through its US-supplied ATACMS months ago, and US approvals came slowly. Buying 70 more through Türkiye lets Ukraine rebuild without waiting on fresh US aid.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:00:57 UTC
02:00:57 KST

Israel is increasingly concerned that a new defense pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan is directed not only at Iran but also against Israel, a senior Israeli official said Monday, warning that Egypt could eventually join the alliance.
“This agreement troubles us. This is an alliance aimed against Israel,” the official said of the defense agreement signed over the weekend in Mecca.
Reports following the signing suggested Egypt could become the next country to join the emerging bloc.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told the state-run Anadolu news agency that the agreement is effectively modeled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
Fidan said the alliance would also include a ministerial committee and a general secretariat headquartered in Saudi Arabia.
The senior Israeli official said the agreement reflects a broader regional shift.
“The Shiite axis has weakened, and for a long time we have seen the Sunni axis getting stronger,” the official said. “Israel needs to build alternative alliances, especially with the Hellenic axis, Greece and Cyprus, together with India and the United Arab Emirates.”
Israel, he added, must become “very, very strong” and make other countries dependent on it.
“Israel needs a massive force-building program,” the official said.
The official singled out Turkey and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as a particular concern.
“The story of Turkey and Erdogan is dangerous,” he said. “We would not be surprised if the Egyptians join the ‘Mecca Alliance.’ This alliance is aimed against Israel. Who do you think they are doing this against? Allow me to be skeptical when they say it is really aimed at Iran.”
The agreement was signed Friday during a meeting in Saudi Arabia between Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
Dubbed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, the pact is the result of nearly a year of negotiations among the three countries.
‘Unite against Israel’
The signing comes as Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan seek greater strategic independence amid regional upheaval.
Reuters noted that although all three countries remain concerned about Iran and its proxies, they are also increasingly troubled by Israel’s military policies in the region, while doubts are growing over the ability of their longtime ally, the United States, to restrain further escalation.
Pakistan said the agreement also calls for expanding security cooperation across multiple fields.
The alliance brings together three very different powers: Saudi Arabia, a major oil producer; Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state; and Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest military and a rapidly expanding defense industry.
Turkish media said the pact is likely to lead to joint military exercises and training, as well as increased intelligence and technological cooperation.
Following the agreement, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif directly invoked Israel, calling on the Muslim world to “unite to confront the common threat posed by Israel.”
“Israel poses a threat to all of us,” Asif said. “Islamic countries must adopt a coordinated approach to confront this threat.”

Rhine River hits record-low flow amid severe drought in western Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:00:09 UTC
02:00:09 KST

Aysu Bicer
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
The Rhine River has reached its lowest recorded water flow under normal conditions, with drought across western Europe raising concerns for shipping, agriculture and industry.
The average discharge of the Rhine at Lobith in the Netherlands fell to 614 cubic meters per second over the past 24 hours, breaking the previous record of 620 cubic meters per second recorded in 1947.
The 1947 record was set on Nov. 4, making the current record particularly unusual because it has been reached much earlier in the year.
Jan Verkade, a hydrometeorologist at Deltares and the Dutch water authority Rijkswaterstaat, told Dutch broadcaster NOS that exceptionally warm weather and a lack of rainfall had contributed to the sharp decline.
"Due to the exceptionally warm spring, the snow in Switzerland melted about three months earlier than usual this year. Rain also stayed away and continues to stay away, and as a result, the Rhine is now more or less emptying," he added.
The Rhine normally carries about 2,000 cubic meters of water per second at this time of year.
The river is a major European transport route, and falling water levels are already disrupting inland navigation. Ships cannot be fully loaded because of the risk of running aground, while some waterways, including the Delftse Schie and Twentekanaal, have been closed.
Germany's inland shipping association BDB has warned that navigation on the Rhine could soon become impossible between Koblenz and Mainz if water levels around Kaub fall further.
The drought is also affecting agriculture, industry and ecosystems. Water quality is deteriorating in many areas, while restrictions on water extraction are creating difficulties for farmers and market gardeners.
The lowest Rhine discharge ever recorded was 575 cubic meters per second in February 1929, when ice obstructed the river.
Verkade said the current flow could potentially fall below that level. "I do not rule out that the discharge will fall below that level in the coming weeks as well."
Climate researchers say climate change is increasing the likelihood of extreme droughts in Europe, while also contributing to more intense periods of heavy rainfall.

US court rules Meta, other tech firms must face 3,000+ lawsuits over social media addiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:00:02 UTC
02:00:02 KST

A US appeals court has allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet's Google, ByteDance's TikTok, and other social media companies over claims they designed their products to be addictive to young users.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday rejected the companies’ bid to reverse a lower court's ruling forcing them to face more than 3,000 lawsuits over the claims filed in federal court, concluding that the appeal came too early in the litigation.
The defendants, which also include Snap Inc's Snapchat, had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 — which generally shields online companies from claims over content posted by their users — also bars lawsuits claiming they failed to warn the public about the addictive nature of their platforms.
Most appeals come after a case has concluded with a ruling or a verdict. Meta had argued that Section 230 provided it broad immunity and that it should be able to appeal the lower court's decision immediately. But the 9th Circuit said Section 230 provides a defence to liability, not immunity from lawsuits, so the appeal was premature.
The court also denied Meta's bid to postpone a trial beginning Wednesday in a lawsuit brought by 29 state attorneys general alleging that the company illegally collected and used children’s data, designed their social media platforms to keep young users hooked, and misled consumers about their safety.
The company had argued that the trial couldn't go forward while the appeal had been outstanding.
A representative for Meta and a spokesperson for the lead attorneys in the appeal did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Social media intentionally targeting young users
Filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals, the lawsuits allege that social media companies intentionally addicted young users, contributing to surging depression, anxiety and body-image issues and a broader mental health crisis among American youth in recent years.
Parents, school districts, states and other plaintiffs had argued that the trial court’s ruling was not final and therefore could not be appealed. But they also objected to the companies’ arguments about Section 230, saying it does not cover claims related to how they operate and design their products.
The cases, which have been centralised before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, seek damages, penalties and restitution from the companies. The companies appealed Rogers' orders in 2023 and 2024 that largely allowed the litigation to move forward.
The companies are facing hundreds of additional lawsuits over similar claims in state court, with approximately 3,300 of them in a consolidated proceeding in California state court.
In the first lawsuit to go to trial in the California litigation, and a closely watched test of how juries might respond to similar claims, a Los Angeles jury in March found Meta and Google negligent for designing social media platforms that harm young people.
The jury awarded $6 million to a now-20-year-old woman who says she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.
And, Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico in state court. A jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms.
On Thursday, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional $567 million and implement youth-safety measures.
Both Meta and Google, which have denied the claims in those cases, said they would appeal.

Yemen's presidential council says government will no longer allow Houthis to monopolize decisions on war, peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

01:59:58 KST

Mohammad Sio
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
The chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council said Monday that the government will no longer allow the Houthis to monopolize decisions on war and peace, following a recent escalation that included a Houthi attack on the port of Mokha in southwestern Yemen.
Speaking at a meeting with ambassadors of countries sponsoring Yemen's political process, Rashad al-Alimi said the Yemeni state did not initiate the latest escalation but would not allow its commitment to peace to give the Houthis the freedom to decide when and where to attack, according to a statement by his office.
He said the missile and drone attack on Mokha caused civilian casualties, including women and children, and damaged the port's maritime pier, service facilities, cargo-handling cranes, food supplies, and commercial vessels.
Al-Alimi said the attack also damaged a Saudi hospital, the immigration and passport authority, and water projects.
He described the Mokha attack as part of a broader escalation that has continued for weeks, adding that the government has repeatedly warned the international community that “lasting peace cannot be built with an armed group that has ballistic missiles and controls decisions of war and peace.”
He said the government has prioritized peace and exercised restraint, facilitating air and port traffic and the flow of goods while cooperating with UN, regional and international efforts.
Al-Alimi said the latest developments showed that the political and military equation had changed and warned that “the period of Houthi attacks without consequences has ended.”
“The state will no longer allow the (Houthis) militias to monopolize the decision to start the confrontation, its timing, location and scale, and then also monopolize the decision on when it should stop,” he said.
He called on the international community to protect civilians, civilian facilities, and commercial ports, respect state sovereignty, and reject the use of missiles and drones to obtain “illegitimate gains.”
The ambassadors strongly condemned the latest Houthi attacks on government forces, civilian sites, and economic facilities, including the port, as well as attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels, according to the statement.
On Sunday, at least seven civilians and military personnel were killed and around 35 others injured in the Houthi attack on the port near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and nearby residential areas, according to official Yemeni sources.
Fighting has periodically intensified along several Yemeni fronts since last month, leaving dozens of people dead and wounded on both sides.
Yemen had been under a relative lull since April 2022 after nearly 12 years of war between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Iranian-backed Houthis, who seized control of the capital Sanaa and large parts of the country in 2014.

Nearly 6,000 displaced in one day by clashes in Sudan’s West Darfur: UN migration agency

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

Adel Abdelrheem and Rania Abushamala
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
Nearly 6,000 people were displaced from seven villages in Sudan’s West Darfur state in a single day amid clashes between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday.
The UN agency said in a statement that 5,975 people fled the villages of Lakisa, Rofeid, Shibeit Ardu, Um Ghadara, Hajar Sangeid, Salamtar and Abu Suruj in Sirba locality on Sunday because of “deteriorating security conditions.”
Most households crossed the border into Chad, while others sought refuge in locations within El Geneina locality, the capital of West Darfur, it added.
The situation remains tense, the agency said, noting that it continues to monitor developments closely.
On Sunday, the IOM reported that 5,135 people had been displaced from 10 villages in Sirba a day earlier because of escalating security tensions.
On Saturday, Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi said the Sudanese army had repelled a large-scale attack by the RSF on Bir Saliba.
Bir Saliba lies north of El Geneina, the capital of West Darfur, and is considered strategically important because of its location along routes leading to the city. The area has repeatedly witnessed fighting between the RSF and the army and its allied forces.
Fighting between the Sudanese army and the RSF has continued since April 15, 2023, following disputes over integrating the paramilitary force into the regular military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions.
As of the end of June 2026, the IOM had recorded about 8.69 million internally displaced people in Sudan, along with more than 4.64 million people, who had returned to areas inside the country or from abroad.

Russia’s Supreme Court on Monday canceled the registration of the liberal Yabloko party’s federal slate of candidates for next month’s State Duma elections.
In a high-stakes hearing, the court granted a lawsuit filed by the small nationalist party Rodina, which accused Yabloko of receiving foreign funding, violating copyright law and promoting “extremism.”
The Supreme Court disqualified Yabloko from the parliamentary elections primarily for alleged copyright violations during campaign activity. Election authorities and state prosecutors said they also documented the violations.
In the court’s view, campaign materials linked to Yabloko’s website used protected intellectual property without acquiring the proper rights or permissions. This included song lyrics, film footage, photographs and even images generated by ChatGPT.
The ruling removes Russia’s oldest liberal party — and what was the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform — from the nationwide party-list ballot.
Yabloko chairman Nikolai Rybakov said the party would appeal the ruling within the five-day deadline and that it would do everything possible to take part in the election.
Rybakov told supporters outside the court that he could see how many people wanted peace and an end to the loss of life, in a reference to the war in Ukraine.
Hundreds of people had gathered outside the Supreme Court in Moscow on Monday morning to support Yabloko. The party estimated that around 500 people had lined up to enter the building, though the courtroom had space for only 150.
Supporters responded to the ruling with chants of “Shame! Shame!” as law enforcement prepared to disperse the crowd.
“You have two minutes to leave. No one will come to get you out of the military enlistment offices afterward,” a police officer warned through a loudspeaker in footage published by the RusNews media outlet.
During Monday’s hearing, Central Election Commission officials said that it had uncovered evidence indicating that candidates from Yabloko received funding from abroad.
Election officials told the court that data provided by Russia’s financial watchdog, Rosfinmonitoring, revealed foreign financial transfers to several Yabloko candidates in 2025, the newspaper Kommersant reported.
Because the Rosfinmonitoring document was classified “for official use only,” judges briefly adjourned the hearing to require non-disclosure agreements from Yabloko’s legal defense team before permitting them to review the evidence.
Rybakov rejected the allegations that his party received funding from abroad.
“We’re being funded by Russian citizens, and we answer to Russian citizens, as well as the Central Election Commission,” Rybakov told the Supreme Court.
The legal push to remove Yabloko from the ballot comes after the Central Election Commission last month unexpectedly approved more than 400 candidates from the party to run in September’s parliamentary elections.
Russian authorities have jailed several prominent Yabloko members in recent years over their opposition to the invasion of Ukraine.

Colombia earthquake 'reminded me of Israel with the sirens,' Israeli tells 'Post' - interview

Unknown Publisher

“It reminded me of Israel with the sirens and the bombs,” Israeli resident Fernando Chaim Bisker told The Jerusalem Post from Bogota, Colombia.
An earthquake with a magnitude of 7.4 shook Colombia’s coastal Choco province at 7:34 a.m. local time on Monday, killing at least 21 people and trapping an unknown number of people underneath rubble.
According to the geological service, the quake struck at a depth of 79 kilometers, with its epicenter near San Jose del Palmar.
Bisker, his wife Chaya, and their two children were in Cali for Shabbat and to see the inauguration of the new president, before returning to Bogota to continue their vacation on Sunday.
Bisker said they are safe as the building is new and is built to be protected in case of an earthquake.
Nevertheless, the earthquake was frightening.
“I was having my breakfast after Shacharit [morning prayers], and then we noticed it was shaking stronger and stronger. And I always saw it in the movies, not in my life. And we went down to the street, and we needed to hold on to the walls because we could not walk; it was shaking so much.”
Down in the street, he said he could see all the buildings shaking.
“It’s not an easy feeling.”
While standing in the street in his pajamas holding his two children, Bisker said something “beautiful” happened.
Something 'beautiful' happened on the street in Colombia
“I went to the street with kippah; I’m a religious Jew. And the people there in the street started saying, ‘Viva Israel’ and ‘bless us.’ That was very touching to see the people in the street ask me to bless them.”
“Usually people think that there is so much hate, but there is so much love toward the Jewish people.”
Cliff Katz was in a synagogue in Cali when the earthquake struck.
“We started to feel shaking,” he told the Post. “We’ve experienced it before, but usually it’s just a little shake for a few seconds, and that’s it. But then we started to hear banging; things were falling. And then the earthquake alarm went off, which I’ve never experienced before.”
Everybody inside the synagogue proceeded very quickly to get out of the building. Katz said that the earth was “moving up and down and sideways pretty strong.”
He said the synagogue suffered significant structural damage.
“Certain parts of the walls collapsed or opened up or separated. There was ceiling damage, glass broke in. I’m sure nothing that can’t be fixed, but it looked like it was pretty significant.”
However, Katz said that since this morning he has driven around the city and estimated that 90% of the buildings did not sustain any damage. The other 10% suffered damage to the facade, he said.
“It depends on the quality of the structure,” he said.
The Post also reached out to Cali Rabbi Asher Abarbanel, who said he is busy assisting community members “going through a very difficult time” and therefore was unable to speak further.

Canals can help cool your neighbourhood during heatwaves, study finds
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:56:20 BST
01:56:20 KST

Canals can help cool your neighbourhood during heatwaves, study finds
While canals are found widely throughout UK and Irish cities, reflecting the legacy of the Industrial Revolution, their role in combating urban heating had been largely unknown
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Canals in Great Britain and Ireland cool city neighbourhoods up to 50 metres from their banks, particularly during heatwaves. That’s the key finding of our new research which modelled the impact of canals on urban temperatures – quantifying their importance for the millions of people who live and work nearby.
While canals are found widely throughout UK and Irish cities, reflecting the legacy of the Industrial Revolution, their role in combating urban heating had been largely unknown.
Our team found that canals cool their immediate surroundings during the day, typically extending 20–50 metres from canal banks. This cooling effect is greater during spring and early summer (approximately −1.2°C to −1.4°C), and is particularly pronounced during heatwaves, with cooling of more than 2°C.
Canals also warm their surroundings at night, but this effect is much smaller (approximately +0.2°C).
Health and economic benefits
To study whether canals cool or warm their surroundings, we developed a model simulating changing water temperatures over a year and how this interacts with the air around it, using key features of the canal and environment (such as weather and shading by buildings). We studied 68 canals for this research.
This allowed us to look at all the urban canals of Great Britain and Ireland for an entire year, and how effects varied day to day and across the seasons. Our analysis focused on 2022, which until recently was the warmest year on record, and still features the UK’s highest ever recorded temperature of 40.3°C.
Even small reductions in temperature can benefit people’s health and wellbeing, particularly for vulnerable groups. Canal cooling also provides economic savings – estimated by the Canal and River Trust at £14.4 million per year – due to reduced losses in labour productivity, for example.
Other potential benefits include reductions in carbon dioxide emissions due to walking or cycling to work (active travel), and reduced demand for air conditioning.
Natural spaces in cities provide important ecosystem services, including improved biodiversity and flood protection – worth an estimated £17.6 billion to the UK economy each year. Being able to see and access canals is also important for physical and mental health.
Why canals matter
Around 6.2 million people live within 1km (roughly a 15-minute walk) of urban canals. Many more walk along canals on the way to work or go for a stroll at the weekend. In all, 791 million visits to UK canals were made between April 2024 and March 2025.
Direct benefits of lower temperatures during periods of hot weather include improved thermal comfort, with canal cooling reducing the number of hours of “moderate” and “high” risk – although this is partly offset by higher humidity.
Extreme heat is deadly. The May and June 2026 heatwaves, which included the UK’s highest recorded June temperature of 37.7°C, have been linked to more than 2,700 excess deaths in England and Wales.
Heatwaves in Great Britain and Ireland are particularly dangerous, as most of our homes and infrastructure have been built for a climate that has changed. Around 92% of existing homes would overheat under a 2°C global warming level by 2050. Adapting to new extremes in heat will require monitoring, social change and improved urban design.
Parks, woodlands, lakes and rivers are often included in government strategies on how to adapt to rising temperatures.
However, while green areas can lower urban temperatures (approximately −1°C during the day), the effects of “blue spaces” such as rivers and canals are much less certain. Differences in the characteristics of waterways (such as size and depth) and those of the surrounding environment (including weather and nearby buildings) can significantly impact this cooling effect.
Our findings emphasise the important role that canals play in making cooler and more liveable cities.

Feds charge speedboat operator after mother and infant are killed in New York Harbor capsizing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:53:02 UTC
01:53:02 KST

Speedboat driver charged after capsizing on Statue of Liberty tour, killing infant and mother
NEW YORK (AP) — A speedboat that capsized during a nighttime tour around the Statue of Liberty, drowning a baby girl and her mother, was illegally chartered, overcrowded and operating with a slew of safety violations, federal prosecutors said Monday.
The boat’s pilot, Manuel Hernandez, was charged with causing the deaths of 5-month old Antonella Garcia and 27-year-old Sara Sanchez through misconduct or neglect.
Hernandez wasn’t licensed by the U.S. Coast Guard, wasn’t aware of basic safety rules and told investigators he had borrowed his friend’s personal vessel for the excursion in New York Harbor, prosecutors said.
Antonella wasn’t wearing a life preserver because the boat didn’t have any for small children, prosecutors said. Instead, Hernandez told Sanchez she needed to wear a life vest and hold the infant throughout the hourslong tour, a violation of federal regulations, prosecutors said.
Hernandez, 46, of Manville, New Jersey, wiped his eyes as he arrived for his initial appearance in Manhattan federal court. He was not required to enter a plea and was released on $50,000 bail. He and his lawyer, Amy Gallicchio, declined to comment as she led him to a waiting vehicle.
The tour was organized through Zeus Luxury Rental Inc., which had a boat catch fire last year during a birthday charter cruise on Long Island Sound. A Coast Guard investigator said in Hernandez’s criminal complaint that the company does not appear to have applied for Coast Guard licensing.
Messages seeking comment were sent to a phone number and email address listed on Zeus Luxury’s website. The voicemail box for the phone number was full, according to an automated recording.
Charter company had a boat burst into flames last year
Authorities said the 21-foot Yamaha AR210 had 14 people aboard — well over its 10 person capacity — when it swamped and sank around 10:20 p.m. Saturday as Hernandez made a U-turn in choppy waters possibly caused by the wake of a larger vessel.
The boat was later pulled from the water and taken to a New York Police Department facility.
Zeus Luxury advertises its services on social media platforms including Instagram and TikTok, marketing itself as “one of the leading companies in limousine, party bus, and yacht rentals in the tri-state area” and touting a fleet of vehicles including such high-end brands as Mercedes, Hummer, Rolls-Royce, and Cadillac.
According to his criminal complaint, Hernandez told investigators he had worked for Zeus Luxury on a freelance or contract basis since last year, starting as a limousine driver. He said that twice recently he used his personal boat, a slightly larger Yamaha AR250, but used a friend’s boat on Saturday because his needed repairs, the complaint said.
In June 2025, a boat on a company-organized charter cruise burst into flames near the Bronx. All 22 passengers survived. Some were pulled from the water and others swam to safety on nearby Hart Island. Three passengers were injured, authorities said. Loriann Garcia went into cardiac arrest and is now suing the company. Two others had severe burns.
The pilot of that boat, Joshua Brito, was indicted on charges including vehicular assault, reckless endangerment and operating a vessel while intoxicated. He has pleaded not guilty and remains free on bail.
“This is just a fly-by-night company,” Garcia’s lawyer, Rose Day, said. The vessel Garcia was on didn’t have life preservers and Zeus Luxury wasn’t properly insured, she said.
“Here we are, same thing, one year later. Same company, same reckless acts,” Day said. “It’s shocking that this has happened and sickening at the same time.”
A mother and daughter gone, a partner and father left grieving
Saturday’s tour began around 7 p.m. and the vessel capsized more than three hours into its journey. Hernandez tried to accelerate to pass through the swell, but water swamped the bow and the boat immediately capsized, prosecutors said.
Hernandez admitted to investigators that had never sought required licensing and claimed he was unaware it was needed, according to the complaint.
Hernandez said he capped trips using his personal boat at 12 passengers, but that he did not know the maximum capacity for the boat he used on Saturday. Hernandez said he thought there would be 12 passengers on the tour but ended up agreeing to take 13, the complaint said.
An online campaign to help Sanchez’s partner, Andres Garcia, pay for funeral and other expenses had topped $25,000 by Tuesday afternoon. Garcia also was on the boat.
Sanchez’s neighbor, Diego Naranjo, said he first met her last spring when her son threw a ball into their Queens backyard. After recovering the ball, Naranjo invited her son to play on a trampoline with his children.
“They were really nice people,” Naranjo said. “You can see when a person is noble.”

Ben Jones, good ol’ boy ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ actor and 2-term US House member, dies at 84
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:53:02 UTC
01:53:02 KST

Ben Jones, good ol’ boy ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ actor and 2-term US House member, dies at 84
Ben Jones, who played the good ol’ boy mechanic in “The Dukes of Hazzard” TV series and parlayed his fame into a political career and two terms in the U.S. House, has died. He was 84.
Jones had a heart attack in his home Sunday in Washington, Virginia, as he was waiting to watch his beloved Atlanta Braves play baseball, his wife, Alma Viator, said on social media. Rappahannock County Sheriff Connie Compton confirmed his death.
Jones’ fame came from his role as Cooter Davenport, the mechanic who got the Duke boys out of jams as they tried to do the right thing and fight the corrupt Boss Hogg in the fictional Hazzard County, Georgia.
After playing Cooter for all seven seasons of the series from 1979 to 1985, Jones turned to politics and was elected to the U.S. House from a district near Atlanta in 1988. The Democrat served two terms before he was redistricted out of the seat.
Jones was born in North Carolina and in college got involved in acting and civil rights, he wrote in his autobiography “Redneck Boy in the Promised Land: The Confessions of ‘Crazy Cooter.’”
Acting took over his life. Jones performed in numerous stage productions and had a few minor TV and movie roles in Atlanta during the 1970s before his life-defining break came on a TV show Jones defended as a modern-day morality tale and a fine example of Southern values.
For seven seasons, Jones was one of a small band of friends and family helping Bo and Luke Duke in “The Dukes of Hazzard.” The cousins were on probation for running moonshine and were constantly trying to clear their names and stop the crooked and powerful Boss Hogg from stealing or cheating.
The Duke boys drove a modified 1969 Dodge Charger called the General Lee with a Confederate flag on its roof. Cooter owned “Cooter’s Garage” in the town square. Nearly every episode involved a car chase with jumps and stunts and a patrol car badly in need of repairs.
Cooter was often on the CB radio in his pickup truck saying “Breaker one, Breaker one. I might be crazy but I ain’t dumb. Crazy Cooter coming at you.”
“The Dukes of Hazzard” was a hit for CBS and its popularity never waned. It went into syndication and later became a prominent fixture on cable’s The Nashville Network.
Jones also credited the series with pulling him out of a self-destructive, alcoholic lifestyle that led to the failure of several marriages.
″It was like being in a Beatles movie,″ Jones said. ″Our lives changed.″
Tom Wopat, who played Luke Duke, said Jones was an integral part of making the series work.
“Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed,” Wopat wrote on Instagram.
After “The Dukes of Hazzard,” Jones went into politics. He kept his aw shucks personality, but took the issues seriously. In his four years in Washington, Jones was known as a Democrat who could buck his party. He was liberal on social issues and conservative on economics.
But even in politics, he made a splash. After losing in 1992 in his redrawn district, Jones ran for Congress again in 1994. He lost to Newt Gingrich in the elections that elevated the Republican to the Speaker’s Office.
Jones would file an ethics complaint that Gingrich used tax-deductible donations to fund his partisan college course leading to a House reprimand and Gingrich’s decision to leave the body.
Jones always embraced his role as Cooter. After moving to Virginia, he would open at least three “Cooter’s” country stores in Nashville and Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, and near his home. They sold plenty of T-shirts, key chains and insulated tumblers and included Dukes of Hazzard memorabilia like one of the 300 or so General Lee cars used and abused in the TV series.
The show and Cooter lived on because it was funny, had plenty of action and car chases and had a good, family-friendly heart, Jones told the Richmond Times-Dispatch at a 2001 car show where he played in a band, signed autographs and met fans.
“The show reflects the values of the heartland of America. The good guys always win,” Jones said.

This story has been updated to correct that Bo and Luke Duke were cousins, not brothers.

What doctors want everyone to know about CKM syndrome - a condition that 90% of Americans face
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:52:24 BST
01:52:24 KST

What doctors want everyone to know about CKM syndrome - a condition that 90% of Americans face
This extremely common and life-threatening condition connects the biggest areas of your health
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, or CKM syndrome, affects millions of Americans - but many may not know what signs to watch out for.
The condition that includes heart and kidney disease along with diabetes is linked to a higher risk of developing cancer and premature death.
Some 90 percent of Americans have at least one risk factor for CKM syndrome, such as excess body fat, high cholesterol and high blood pressure.
Doctors say knowing risk factors and disease symptoms can help people take steps to delay or prevent them, including changing contributing behaviors and seeking out screening and treatment.
“Heart, kidney, and metabolic conditions don’t occur in isolation — they are deeply connected,” Dr. Chiadi Ndumele, director of obesity and cardiometabolic research at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, said in a release.
Early warning signs
There are several symptoms to look out for that indicate you could be affected by CKM syndrome.
Chest pain, shortness of breath, passing out, pain in the legs while walking, dry skin, gout, sleep apnea, a need to pee more often, a loss or increase in appetite and swelling the legs, feet, hands and ankles are all telltale signs, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
“These symptoms can be an early warning sign of CKM syndrome, so it’s important to see your doctor if you have concerns,” University of Utah Health says.
100 million Americans...for now
These symptoms are driven by multiple health risks, including obesity.
Obesity, which refers to having too much body fat that presents a risk to health, impacts more than 100 million Americans and is also a risk factor for every facet of CKM syndrome.
The number of Americans living with obesity is projected to more than double by 2050, due to an increasingly sedentary lifestyle and a diet that relies on processed foods.
The big three
But eating a healthy and balanced diet, exercising enough and getting enough sleep can help people stave off obesity and reverse CKM syndrome symptoms.
Avoiding foods that are high in bad fats, sugar and salt is important for all facets of our health, but is especially key to ward off obesity.
Sleep is just as important to keep extra weight off, too.
Adults should get seven to nine hours of sleep a night for optimal health, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Working to find ways to clean up sleep hygiene may help people to extend sleep time to the recommended seven to nine hours per night," Dr. Beth Frates, director of lifestyle medicine and wellness in the department of surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital, told Harvard Health.
"This could, in turn, lead to consuming fewer calories and even weight loss in people who are in the overweight category by [body mass index],” she said.
Lastly, adults should also get 150 minutes of aerobic exercise and do two days of strength training a week, the CDC says.
However, you don’t need to become a gym rat or marathon participant to make a positive change for your health. Walking more is a big and easy way to meet your weekly goals.
“Light exercise improves heart health and metabolism. It helps lower insulin and fat levels as well as blood sugar,” says Dr. Randy Gould, a doctor with Manhattan Cardiology, told Prevention.
Disease in stages
When you catch signs of CKM syndrome is also important.
There are four stages of the condition, with stage one leading to early warning signs and stage four including noticeable kidney and cardiovascular problems.
“Recognizing what stage of CKM syndrome you have and talking about it with your doctor can really make a difference in being able to identify the condition early and prevent further progression of disease,” Dr. Rahul Aggarwal, a Mass General Brigham cardiovascular medicine fellow, said in a statement.

Belarus to digitalize mobile retail services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:52:00 UTC
01:52:00 KST

File photo
                    
                    MINSK, 10 August (BelTA) – Belarus is implementing a project to digitalize mobile retail, BelTA learned from the Belarusian Ministry of Communications and Informatization.
The initiative is aimed at fulfilling the head of state’s instructions to ensure high-quality and uninterrupted retail services for rural residents. The project was approved by the council for development projects under the Ministry of Communications and Informatization. 
The new functionality will complement the ecosystem of services of the Smart City platform. The service under development will automate notifications for rural residents about mobile shops: users will receive push notifications about the scheduled arrival time of a mobile shop, possible delays, new routes and changes to the schedule. 
“For the state, this provides end-to-end real-time monitoring of compliance with social standards, an objective assessment of the efficiency of rural retailers, and guaranteed coverage of all remote communities. For businesses, it enables automatic creation and optimization of logistics routes, minimizes vehicle downtime and reduces empty runs,” the ministry said. 
The new service will become available to residents of Grodno Oblast by the end of 2027 and, following pilot testing, will be rolled out nationwide.
