Big Four accounting firm ends intern Disney trip to cut costs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:50:33 BST
01:50:33 KST

Big Four accounting firm ends intern Disney trip to cut costs
The company had taken the trip 15 times in the past 20 years
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Last summer, Big Four accounting firm PwC’s summer interns celebrated job offers by heading to the Magic Kingdom on the company’s dime. This year? The summer trip lost its magic.
PwC has axed the summer trip to Florida’s Disney World, according to interns who gave an exclusive interview about PwC’s decision to Business Insider in an article published Friday. The trip, known as “Impact,” happened 15 times in the past 20 years, according to Business Insider.
A company spokesperson told the publication the company will use the trip funds to reinvest in its talent.
“As part of that approach, we're intentionally focusing our programs on experiences that provide more time with colleagues, greater exposure to clients, and stronger opportunities to build relationships within the offices and teams where interns begin their careers,” the spokesperson said.
News of the trip cut prompted a wide range of responses from interns and Reddit users.
Interns said that the company was planning alternative celebrations, such as dinner at an Italian restaurant and organized happy hours. One participant said those options are “nothing compared to what Impact would have been.”
Another intern said they didn’t mind the cut.
Generational observations and arguments about ending the trip took over a Reddit thread in an accounting subreddit.
“Boomer’s parents preached loyalty and treating your workforce with respect,” user danceswithshibe wrote. “All that ... went out the window as soon as boomers and GenX see an opportunity to put more money in their pocket. Then tell us it’s just how it is. Taking away bonuses and in-person training events.”
Another user pointed out the hypocrisy involved in the decision.
“Companies saying they want people in office so that communication improves, while simultaneously stripping away any non-active working time that would build better teamwork and communication will never not be funny to me,” sokuyari99 wrote.
The Independent contacted PwC for comment.
PwC called workers back to the office for three days a week in 2025.
The accounting firm’s decision to drop its Disney World intern trip is part of a wider trend of companies turning to benefits for cost-cutting that, in many cases, is related to AI.
More than half of companies have already or will cut employee compensation to generate AI capital in 2026, according to a March survey of 866 U.S. business leaders by career site ResumeBuilder.com.

Teen fatally stabbed De Montfort student in heart after dispute over fake Rolex, court hears
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:49:06 BST
01:49:06 KST

Teen fatally stabbed De Montfort student in heart after dispute over fake Rolex, court hears
Harper Dennis is accused of stabbing his former friend Khaleed Oladipo to death
- Bookmark
A student stabbed a man from another university five times in the chest, including once in the heart, after a row over a fake Rolex, a court has heard.
Leicester Crown Court was told on Monday that Harper Dennis, 18, fell out with De Montfort student Khaleed Oladipo, 20, in a dispute over money before plunging a knife 13cm-deep into him near the university’s campus in February earlier this year.
Dennis, who is charged with murder, having an article with a blade or point and failing to provide the Pin for his phone, sat in the dock while prosecutor Jane Osborne KC alleged that he killed his former friend.
Opening the Crown’s case, Ms Osborne told the jury: “It was the 3rd of February this year, 2026, shortly after 5pm, on a wet evening in Leicester, near to the university campus, where Khaleed Oladipo, who was a student at De Montfort University, was stabbed.
“He was stabbed not once, but a number of times. Only one of those stab wounds was fatal. That one fatal wound unfortunately penetrated his heart.”
Ms Osborne then told the court that Mr Oladipo collapsed in the street and never regained consciousness.
She added: “Khaleed Oladipo was killed not by a stranger, but by somebody who knew him. Khaleed Oladipo and Harper Dennis, this defendant, knew each other from online gaming.
“Whereas Khaleed Oladipo was in his third year at De Montfort University, Harper Dennis was in his first year at the University of Leicester.
“They had previously been friends. They were part of a Snapchat group together, but there had been a falling out seemingly over money that, at the very least, Harper Dennis perceived was owed to him by Khaleed Oladipo.
“It would seem the perceived debt was the reason that Harper Dennis attacked Khaleed Oladipo in the street on the 3rd of February.”
The prosecutor said Khaleed Oladipo and Harper Dennis were both in Oxford Street, close to De Montfort University’s Innovation Centre, when the stabbing, which was captured on dashcam footage, happened.
Ms Osborne added that the two men engaged in a “short struggle” before they both went to the floor.
The prosecutor told the court the footage shows the defendant’s arm in a “backwards and forwards” motion, “consistent with the stab wounds inflicted to the left hand side of Khaleed Oladipo’s chest”.
She continued: “Having been stabbed, Khaleed Oladipo rises to his knees and the defendant runs off. He isn’t pursued. It’s clear Khaleed Oladipo is not capable of pursuing Harper Dennis. It was an incident that lasted, in reality, seconds.”
The court was told Mr Oladipo was on the phone with his girlfriend, who heard him say “Why did you come up to me and stab me?”
A witness who had been driving in traffic recalled seeing a “snowstorm of feathers from one of their coats” during the altercation, Ms Osborne said.
The woman got out of her car to help Mr Oladipo, the jury heard, and saw a knife “parallel” to where he lay on the ground.
Ms Osborne told jurors Mr Oladipo’s cause of death was a 13cm-deep stab wound to the left side of his chest which went into his heart.
The prosecutor said there were four other stab wounds to his chest area, which did not contribute to his death, while a defensive wound was found on his hand.
Ms Osborne told the jury two calls were made by Dennis to Mr Oladipo’s girlfriend Shekeizah Fowler-Palmer on Christmas Day last year.
The barrister said: “The caller said to her Khaleed was a bad guy and that Khaleed owed him £3,000. That caller intimated if Khaleed did not give the money, he, the caller, would come to her.”
Ms Osborne said there was an occasion when Mr Oladipo gave Dennis a watch to sell and advised him not to go to certain jewellers because it was a fake Rolex.
When Dennis went to sell the watch, he was “laughed at” because it was fake and was “embarrassed and angry” with Mr Oladipo, jurors were told.
The prosecutor said messages between the two suggest they had fallen out for an unknown reason, including one from Dennis which said he “won’t ever forget” what Mr Oladipo did.
In a Snapchat message from Dennis to Mr Oladipo on Boxing Day last year, he said he would “dedicate his life to making sure you suffer for what you did”, the court heard.
Dennis, of North Road in West Drayton, London, denies the charges against him.
The trial, which is expected to last three weeks, continues.

Photos: 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocks western Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:48:50 UTC

In Pictures
Photos: 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocks western Colombia
A powerful earthquake kills more than 69 people and topples buildings across western Colombia.
At least 69 people have been killed and dozens of buildings have collapsed in cities across western Colombia after a powerful magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck the South American nation.
The quake on Monday trapped residents under debris, injured many more and forced people to flee their homes as far away as the capital, Bogota.
The epicentre was near San Jose del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region, roughly 250 miles (400km) west of Bogota, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and Colombia’s geological service. The USGS said the earthquake struck at a depth of 66 miles (107km). Tremors were also felt in neighbouring Ecuador.
The quake left cities across western Colombia, including Pereira, Quibdo, Cali and Manizales, badly damaged, with residents picking through the rubble of collapsed buildings amid official warnings of possible aftershocks.
The Colombian Geological Service said it was “the highest-magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade” and that it was followed by two aftershocks of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8 on the Richter scale.
Small earthquakes, known locally as “temblores”, are common in central and western Colombia, but quakes above magnitude 6.0 are rare. In 1999, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people.
Colombia’s newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Monday that he had personally taken charge of the government’s response to the emergency in San Jose del Palmar following the earthquake.

Russia’s central bank has recommended that lenders support small and medium-sized businesses hit by what it called “terrorist attacks,” a reference to Ukrainian drone strikes on warehouses and logistics centers.
In an information letter posted on its website, the Bank of Russia advised lenders to approve requests to modify loan terms regardless of whether the borrower is legally entitled to defer payments.

The Bank of Russia also proposed that banks treat these loan restructurings as a standalone measure to support businesses — recommendations that will remain in effect until August 31, 2027.
Since mid-July, Ukrainian drones have regularly struck logistics centers belonging to the Russian marketplace Wildberries. Many of these attacks have caused major fires at the company’s warehouses.
According to a source cited by The Bell, Wildberries’ direct losses from these strikes may already exceed 100 billion rubles. In early August, the damage to the sellers was estimated at 215–280 billion rubles.

Russia's Supreme Court bars only 'pro-peace' party from parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:48:39 UTC
01:48:39 KST

Russia's Supreme Court barred the Yabloko party from participating in September's parliamentary elections, citing alleged violations of election campaigning rules, according to a ruling published Aug. 10.
The decision comes just weeks after Russia's Central Election Commission registered Yabloko's candidate list, allowing the party to participate in the election. The case was brought by the nationalist, pro-Kremlin Rodina party, which is also running in the election.
Rodina leader Alexei Zhuravlev told state-owned media outlet TASS that his party had identified numerous violations, particularly those involving campaign financing.
Zhuravlev also told the pro-state outlet Kommersant that Yabloko had placed advertisements on social media platforms banned in Russia and violated copyright rules by using Soviet songs.
The decision removes Russia's only remaining liberal political group from an election in which Yabloko had campaigned on a platform calling for an end to the war against Ukraine.
"Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing to engage in dialogue with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for those in power," Grigory Yavlinsky, the party's founder and head of its political council, said.
"We disagree with the decision and will appeal it."
After its registration, Yabloko published what it described as "the shortest in the party's history" campaign platform.
"For peace and freedom! For a life without fear! For a ceasefire agreement, diplomacy, and the achievement of peace!" the platform says.
Yabloko's registration had already prompted attacks from lawmakers, who accused the party of "betraying the motherland" and failing to support Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
On Aug. 6, allies of late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, including his widow, Yulia Navalnaya, and other opposition figures in exile, urged voters to support Yabloko.
"We must view the upcoming elections — no matter how unfair they may be — as the only legitimate and safe opportunity to express our disagreement with the government," Navalnaya said.
Yabloko members across Russia have also faced pressure that has prevented some candidates from participating in elections.
Regional party members have been fined under legislation targeting extremist symbols, with some cases triggered by photographs of Navalny posted on social media, whose organizations have been designated as "extremist" and "terrorist" by Russian authorities.
Yabloko is not a totally Kremlin-controlled party, but its ability to operate has been sharply constrained under Russian President Vladimir Putin's political system.
The party entered the State Duma in 1993, 1995, and 1999 but has failed to clear the 5% electoral threshold in federal elections since 2003.
Some independent pollsters had assessed that Yabloko had a small chance of crossing the threshold in September. The state-run Russian Public Opinion Research Center, known as VTsIOM, previously put the party's support at around 3%.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was ready to "bring more help" to Colombia after mobilizing its Copernicus satellite service to facilitate relief operations.
City of Cali hit hard
The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Éder, announced a toll of 15 dead and 380 injured in his city, the third largest in the country.
He said he was waiting for the arrival of the first 130 rescuers from other cities in Colombia.
'We aren't going to leave people alone', Colombia president says
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said: "We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination."
Around 1,600 buildings damaged, including at least 61 completely destroyed
Epicentre of quake in San Jose Del Palmar
The epicentre of the quake was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles (400 kilometers) west of Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. The quake also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.
The quake ravaged cities across the west of the country, including Pereira, Quibdo, Cali and Manizales.
EU 'ready to provide support'
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday the European Union was "ready to provide more support" after a powerful earthquake struck Colombia.
"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia after the terrible earthquake in the Choco region. We have already mobilised Copernicus, our satellite service, to help with rescue operations," von der Leyen said on social media.
At least 111 killed, 87 injured, Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella says
Colombian police deployed to support search and rescue efforts
At least 30 buildings collapsed, Cali mayor says
Cali, one of Colombia's biggest cities, was among the worst hit, though authorities have yet to confirm deaths there.
Mayor Alejandro Eder told Caracol at least 30 buildings had collapsed and rescue crews were working at 10 of them.
Caracol showed firefighters and Colombian Red Cross workers carrying a survivor on a stretcher from one collapsed building.
Tremors felt in Venezuela
Reuters witnesses in the Venezuelan border state of Tachira and central-western city of Barquisimeto reported the quake had been felt there.
Venezuela was hit by twin earthquakes in June, which killed more than 6,000 people, mostly on the coast near the capital, Caracas.
Flights suspended at several airports in Colombia
Colombia's civil aviation authority said flights were suspended at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura while inspectors checked for structural damage.
'I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake', eyewitness says
Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in hills of the city as buildings collapsed. Residents in the city and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors.
“My entire house shook,” he said. “I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake.”
Colombia declares national emergency after deadly earthquake
ICRC says it is closely monitoring the quake affected regions
Manizales mayor urges people to remain outdoors because of possible aftershocks
Colombia declares national emergency after earthquake
Colombia government has declared a national emergency after Monday's deadly quake, local media reported.
Province of Risaralda reports highest death toll – 42 people – so far
The highest reported death toll was in the western province of Risaralda -- where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located -- in Colombia's coffee-growing region, where Governor Juan Diego Patino, speaking by phone to Caracol Television, reported 42 fatalities.
The powerful earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday killed at least 69 people, local officials said.
The 7.4 magnitude quake killed 40 people in the coffee-growing Risaralda region, 27 in Valle del Cauca department and two more in the city of Manizales, according to new tolls from these officials.
Local officials confirmed that at least 40 people were killed in the Risaralda region, where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Colombia's third-biggest city, Cali, is located. At least three of those killed in Valle del Cauca were children, the governor said.
Authorities also confirmed nine people were killed in Choco, two more in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. Many more people across the country were injured.
"The situation is critical," Salazar told Caracol Radio after the quake centred in neighbouring Choco province.
The Colombian geological service put the magnitude of the quake at 6.6 while its American counterpart USGS put it at 7.4, with an epicenter 100km (62 miles) underground in the west of Colombia.
It was felt in Ecuador and as far away as Panama to the north, and prompted building evacuations in Bogota, AFP reporters saw.
The governor of Colombia's Choco province wrote on X that there were injuries and serious damage to buildings in the department's capital Quibdo.
The mayor of Cali, Colombia's third largest city, also reported "major damage".
News outlets aired footage of some buildings with their facades ripped off by the quake.
In Bogota some people ran out into the street in their pajamas as emergency sirens rang out, AFP reporters saw.

Drought declared in nearly three-quarters of England as conditions worsen
- Almost three-quarters (71.3 per cent) of England has now been officially declared in drought following persistent historically dry and hot weather, according to the National Drought Group.
- The East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs are the latest regions to move into official drought status.
- With no area in England currently deemed to be in normal status, all regions are experiencing severe pressure on water resources, impacting public supplies, agriculture, navigation, and the environment.
- The North East and Yorkshire have been moved to prolonged dry weather status, which represents the final stage before an official drought is declared.
- The ongoing water crisis follows provisional statistics showing that England and Wales recorded their driest July since 1836, with 19 English counties receiving no rain at all during the month.

Mental health: one step forward and two steps back? | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:46:30 UTC
01:46:30 KST

It’s very encouraging to hear the announcement about the new network of community mental health clinics in England (Editorial, 6 August). The focus on early intervention is crucial, as it means that people can access treatment as early as possible, rather than waiting for their mental health to reach a crisis point. The centres should improve access, reaching people where they are. The government should make sure that they meaningfully involve people with lived experience of mental health problems to ensure the centres are co-designed and co-led with them.
As your editorial says, parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011. Mental health is an issue that unites us. According to new research, which we commissioned from More in Common, nearly three-quarters of the public believe that mental health is as important as physical health, most people are comfortable talking about it, and support for early intervention is high across the political spectrum. Three-quarters also say the government should do more to improve services.
The centres are an important step forward, but the government needs to make sure that people can access the many new and improved mental health interventions that have the potential to transform lives. New evidence-based mental health treatments must be rigorously evaluated, adopted and made available across the NHS. This will help people get the right treatment at the right time, and lead fulfilling lives.
Dr Kate Martin
Head of field building and lived experience, Wellcome Trust
While the announcement of a new initiative on early access to mental health care must be welcomed, there is a danger that without a parallel programme on mental health promotion, it could compound an already disastrous situation by uncovering massive further unmet need.
A public health approach to mental health is long overdue. I refer to one which takes its cues from the history of tuberculosis, the “captain of the men of death” that was brought under control not by pharmaceuticals alone, but by paying attention to the environmental conditions that predisposed to transmission.
The initial prescription for action was written 60 years ago by the Manchester psychiatrist Gerald Caplan, who identified how those with psychiatric training might best be deployed to build population-level mental health resilience through their support in the community, school, places of work and recreation; in Caplan’s blueprint, clinical work was only one aspect of the daily round of the psychiatrist and their team.
The forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp this nettle; for too long these opportunities have been missed.
Prof Dr John R Ashton
Former president, Faculty of Public Health
Your report (NHS mental health trust plans £25m in cuts to jobs and services, 3 August) is concerning. As the NHS faces yet another reconfiguration, patients and staff can only look forward to an uncertain future as not only this trust but other mental health trusts are expected to make savings to already impoverished levels of care. This is in stark contrast to the recent announcement of a major expansion of community mental health support in England.
Successive governments have insisted that mental health should be given the same priority as physical health, yet each year psychiatric services undergo ever more cuts to funding, services and beds. This has left people with minimal help and nowhere to go in times of loneliness or crisis.
Marjorie Wallace
Chief executive, Sane

Katriona O’Sullivan’s story of growing up in poverty is one that we can all learn from | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:46:25 UTC
01:46:25 KST

Adrian Chiles’s emotional response to Poor by Katriona O’Sullivan really resonated with me (I’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbing, 30 July). I read it and my heart both sobbed and cheered for Katriona’s younger self and the woman she has become.
With its linear narrative, rich cultural references and “rags-to-riches” form, it might be taken for a tale of “that was then but this is now”. However, the defining part of the book is the epilogue, making clear that Katriona’s account of growing up in grinding, abject poverty is a story of then and now. Every day, countless Katrionas enter schools with “pissy pants” and empty bellies, their nervous systems on high alert, in fight, flight or freeze.
School is a place to survive, not thrive. I know, because I have worked in a primary school for over 20 years. I provide mental health support to vulnerable children and their equally vulnerable and disadvantaged families.
My job is not to educate, but to help make children feel seen, heard, cared for and valued – to try to reduce the stigma attached to being poor ie, the misconception that having less means being less.
Reading Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty as an issue – it can feel “too big”. But that doesn’t prevent each of us from treating others with dignity, respect and kindness, noticing when someone is struggling, is hungry, dirty or alone, and offering a supportive hand.
Pollyanna-ish? I don’t think so. It was heart-warming and affirming to read about the lasting, positive impact certain school staff had on Katriona. When school reopens in September, my copy of Poor will be available in the staffroom – anyone who works in a school (or indeed anyone at all) should read it.
Sarah Schofield
Whitefield, Greater Manchester

Alertswiss said Monday that outdoor fires are banned in Geneva, Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, while fireworks are prohibited in Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, with authorities warning of severe or maximum forest fire danger.

MeteoSwiss said Sunday that a Level 3 heat wave warning had taken effect for the Lake Geneva basin, the Three Lakes region and much of German-speaking Switzerland.
Maximum temperatures are expected to reach between 31C (87.8F) and 36C (96.8F) nationwide, with the heat wave forecast to peak from Thursday and persist until at least Friday, Aug. 14.

An unnamed Republican official in Washington said fears of Ukrainian competition may be obstructing a Patriot license, The Atlantic reported on 9 August. RTX’s Raytheon and Lockheed Martin may worry Ukraine would improve Patriot interceptors and make them faster and cheaper than US production lines, he said.
The official said the manufacturers would frame their concerns around intellectual-property theft and technology transfer. Their deeper concern, he claimed, is that Ukraine could eventually outcompete them. Neither company has publicly confirmed that motive.
Meanwhile, Russia’s missile threat is growing. July was Ukraine’s deadliest month for civilians since 2022, while Moscow can reportedly launch 77 ballistic and cruise missiles at once and aims to raise that capacity to 200. Ukrainian intelligence separately said Russian plants reached 110–120% of their July missile-production targets and are unlikely to pause their attacks.
Why the Patriot license remains unfinished
US President Donald Trump promised the license at NATO’s 8 July summit. Yet Lockheed Martin and RTX had not been informed, and by 23 July, both described the process as only beginning.
On 8 August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump had agreed to grant Ukraine Patriot production licenses, but paperwork was delaying their issuance.
Current interceptor supplies are also failing to keep pace with Russian attacks. After a 5 August strike killed 17 people, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had received three times fewer anti-ballistic missiles since the beginning of 2026. He suggested the reduction might partly be intended to make Kyiv more compliant.
At their 28 July White House meeting, Zelenskyy asked Trump for 300 Patriot interceptors before winter, Axios reported. Trump declined, citing depleted US stocks and demand for interceptors in the Middle East.
Why Ukraine might look like a competitor—and why it is also part of the solution
Ukraine’s expanding defense industry is testing Western allies’ willingness to strengthen a potential competitor.
In January, French President Emmanuel Macron warned that French arms manufacturers faced “fierce competition” from Ukrainian and other European rivals. By July, Le Monde reported that many European allies remained torn between helping Ukraine and creating a new continental competitor.
Yet Kyiv has also proven willing to cooperate with its partners on mutual defense. Ukrainian military specialists have already helped the US counter Iranian-designed Shahed drones and protect American bases in the Middle East. After Washington requested assistance in March, Kyiv sent interceptor drones and military specialists to Jordan the following day.
Kyiv has also spearheaded the ten-country FREYJA initiative, combining Ukrainian launchers and interceptors with European radars and sensors to counter Russian ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy said the system could eventually protect countries across Europe.
Industrial cooperation extends to the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Program. Kyiv approved its first export of finished combat drones after F-Drones’ F10 placed sixth among 25 competitors. The company won a prototype order for 2,000 drones and plans to open a factory in Ohio.

US strategic oil reserves fall to lowest level since 1983
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
Crude oil stocks in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell by 6.1 million barrels last week to their lowest level since 1983, according to Department of Energy data released Monday.
The reserve held 298.7 million barrels as of Aug. 7, comprising 105.3 million barrels of sweet crude and 193.4 million barrels of sour crude.
The latest decline followed a draw of about 2.8 million barrels in the previous week, when inventories stood at 304.8 million barrels.
The drawdowns are part of Washington’s commitment to release 172 million barrels from the SPR under a coordinated action by International Energy Agency members to address global supply disruptions and elevated energy prices.
The broader initiative involves the release of 400 million barrels of oil and refined products from participating countries’ emergency reserves.
The Energy Department has largely structured the US releases as exchanges, requiring companies receiving crude to return the borrowed volumes with additional barrels as a premium at a later date.
Located in underground salt caverns along the Gulf coasts of Texas and Louisiana, the SPR has an authorized storage capacity of about 714 million barrels and a maximum nominal drawdown capability of 4.4 million barrels per day.

Colombia announces recognition of Israeli sovereignty over Golan Heights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

Colombia has recognized Israel’s sovereignty over the Golan Heights, the country’s Foreign Ministry announced on Monday.
In a statement released on X/Twitter, the ministry stated that it recognizes Israeli control over the area as “an essential component of its national defense and its ability to protect and safeguard its citizens."
The recognition resulted from a commitment made by both Israel and Colombia on Saturday, the ministry said.
In its declaration, Bogota became only the second UN member state to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the territory captured from Syria in 1967 and effectively annexed by Israel in 1981, after the United States recognized Israeli sovereignty in 2019 during US President Donald Trump’s first term in office.
Gideon Sa'ar: Colombia demonstrated 'commitment to Israel' in declaration
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar thanked Colombian President Álvaro de la Espriella for the move and Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bola Escobar for his cooperation on the matter.
"Israel is a small country without strategic depth. Defensible borders are essential to ensure the continued existence of the Jewish people in their historic homeland," the foreign minister wrote on his social media accounts.
"I will continue working to see more countries join the United States, under President Trump’s leadership, and Colombia, under President de la Espriella’s leadership, in recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan, to which Israeli law was extended 45 years ago."
Sa’ar also praised the recognition as a show of the newly-elected Espriella’s leadership, values, and commitment to Israel, coming in the wake of the foreign minister’s recent visit to South America.
Golan Regional Council Head Ori Kallner congratulated Colombia on the recognition and expressed gratitude for Sa’ar’s efforts to advance the move.
Kallner described the recognition as “right and just from a moral, diplomatic, and strategic standpoint,” vowing to continue working to strengthen the Golan Heights’s standing in the international arena.
Colombia's recent push to strengthen Bogota-Jerusalem ties
The declaration is the latest move in Bogota’s recent push to strengthen ties with Jerusalem.
In July, Colombia ordered the full restoration of diplomatic relations, immediate appointment of ambassadors, and relocation of Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem.
Colombia also withdrew from South Africa’s International Court of Justice lawsuit against Israel, in which South Africa accused Israel of committing genocide during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.
The renewal of ties with Colombia is part of Sa’ar’s broader initiative to improve relations with South American countries, with the Foreign Ministry designating 2026 as the “Year of Latin America.”

OpenAI pauses work on ChatGPT update over fears it is too dangerous
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:39:58 BST
01:39:58 KST

OpenAI pauses work on ChatGPT update over fears it is too dangerous
System could launch dangerous hacks, company warns amid ongoing controversy over similar cyber attacks
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
OpenAI will pause some of its work on a planned update to ChatGPT amid fears it could be too dangerous.
The new model, named Astra, brings “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, the company said. But testing showed that it might be too powerful – and represent a threat if it was released.
The announcement comes as OpenAI continues to deal with the fallout from an experiment in which one of its unreleased models launched a hack on a fellow AI company entirely by itself. The discovery of that cyber attack led to a run of similar disclosures from other artificial intelligence firms, and fears that new AI systems could prove too powerful to contain.
Astra was not involved in that incident, in which the experimental model attacked AI platform Hugging Face. But its performance meant that it may not be safe enough to release publicly for now, it said, and that new safeguards would be required before it did so.
Cyber security experts and AI companies have promoted artificial intelligence tools as important ways of discovering possible vulnerabilities in software, and allowing companies to fix them. But those same capabilities mean that they could prove similarly useful to cyber attackers – who may be able to use them for hacks that they do not even have to manage, recent incidents suggest.
In part to address such fears, OpenAI rolled out a “Preparedness Framework” at the end of 2023. It is intended as a way for the company to identify progress in models’ capabilities and respond to breakthroughs in a way that kept them safe.
The new Astra model may have reached the “Critical” threshold set out in that framework, OpenAI said. That happens if a system is able to find and develop exploits in real-world critical systems without human oversight, or if a system is able to execute new strategies for advanced cyber attacks on its own.
It said that it was continuing its evaluations, but that the performance of the new model was such that it was unable to rule out Astra having reached that level.

In response, OpenAI has increased its testing of its safeguards and security controls, it said. That includes putting it in better isolated testing environments to try and keep it from escaping those safeguards, as its other model did in the Hugging Face attack.
It will pause work on the Astra model in situations that do not meet those higher safeguards and security controls, it said.
And it will also closely monitor Astra for “risky actions” and misbehaviour, as well as working with “relevant government agencies and select AI safety organisations to test the capabilities for this model” and giving better security controls to third parties who are testing it.
“We believe advanced cyber-capable models should help defenders identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers do,” OpenAI said. “We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity.”

Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei issued decrees Monday appointing six senior military commanders, including successors to four commanders killed in the Israeli-US attacks, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.
Ali Abdollahi was appointed chief of staff of the Armed Forces, succeeding Abdolrahim Mousavi, while Ahmad Vahidi was named commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), succeeding Mohammad Pakpour.
In separate decrees, Kioumars Heydari was appointed deputy chief of staff of the Armed Forces, while Mostafa Izadi was named deputy commander-in-chief of the IRGC.
Khamenei also appointed Ali Azmaei commander of the IRGC Navy, succeeding slain Alireza Tangsiri.
Hossein Taeb was appointed head of the IRGC’s Basij Organization, succeeding slain Gholamreza Soleimani.
In the decrees, Khamenei called for the “continuous and comprehensive development” of military capabilities to achieve “maximum deterrence,” along with readiness to conduct “powerful offensive operations against the enemy.”
He also ordered the enhancement of the Armed Forces’ and Basij’s “comprehensive and up-to-date defense and security capabilities” and the provision of an effective response to all levels of conventional, modern, cognitive and hybrid military threats.
Khamenei further called for completing the integration of the Armed Forces General Staff and the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, based on directives from the late supreme leader.
Iran is engaged in military conflict with Washington since the US and Israel launched a joint offensive against Tehran in February, fueling regional tensions. Tehran retaliated with attacks targeting regional countries hosting US military assets.
Iran and the US agreed to a ceasefire in April and subsequently signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending their military conflict and reaching a lasting peace agreement.
The deal, however, collapsed last month with Tehran and Washington exchanging attacks for nearly two weeks before US President Donald Trump abruptly halted the bombardment amid reports of talks to resolve the conflict.

The same hostage economics playbook, from Havana to Tehran to Beirut
Washington uses civilian suffering as its primary foreign policy tool

When Israel launched its barbaric campaign of aggression on Lebanon in March, the opening salvos bypassed command centers. Warplanes targeted civilian banks, local exchange shops, and neighborhood gas stations. The architects of this aggression admit their primary objective was “Hezbollah’s money,” functionally confessing to holding the daily survival of Lebanese families hostage.
As it fails on the battlefield, the imperial apparatus targets the working class.
Engineering mass destitution
Western policy consistently labels Al-Qard al-Hassan “a shadowy militant front,” ignoring its entirely mundane reality.
The institution holds a Lebanese NGO license, providing interest-free loans across the Bekaa Valley and the south.
After the Western-backed commercial banking sector collapsed in 2019, this network became the sole financial lifeline for hundreds of thousands.
Blatantly dropping American munitions on these branches incinerates university tuition payments, chemotherapy funds, and small business capital. By bombing Amana fuel stations, Washington and Tel Aviv deliberately paralyzed civilian mobility.
Hezbollah spokesman Youssef al-Zein says that massive displacement forced the group to halt $12,000 compensation payments promised to families whose homes were destroyed.
A taxi driver named Hassan, whose daughter was widowed by the strikes, told reporters his family remains waiting for reconstruction support. Denying a widow medical coverage and freezing a displaced family’s rebuilding fund is economic torture designed to break a targeted demographic.
The neocolonial hijacking
This blockade operates through the hijacking of sovereign Lebanese institutions. The Trump administration aggressively bullied Beirut into installing Karim Souaid as the central bank governor.
Once seated, Souaid functioned as a proxy for the U.S. Treasury. He purged officials suspected of Resistance ties and choked off the cash economy that ordinary citizens rely on to buy groceries.
The interference extends to the borders. Washington forced Lebanese authorities to suspend civilian flights from Iran.
Security personnel coordinating directly with American intelligence replaced local airport staff. Washington’s inhuman Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent treats the Lebanese financial system as a subordinate division of the Pentagon.
American officials sitting thousands of miles away presume the legal authority to dictate who receives a micro-loan in Nabatieh.
It is none of Washington’s business how people in West Asia move their wealth or organize their social welfare.
The global geography of pain

Former U.S. sanctions architect Richard Nephew previously published an abhorrent manual explaining that inflicting sustained pain on civilian populations is an intentional policy mechanism.
Syria served as the immediate regional laboratory. The Caesar Act was marketed as “humanitarian” while systematically blocking fuel and medical imports.
Once the Assad government fell in late 2024, Washington began to suspend those same sanctions. The suffering of the Syrian people was always a disposable bargaining chip.
In Cuba, the U.S. has weaponized the energy grid. The blockade forced daily blackouts exceeding 20 hours, postponed 96,000 surgical procedures, and doubled the infant mortality rate. The suffering is the point.
An unbreakable bond
Western planners believe cutting off the cash supply will cause fighters to desert and the base to riot. This assumption is fatally flawed.
The economic blockade merely accelerates adaptation. Resistance networks rapidly bypass the weaponized dollar.
Despite billions of dollars in damage, the popular base refuses to fracture. Families sleeping in temporary shelters understand exactly who dropped the bombs on their savings.
The siege only hardens the people. Smashing a community’s infrastructure does not separate the people from their defenders. It binds them together permanently.

Best paper shredders for home use, reviewed by a tech expert
I’ve found the best paper shredders that destroy documents with a confidence akin to an SIS operative
- Bookmark
Face it, we all have paperwork that we need to destroy. Whether it’s because you’ve made some incriminating “mistakes” in political office, you need to rustle up some packing material to send a parcel via a low-cost courier service, or it’s just taking up space and you need to ensure you can recycle-bin it securely, the best way to rid yourself of problem paper is, of course, by buying yourself one of the UK’s best paper shredders. Or fire; but that can bring its own problems.
Available in three distinct and largely self-explanatory flavours, Strip Cut (strips), Cross Cut (confetti), and Micro Cut (basically granules), each type comes offering security on one of seven levels, from P-1 and P-2 for innocuous day-to-day waste and general non-sensitive stuff, respectively, to P-3 and P-4 for personal correspondence and bank statements etc, respectively, all the way up to P-6 and P-7 for legal documents and government/military/classified bumf, also respectively.
So, for home use and the sake of your bank account, you’ll probably have no need to buy above P-4. Which is what we have here, the very best of the first four Ps paper shredders for destroying docs at home. Let’s tear it up…

Your paper shredder questions answered
What’s the best paper shredder?
Without wishing to state the obvious, the best paper shredder for you all comes down to what your individual/household shredding needs are, for light duties, stick with a sub-£100 model. But for me and my need to securely dispose of all manner of sensitive financial and medical documents relating not just to me but also my youngish kids, the Fellowes Powershred LX70 with its quick cool-down time and ability to deal with staples, paperclips and credit cards, proved ideal. I mean, the Leitz IQ OptiMax Home Office 225 is amazing, but at over £200, I just don’t feel my shreddables would be of that much interest to anyone else!
How I tested
The answer to that may seem both blunt and blindingly obvious – plug in, turn on, shred. But as with all tech tests, it’s vital to approach each review unit with equal measures of scientific curiosity and downright cynicism. So, this one claims it can shred ‘X’ number of A4 pages simultaneously, staples and all, but can it? I see that this one boasts a duty cycle (its run-time before needing to cool down) of ‘X’ minutes, but is this the actual case in real-life usage? This one spuriously spouts on about having an anti-jam function, but how effective is that under proper pressure on the test bench? Am I desperately trying to build my part up when in reality I pretty much just plugged them in, turned them on and shredded? Okay, you’ve got me there, but these things were how I judged and how I arrived at… the Best Paper Shredders of 2026!
- Number of pages shredded simultaneously: I tested this against the brands’ claims to test the shredders to their limits.
- Duty cycle time: How long could the shredders work for before needing to stop to cool down?
- Ability to handle staples and paperclips: Would the hardware cause jams or be dealt with without any fuss?
- Bin size: The more capacious the better.
- Noise: Would shredding incriminating documents in the dead of night wake the family?
- Jams: Have the shredders been successfully designed to reduce or completely prevent paper jams?

Britons lead spending, but average tourist spend in Portugal falls

Foreign tourists are spending less per purchase in Portugal, with the average amount falling to its lowest level since 2019. Britons and Americans stand out among the main markets.
Foreign tourists holidaying in Portugal are spending less and less money in the country. According to the latest data from Turismo de Portugal, based on statistics from SIBS and published by Jornal de Negócios (source in Portuguese), the average value of transactions has fallen to its lowest level since 2019.
The overall average spend per foreign transaction was 35.70 euros in the first half of 2026.
Even so, in the first six months of the year, the volume of purchases made with foreign cards grew by 6%, surpassing 3.7 billion euros.
Beyond accommodation, restaurants and shops continue to absorb a significant share of spending. The retail sector accounted for the largest share of foreign expenditure in the first half of the year, totalling approximately 1.4 billion euros. The restaurant sector recorded more than 1 billion euros, while accommodation establishments registered around 735 million euros in electronic payments.
More than half of the expenditure by foreigners remained concentrated in the Greater Lisbon (35.7%) and Algarve (21.6%) regions. Northern Portugal accounts for just 1.9% of tourists' purchases.
Among the main source markets, British tourists top the list, having carried out 16 million electronic transactions in the country, amounting to 518 million euros in spending.
Tourists from the United States rank second among the biggest foreign spenders. However, the total volume of expenditure associated with the North American market stood at 2.4 million euros, considerably below the amount generated by British visitors.
Even so, they display different consumption patterns. Although British visitors make more purchases, North Americans are among those who spend the most per tourist, with an average of 45 euros per transaction.

A rare amber warning for extreme heat has been issued by the Met Office as a fifth heatwave looms with the risk of temperatures reaching 38C.
The forecaster warned there was a risk of travel delays, adverse health effects and potential power cuts. The warning covers large parts of England from 9am to midnight on Thursday.
Amber heat health alerts are already in place across large parts of England and Wales. Highs of 29C in Cardiff, 28C in Manchester and 25C in London are forecast for Tuesday.
Firefighters are working “tirelessly” to contain a blaze in the New Forest which is burning for a third day, covering an area as wide as 140 football fields.
Some 45 million people have been plunged into drought conditions as dry and hot weather continues. The National Drought Group has declared 71.3 per cent of England is now suffering a “flash” drought.
England and Wales recorded their driest July in records dating back to 1836, after 19 counties of England had no rain for the entire month, provisional statistics show.
Heatwaves set to drive prices higher, food producers warn
Soaring temperatures and droughts across the UK and Europe are set to drive prices higher, food and drink producers have warned.
The Food and Drink Federation (FDF) said “fruit, vegetable and grain supply” are being hit by recent heatwaves, with these crop shortages then set to feed into supermarket prices.
Economists from the trade group suggested that this will put upward pressure on food inflation going into 2027.
It is understood that the supply of a number of UK-grown fruit and vegetables has already come under pressure, such as broccoli and cherries.
Meanwhile, poor grain harvests are driving the cost of animal feed higher, with predictions that this could lead to more expensive meat as farmers are forced to reduce herd sizes.
It comes ahead of a fresh heatwave in the UK, with the Met Office warning that temperatures will soar to the mid-30s in some areas on Thursday.
Invest in climate defence rather than heed Trump on military spend – Polanski
The UK should be investing money in defending the country against the climate crisis rather than listening to Donald Trump on security spending, Zack Polanski has said.
The Green Party leader on Saturday reiterated his view that the climate crisis is “the biggest threat to our national security since the Second World War”.
Appearing at Iain Dale All Talk at the Edinburgh Fringe, he was asked by an audience member whether he and his party agree with increasing defence spending to 3% of GDP when there are “so many competing environmental needs.”
Mr Polanski said that if defence spending includes money for climate adaptation such as dealing with floods and wildfires then we “clearly need to up our spending”.
He suggested that was more important than listening to US President Donald Trump, who has called for Nato allies to shoulder more of the burden of European defence.
Mr Polanski said: “If we’re talking about spending 3.5 per cent of our GDP on military spending to please Donald Trump, then I think there’s an absolute incoherency in that.
“We’re already, I think, one of the fifth biggest spenders on military capacity, and actually, I think we need to look at defence as a much more holistic issue.
“I said this week, and I really believe, that the climate crisis is the biggest threat to our national security since the Second World War.
“It’s not some distant threat – it’s right here, right now. We’ve had wildfires not far away from here, where we’re talking in Edinburgh, and we know that what’s happening right now is not the new normal.
“This is the beginning of what will be the least extreme temperatures and least extreme weather in our lifetimes.
“It is going to get worse and worse and worse. And in many ways, it’s a grim message.
“We can’t stop some of that breakdown, what we can do, though, and it’s important that people hear this, is we can stop total breakdown, and that feels beyond important to do, and that’s where we should be investing right now, not on listening to what Donald Trump says or creating arbitrary numbers of GDP.”
Historic gardens, parks and cemeteries under threat from climate change
The UK’s treasured historic green spaces are under increasing threat from climate extremes, a report warns.
The National Lottery Heritage Fund and Historic England warn that historic parks, gardens and cemeteries across the country are vulnerable to damage from harsher, more widespread drought, intense rainfall, more severe storms and pests which can thrive in warmer conditions.
These impacts, driven by climate change – which is mostly caused by burning fossil fuels for power plants, cars, heating and industry – are affecting all aspects of these heritage landscapes, from trees and plant collections to paths, terraces and lakes.
The report says historic parks and gardens, including Chiswick House and Gardens, Kew and the Royal Parks, in London, and Princes Street Gardens in Edinburgh, employ more than 32,000 people and contribute £2.9 billion to the UK economy each year from international visitors alone.
But they are already being hit by increasingly extreme weather caused by climate change, with paths and drainage systems not fit for current conditions, trees lost to drought and high winds, and potential loss of entire groups of plants to diseases affecting box, ash, sweet chestnut and oak.

Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, Chelyabinsk, and Omsk are leaders in providing convenient public transport.

Reform backer Arron Banks urged to set out extent of surveillance of journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:30:47 UTC
01:30:47 KST

The businessman and Reform UK backer Arron Banks is facing calls to lay out the extent of his surveillance of journalists, described by an industry body as an “attack on our democracy”.
The News Media Association (NMA), which represents regional and national media, raised concerns after Banks appeared to admit over the weekend to hiring private investigators to spy on a Sunday Times journalist.
The revelation, first reported in the New Statesman, has led to fears that other journalists examining the funding of Reform and Nigel Farage, including those at the Guardian, could have been targeted.
When asked over the weekend whether he had commissioned investigators to surveil reporters at the Guardian, Banks, a Reform UK member and former mayoral candidate, said he was “not really interested in the Guardian” but declined to comment further.
The Guardian, along with the Sunday Times, has broken a series of stories in recent months revealing how cash has been given to Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors.
Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said aggressive attempts to deter journalistic inquiry were at risk of becoming normalised.
He said: “Using private investigators to try to deter journalists from making legitimate inquiries about public figures is an attack on our democracy. Sadly, intimidation and abuse of local and national journalists is increasingly used as a weapon to limit scrutiny and deflect attention away from matters of public interest. This must not become normalised.
“Ministers must wake up to this threat to our democracy and do much more to protect the independent journalism which underpins our democratic way of life.”
According to the New Statesman, Banks instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a private investigations company he once owned, to examine Gabriel Pogrund, the editor of the Sunday Times’ Insight investigations team.
In response to inquiries, Banks told the magazine: “We believe the Sunday Times used hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.”
The Sunday Times has strongly rejected Banks’s suggestion.
Banks, when asked directly by the New Statesman whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, responded: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.”
Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of Index on Censorship, said Banks should be open and transparent about the extent of his surveillance of journalists.
She said: “I really, really hope that it’s not happening to other journalists. But my fear is that it will be, because Gabriel is not the only one who’s asking the right questions about Reform.
“These tactics are often used to just stop the questions, to stop accountability, and that can have hugely detrimental effects on our democratic structure.”
Reform UK has denied any knowledge of Banks’s alleged use of investigators.
Gawain Towler, a member of Reform’s board and a former head of press for Ukip, said he was uncomfortable with the development but there were legitimate questions as to where journalists were sourcing private information.
“Personally I don’t like it,” he said. “But truly how in the light of the situation does one ask questions with a possibility of getting an answer …
“I think the issue with Banks is that there was actually silence about this possible collusion with the [National Crime Agency and journalists] … It would be ridiculous of us not to ask questions. So how do you ask questions?”
Nicky Morgan, a former Conservative secretary of state for culture, media and sport, said such intrusions in press freedom were “not compatible with an open democracy”. She said: “Investigating a journalist can only be intended to have a chilling effect on free speech.”
Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrats’ Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “Hiring private investigators to target journalists who are simply doing their jobs is a desperate attempt to dodge accountability.
“Anyone who uses or condones these tactics demonstrates complete contempt for a free press and should have no business in British public life.”
Banks, who helped run the pro-Brexit campaign group Leave.EU, is reported to have previously hired what he described as “ex-MI5 and SAS” operatives to surveil political opponents in the run-up to the EU referendum.
Included among those was Matthew Elliott, a Conservative peer who was the chief executive of the rival Vote Leave campaign. He has warned that such tactics will “drive out the decent people we need in public life”.

Hecklers in San Antonio, Texas, interrupted Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s campaign event Saturday with jeers about his alleged infidelity and accusations that he was too lenient with a child sex abuser.
Paxton, the controversial Texas attorney general locked in a competitive Senate race with progressive Democrat James Talarico, faced public criticism after taking the stage at The Angry Elephant for his latest rally.
“You cheated on your wife!” One heckler yelled at Paxton after he criticized Talarico’s Christian beliefs.

Paxton supporters at the bar countered the hecklers' jeers with chants of “USA.”
The Independent has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment.
The San Antonio Current was the first to report on the heckling.
Paxton was President Donald Trump’s choice to take on Talarico in the upcoming midterm elections. While Paxton has a lengthy political career and history of being staunchly conservative, he also has several controversies that are being used against him.
In 2023, the Texas legislature impeached Paxton on allegations of bribery and abuse of public trust. Former staffers accused Paxton of using his position of power to benefit himself and a Texas real estate investor.
Among other allegations that emerged from the impeachment trial, Paxton was accused of having an extramarital affair.
Although Paxton was later acquitted by Texas lawmakers, the details of the impeachment have continued to haunt his campaign.
The affair allegations, in particular, were re-ignited last year when Angela Paxton filed for divorce, appearing to accuse her soon-to-be ex-husband of cheating. Paxton himself has not publicly commented on those allegations directly.
The divorce proceedings have also cast light on Paxton’s wealth – specifically his expansive $9 million real estate portfolio that includes a luxury cabin in Oklahoma, three homes in Florida, a plot of land in Hawaii and three condominiums in Utah.
Some have raised questions about how Paxton acquired such wealth and real estate.
When asked about his multi-million-dollar real estate portfolio after the rally Saturday, Paxton declined to answer, according to San Antonio Current reporter Michael Karlis.
Other controversies, such as the child sex abuse plea deal, have become a talking point for Paxton’s opponents, such as Talarico, to criticize.
A campaign spokesperson for Paxton previously defended the attorney general’s decision in the case, telling the New York Times that the child victim did not want to testify and a first trial ended in a hung jury. The spokesperson accused Talarico of using the victim as a “political pawn.”
Most polls show Talarico and Paxton tied – some have Talarico with a narrow lead.

Belarus’ energy intensity drops 54% over 20 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:30:00 UTC
01:30:00 KST

An archive photo
                    
                    MINSK, 10 August (BelTA) – Belarus’ energy intensity has decreased by 54% over the past 20 years, Deputy Director of the Department for Energy Efficiency of the State Committee for Standardization Leonid Poleshchuk said during a press conference on 10 August, BelTA has learned.
Belarus is pursuing economic development by improving its energy efficiency. “Over the past 20 years, the energy intensity of Belarus’ gross domestic product has decreased by 54%. This is the best performance among the EAEU countries. For comparison, over the same period, Russia reduced its energy intensity by 35%, and Kazakhstan by 40%,” Leonid Poleshchuk said.
In addition, the reconstruction of air purification systems at Grodno Azot reduced energy consumption by 40%. Krichevtsementnoschifer cut its energy resource consumption by 3.8%, while the replacement of refrigeration equipment at the Integral enterprise led to a 21% drop in specific energy consumption.
According to the deputy director, electricity consumption in Belarus is increasing due to the implementation of an inter-branch set of measures. It outlines areas for improving economic efficiency by boosting power consumption and shifting away from or replacing imported natural gas. By 2035, the country plans to increase electricity consumption by 4.8 billion kWh. “Work in this area is progressing successfully. Electricity consumption has already increased by about 2 billion kWh. This is a solid contribution to the economy,” he explained.
Belarus focuses on the construction, reconstruction, and modernization of electrical systems, reducing technological losses, digitalizing the management of generation and power consumption modes, and improving grid resilience during peak load periods. The country has implemented the state program Sustainable Energy and Energy Efficiency for 2026–2030. It targets a 4% reduction in energy intensity, an increase in energy independence to 33%, and expanded utilization of local fuel and energy resources.
Leonid Poleshchuk added that the department, in cooperation with the Energy Institute of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus, is working on a concept for the deployment of local electric heating systems through 2035. “The result of this work could be a state standard on seasonal energy efficiency. Its potential introduction is scheduled for 2027–2028,” he noted.

DRC’s Ebola outbreak began months before it was officially declared, says WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:28:34 UTC
01:28:34 KST

DRC’s Ebola outbreak began months before it was officially declared, says WHO
Earlier cases of the disease were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid, WHO said.
The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record started in February, months before it was officially declared in mid-May, said the World Health Organization (WHO) as responders in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) battle the surge in cases.
Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional director for Africa, told a news conference on Monday that sequencing indicated the outbreak’s start, with some cases early on wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Ebola outbreak accelerates as healthcare workers strike over pay
- list 2 of 4DR Congo Ebola health workers protest unpaid wages as deaths surpass 1,800
- list 3 of 4WHO chief: Ebola outbreak in DRC spreading at ‘unprecedented rate’
- list 4 of 4Ebola cases top 4,000 in DRC as WHO urges Ervebo vaccine trial
“So we are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us,” Janabi said.
Confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have reached 4,200, including at least 1,900 deaths, according to latest government figures.
The Ebola outbreak declared on May 15 is unlike most previous ones because the rare Bundibugyo virus has no approved vaccines or treatments. Early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola, contributing to delays.
The outbreak is unfolding in challenging conditions, with strikes by some unpaid health workers, threats by rebel groups, anger among long-traumatised communities and misinformation asserting that Ebola isn’t real.
Health teams travel on remote, unpaved roads and have reported shortages of protective gear, while the vast population of displaced people struggles to find reliable water sources for washing hands hygienically.
This Ebola outbreak has killed more people at a faster rate than any other, including the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa that is considered the worst on record with over 11,000 deaths in at least 28,000 cases. That outbreak took about eight months to reach 1,000 deaths.
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted via contact with bodily fluids, such as blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Cases doubling in some regions
Last week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to fight it. New cases are doubling in some hotspots, Tedros said on X after meeting with officials in the capital, Kinshasa.
Access to healthcare in the region had already been challenged by years of rebel conflict in one of the DRC’s most remote and vulnerable areas.
On Friday, the WHO recommended the start of full-scale human trials for the Ervebo vaccine, the only licensed Ebola vaccine. While Ervebo has proven to be safe and effective against the more common Zaire strain of the Ebola virus, WHO experts said early data showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain.
A specific Bundibugyo vaccine is the preferred option for fighting the current outbreak, according to experts from the United Nations’ health agency. Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on people, while a third is being worked on to get it to that stage.
Several previous Ebola outbreaks have also been declared weeks or months late, including the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. That was declared in March 2014, although the first human case was later found to have occurred in December 2013.

Russia's Syria bases remain but their military power has faded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:27:45 UTC
01:27:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Russia's Syrian bases remain, but their days as centres of regional power are over
Syria and Russia have agreed to restructure Moscow’s military presence in the country, with Damascus taking greater control over facilities at Hmeimim and Tartous as the two sides redefine ties following the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
The agreement came as footage from Hmeimim showed Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and other officials walking ahead of Russian personnel during a tour of the facility, prompting comparisons with a widely shared 2017 clip in which Assad was physically stopped from following Russian President Vladimir Putin at the same base.
Under the new arrangement, Syrian authorities will assume control of civilian facilities at Hmeimim and commercial facilities at Tartous, while Russian military sites are to be reorganised as joint training and qualification centres during a three-month transition period.
The deal follows months of negotiations over the future of Russia’s presence in Syria after Assad’s government collapsed.
Russia intervened militarily in Syria in 2015 and became Assad’s most important military backer, using Hmeimim as the centre of its air operations and Tartous as a naval foothold on the Mediterranean.
But Anton Mardasov, a Russia and Syria specialist at the Middle East Institute, told The New Arab that Moscow’s military position in the country had already been significantly reduced before the latest agreement.
"The partial reconfiguration of the bases has already taken place," he said. "These facilities have long ceased to perform military functions and, even more so, no longer provide any capacity for regional deterrence."
Mardasov said Russia withdrew almost all of its major weapons systems from Syria to Russia or Libya as early as January 2025, including S-300 and S-400 air-defence systems.
As a result, he said, Moscow can no longer use Hmeimim and Tartous to project military power across the region as it did under Assad, including through the temporary deployment of strategic aircraft.
Russia nevertheless has strong reasons to retain access to Syria.
"For Russia, the main objective is to continue using the Syrian airfield as a transit hub on the way to Africa and to secure the conditions for maintaining a long-term presence there," Mardasov said.
Damascus has continued to allow Russian personnel to use Hmeimim as a transit point for cargo bound for Africa, where Moscow maintains military and political interests.
The new arrangement could also allow Russia to retain influence through cooperation with Syria’s armed forces.
Mardasov said Russian participation in training Syria’s new army would allow Moscow to “keep its finger on the pulse of developments” and provide a counterweight to Turkish influence.
He added that this was also in the interests of President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government.
The footage from Hmeimim has meanwhile been widely shared as a symbol of the changed relationship between the two countries.
In the December 2017 footage, Assad was stopped by a Russian serviceman as he attempted to follow Putin towards a group of Russian troops at Hmeimim.
The 2017 incident was widely seen as emblematic of Assad’s dependence on Moscow, with the Syrian dictator appearing subordinate to Russian personnel at a base on Syrian soil after Russia’s military intervention had become crucial to his government’s survival.
By contrast, Sunday’s images showed Shaibani and other Syrian officials leading the delegation through the facility as Russian personnel walked behind them.
The visual reversal comes as Moscow adjusts from its former role as Assad’s dominant military patron to a more restricted presence negotiated with Syria’s new authorities.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday used illegal settlement expansions in the occupied West Bank, assassinations and home demolitions in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran as part of his campaign ahead of the Likud party's primary election.
Katz posted a video on the US social media company X showing assassination operations and destruction in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran under the title “Israel Katz Boom Boom,” an apparent reference to explosions.
He also posted another video highlighting illegal settlement activity in the occupied West Bank and support for Israeli occupiers’ violence against Palestinians.
“Our settlement revolution in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank): decisions to establish 104 new settlements, legalize 160 farms, cancel administrative detention orders against settlers and expand settlement activity in the Jordan Valley,” he said.
Katz also highlighted the displacement of 40,000 Palestinians from the Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps in the northern West Bank and the continued presence of Israeli forces in the camps.
He urged Likud members to vote for him in the party's primary as a “right-wing defense minister.”
According to the daily Israel Hayom, Katz has intensified his political campaign ahead of the Likud primary election next week.
Alongside the settlement expansion, Israeli forces and occupiers have intensified attacks in the West Bank, including damaging and demolishing homes and other structures, burning mosques and vehicles, bulldozing agricultural land and preventing farmers from reaching their fields.
In Gaza, a ceasefire agreement was reached to halt Israel's genocide, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 174,000 since October 2023. The war has caused extensive destruction, affecting 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure, with reconstruction costs estimated by the UN at about $70 billion.
Despite peace negotiations with Beirut, Israel has continued its daily assaults in Lebanon, killing 4,335 people, wounding 12,277, and displacing more than 1 million since March 2, according to Lebanese authorities.
Israel also launched a joint offensive with the US against Iran in February, fueling regional tensions despite ongoing efforts to reach a peace deal between Washington and Tehran.
