Why is Yemen confronting Saudi Arabia?
TEHRAN – Operations by Yemeni Armed Forces targeting Saudi Aramco facilities and imposing a naval blockade on Saudi-linked shipping aim to pressure Riyadh to lift its blockade on Yemen and, ultimately, secure Yemeni sovereignty.
The government in Sanaa has been compelled to impose such measures as a necessary response to Saudi efforts to entrench the 12-year blockade, which it says is aimed at strangling the Yemeni people and pushing the country toward collapse. Critics accuse Riyadh of seeking to further tighten its grip on Yemen in partnership with the United States.
This was confirmed by the Ansarullah leader, Sayyed Abdul-Malik al-Houthi in his most recent speech, when he stated that “serious action was necessary in response to the Saudi blockade.” He stressed that this did not mean turning Yemen’s back on the issues of the Islamic and Muslim world, foremost among them the Palestinian cause.
He underlined that “Yemen’s action in confronting Saudi aggression is consistent with its position on the issues of the Islamic world … because our Yemeni people are among the peoples suffering and being targeted most severely by the Saudi regime within the framework of the American plan, in a manner that serves the Israeli enemy.”
Ansarallah authorities maintain that Saudi Arabia, the United States, Britain, and others have no right to “confiscate the humanitarian rights of our people, which are recognized in all international charters and laws.”
Saudi Arabia has been waging a humanitarian and economic war against the Yemeni people for the past 12 years, before Ansarallah came to prominence in Yemen. The main aspects can be summarized as follows:
The destruction of the Yemeni economic infrastructure through airstrikes and economic warfare, with direct and indirect losses exceeding $1 trillion, according to official sources in Sanaa.
Saudi Arabia has recently imposed arbitrary and unjustified measures and restrictions on commercial imports and goods, contributing to a 400% increase in commodity prices, with the aim of worsening and deepening the Yemeni citizens’ living conditions under circumstances created by the aggression and blockade.
The Saudi kingdom has deepened humanitarian and health catastrophe in Yemen through imposing air blockade on Sanaa Airport, depriving Yemenis of revenues from 90 million barrels of oil annually, denying them access to substantial gas resources that could fund salaries and public services, and cutting off electricity from the gas-fired power station in Marib.
Saudi Arabia openly intervened to prevent previous Yemeni governments from extracting oil in the provinces of Al-Jawf and Al-Mahrah, while imposing a ceiling on the amount permitted to be extracted according to what Saudi Arabia wanted, because it continues to covet that oil.
These manifestations reveal Saudi Arabia’s conduct toward Yemenis throughout history and demonstrate that its policy of impoverishment and deprivation is linked to a historic Saudi hostility, rather than to the choices of liberation and independence pursued by national forces, including Ansarallah.
This Saudi conduct aims to keep Yemenis, all Yemenis, in a state of poverty, misery, dependence, and subordination to the Kingdom, a measure that critics say only benefits the Zionist agenda. The blockade imposed and tightened today is a continuation of an old policy of collective punishment.
The latest measures came against the backdrop of Yemen’s support front for Palestinians in Gaza amid the U.S.-backed genocide in the Strip. The Saudi blockade has become an unjust practice that deepens the suffering of Yemenis in every area of their lives in an effort to subjugate them or recruit them into the dwindling Saudi-backed camp in return for financial aid.
This is something free Yemenis categorically reject (including mass rallies every Friday), and hence see the battle as no longer an economic and humanitarian one, but a battle for freedom and dignity.
The Saudi role is not a product of the past decade or two. Rather, it is a historical reality demonstrating that the Kingdom does not respect good-neighborly relations, nor does it respect Yemenis or Yemeni sovereignty.
Saudi Arabia’s military campaigns against Yemen began in 1934, when King Abdulaziz Al Saud launched a full‑scale offensive that overran the disputed provinces of Asir, Jizan, and Najran, forcing the Yemenis to accept the Treaty of Taif and cede those territories.
For decades afterward, Riyadh waged a strategy of political meddling, tribal patronage, and proxy support, most notably during Yemen’s civil war in the 1960s, when Saudi funds and arms flowed to royalist factions. Through these indirect means, Saudi Arabia exerted considerable influence over Yemeni affairs.
Because Yemen today is a revolutionary nation that has broken free and seeks independence and sovereignty while respecting good-neighborly relations, Saudi Arabia refused to accept this reality. It therefore launched its unjust aggression against Yemen on March 26, 2015, without justification, with U.S. support, and following an announcement from Washington.
And because Yemen, at this stage, is demanding its rights and imposing deterrence equations to secure them, Saudi Arabia, with clear American-British-Israeli backing, is seeking to establish a “naval coalition” under the pretext of “protecting international shipping,” a coalition by only a dozen or so countries, as a gesture of courtesy.
Yet the Yemeni operations threaten no one and do not mean closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait to international shipping; they are exclusively restricted to Saudi shipping. So what’s behind this coalition, where did the idea come from, and what is Sanaa’s position on all of this?
Recently, Arab and Western media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had formed a “naval coalition… to protect international shipping.” The reality, however, is precisely the opposite. What was unmistakably a Zionist idea dating back to late 2023 has become, in 2026, a project that the Saudis are undertaking and mobilizing for as an executive manager.
This is reinforced by the Israeli regime’s broadcaster Kan, which revealed in 2023 that “Israel officially approached several countries, to form a naval force as part of an international coalition operating in the Bab al-Mandab area, to guarantee freedom of navigation in the region.”
Authorities in Sanaa say this initiative came amid Zionist frustration over the failure of the U.S.-British “Prosperity Guardian” coalition and the European “Operation Aspides” to secure Israeli ships in the Red Sea amid Ansarallah’s Red Sea blockade on the regime during its military support front for Gaza.
Riyadh hosted an international conference in September 2025 in partnership with Britain, launching the Yemen Maritime Security Partnership. While the initiative was officially presented as an effort to strengthen maritime security and protect international shipping, it was widely viewed as part of a broader effort to counter the Ansarallah blockade and attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea.
The conference coincided with a meeting between Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and U.S. Central Command commander Admiral Brad Cooper. A similar sequence emerged in 2026, when Trump met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Washington on July 28, followed the next day by a meeting with Khalid bin Salman. Taken together, the timing of these meetings is viewed in Yemen as reflective of the close relationship between U.S., Israeli, and Saudi security discussions in the region.
In response to this coalition, which was effectively dead on arrival and emerged from previous alliances that had failed to break Yemeni resolve, Sanaa emphasized to all countries in the world that its battle with Riyadh is aimed at “restoring humanitarian rights and lifting the unjust blockade that has lasted for 12 years.”
Ansarallah has warned that “any militarization of the Red Sea will create a state of instability and affect safe navigation currently taking place in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab.”
Sanaa further stresses that “security is indivisible” and that the quickest way to secure Saudi interests is contingent upon ending the aggression and completely lifting the Saudi blockade on Yemen.

Ukraine strikes Russian petrochemical plant more than 2,000 kilometers from border, General Staff says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine strikes Russian petrochemical plant more than 2,000 kilometers from border, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck the Tobolskneftekhim petrochemical plant in Russia's Tyumen Oblast on Aug. 10, the General Staff said.
An air raid alert was issued in Tyumen Oblast at around 1 p.m. local time amid a drone attack. Regional Governor Alexander Moor said around 4:40 p.m. that falling drones caused a fire at an industrial facility, but did not specify where the incident occurred.
The damaged facility is located in the city of Tobolsk, about 2,200 kilometers (1,370 miles) from the Ukrainian-Russian border. The attack struck the plant's central gas fractionation unit, according to the General Staff.
The unit processes 6.6 million tons of feedstock annually and produces materials considered critical to Russia's military-industrial complex, including butadiene, isobutylene, maleic anhydride, and MTBE, a high-octane oxygenate additive.
These products are used to manufacture rocket fuel components, aviation fuel, composite materials for drones, and high-octane gasoline, the report read.
The extent of the damage caused by the attack is still being assessed, the General Staff added.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the depth of the strike represented "a very significant achievement" for Ukrainian forces.
"This region is now within range of our precision strikes. ... I thank everyone for their accuracy," he said in his evening address on Aug. 10.
"There will be more Ukrainian precision strikes to demonstrate to Russia and the Russian people that peace is necessary."
Earlier on Aug. 10, Ukrainian forces also struck another facility in Russia's oil industry, an oil refinery in Tatarstan, as Russian air defenses reportedly intercepted 456 drones overnight.
The Ukrainian General Staff later confirmed the strike on the Taneco refinery, saying a fire was reported at the facility in Nizhnekamsk. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep inside Russia and in occupied territories as part of efforts to weaken Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.

Russia's Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk lose power amid Ukrainian drone threat
Residents of the Russian cities of Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk have begun complaining about power outages.
Source: Meduza, a Latvia-based Russian media outlet
Details: A warning about a possible Ukrainian drone attack has been in effect in Gelendzhik since early morning, with sirens sounding intermittently and beaches closed.
There is also no electricity in the surrounding villages and in Novorossiysk. In the city of Krasnodar, more than 70 traffic lights are not working because of an emergency power cut.

The so-called operational staff in Russia's Krasnodar Krai claimed that the power supply will be restored within the next two hours.
Background: Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces struck 102 Russian assets on 6-7 August, including ten energy facilities and six shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.

Inside Putin’s aggressive army recruitment drive as Russians snatched off streets to feed Ukraine war
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
17:06:56 BST
01:06:56 KST

Inside Putin’s aggressive army recruitment drive as Russians ‘snatched off streets’ to feed Ukraine war
Moscow denies Ukrainian claims that Kyiv’s forces are killing Russian troops faster than they are being recruited
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Moscow appears to be adopting increasingly aggressive strategies to recruit fresh troops for its war of attrition in Ukraine, as Vladimir Putin looks to make up for heavy battlefield losses.
Men are reportedly being snatched off Russian streets and students offered significant financial incentives to join drone units as Moscow looks to avoid another forced mobilisation.
Local officials have been issued recruitment quotas by the Kremlin and Moscow’s defence ministry as it looks to meet this year’s 409,000 target, sources familiar with the matter told the Financial Times.
Russians are given referral bonuses for encouraging others to sign up while officials exploit knowledge of potential recruits’ debts and legal problems to pressure them into signing up, the FT adds.
It comes as Putin seeks to regain the initiative in Moscow’s stalling four-and-a-half year invasion, after Kyiv’s increased long-range attack capability has seen it inflict major damage on Russia’s energy industry.
The Russian army has suffered 1.4 million casualties, including 450,000 deaths, since its invasion began in February 2022, according to data from the Centre for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS).
According to Ukrainian estimates, Russian recruitment rates are not keeping up with casualty rates, with 222,500 troops lost – including 131,000 killed – but only 221,000 recruited so far in 2026.
“Year by year and month by month, it’s harder for the Russian army to find people,” Grigory Sverdlin, director of a charity, Get Lost, helping Russian troops desert, told the FT.
“Putin is evidently putting off a new wave of mobilisation, so the defence ministry has to put more pressure on all sorts of people to sign contracts.”
Human rights campaigners say police have raided workplaces and snatched people off the street to take them to military recruitment offices, where they were forced to sign contracts in several incidents in recent months.
Raids in Russian cities and towns like Penza, Kamenka and Kuznetsk saw men being rounded up by police officers and other military enlistment officials, it is claimed.
“In Penza, they’re taking everyone indiscriminately, stopping cars and public transport, rounding up men and taking them away to sign contracts. Raids are happening across the entire city,” one local resident told human rights group Idite Lesom, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
The raids have intensified since the authorities began “catching men” in January, a Penza resident told the Mobilizatsiya channel, according to the outlet.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed that the Kremlin is preparing to carry out a “significant” wave of involuntary reserve call-ups this autumn.
The Institute for the Study of War reports that Russia has been preparing conditions to conduct rolling partial reserve call-ups since last October, and has passed bills to expand the pool of criminals who may be recruited.
Targeting sign-ups from students also suggests that Moscow is keen to pour more skilled human resources into its drone forces which, like those of Ukraine, are playing an increasingly vital role in the war.
Drone operators typically work some distance from the front line, but they are regarded as high-value targets who are hunted down and killed if their positions are revealed.
Russia has denied that any kind of general mobilisation drive is on the agenda, and says it is not running short of recruits despite Ukrainian claims.
Similar recruitment tactics have been reported in Ukraine, where footage from October 2024 purportedly showed Ukrainian military recruitment officers raiding restaurants, bars and a concert hall in Kyiv in search of men not registered for conscription.
Officers positioned outside the doors of the capital city’s Palace of Sports were seen carrying out checks as people left a concert by Ukrainian rock band Okean Elzy on Friday night, local media and witnesses said.
Moscow has also sought to bring in thousands of foreign troops to help fight in its war. Mr Zelensky said on Sunday that up to 50,000 North Koreans were set to be deployed on Russian territory.
It has used a network of online recruiters to deceptively funnel thousands of Africans from nearly every country on the continent into the frontlines, according to the Africa Centre for Strategic Studies.
Cuba and Colombia have also been targeted by Moscow for recruitment to the Russian army, according to a report published in April by the International Federation for Human Rights.

Meta launches new AI model as Zuckerberg warns against concentration of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:05:52 UTC
01:05:52 KST

Halis Sunnetci
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg called for advanced artificial intelligence to be distributed widely on Monday, warning that concentrating superintelligence in the hands of a few companies, governments or other institutions could pose significant risks.
In a letter titled The Future is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future, Zuckerberg said superintelligence should primarily expand people’s ability to create, discover and solve problems rather than merely automate existing work.
“We propose a philosophy based on individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, invention as the primary purpose of superintelligence, and balance of power as the foundation of safety,” he wrote.
Zuckerberg argued that no single superintelligent system could reflect humanity’s competing values and interests. Instead, he proposed distributing advanced AI broadly so individuals, businesses, governments and different AI systems could act as checks on one another.
“The key to a positive future for everyone is achieving a balance of power that favors individuals,” he said.
The letter coincided with Meta’s launch of Muse Glimmer, an open-weight AI model with 30 billion learned parameters that is designed to run local AI agents on consumer devices.
Unlike many cloud-based AI assistants, it can run on a Mac or PC with a single consumer GPU, allowing it to perform multi-step tasks without internet access while keeping data on the device.
The letter also reaffirmed Meta’s support for open-source AI, with Zuckerberg saying the company would resume releasing some open-source models. He argued that wider availability could help prevent excessive concentrations of technological and economic power.
Zuckerberg acknowledged risks involving cybersecurity, biological and chemical misuse, employment disruption, government surveillance and the possibility that increasingly autonomous AI systems could escape human control.
To reduce the longer-term risk of a single dominant superintelligence, he advocated maintaining several competing AI systems and ensuring that most computing resources remained directed toward people’s goals.
“Alignment should be about helping people pursue the many diverse goals and views held across society rather than a method of enforcing a centralized dogma,” he wrote.
Zuckerberg also proposed closer cooperation between governments and leading AI developers to address vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure without delaying the release of new models.
He warned that unnecessarily slowing American AI development could weaken the US technological lead over rivals, including China, posing economic and national security risks.

Economy Ministry drafts changes to war risk insurance program
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
19:03:59 EEST
01:03:59 KST

Ukraine’s Economy Ministry is preparing amendments to Resolution No. 1541, which established a state mechanism for war risk insurance and compensation for businesses via the Export Credit Agency (ECA), lawmaker Olha Vasylevska-Smahliuk said on Telegram.
The draft amendments have been sent to central executive authorities for approval and will then go before the Cabinet of Ministers, she said.
The Economy Ministry proposes expanding the program to Kyiv and Kyiv region as high-risk territories and allowing leased property to be insured, which is important for businesses operating out of leased warehouses, terminals and other premises, she said.
The ministry also proposes adding agricultural machinery and heavy freight transport to the program, expanding coverage for the fuel sector by adding fuel tanks, fuel stocks, fuel in transit and transport used to carry it to the list of insurable gas station premises and equipment, and raising the maximum amount the state compensates businesses for insurance premiums to UAH 5 million.
"The maximum insurance coverage limit under the program currently remains UAH 30 million. Representatives of affected businesses consider this limit extremely low," she said.
As reported, the Cabinet of Ministers adopted Resolution No. 1541 in March 2026, expanding the war risk insurance program. The maximum insurance premium compensation for businesses was increased from UAH 1 million to UAH 3 million, and the deadline for submitting a payout application was shortened to 31 days after signing the contract. Businesses operating in frontline regions were given the option of compensation for damaged property of up to UAH 30 million.
Under the resolution, Export Credit Agency PJSC (ECA) has been authorized, starting Jan. 1, 2026, to make partial compensation payments on behalf of the state for property destroyed or damaged by the war and partial compensation of insurance premiums under war risk insurance contracts.

Sudan’s army chief holds unannounced talks on national dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:03:43 UTC
01:03:43 KST

Sudan’s army chief holds unannounced talks on national dialogue
Al-Burhan engaged in discreet consultations aiming to pave the way for a comprehensive Sudanese dialogue conference.
Khartoum, Sudan – Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has held unannounced consultations with political and civil society groups and figures, resulting in agreement on steps to create the conditions for a Sudanese dialogue conference, political sources aware of the discussions have told Al Jazeera.
The consultations include proposals to drop charges punishable by death against opposition leaders and to form a preparatory committee for the proposed conference.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Photos: Sudan war leaves ancient Meroe pyramids at risk of collapse
- list 2 of 3Sudan’s war threatens an ‘entire generation’s’ future, UN warns
- list 3 of 3Sudan sentences RSF chief Hemedti to death: Who’s he, what’s he accused of?
The political sources, who requested anonymity, said the consultations focused on the need for a comprehensive Sudanese conference involving key political players.
The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have been at war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023.
Those involved in the consultations have largely agreed on the need for practical steps to create a climate conducive to dialogue, including an end to media campaigns against political opponents.
According to the same sources, a majority of those taking part have agreed on practical steps to create a climate conducive to dialogue, including halting negative media campaigns and suspending criminal charges carrying the death penalty against dozens of opponents of the army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council – primarily members of the Somoud Alliance, a political grouping led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok.
The charges against Hamdok and other political figures tied to Somoud include war crimes, inciting war against the state, and undermining the constitution. Somoud has been accused of supporting the RSF, but has always denied such claims.
No preconditions
Participants in the consultations have agreed on the need to select a preparatory committee for the dialogue conference, made up of independent, widely accepted figures with specialised expertise. The committee would determine who takes part, the agenda, and the venue and date of the conference, as well as invite international and regional parties to monitor it, according to the political sources.
Hatem al-Sir, adviser to the head of the Democratic Unionist Party-Original, said Khartoum is witnessing intensive political activity and ongoing consultations in preparation for an intra-Sudanese dialogue, with the support of regional forces.
In a post on X, he said al-Burhan had held meetings with leaders of political blocs, chiefs of native administration, Sufi order leaders, independent national figures, academics, professionals and resistance committees. The meetings focused on strengthening national consensus and reaching an agreed national project.
The Quintet – made up of the United Nations, the African Union, the European Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the Arab League – has also been attempting to secure an agreement among Sudan’s competing political blocs on the structure of a proposed national dialogue, but has so far struggled.
Its latest round of discussions, which began in Ethiopia’s Addis Ababa on July 29, failed to bridge differences among Sudanese parties over arrangements for the conference. Several political groups, including Somoud, did not attend the meetings.
A cosmetic process
Babiker Faisal, a leader in the Somoud alliance, accused the Quintet of retreating from understandings that had previously been reached over arrangements for the political process. Faisal described the Quintet as “no longer a neutral umbrella” for sponsoring dialogue, saying that it had strayed from the principle of Sudanese ownership of the political process.
In a social media post, Faisal said the Quintet had recently called for consultations involving alliances and individuals, some of whom, he said, “have no presence in the political arena”. He added that most participants represented parties supportive of the army, which he said contradicted pledges by the Quad – the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Egypt – to launch a political process not dominated by either side of the conflict.
He also accused Sudan’s army leadership of seeking to exploit military developments to launch a “cosmetic political process” aimed, in his words, at bolstering the legitimacy of its authority, restoring regional and international recognition, and forming governing institutions loyal to it that would grant the army chief broad powers for an extended period.
In a statement issued Friday, the Quintet said it would continue efforts to advance Sudan’s political process through renewed consultations with civilian forces and stakeholders, seeking to narrow differences over the path ahead and reach common ground that could pave the way for a Sudanese-led political settlement.
The group said broadening the scope of consultations and ensuring their inclusiveness were essential to building trust, establishing legitimacy and reaching a shared understanding that could support a credible, Sudanese-led political process.
The Quintet also reaffirmed its respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity and rejected parallel governing structures, while calling for de-escalation and efforts towards a negotiated, sustainable peace.
No exclusion
Separately, leading figures in the National Congress Party (NCP) – which led Sudan during the rule of President Omar al-Bashir until his overthrow in 2018 – criticised al-Burhan’s announcement that their party would not be part of the political process.
Al-Bashir had made the announcement last week, saying that an intra-Sudanese dialogue conference would be held, but that it would not include figures associated with the RSF – namely the political group Tasis – and the NCP.
Former Federal Governance Minister and National Congress Party leader Hamid Mumtaz said that equating the NCP with RSF-aligned forces was “a catastrophic mistake and a statement out of touch with a complex political reality”.
Mumtaz said it was untenable to place the RSF, which he described as “a rebel militia that hijacked the state and waged war against citizens”, on the same footing as the NCP, which he said had “sent its grassroots supporters and cadres to fight alongside the armed forces to reclaim the state”.
The politician warned against the exclusion of the NCP, citing the example of the banning of the Ba’ath Party in Iraq and what he described as its catastrophic consequences. He added that any partial political dialogue, or one dominated by any particular party, would remain isolated and be doomed to fail, and would not lead to a stable Sudan.

"On August 10, 2026, the investigative judge partially granted the motion of the defense of the former head of the President’s Office of Ukraine, suspected of laundering property obtained through criminal activity during the construction of a private cottage community near Kyiv, and changed the procedural obligations previously assigned to him," the SAPO said on Telegram on Monday.

"Thus, the obligation not to leave Kyiv and Kyiv region without permission from a detective, prosecutor, and court has been replaced with an obligation not to leave the city of Kyiv, Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Kherson regions without such permission, with the possibility of transit through other regions," the SAPO reads.
The defense explained the suspect’s trips to these regions by citing his participation in a project providing legal assistance to military personnel. The defense filed this motion with the court after the SAPO and NABU simultaneously received several similar letters from military unit commanders on behalf of the suspect.
The court denied the defense’s motion to remove the electronic bracelet (monitoring device) from Yermak.
As reported, on May 11, the NABU and SAPO announced the uncovering of an organized group suspected of laundering UAH 460 million through luxury construction near Kyiv. Former Head of the Presidential Administration Yermak was one of the participants in the scheme, and he was charged.
On May 12, anti-corruption agencies served notice of suspicion in this case to six more members of the organized group, including a former deputy prime minister and a businessman (one of the leaders of the criminal organization exposed in November 2025 as part of the special operation Midas). These are likely businessman Tymur Mindich and former Deputy Prime Minister of Ukraine Oleksiy Chernyshov.
According to investigators, between 2021 and 2025, the suspects laundered over UAH 460 million through the construction of a cottage community in Kozyn, Kyiv region. The project involves the construction of four private residences with auxiliary buildings and structures, as well as a spa area (the so-called Dynasty Cooperative), on land plots totaling approximately 8 hectares.
On May 14, the High Anti-Corruption Court ordered Yermak to remain in custody with the right to post bail in the amount of UAH 140 million. On May 18, Yermak’s bail was fully paid, and he was released from pretrial detention.

Signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on August 7, the agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence and expand defence cooperation among the three countries.
The pact, described as reflecting their "deep historical ties, longstanding brotherhood, Islamic solidarity and shared strategic interests," has also been brought into the public spotlight in Türkiye through a special visual communications campaign.
Digital screens, architectural lighting and large-scale visual displays have transformed some of Ankara and Istanbul's best-known landmarks into platforms highlighting the Mecca agreement's messages of solidarity, cooperation and a shared future.
Here are some of the landmarks illuminated as part of the campaign:
Presidential Communications Directorate Building — Ankara
The Presidential Communications Directorate building in Ankara was among the capital's prominent landmarks selected for the campaign.
Digital displays highlighted the Mecca agreement and its message of strategic cooperation and solidarity among Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

The campaign was also displayed on the Turk Telekom building in Ankara.
Similar visuals were presented across more than 600 Turk Telekom branches throughout Türkiye, extending the campaign beyond the capital and bringing the agreement's message to audiences nationwide.
Atakule — Ankara
One of Ankara's most recognisable landmarks, Atakule was illuminated as part of the campaign.
The visuals emphasised the agreement's themes of cooperation, unity and a shared future.
Ataturk Cultural Center — Istanbul
In Istanbul, the Ataturk Cultural Center became another prominent backdrop for the campaign.
The visual displays presented the Mecca agreement as a symbol of partnership and solidarity between the three countries.
15 July Martyrs Bridge — Istanbul
The campaign reached one of Istanbul's most iconic structures, the 15 July Martyrs Bridge, which connects the city's European and Asian sides.
The display carried the agreement's message across one of Türkiye's most recognisable urban landmarks.
Galata Tower — Istanbul
The historic Galata Tower was also illuminated as part of the campaign.
The display brought the message of the Mecca agreement to one of Istanbul's most prominent landmarks, linking the contemporary defence partnership with the city's centuries-old role as a crossroads between regions.

Source: Business Insider, a global news website, referring to satellite imagery as of 4 August
Quote: "The new images, collected on Tuesday [4 August – ed.] by the US spatial intelligence firm Vantor, show more than half a dozen submarines covered by anti-drone netting at the Rybachiy Nuclear Submarine Base on Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula."

Quote: "The appearance of these defences so far from the conflict suggests Russia sees its vulnerability to drone attacks extending well beyond the immediate fighting, including to its Pacific Fleet."

Anti-drone netting has also appeared at other Russian bases.

This facility serves as a base for Russia's Black Sea Fleet and has already been targeted by Ukrainian drones on multiple occasions.

‘They need each other’: What’s behind the new Syria-Russia accord?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:01:06 UTC
01:01:06 KST

‘They need each other’: What’s behind the new Syria-Russia accord?
The Syrian-Russian agreement reflects a pragmatic approach redefining past alliances amid shifting geopolitical realities.
Syria and Russia have spent the past 18 months negotiating the fate of Moscow’s military presence in Syria following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024.
On Sunday, at least part of that question seemed to be settled after the post-Assad government in Damascus announced a memorandum of understanding regarding Moscow’s Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Lebanon ‘detains’ former al-Assad-era general, weighs handing him to Syria
- list 2 of 3What will it take for Syrians to return to Aleppo after years of war?
- list 3 of 3As Syria marks 15 years since anti-Assad uprising, security issues remain
Russia was a major Assad ally during Syria’s near 14-year civil war which began with Arab Spring protests in 2011 and ended when the current President, Ahmed al-Sharaa, led a lightning strike on Damascus and toppled the regime. Assad fled to Russia where he and his family were granted asylum.
Under the new accord, Syria will take control of civilian facilities at the Hmeimim airbase and the commercial section of Tartus port.
The military facilities will be transformed into joint Russian-Syrian training and qualification centres, with the transition expected to be completed within three months. Moscow has yet to comment on the deal.
It marks a significant shift from the role both bases once played in service of al-Assad during the civil war which killed hundreds of thousands of Syrians and displaced millions.
However, analysts say it could represent something more pragmatic, with Damascus reclaiming greater sovereignty over strategically important facilities while Moscow preserves a foothold and avoids being pushed entirely out of a country in which it has invested heavily for decades.
“The agreement between Russia and the Syrian government indicates that both countries need each other,” Alexey Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia, told Al Jazeera, adding that Damascus is likely “not interested in terminating its prolonged relationship with Russia”.
Russia’s military foothold in Syria
Moscow was a key Assad ally during Syria’s civil war, helping to keep the former leader in power by providing vital military support.
The Russian military intervention in 2015 helped to turn the tide of the war in favour of the al-Assad-led government. Hmeimim became the centre of Russian air operations, while Tartus provided Moscow with its principal naval foothold in the Mediterranean.
However, Russia did not interfere during the major advance towards Damascus that led to al-Assad’s overthrow in December 2024.
Following Assad’s ousting, Russian troops still in Syria gradually left the country except for those stationed at the two bases.
The Syrian foreign ministry said in a statement that the new arrangements for the bases represent a “reorganising of the Russian presence” along Syria’s coast.
“This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations,” the statement read.
‘No permanent enemies, only permanent interests’
According to political analyst Ruslan Trad, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council, Damascus has already moved on from Russia’s role in the war.
“Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa’s government fought al-Assad’s Russian-backed forces for years, yet within weeks of taking power, it began quiet negotiations to keep Moscow present rather than expel it,” Trad told Al Jazeera.
“This confirms the classic realist maxim that in politics there are no permanent enemies, only permanent interests.”
In the same vein in which al-Sharaa has gone in efforts to strike cordial relations with Western powers such as the US – which bestowed him with the status of Specially Designated Global Terrorist in May 2013 during the civil war – Trad said the post-al-Assad government has likely calculated that punishing Russia for its wartime role would cost more than it was worth.
“Moscow controls Bashar al-Assad’s asylum, holds Syrian debt and reconstruction contracts, supplies subsidised oil and grain and remains a veto-wielding Security Council power that shielded Sharaa’s own past terrorism designation,” he added.
Aron Lund, a fellow at Century International, said there is “lots of military and civilian technology” in Syria that comes from Russia and the former Soviet Union.
“There is an old legacy of military, administrative and technical cooperation between Damascus and Moscow. It would be very painful for Syria to break that relationship completely,” he told Al Jazeera.
“It’s transactional pragmatism on both sides,” he told Al Jazeera. “Al-Sharaa’s government, chronically cash-strapped and needing wheat, energy and technical support, has visited Putin twice in Moscow since taking power.”
“The leaders of both Syria and Russia have proven themselves to be very flexible and pragmatic.” Lund said.
That is reflected in the fact that the two sides began meeting and negotiating even before the toppling of the al-Assad regime was complete, he added.
“They began to meet only some weeks after Assad’s ouster. In practice, they were meeting and negotiating just weeks after Russian jets bombed al-Sharaa’s fighters. In fact, the first agreements were made even before Assad fell, during the offensive that toppled his regime,” he said.
Sovereign gatekeeper, not ‘Moscow client’
To this end, Al-Sharaa’s government, “chronically cash-strapped and needing wheat, energy and technical support”, says Trad, has visited Putin twice in Moscow since taking power.
The Syrian president has taken pains to publicly acknowledge Russia’s role “in stabilising the situation, not only in Syria but also in the region”.
Putin has welcomed al-Sharaa and signalled support for Syria’s territorial integrity.
Moscow, Trad said, needed to preserve its “only Mediterranean military platform for projecting power into Africa and the eastern Mediterranean”, while offering “debt relief, economic cooperation and UN cover on terrorism designations in exchange”.
“So yes, both sides still need each other, just on renegotiated terms that reflect Syria’s new leverage as sovereign gatekeeper rather than as Moscow’s client,” he added.
Resisting or balancing Western meddling?
Since the fall of al-Assad, Western and regional actors have sought to use Syria’s political transition to curb Russian influence, said Muraviev.
“Clearly, there was an attempt by the US and, to some extent, perhaps, the Israelis to push the new Syrian regime to terminate Russia’s presence in Syria,” he said.
“But … an agreement means that the Syrian government has retained an interest, and withstood the pressure from other parties, because they clearly see the dividends of maintaining the relationship with Russia.”
The prolonged negotiations between Damascus and Moscow were themselves telling, he said.
“The fact that those negotiations were held for about a year and a half meant that both sides were interested in not seeing these negotiations collapse,” he added.
Nevertheless, Muraviev stressed that keeping Russia in the picture does not mean Syria will close off avenues to other powers: “The new government would be open to develop strategic links with the US, Turkey, even working with Israel,” he said.
“But they would probably want to keep a multi-vectoral engagement … and having Russia in the equation will help them to use it as perhaps even a bargaining chip in their power game with other major powers.”
Lund noted that negotiations have been “very discreet”, perhaps because Russia and Syria appear to have been concerned that “talking too much about the bases” could trigger US and European demands for their closure.
“Al-Assad’s fall was a major blow to Russia, but that has already happened. This agreement is about the post-Assad future, and it could be positive or negative for Russia. We shall see whether the new arrangement will constrain Russia even more, or, to the contrary, whether this deal will formalise and reactivate Russia’s military presence.”

Belarus to introduce new wildlife protection system on M6 highway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:59:00 UTC
00:59:00 KST

File photo
                    
                    MINSK, 10 August (BelTA) – A new system to protect roads from wild animals will be introduced on the M6 highway. A pilot version of the system is already operating on the M10 highway. Sergei Kabak, Head of the sectoral road laboratory at the Belarusian Road Research Institute (BeldorNII), explained how it works in BelTA’s The Nation Speaks project.
“In Belarus, a pilot project to build a wildlife overpass is being implemented jointly with the National Academy of Sciences on the M10 highway (Russian border - Gomel - Kobrin),” Sergei Kabak said. “Drivers are warned that an animal is approaching the roadway by motion sensors installed in openings in the fence. The corresponding signal is sent to a variable-message road sign. It lights up when an animal is in the sensor area. The animal may not be on the roadway itself but in its immediate vicinity. Rumble strips made of coarse crushed stone have been installed on the approaches to the crossing to create discomfort for the animals’ hooves, discouraging them from jumping over this surface treatment. Lighting has also been installed, serving two purposes: it illuminates the area and scares animals away from the illuminated space.”
 
  
  
 
In addition, so-called Texas gates (or Canadian cattle grids) will be used on the M6 section. The structure addresses the problem of junctions and intersections, where conventional fencing is less effective: a special plate creates discomfort for animals, prompting them to turn back. The ends of the fences will also be fitted with special one-way flaps. This will prevent situations where an animal reaches the end of the fence and enters the road. The flap will allow the animal to leave for the forest but prevent it from entering the highway from there.
 
 
 
                    
                    
                                        
                                    
                                                        
                
                
            “In Belarus, a pilot project to build a wildlife overpass is being implemented jointly with the National Academy of Sciences on the M10 highway (Russian border - Gomel - Kobrin),” Sergei Kabak said. “Drivers are warned that an animal is approaching the roadway by motion sensors installed in openings in the fence. The corresponding signal is sent to a variable-message road sign. It lights up when an animal is in the sensor area. The animal may not be on the roadway itself but in its immediate vicinity. Rumble strips made of coarse crushed stone have been installed on the approaches to the crossing to create discomfort for the animals’ hooves, discouraging them from jumping over this surface treatment. Lighting has also been installed, serving two purposes: it illuminates the area and scares animals away from the illuminated space.”
The system has been in operation for about two years and is constantly being improved. “It is expected that this experience will be rolled out across the country in the near future,” Sergei Kabak said. Similar infrastructure is being built on the M6 highway (Minsk - Grodno) in the Volozhin District.
 
In addition, so-called Texas gates (or Canadian cattle grids) will be used on the M6 section. The structure addresses the problem of junctions and intersections, where conventional fencing is less effective: a special plate creates discomfort for animals, prompting them to turn back. The ends of the fences will also be fitted with special one-way flaps. This will prevent situations where an animal reaches the end of the fence and enters the road. The flap will allow the animal to leave for the forest but prevent it from entering the highway from there.
Sergei Kabak noted that the development and implementation of these solutions involves not only BeldorNII specialists but also BelDorSvyaz (which is responsible for installing the sensors), as well as road operators, which install the structures. Work in this area is ongoing with the aim of improving the effectiveness of road safety measures.

Trump steals Game of Thrones ‘Iron Throne’ to declare ‘order restored’ in latest White House pop culture takeover
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:58:55 BST
00:58:55 KST

Trump steals Game of Thrones ‘Iron Throne’ to declare ‘order restored’ in latest White House pop culture takeover
In the minute-long video posted to social media, the Resolute Desk is transformed into the Iron Throne
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The White House ripped off Game of Thrones in a new social media video that transformed the Resolute Desk into the Iron Throne — using the fantasy reference to declare order restored in the nation’s capital.
The minute-long video, posted to X on Monday, spoofs the iconic Game of Thrones opening sequence, with the realm of Westeros swapped out for Washington, D.C. The HBO show’s ominous, minor-key melody plays over the visuals.
“THE CAPITAL: RESTORED,” the White House captioned the video. “Order restored. The capital reclaimed.”
The video depicts various parts of Washington rendered like clockwork, including architectural features that have been restored by the Trump administration as a part of its beautification campaign. Among them is the cascading fountain in Meridian Hill Park, where water began flowing again earlier this year for the first time since 2019.
Other fountains touched by the administration’s restoration campaign, including those at Dupont Circle and beside Union Station, are also featured.
Conspicuously missing, however, is one of Trump’s most expensive restoration efforts: the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The $16 million project has been dogged by problems — including algae blooms and peeling sections of its newly installed liner.
As the video nears its close, the camera glides toward the White House and into the Oval Office, where the presidential seal on the carpet has been replaced by the sigil of House Targaryen.
The Resolute Desk then morphs into the Iron Throne — the seat fashioned from swords from which a monarch rules in the HBO series.
The suggestion that President Donald Trump wields — or aspires to wield — the unchecked power of a king is hardly new.
Last year, the White House circulated a fake Time magazine cover depicting the Republican president in a golden crown alongside the headline: “Long live the king.” Trump also shared a seemingly AI-generated video of himself piloting a jet emblazoned with the words “King Trump” and dropping excrement on protesters. He has, meanwhile, repeatedly floated the prospect of seeking an unconstitutional third term.
The White House’s communications strategy has also leaned on pop-culture imagery. Earlier this month, it posted a video likening ICE agents to Spider Man, with detainees shown ensnared in webs. And last year, capitalizing on a social-media trend, the White House shared a Studio Ghibli-style illustration of a detained migrant.
HBO has previously pushed back against Trump using imagery from Game of Thrones. In 2018, the president posted “Sanctions are coming” on Twitter, seemingly referencing the show’s “Winter is coming” tagline. The font appeared similar to that used by the show.
“We were not aware of this messaging and would prefer our trademark not be misappropriated for political purposes,” HBO said in response, according to Time.

In Malaysia, wave of hate speech threatens Rohingya refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:58:37 UTC
00:58:37 KST

In Malaysia, wave of hate speech threatens Rohingya refugees
Malaysia – The spread of hostile content on social media in Malaysia has intensified tensions towards the Rohingya refugee community, leading to the eviction of more than 100 people from their village and the temporary closure of schools attended by refugee children.
Malaysia has long been considered a safe haven for Rohingya Muslims fleeing persecution in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar. As of the end of February 2026, 126,000 Rohingyas were registered with the UN refugee agency in Malaysia, out of a total of around 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers.
However, they have faced growing hostility since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, culminating in a wave of online hate and disinformation that began in April 2026. On July 27, around 1 hundred Rohingya refugees were forced to leave their homes in a fishing village after their neighbours put up signs urging them to leave.
#SaveMalaysiaFromRohingya
Maryam* works for the NGO Article 19, which defends freedom of expression in Malaysia and combats hate speech.
 "The latest wave of anti-Rohingya rhetoric has undoubtedly been one of the most intense in terms of both scale and duration. It began towards the end of April and is still continuing today.
It all started with a disinformation campaign claiming that Rohingya refugees were demanding land and special rights. In May, an online petition was launched calling on the Malaysian prime minister to expel Rohingya refugees from Malaysia. Organisations such as UNHCR, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (SUHAKAM), and NGOs came under pressure and received threats on social media."
To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Some Malaysian influencers regularly post anti-Rohingya content and contribute to the spread of hostile hashtags such as #SaveMalaysiaFromRohingya.
Maryam* explains :
 "We reported some of the problematic content to Meta so that action could be taken immediately. However, Meta's content moderation, complaint handling, and reporting mechanisms remain far too slow to deal with harmful content."
She adds that the situation is particularly alarming because refugees are neither officially recognised nor protected under Malaysian law, as the country is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Although they are registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), they have no legal protection and are not allowed to work, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation and abuse.
'Rohingyas Are Banned from Kuala Muda'
This wave of online hatred has had dramatic consequences. On July 27, more than 1 hundred Rohingyas were forced to leave their homes in the village of Kuala Muda, in the state of Penang.
To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
According to the local newspaper Sinar Harian, the Rohingya population in this village has almost quadrupled, rising from 108 people in 2018 to around 400 in 2026. A non-Rohingya resident told the media outlet Bharian: “The locals feel disadvantaged, particularly economically, because many Rohingya have taken up fishing, creating competition with local residents who depend on fishing for their livelihoods."
The refugee families were reportedly escorted to buses bound for Kuala Lumpur. On arrival in the capital, they went to the office of the UNHCR to seek assistance. They then set up tents outside the organisation’s offices while awaiting a response. The Malaysian police then intervened and detained them for a day to check their documents and legal status. They were eventually released and placed in the care of local NGOs.
'Many children were chased and harassed on their way to school'
Children are also being targeted. At least nine community schools for refugees have temporarily closed to protect their students. The exact number of affected schools remains difficult to determine.
Amira* is the founder of an NGO that provides education for refugees in Malaysia. She describes the climate of fear that has forced many refugee schools to shut their doors.
 "Many children have been chased and harassed on their way to school. Some of these incidents have been shared on social media. Youth teams from several NGOs are now afraid to go in the field. The content being posted online is extremely radical. It is highly aggressive, using dehumanizing and threatening language. There is a real sense of fear within the Rohingya community."
Ahmad* is a Rohingya teacher and activist in Kuala Lumpur. He teaches at two schools in the capital that decided to close.
 "One school remained closed for a month, the other for two weeks because of all this chaos. We have only just reopened. Despite the risks, the staff felt it was essential to resume classes so that the children could continue their education. We advised students not to wear their school uniforms so that they would not attract attention on their way to school."
He also points out that his students come from different refugee communities, but many Malaysians assume they are all Rohingya. According to him, this misconception is reinforced by media coverage that often labels all refugees as Rohingya.
To display this content from Facebook, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Amira* explains that refugees have no legal right to formal education in Malaysia, as the country is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention.
 "Schools like ours operate in a grey area. If someone were to ask, ‘Is this school legal? Do you have the right to be here?’ Of course, the answer is no. Some schools have been closed down by the authorities because they did not have the necessary authorisations.
The lack of the right to work and access to education marginalises the Rohingya and limits their integration in Malaysia. At the same time, disinformation campaigns wrongly portray them as economic migrants or invaders. On social media, many ask why the UNHCR does not send them to other countries, but they are unaware that its ability to organise resettlement depends on the willingness of states to offer places to refugees."
'We cannot trust the Myanmar government to guarantee our safety'
On 23 July, the deputy foreign minister informed Parliament that 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently held in immigration detention centres would be repatriated to Myanmar.
On 28 July, Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said that the presence of the UNHCR office had made Malaysia "a magnet" for refugees and warned that the government could reconsider the agency's presence in the country if it refused to resettle more refugees.
Despite allegations of genocide against the Rohingya in Myanamar, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced on 30 July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya asylum seekers currently living in Malaysia.
The Myanmar Ethnic Rohingya Human Rights Organization Malaysia (MERHROM) expressed serious concern over the announcement:
"We cannot trust the Myanmar government to guarantee our safety while the massacres continue. Rohingyas will be forced to join the Myanmar military without any training and used as human shields in the army's war against various ethnic armed groups. That is the only reason the Myanmar military has agreed to take the Rohingyas back."
However, the Malaysian government later appeared to reverse its position. On 5 August, Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil announced that the government would not deport refugees if they faced a risk of persecution.
Denied citizenship under Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law, the Rohingya fled the country in large numbers in 2017 following a military campaign marked by massacres, sexual violence, and the systematic destruction of villages. The International Court of Justice is currently examining allegations of genocide against Myanmar over those events, following hearings held in January 2026.
* For security reasons, the people interviewed for this article asked to speak anonymously and their names have been changed.

Navy warship that sank during fatal training exercise uncovered after 118 years
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:57:35 BST
00:57:35 KST

Navy warship that sank during fatal training exercise uncovered after 118 years
The warship was cut in two in 1908 after straying into the path of another warship
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A team of divers off the Isle of Wight has discovered the wreck of a Royal Navy warship that sank 118 years ago, claiming the lives of more than half its crew.
HMS Tiger was cut in two in 1908 after straying into the path of another warship during a training exercise.
Fewer than half of its 57 crew survived. The torpedo boat destroyer was unable to take evasive action to avoid colliding with the cruiser HMS Berwick during night manoeuvres.
A Royal Navy spokesman said: “The tragedy made front page news, King Edward VII sent a telegram of sympathy and commemorative postcards were produced remembering the crew.”
The discovery of the wreck by the ProjectXplore group of divers and historians, which spent five years working through the archives to pinpoint the Tiger’s resting place, comes as the Government is considering new powers to protect military shipwrecks.
Under the new Armed Forces Bill, military shipwrecks would be safeguarded with a “protected place” designation once the remains had been found.
The change in the law would expand existing safeguards under the Protection of Military Remains Act, which only cover vessels lost within the past 200 years.
Minister for the Armed Forces Louise Sandher-Jones said: “As well as protecting UK national security, defence has a role to play in preserving our maritime heritage and the memory of those who gave their lives serving their country.
“These protections go further to ensure that these vulnerable and nationally significant monuments are protected from day one of discovery, giving lost sailors the dignity and respect they deserve.
“This Armed Forces Bill is wide-ranging in the measures it proposes – from protecting our rich cultural heritage, to transforming the lives of military families by upgrading and improving the defence housing estate.”
Leo Fielding and Dan McMullen, co-organisers of ProjectXplore, said in a statement: “It has been the privilege of a lifetime to research, discover and document the wreck of HMS Tiger.
“We sincerely hope that our work will ensure that HMS Tiger, her story and the memory of those connected with her endure for future generations.
“ProjectXplore welcomes the proposed amendments in the Armed Forces Bill.
“We believe they represent a constructive step forward in protecting the United Kingdom’s maritime heritage and ensuring that wreck sites of historical and archaeological significance are appropriately safeguarded.”
Royal Navy Deputy Fleet Wreck Officer Lieutenant Commander Jen Smith said: “Protecting military wrecks helps to ensure they are preserved for future generations.
“This is beneficial for our rich maritime heritage and the diving community who keep the stories of our lost shipwrecks alive.
“Divers are still able to visit these sites and witness history first hand, which is key to ensuring that these ships and their crews are not forgotten.
“All we ask of divers is this – enjoy looking, learning and paying your respects at these incredible sites, but do so in a manner that does not disturb them.”

US intelligence ‘believes Russia was behind Leipzig airport drone bomb’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:55:26 UTC
00:55:26 KST

American intelligence experts believe Russia was behind an attack on a German airport last week with a drone laden with explosives, US media have reported, as Berlin remained silent on the likely culprit.
Last week’s security emergency prompted the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, to break off his summer holiday in Italy and rush to the scene in the eastern city of Leipzig, as he spoke of a “new level of danger” for Germany.
Dobrindt called the incident, in which a quadcopter with semtex plastic explosives attached was found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at the major shipping and military hub, part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario” by a well-equipped foreign actor.
As the German investigators raced to identify the perpetrators, the tabloid Bild reported that authorities had found DNA traces at the scene that matched a sample from a firebomb, posted via DHL, that exploded at Leipzig airport in July 2024.
Five men suspected in a related series of mailed incendiary devices are on trial in Lithuania, where it emerged in court last week that the plane that was the target of the firebomb only avoided being set on fire in mid-flight because it was delayed. The suspects are alleged by Lithuanian prosecutors to have been employed by Russian intelligence.
Even as MPs and security analysts pointed the finger at the Kremlin over the latest incident in Leipzig, German government officials have not levelled a specific accusation against Moscow.
The Wall Street Journal, however, has quoted US officials familiar with intelligence reports about the incident as saying that the drone probably belongs to the Russian government.
CNN reported that Washington had concluded the drone came from a Russian secret service, citing a US defence official in Europe noting the explosive material found on the drone suggested a military manufacturer.
German officials said the drone managed to fly past Leipzig airport’s defences.
It was only immobilised when an alert airport bus driver ferrying a group of late-night passengers spotted and reported it, an estimated four hours after it breached the facility’s security, averting what authorities have said could have been a multiple casualty event.
The same night, a DHL cargo plane, which had been forced to abort its landing at the airport due to the discovery of the drone, then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere, with minor damage.
Investigators now believe it hit a second hostile drone being flown that night.
A day later, drones were detected above an army installation in western Germany housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine has often requested to help fend off Russia’s aerial bombardments.
In response to the increased threat, the German interior ministry said on Monday it plans to double its federal team of anti-drone experts to 300, with the number of operational bases for the unit to rise to eight from four.
Germany and other European countries have long reported suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies, and accused Russian agents of spying as well as a targeted campaign of sabotage, disruption and intimidation.
Moscow has denied this, and late last week its embassy in Berlin called any suggestion it had a hand in the Leipzig case a “rashly contrived provocation” that “serves only the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political establishment”.
Berlin is Ukraine’s biggest national supplier of military aid in its defence against the Russian onslaught.
Next month, Germany will hold three pivotal elections in eastern states, where support for defence assistance for Kyiv is controversial among voters and fears of “provoking” Moscow run high.
The pro-Russian far-right Alternative für Deutschland is poised to perform well in all three races, polls show, amid reports of Russian disinformation targeted at its principal rivals, the mainstream democratic parties.
The opposition Greens have criticised the government for not naming and blaming Russia at this stage of the Leipzig investigation.
Political scientist Wolfgang Schröder of the University of Kassel in western Germany said two factors could be shaping Berlin’s restraint.
Firstly, Russia had been named early on as a prime suspect behind the 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, which German prosecutors now say was ordered by Ukrainian “state authorities”.
More important, Schröder said, were the incalculable consequences of accusing Moscow of a botched military attack on German soil amid warnings of an escalation in tensions.
“If it were to be defined as an act of aggression – that is, a military attack by Russia against (Germany’s) critical infrastructure – then we would be on the brink of entering a state of war, and that would have implications not only of a diplomatic nature but also with regard to Nato,” he told local news broadcaster n-tv.
“A cautious approach is being taken here, precisely because the aim is to prevent being drawn in, and that would mean turning this into a matter of European security – a matter of Nato security – and that would certainly take Germany’s involvement in the armed conflict between Russia and Ukraine to a whole new level.”

Why the Rhine drought is bad news for Germany's recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:55:00 UTC
00:55:00 KST

Why the Rhine drought is bad news for Germany's recovery
August 10, 2026
Water levels on the Rhine River — a small but critical artery for goods vital to Germany’s industry — remain critically low as a result of weeks of drought.
At one of the river's shallowest stretches, Kaub — between Mainz and Koblenz — the water level stood at around 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) at Monday lunchtime, according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV).
Although the real navigable channel is roughly a meter deeper, 40 centimeters is regarded as the lowest for standard commercial vessels at Kaub.
Ship operators use the reading at Kaub to decide how much cargo their barges can safely carry and whether a passage is feasible at all.
According to local media, in recent weeks, carriers have significantly cut their cargoes along the Rhine — in many cases to as little as one-fifth of normal capacity.
The problem isn't just limited to the Middle Rhine, the 130-kilometer (80-mile) stretch between Mainz and Bonn that is the narrowest and shallowest section of the river.
Areas around Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg-Ruhrort and Emmerich are also at historic lows.
Jens Schwanen, the head of the BDB association of inland shipping, told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Monday that the Rhine may become impassable at Kaub before the end of the week.
This would effectively split the river in two for commercial traffic.
What effect will the drought have on the German economy?
The drought could not come at a worse time for Germany’s economy, which is already grappling with weak growth, high energy costs and fading industrial competitiveness.
Germany still relies on its long rivers and waterways to transport some 5% of goods around the country, most of them bulk materials, including iron ore, coal, sand and petroleum products.
Out of 3.28 billion tons of goods transported in 2024, 173 million tons were carried by inland water, including the Rhine, according to BDB.
Eurostat, the European Union's statistics agency, calculated in 2023 that the Rhine corridor — from the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands to the German-Swiss border — accounts for around 40% of freight by ton-kilometers.
After two previous droughts, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated in 2023 that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.
In an economy that has barely grown for the past two years, even a temporary 1% hit to industrial output is highly damaging.
The German Economic Institute (IW) now predicts a 0.4% drop in gross domestic product, effectively wiping out this year's economic growth, which was expected at 0.5%.
"A prolonged disruption of navigability on the Rhine could completely stifle the tiny seed of growth we have," warned IW economist Thilo Schäfer in an interview with Bild newspaper last week.
Other experts have warned of losses of €1 to €2 billion ($1.2 to $2.3 billion) in the third quarter alone, with the steel, chemicals and energy sectors hit especially hard.
What happens if the River Rhine is effectively split in two?
The BDB's Schwanen warned that "due to the lack of rainfall, a single-digit reading is forecast for the first time this week at the Kaub gauge."
"In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer navigable along its entire length and is therefore effectively divided in two," he told the Rheinische Post.
This would result in two separate areas. On the one hand, shipping traffic would continue between the North Sea ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp and the Cologne region via the Rhine and the Western German canal system.
Further south, shipping would operate on the tributaries of the Neckar, Moselle, and Main, as well as the Main-Danube Canal, which is regarded as a key global link on the route to and from Southeast Europe.
Between the two sections, shipping companies would then try to move cargo onto trucks and freight rail services.
However, Germany's roads cannot absorb the typical 50 to 150 truckloads that a single large barge can handle without severe congestion and substantially higher costs.
Baden-Württemberg said Monday it would join four other German states in easing restrictions on truck movements on Sundays to help ease congestion.
Following urgent talks last Thursday, Transport Minister Steffen Bilger announced several other measures to shore up Germany's supply chain.
These include cutting red tape for heavy loads shifted to the road network, stopping unnecessary roadworks and better coordination with DB Cargo, the rail freight arm of Deutsche Bahn.
Are regular droughts a new reality for Europe's waterways?
Extremely low water on the Rhine and other major European rivers used to be rare events.
Yet, many scientists believe climate change is now making them more frequent, longer and more severe.
According to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, western Europe has just experienced its warmest June and July on record, with exceptionally low rainfall driving much lower than average water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Seine.
The current crisis marks the third major low‑water episode in eight years, after major droughts in 2018 and 2022.
The Rhine has traditionally been supported during dry summer months by meltwater from Alpine snow and glaciers. As those glaciers retreat and snow cover declines, this natural buffer is weakening.
Germany’s Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) projected in 2023 that severe low-water events like 2018 could strike every five to 10 years by mid-century.

National Guard unveils new armored vehicle for radiation and chemical reconnaissance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:55:00 UTC
00:55:00 KST

National Guard unveils new armored vehicle for radiation and chemical reconnaissance
According to Ukrinform, Pivnenko announced this on his Facebook page.
Pivnenko said that the National Guard was continuing to modernize its equipment and replace outdated models with modern ones that met current requirements for safety and efficiency.
According to him, one of the areas of this work was strengthening the radiation, chemical, and biological protection units.
Pivnenko explained that their task was to detect radiation, chemical, and biological threats in a timely manner, determine the scale of contamination, monitor the situation, and promptly transmit information to the command.
The general emphasized that the safety of service members, the performance of combat missions, and the protection of civilians depended on the speed and accuracy of this work.
For this reason, Pivnenko said, the National Guard had commissioned the development of new radiation and chemical reconnaissance vehicles based on the Tisa light armored vehicle chassis.
The vehicle is a modern system that allows crews to conduct reconnaissance and monitor hazardous areas without having to leave the protection of the armored vehicle.
The radiation and chemical reconnaissance vehicle is equipped with:
- radiation and chemical reconnaissance instruments;
- an automated information collection and processing system;
- a weather station;
- modern communications equipment;
- satellite navigation.
Pivnenko emphasized that these systems allow personnel to receive and transmit data in real time, assess the situation more quickly, and make the necessary decisions.
The armored vehicle is based on the Toyota Land Cruiser 79 and complies with the NATO STANAG 4569 protection standard. This provides the required level of ballistic and mine protection.
It is also equipped with night-vision, ventilation, and air-filtration systems, allowing the crew to carry out missions in difficult conditions while maintaining a high level of safety.
Pivnenko said that the National Guard was working to ensure that every unit had modern equipment for carrying out its missions and was prepared to respond to any threats.
On Telegram, Pivnenko reported that the outdated Soviet UAZ-469RKhB had been replaced with a modern armored vehicle for radiation and chemical reconnaissance.
According to him, the National Guard of Ukraine had already received the first radiation and chemical reconnaissance vehicles in Ukraine based on the Tisa armored chassis.
The general emphasized that the vehicle was a modern development created according to the National Guard’s technical specifications and had no analogues.
Pivnenko explained that the new vehicle had replaced the outdated Soviet UAZ-469RKhB, a chemical reconnaissance vehicle developed in the 1980s on the basis of a civilian off-road vehicle without adequate armor protection for the crew.
Pivnenko added that its equipment had also failed to provide adequate monitoring and threat detection capabilities.
The National Guard commander stressed that Russia had repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to use prohibited chemical substances on the battlefield, while attacks on critical infrastructure, particularly near nuclear power plants, made radiation monitoring an extremely important issue.
As Ukrinform reported, the National Guard of Ukraine had also received upgraded Shilka self-propelled anti-aircraft systems.
