A short tenure? Trump frustrated and MAGA furious with DHS head Markwayne Mullin: report
President and allies having buyer’s remorse over ex-Oklahoma senator’s perceived squishiness on harsh anti-immigrant moves
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Less than six months into Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s tenure atop America’s sprawling immigration and internal security bureaucracy, President Donald Trump and some of his most vocal allies are having second thoughts about the former Oklahoma senator’s job performance.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Trump’s angst over his decision to elevate the 49-year-old ex-mixed martial arts fighter and plumbing business owner to lead one of the cabinet’s most important departments has been simmering since his March confirmation, which followed the president’s decision to fire Mullin’s predecessor Kristi Noem amid outrage over a series of shootings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and other scandals that had plagued her tenure atop the department.
Though Mullin was tasked with calming public anger at DHS after ham-handed deployments in Minneapolis gave the administration a black eye, Trump allies have bristled at anything that even smacks of moderating the harsh immigration and deportation policies that have become a staple of the president’s second term.
After a June Supreme Court ruling allowing DHS to end temporary protections for as many as 350,000 Haitians living across the U.S., Mullin suggested that some could “fill out the paperwork” to gain some form of legal status — something that directly contradicted Trump’s promise to deport as many Haitians as possible from the U.S.
A month later, Mullin got crosswise with Trump after he directed ICE to stop most traffic stops after a pair of fatal shootings — a move that prompted Trump to publicly overrule the DHS boss, writing that Mullin’s attempt to curb the practice was something “the Radical Left [Democrats]” had wanted.
The decision sparked outrage from MAGA personalities, including right-wing legal activist Mike Davis, who complained on ex-Trump adviser Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast that Mullin “needs to stop being a wimp, he needs to stop being weak, he needs to stop being stupid” and upbraided him for seemingly bowing to a request from Maine Senator Susan Collins.
“You work for President Trump, you don’t work for Senate Democrats, you don’t work for Susan Collins ... If he’s not up to doing the job, get the hell out of the job and we’ll put someone there who can,” Davis said at the time.
Earlier this month, Mullin triggered MAGA fury once more when he told National Governors Association members that immigration could be a benefit to some industries, directly contradicting the administration position that immigrants steal jobs from American citizens, and suggested that immigration could provide needed workers in some industries.
One Trump ally, activist Laura Loomer, reacted by posting on X that Mullin should be sacked because he has “done absolutely nothing to increase the rate of mass deportations.”
Trump himself has also groused about Mullin’s attempt to postpone an Independence Day fireworks display Trump had touted after severe thunderstorms threatened the safety of those who’d been waiting on the National Mall to watch the show.
At the time, the president complained that “one of my very brilliant people” had suggested postponing the show after lightning forced the Mall’s evacuation.
“I said, ‘It doesn’t work next week. This is the big day. We want July Fourth. We’re not looking for July something else,’” he said.
The White House denied any tensions between the president and his DHS pick, with spokesperson Lauren Bis noting in a statement that Trump “has confidence in his Cabinet to carry out the agenda the American people voted for.”
“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership we have the most secure border in history, we are deporting record numbers of illegal aliens, we have cracked down on illegal alien fraud, and we are denaturalizing individuals who illegally procured American citizenship,” she said.

Hong Kong to review warning system after record heat triggers lowest alert
Pledge follows calls to adopt international measurement that places greater weight on direct sunlight and to increase monitoring stations
Hong Kong labour authorities have pledged to review the city’s heat stress warning system, a day after the lowest-level alert for outdoor workers was issued despite record-breaking temperatures, prompting questions about the index’s effectiveness
The pledge on Monday followed calls from experts for the government to adopt an international measurement that gives greater weight to direct sunlight, and to increase the number of heat stress monitoring stations so that all districts are covered and the risks faced by outdoor workers are better reflected.
“We will review the current mechanism while maintaining our close communications with relevant departments,” Undersecretary for Labour and Welfare Ho Kai-ming said on Monday.
“The Labour Department has been working with different departments, including the Observatory, to mitigate the occupational safety risks faced by workers.”
The city reached a scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) on Sunday, the highest temperature recorded since the Hong Kong Observatory began operating in 1884. Yet the lowest-level amber heat stress alert for outdoor workers remained in place.
The Observatory said the scorching conditions would persist in the coming days, with temperatures in some areas forecast to reach at least 37 degrees, although more frequent showers are expected later this week.

Smart glasses give men tools to ‘stalk and harass’ women in private spaces, study finds
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:02:38 BST
00:02:38 KST

Smart glasses give men tools to ‘stalk and harass’ women in private spaces, study finds
Women are being filmed at work and in the gym by men wearing smart glasses, a new study has found
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Smart glasses such as Meta Ray-Bans are giving men the tools to “stalk and harass” women in private spaces including at work and in the gym, researchers have warned.
Women are facing a growing threat of being filmed without their consent in places they would normally expect privacy by men wearing the glasses, and facing these videos being shared online for views, a new study from the University of Sydney (UoS) found.
The authors analysed hundreds of videos from “pick-up” content creators posted on Instagram between 2023 to 2026. In the videos, men wearing smart glasses approach women with the aim of getting their phone number or Instagram handle and then share that online for engagement. Some of the women in the study were filmed at work, the gym, or the beach in swimwear, researchers said.
Around 60 percent of covert point-of-view Instagram videos analysed by the researchers showed behaviour classified as potential harassment, and in 43 per cent of videos, the women were further exposed to derogatory commentary, some being identified and doxxed.
Many women showed discomfort or refusal, yet filming and interaction often continued, according to the study.
“Smart glasses have given pickup artists a new tool to further exploit women,” Dr Milica Stilinovic, a postdoctoral research associate at UoS said. “We call it ‘ambient capture’ because it is a state of play in which men might seem disarming. They will stalk and harass you in places of work, the stairwell of your apartment building, on the street, in the gym, and at the beach – places where you’d assume some sort of right to privacy.
“You don't know if you’re being filmed; that footage is then uploaded, exposing you to a wider web of harassment.”
The researchers have now called on governments and tech companies to slow down the release of more smart glasses so that they can be better regulated to protect privacy and against misuse.
“Tech is running at breakneck speed and regulators, a pace behind, cannot regulate harms once they’ve already manifested in the wild,” Dr Stilinovic said. “It’s time for Big Tech to come to the table and slow down the release of more smart glasses so that regulation gets a better scope of what they’re dealing with.”
Meta said its glasses come with a built-in LED light that turns on when the wearer is filming. It later made changes to stop the glasses working when the light is tampered with after dozens of videos online showed users how to disable the light.
It added it has cracked down on pick-up style videos following recent comments from Instagram chief executive Adam Mosseri, who said the company is trying to fight the videos “every way we can”.
Filming in public places is currently legal in the UK, but filming in areas where people have a reasonable expectation of privacy is not generally allowed without the explicit consent of the landowner.
It comes after popular pub chain Wetherspoon said Meta glasses would be banned inside its venues last week, accusing the glasses of “enabling surreptitious surveillance”.
Meta glasses have been at the centre of a controversy over privacy rights as women reported feeling “scared” and “violated” by being filmed without their consent.
Domestic abuse charity Refuge has repeatedly warned the glasses “threaten the safety of all women and girls in public, facilitating harassment, surveillance and other abuse”.
The glasses have also been banned in some schools and recently by Monopoly Events, the company behind Comic-Con, who banned Meta glasses from its events to stop "secret filming" of guests and attendees.
A Meta spokesperson said: "We designed our AI glasses with privacy and safety features built in from the start — informed by engagement with safety experts. Our glasses have always had an LED light that activates whenever someone captures a photo or video for their gallery. They also feature tamper detection technology, and we are updating the glasses to disable the camera if they detect the LED was physically tampered with or destroyed.
“No other kind of camera has done this and we're proud to lead the industry forward. We have teams dedicated to ensuring our glasses feel great for wearers and the people around them, so we can continue delivering products that make everyday life better."
A government spokesperson said: "Recording someone in public to cause alarm or distress may constitute offences such as harassment or stalking. We are already further strengthening protections for victims of intimate image abuse through new offences in the Crime and Policing Act.
"We will continue to engage with the Information Commissioner's Office to ensure regulation remains effective as technology evolves and that people's information rights are protected."

Germany boosts police anti-drone unit after incident at strategic airport

- The incident involved an explosives-laden drone that struck a Ukrainian cargo plane but did not detonate; it was described as a "hybrid attack scenario" possibly involving a foreign power.
- Germany suspects Russia's involvement in such drone incidents targeting sensitive sites, while Russia denies the accusations and calls the Leipzig event a provocation benefiting Kyiv and European militarists.
AI generated
BERLIN – Germany will beef up its anti-drone police unit, the government said on Aug 10, days after an explosives-laden unmanned aerial vehicle was flown into a strategically important airport.
Berlin was shocked by the incident last week when the UAV was defused after it was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig-Halle airport, a key hub for military equipment transport.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt – who labelled the incident a “hybrid attack scenario” potentially involving a “foreign power” – now plans to double personnel in the federal police anti-drone unit to 300.
The number of operational bases for the unit will be increased from four to eight, a ministry spokeswoman said at a press conference.
She said that Dobrindt would next week formally open a new drone technology research centre, attached to the German Aerospace Centre.
According to news weekly Die Zeit, the drone at Leipzig airport bounced off one wing of the Antonov plane hours before it was discovered by an airport employee around midnight.
The reason the explosives failed to detonate remained unclear, said the unconfirmed report that cited security camera footage.
The airport in eastern Germany plays a key role in the transport of military goods by the German armed forces and NATO allies. It also serves as a base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines.
Germany and other European countries have observed UAVs frequently flying over sensitive sites such as airports, military bases and industrial plants.
The authorities in Germany, one of Ukraine’s biggest military supporters, have said they suspect Russia of orchestrating many of the incidents as part of a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation.
Russia has denied being behind any such incidents.
Russian embassy last week dismissed the Leipzig incident as a “hastily contrived provocation” that “serves only the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political establishment”.
Also on Aug 11, Die Zeit and the Bild daily said investigators had found traces of DNA on the drone discovered at Leipzig airport.
Die Zeit reported that the DNA in question had previously been registered in Lithuania but gave no further details. AFP

Shoppers warned of supermarket price rises ‘within months’ due to extreme heat
Senior MP says consumers could feel impact of shortages on their food shop within the next six months
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Shoppers have been warned they can expect to pay more for their food shop “come the later part of this year”, as extreme heat and drought bring farming to the brink.
The chair of the House of Commons’ Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee, Alistair Carmichael, has said consumers can expect to see the impact of this summer’s record-breaking weather in six to 12 months, as growers have warned that this year’s barley and wheat yield is expected to be lower than previous years.
“The problems for farmers today will be the problems for consumers in six or 12 months’ time because you see massively decreased yield for wheat and for barley,” said Mr Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP for Orkney and Shetland, on BBC Radio 4’s The World At One.
“And you’re seeing increasingly sort of concerned noises coming from vegetable producers as well.”
He added that shoppers will not be able to rely on imports to buy cheaper food because of the extreme heat throughout Europe.
“We can’t look to some of the alternative markets that we might have done in continental Europe in recent years because they are experiencing the same problems that we are,” he said.
“If you decrease the supply but you maintain the demand, then you’re going to pick the price up, so we will be seeing further food price inflation shocks for everybody come the later part of the year.”
Experts in the food industry have warned that UK food security is growing more fragile due to the extreme weather after England and Wales experienced their driest July since records began, while the south of England saw the driest month ever recorded.
Analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) last week estimated that the hot and dry conditions that have plagued spring and summer could cut the country’s cereals and oilseed harvest by 2.5 million tonnes compared to earlier projections.
The National Drought Group revealed on Monday that almost three-quarters – 71.3 per cent – of England is now in drought. The National Farmers’ Union president Tom Bradshaw said conditions had left the agricultural sector struggling.
“This is one of the most severe droughts many farmers and growers have lived through,” Mr Bradshaw said. “Harvest yields are looking poor, farmers are struggling to access water to irrigate fruit and vegetables, and livestock farmers are having to use grass they cut this spring for their stores of winter feed for cattle as there’s very little grass growing now.
“The picture is even worse when we look across Europe to many of the countries we import food from, with huge wildfires across France and Spain. While retailers are used to managing variations in global supply, we’re not going to be able to trade our way through this potential crisis.
“If this summer teaches us anything, it is that we must prioritise food production. We have taken food production for granted for too long; we must create a more resilient food system to feed the 29 million households across the country, and we can’t produce food without water. This means urgent action to bolster our water security and ensuring our food security is treated as a vital part of our nation’s critical infrastructure.
“Central to this will be fast-tracking investment and planning changes, meaning we can build new reservoirs on farms. We need a common sense approach to water use, with water access prioritised for livestock, particularly poultry and pigs. More flexible abstraction rules are also needed so farmers can access water for irrigation. This would enable us to grow more of the food we can and should produce here ourselves, especially fruit and vegetables.”

The strike reached a strategic plant more than 2,000 kilometers from Ukraine. ZapSibNeftekhim is Russia's largest petrochemical complex and a strategic chemical-industry enterprise.
The plant makes materials with military uses
The target feeds Russia's industry, including its war production. The Tobolsk complex produces basic raw materials for a wide range of industrial products, some of which have applications in the defense-industrial sector.
Its scale is substantial. The complex produces about 2.5 million tons of polymers a year, including dual-use materials, making it a flagship of Russia's chemical industry rather than a peripheral target, according to the insurgent movement Chornaya Iskra.
The plant belongs to Putin-linked billionaires
The strike hit assets tied to Russia's ruler, Vladimir Putin's inner circle. ZapSibNeftekhim is the flagship of the SIBUR holding, which is owned directly and indirectly by billionaires, including Gennady Timchenko and the Kovalchuks, figures who built their fortunes on their closeness to the leadership, Chornaya Iskra reports.
The partisans framed the strike in those terms.
"This is not just a money flow feeding Putin's economy burning, this is the money of his accomplices burning," Chornaya Iskra said, casting the strike as hitting the oligarchs who fund and profit from the war, not just the Russian economy in the abstract.
The strike extends Ukraine's deep campaign
Reaching Tobolsk marks the range of Ukraine's long-range campaign. The SOF said it continues to implement Ukraine's long-range sanctions against Russia's military-economic sector.
Striking a petrochemical complex over 2,000 kilometers inside Russia, in western Siberia, extends the deep-strike campaign far beyond the refineries and depots of European Russia. Each such strike raises the cost of the industry that funds and supplies Russia's war.

At the end of a long day I made a mistake at work. No patient was harmed and yet it weighs on me | Ranjana Srivastava
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:00:48 UTC
00:00:48 KST

The other day, I made a mistake at work.
It was the end of a long day. I had already run an outpatient cancer clinic with dozens of unwell patients and then moved on to inpatient rounds on a busy medical unit.
My small team cares for 30 patients aged 25 to 100.
The younger ones often live with disability and mental illness. Elderly people present with falls, organ failure and dementia. The diagnoses are common, but the stories are distinct.
People have tripped, taken too many pills, or have “no idea what happened”. Some are delirious and dying, though no one has quite said it aloud. Others report pain. A few are homeless. Nearly everyone has undergone a battery of tests – many of them unnecessary.
The carer of a disabled young man finds me to tell me gently but firmly that he’s in pain.
“I believe you,” I reply, scrambling to prescribe analgesia. Thank goodness for carers.
Another patient is agitated after weeks in hospital. Each day we try something new with no result. I make a mental note to call his wife.
Elsewhere, a patient with dementia has been effectively evicted from her nursing home for periodic aggression. Everyone agrees this is wrong, but the responsibility for advocacy falls, once again, to the medical team. She will languish here.
A tidy ward round requires clearing the mind between patients. But when the problems are deeply human, that is impossible. Each interaction leaves a residue until the individual concerns blur into a dense mass, most of them requiring some form of medical oversight.
Unsurprisingly, my mind is saturated with everything I must do, cannot do, and am not equipped to do. It’s a peculiar feeling to work at the height of your capacity and still know that you have not done enough.
My mistake comes at the end of the day. I prescribe a medication I have ordered hundreds of times before, but I get the dose wrong. An attentive pharmacist queries it and I correct the error.
Thankfully, no patient was harmed. Still, the mistake lingers.
One interpretation is that human error is inevitable and that the system worked as intended. But that is false comfort. When lives are at stake, the error should not occur.
I consider the usual explanations. Poor sleep, exercise, diet, unusual stress: not much is relevant here.
I worry whether after 25 years my attention is slipping. But experienced clinicians are often better at filtering noise and focusing on what matters. This aligns with what I see in students and junior doctors.
Eventually, I arrive at a simpler explanation: cognitive overload.
There were too many patients, each with competing needs where prioritisation is not always straightforward. It is one thing to choose between cooking and laundry; it is another to weigh stroke against trauma, delirium against dying.
The standard response is that there are too few doctors managing too many patients. That is true, but an incomplete explanation. No health system is overstaffed or overfunded. Across the world, outpatient clinics are crowded, and many doctors work under unthinkable conditions.
Comparison, however, is not the point. Patients are entitled to careful, attentive care. They should not feel fortunate simply because their doctor listens.
An ageing population with a high burden of chronic disease is poorly served by a hospital-centred system. The prescription for a different kind of healthcare demands political courage and long-term thinking.
Nearly half of my inpatients could be managed in the community. Patients who fall would benefit more from preventive allied health interventions. Nursing home residents often endure the indignities of hospitalisation when care could be delivered in place. Patients with primarily social needs require social workers, not doctors. Mental illness requires an array of providers. Patients on chemotherapy or dialysis become unwell at all times, yet their support is confined to business hours.
Initiatives such as virtual emergency departments and urgent care clinics attempt to reduce hospital demand. Even so, the default pathway for most patients remains the public hospital. Despite their well-documented shortcomings, hospitals are still perceived as the final bastion of safety.
The more important question is whether every patient needed to be there at all.
The most common reason people become doctors is because they want to help people. That is precisely why it feels so awful to make mistakes that could harm.
When doctors err, the instinctive question is often: is it time to quit?
Self-reflection is important but it is misplaced when the primary constraint is a system that is not fit for purpose.
Mistakes leave permanent impressions – on patients who trust us and doctors who want to deserve that trust.
The reflex solution is to train and employ more doctors. A more realistic one is to reduce the number of patients who require hospital care.
Not because patients deserve less care, but because they deserve better care – delivered in the right place, by the right people, at the right time.
- 
  Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the Public

Dogs can distinguish between fearful and angry or sad human faces, brain scans suggest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:00:47 UTC
00:00:47 KST

While dogs are known to turn the puppy eyes on their owners, it seems our pets are keeping a close eye on us too: research has revealed dog brains can distinguish different types of unhappy human faces.
Dr Laura Cuaya, a co-author of the study from the University of Vienna, said previous behavioural studies had shown dogs could tell apart some human facial expressions, but such studies tended to only test two at a time, one positive and one negative. As a result, it was not clear if dogs could distinguish different types of happy or unhappy faces.
Now Cuaya and colleagues have revealed dog brains can not only distinguish happy faces from other expressions, but can tell apart different negative expressions, distinguishing fearful faces from those that are angry or sad.
“This is the first demonstration that the dog brain can distinguish between emotions from the same valence,” she said.
While the team’s previous research has suggested dogs do not have a particular region of the brain devoted to processing faces, Cuaya noted that did not mean the brain activity pattern was the same for the front and back of the head.
Writing in the journal iScience, Cuaya and colleagues report how they worked with pet dogs that had been trained to voluntarily lie still, awake and unrestrained, within an MRI scanner.
In the first experiment, eight dogs were shown five sets of happy faces and five sets of neutral faces. Each set contained four photos of humans that were unfamiliar to the dog but were of the same gender as their primary caregiver. This was repeated five times for each dog.
The results revealed increased activity in certain parts of the brain when the dogs were shown happy faces compared with neutral ones.
Cuaya said these areas were associated with higher visual processing, social processing and reward processing – suggesting the dog was processing something positive.
Dr Raúl Hernández Pérez, the first author of the study, said the results raised another question, however: “We don’t know if these regions are related just to happy faces or to emotional faces in general.”
The team then carried out a second MRI experiment involving 12 dogs. Each was shown new sets of unfamiliar male and female human faces, this time bearing four different expressions: happiness, sadness, fear and anger.
The researchers used machine learning to analyse activity in the same brain regions identified in the first experiment, revealing such activity could distinguish happy faces from each negative expression – but could not distinguish between different types of unhappy face.
However, when the team analysed activity in the whole dog brain, they found it was possible to distinguish between sad v fearful faces, and angry v fearful faces – with differences in activity in different parts of the brain – but not angry and sad faces.
Hernández said different negative expressions might trigger different responses as they represented a different type of threat.
The authors said it might be harder for dogs to tell apart two human facial expressions if they were both negative or both positive, and dogs might also need additional information – such as body language – to distinguish anger from sadness.
The research has limitations, including small sample size; most of the dogs being border collies, and all were healthy and without behavioural problems.
Cuaya said the study could have practical implications: for example, expressing happiness when training a dog could aid the learning process.
Bridget Waller, a professor of evolution and social behaviour at Nottingham Trent University, who was not involved in the study, described the work as fascinating, saying it showed how dogs have been shaped through domestication to understand human behaviour.
“Smiling is the most commonly used human facial expression, vital to our social interactions, and so it makes sense that dogs have developed a particular ability to distinguish this from other facial movements,” she said. “It seems less clear that they can distinguish between the other facial expressions, and again this would make sense as these are much less commonly produced in human social interaction.”

Mecca pact: How the Middle East is building a new security order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:00:43 UTC
00:00:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Mecca pact: How the Middle East is building a new security order
After more than a year of talks, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a landmark defence pact last week in Mecca.
Bringing together Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim country, Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters and custodian of Islam’s holiest sites, and Turkey, NATO’s second-largest military, the agreement marks a significant shift in the regional security architecture.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack against one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all, echoing NATO’s Article 5. It also builds on the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) signed by Riyadh and Islamabad last September. Unlike that bilateral accord, however, the new arrangement could be expanded to include other countries.
Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, stressed that the agreement does not “supersede or replace” existing bilateral or multilateral arrangements. Nor, he said, is it linked to nuclear ambitions or an arms race, but rather to building “sustainable capabilities”.
He was equally pointed that the pact was not an escalation between any two states or a threat to any country in the region.
This careful language suggests that the pact is intended less as a military coalition against Iran, Israel or any other specific adversary, than an attempt to build a more durable regional security order based on mutual defence and non-aggression.
That ambition has gained urgency. The Iran conflict has exposed the fragility of the region’s existing security arrangements, while uncertainty over the reliability of external security guarantees has grown. Houthi threats to Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping routes have added another layer of vulnerability.
A new model of mutual defence
Significantly, the Mecca agreement has institutionalised collective deterrence, raising the costs of aggression against any member.
By consolidating their military and economic capabilities, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan troika seeks to create a security shield that makes deterrence a shared rather than national responsibility.
But each member gets the space to join the fray at a time and place of their own choosing, as the mutual defence clause does not specify any automatic, mandatory obligations. Diplomatic support would certainly be there, and maybe weapons or economic help, but putting troops on the ground has not yet been mentioned, and no further details were made available. In this initial stage at least, the Mecca alliance seems to be more of a diplomatic bloc.
Torek Farhadi, a senior geo-economic advisor based in Geneva, told The New Arab that the “sheer fact that these three countries are aligned in their political thinking is by itself a stabilising factor in an otherwise fractured Middle East”.
With Turkey and Pakistan both energy-importing countries, Saudi Arabia provides their economies with important resource security. Turkey being a NATO member, meanwhile, is positively viewed by Western capitals as a “provider of much-needed stability”, Farhadi said.
But it was the maturation of “two bilateral tracks that laid the political and military groundwork necessary for the Joint Defence Agreement signed in Mecca,” Zeynep Gizem Ozpinar, a Turkish foreign policy expert, told The New Arab.
In her opinion, the complementary capacities of the three countries are “Turkey’s defence industry and operational experience, Saudi Arabia’s financial strength and strategic geography, and Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence”.
The Mecca pact has brought together relationships that had previously advanced along separate channels within a shared strategic framework.
Explaining the depth of ties, Ozpinar noted that Turkey’s defence relationship with Pakistan rests on a foundation spanning decades, nourished by a discourse of brotherhood and gradually institutionalised over time.
Ankara’s ties with Riyadh, meanwhile, have undergone a visible process of “normalisation and rapprochement” in recent years. Reciprocal high-level visits, memoranda signed in the defence sector, and a rising volume of trade have all served as concrete indicators of trust-building on the Ankara-Riyadh axis, she said.
Where Saudi-Turkish ties are concerned, Ozpinar said that it was “Riyadh’s pursuit of strategic depth in the face of uncertainties within the regional security environment” that produced “favourable ground that aligns with Turkey’s defence industry capacity”.
Looking ahead, Junaid Javeed, a risk and security management expert, told The New Arab that the Mecca agreement has the potential to alter the strategic equation across a region stretching from the eastern Mediterranean to the northern Indian Ocean.
Comparing the Mecca pact with NATO, Javeed said that the latter has more than just a mutual defence clause. “It is a deeply institutionalised alliance with established command structures, planning mechanisms and decades of operational integration, and the Mecca alliance is not on that level yet,” he told The New Arab.
Assessing the geopolitical impact of this agreement, Javeed said that Iran would “closely watch the agreement’s Gulf and maritime potential” while India would “assess what it means for Pakistan’s strategic capabilities”.
China, he said, will have “an interest in its effect on Gulf stability, while the United States will consider whether the arrangement strengthens or complicates the existing regional security architecture”, Javeed added.
While a political commitment has been created, the real challenge is building the machinery to get “military credibility”.
However, the analyst added that the maritime dimension may prove to be the most practical area for cooperation.
“Naval interoperability, coordinated exercises, and the protection of critical shipping routes could become important components of trilateral ties,” Javeed told The New Arab.
Putting the pact to the test
With collective deterrence a central part of the deal, the first challenge is keeping the Bab al-Mandab and Strait of Hormuz open.
Ever since the US- Israel war on Iran started, Gulf states have been on the receiving end of Iranian attacks. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has also severely restricted their energy shipments, bringing the GCC’s oil industry to a halt.
Due to joint mediation efforts with Pakistan, Turkey, and Egypt, Riyadh emerged from attacks in the Gulf relatively unscathed. But that has now all changed.
A Houthi blockade on Saudi-linked shipping, threats to expand it to the Bab al-Mandab, and attacks on oil assets in the kingdom have forced Riyadh to change its strategy.
So far, Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes and announced a maritime defence coalition to protect shipping routes. Along with Pakistan and Turkey, 14 other countries have joined to play a supporting role, though avoiding direct attacks on the Houthis.
Under the SMDA, Pakistan had already added 8,000 more troops to its permanent unit deployment in the kingdom, along with fighter jets, drones, and air defence systems. And now with the Mecca pact, Ankara, Riyadh, and Islamabad are expected to make a show of strength.
“The most consequential feature of the pact is the collective defence commitment, but it will all depend on what follows the signing,” Javeed told The New Arab.
“A defence commitment on paper is one thing, and turning it into workable planning, interoperability, intelligence coordination, and military capacity is another.”
Nevertheless, with Pakistan’s position on the Arabian Sea, Saudi Arabia’s strategic access to the Gulf and Red Sea, and Turkey’s naval capabilities, the three countries naturally complement each other.
What each country brings
Seeking regional stability rather than getting into unwanted war scenarios, this trilateral accord may remain focused on proactive defence. But if implemented effectively, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan agreement could rebalance the Middle East.
Ostensibly, Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, diplomatic influence, and its central role in Gulf security. Turkey offers one of NATO's most capable militaries alongside a rapidly expanding indigenous defence industry that has emerged as a global exporter of drones, missiles, naval platforms, and armoured vehicles.
Meanwhile, Pakistan provides one of the region's largest and most experienced armed forces, extensive counterterrorism expertise, and the unique status of being the only nuclear-armed Muslim state.
Discussing the implications of the deal for Pakistan, Abdullah Khan, Managing Director at the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies in Islamabad, told The New Arab that the trilateral defence MoU significantly strengthens Pakistan’s strategic standing both in the Gulf and across South Asia.
“The space Pakistan had progressively lost to India in the Middle East is being reclaimed - and in many ways exceeded - through this institutionalised partnership with two major regional powers,” Khan told The New Arab.
The agreement will also have an impact in South Asia, creating “new openings for Pakistan-India dialogue as Saudi Arabia, bound by mutual defence commitments with Pakistan, has no interest in being drawn into a military confrontation involving India”.
Therefore, Arab states may “use their diplomatic influence to encourage New Delhi toward meaningful engagement with Islamabad for regional stability”.
In Javeed’s opinion, Pakistan brings operational experience, military expertise and geography, with its armed forces having decades of experience in conventional operations and counterterrorism, and its location connecting South Asia with the Gulf, Arabian Sea, and the wider Indian Ocean.
Together, these capabilities can create a complementary rather than overlapping security partnership. Turkey’s advanced defence manufacturing complements Pakistan’s production capabilities, while Saudi investment could accelerate joint research, technology transfer and large-scale production.
A regional reset?
More countries will likely join the Mecca alliance, and it is expected to be a more flexible security partnership than a focused military alliance, as the ethos of the grouping is going to remain “collective deterrence”.
In line with Turkey’s defence diplomacy and Pakistan’s customised security deals with regional states, it may turn out to be a win-win situation.
Putting less pressure on the US, which would continue as a main security guarantor, and, hopefully, keeping oil routes open for the GCC, the Mecca alliance may be exactly what the region needs.
The pact could extend beyond these three initial signatories and a wider trend could emerge whereby local states would “seek greater control over their own defence”, Javeed told The New Arab.
But it all depends on whether the pact develops as a sustainable partnership without drifting into “bloc politics” or commitments that partners are unwilling to sustain.
“We may see Egypt joining in the near term, with Kuwait and Qatar potentially following. Overall, this is a defensive, stabilising step that enhances collective deterrence while reinforcing Pakistan’s role as a key security partner in the Muslim world,” Khan told The New Arab.
“For Ankara, the principal gain of the agreement lies in multiplying its strategic options and expanding the scope of its foreign policy,” Ozpinar said.
“Operating within a framework built on the principle of collective deterrence, Turkey is opening new markets for its defence industry exports and positioning itself as one of the founding actors in the emerging security architecture of the Islamic world.”
She noted that this could be regarded as a “natural extension of the multidimensional, multi-vector foreign policy approach Ankara has pursued for some time, and the defence industry dimension constitutes the most tangible aspect of these gains”.
Pakistan’s large military and missile technology further completes this picture.
“As integration deepens among the three countries in areas such as air defence, early warning systems, maritime security, and intelligence sharing, Turkey’s position within the regional defence market will strengthen.”
Sabena Siddiqui is a foreign affairs journalist, lawyer, and geopolitical analyst specialising in modern China, the Belt and Road Initiative, the Middle East, and South Asia

Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg outlines vision for 'personal superintelligence'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:00:35 UTC
00:00:35 KST

Meta has introduced a new model that can run on a personal computer, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg laying out a philosophy for the development and deployment of superintelligence, arguing that the technology should prioritise individual empowerment, invention, and a balance of power rather than centralisation in the hands of a few institutions.
In a detailed statement on Monday, Zuckerberg described the current era as an "incredible moment in history," predicting that within the next few years people will gain access to superintelligence exceeding human capacity.
This, he said, will enable the creation of extraordinary new things, the building of businesses, the expression of ideas, accelerated learning, and advances in health and quality of life.
The defining questions, according to Zuckerberg, are who will control superintelligence and to what ends it will be directed. He contrasted two paths: one in which the technology is centralised and restricted to a limited number of institutions, and another in which it becomes a widely available tool that empowers everyone.
The new model lunched by Meta, Muse Glimmer, is much smaller than leading AI models from rivals and is instead designed for agentic tasks and can run on a Mac or PC with a single graphics card, aiming to tap demand for AI systems that run directly on people's devices.
Open-weight models are typically cheaper than leading models from so-called frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. They also come with publicly accessible core components for easy customisation, unlike closed models that companies keep fully under their control.
Meta's launch comes as the social media giant seeks to strengthen its position after forming a costly, new superintelligence team last year to propel itself back into the high-stakes AI race.
Zuckerberg acknowledged that transformative technologies bring both opportunities and challenges, and that superintelligence’s scale will make those greater than any seen in recent lifetimes.
On job losses
He expressed surprise at the prevalence of "doom" in discussions among some AI developers, questioning why anyone who believes AI will eliminate most jobs and diminish human relevance would accelerate towards that outcome.
"The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes," he said.
Drawing parallels to past technological shifts, Zuckerberg argued that fears of people being left behind have repeatedly given way to broader prosperity, health, and freedom.
He expressed confidence that AI will follow the same pattern if guided by values such as liberty, open inquiry, free enterprise, and equal opportunity.
He emphasised that invention, not mere automation, will be superintelligence’s greatest contribution.
"Early AI could answer questions and do routine work. Soon it will increasingly help discover new knowledge — ranging from discovering new drugs to cure a family member’s disease to finding new ways to improve your business. While the number of questions a person can ask in a day is limited, the number of valuable things superintelligence can invent to help achieve your goals is unlimited," he argued.
Zuckerberg also stressed the need to remain competitive against countries like China, among other issues.
"There are also national interest and national security aspects of development as well. American communities will have greater prosperity and security if America and its allies lead in AI compared to geopolitical rivals. Yet one significant disadvantage that the US has compared to countries like China is that it is more difficult to build infrastructure here," he said.
Rather than allowing a singular superintelligence or a small group of experts to decide what is best for humanity, Zuckerberg advocated distributing the technology so individuals can direct it according to their own goals and values.
"The history of democracy and economics has shown that there is no single objective answer to how people define the best life, and therefore the best approach is letting people decide what matters in their own lives," he stressed.
He compared this approach to the earlier democratisation of supercomputers and the internet. Meta, he said, is actively building towards this vision of personal superintelligence.
Data centre development
The Meta boss also addressed risks including job displacement, local impacts of data centres, cybersecurity and biological misuse, government overreach, and the need for democratic countries to maintain leadership while ensuring humanity retains control.
Amid growing public opposition to data centre development in the US, Zuckerberg added that Meta is launching a fund to directly support communities around its facilities.
He rejected the view that aligning a single superintelligence resolves these issues. Humanity lacks uniform values, he argued, so no single system can align with everyone's competing interests.
Instead, he proposed viewing the challenges through the lens of power balance, similar to democratic institutions.
Widely distributed superintelligence, he said, would enable people and institutions to check one another, producing fairer and more secure outcomes — whether in legal representation, cybersecurity, or economic competition.
“If superintelligence remains concentrated in a few hands — whether individuals, companies, governments, or AI systems themselves — outcomes will favour those few at the expense of others.”
Meta’s focus on personal superintelligence for everyone, Zuckerberg concluded, is intended to tip the balance of power towards individuals and produce a future reflecting the full range of human values and perspectives.
"The arc of human civilization has bent towards putting more power in people’s hands to live and shape the world in the ways we believe are best. Superintelligence holds the promise of giving everyone that power, and building a positive future for everyone," he added.

Wave of US tariff refunds flows back to Chinese firms, buoying profits by millions
Five listed firms, operating mainly in automotive and healthcare sectors, disclosed payouts, as reversal of duties strains US customs revenue
The wave of US tariff refunds is reaching Chinese companies. More than US$38 million in tariff rebates, plus accrued interest, from US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has landed in the bank accounts of five listed Chinese firms since last month, providing a windfall that is expected to bolster their earnings.
The five listed firms primarily operate in the automotive and healthcare sectors. Each secured an average tariff refund of US$7.64 million, representing between 13.12 per cent and 53.58 per cent of their 2025 net profit, according to the companies’ annual reports and filings. The funds were disbursed through accounts held by their US subsidiaries.
The largest payout went to the US subsidiary of Zhejiang-based Huahai Pharmaceutical, which has received more than US$14.2 million in tariff refunds.
The sum is substantial for the drug maker, equivalent to 36.36 per cent of its full-year 2025 net profit. In its exchange filing, the firm noted that the refunds would “impact its profit in the second half of this year”.
Guizhou Tyre, based in southwest China, generated more than 45 per cent of its annual revenue from overseas markets last year. Its core products sold in the US are trailer and off-road tyres.
In an announcement released on Friday, the tyre maker disclosed that its US subsidiary had received more than US$11.98 million in combined tariff refunds and interest, which would be factored into its 2026 financial statements.

FACTBOX - World Lion Day: How many lions remain in the wild?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:59:21 UTC
23:59:21 KST

Once ranging across much of Africa, Europe, the Middle East and southwestern Asia, wild lions are now largely confined to fragmented populations in sub-Saharan Africa and a single population in western India.
World Lion Day, observed annually on Aug. 10, draws attention to the decline of one of the planet’s most recognizable predators and the conservation efforts that have produced sharply different results across its remaining range.
Determining exactly how many lions remain is difficult. Unlike India, which conducts a coordinated count of its Asiatic lions, Africa has no single continentwide census.
Estimates combine camera-trap surveys, sightings, tracking data, population models and expert assessments from different countries and years. Some figures include cubs, while others count only adults and older juvenile lions, meaning national totals cannot always be compared directly.
Here is the state of the world’s remaining wild lions in numbers:
The Lion Recovery Fund estimates that about 23,000 wild lions remain in Africa, based on information compiled by the IUCN Cat Specialist Group’s African Lion Database.
The IUCN Cat Specialist Group estimated the African population at between 22,000 and 25,000 adult and subadult lions in 2025.
The group stresses that lion numbers remain uncertain because only a small proportion of their range has been systematically surveyed.
Earlier assessments estimated that Africa had about 35,000 lions in 2013. Differences in survey coverage and methodology mean the figure cannot be directly compared with the latest estimate, but long-term evidence points to a significant overall decline.
Lions occupied an estimated 566,675 square kilometers (218,795 square miles) in 2025, equivalent to just 6.13% of their historical range, according to the IUCN Cat Specialist Group.
They have disappeared from at least 16 African countries, including Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, Eritrea, Gambia, Lesotho and Sierra Leone, and may be extinct in several others.
Outside Africa, wild lions survive only in the Indian state of Gujarat.
Lions disappeared from Europe in ancient times and were gradually lost from North Africa, the Middle East and most of Asia between the 19th and mid-20th centuries. Türkiye’s last lions are believed to have disappeared in the late 1800s.
Tanzania is widely regarded as home to the world’s largest national population of wild lions, with conservation organizations estimating that around 8,000 remain in the East African country.
Other major populations are found in southern and eastern Africa.
South Africa has an estimated 3,490 free-roaming lions, including animals in transfrontier conservation areas, according to the South African National Biodiversity Institute. The country’s populations are considered stable or increasing in major reserves, although many live in fenced and intensively managed areas.
Botswana’s lion population is estimated at around 2,800, while Kenya’s 2021 national wildlife census counted 2,589.
Significant populations also survive in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Namibia, including in ecosystems extending across national borders.
West and Central Africa remain the regions of greatest concern. The largest West African population is estimated at only about 187 lions in the W-Arly-Pendjari complex spanning Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger.
India’s Asiatic lion population increased to 891 in 2025, up from 674 in 2020, according to the Gujarat government.
The rise to 217 animals represents an increase of about 32% in five years.
The recovery is even more striking over the longer term. Only about a dozen lions were believed to remain in Gujarat’s Gir forests in the late 19th century following widespread hunting and habitat loss.
Conservation measures helped the population recover steadily, but all remaining Asiatic lions are still confined to Gujarat’s Greater Gir landscape. Their concentration in one region leaves them vulnerable to disease outbreaks, extreme weather and other large-scale disasters.
As the population expands beyond protected areas, encounters with people, livestock, roads and settlements are also increasing.
The IUCN Cat Specialist Group estimates that the lion’s occupied range contracted by 34% between 2004 and 2025, a period spanning approximately three lion generations.
It suspects the species’ population declined by a similar proportion during the same period, with the heaviest losses occurring in West and Central Africa.
The picture, however, is not uniformly negative.
In Senegal’s Niokolo-Koba National Park, the lion population has recovered from fewer than 10 animals to nearly 40 following increased protection and conservation work.
Lions have also been successfully reintroduced in protected areas in Rwanda, Malawi and Zambia.
Botswana provides an example of movement in the opposite direction, with its estimated population declining by about 20% from approximately 3,500 in 2015 to 2,800.
All living lions belong to the species Panthera leo, which is classified as “Vulnerable” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List.
Scientists recognize two subspecies.
Panthera leo leo, which includes the Asiatic lion and populations in West and Central Africa, is classified as “Endangered.”
Panthera leo melanochaita, covering populations in eastern and southern Africa, is classified as “Vulnerable.”
The lion has also been assessed as “Largely Depleted” under the IUCN Green Status of Species, which measures how far a species is from fully recovering across its historical range.
Habitat loss and fragmentation remain among the greatest threats as farmland, settlements, roads and other infrastructure expand into lion territory.
The decline of wild prey through poaching and the bushmeat trade can force lions to attack livestock, increasing conflict with farmers and leading to retaliatory killings through shooting, spearing or poisoning.
Lions are also caught and killed in wire snares set for other animals.
Other threats include targeted poaching for body parts, poorly monitored or unsustainable trophy hunting in some areas, disease, civil unrest and armed conflict that make protected areas harder to manage.
Conservation groups say the survival of lions will depend not only on protected areas but also on securing wildlife corridors, restoring prey populations and helping communities protect their livestock while benefiting economically from living alongside the predators.

Al Jazeera reporter on the ground as Colombia quake death toll rises
At least 132 people have been killed and hundreds remain missing after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia, the most powerful to hit the country this century, according to the Colombian Geological Service.
The earthquake on Monday ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Cali, Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama.

The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar in the Choco region, about 400km (250 miles) west of the capital, Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. The quake struck at a depth of 107km (66 miles).
At least 21 aftershocks followed within hours.
In Cali, the country’s third-largest city, search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. Local officials said at least 20 buildings crumbled, while 380 were damaged, trapping many people.
Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, told The Associated Press news agency that he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed.
“My entire house shook. I’ve never lived through such a powerful earthquake,” he said. “We’re thanking God we’re alive.”
Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television that the collapse of one building “sounded like a bomb”, as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali.
“All of us neighbours are working together, forming human chains. We need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped.”
State of emergency
The earthquake struck just days after Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as president, thrusting the new administration into its first major crisis, with memories still fresh of devastating twin earthquakes in neighbouring Venezuela in June.
“The national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed,” he said in a national address at about 1pm local time (18:00 GMT), upon declaring a national state of emergency.
“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”
De la Espriella said preliminary reports indicated 111 dead and 87 injured, along with dozens of collapsed buildings and damaged homes. The Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a think tank, said at least 132 people were killed and 570 others injured.
Local authorities said at least 40 people died in the Risaralda region, part of Colombia’s coffee-growing area. Pereira, the region’s capital, suffered extensive damage, with rescue workers continuing to search collapsed buildings for survivors.
At least 27 people died in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children.
Reports from Choco, near the epicentre, were slowed by communications outages, with some areas still lacking mobile phone service hours after the earthquake. Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said 12 people had been killed and 84 injured in the largely rural area.
Luis Gregorio Moreno, a community leader in the region’s capital, Quibdo, told the AFP news agency that many people were missing.
“We are all devastated,” he said. “At this moment, there are reported deaths, dozens of wounded, but what there are most of are missing people.”
Hundreds missing
By Monday afternoon, people had begun reporting their loved ones missing on digital databases, one of which had more than 1,400 people, mostly in Cali and Pereira, with the number steadily climbing.
In Pereira, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport’s ceiling falling on travellers, who were taking shelter and screaming. The footage also showed a four-storey building crumbling.
Pereira’s mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped.
In nearby Manizales, footage showed one of the side towers of the city’s landmark neo-Gothic cathedral collapsing and scattering debris onto nearby streets.
The civil aviation authority suspended operations at several airports in Colombia’s west, including Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura, while engineers carried out structural inspections.
Low-intensity earthquakes, or tremors, are common in Colombia, which sits along the seismically active Pacific Ring of Fire, but those above magnitude 6 are rare. In 1999, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people.
The Colombian Geological Service said Monday’s earthquake was the country’s strongest recorded “in the 21st century”.
Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the earthquake’s magnitude, inland location and strike-slip motion may have amplified damage in populated valleys despite its considerable depth.
“This one was far below the crust, and in theory, it shouldn’t cause as much shaking. At this magnitude, it did actually cause a lot of shaking,” she told the Reuters news agency.
Countries pledge help
On Monday night, the US Department of State announced it would provide $15.5m for emergency shelter, food and other earthquake response aid.
Washington is “closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia”, Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X.
Governments across Latin America also lined up to help.
El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum – whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela following its recent crisis – offered help to Colombia.
“From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary,” Bukele said.
President Jose Antonio Kast said Chile, one of the region’s most earthquake-prone countries, “knows the pain and the challenge left by earthquakes” and pledged help.
Israel, Ecuador and France also offered assistance.

Colombia: Several killed after large earthquake rocks region
Unknown

2026-08-10

Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026
A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.
Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.
Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.
The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.
The government has declared a state of emergency.
What is the latest?
Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.
He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.
"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.
"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."
What's happening on the ground?
The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.
"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."
Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.
Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.
The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.
And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.
Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.
"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.
What do we know about the quake's size and location?
The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.
The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.
The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.
The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.
The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.
Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.
USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.
The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Russian publisher blacks out mention of Stalin and Hitler in book by Nobel laureate Günter Grass
Users of the Russian marketplace Ozon have complained about censorship in The Rat, a novel by German writer and Nobel Prize in Literature laureate Günter Grass. The independent Russian news outlet Verstka first reported on the complaints.
The original text includes the phrase “until a certain Hitler and a certain Stalin devoured all of Poland,” a reference to the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the 1939 agreement that led to Poland’s division between Germany and the Soviet Union.
A video posted by one user shows the phrase “a certain Hitler and a certain Stalin” blacked out in the 2026 Russian edition, which includes a footnote reading, “This fragment of text has been removed in accordance with the requirements of the legislation of the Russian Federation.”
The censorship appears in both the print and digital editions. Meduza found no other examples of hidden text, and none are mentioned in the footnotes.
Buyers have complained in the comments that the publisher never warned them about the censorship. But the “Questions About the Product” section includes a January response from Alpina Publisher stating that “some fragments of the book were blacked out in agreement with the rights holders.”
Günter Grass was one of the most important German writers of the 20th century. He gained worldwide recognition with his debut novel, The Tin Drum, published in 1959. Along with Cat and Mouse (1961) and Dog Years (1963), the novel later formed part of the Danzig Trilogy. Grass won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1999. He died in 2015.
His apocalyptic novel The Rat, built around a dialogue between the narrator and a rat, was published in 1986 and had never before appeared in Russian.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

Russia is seeking to nearly triple the number of ballistic missiles it can launch simultaneously against Ukraine, the commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said.
Maj. Robert “Madyar” Brovdi said Russia’s military can currently fire a simultaneous salvo of 77 ballistic missiles and plans to increase that capability to 200, according to an interview with The Associated Press (AP).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He did not provide a timeline for when Russia could achieve that capacity.
Brovdi described the potential expansion as one of Ukraine’s most vulnerable points because the country is running short of interceptor missiles for US-made Patriot systems, the only air-defense system in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of intercepting ballistic missiles.
The shortage means that dozens of ballistic missiles launched by Russia during massive attacks can penetrate Ukraine’s defenses and reach their targets, according to AP.
“Even if they only manage half of that, it will all be flying at us,” Brovdi added.
He said there was only one way to reduce the number of missiles Russia could launch: strike every facility involved in their production.
His comments underscored the importance of Ukraine’s long-range strikes against missile plants and other military-industrial facilities deep inside Russia.
Brovdi also warned that Russia was expanding its use of jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are substantially faster than conventional propeller-driven models and more difficult to intercept.
Zelensky in Belgrade: Vučić Refused to Let Serbia Foot Putin’s Bill
He said the concentration of jet-powered Shaheds had increased 2.5 times in recent weeks.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces have intensified attacks on Russian military, logistics, and energy infrastructure, including targets in Russian-occupied Crimea.
Brovdi told AP that Ukraine could conduct seven times as many strikes in Crimea if funding promised by Western partners arrived more quickly. He said his forces had received only 14% of the funding required to conduct the campaign at full capacity.
Ukrainian manufacturers have the capacity to produce the necessary drones, but delays in financing have restricted production, he said.
Brovdi described Crimea as a key target because Russia uses the occupied peninsula to support its military operations against Ukraine.
Russia has increasingly used ballistic missiles in large-scale attacks designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
During an overnight assault on Kyiv and the surrounding region on Aug. 5, Russia launched 24 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, four Zircon or Oniks missiles, and 115 attack drones, according to Ukraine’s Air Force.
Warehouses, logistics facilities, businesses, residential buildings, and a railway station were among the sites damaged.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on Ukraine’s partners to accelerate deliveries of Patriot systems and interceptor missiles, warning that delays leave Ukrainian cities exposed to Russian ballistic attacks.

OnlyFans model sentenced to just six years for fatally stabbing her boyfriend in Miami condo
Courtney Clenney pleaded guilty to manslaughter for the April 2022 fatal stabbing of her boyfriend, Christian Obumseli
- Bookmark
OnlyFans model Courtney Clenney, who pleaded guilty to manslaughter for the fatal stabbing of her boyfriend in their Miami condo, was sentenced to just six years in prison.
Clenney, 30, who had been behind bars since April 2022, pleaded guilty to manslaughter Monday, receiving a six-year sentence and five years of probation following the 2022 killing of 27-year-old Christian Obumseli.
The former OnlyFans model, who was known online as Courtney Tailor, received credit for time served. She had been jailed in Miami since 2022 on a second-degree murder charge. That means she will only serve two more years behind bars before being released.
Clenney became emotional and was seen wiping away her tears while listening to a victim’s statement written by Obumseli’s mother, who described her son’s death as “the darkest day” of her life.
“No sentence, no plea, can bring back my son to me,” a family spokesperson said on behalf of Obumseli’s mother.
“Since April 4, I have lived with fear, anxiety, sleepless nights, heartache and more tears than I can count,” she said. “There was a joy in my life and my family’s life that has never completely returned.”
Police were called to a luxury Miami apartment on April 3, 2022, after an altercation between the couple, who were in an on-and-off relationship.
Authorities found Obumseli with a single stab wound to the torso, while body camera footage showed Clenney covered in his blood.
Clenney told investigators that Obumseli pushed her and that she threw a knife at him from about 10 feet away. A medical examiner determined the knife wound to Obumseli’s chest was about three inches deep.
The model’s attorneys argued that she acted in self-defense, claiming Obumseli was abusive and that he grabbed her by the throat before she stabbed him. They said Clenney was a victim of domestic violence, which Obumseli's family strongly disputed, claiming he was the one who suffered abuse in their turbulent, on-and-off relationship.
While on the outside, Clenney and Obumseli appeared to be in love and living a lavish lifestyle, prosecutors described their relationship as “tempestuous and combative,” saying the fatal stabbing came after a history of conflict between the two.
Following Obumseli’s death, videos emerged showing the turbulent side to their relationship. In one clip, Clenney was seen hitting Obumseli in an elevator, while in another, she was seen repeatedly slapping him.
The videos were just some of the evidence prosecutors planned to use as evidence to prove their case at trial, before the plea deal.
Meanwhile, Clenney claimed in recently filed court documents intended to be used in trial that Obumseli abused her at least nine times before his death, including allegations that he punched her and fractured her ribs, according to the New York Post.
Her trial was scheduled to begin this year, but repeated delays pushed the case back as attorneys continued battling over evidence, legal motions and courtroom issues. Repeated attempts for her release on bond were also unsuccessful.
In a statement Monday, Miami-Dade State Attorney Katherine Fernandez Rundle said that with the plea deal, Obumseli’s family “finally heard what they long sought: Courtney Clenney accepting full responsibilty for his death.”
“This plea was reached in full consultation and approval of Christian’s family,” Fernandez Rundle said. “The Assistant State Attorneys handling this case have remained focused on the core evidence that Clenney stabbed Christian Obumseli as part of a pattern of escalating violence toward him. While nothing can heal the wounds caused on that day in April, I hope today’s guilty plea brings his family a measure of justice too long denied.”

Student loans should be taught in school maths lessons, Ucas boss says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:55:37 BST
23:55:37 KST

Student loans should be taught in school maths lessons, Ucas boss says
Calls for student loan finance to feature on GCSE maths curriculum after recent backlash over system
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Student loan finance should be added to the maths curriculum at secondary schools, according to the head of the university admissions service.
Backlash over student loans has simmered in recent months - particularly regarding plan two student loans, which have left some graduates with snowballing debts despite years of making repayments.
Interest on plan two loans, taken out between 1 September 2012 and 31 July 2023 in England, is charged at the rate of Retail Prices Index (RPI) inflation, plus up to 3 per cent extra depending on income.
Repayments start when graduates earn a salary of £29,385 and the interest rate means that many people see the balance of their loan rise significantly, despite making regular repayments.
As such, the Labour government has faced calls to reverse the freeze on the threshold at which repayments start.
Dr Jo Saxton, chief executive of the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas), said pupils should be taught how the loans work before they arrive at university, telling The Times that many young people understand the concept but they struggle to calculate repayments.
She said: “As somebody who used to work with schools and has done a lot on qualifications, it made me think this should be in the national curriculum.
“It should actually be in GCSE maths as a real example. Because the concepts of percentage and compound interest and all of those things are taught.
“But giving the applied example - given that we’re in a position where just under half of young people are proceeding to university - I think it should be in there.”
Dr Saxton also said that 90 per cent of incoming university students intended to work alongside their studies, which has risen sharply in recent years.
This has a big impact on whether students live at home or move away for university, with some not wanting to give up their part-time jobs.
“They don’t want to go too far. Often students start a part-time job in sixth form and they know that it’s difficult to get jobs,” she said.
“Once they’ve got them, they’re reluctant to give them up so they will study somewhere where they can come back at weekends or it might be part of what’s contributing to the growth in the live at home students.”
Last month, education secretary Lucy Powell said the “egregious” student loans system “needs looking at” amid concerns over costs for graduates.
She told BBC Radio 5 Live: “The Government has committed to a review of that.
“It is… very much at the top of my in-tray as the secretary of state.
“And, you know, I want to make sure that we look at this so that it’s fair for students. And it’s a real cost-of-living issue for young people because there’s about a 10-year sort of timeframe for people on this plan two as well.
“So, they’re paying high repayments and never, ever paying off the capital of their student loan.”
Asked whether it was something she would deal with, Ms Powell said: “I can’t make any promises, but, you know, it needs looking at.”
At the last budget, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves caused a furore when she froze the repayment threshold at £29,385 for three years from 2027, leaving graduates worse off than if it had risen with inflation.
Above that level, graduates pay back nine per cent of everything they earn.
When they were first created in 2010, the plan two loan threshold was meant to be uprated with inflation each year, but it has been frozen on several occasions since 2016.
