Europe is running out of Patriot missiles as Ukraine braces for Russia’s winter attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:54:52 UTC
23:54:52 KST

BERLIN — Europe is scrambling for more Patriot interceptors to donate to an increasingly desperate Ukraine, which is racing to reinforce its ballistic missile defenses before Russia’s expected winter assault.
Kyiv is seeking hundreds of interceptors, but new production will come too late, the war with Iran has strained U.S. supplies, and several of Ukraine’s leading European backers say they have few left that they can safely donate.
“Over the last few months, Russia fires more missiles a week at us than we get from partners over months," former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said last week. In July, Ukrainian air defense intercepted only 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, with another 40 failing to reach their targets, Ukraine's defense ministry said.
Advertisement
Germany, one of Ukraine’s top military aid donors, has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. But Berlin must now balance Kyiv’s increasingly urgent needs against the minimum stocks required to protect Germany and meet its NATO commitments. Other European countries are also weighing whether to hang on to their interceptors or give them to Ukraine.
“We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defense ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin shortly after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.”
Berlin and other Northern European capitals have urged counterparts elsewhere on the continent to examine what more military equipment and financial support they could release.
“I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.”
That's putting pressure on countries with stocks of Patriot interceptors like Poland, Spain and Greece. The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, which are among Ukraine’s few effective defenses against fast-moving Russian ballistic weapons.
Ukraine can use other, often cheaper, air-defense systems against drones and cruise missiles. The country is racing to develop its homegrown Freyja interceptor, but the anti-ballistic system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can fill that role.
Advertisement
Until Freyja is ready, Ukraine needs an immediate answer to Russia’s ballistic missiles. “One of the priority directions is Patriot — PAC-3 or PAC-2,” Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told POLITICO. “The first [solution] is buying, or receiving from stockpiles, PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors.”
Stuck in Washington
The Patriot dependence makes U.S. President Donald Trump essential to Kyiv: Most PAC-3 interceptors are produced in America, which means their sale and any production deals are subject to White House decisions.
During Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's meeting with Trump last month, “The main topic was Patriot interceptors,” according to a senior official familiar with the talks.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump speak on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 8, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
Trump raised hopes at the Ankara summit when he said Ukraine would be allowed to produce U.S.-designed Patriot interceptors under license — a step that could eventually reduce Kyiv’s dependence on scarce American deliveries.
U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker made clear that production would not solve the immediate shortage.
“A long-term production agreement will not be concluded before this winter,” he told Fox Business, and manufacturing the first missiles would take longer still.
Advertisement
But Trump has now walked that back, last week saying: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."
Following a Reuters report that the U.S. had almost exhausted its missile stocks thanks to the war against Iran, Trump is now focusing on rebuilding U.S. supplies. Asked on Thursday about Zelenskyy’s calls for more Patriot missiles, he said: “We want missiles too.”
Ukraine has also signed a deal to get PAC-2 interceptors being made in Germany, but they are unlikely to arrive before next year.
Faced with a shortage of interceptors, Kyiv is now looking at a more aggressive campaign to hit Russian launchers.
"The Russians must understand that a few minutes after the launch, the entire team that launches the rocket must die from our ballistic missile," Fedorov said.
Europe’s unbalanced effort
That puts the immediate burden on Europe, where allies are once again searching their own arsenals — and one another’s — for interceptors that could reach Ukraine before winter.
Advertisement
Germany supplied three Patriot systems from its own military stocks and subsequently arranged two more through a deal under which the U.S. would replenish the Bundeswehr. The Netherlands assembled the components for another complete system, including five launchers, a radar and missiles.
But with stocks now stretched thin, governments face limits of their own.
Warsaw confirmed in July that it had released several PAC-3 interceptors after requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior U.S. commanders. Polish outlet Defence24 reported that just five missiles were transferred.
Mark Rutte speaks at a press conference ahead of a NATO summit in Ankara on July 6, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images
Even that triggered a political backlash. Opposition lawmakers accused the government of weakening the country’s defenses at a time when Russian missiles and drones have repeatedly strayed across its border.
Countries closer to Russia are now becoming less likely to give up existing Patriots because their armed forces already regarded their air defenses as insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic contacts.
That is shifting attention toward Southern European countries, which have contributed less to Ukraine than Germany and many Northern European donors.
Advertisement
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez confirmed in 2024 that Madrid was sending missiles to Ukraine, but the government has not disclosed their type or amount.
Spain's defense ministry did not respond to a question from POLITICO whether it had recently been approached for more interceptors or was considering another transfer. It instead pointed to Spain’s wider military support for Ukraine and its NATO commitments.
Greece — which traditionally sees fellow NATO member Turkey as its greatest security threat — has not announced any Patriot transfers to Ukraine. Greek media reported in July that Ukraine had requested as many as 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens.
The Greek defense ministry did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.
Prying open Europe’s arsenals
This isn’t the first time European allies have had to cobble together Patriot missile deliveries from their own limited stocks.
At a February meeting, Ukraine's Fedorov said he and Rutte worked through a list of interceptors held by European allies, asking governments for whatever they could spare.
Advertisement
“Dear defense minister of Poland, can you give us five?” Fedorov recalled in this week's interview.
Berlin offered to top up the effort. “If you get 20 out of all the countries, I'll give you an extra five,” Fedorov quoted German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius as saying. “That’s the exercise we had to perform to get more than 20. And it is a hard mission.”
Kyiv is continuing those types of talks with its allies.
“Of course, Ukrainian diplomats have been working with Spain, Greece and everyone in the world who has [PACs],” said the senior official familiar with the talks. “Everything depends on the U.S., and the lack of political will to help influences everyone else.”
“The American administration could have helped, but they don’t do this. And as the result it’s been hard with everyone else,” they added.
For Kyiv, the arguments over allied stockpiles are unfolding against a ticking clock. With demand for PAC-3 interceptors surging in the Middle East, the Pentagon replenishing its own stock and many European countries worrying about their own ability to fend off a future Russian attack, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was struggling to buy, exchange or secure any available rounds.
“We are literally fighting for every missile,” Sybiha said.

Israel cuts funding for local LGBTQ programs, putting them at risk of closure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:53:32 UTC
23:53:32 KST

The Social Equality Ministry has cut funding for LGBTQ programs in 20 local authorities. Under the new funding arrangement, each local authority will receive a uniform annual budget of 150,000 shekels (about $50,000).
The budgets of Be'er Sheva, Haifa, Rishon Letzion, Ramat Gan and Rehovot will be cut by more than 90 percent, while those of other local authorities will be cut by 53 percent. Local officials said the cuts would effectively bring activities to an end, including support groups, workshops and assistance in accessing rights.
About 100 local authorities participate in the ministry's program, which is intended for people aged 18 and over and seeks to strengthen LGBTQ people's sense of belonging, particularly in areas where the LGBTQ community is small or not well established. Former minister Meirav Cohen (Yesh Atid) launched the program in 2022. It provides community activities and services tailored to LGBTQ people, including classes, workshops, assistance in accessing rights, professional training, therapy groups, guidance for LGBTQ parents and social groups aimed at reducing loneliness.
Until now, funding was determined by the size of the local authority. Those classified as very large received about 760,000 shekels (about $253,000), large authorities received about 470,000 shekels (about $156,000), and medium-sized authorities received about 210,000 shekels (about $70,000). Small local authorities already received about 150,000 shekels and therefore will not be affected by the cuts. The previous budgets covered eight months, while the new agreements cover a full year, further reducing the amount available each month.
The ministry, which is headed by Minister for Social Equality and the Advancement of the Status of Women of Israel, May Golan, says the 150,000-shekel limit is due to its lack of a director general. Local authorities joined the program at different times, so their agreements also expire at different times. Agreements worth more than 150,000 shekels require the approval of a ministry committee chaired by the director general, a position that has been vacant since December 2025.
The Finance Ministry, however, told Haaretz that the lack of a director general did not make the cuts necessary. It said the Social Equality Ministry could apply to the Higher Exemption Committee, which is authorized to consider exceptional requests, and seek approval for agreements exceeding 150,000 shekels.
No community Shabbat gatherings
The reduced funding leaves little money for the programs themselves. More than 110,000 shekels (about $37,000) of each local authority's annual allocation is expected to go toward the salaries of program coordinators, who are essential to running the programs. If coordinators are not employed, the authorities will have to pay external providers, which would in any case consume a significant portion of the budget.
In previous years, for example, the Be'er Sheva municipality transferred about 200,000 shekels (about $67,000) to Pride House, the city's LGBTQ center. The center used the full amount to run support and social groups, including groups for parents, bisexual people and Russian- and English-speakers. This year, the municipality will be able to transfer only about 12,000 shekels (about $4,000) to the center. The groups are still meeting for now, but planned activities have been canceled since June, including a conference for school counselors organized in cooperation with LGBTQ organizations, creative events and community Shabbat gatherings.
"I have no way to fund anything," said Avishag Tabib, director of Be'er Sheva Pride House. "It looks like a calculated move. I don't know why May Golan has decided to target the LGBTQ community. Maybe it's to curry favor with hate groups."
The Haifa Municipality contacted the Social Equality Ministry and Golan, warning that the new funding framework could effectively bring the program's activities in the city to a halt.
"The budget for activities will effectively run out within two weeks to a month," Mayor Yona Yahav wrote. "Ending this funding will lead to the cancellation of significant programs that affect the lives of thousands of residents of Haifa and northern Israel."
Yahav added that "the Haifa municipality has provided life-saving services, including groups that foster a sense of belonging and combat loneliness, assistance and guidance in accessing rights, professional development, and tools to help people transition to independent living."
The LGBTQ Union in Local Authorities also contacted the ministry. "In medium-sized local authorities, the budget will be enough for about six months of activity. In large authorities, it will last one month, and in the largest ones, just two weeks," warned Elisha Golani, chairman of the union's executive committee. "We can't wait for future exemption committees. Without funding for activities, the program will effectively cease to exist."
The ministry did not respond to either letter.
"This is the first time a government body has entered this field and worked directly through the local authorities," said an LGBTQ program director in northern Israel. "The initiative allows LGBTQ people to receive social, cultural and therapeutic services where they live, without feeling that they have to move to Tel Aviv when they turn 18."
"When you see Pride flags in the Valley of Springs in northern Israel, the Eilot region [Israel's southernmost regional council] or Arad, that is entirely a result of this program," he said. "It shifts the center of gravity of the LGBTQ community."
Another program director said the services reach people from a wide range of backgrounds. "We see people from a wide range of groups, including elderly people who have no one, people who have left prostitution and Arab LGBTQ people."
Last year, Kan 11 reported that the Social Equality Ministry had asked LGBTQ program directors in local authorities not to use the ministry's logo in their activities. The ministry denied issuing any such instruction.
In September, Omer Ohana, the partner of Maj. Sagi Golan, who was killed in the October 7 attack, told the Knesset that he had been promised funding for an LGBTQ project established in his partner's memory, but that the money was never transferred. Ohana said that after working on the project for months, he was told that its activities were "not sufficiently value-based" and were "activities for leftists."
The Social Equality Ministry said in response: "Throughout her term, the minister for social equality and the advancement of women has worked to maintain the division's operations, despite significant budget cuts across the ministry and the budgetary constraints imposed as a result of the war."
The ministry said the claim that it had failed to approach the Higher Exemption Committee "is not based on facts and reflects an incorrect interpretation of the legal and administrative situation. The ministry acts, and has at all times acted, in accordance with the law, including the framework of powers and procedures by which it is bound."
The Finance Ministry said: "There is no fundamental obstacle to approving an agreement worth more than 150,000 shekels even when there is no serving director general. In such a situation, the ministry can apply to the Finance Ministry's Higher Exemption Committee, which is authorized to consider requests that exceed the authority of the ministry's own exemption committee. Therefore, the decision not to apply to this committee was made by the Social Equality Ministry and does not stem from any restriction imposed by the Finance Ministry."

Jerusalem cafe becomes flashpoint in growing haredi protests over Shabbat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:53:23 UTC
23:53:23 KST

By mid-morning on Saturday, the alleys surrounding Cafe Basimta were filled with haredi Orthodox demonstrators protesting the cafe’s decision to open on Shabbat.
It was the sixth consecutive Shabbat that the small cafe off Agrippas Street had faced demonstrations, with no sign of change.
Israeli police were out in full force after demonstrators broke through the barricades last weekend.
Shabbat cafe becomes flashpoint in Jerusalem tensions
Close to 100 restaurants, bars and coffee shops in Jerusalem open on Shabbat, according to Laura Wharton, a Jerusalem city council member from the Democrats party who founded Shabus, a cooperative that runs buses on Shabbat. Only one, Basimta, has drawn a crowd.
Basimta, which opened at the end of May, is new, Wharton said, whereas the others have been open for decades. The cafe sits near what she called the undeclared border between the city’s haredi neighborhoods and the rest of the city.
Agrippas Street runs along the Mahane Yehuda market, where almost every business closes for Shabbat. The cafe also opened its doors during the period when haredi yeshivas are on break, so teenagers who make up the bulk of the protestors have more free time to demonstrate.
“There have been weeks when the average age was probably about 16 there,” Wharton said..
The cafe is not only a flashpoint in the long-running fight between secular and religious Israelis over the character of the holy city. It has become the most visible front in a hot summer of protests and riots across Jerusalem, over a light rail line and extending forced army conscription to yeshiva students, both opposed by the Haredi community.
Haredi protests extend beyond Shabbat observance
For six years, hardline haredi demonstrators who say the light rail was planned without accounting for the community’s sensibilities have fought construction through Bar-Ilan Street, a haredi thoroughfare, breaking into work sites and pulling down fencing. The vandalism and delays have cost an estimated 400 million shekels.
The light rail project is going ahead despite years of obstruction, Wharton said, and Saturday is the one day there is no work at the site to disrupt, freeing up protesters to target the cafe.
Nationally, 44% of Israeli Jews identify as secular and 16% as haredi, according to figures provided to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency by the Jerusalem Institute for Policy Research. That breakdown is vastly different in Jerusalem, where among the city’s Jewish residents, 46% identify as haredi and 25% as religious-Zionist, while 13% identify as secular, according to the institute.
That arithmetic, which speaks to the struggle over the city’s identity, is what non-haredi Jerusalemites say is really at stake in an alley off Agrippas Street.
Avi Dabush, a rabbi who directs Rabbis for Human Rights and is running for the Knesset as part of the left-wing Democrats party, said the cafe was symbolic of the larger national issue.
“It’s kind of an example for the battle that we are doing about the identity of Israel right now,” said Dabush, who was raised in the religious-Zionist school system. He was there on Saturday along with Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats party, for whom the cafe has become an issue ahead of the Oct. 27 election.
“We are in the midst of elections,” Dabush said. “So it’s part of it.”
Confrontations grow increasingly aggressive
Outside Cafe Basimta Saturday, demonstrators took turns screaming at each other in the alleys. The haredi teens, dressed in their black Shabbat best, yelled “One who desecrates the Sabbath, his sentence is death,” a verse from Exodus. They also shouted “stop destroying Jerusalem,” while at other times they gathered in circles to sing Shabbat hymns.
Secular Israelis shot back with a slew of chants, of which “enlist!” appeared to be the most popular. They also shouted, “Only cowards send children,” and carried signs reading “Haredim for our coffee,” a play on a Hebrew word that means both ultra-Orthodox and devoted.
Haredi children followed and tried to defend older members of the community during altercations. Lior Leon, a Jerusalem tour guide, blamed the adults. “The problem is not the kids; they push them,” he said.
The confrontations have grown more aggressive since the protests began in early July. Before dawn on July 25, someone threw a bag of feces at the entrance, and on Thursday, Israel Police announced the arrest of a 15-year-old boy.
On Saturday, the JTA reporter at the scene was spat on by a demonstrator, as were other journalists, and Orthodox residents of the buildings lining the alley threw bags of water down at counter-demonstrators until police shouted a warning that they would be arrested.
Israel Police said in a written statement to JTA that officers acted where they identified people “attempting to instigate violence or disrupt public order.”
Dispute over Basimta’s Shabbat opening
Cafes and restaurants are granted an exemption from the city’s prohibition on businesses opening on the Shabbat. Yohanan Weitzman, a Jerusalem city council member from the haredi Agudat Yisrael faction, told JTA that there was an unwritten status quo governing which businesses and cafes open in the city, which Basimta had violated. It “is not the desire of either party, but it is a necessary compromise to prevent conflicts,” Weitzman said.
There has been widespread violation of those agreements and a failure to enforce municipal bylaws, he said. Opening the cafe was “the straw that broke the camel’s back.”
The protests are organized by the Committee for the Sanctity of Jerusalem, which acts for the Edah HaChareidis, the anti-Zionist body that includes some of the city’s most militant Hasidic groups. Demonstrators are summoned by pashkevilim, the broadsheet notices pasted on walls in haredi neighborhoods with the time and place of each week’s protest.
Haredi groups who are more involved in Israeli society have been unsettled by the protests. “I am strongly opposed to any kind of violence,” Eliezer Rauchberger, the deputy mayor who heads Jerusalem’s Degel HaTorah faction, the Lithuanian stream that sits in Mayor Moshe Lion’s coalition, said in a written statement. Asked which haredi groups were organizing the protests and which rabbis stood behind them, he declined to answer.
One haredi demonstrator, who asked to be identified only by his first name, Avraham, told JTA the protests would not stop until the cafe closes. “We want it gone,” he said. “It is desecrating our Sabbath.”
Wharton said a Supreme Court ruling exempts entertainment, food service and sports from the city’s Shabbat closures, which is why three of Jerusalem’s four cinemas and its municipal swimming pools operate on Saturday. Basimta, she said, is running legally.
The cafe’s ownership by a sect of Jews who have embraced Christian beliefs has also stirred some opposition. Or LeAchim, an anti-missionary organization, told JTA it is pursuing municipal channels to have Basimta shut, arguing it lacks a valid business license. Wharton said the only substantive complaint concerned tables and chairs placed outside without a permit, and that the furniture has since been brought inside.
Yoel Ben David, who runs the cafe, told JTA in July that the municipality and police had been “incredibly supportive,” and that city officials asked him to bring the tables in as a compromise, which he accepted.
Wharton said the effort to shut the cafe had backfired. Basimta has been doing record business, boasting lines of customers from the moment it opens until it closes.
Ben David is a member of the Jews for Jesus community, which owns and operates the cafe, as JTA reported last month. The revelation cost him support from some Israeli institutions, but it has not thinned the crowds, and demonstrators told JTA it is not what they care about.
For Liora Bamberger, who lives in one of the high-rise buildings encircling the Basimta courtyard, the fight has taken away the one quiet morning of her week.
“The only day in the week that we have a little bit of quiet,” she said, before pausing. “Not anymore.”
Bamberger, who observes Shabbat, said the cafe should be allowed to open and that she did not expect this to end well. “When you have extremism, it’s not gonna end,” she said. “It’s gonna be a boom.”
Asked whether she found common ground with the demonstrators, she said she found it with everyone.
“This is the problem.”

In 2024, Sweden ended two centuries of military non-alignment and joined NATO, spurred into the alliance by Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Säpo has repeatedly pointed to Russia, along with China and Iran, as the main intelligence threats to the country.

Powerful 7.4 quake rattles Colombia, neighbouring countries, collapses buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:52:03 UTC
23:52:03 KST

At least 69 people have been killed, and more were trapped below buildings after a powerful earthquake shook Colombia, damaging or collapsing buildings in several cities and sending residents rushing into the streets, officials and witnesses said.
The Colombian Geological Service and the US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at 7.4, with its epicentre about 100 kilometres (60 miles) underground in western Colombia early on Monday.
Colombian authorities initially recorded the magnitude at 6.6.
Local officials said at least 40 people were killed in the coffee-growing Risaralda region, 27 in Valle del Cauca department and two more in the city of Manizales.
The tremor was felt across Colombia and in neighbouring Ecuador, Panama and Venezuela.
Officials said there was no immediate tsunami threat.
Damage reported across western Colombia
In Choco province, the governor reported injuries and significant damage in the capital, Quibdo, where footage showed a collapsed building.
Buildings were also damaged in Pereira and Manizales, in Colombia's coffee-growing Eje Cafetero region.
Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said the city had suffered major damage and that authorities were using drones to assess the situation.
Several airports in western Colombia suspended operations as authorities checked infrastructure.
In Bogota, residents evacuated buildings and gathered outside as emergency sirens sounded.
Mayor Carlos Galan said initial assessments suggested the capital had largely avoided major structural damage, with cracks reported on some building facades.
Residents describe a violent jolt
Martha Estrada, a 66-year-old resident of the coffee-growing region, told AFP that power and mobile phone services were disrupted.
"There is no electricity or cell phone coverage," she said. "It was strong, really strong. Things fell in my house."
In Bogota, 29-year-old Valeria Polo described the earthquake as "very, very strong."
Emergency and medical teams moved into affected areas to assess casualties and damage, while authorities continued monitoring for aftershocks and additional structural failures.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would travel to the affected region as emergency operations continued.

Strong Colombia earthquake leaves buildings collapsed, injuries reported across western cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:51:30 UTC
23:51:30 KST

The deadliest known scene so far was in the western city of Pereira, where 18 people were killed. Fatalities were also reported in Manizales, Buenaventura and Valle del Cauca, including three children who were killed when a wall collapsed on them.
In Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city, the mayor said at least 20 buildings had collapsed and rescue teams were working to reach people trapped inside.
Heavy structural damage was also reported in Quibdó, which along with Pereira appeared to be among the main centers of destruction. In Bogotá, buildings swayed and frightened residents rushed into the streets, but authorities said no significant damage had been reported in the capital.
Local media broadcast images of buildings with shattered facades, while videos circulating online showed residents fleeing as debris fell around them. In one video, a woman struggled to stay on her feet as the facade of a nearby building collapsed before jumping across the road to escape.
Buildings collapse as survivors jump and flee: Footage from the Colombia earthquake
The earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time. Its epicenter was near San José del Palmar, about 400 kilometers west of Bogotá, at a relatively deep 96 kilometers below the surface.
The tremor was also felt in neighboring Ecuador, including the capital Quito, as well as in Venezuela and Panama. No tsunami warning was issued.
In Bogotá, the powerful shaking triggered panic as residents and tourists evacuated buildings, though significant damage was not reported there. Farther west and in central Colombia, however, authorities reported widespread destruction, including the collapse of dozens of structures.
Colombia’s aviation authority reported damage at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura and said operations at all six had been suspended.
Video from Pereira airport showed pieces of ceiling falling as passengers struggled to remain on their feet during the earthquake.
In Manizales, the city’s neo-Gothic cathedral was also heavily damaged, with one of its towers collapsing.
Less than an hour after the main earthquake, a magnitude 4.6 aftershock was reported in Chocó, the department closest to the epicenter. The aftershock occurred somewhat closer to the surface.
The earthquake came less than two months after two devastating quakes struck Venezuela in June. Those earthquakes, measuring magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, killed more than 5,000 people and destroyed hundreds of buildings.
Colombia and its neighbors lie along the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” a region of intense seismic and volcanic activity caused by the movement of tectonic plates.
Minor earthquakes are common in central and western Colombia, but tremors above magnitude 6 are relatively rare. In 1999, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake near Armenia killed more than 1,100 people. The deadliest earthquake in Colombia’s history struck in August 1868 and killed about 70,000 people.
‘I ran out wearing my kippah, and people asked me to pray for them’
Israeli Rabbi Yosef Garmon, who was in Bogotá during Monday’s earthquake, said he had arrived in the city only hours earlier with a volunteer delegation that had been assisting communities affected by the Venezuelan disaster.
“I arrived in Bogotá before dawn, went to sleep at 5 a.m., and then the earthquake woke me up,” Garmon said. “I’m on the eighth floor and everything here was shaking. It was long, seconds that felt like an eternity, and then I heard screaming. Everyone went down through the stairwell.”
Garmon said frightened residents remained outside and that the ground continued to shake. He added that his delegation was assessing whether assistance was now also needed in Colombia.
Colombia’s newly inaugurated president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in a post on X that he would personally oversee rescue and recovery efforts and establish an emergency center in San José del Palmar, near the epicenter.
De la Espriella, who took office only days ago, is a vocal supporter of Israel and announced after winning the election that Colombia would restore ties with Israel and open an embassy in Jerusalem.
Against the backdrop of warming relations between the countries, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said Israel was closely following developments and had offered assistance.
“We are following with concern the reports of the earthquake that struck Colombia,” Sa’ar wrote on X. “I offered my Colombian counterpart any assistance Israel can provide. Israel is prepared to help Colombia as needed.”
Israeli businessman Fernando Haim Bisker, who attended de la Espriella’s inauguration, said he experienced the earthquake at his home in Bogotá with his wife, Haya, and their children.
“In the middle of breakfast there was a strong earthquake. Everything started shaking. You hear an alarm like in Israel, and I thought, like in Israel, that it was because of missiles, until my brain understood that it was an earthquake,” he said.
“All the buildings were shaking, all the power lines were falling like in a hurricane. We immediately ran into the street. We didn’t know whether the building would collapse or not. It was very frightening, and everyone in the street was crying. There were people in pajamas and children.”
Bisker said strangers noticed that he was Jewish after he fled the building wearing his kippah.
“I came down wearing my kippah, and suddenly non-Jews said to me, ‘Bless us, pray for us,’” he said. “The opposite of hatred.”

Rush to find solar eclipse glasses as UK high street stocks run short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:47:48 UTC
23:47:48 KST

A frantic rush is on across the UK to find the right kind of protective eyewear ahead of Wednesday’s partial solar eclipse.
High street stores are running out of eclipse glasses and online shoppers who track down a pair are being told they may not reach them until the end of the week. In other words, in plenty of time for the next comparable UK eclipse – in 2081 – but no good at all for Wednesday’s show.
The Royal Observatory Greenwich said it was aware of a shortage of glasses. A spokesperson said: “We have sold out of solar eclipse glasses, both online and in our shops, due to an unprecedented volume of orders.”
Ordinary sunglasses are not safe to use and over the last few weeks consumer experts have been recommending specialised glasses. But try to get, for example, a pack of Lunt solar eclipse glasses (£14.99) on Amazon and the dispiriting message “free delivery Thursday 13 August” pops up.
The Robert Dyas store was offering Bresser eclipse glasses for £2.99, but there was an “out of stock” message on its website.
Emma, from Tonbridge in Kent, described her mission to find pairs for herself and three relatives. “They were sold out everywhere,” she said. When she called her local opticians, she received short shrift. “They sounded really angry. I said: ‘I’m calling to see if you have any glasses for the …’ The assistant interrupted and said no and hung up.”
Emma managed to get one from a friend whose forward-thinking mum had bought a multipack. “If we can’t get any more, we’ll have to share,” she said.
Neill Sanders, the founder of Go Stargazing and the UK coordinator of Astronomers Without Borders, said there wasn’t a shortage – it was just that people had not planned ahead.
He said: “I’m getting loads of calls, text messages, emails with people asking ‘Do you have some glasses?’. Everyone’s suddenly realising we need glasses for Wednesday.”
Sanders said he had imported 300,000 pairs from the US. He had sent out 100,000 pairs in the last few weeks at discount prices to astronomy clubs and community groups but it was too late to get most of the others out.
Another distributor said: “We have good stocks, our issue is everybody has left it until the last minute to order and we only have so many people we can put into packing at a time.”
Jake Foster, an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, said: “If you don’t have a pair of eclipse glasses, you can still view the eclipse indirectly. Any household item with small round holes in it, such as a colander or even a piece of paper with a small hole poked in it can project an image of the eclipse on to a flat surface.
“Don’t look at the sun itself but instead at the shadow that’s being produced – you should be able to see the shape of the eclipse within it.”
After the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems from watching it.
The UK Health Security Agency and the royal college have issued detailed advice on their websites on the sort of glasses that are safe and other ways of watching the eclipse.

Finland reopens train service to Sweden, putting Europe in reach
- Finland restarted a passenger train service to Sweden on Aug 10, linking northern Finland to southern Europe for the first time since the 1990s.
- The route runs twice daily from Oulu, Finland to Haparanda, Sweden, with transfers needed due to differing track widths.
- Officials see the service as a boost for security, economy, and growing cooperation, while passenger train travel in Europe is experiencing a renaissance.
AI generated
OULU, Finland – A new passenger train service linking Finland to Sweden began running on Aug 10, creating a rail route stretching from northern Finland to southern Europe for the first time since the 1990s.
The atmosphere at the Oulu train station in northern Finland was filled with excitement as passengers boarded a train headed for neighbouring Sweden early on Aug 10.
Vaino Jalkanen, 37, woke up at dawn to witness the “historic” resumption of Finnish cross-border trains that were discontinued in 1988.
“Now, it will be possible to travel from Paris to Rovaniemi, for example,” he told AFP as he had found his seat, referring to a city deep in central Finland.
Services will run from Oulu on Finland’s north-west coast to Haparanda, Sweden, twice a day.
From Haparanda, passengers can transfer to trains and routes that run west to the Norwegian sea or south through Stockholm as far as Portugal.
The transfer is necessary because Finland uses the same track widths as in neighbouring Russia, which are wider than the European standard – a legacy of when the Nordic country was part of the Russian Grand Duchy in the 19th century.
After crossing a bridge over the Torne river from Finland’s Tornio, the inaugural train on Aug 10 was welcomed by a crowd of people waving Finnish and Swedish flags at the red-brick station in Haparanda.
“It’s about security, it’s about the future, it’s about economy,” Finland’s Transport Minister Lulu Ranne told AFP.
She added that cooperation between the two countries was growing “all the time”.
Elisa Markula, chief executive of Finland’s state-owned railway operator VR, said she was hopeful the service would attract passengers because “travelling via land is very popular at the moment”.
“Train travelling in all Europe is having a renaissance. Also in Finland, our passenger numbers are increasing a lot,” Markula added. AFP

A boat captain in cuffs and a family grieving: How a birthday celebration turned deadly in NYC harbor
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:45:27 BST
23:45:27 KST

A boat captain in cuffs and a family grieving: How a birthday celebration turned deadly in NYC harbor
The boat’s operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan man, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A sightseeing cruise in the New York Harbor ended in catastrophe Saturday night when a small motorboat carrying 14 people capsized near the Statue of Liberty, killing a mother and her 5-month-old daughter.
The passengers, who had gathered to celebrate a birthday, were thrown into the dark water after the vessel overturned, screaming for help as rescuers raced to the scene.
The disaster has prompted a joint Coast Guard and New York City Police Department investigation into what caused the boat to flip — and whether the trip was operating as an unlawful charter. The vessel’s operator has been arrested and charged.
“We are deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life,” Captain Doreen McCarthy, the Coast Guard Sector New York Commander, said in a press release. “We are committed to holding illegal operators accountable to [the] highest extent of the law.”
What happened?
Fourteen people boarded a 22-foot bowrider at Randall’s Island at about 7 p.m. for a surprise 41st-birthday celebration for Paula Rivera, her 20-year-old daughter, Sara Raez, told The New York Post. The family and friends had chartered the vessel through Zeus Luxury.
Hours after embarking, as the group returned from the Statue of Liberty, the boat — described by the Post as “dangerously overcrowded” — capsized.
“When we were heading back, we were slow, but out of nowhere, people started screaming because the front of the boat went into the water,” Raez told the Post. “The water got into the boat. The boat went up, and when it went down — it was in seconds — it flipped over.”
“Everyone was on the bottom of the boat,” she continued. “We were just trying to get out. Then, when finally everyone got out, everyone was screaming, because we were still missing them, too.”
Some passengers climbed onto the hull of the overturned boat and tried to signal a distant vessel for help, Raez said. A nearby “party boat” eventually came to their aid, throwing life jackets to those in the water.
The Coast Guard, New York City Police Department and New York City Fire Department responded with eight boats and a helicopter.
“While all persons on the overturned vessels were recovered, two of the passengers, a mother and child, were pronounced deceased shortly after recovery,” the Coast Guard said. “The remaining survivors are reported to be in stable condition.”
Adam Schwartz told The Associated Press that his company’s boat, Sea the City II, was in the area when the accident occurred and took on the 12 survivors.
“Our captain and both crew members immediately assisted, called in to the Coast Guard and...then coordinated with the Coast Guard and NYPD Harbor units to bring them to land in Brooklyn,” Schwartz told the outlet.
Who were the victims?
The victims were identified as 27-year-old Sara Sanchez and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, according to WABC. Both were taken to a local hospital in critical condition and later pronounced dead. Sanchez lived in College Point, Queens.
Among those rescued was Andres Garcia, Sanchez’s partner and Antonella’s father. The Post reported that Garcia was photographed weeping after the rescue.
Raez told the outlet that the couple also have a 6-year-old son, Salvador, who was not on the boat Saturday.
A GoFundMe fundraiser says Garcia suffered “a loss that no husband or father should ever have to endure.”
“No amount of money can replace Sara or Antonella,” the online fundraiser states. “But together, we can give Andres some breathing room to grieve, take care of their son, Salvador, and begin facing a future that changed in an instant.”
“I’m in shock,” Diego Naranjo, a neighbor of the family, told WABC. “For the family, sending condolences to the family. May they rest in peace in heaven.”
Who was charged?
The captain of the 22-foot vessel, 46-year-old Manuel Hernandez, was arrested and charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment, the Post reported.
“Coast Guard Investigators are also determining whether the operation constitutes an illegal charter operation and are coordinating efforts in conjunction with NYPD,” the Coast Guard said. “An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that lacks required U.S. Coast Guard credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection.”
Although 14 people were aboard Saturday night, the boat had a maximum seating capacity of 10, the Post reported, citing police sources. Passengers were not required to wear life jackets, except for 5-month-old Antonella.
The case against Hernandez, who is from Manhattan, has been taken over by federal prosecutors, CNN reported.
Zeus Luxury describes itself as “one of the leading companies in limousine, party bus, and yacht rentals in the tri-state area,” with a fleet that includes “40 high-end vehicles from top brands.”
The Independent has contacted the company for comment.

Swimming pools and car washes could be banned as drought declared across most of England
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:45:09 BST
23:45:09 KST

Swimming pools and car washes could be banned as drought declared across most of England
Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales plunged into drought as UK on the verge of fifth heatwave
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Swimming pools and car washes are among the UK businesses that could be hit by a water ban as providers look to conserve resources amid drought conditions and an upcoming fifth heatwave.
Southern Water has applied to the government for permission to issue a “non-essential use ban” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. If granted and put into action, the policy would prevent businesses from activities like washing cars with hosepipes and filling private swimming pools.
It comes as almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been plunged into drought.
Temperatures are set to soar to as high as 36C this week as parts of the country face their fifth heatwave this summer.
A Southern Water spokesperson confirmed it had applied for a drought order and a non-essential use ban as a precaution, but that it does not currently plan to enact the measures.
“This isn't a choice between protecting the river and supplying customers,” they said.
“We have to do both. The drought order process helps ensure we can maintain essential water supplies during an exceptional drought, while operating within a regulatory framework designed to balance environmental protection with the needs of the communities that rely on the river test."
Almost three-quarters of England is now suffering from drought as weather conditions continue to worsen into August, piling pressure on vital industries.
The East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs moved into drought status on Monday, bringing the total number of people affected up to 45 million as a fifth heatwave of the summer sweeps through England and Wales.
It means that more than 71 per cent of England is now experiencing a “flash drought”, after drought was declared across East Anglia, Hertfordshire and London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the west Midlands, and Wessex on 29 July.
“Flash drought” has a rapid onset or is intensified very quickly. It is brought about by low levels of rain and abnormally high temperatures.
Some 27 million people are currently living under restrictions on water use, with millions under hosepipe bans, including all South East Water and Thames Water customers.
A non-essential use ban comes as part of the next level of drought restriction that applies to business and commercial activities that use large amounts of water but aren't considered essential.
There is no specific date set for the hosepipe bans to end, but water companies have explained that it will be lifted once water sources have recovered back to normal levels.
Southern Water has previously said it needs enough water in reservoirs, rivers and underground aquifers to meet demand before it can lift the ban.
Met Office science manager Dr Amy Doherty described July as a “truly remarkable month” in the UK’s climate record.
“The combination of record-breaking dryness, exceptional warmth and unprecedented sunshine has delivered one of the most notable summer months in our historical records,” she said.
Last summer, the government granted two drought orders during a season which saw four heatwaves and the driest August for England since 2003.

Are UFOs inspiring a new religion around the search for alien contact?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:43:52 BST
23:43:52 KST

Are UFOs inspiring a new religion around the search for alien contact?
Many CE-5 practitioners believe that the U.S. government, in tandem with defence contractors, possesses recovered extraterrestrial craft and that scientists have secretly reverse-engineered alien technologies
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
For years, whistleblowers have publicly alleged that the United States government is withholding what it knows about UFOs (now formally referred to as “unidentified anomalous phenomena” or “UAP”).
Those allegations gained new weight this past May, when the U.S. Department of War began the process of releasing hundreds of declassified documents, images and videos as part of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters.
These recent disclosures raise an old question: If the U.S. government is officially acknowledging that UAP have been observed, could claims of contact with the non-human intelligence allegedly operating them also be true? To understand what a claim of actual contact would even mean, it helps to start with the framework that first tried to categorize these encounters.
In 1972, American astronomer J. Allen Hynek proposed a three-part “Close Encounters” framework for classifying UFO experiences that has shaped the field since the late 1940s.
A “Close Encounter of the First Kind” (CE-1) is a visual sighting from less than 150 metres away. A CE-2 involves physiological effects on the surrounding environment. A CE-3 involves observing non-human entities operating the UFO.
Five years after Hynek’s book appeared, Steven Spielberg’s 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind established CE-3 in popular culture.
Communicating with UAP
Later researchers expanded Hynek’s classification. A “Close Encounter of the Fourth Kind” refers to abduction into a UAP. A “Close Encounter of the Fifth Kind” (CE-5) alleges human-initiated communication with the non-human intelligence operating UAP, whether extraterrestrials, time-travellers or so-called interdimensional beings.
Those who claim to have had such encounters are commonly called — as in Spielberg’s newly released film, Disclosure Day — “experiencers.”
CE-5 is not just a category of experience, though. During the past three decades, it has developed into a ritual protocol practised by a global community. Groups gather in wilderness settings around the world with the intention to initiate contact using various techniques. Some use laser pointers to send visual signals into the sky and geiger counters to measure fluctuations in radiation levels.
Stroboscopic light and musical entrainment have also been observed alongside mantra recitations, and transcendental meditation focused on “coherent thought sequencing” (where practitioners visualize their consciousness extending into deep space before sending a telepathic invitation to the operators of UAP to visit Earth).
Practioners of CE-5 ritual protocol also report telepathic communication, “photon dialogue” through flashing lights and bodily sensations from UAP that they interpret as interspecies communication.
Shamanism with a technological twist
Is CE-5 a new religious movement?
Although practitioners reject the label “religion,” their activities constitute a protocol enabling extraordinary experiences with superior, sky-dwelling entities. The fact that their efforts to connect with extraterrestrials draw upon telepathy and altered states of consciousness suggests a ritual form commonly associated with shamanism, yet with advanced technological mediation.
Calling CE-5 a “religion” may also reduce convictions about extraterrestrial presence from questions of reality to matters of belief or conspiracy, reflecting the long-standing cultural dismissal of UFOs and “little green men.”
Religious or not, CE-5 practitioners draw on 80 years of UFO lore to advance a cosmology in which consciousness is a fundamental property of the universe that enables telepathic communication with superior, non-human intelligence visiting Earth.
CE-5 protocol also resembles a ritual séance. It combines transcendental meditation, cosmic visualization, telepathic communication and an experience of “internal communication” through which bodily sensations become direct signs of extraterrestrial contact.
This has interesting parallels with anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann’s research on Evangelical Christianity in America and how church-goers feel themselves to be in direct communication with God through bodily sensations and religious interpretations of their inner voice.
CE-5 practitioners regard extraterrestrials as benevolent, highly intelligent beings physically present in space and around Earth.
Are they, as religious studies scholar Diana Pasulka asked in her 2019 book American Cosmic: UFOs, Religion, Technology, the angels of the secular space age? Rather than genuine contact, do they instead represent an unconscious desire to re-enchant the de-spiritualized cosmos?
A salvation narrative
Many CE-5 practitioners believe that the U.S. government, in tandem with defence contractors, possesses recovered extraterrestrial craft and that scientists have secretly reverse-engineered alien technologies.
These claims have been advanced by figures with overlapping views such as former military and intelligence officers Col. Philip J. Corso, Luis Elizondo and David Grusch (who testified under oath before U.S. Congress that a secret arms race exists to recover and exploit non-human technology that has crashed or landed on Earth). The U.S. government has denied these claims.
Within CE-5 communities, the “disclosure” event in which the government admits to possessing alien technology also functions as a salvation narrative. That’s because official confirmation promises technological liberation from fossil fuels, leading to the dawn of a free energy civilization.
As in millenarian movements, the anticipated post-disclosure world is always imminent but perpetually deferred.
What if close encounters are real?
CE-5 bears many hallmarks of a new religious movement emerging from the intersection of science, technology and modern anxieties. It may indeed re-enchant a desanctified universe viewed through secular scientific frameworks.
Yet, UAP present an unusual challenge. The U.S. government has acknowledged that UAP are real, even as it maintains there’s no confirmed evidence of extraterrestrial origin. And so it’s possible that CE-5 may not be based solely on faith and imagination but on experiencers’ interpretations of authentic encounters with an advanced, non-human intelligence.
Regardless of whether the anomalous experiences reported during CE-5s involve genuine contact with non-human intelligence, the practice has certainly emerged as a ritual of cosmological transition.
It encourages participants to experience the universe not as dead empty space but as a cosmic community in which we, ancient by our own reckoning, have only just awakened to our place in the galactic neighbourhood.
Either way, it’s time for scholars of the humanities and social sciences to take seriously UAP and the possibility of non-human intelligence. The stigma is fading.

Trump predicts the future and claims he will have the lowest inflation of all presidents for the rest of his term
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:42:14 BST
23:42:14 KST

Trump predicts the future and claims he will have the lowest inflation of all presidents for the rest of his term
Inflation has steadily risen under Trump’s second term, largely attributed to his war with Iran
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
President Donald Trump believes that cumulative inflation under his second term will be the lowest of the past six administrations – despite persistently high prices that his administration continues to struggle with.
The president posted an infographic on Truth Social Sunday showing cumulative inflation rates for each of the last six administrations, measuring the total percentage change in consumer prices over four years under each president.
At the top is former President Joe Biden, who saw a cumulative inflation rate of 21.20 percent over the four years he was in office.
At the bottom of the chart sits Trump’s second administration with a 4.71 percent inflation rate – however, the data is incomplete because Trump is only 18 months into office. The president pointed that out in a separate Truth Social post.
When examining cumulative inflation at the 18-month mark of each presidential term, Trump’s second term has the fourth-highest inflation rate.
Mediaite was the first to report on the Truth Social post.
Though Trump ran on a platform to lower everyday costs, in part by lowering inflation, the president has struggled to maintain that promise because his war with Iran has pushed consumer prices up.
The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted global trade and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, causing gas and oil prices to rise. As of August 10, Americans are paying, on average, $4 per gallon of regular gasoline.
Between June 2025 and June 2026, consumer prices rose 3.5 percent overall.
Rising costs have reflected poorly on the Trump administration.
In a July Fox News poll of 1,003 people, just 24 percent said they approved of Trump’s handling of the economy.
Just 33 percent of people said they felt they were “living comfortably” in a recent Marquette Law School poll – a 7 percentage point decrease from the number of people who said they were living comfortably in January.
Yet, Trump has consistently tried to insist that he’s bringing costs down.
While delivering remarks in Michigan last month, the president said that “inflation dropped by the largest amount in more than six years, because we’re doing it right”
“They tried to blame high prices on me,” Trump told rally-goers.
While Trump is correct that inflation dropped quickly in June, his statement excludes some key context.
The decrease in inflation in June came after months of increases largely attributed to higher oil and gas prices due to the Iran war. The U.S. and Iran were following a ceasefire agreement in June – which subsequently fell apart in July.
Inflation was also still higher in June 2026 than it was at the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025.
The infographic, posted by the president, appears to have originated from an Instagram account called Yung Geeski.
Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, re-posted the infographic on Instagram earlier Sunday, calling it a “great chart” and including the caveat that the information was incomplete for Trump’s second term.

Israel advances 3 major illegal settlement projects in East Jerusalem in weeks: Rights group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:41:50 UTC
23:41:50 KST

Abdelraouf Arnaout Mohammad Sio
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
The Israeli government has advanced three major illegal settlement projects in East Jerusalem within a few weeks, involving more than 3,400 units, in an effort to strengthen Israeli control over the occupied city, an Israeli rights group said Monday.
Ir Amim, an Israeli organization focused on East Jerusalem, said in a statement that Israeli authorities had advanced the three projects, less than three months before legislative elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
The organization said the Jerusalem District Planning and Building Committee last month deposited a plan for a new illegal settlement of about 650 housing units in the Palestinian neighborhood of Umm Tuba.
The committee also approved two other plans: one for a new illegal settlement of about 450 housing units in the heart of the Palestinian neighborhood of Umm Lison, and another to expand the Gilo illegal settlement by more than 2,300 housing units.
Umm Tuba, Umm Lison and Gilo are located in southern East Jerusalem.
Ir Amim said the projects, which together include thousands of illegal settlement units, would “deepen the fragmentation of Palestinian neighborhoods in East Jerusalem, strengthen Israeli control over the city and undermine prospects for any future political settlement.”
Aviv Tatarsky, a researcher at Ir Amim, said the developments are not a series of separate planning decisions but “an integrated policy implemented according to a calculated timetable.”
“Within a few weeks, and ahead of the elections, the Israeli government is advancing three of the largest settlement projects in East Jerusalem,” he said.
Tatarsky described the moves as “an attempt to create new facts on the ground, redraw the city's landscape, deepen its separation from the West Bank and make any future political settlement more difficult.”
“This government may be in its final days, but it is racing against time to leave behind a reality that will be extremely difficult to change,” he said.
Israeli officials have touted the current government as one of the country's most supportive of illegal settlement expansion.
At the end of June, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced an acceleration of illegal settlement activity in the occupied West Bank, saying his government had established 160 illegal settlement farms and approved more than 100 new illegal settlements.
The UN and most countries consider Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land illegal under international law and say they undermine prospects for a two-state solution.
The Israeli Peace Now movement estimates that about 500,000 occupiers live in the West Bank, in addition to about 250,000 in illegal settlements in East Jerusalem.
Palestinians say the projects are part of an accelerating Israeli policy aimed at expanding illegal settlements, seizing land and creating new facts on the ground.

Ukrainian teen from occupied territory found serving in Russia’s army, says Back to Ukraine project
Oleksandr Mustiatse, a Ukrainian teenager stranded in occupied territory in the Kherson region after Russia’s full-scale invasion, is now fighting on Russia’s side, the Ukrainian initiative Back to Ukraine reported on July 28. According to the group, this is one of the first such cases to come to light.
Mustiatse appears in a database of Ukrainian children under Russian occupation, which lists his hometown as the village of Krynky in the Kherson region — captured and later destroyed after 2022. He was 14 when the full-scale invasion began. He’s now 19. Back to Ukraine located his page on VK, where he had posted photos of himself in Russian military uniform and displaying the letter Z, a symbol of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
That VK page was deactivated in November 2025, leading Back to Ukraine to speculate that Mustiatse might have been killed. The group later reported that he was alive: with help from one of his fellow soldiers, it learned that Mustiatse had been wounded in the fall of 2025, treated at the Burdenko Main Military Hospital in Moscow, and sent back to the front.
On August 3, Back to Ukraine revealed it had found another VK page belonging to Mustiatse — this one under the name Alexander Famenok — and messaged him directly. The activists told him that Ukraine had learned of his fighting on Russia’s side and asked him to explain himself. Mustiatse didn’t deny it. “I’ve always been for my own country. Russia has always been in my heart,” he replied.
“When a person born in Ukraine sincerely considers russia to be ‘their side,’ that’s not an accident, but the result of systemic work. That’s why we insist on the need to launch a full-fledged state information strategy to fight for the population of temporarily occupied territories. Every month and year of occupation leads to the mental loss of [these] people,” Back to Ukraine stated.
The Ukrainian project Myrotvorets added Mustiatse to its database on August 3 as an accomplice in Russian aggression against Ukraine.
Back to Ukraine describes its goal as documenting the militarization and Russification of Ukrainian children under Russian control. Publicly, the project exists only as Instagram and Threads accounts, both created in the second half of July, and it’s unclear who is behind it.
Mustiatse’s story, as told by Back to Ukraine, drew coverage from many Ukrainian media outlets, as well as the attention of Mykola Kuleba, Ukraine’s former presidential commissioner for children’s rights and head of the charity Save Ukraine. As far as Meduza knows, however, no one besides Back to Ukraine has tried to reach Mustiatse.
Back to Ukraine also publishes information about other Ukrainian children who remained in Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine or were taken to Russia after the war began. Mustiatse isn’t the only one fighting for Russia, according to the group: 19-year-old Hryhorii Chymbur, for instance, is a member of Russian military intelligence. Other teenagers taken from Ukraine and identified by the project have been photographed displaying Russian military symbols.
Back to Ukraine also highlighted the case of Pylyp Holovnia, a teenager from occupied Mariupol adopted in 2022 by Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s presidential commissioner for children’s rights. Lvova-Belova is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of complicity in the deportation of Ukrainian children. She said on August 4 that Holovnia had enrolled at a university in Moscow to train as a prosecutor, though she had previously said the teenager was critical of Russia and didn’t want to live there.
According to the Ukrainian project Bring Kids Back, launched at the initiative of Volodymyr Zelensky, 1.6 million Ukrainian children remain under Russian control — either in Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine or in Russia itself — after being taken there since 2014. Only 2,441 have been returned.

NEW DELHI, August 10. /TASS/. India has increased its number of oil suppliers from 27 to 41 to mitigate risks associated with supply chains and global energy market instability, the ANI news agency reported, citing the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
The number of nations exporting liquefied natural gas (LNG) to India has also grown from 6 to 15. Speaking in the upper house of parliament, India's Minister of State for Petroleum and Natural Gas, Suresh Gopi, stated that "diversification has reduced dependence on any particular country, region, or transit route and increased India's ability to cope with supply disruptions and market volatility." He added that amid ongoing geopolitical upheavals, the ministry continuously monitors risks to energy supplies and assesses global market conditions in coordination with state-owned oil and gas enterprises and other stakeholders.
Local media outlets note that Russia retains its position as India's top oil supplier, playing a key role in securing supplies amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty due to competitive pricing, reliable availability, and flexible logistics. Purchasing Russian crude has helped India mitigate losses from supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz and reduced its reliance on higher-cost imports from Atlantic Basin nations.
Alongside Russia, India's top five crude oil suppliers include the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, and Venezuela.

China eyes humanoid robots to patrol future Moon bases
- Chinese scientists are considering using quadrupedal robot dogs, humanoid machines, and wheeled rovers to guard and maintain future bases on the Moon.
- A study published in Chinese Space Science and Technology proposes a collaborative model where astronauts provide high-level decision-making while robots execute physical tasks.
- Researchers argue that hostile lunar conditions, extreme temperatures, and radio signal delays from Earth make human-only or robot-only missions inefficient.
- Proposed concepts include three astronauts working alongside robot dogs that carry out daily patrols, sample collection, environmental sensing, and cleaning.
- China aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030 and build the International Lunar Research Station near the lunar south pole in collaboration with international partners.

Grease actor says they’re living ‘reclusive’ life after death of partner

Grease actor says they’re living ‘reclusive’ life after death of partner
‘The West Wing’ star, 82, has lived in London since her partner’s death in 2014
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Grease and The West Wing star Stockard Channing has admitted that she’s becoming a “recluse” since the death of her partner in 2014.
The American actor, 82, currently lives in London, having taken on fewer screen roles in recent years. Channing is best known for playing Betty Rizzo in 1978 musical Grease as well as roles in To Wong Foo Thanks for Everything! Julie Newmar, The West Wing and Practical Magic.
In a new interview, Channing spoke about how her life has been since the death of her cinematographer partner Daniel Gillham in 2014. The couple were in a relationship from 1990 until Gillham’s death after meeting on the set of war drama A Time of Destiny.
“I’ve lived alone since I lost Daniel and I’m happy being a recluse,” she told The Sunday Times, adding that she moved to London from Maine after his death.
“My partner, Daniel, died in 2014 and it was more devastating than I realised; it had a lag effect,” she said. “The pattern of my life shifted, so I shifted my life from Maine.”
Channing was married and divorced four times before her relationship with Gillham – first to sculptor Walter Channing Jr in 1963 until their divorce in 1967, and second to Slavic language professor, Paul Schmidt, from 1970 until 1976.
She married her third husband, writer-producer David Debin, in 1976, but the couple split four years later. In 1980, she wed businessman David Rawle, with their marriage lasting eight years.
Speaking about her relationship history, Channing said that her marriages “all represent epochs of me” and that she did once think about having children but decided against it.
“I think about them now because it’d be great to have someone taking care of me,” she added. “But hey, children can be just as selfish as everybody else out there.”
While Channing is currently directing the play Krapp’s Last Tape, she admitted that she’s “not sure” if she’ll take on any work after that. “Acting is like everything in life; you never know what’s going to happen,” she said.
Channing last appeared in the Paramount+ miniseries Knuckles as Wendy Whipple, the mother of witless deputy sheriff Wade (Adam Pally) in the 2024 Sonic spin-off.
She has regularly taken on theatre work, appearing at Clytemnestra in Greek tragedy Elektra at Brighton’s Theatre Royal last year. In September, she is due to reprise her Practical Magic role of Frances Owens – the witch aunt of Sally (Sandra Bullock) and Gillian (Nicole Kidman) – in its forthcoming sequel.

Solar power output set to fall during eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:38:51 UTC
23:38:51 KST

Portugal's grid operator REN estimates that solar power generation on Wednesday will fall by about 45% during the eclipse compared with usual levels for that time of day.
Portugal's grid operator Redes Energéticas Nacionais (REN) expects it will have to tap additional energy reserves to offset the loss of solar power generation caused by Wednesday's eclipse.
In the statement REN published on its website this Monday (source in Portuguese), the company says that "additional reserves from hydro and/or thermal generation will have to be mobilised" to mitigate the impact the phenomenon will have on the balance between energy consumed and generated in the National Electricity System (SEN), as well as the deviations the eclipse will cause in the interconnection between the Portuguese and Spanish grids. In neighbouring Spain, the eclipse will be 100% in a large part of the territory, while in Portugal it will be "almost total", ranging from 92% in the Algarve to 100% in the municipality of Bragança. The village of Guardamil is considered the best place in Portugal to see the eclipse in full.
According to REN's statement, the phenomenon, which will occur between 18:30 and 20:30 on Wednesday 12th, "will lead to an estimated loss of solar generation of 450 MW", which will represent around 7% of consumption and 45% of the solar output of the National Electricity System forecast for this time slot (average values). REN further indicates that "compared with the peak solar output forecast, the impact of the eclipse is estimated at around 15%".
For these figures, REN considers only centralised solar production and that recorded/measured by the company, excluding the solar energy generated by households for self-consumption. However, the impact that the drop in this household production will have on demand is factored into the consumption forecasts for that day.
The company says that "preparations for this event have been carried out in coordination with the other European transmission system operators, in particular through the Short Term Adequacy (STA) load-coverage assessment service, which ensures the balance between electricity generation and consumption over a seven-day horizon".
At the level of the European synchronous area, REN says the approximate loss of generation is estimated at 9,700 MW.
REN also points out that the phenomenon will occur in the late afternoon/early evening, a period when solar power generation is already declining, and so the impact will be smaller.
Solar power generation in Portugal reached an important milestone in July, the first month in which this energy source was the most used, accounting for 19% of consumption. Renewable sources represented 53% of total energy consumption.
