7.4 magnitude earthquake shakes Colombia, causing serious damage – latest news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:35:16 UTC
23:35:16 KST

We’re about to wrap up this live coverage of Colombia’s devastating earthquake but you can read an updated full report here – and below is a recap of the day’s news. It’s now a little after midnight local time.
Search and rescue efforts were under way early on Tuesday in dozens of cities and towns in western Colombia after a powerful earthquake struck the region.
At least 110 people were killed after the 7.4-magnitude quake struck on Monday morning local time, toppling buildings, damaging hospitals and infrastructure and trapping people beneath the rubble in Colombia’s strongest earthquake this century.
More than 2,700 people had been reported missing by Monday night.
New president Abelardo de la Espriella – sworn in just days earlier – declared a state of emergency and said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”.
“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” de la Espriella said after about 1,600 buildings had been damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed.
Colombian volunteers and rescuers were sifting through rubble into Monday evening searching for survivors. A person among those who joined a make-shift crew in Cali – western Colombia’s largest city – said: “We are trying to get everyone out alive.”
Local officials confirmed deaths across several regions, including the coffee region of Risaralda. Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, with at least 40 deaths reported; the department of Chocó, with at least 12; and the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department with at least 27, including 15 in Cali, Colombia’s third most populous city.
The quake hit the remote Chocó region about 7.30am local time and was felt as far as Bogotá, the national capital, about 400km (250 miles) away, as well as in neighbouring countries Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two aftershocks of 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude.
Authorities in the cities of Cali, Armenia and Manizales announced curfews in the aftermath of the quake, with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets.
The US state department announced it would provide $15.5m for emergency shelter, food and other aid. Governments across Latin America also offered help.
The earthquake comes less than two months after back-to-back quakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people.
Amid the quake devastation in western Colombia, little is known about the extent of the damage in Chocó, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details.
Phone signals were out in many parts of the region’s capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake’s epicentre, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira.
In Pereira, further south in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling onto travellers taking shelter and screaming, the Associated Press reports.
People ran through rubble and plumes of dust, and residents said collapsed stores, residential buildings and homes lined the city.
Pereira mayor Mauricio Salazar told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped.
In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks.
Authorities said flights were suspended at the airports in Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage.
The Colombian Geological Service said by late Monday it had recorded 21 aftershocks, including a 2.8- and 4.8-magnitude aftershock. The service has warned additional tremors are likely.
As the nighttime search to find Colombian quake survivors continues, a Cali resident and rescue volunteer has been quoted as saying her group helped seven people out of a fallen building but there were still four people and a dog trapped underneath.
“A moment ago there was scratching but now we can’t hear anything,” Carmen Yasmin Garcia, 43, said. “We still have faith that the dog is alive and we can get these people out.
The more people lending a hand the better.
Reuters also quotes Saul Paz, a resident of a Cali residential complex that partially collapsed, as saying he had been in the dining room with his son and wife when the shaking began.
“I think if it had lasted five seconds more there would be nothing left,” the 69-year-old said.
There are people who went to bed last night with a house and a car and today they won’t have anything.
Authorities in the western Colombian cities of Cali, Armenia and Manizales have announced curfews in the aftermath of the quake, with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets.
President Abelardo de la Espriella promised 1,000 additional security personnel for the city, the largest in western Colombia.
As night fell in Colombia, rescue workers and volunteers with headlamps have hurried to find people still trapped under rubble.
Video broadcast by Caracol Television showed a group of people pulling a small baby covered in dust from under a pile of debris. The six-month-old girl and her mother were rescued from under a five-story building in Cali, it reported.
Video from Cali also showed rescue workers rappelling people out from the windows of a local hospital, Reuters reports.
In the hard-hit city of Pereira, rescue workers told local TV they were in contact with a young boy trapped under a bakery, and crane operators were working to remove badly damaged parts of buildings.
Cali authorities said the Petronio Alvarez festival, an annual celebration of Pacific music which was due to start on Wednesday, has been postponed.
Colombia’s earthquake struck just three days after Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as president, thrusting his new administration into its first major crisis, with memories still fresh of devastating twin earthquakes in neighbouring Venezuela in June.
“The national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed,” he said in a national address about 1pm local time on Monday, declaring a national state of emergency and giving a death toll of 111.
The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.
De la Espriella visited Quibdo, the capital of coastal Chocóprovince, where he promised rent subsidies for those who had lost homes, and then travelled to Cali, western Colombia’s largest city, Reuters reports.
He had been expected to give an updated national death toll on Monday evening but only gave figures for Valle del Cauca province, where Cali is located, saying 35 people had died there and 700 been injured.
Some local media have cited a national total of 132 deaths, though the figure’s origin is unclear.
Rescuers race to find quake survivors under building rubble
Colombian volunteers and rescuers have been sifting through rubble with bare hands and buckets into Monday evening, hunting for survivors after the huge quake in the country’s west that left at least 111 people dead.
Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, declared a state of emergency and vowed a concerted rescue effort.
In the city of Cali, volunteers quickly went to work with picks, basic tools and their own hands to try to find survivors.
Andres Felipe Mejia was among those who joined a make-shift crew, telling Agence France-Presse:
We are trying to get everyone out alive. One of the rescuers asked anyone trapped to whistle, and someone whistled back.
“They pulled out a man and a baby, but the wife is still in there,” he said near a collapsed multi-story building.
Rescuers formed human chains to remove bricks and masonry, stopping every few minutes to listen for signs of life from those trapped below.
Mejia said:
A lot of people have come, with supplies, with food, helping the firefighters, helping the people.
Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert on Monday and a nighttime curfew was declared in Cali, according to local authorities. At least six local airports suspended operations, the civil aeronautics agency said.
The quake was felt across Colombia including Bogotá, the capital, where crowds of people rushed out into the street in their pyjamas.
More reports are emerging of the chaotic scenes that followed the earthquake that struck several cities across Colombia’s picturesque coffee region and Pacific, sending panicked residents on to the streets and damaging at least 1,500 buildings.
“People ran out naked, people jumped from the second floor of their homes” Wilmer Cuesta, a law student in Quibdo, told Agence France-Presse, recounting violent shaking.
Dentist Julian Pena was at home in Quibdo when he felt “very, very strong” shaking.
“People were praying in the street. It was overwhelming,” he told AFP. “I ran outside carrying nothing and found hundreds of people there.”
There are many buildings with gaps, with cracks. There are others that have completely collapsed.
There were scenes of destruction in several cities, with furniture and fabrics sandwiched between concrete, walls and floors tossed into irregular angles, and cabling strewn across roads.
Rescuers search for quake victims – latest pictures
Here are some of the latest images coming in from western Colombia as searches continue through the rubble of damaged buildings after the 7.4-magnitude earthquake – the country’s strongest recorded this century.
Colombian president says aid allocated to quake victims
Colombia’s president says the national government “stands with the people of Chocó” and that “immediate economic resources and humanitarian aid have already been allocated to support the more than 1,400 affected families and individuals”.
Abelardo de la Espriella – facing his first major crisis as president – also said on X that injured people and those requiring priority medical attention were being transferred to Medellín “with all available hospital capacity”.
His post said (in a translation):
Additionally, temporary rental subsidies will be implemented for families whose homes were damaged.
Our priority is and will continue to be the lives and well-being of the affected communities.
De la Espriella finished his post:
¡Firme por la Patria!” (Steadfast for the Homeland)
The US has announced $15.5m in earthquake aid for Colombia and said it is ready to support the new president’s response.
The state department said on social media the funding would go to “emergency shelter, food, protection and earthquake assessments”.
The post said:
We are united in prayer with the Colombian people and stand ready to support President [Abelardo de la Espriella] and his government as they assess the needs on the ground.
At the weekend the state department announced the Trump administration would provide $1bn in security assistance to the government of the new rightwing president, who used his inaugural speech to pledge a fight against drug trafficking as well as austerity measures to restore economic confidence.
Further to the last post: Mauricio Andrade, a firefighter in Colombia’s third most populous city of Cali, said his team had rescued two adult women and two children from a collapsed building.
As he spoke, his team was preparing to rescue more people from the rubble.
“They are alive,” he told Reuters. “We are making space so we can free them and get them out.”
Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television that the collapse of one building “sounded like a bomb”, as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali.
All of us neighbours are working together, forming human chains. We need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped.
Reports from Chocó, near the epicentre of the quake, have been slowed by communications outages, with some areas still lacking mobile phone service hours after the earthquake. 
Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said 12 people had been killed and 84 injured in the largely rural area.
The quake’s heaviest casualties appeared to be concentrated in Risaralda, part of Colombia’s coffee-growing region. Pereira, the department’s capital, suffered extensive damage, with rescue workers continuing to search collapsed buildings for survivors.
A four-story building crumbled in Pereira during the quake, according to Reuters-verified video, while footage from Manizales showed one of the side towers of the city’s landmark neo-Gothic cathedral collapsing and scattering debris onto nearby streets.
Reuters footage showed rescue workers, police and volunteers shovelling debris by hand and loading rubble into trucks as they searched for trapped survivors. Other footage showed damage to residential towers and emergency-service facilities, with debris crashing onto ambulances parked below.
Colombia’s Pacific region around the epicentre of the earthquake lies along the Ring of Fire, the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s quakes occur.
The Pacific, particularly the Chocó region where the quake hit, is one of Colombia’s poorest and is nestled in dense jungle. Much of the region is reachable only by boat or plane, which may pose a problem for authorities in assessing the wider toll, as the AP reports.
Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the quake’s powerful magnitude, inland location and strike-slip motion may have amplified damage in populated valleys despite its considerable depth.
“This one was far below the crust, and in theory it shouldn’t cause as much shaking,” she said, quoted by Reuters. “At this magnitude, it did actually cause a lot of shaking.”
The Colombia earthquake has left many people trapped under the debris of damaged buildings as their loved ones and rescue workers search through the rubble.
Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country’s third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers.
“Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed,” said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search.
The desperate scene recalled the searches still ongoing in neighbouring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by back-to-back quakes in June, the Associated Press reports.
Besides Cali, the quake-ravaged cities across western Colombia including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama.
At least 111 have died and 87 people injured after dozens of buildings collapsed following a 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday morning – the largest to hit the country so far this century. After declaring a state of national disaster, Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” he said after around 1,600 buildings had been damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed.
The president declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery while saying he would visit the disaster zone. “We aren’t going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination,” he said.

The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.

Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, where at least 40 people have been killed, according to the mayor. In the department of Chocó, at least 12 people were killed, according to the local governor there, and at least 27 deaths have been reported in the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department, including at least three children and including 15 people in Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city.
The United States and countries across Europe and Latin America offered support. Other countries including Ecuador, France, Mexico and Brazil also offered support.
It all comes less than two months after two earthquakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people.

Retail investors dispose of SpaceX shares for first time on Aug 7, with $5.8m in net sales
- Retail investors sold a net US$4.5 million in SpaceX shares on Aug 7, marking their first net selling since its June IPO debut.
- The shift to selling was driven by profit-taking and reassessment of risks, not panic, despite shares rebounding near the IPO price.
- SpaceX shares have fallen over 22% below IPO price recently, with increased public trading liquidity after lock-up expiries influencing investor behaviour.
AI generated
Retail investors who spent weeks defending SpaceX through its post-IPO run turned net sellers on Aug 7, marking the first such instance since the company’s blockbuster debut in June.
Mom-and-pop traders sold a net US$4.5 million (S$5.8 million) in Elon Musk’s rocket company, the first net negative reading since the company went public on June 12, according to Vanda Research data.
“A shift from persistent net buying to selling is rarely about one catalyst, it is usually a mix of profit-taking, position fatigue and investors reassessing the risk-reward,” said Sam North, market analyst at eToro.
“Friday is particularly interesting because retail turned net sellers while the shares were rebounding strongly and trading back around the IPO price. That looks more like investors using strength to take some money off the table than panic selling.”
By comparison, the highest single-day net buying in SpaceX’s trading history reached US$144.6 million on June 16, suggesting the outflow remains modest by the stock’s own standards.
This comes just days after individual investors “bought the dip” as shares slumped 13.6 per cent on Aug 5, when retail net-buying was the fourth-highest since the company’s June debut.
Shares had dropped as investors reacted to SpaceX’s first-ever quarterly earnings report as a public company, in which it touted faster returns from AI spending, but concerns remained about how long its profitable Starlink business would bankroll costly investments in artificial intelligence.
The reversal in sentiment tracks a broader unwind in SpaceX’s share price. The stock surged as much as 67 per cent above its US$135 IPO price in June before giving back all of the gains and falling more than 22 per cent below its debut price earlier in August.
Shares were last up 1.4 per cent at US$134.95 in early trading after surging nearly 23 per cent last week.
Despite the recent jump, its shares have closed below the IPO price every day since July 16.
Small investors have been crucial in the company’s history on the public markets, as at least 30 per cent of shares that were made available on debut were set aside for retail buyers.
Jai Malhi, senior equities strategist at Vanda, estimates that retail traders on average paid US$147 for SpaceX shares since the IPO, so “the selling may have been a function of cutting losses at an opportune time”.
In the last one week, SpaceX was the second most mentioned ticker on Reddit forum r/WallStreetBets, per sentiment aggregator SwaggyStocks.
Liquidity conditions have also changed as the number of SpaceX shares available for public trading more than doubled following the expiry of the first of several lock-up restrictions last week. REUTERS

Putin speaks on Russia's demographic situation, balancing act of modernizing cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:34:35 UTC
23:34:35 KST

ULAN·UDE, August 10. /TASS/. The depopulation of territories is unacceptable for such a vast country as Russia, President Vladimir Putin said at a meeting with representatives of the urban planning and spatial development sector.
He also noted that Russia's cities must not lose their historical character amid modernization efforts.
TASS has compiled the key statements made by the head of state.
The unacceptability of territorial depopulation
The depopulation of territories is unacceptable for such a great country as Russia: "For a country as vast in territory as Russia, allowing depopulation is unacceptable. This is why we need to steer a course between Scylla and Charybdis, we need to find an optimal, balanced solution, taking into account today’s opportunities to use modern technologies, the internet and artificial intelligence, and other IT opportunities."
Supporting young people
The Russian government needs to support young people’s desire to live and work in their native towns: "A list of 2,160 key towns has been identified, in which 75% of Russia’s population lives." A development program has been prepared for these places, designed to strengthen the country’s economic, social, and infrastructure framework. And, crucially, [the program is intended to] improve the quality and standards of life for millions of people, to support young people’s desire to stay in their hometown or village and build their future there.
Active, systematic work is underway on all these projects and programs, and promising infrastructure projects are being implemented.
Veterans of the special military operation
Veterans of the special military operation "should not just be returned to civilian life; they should be given the opportunity to find their way in life, to acquire some kind of profession again, to create the necessary barrier-free environment."
Modernization of cities
When modernizing Russian cities in line with modern trends and digital technologies, it is necessary to preserve their unique character: "By changing and rebuilding cities in accordance with modern trends and using digital information technologies, it is necessary to preserve their unique character: to seemlessly integrate new facilities into the already established space, to preserve the historical appearance of Russian cities and towns, their uniqueness, and to restore and give new life to cultural heritage sites."
This palette of diversity among cities and regions is the treasure of Russia.
There are many sites across the country that require the state’s attention: "I am convinced that together, as a single team, we can achieve maximum results in the development of large and small cities, villages, settlements, and historical settlements. And here, and in the Far East, and in Siberia, and in the Arctic, and in Donbass, and in Novorossiya - throughout the country."
The architectural appearance of cities should combine distinctive and national features so that local residents appreciate their symbiosis. "It’s important to link this in such a way that those who live in these spaces, who benefit from something, themselves come to the conclusion that one thing is impossible without the other, that one doesn’t just complement the other -- rather, this combination creates a force that allows local and unique things to be preserved and to develop on the basis of the power that represents a nationwide and unifying principle."
"As for the law on master plans, I agree, of course. What is a master plan? It says what needs to be built, when, what the goals are, what the returns will be, the feasibility study, and so on. Everything becomes a document that can be implemented not just as some kind of wish. And here, of course, it’s better if everything is described appropriately in a regulatory document. This is why I agree with you -- such a law is needed."
Development of the Far East
The Russian authorities are paying "special attention" to the development of the Trans-Baikal and Far Eastern regions.
Recently, a lot has been done to develop the economy, industry, and infrastructure in these territories; however, if creative spaces and conditions for people’s lives are not created there, "there will be no success: People will come here temporarily, and we will never create a stable environment here where people would want to live and raise their children."
Work in remote settlements
Workers will be employed in remote settlements across Russia exclusively on a rotational basis if they do not have a decent living environment: "You can try as hard as you like to develop the economy, and invest. But if there is no decent living environment, then people will only work on a rotational basis and will not live permanently in these settlements.".

Israel pushes 3 major illegal settlement projects in East Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:34:00 UTC
23:34:00 KST

Israel has advanced plans for more than 3,400 illegal settlement units across three projects in occupied East Jerusalem in recent weeks, a rights group said Monday, amid efforts to expand Israeli control over the city.
Ir Amim, an Israeli organization focused on East Jerusalem, said in a statement that Israeli authorities had advanced the three projects, less than three months before legislative elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
The organization said the Jerusalem District Planning and Building Committee last month deposited a plan for a new illegal settlement of about 650 housing units in the Palestinian neighborhood of Umm Tuba.
The committee also approved two other plans: one for a new illegal settlement of about 450 housing units in the heart of the Palestinian neighborhood of Umm Lison, and another to expand the Gilo illegal settlement by more than 2,300 housing units.
Umm Tuba, Umm Lison and Gilo are located in southern East Jerusalem.
Ir Amim said the projects, which together include thousands of illegal settlement units, would "deepen the fragmentation of Palestinian neighborhoods in East Jerusalem, strengthen Israeli control over the city and undermine prospects for any future political settlement.”
Aviv Tatarsky, a researcher at Ir Amim, said the developments are not a series of separate planning decisions but "an integrated policy implemented according to a calculated timetable.”
"Within a few weeks, and ahead of the elections, the Israeli government is advancing three of the largest settlement projects in East Jerusalem,” he said.
Tatarsky described the moves as "an attempt to create new facts on the ground, redraw the city's landscape, deepen its separation from the West Bank and make any future political settlement more difficult.”
"This government may be in its final days, but it is racing against time to leave behind a reality that will be extremely difficult to change,” he said.
Israeli officials have touted the current government as one of the country's most supportive of illegal settlement expansion.
At the end of June, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced an acceleration of illegal settlement activity in the occupied West Bank, saying his government had established 160 illegal settlement farms and approved more than 100 new illegal settlements.
The UN and most countries consider Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land illegal under international law and say they undermine prospects for a two-state solution.
The Israeli Peace Now movement estimates that about 500,000 occupiers live in the West Bank, in addition to about 250,000 in illegal settlements in East Jerusalem.
Palestinians say the projects are part of an accelerating Israeli policy aimed at expanding illegal settlements, seizing land and creating new facts on the ground.

Mapped: Where in Spain and France temperatures could hit 43C as another heatwave hits
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:33:39 BST
23:33:39 KST

Spain and France heatwaves mapped as extreme 42C temperatures sweep across Europe
Europe is bracing for its fifth heatwave of a record-breaking summer, with the threat of further devastating wildfires
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Europe is bracing for another scorching heatwave set to sweep across the continent, once again driving up the threat of devastating wildfires.
Spain could see temperatures as high as 42C later this week in what will be Europe’s fifth heatwave of a record-breaking summer, which has seen several countries suffer a record-breaking number of fires due to persistent dry conditions and extreme heat.
France and Italy will also see scorching temperatures, before the heatwave moves eastwards into Central and Eastern Europe, with temperatures set to near the 40s in Hungary, Serbia and Romania early next week.
The extreme heat has led to 25,000 related deaths this year, according to Bloomberg research covering Spain, France, the UK, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Wildfires have scorched more than 550,000 hectares of land across the continent during the same period.
Western Europe is in the midst of its hottest ever summer, with a record-breaking 24-hour average temperature of 21.62 degrees for June and July recorded this year, according to a report the EU’s Copernicus climate change service released on Monday.
This is 2.79C above the average temperature during the 1991 to 2020 period, smashing the previous heat record set in 2022.
Spanish forecaster Aemet says that tourist hotspots in Spain including Cordoba (42C), Sevilla (40C), Granada (39C), and Madrid (39C) will all see temperatures in the region of 40C on Thursday, while other touristy areas including Barcelona, Malaga and Alicante are all forecast to be in the low-to-mid 30s in the coming days.
Large parts of Spain, barring the eastern, southern and northwestern coasts, will be placed under yellow and amber warnings for the next three days.
France will see temperatures in the mid-to-high 30s, Meteo-France says, including in Paris (35C), Toulouse (36C) and Bordeaux (39C), which was the site of a vast wildfire last month that forced 200,000 people from their homes.
Meteo-France has placed much of the country’s south east under an amber heatwave warning, with the rest of the country, barring the north, under a yellow warning. On Wednesday, almost the entire country will be under an amber warning, other northern areas.
Last Thursday, all 27 Italian cities that are monitored through the Health Ministry’s national heat surveillance system were placed on red alert.
In the next three days, Rome (38C), Milan (37C), Florence (37C) and parts of central Sardinia (40C) will be among the hottest parts of Italy in the coming week, Italy’s Meteo Agency said.
It comes after Slovakia recorded a temperature 42.2C, becoming the latest country, including Hungary and Austria, to set an all time record.
Greece, which earlier this month was battered by dramatic wildfires in which several people were killed, is set to avoid the worst of the upcoming heatwave, with temperatures not expected to surpass the mid-30s.
Three consecutive months of exceptional heat in western Europe are the result of persistent high-pressure systems which have trapped heat over the region, a weather event also known as a ‘heat dome’, said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service.
Half of England and Wales have already been plunged into drought, with more regions likely to be declared on Monday afternoon when officials meet at the National Drought Group, before temperatures soar as high as 36C later this week.
“The extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought,” said Dr Burgess. “As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily. This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another.”
Eastern Europe is also currently in the grip of an intense heatwave, with temperatures as high as 36C in Serbia and Hungary on Tuesday, and set to hit 38C on Tuesday.
After a brief midweek reprieve, scorching temperatures will return to Croatia, Hungary, Serbia and Romania this weekend, as most of France and Spain cool into the mid-to-low 30s.
Some parts of Hungary, Romania and Serbia - particularly around the borders where the three countries meet - are also bracing for an ‘extreme danger’ of wildfires this week, according to the Copernicus European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS).
The danger will peak on Wednesday, after a spell of extreme high temperatures this week. Towards the end of the week, large parts of Spain and patches of France will be under ‘extreme’ and ‘very high’ wildfire danger warnings.
“Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extending the fire season northwards,” said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) at ECMWF.
“Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, meaning it can travel further and impact air quality not only locally, but across the wider region.
“Countries that experience relatively few wildfires may be increasingly impacted by long range transport of smoke, even if they are thousands of kilometres away.”
The threat from wildfires in western Europe far from over, with vast swathes of the continent under extreme wildfire warnings, as experts warn that the wildfire season is increasing in length and intensity each year.
In France and Spain, more than 300,000 people were forced to flee their homes, in an evacuation operation that now ranks among the largest the continent has seen since World War II.
The fires have already cost the continent up to £16.4 billion in economic costs, estimates published by forecaster AccuWeather showed on Thursday. This includes the cost of emergency response, damage to property, and health impacts.
The cumulative number of wildfires in France, Spain and Italy this year dwarfs the average from the previous two decades, figures from Copernicus’ European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) show.

In the first six months of 2026, JTI Ukraine transferred UAH 23.7 billion in taxes to the state budget — 12% more than in the same period of 2025. Increased excise tax rates and changes in product prices are the main factors behind this growth.
The excise tax, including a 5% retail excise, accounted for the largest share of tax deductions, reaching nearly UAH 18.8 billion. This is 15% more than in the first six months of 2025. The excise tax makes up 79% of the overall tax structure.
The volume of paid VAT increased by 33% to UAH 3.69 billion, in particular due to changes in product prices. Enterprise income tax amounted to UAH 578.6 million, which is 5% higher.
Personal income deductions and military fee increased by 16% to UAH 141.9 million, while the single social contribution grew by 12% — to UAH 98.4 million. The growth of these payments is associated with the company’s annual salary review. Customs fees, including VAT, amounted to UAH 405.2 million, which is 69% lower than the same period in 2025 due to reduced imports and the shift of some products to local manufacturing.
JTI Ukraine’s responsibilities are not limited to tax liabilities. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the company has directed over UAH 500 million to support its employees, communities, and people affected by the war. JTI Ukraine’s social programmes cover the reintegration of veterans, support for senior citizens, internally displaced persons, and persons with disabilities, the development of social institutions, and humanitarian demining. Silver Economy of Ukraine, aimed at preserving the professional potential of the 50+ generation, has become a separate focus area.
Simultaneously, the company continues to invest in the development of business in Ukraine. As part of the programme intended for 2024–2026, JTI Ukraine plans to invest up to $60 million in the HTP (heated tobacco products) category. The overall volume of the company’s investment into the Ukrainian economy since 1999 amounts to nearly $440 million. In 2025, JTI Ukraine paid UAH 45 billion
Аbout JTI Ukraine
JTI Ukraine is part of Japan Tobacco International (with its headquarters in Geneva), the international tobacco business of the Japan Tobacco Group of Companies (with headquarters in Tokyo). Since 1999, the company has been one of the leading tobacco manufacturing companies in Ukraine, bringing together over 800 employees in the central office in Kyiv, regional representative offices and the factory in Kremenchuk. JTI Ukraine manufactures products both for the domestic market and for export into 20 countries of the world. In 2024, the company introduced an innovative Ploom system in the heated tobacco products (HTP) category on the Ukrainian market, and in 2026 — a new-generation Ploom AURA device.
Over 27 years of its operations, the company invested almost $440 million in the country’s economy, and an additional $60 million in investment is planned for 2024-2026. The company actively implements social initiatives aimed at supporting Ukrainians in the times of war, the development of inclusive corporate culture and the strengthening of local communities. JTI Ukraine is among the top 10 largest taxpayers to the state budget and among the 10 leading companies in the Ukrainian corporate equality index.

Thales wins deal to run Britain’s Link 16 network
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:33:15 BST
23:33:15 KST

The Ministry of Defence has awarded Thales UK a contract worth £9.8 million to support the system that manages and monitors all Link 16 activity across the United Kingdom, the department stated in a contract award notice.
The notice was published on 10 August 2026 and records the contract as concluded on 7 August. It covers in-service support of the Link 16 Network Management System for an initial two years, with two further one-year options and additional options for out of hours support during crisis operations. Work will be performed at Templecombe in Somerset, where Thales UK is based.
According to the notice, UK defence has an enduring requirement to manage and monitor Link 16 activity across the country and to support up to two deployed operations simultaneously. The system allows operators to watch network activity and adjust the network architecture to keep conditions optimal. It also monitors activity for compliance with the frequency clearance agreement held between the department and the Civil Aviation Authority, which governs how the waveform may be used in UK airspace.
The contract was placed without competition, and the department sets out its justification in some detail. Only one tender was received. The equipment configuration is described as unique, with the installed software owned and supported by Thales as the original equipment manufacturer holding proprietary rights, meaning the company alone possesses the technical information, tools and expertise required. Changing the system in the immediate term, the notice states, could result in an inability to use the Link 16 network across all platforms in the UK Flight Information Region, significantly curtailing the ability of platforms across domains to train for operations.
Link 16 is the NATO standard tactical data link, operating in the L-band and allowing aircraft, ships and ground stations to exchange track, position and command information in near real time without voice traffic. British platforms carrying it include Typhoon, F-35B Lightning, P-8A Poseidon, E-7 Wedgetail, the Type 45 destroyers, Type 23 frigates and the Queen Elizabeth-class carriers, alongside ground-based air command and control nodes.
The network is a finite resource rather than an open channel. Link 16 divides transmission into time slots allocated in advance, and participants must be assigned slots through a network design before they can join. Managing those designs, deconflicting them between exercises and operations, and ensuring transmissions stay within agreed frequency bounds is what the management system exists to do.
That last point matters beyond the military, because Link 16 operates in a band shared with civil aeronautical navigation aids, which is why its use in UK airspace is governed by a formal agreement with the aviation regulator.
Thales UK’s Templecombe site has a long history in underwater systems and sonar work for the Royal Navy, and also houses communications and command and control activity. The company employs several thousand people across UK sites including Crawley, Belfast, Glasgow and Bristol.

Ukrainian defence companies gain access to 5m battlefield images to train AI
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Ukrainian defence companies gain access to 5m battlefield images to train AI
Ukraine's Ministry of Defence has granted domestic defence companies access to the Avengers Labs platform to train AI models for unmanned systems using real battlefield data.
Source: Ukraine's Defence Ministry
Details: The ministry noted that the platform was developed by the team at the Centre for Innovation and Defence Technology Development, which also created the Delta combat system.
Delta is a Ukrainian digital battlefield-management system that provides military personnel with a real-time picture of the battlefield by combining data from drones, satellites, sensors and other sources. It allows commanders to track enemy and friendly forces, identify targets and coordinate operations through a single digital platform.
"At the core of Avengers Labs is an annotated dataset of 5 million images collected on the battlefield. Most of this material comes directly from the Delta combat system and is continuously supplemented with new data that has practical value in combat conditions," the defence ministry said.
According to the Defence Ministry, the data covers:
- tanks
- artillery
- air defence systems
- infantry
- aerial assets, including Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs.
The ministry also reported that a target auto-detection system trained on the Avengers Labs dataset has proved effective within Delta and analyses more than 100,000 drone video streams each month.
"While processing video, artificial intelligence detects 70% of all enemy assets in real time and helps identify them both day and night," the Defence Ministry added.
Models trained on Avengers Labs can be used, among other things, in scenarios where an operator identifies a target and the drone independently adjusts its trajectory during the final phase of a mission. In another scenario, an unmanned system independently reaches a designated area, detects a target and then acts according to the mission logic.
The Ministry of Defence notes that these scenarios gradually reduce unmanned systems' dependence on constant manual control.
The first Ukrainian defence companies have signed licensing agreements with the Defence Ministry to use Avengers Labs. The platform may also be opened to Kyiv's partner countries in the future.
To gain access, companies can apply via the website. They must then undergo screening, including having no ties or business activities in Russia, not being subject to sanctions and not operating in temporarily occupied territories.
Background:
- Previously, the Defence Ministry reported that more than 75,000 video streams pass through Delta daily, and that, thanks to the built-in Avengers AI platform, battlefield video feeds can be automatically analysed to detect enemy assets.
- Ukrainska Pravda also reported that Ukraine has opened up the possibility for its partners to train AI models for unmanned systems using real combat data.

Latvia brings international defence and dual-use companies to NATO’s eastern border  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:32:09 UTC
23:32:09 KST

More than 150 participants from 19 countries are coming for the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum in Rēzekne on 6–7 September, bringing international companies together with Baltic manufacturers as Europe increases defence investment and restructures its industrial supply chains.
One month before the second Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum, more than 150 participants from 19 countries have already confirmed their participation, reflecting rapidly growing international interest in Latvia’s dual-use technology and defence industry potential.
The forum will take place on 6–7 September in Rēzekne, in Latvia’s easternmost region and on the EU and NATO eastern border. It will bring together defence and dual-use manufacturers, technology companies, investors, suppliers and system integrators looking for new partnerships and opportunities in the Baltic region.
This year’s international representation is broader than ever before. Companies from the United States, Germany, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, the Czech Republic, Romania, Serbia, Ukraine, Lithuania, Estonia and other countries have registered for the forum. International participants among others include GDELS, Analog Devices, HISDESAT, Gühring, Fischer Panda and Sine Engineering.
Overall, representatives of around 50 international companies and up to 120 Latvian companies are expected to participate, with more than 180 business meetings planned.
“One month before the forum, we have already reached the highest level of international interest since the forum was established. More than 150 participants from 19 countries demonstrate that Latvia is becoming increasingly visible on the European dual-use and defence industry map. Our goal is to create an environment where companies not only make contacts, but find new cooperation partners, customers and supply chain opportunities. Rēzekne was not chosen for this forum by chance – it is a place where security, industry, innovation and export potential come together,” says Līva Stūrmane, Chairwoman of the Board of the Latvian Exporters Association “The Red Jackets”.
Europe’s growing defence industry creates new export opportunities
Dual-use technologies – solutions that can be used in both civilian and defence sectors – are currently one of the fastest-growing segments of European industry. European countries are significantly increasing defence investment, restructuring supply chains and actively seeking new, reliable partners.
For companies able to become part of NATO and European defence industry supply chains, the current shift creates an opportunity to establish strong positions for the long term.
At the same time, working across civilian and defence markets can make businesses more resilient to market fluctuations. The quality, security and certification standards required by the defence sector can also strengthen companies’ competitiveness in other industries.
“Strengthening Latvia’s defence capabilities and developing local industry are closely connected. Every company capable of developing technologies, systems or components for defence needs simultaneously strengthens both national security and its own export potential. It is also important for us that the industry has opportunities to demonstrate its solutions in a real-world environment, while receiving direct feedback from soldiers and international partners,” says Raivis Melnis, Minister of Defence of the Republic of Latvia.
The choice of Rēzekne gives the forum particular relevance in the current European security environment
Latgale forms the eastern border of Latvia, the European Union and NATO, while Rēzekne is a regional centre with significant manufacturing, technology and logistics potential and is increasingly becoming an important location for defence industry development.
Holding the forum there brings discussions about European defence capacity, industrial resilience and new supply chains directly to a region where security, industrial development and export potential increasingly intersect.
From technology demonstrations to direct business meetings
The forum will begin on 6 September with Industry Day, featuring defence technology demonstrations. Participants will have an opportunity to explore Latvia’s defence innovation ecosystem, visit LEAX Rēzekne, Bee Tactics and VEREMS, and take part in networking activities and individual business meetings.
On 7 September, the main forum programme will take place at the GORS Concert Hall in Rēzekne, featuring expert panel discussions on the development of the dual-use and defence industries, technology presentations by Latvian companies, an EXPO area and pre-scheduled individual meetings with potential customers, investors, suppliers, as well as NATO and European Union system integrators.
On 8 September, international delegations and other interested participants will have an opportunity to take part in company visits in Riga.
The Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum is organised by the Latvian Exporters Association “The Red Jackets” in cooperation with the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), the Ministry of Economics and the Ministry of Defence.

Vilnius mayor asks agencies to assess Russian rapper Morgenstern's threat  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:32:06 UTC
23:32:06 KST

VILNIUS - Vilnius Mayor Valdas Benkunskas has asked Lithuania's State Security Department and police to assess whether Russian rapper Alisher Morgenstern poses a threat to national security, as the artist plans to perform in Lithuania following a favourable court ruling.
In April, the Supreme Administrative Court of Lithuania upheld the rapper's appeal and overturned a Migration Department decision that had banned Morgenstern from entering the country for 10 years.
The court ruled that the Migration Department had unjustifiably relied on information provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as the primary basis for assessing the threat to state security.
Meanwhile, the State Security Department, which is legally mandated to perform such assessments, provided no conclusion. Consequently, the court found that the entry ban was based on data from an incompetent authority.
Benkunskas announced on Monday that Morgenstern is planning a concert in Vilnius on October 31 and that he had turned to the security services to assess potential risks.
"In order to close this matter, I have appealed to the State Security Department and the police with a request to evaluate possible risks regarding threats to our national security and public order," Benkunskas said. He added that if such assessments are provided, the Foreign and Interior Ministries should move to block the rapper's entry.
The mayor emphasised that while a lower administrative court had previously found the ban justified, the Supreme Administrative Court overturned it due to "procedural violations."
In lifting the ban, the court also noted that Morgenstern's inclusion on the blacklists of other states, public-source information, past statements or creative work did not in themselves prove a threat to Lithuanian national security.
Morgenstern has previously expressed support for Russian President Vladimir Putin on several occasions. However, following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, he criticised Russian military actions in his songs. In May 2022, the rapper was designated a "foreign agent" in Russia.

VILNIUS - European Union Ambassador to the US Jovita Neliupsiene said it was unclear whether Washington had finalised decisions on its military presence in Europe, leaving the future of US deployments in Lithuania uncertain.
"First of all, the Americans themselves need to know what to expect and what the final decisions will be. (...) We must answer the question: do the Americans know and do they have decisions made? I would not be sure about that," Neliupsiene said in an interview with the 15min news portal.
Neliupsiene also noted that Europe is not the top priority in the US National Security Strategy. According to her, strategic documents focus primarily on Latin America, migration and drug control issues, as well as Asia and economic threats from China, while Middle Eastern security has become a major priority due to the conflict with Iran.
"Only then can we talk about Europe. If you are the fourth priority in strategic documents, it is probably difficult to expect a great deal of attention," Neliupsiene said.
The US is currently reviewing its troop presence in Europe. Laurynas Kasciunas, deputy chairman of the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence, said in early August that decisions on US troop rotations in Lithuania would be clear by early autumn. However, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas did not confirm this, saying partners had requested that too much information on the matter not be disclosed.
More than 1,000 US troops ended their rotation in Lithuania this summer. According to Kaunas, some American soldiers remain in the country, but the rotation process has not yet returned to regular levels.
The US has regularly deployed troops to Lithuania since 2019, and following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Washington changed their status to continuous rotational deployment. These reinforced battalions typically consist of 1,000 or more troops with various combat equipment. Lithuania has indicated it is prepared to host up to 1,500 US soldiers.

The Baltics' miracle: Geography doesn't determine economic performance – yet  - The Baltic Times

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

23:31:48 KST

The economies of the Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – although differing in their performance, are doing remarkably well amid geopolitical tensions.
Instead of buckling under the weight of the war in neighbouring Ukraine, soaring defence budgets and the loss of key eastern markets, the Baltic states have shown remarkable resilience.
The numbers tell the story. The Lithuanian economy is expected to grow by around 3 percent in 2026, according to forecasts by the European Commission, the OECD, the IMF and the EBRD, making it one of the faster-growing economies in the European Union. Latvia has returned to moderate growth, supported by EU investment and a resilient services sector, while Estonia is finally emerging from a prolonged slowdown as investment begins to recover.
Do delve into the business stories in the latest edition of The Baltic Times Magazine, and you’ll likely be fascinated by the growth, innovation and far-reaching plans.
"We have no intention of slowing down this year – in 2026, we plan to double our revenue once again," Paulius Grigas, CEO of KRS and our cover hero, who spent 14 years in the United States before returning to Lithuania and significantly strengthening the company's position in the country's construction sector, told The Baltic Times Magazine.
During 2025, KRS added more than 70 general construction and infrastructure projects to its order portfolio, with a combined value of nearly 130 million euro. The company's revenue surged from around 30 million euro to 69 million euro in 2025 alone, and it expects to double its revenue again in 2026.
Be it this story or any of the others, the bottom line is clear: geography alone does not determine economic performance. Institutions, policy choices and adaptability matter far more.
Amid the sabre-rattling, the Baltics should no longer be described as Europe's vulnerable frontier. They are becoming one of its most resilient regions. Investors who continue to apply a blanket "geopolitical discount" risk overlooking a simple reality: resilience and endurance have become one of the Baltics' strongest economic assets.

VILNIUS - Belarusians living in Lithuania gathered in Vilnius on Sunday to mark the sixth anniversary of mass protests against the rule of President Alexander Lukashenko.
The commemoration began with a rally in Cathedral Square, drawing about 100 people. Former political prisoners, politicians, civil society representatives and supporters of Belarus spoke about the struggle for democracy. Participants carried the historical white-red-white flags of Belarus, chanting "Long Live Belarus!" and singing songs that have become symbols of Belarusian solidarity.
Most Belarusians interviewed said they still believe the political situation in their country can change, although optimism has faded compared with 2020.
"I am not as optimistic as I was six years ago," said Anatolij Chinevic, a 32-year-old IT specialist who spent two and a half years in prison for participating in protests.
Meanwhile, 31-year-old Kaciaryna Kanapliova, a French teacher who moved to Lithuania four years ago, said she still holds onto hope for change.
"Of course we have hope; the faith hasn't died out. Maybe in a few years the situation will change. Our goal is to preserve our Belarusian identity within ourselves. Even if we live in different countries, we want to keep our identity," Kanapliova said.
Kanapliova emphasised that the events aimed to remind the world that the people of Belarus still resist the Lukashenko regime and support Ukraine.
Tatjana, a 53-year-old former medical centre administrator, said that even after six years she hopes for change and attended the rally to remind others that "Lukashenko lost the 2020 elections."
"Today we continue the fight for a free, democratic Belarus. We are doing what the people in Belarus cannot. I left to escape criminal prosecution after being detained twice, in 2022 and 2024," she said.
Ilja Mironov, a 44-year-old logistics specialist from Gomel who was previously imprisoned in Belarus, also expressed belief in future political change.
"We all remember the Soviet Union - it collapsed literally in six months, and in 1990 no one could imagine it was possible. But that Soviet empire fell, and independent republics emerged, including the Baltic states and Belarus. So, everything can change in Belarus too," Mironov said.
Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Cichanouskaja, who moved from Vilnius to Warsaw this year, said in a statement released on Sunday that the struggle for democracy was not over.
"We are determined to finish what we started in 2020. I truly believe Belarus can become a success story - a story of transition from dictatorship to democracy. Today I ask you to support Belarus, fight for the release of political prisoners, keep pressure on the Lukashenko regime, and, of course, stand firmly with Ukraine," Cichanouskaja said.
According to the Migration Department, about 48,000 Belarusian citizens hold residence permits in Lithuania. Most arrived after the events of 2020, primarily as labour migrants.
Following the rally, participants marched to the Belarusian embassy, where they observed a minute of silence for victims of political repression and those killed fighting for Ukraine's freedom. The events concluded with an acoustic concert by Jurij Stylski, leader of the Belarusian rock band Dai Darogu!.
Mass protests erupted in Belarus in August 2020 after Lukashenko claimed victory in a presidential election widely viewed as rigged. The authorities responded with a crackdown, detaining approximately 65,000 people. Key opposition figures were either jailed or forced into exile, leading to Western sanctions against the regime.

How the US Sports Betting Boom Changed the Way the World Watches American Sports  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:31:25 UTC
23:31:25 KST

If you weren't paying close attention, you probably missed how fast this all happened. Back in 2018 the US Supreme Court knocked down a federal law that had basically kept legal sports betting locked inside Nevada for something like 25 years. Fast forward to now, and most states have some version of it on the books. The industry that grew out of that decision is tangled up in pretty much everything about how American sports get broadcast, sponsored, even talked about on air.
You don't have to set foot inside a sportsbook to notice the change if you're watching from outside the US. Odds show up right on the broadcast graphics during NFL and NBA games now. Betting companies have their names on stadiums, on jersey patches, on entire pregame shows. Commentators throw around spreads and totals like it's nothing, the same casual way they used to talk about stats. A decade ago basically none of that existed in any mainstream sense. It's honestly a different media landscape at this point, and it happened fast enough that plenty of casual fans watching from abroad probably haven't clocked just how much shifted.
What's interesting from the outside is how messy the rollout has actually been. Betting regulation in the US gets handled state by state rather than federally, so the experience differs a lot depending on where you happen to be. Some states let you bet online with a bunch of different operators to choose from. Others only allow betting in person at a physical casino sportsbook. A few states still don't allow any of it. That's a pretty unusual setup by European standards, where gambling tends to get regulated at the national level, and it's a big reason the American market feels so scattered compared to how things work across the Baltics or the wider EU.
That patchwork has real consequences too. A sportsbook that's licensed and widely used in New Jersey might not exist at all in Texas. Bonuses, deposit limits, even which sports you can actually wager on — all of that can vary state to state, sometimes by a lot. Anyone trying to actually get a handle on the landscape, rather than just watching from a distance, is probably better off looking at a breakdown of sports betting sites in united states that covers how the market splits by state, since "US betting" isn't really one thing you can generalize about.
The numbers involved are still wild even with all that fragmentation. Industry tracking has put the amount wagered legally in the US at billions of dollars in a single year since things opened up after 2018 — a figure that would've sounded made up under the old Nevada-only rules. The American Gaming Association tracks a lot of this and puts out regular updates on state-by-state legal handle, which honestly tells you more than most of the headline numbers floating around do on their own.
For readers in the Baltics, the more interesting angle probably isn't the US market by itself — it's what this whole shift says about where sports broadcasting is headed generally. American leagues have leaned hard into betting-adjacent content, mostly because it keeps people watching deep into games that might otherwise be decided by halftime. Whether that catches on elsewhere or just stays a weirdly American thing is anyone's guess at this point. For more on how audiences outside the US are following American sports coverage, [FILL IN: link to a relevant existing baltictimes.com article/category] has more on that.
Either way, what's happened since 2018 counts as one of the bigger shifts in American sports culture in recent memory, even for people with zero interest in placing a bet themselves. It's changed what's on screen, who's sponsoring what, how broadcasters fill dead air during a blowout. Not a small thing for an industry that spent most of the last century operating on the exact opposite assumption.

VILNIUS - Lithuania's Culture Ministry has urged lawmakers to wait for a unified European Union position as parliament considers a proposal to ban social media use by minors under 16.
"A legislative initiative is currently being prepared at the EU level to establish a uniform age limit for social media users. Therefore, changing national legal regulations before a specific EU legal proposal is presented would be a suboptimal measure," the ministry stated in a report this week.
The European Union is weighing a potential social media ban following calls from member states, including Greece and France, to restrict access. Pressure is mounting for a bloc-wide ban similar to that in Australia, which requires platforms to remove accounts of children under 16.

In early April, the Seimas gave initial approval to a proposal by opposition lawmaker Daiva Ulbinaite to legalise a "digital age of majority." The bill would oblige social media providers to prevent individuals under 16 from becoming independent users.
Under the proposed changes, platforms would be required to ensure that minors under 16 cannot register or use services without legal grounds. Networks failing to comply would face fines.
The Ministry of Culture, which drafted the evaluation of the project, argues that changes should not be initiated now to avoid regulatory inconsistencies between Lithuania and European Union law.
Opinions on the proposed restriction remain divided in Lithuania. Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginiene argued that the most effective tool against addiction is youth engagement rather than bans. Speaker of the Seimas Juozas Olekas expressed scepticism, though he did not rule out potential restrictions. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas supported some level of restriction for those under 16, while Education, Science and Sport Minister Raminta Popoviene urged public consultation before proceeding.
A Baltijos Tyrimai poll commissioned by public broadcaster LRT in March showed that 75 percent of Lithuanians support restrictions for minors under 15, though nearly half, or 40 percent, of pupils and students oppose such a ban.

TALLINN, August 10 (BNS) - On Saturday, the V&K Teed One Mile Challenge 2026, a 1-mile standing start top speed competition, was held at the Kiltsi airfield, where a new Estonian speed record for passenger cars was set at 416 km/h.
The goal of the competition was to achieve the highest possible speed by the end of the one-mile (1609-meter) distance. Competitors also had the option to participate in a half-mile category. The event drew participants from Estonia as well as neighboring countries.
This year's fastest competitor was Aleksandr Ljahh in a Nissan Skyline GT-R, who set the new Estonian passenger car speed record at 416 km/h. With this, he broke his own record of 402 km/h, which had stood since 2020. This is likely the highest speed ever achieved by a passenger car on land in Estonia.
A speed of 416 km/h significantly exceeds the takeoff speed of large passenger aircraft such as the Boeing 747 or Airbus A380, and is surpassed only by the world's fastest high-speed trains. This means the car travels nearly 116 meters per second.
A total of 12 competitors broke the 300 km/h barrier during the competition. One of them, Anti Kevvai in a BMW 1M, reached this speed in the half-mile category.
In the overall standings, Ljahh was followed by Virgo Rikk in a Porsche 911 Turbo at 351 km/h and Aron Voola in a Ferrari 849 Testarossa at 343 km/h.
The fastest female competitor was Smilla Sangernebo, who reached 305 km/h in a Chevrolet Corvette. In the diesel category, Tarmo Pillerpau was the fastest, with his BMW 840xd clocking a final speed of 255 km/h.
Full results are available on the website https://www.onemile.ee/?lang=et&page=tulemused&year=2026.
The 416 km/h record set at the Kiltsi airfield demonstrates that Estonia's acceleration and top speed scene has reached a level where the benchmarks are no longer other cars, but airplanes and high-speed trains.

Russia currently lacks military capability to open another front against NATO countries - Sarts  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:31:10 UTC
23:31:10 KST

RIGA - As long as Russia's war in Ukraine continues, Russia will lack the military capability to open another front against NATO countries, and there are no signs that Russia is currently preparing for such an attack, Janis Sarts, Director of NATO Strategic Communications Center of Excellence, said during LETA podcast "What Was That All About?! (Kas Tas Vispar Bija).
"Russia is and will remain a threat to us, but that does not mean it is going to happen right here and now," said Sarts. For a military attack to occur, Russia must be capable of carrying it out, but it currently lacks that capability. NATO, meanwhile, has been working on its defense plans, he said.
Russia's military capabilities are currently constrained by the war in Ukraine. "As long as the war in Ukraine continues, Russia is unable to open another military front against NATO countries, and there are no signs that it intends to do so," said Sarts.
At the same time, this does not mean that the Baltic countries are not under threat. The threat of hybrid attacks always exists, but it is not unique to the Baltics - similar threats also exist for Germany and France.
The situation could change if the war in Ukraine were to end and Russia were to gain time to rebuild its military capabilities. Russia would most likely continue to build up its military, but experts differ in their assessments of how quickly it could restore its capabilities for a larger-scale war, said Sarts.
Therefore it is essential to distinguish between an immediate military threat and a risk that could grow over the course of several years. "It is one thing to pour all your resources into capabilities because someone is going to attack you in two weeks. It is another thing to allocate resources with the understanding that there is a specific time frame in which they must be maximized. These are two different decisions," Sarts explained.
He also spoke critically on statements about a possible imminent Russian attack on the Baltic countries. Such scaremongering is counterproductive, he said, because it hinders serious discussions about what Latvia actually needs to prepare for.
"I like that we base our discussions on data and facts," said Sarts, emphasizing that defense decisions must be made by assessing the actual situation, rather than by maintaining a constant state of panic among the public.

How Wes Streeting is faring as Defence Secretary
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:30:42 BST
23:30:42 KST

Three weeks into the job, Wes Streeting has delivered a keynote at Farnborough, stood alongside the Prime Minister in Barrow for an £8.4 billion submarine announcement, toured the frigate hall at Rosyth, and repeatedly declined to guarantee the spending target that his predecessor resigned over, which is a reasonable summary of both the energy he has brought to the role and the one question hanging over it.
He arrived at Main Building on 20 July, appointed by Andy Burnham in his first cabinet, becoming the department’s third Secretary of State in a matter of months following John Healey’s resignation on 11 June and Dan Jarvis’s brief caretaker tenure. Healey, who quit saying the Treasury had been unwilling to commit the resources the country needed at a time of rising threats, is now Chancellor, which means the man who walked out of Defence over funding is the one now holding the purse strings, an arrangement Streeting has been quick to point to as grounds for confidence.
The appointment drew a mixed reception, with a former head of the British Army reported as disappointed by the choice and some in the defence community questioning what a politician with no service background would bring to a warfighting department, though that reading rather undersells the record he arrived with, doesn’t it?
He had run Health for two years and shadowed it for three before that, which is a longer apprenticeship in a major department of state than most Defence Secretaries bring to the post, and his time there involved negotiating and then delivering a substantial spending settlement while driving down staff vacancy rates, experience that translates more directly to the Ministry of Defence than his critics allowed, given that recruitment, retention and the management of very large procurement budgets are among the department’s most persistent difficulties.
His framing on the day of the appointment was characteristically direct, saying that keeping the country safe is the first duty of government and that the armed forces would have the resources they need, with particular emphasis on standing steadfast alongside allies and Ukraine, and he has stuck to that line since without embellishment.
His first substantial outing came two days later at the AGF Defence Summit at Farnborough, where he told the audience that more than £11.8 billion in contracts had been agreed in the ten days following publication of the Defence Investment Plan, declaring that defence was up and flying again.
Alongside over £1 billion for Typhoon upgrades and continued commitment to the £8.6 billion GCAP programme with Italy and Japan, he set out work on the Storm Fighter collaborative combat aircraft and an ambition for a prototype of the uncrewed Brontanax to conduct a test flight next year, while also thanking industry for persevering through the delays to the investment plan, an acknowledgement that the document had arrived late and amid considerable friction.
Where the questions concentrate is on money, because when pressed at Farnborough and repeatedly since on whether the government will reach three per cent of GDP by 2030, Streeting has declined to give the guarantee. His argument is fiscal rather than strategic, namely that announcing a figure without setting out how it will be funded invites a loss of market confidence and rising borrowing costs, a trap he says previous governments fell into repeatedly, and he has been consistent in saying that this government will pair any new commitment with an explanation of how it is paid for. He has said that he supported Healey’s resignation over the funding question, describes the new Chancellor as a firm friend of defence, and insists he has every confidence the investment plan will be fully funded, while declining to rule out tax rises as part of the answer.
Critics have not found that entirely satisfying, given that Healey resigned saying he was certain Britain should reach three per cent by 2030 and his successor is now defending the absence of precisely that commitment, though it is worth noting that Burnham himself declined to commit to the target the day before the Barrow visit, and supporters would argue that a pledge arriving with a funding mechanism attached is worth considerably more than one that does not. Sitting behind all of it is NATO’s push towards 3.5 per cent by 2035, alongside the Office for Budget Responsibility’s earlier assessment that reaching three per cent would cost an additional £17.3 billion in 2029-30.
On delivery, the record so far consists largely of announcements he inherited rather than initiated, since the £8.4 billion Dreadnought contract with BAE Systems was agreed before he took office and the Defence Investment Plan, which converts the 2025 Strategic Defence Review into commitments spanning naval base modernisation, the frigate programmes, the F-35A purchase and the Hybrid Navy, was published three weeks before he arrived. That is less a criticism than an observation about timing though, because any Secretary of State three weeks into the post is by definition executing a plan drawn up by someone else, and his visit to Rosyth and Edinburgh on 7 August, taking in Type 31 construction and service family accommodation, followed a well-established pattern of demonstrating that defence spending reaches well beyond the south east.
The tests that will genuinely define the tenure remain ahead of him, among them whether the investment plan survives sustained contact with the Treasury, whether the frigate and submarine programmes hold their schedules, whether recruitment and retention begin to improve, and whether the three per cent question is eventually settled with a funding route attached.
On the evidence of the first three weeks, though, there is rather more to be encouraged by than not, because he has been visible where it matters, notably fluent in front of industry audiences who had every reason to be sceptical, and clear that his purpose is deterrence backed by the capability to fight if it fails. A department that has churned through three Secretaries of State since June needed someone willing to grip it quickly and make the case for defence in terms the Treasury understands, and on both counts he has started well, with a Chancellor who resigned this very job over funding sitting across the table from him and a Prime Minister who has pledged to fund the plan in full.
The commitments still have to arrive, but the groundwork looks sound.
This article is the opinion of the author and not necessarily that of the UK Defence Journal. If you would like to submit your own article on this topic or any other, please see our submission guidelines.
