Rare astronomical spectacle: Partial solar eclipse to darken much of Lithuania’s sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

A partial solar eclipse will offer Lithuanians a rare astronomical spectacle on August 12, with the moon expected to cover about 75% to 81% of the sun’s disk, according to astronomers at Vilnius University.
The eclipse will not be equally visible across the country. Because it will occur in the evening, the sun will be very low over the western horizon, making Lithuania’s western coast the best location for viewing the event.
Astronomer Edita Stonkutė said the last time Lithuanians witnessed such a prominent partial solar eclipse was March 20, 2015.
A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes directly between the sun and Earth, casting its shadow across part of Earth’s surface, according to Vilnius University astrophysicist Kastytis Zubovas.
A total solar eclipse will be visible along a narrow path stretching across northern Russia, Greenland, Iceland, the Atlantic Ocean, northern Spain and a small part of northeastern Portugal. Areas outside that path, including Lithuania, will see a partial eclipse.
Because the sun and moon are not point-like objects, the moon casts two types of shadow: a central shadow, where the sun is completely obscured, and a wider penumbral region, where only part of the sun is covered. The latter extends thousands of kilometres on either side of the path of totality.
Best viewing times
In Lithuania, the eclipse will begin at about 20:08 in the Klaipėda and Šiauliai regions. The maximum phase will occur between 20:53 and 21:00, depending on location.
In Klaipėda, the eclipse will reach its maximum at 21:00, with the moon covering about 81.34% of the sun’s disk. The eclipse will end at about 21:50.
Klaipėda and the coastal resorts of Nida and Palanga are therefore expected to offer some of the best viewing conditions in Lithuania.
In Vilnius, the eclipse will begin at 20:09, reach its maximum at 20:53 and end at 21:49. About 75.04% of the sun’s disk will be covered.
But the sun will set before the eclipse ends.
“In Vilnius, the sun will set at 20:57 p.m., so after that we will no longer be able to see it, even though the eclipse will not yet have ended,” Stonkutė said. “Because the coast is farther west, the sun sets there about 20 minutes later than in Vilnius, so the eclipse can be observed for longer, although we still won’t see it through to the end.”
The most dramatic phase of the eclipse will last only a moment, but Stonkutė said the most impressive portion should be visible for about 15 to 20 minutes around the maximum.
Because the sun will be close to the horizon, astronomers recommend choosing a location with a broad, unobstructed view to the northwest. Beaches, lake shores, elevated areas and open fields are among the best options.
The Vilnius University Molėtai Astronomical Observatory will also invite visitors to observe the eclipse, weather permitting.
Do not look directly at the sun
Astronomers warn that the eclipse must not be viewed directly with the naked eye, even briefly. Ordinary sunglasses do not provide adequate protection.
“Even normally, you should not look at the sun without proper eye protection or with ordinary sunglasses,” Zubovas said. “During an eclipse, there is an additional danger: As the amount of visible light decreases sharply, the pupil naturally dilates, allowing much more ultraviolet radiation from the sun to enter the eye.”
Stonkutė said even the uncovered portion of the sun during a partial eclipse remains bright enough to damage the retina.
“The danger is increased by the fact that the retina has no pain receptors, so vision can be damaged without the person noticing it and without pain or discomfort,” she said.
Astronomers recommend using specially designed solar-viewing glasses with filters that block both visible and ultraviolet radiation.
Stonkutė said safe eclipse-viewing glasses cannot be reliably made at home. She also advised against improvised methods involving smoked glass, X-ray film, photographic film, CDs, tinted plastic or multiple pairs of sunglasses.
If certified solar glasses are unavailable, the safest alternative is indirect viewing. A simple pinhole can be made in a piece of cardboard or paper, allowing an image of the sun to be projected onto a light-coloured surface without looking directly at the sun.
A rare opportunity
Partial solar eclipses are not particularly rare in Lithuania, Zubovas said, but the August 12 event will stand out because of the large portion of the sun that will be covered.
Stonkutė said the last similarly impressive eclipse visible in Lithuania occurred in 2015, when up to about 78% of the sun’s disk was obscured in the western part of the country.
“Although there will be no total eclipse in Lithuania on August 12, 2026, this will be one of the most impressive opportunities in recent decades to watch the moon cover most of the sun’s disk,” she said.
Partial eclipses will also be visible in Lithuania in 2027, 2029 and 2030. The 2030 eclipse is expected to be relatively large, similar to this year’s event, Zubovas said.
An annular solar eclipse will be visible in Lithuania on June 21, 2039. During an annular eclipse, the moon passes between Earth and the sun but is too far from Earth to completely cover the sun, leaving a bright ring around the moon.
Total solar eclipses are much rarer in Lithuania. The last time the moon’s central shadow crossed Lithuanian territory was June 30, 1954. The next will not occur until May 25, 2142.
“That means 188 years will pass between one total solar eclipse and the next in Lithuania,” Stonkutė said. “These two events are separated not only by time but by several generations, making a total solar eclipse one of the rarest astronomical spectacles in our country.”
Spain prepares for its own eclipse spectacle
While Lithuania will see only a partial eclipse, parts of Spain will experience totality on August 12.
The event will be the first of what astronomers have dubbed a “Spanish trio” of major solar eclipses. A second total eclipse will cross Spain on August 2, 2027, followed by an annular eclipse on January 26, 2028.
Such a sequence of major eclipses in one country is extremely unusual, Stonkutė said.
The eclipse will also provide scientists with opportunities to study the sun and Earth’s atmosphere.
Stonkutė noted that helium was discovered through observations made during a solar eclipse in the 19th century, when astronomers detected an unknown spectral line in sunlight.
During the total solar eclipse of May 29, 1919, British astronomer Arthur Eddington observed stars near the obscured sun and found that their apparent positions had shifted slightly because their light was bent by the sun’s gravity. The observation provided early evidence supporting Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity.
Today, scientists use eclipses to study the sun’s outer atmosphere, or corona, which is normally difficult to observe. Space-based instruments can now create artificial eclipses by blocking the sun’s disk, reducing the scientific importance of natural eclipses for some types of solar research, Zubovas said.
Researchers also study how eclipses affect Earth’s atmosphere. Temperatures can fall by several degrees within minutes, while wind patterns and cloud formation can change.
Animals can respond to the sudden darkness as well. Birds may become quiet or stop singing earlier than usual, bees may return to their hives and some animals may behave as though evening has arrived. These changes are generally temporary and reverse when sunlight returns, Stonkutė said.
Perseid meteor shower and lunar eclipse
The solar eclipse will be followed by another celestial event. The Perseid meteor shower is expected to reach its peak overnight August 12-13, with an average of 60 to 80 meteors visible per hour under favourable conditions.
The meteors are remnants of material about 4.5 billion years old. No special equipment is needed to watch the shower, and activity can also be observed for several days before and after the peak.
The summer astronomical season will end with a partial lunar eclipse early August 28.
During a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the sun and moon, causing Earth’s shadow to fall across the moon. The moon can take on a reddish colour because some red light is refracted through Earth’s atmosphere.
The August 28 eclipse will be partial, with about 96% of the moon’s disk entering Earth’s shadow. In Lithuania, however, only the beginning will be visible because the moon will set before the eclipse reaches its maximum.
The eclipse will begin at 05:34 in Lithuania, and the moon will set at 06:18, when about 58% of the eclipse will have occurred.
Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse can be viewed safely with the naked eye. Astronomers recommend choosing a location with a clear, unobstructed horizon, such as the Lithuanian coast.

Nearly 70 percent of France under water restrictions amid record heat
Nearly 70 percent of France is now under water-use restrictions as successive heatwaves and severe drought intensify pressure on the country’s water supplies. Authorities said Monday that 67 of 101 departments had reached the highest crisis alert, while two-thirds of groundwater reserves were below normal levels. Another heatwave is expected to spread across the country this week.
Nearly 70 percent of France is subject to water-use restrictions as drought conditions worsen amid successive heatwaves, the government said Monday.
A series of heatwaves over the past three months, compounded by drought, have broken temperature records, caused thousands of excess deaths, and fuelled massive wildfires.
"As France is experiencing a particularly severe drought, the effects of climate change continue to increase pressure on water resources," the ministry for ecological transition said, adding that "nearly 70 percent of French territory is subject to restrictions on water use".
As of August 9, the vast majority of mainland France, including Paris, was under at least the first water warning level, with 67 of the country's 101 departments under the highest crisis alert.
In areas subject to the highest alert, water is reserved for priority uses such as healthcare, civil protection, drinking water and sanitation.
Under lower alert levels, restrictions apply to activities such as watering gardens and green spaces, filling swimming pools, washing cars and irrigating crops.
In a further sign of the worsening drought across much of heatwave-pummelled Europe, two thirds of the aquifers that provide most of France's drinking water have dropped below their normal levels, the country's Bureau of Geological and Mining Research (BRGM) said on Monday.
The drawdown of groundwater reserves, common during the summer, is particularly pronounced this year "due to the shortfall in effective rainfall in July and the increase in water demand for various purposes", particularly in agriculture and tourism, the BRGM said.
Read moreWestern Europe lived through hottest June and July ever recorded
July 2026 was the hottest month ever recorded in France and the third driest July in terms of precipitation, with a nationwide rainfall deficit of nearly 70 percent, according to national weather agency Meteo-France.
Ecology Minister Monique Barbut said on July 27 that drinking water supplies were "under strain in several areas", noting that tap water cuts were already affecting "more than 30,000 people", with drinking water supplied to residents by tanker trucks or bottled water.
The minister will convene a crisis meeting on the drought on Wednesday, which comes as France and swaths of Europe face another heatwave.
Meteo-France warned on Monday the southeast would see temperatures as high as 35°C, spreading further across the country as the week progresses.

Expert outlines new technologies for Belarusian roads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:26:00 UTC
23:26:00 KST

File photo
                    
                    MINSK, 10 August (BelTA) – Technologies that could form the basis of Belarusian roads over the next decade were discussed by Sergei Kabak, Head of the sectoral road laboratory at the Belarusian road research institute (BeldorNII) in BelTA’s The Nation Speaks project.
 
 
 
 
  
  
 
Asked about technologies that could form the basis of Belarusian roads over the next decade, Sergei Kabak highlighted solutions already being used on the M4 highway, which are adaptations of foreign experience. 
 
“The ‘washed concrete’ technology has proved effective in the construction of cement-concrete pavements. It was used on the M14 highway (the second ring road) near the Molodechno highway. The essence of the technology is that, when laying a cement-concrete pavement, simple and readily available chemical reagents are used to soften the upper layer. This slows down the setting of the concrete. After some time, brushes remove the weakened cement paste. As a result, the coarse aggregate is exposed, providing a high coefficient of adhesion and high roughness, which significantly improves the pavement’s transport and operational characteristics,” Sergei Kabak said.

“There have been so many amazing moments and shows over these seven seasons. I am forever grateful and honored to have worked alongside the greatest band and crew you could hope for, all the talent and inspiring people who have shared their time and lives with us, all the fans who have supported our show and to NBC for always being such a supportive and incredible partner.
“Because of all of that, this was not an easy decision, but this season will be my last hosting [The Kelly Clarkson Show]. Stepping away from the daily schedule will allow me to prioritize my kids, which feels necessary and right for this next chapter of our lives.”
She assured fans that “this isn’t goodbye. I’ll still be making music, playing shows here and there and you may catch me on The Voice from time to time … you never know where I might show up next.”
“But for now, I want to thank y’all so much for allowing our show to be a part of your lives, and for believing in us and hanging with us for seven incredible years,” Clarkson concluded.

Popular Powerball strategy debunked by math professor as jackpot soars to historic sum
- Monday evening's Powerball drawing features a $905 million jackpot, making it the 16th-largest lottery prize in American history and the eighth-largest in Powerball history after 42 consecutive drawings without a grand prize winner.
- Ahead of the draw, USC mathematics Professor Emeritus Ken Alexander warned that buying tickets at a location where winning tickets with large jackpots have been sold in the past will not increase a player's chance of landing the jackpot.
- "The chance that a given place will sell a winning lottery ticket is just related to how many tickets they sell," Alexander told City News Service.
- Players wanting a better chance of avoiding sharing a jackpot should choose numbers that aren't selected as often, Alexander said. Lottery players frequently choose the date of their birthdays as one of their numbers, so numbers higher than 31 would be played less, Alexander said.
- The odds of matching all five numbers and the Powerball number is 1 in 292.2 million, according to the Multi-State Lottery Association, which conducts the game. The overall chance of winning a prize is 1 in 24.9.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Monday some Iranian missiles can now be guided and change course during flight, allowing them to evade air defense systems.
“Iranian missiles are no longer like they were in the past, merely launched from one point to land at another,” the official IRNA news agency quoted IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohabi as saying at an event in the northern city of Qazvin.
“They now possess guidance and course-changing capabilities, and some can alter their trajectory during flight to bypass the enemy’s air defense systems,” he added.
Mohabi said the Iranian capabilities were used during the recent war with the US to target parts of what he described as the “enemy’s power network.”

Iran is engaged in a military conflict with Washington since the US and Israel launched a joint offensive against Tehran in February, fueling regional tensions. Tehran retaliated with attacks targeting regional countries hosting US military assets.
Iran and the US agreed to a ceasefire in April and subsequently signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending their military conflict and reaching a lasting peace agreement.
The deal, however, collapsed last month with Tehran and Washington exchanging attacks for nearly two weeks before US President Donald Trump abruptly halted the bombardment amid reports of talks to resolve the conflict.

Blink-182’s Travis Barker almost died. A new documentary celebrates his life before and after
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

Blink-182’s Travis Barker almost died. A new documentary celebrates his life before and after
NEW YORK (AP) — The inferno rages onscreen three minutes into “ Travis Barker: Louder Than Fear.” Dashcam footage lifted from a police car shows the blaze: It’s 2008, and Barker has survived a plane crash in South Carolina. Four others did not.
And then, a cut. The documentary, which follows the Blink-182 drummer from 2017 to 2026, is a celebration of Barker’s life before and after the life-altering accident, a central event in a career full of them. The film began as a mirror of his memoir, 2015’s “Can I Say: Living Large, Cheating Death, and Drums, Drums, Drums,” but became something else entirely after a producer suggested it end with the image of Barker, then still unable to fly due to post-traumatic stress disorder, walking toward a plane.
Ending on that note, “where this thing still has power over me,” didn’t sit well with him. Instead, he boards a plane at the end, but the documentary’s final images are a slide show of family photos, including his wife Kourtney Kardashian and kids.
“I almost died,” he says. It “could be helpful to share my life.”
An elastic artist
Barker’s resume is long, and a two-and-a-half-hour documentary can only cover so much of it. The film hits most of the big notes, quickly establishing Barker as a rebellious kid with a supernatural drumming ability from age 4, when he got his first kit, to now, at 50.
And that’s with many projects in-between: From the SoCal punks Feeble, which he joined while working as a trash collector, to his stint in the ska band The Aquabats and multiplatinum, pop-punk legends Blink-182 — the band that skyrocketed Barker into superstardom.
Also covered? His love of skateboarding and car culture, his clothing brands, side-projects Box Car Racer and +44, turntable duo TRV$DJAM, various experiments and collaborations in hip-hop (Bun B, Lil Wayne ) and beyond.
But it all began with drumming, and hilariously enough, Animal from “The Muppets” — his first drumming hero — until he discovered cross-genre greats like jazz legends Buddy Rich, Dennis Chambers and Elvin Jones as well as Mötley Crüe’s Tommy Lee.
“Where drumming got really serious for me was after my mom passed, so it was therapy,” he says, reflecting on his childhood. “It’s like my life. It’s like oxygen to me.”
It’s also a kind of sport. Barker has long been a dedicated, athletic percussionist, and he likens it to a boxer’s meditative state. “It’s like when you see a fighter and he just goes for broke the first round. There’s sometimes where I just feel like that,” he says. “Something just takes over my body.”
Many events in life threatened that euphoria, but none quite as physically as the plane crash. “I was in a burn center for six months on morphine and I had 30 surgeries,” he recounts. “Seventy percent of my body was burned.” At one point, he didn’t only fear if he would be able to drum again — even walking was a question mark.
Lessons from tragedy
Even before the crash, Barker’s life — as marked with musical triumphs as it has been — offered lessons in resiliency.
“Whether it was my mom passing away or my plane crash, I learned — and through watching friends of mine and just living life — I’ve seen traumatic experiences either destroy someone or define them,” he says. “Every loss I had, or every everything I took to the chin, it made me stronger. At the time, I can’t realize it, right? I can’t like really wrap my head around it. But ... that’s why I went so hard and I was so determined to play music and so determined to succeed. Plan B was only making Plan A work. You know? There was no Plan B.”
The same tenacity can be applied to his sobriety and dedication to flying again — a journey emboldened by his family. “I fly all the time now and I feel turbulence and I can’t even tell you what’s going on in my head. And I just look over and my wife’s perfectly OK,” he says. “My son loves airplanes and plays with airplanes and it’s so innocent. It’s so beautiful.”
“They’ve been my greatest joy,” he says of his children, who grow up on screen across the film’s near-decade of filming.
As someone who has lost a lot and thought about what it would be like to lose even more, when it comes to the topic of legacy, Barker has a simple dream. “I think I’d want to be remembered for my music and my drumming and being a great father, husband, and son and brother,” he says.
As for the doc? “Maybe my story helps somebody,” he pauses. “I don’t love how everything happened. I don’t like the losses that happened. But I like how hard I had to work. I like that I wasn’t born with a silver spoon in my mouth. I liked that I had to navigate and find my way. And the journey was awesome.”

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Alabama’s special congressional primaries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Alabama’s special congressional primaries
WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters in four of Alabama’s seven congressional districts will select U.S. House nominees Tuesday under a new map that eliminates one of the state’s two majority-Black districts currently represented by Democrats.
Primaries for all seven congressional districts were originally scheduled for May 19, but Republican Gov. Kay Ivey postponed the contests for the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts following a U.S. Supreme Court decision that prompted a handful of Republican-controlled Southern states to throw out their congressional maps.
The court-inspired actions in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee, as well as earlier legislative actions in other states to redraw their boundaries through mid-decade redistricting, were part of a nationwide Republican effort championed by President Donald Trump to maximize the party’s chances of holding its slim U.S. House majority in the 2026 midterm elections.
Alabama’s U.S. House members will continue to serve in their current districts until the end of 2026. Candidates in Tuesday’s primaries are running under the new Republican-backed boundaries, which go into effect in January 2027. Both of Alabama’s Democratic members of Congress are seeking reelection in their newly configured districts and are unopposed in their primaries.
In the 2nd District, where U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures is running for a second term, the Black population will go from half of the population under the current lines to about 40% under the new lines. In the 2024 presidential election, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris beat Trump in the current district, 53% to 46%. But Trump would have beaten Harris 57% to 42% if the new boundaries had been in effect in 2024.
Six Republicans are running to challenge Figures in November, including state Rep. Rhett Marques, Army veteran Joshua McKee and real estate broker Hampton Harris. Trump has endorsed Marques, who is the field’s top fundraiser.
Black residents will maintain a slight majority in the new 7th District, where U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell is running for a ninth term. Harris beat Trump, 61% to 38%, under the current boundaries and would have beaten him by slightly less, 58% to 41%, if the new boundaries had been in effect in 2024. Two Republicans, Ammie Akin and David Perry, are competing for the nomination to unseat Sewell.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. CT, which is 8 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts.
Who gets to vote?
The special primaries are open to any registered voters in their respective congressional districts. Although Alabama does not register voters by party, voters will be asked to declare a party preference upon selecting a party’s primary ballot.
How many voters are there?
As of June 1, there were 3.8 million registered voters in Alabama. Each congressional district in the state has a total population of about 718,000.
How many people actually vote?
About 409,000 ballots were cast across the state in the May 19 primaries, which was roughly 11% of registered voters. Past vote totals for the four new congressional districts are unavailable.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
Relatively few Alabama voters cast their ballots before Election Day. The state is one of the only holdouts in the country not to offer some form of in-person early voting. In the 2024 primaries, about 4% of Democratic primary voters and about 1% of Republican primary voters voted by mail.
When are early and absentee votes released?
Vote release practices vary from county to county. Most counties tend to release results from absentee voting in the first vote update, sometimes along with results from in-person Election Day voting.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the May 19 state primary, the AP first reported results at 8:28 p.m. ET, or 28 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 12:54 a.m. ET, with more than 99.9% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
In 2010, the Alabama attorney general issued an opinion that Alabama’s automatic recount law does not apply to primaries. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 84 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Israeli closure of Christian village Taybeh harms Palestinians, livelihoods: Mayor

Qais Omar Darwesh and Lina Altawell
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
The mayor of the Palestinian Christian village Taybeh in the occupied West Bank warned Monday of the repercussions of Israel’s decision to declare the area a “closed military zone,” saying it harms residents and their livelihoods.
Earlier Monday, the Israeli army declared the village near Ramallah a “closed military zone” to prevent rising attacks by occupiers. Under the decision, Israelis and foreigners are barred from entering the area.
Speaking to Anadolu, Mayor Suleiman Khoury said municipal authorities have not yet been officially notified of the decision or details on how it would be implemented.
“Preventing foreigners from entering Taybeh would harm residents, as the town is a tourist destination with hotels, restaurants and facilities that depend on visitors and tourists,” he said.
“Some residents make their living from tourism, making restrictions on foreign entry a direct blow to economic activity and income sources,” Khoury added.
He questioned the usefulness of the decision if Israel’s declared goal was to protect Taybeh residents from occupier attacks, particularly as assaults on Palestinians and their property continue.
“Israeli occupiers continue attacking, vandalizing and grazing on the village’s land,” he said, adding that protecting residents should be done “by stopping occupier attacks, not by imposing new restrictions on the village.”
The mayor described the decision as “an attempt to tighten the noose on residents more than a measure to protect them.”
Taybeh is one of the most prominent Palestinian Christian-majority areas and is known for its religious, historical and tourist significance.
The village includes ancient churches and archaeological sites, while tourism is one of the important sources of income for its residents.
The Israeli decision came days after Taybeh came under attack by Israeli occupiers on Friday.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers carried out 3,488 attacks against Palestinians and their property during the first half of this year.
The attacks include assaults on Palestinians, burning homes, vehicles and structures, uprooting trees and razing agricultural land. They also include preventing farmers from reaching their land, establishing new illegal settlement outposts and seizing Palestinian land.
Commission figures show around 750,000 occupiers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 settlement outposts in the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.

“Putinist formalism has arrived”: Contemporary art in Russia is struggling to survive under state repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:22:40 UTC
23:22:40 KST

In July, Russian authorities canceled the Outline music and arts festival, officially due to the threat of drone attacks. After the GULAG History Museum in Moscow was forced to close, in June a state-run institution dedicated to documenting the “genocide of the Soviet people” opened on the vacated site. And in mid-May, photographs by Alexander Gronsky were covered with cloth at the Kontur art fair in Nizhny Novgorod. These developments vividly illustrate the conditions under which the art world now operates in Russia. Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the government has dramatically tightened censorship of exhibitions and art festivals, using curators with ties to the security services and organized groups of informants to monitor the situation. Museums and galleries have been subjected to searches, with staff and artists detained. Some artists continue to resist pressure and persecution, while others have chosen to leave the country. Still others have embraced self-censorship, abandoning any political subject matter altogether. Museum directors have sharply reduced the number of contemporary exhibitions, and staff members deemed insufficiently loyal have been dismissed.
Beginning in the late 2000s, Russia’s contemporary art scene sought to integrate itself into the global cultural landscape. Patrons invested heavily in the sector — billionaire Novatek head Leonid Mikhelson, for example, spent hundreds of millions of dollars setting up the V–A–C Foundation and opening the GES-2 cultural center in central Moscow.
Since 2005, Moscow has hosted the Moscow International Biennale of Contemporary Art, while in 2014 St. Petersburg hosted the major European contemporary art biennial Manifesta 10 as part of the state-sponsored Year of Culture program.
Russian art was also widely exhibited abroad. In 2005–2006, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York hosted the exhibition RUSSIA!, showcasing landmark Russian art ranging from Andrei Rublev’s icons to Socialist Realism and contemporary works. During those years, the state not only refrained from interfering with the development of the contemporary art industry but actively supported it.
The situation changed dramatically after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. On February 25, 2022, several thousand artists signed an open letter calling for the war to be stopped. But in early March, after the government adopted a law criminalizing the spread of so-called “fake news” about the Russian army, the publication Spectate removed both the text of the letter and the list of signatories.
Among the first artists to fall victim to the new laws was Sasha Skochilenko. She was arrested in March 2022 under the “fake news” statute after attempting to replace supermarket price tags with stickers containing information about the actions of the Russian military in Ukraine. She was released only in August 2024, as part of a major international prisoner exchange.
Against the backdrop of the new bans and restrictions, some artists chose to leave the country. One of them was Pavel Otdelnov, who in 2022 published his politically charged “Scenes from a Nightmare” series before relocating to the United Kingdom.
In September 2022, searches were carried out at the homes of Maksim Evstropov and Kristina Bubentsova, members of the art collective Party of the Dead. Citing a law enforcement source, the outlet Peterburgsky Format reported that the searches were conducted as part of a criminal investigation into actions that were suspected to have “insulted the feelings of [religious] believers.” The members of Party of the Dead later explained on their VKontakte page that the case had been prompted by their Easter post containing “an unflattering statement about Patriarch Kirill, who supports the war and kisses the president’s ass.”
On the same day, searches were also conducted at the homes of artists Dmitry Vilensky and Olga Tsaplya of the collective “What Is to Be Done?” The founders of the DK Rozy cultural center and the School of Engaged Art, where Evstropov had taught for the previous several years, also got visits from the authorities.
Evstropov, Vilensky, and Tsaplya all left Russia after the searches, and in June 2023, the “What Is to Be Done?” collective announced that it was closing the DK Rozy space and ending the work of the School of Engaged Art. At the same time, the artists introduced a new initiative, the What Is to Be Done Mutual Aid Fund, intended to support both artists who remained in Russia and those who found themselves in difficult circumstances abroad. Assistance is provided through personal and confidential channels, though the artists noted that they are still “severely restricted in their ability to spend Western grant funding inside Russia” — meaning that the mutual aid effort is financed from their own resources.
The growing crackdown
As the war continued, state repression spread to a much broader circle of artists. In March 2024, searches were carried out in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Nizhny Novgorod, Samara, Yekaterinburg, Perm, and Ulyanovsk. The authorities linked the operation to an investigation into Pyotr Verzilov, a member of the art collective Pussy Riot who left Russia in 2020 before taking up arms for Ukraine. Some of the artists questioned in the probe said they had never even met Verzilov.
According to independent outlet Mediazona, searches were conducted at the homes of at least 20 people, including performance artist Katrin Nenasheva, two additional members of the Party of the Dead collective, Pussy Riot members Margarita Konovalova (Rita Flores), Olga Kuracheva, and Olga Pakhtusova, as well as artist Anatoly Osmolovsky, a co-founder of the Baza Institute. Searches were also conducted at the home of a female acquaintance of the artist Philippenzo, who had left Russia after a criminal case was opened against him on charges of “vandalism motivated by political hatred,” stemming from his street artwork Izrossilovanie. Some of the artists were detained by police as witnesses in the Verzilov case but were released shortly afterward.
In September 2024, searches were carried out at the Baza Institute of Contemporary Art, located on the grounds of Moscow's Winzavod Center for Contemporary Art. Following the searches, Baza director Svetlana Baskova announced that the institution would close: “We realized that we didn't want the people close to us — our students and those who were planning to enroll — to suffer because of this. We simply don't know what may await them. That's why we stopped accepting new students.”
At the same time, Baskova said she did not know why the searches had been conducted: “There was nothing prohibited at the institute. Perhaps some people simply don't like contemporary art. It seems to speak a different language, one that may be difficult to understand and can appear provocative.”
“Some people simply don't like contemporary art: it speaks a different language, one that is difficult to understand and seems provocative”
In an interview with Meduza, Baskova and Osmolovsky said that officers had come to search the institute under Article 228 of the Russian Criminal Code, which covers drug offenses. However, the real reasons for the search remain unclear. Art theorist Boris Klyushnikov, who taught at Baza, told The Insider that Osmolovsky had long irritated the authorities: “He is associated with actionism — he embodies actionism — and that's why they cracked down on Baza.” According to Klyushnikov, that wave of searches was particularly harsh: “They even tortured people to make them hand over our teaching materials.”
Another target of state repression has been the festival culture associated with contemporary art. The festival Kholod i Ogonyok (lit. Cold and Flame), a Russian counterpart to Burning Man, was targeted in a raid by the nationalist group Russian Community, which described the event as “a festival of sodomites and drug addicts.”
Other contemporary art festivals have also faced pressure from state and pro-government actors. In August 2024, security forces shut down the independent contemporary art festival Naiznanku in the Moscow region. Officers ordered participants to leave immediately, threatening to call in a special police unit. They said the reason for the operation was the “unauthorized holding of a mass public event.”
Informants and blacklists
In recent years, the security services have sought to tighten their control over major art institutions using a hybrid system in which denunciations by activists against unwanted participants in exhibitions and festivals are combined with on-site oversight by security service personnel. Irina (name changed for security reasons), a curator who works with several Moscow galleries, told The Insider that the state’s efforts are very thorough:
“The censorship is total. For example, every contemporary art fair, even if it's privately owned and commercial, is inspected by the state. Organizers are required to provide FSB curators with a list of every artist participating in the fair. First they check the names, and then, the day before the opening, the curators come to the venue and inspect the works themselves. If they don't like a particular piece, they can have it removed. They may object to the subject matter. Say you've painted a she-devil — they might take it down. They may not like the colors either. Yellow and blue are an instant ban.”
Irina said that, as a result, “self-censorship has also reached incredible levels,” as all artists, even those with no connection whatsoever to social or political issues, fear that their works could be removed.
Aleksandra (name changed for security reasons), the founder of a contemporary art gallery in Moscow, said that FSB officers themselves compile blacklists of artists — and it is not only public opponents of the war who are targeted:
“I get the impression these lists are compiled based on whether you know someone the authorities dislike. You can barely know another artist, post a social media ‘story’ with them, and end up on the list yourself. But you get used to it. You live with the fact that there's a file on you.”
Asked what legal grounds FSB officers cite when exerting such pressure, The Insider's sources responded with bewilderment: “We've reached the point where they're simply told to shut something down, and it gets shut down without explanation,” said Dmitry (name changed for security reasons), a curator from a major Russian city.
If an institution's management refuses to compromise, however, its leaders themselves may face persecution and dismissal. This is what happened to Nailya Allakhverdiyeva, the director of the PERMM Museum of Contemporary Art. She led the museum for ten years but was forced to resign under the combined pressure of the FSB and various conservative activist groups.
The initial trigger for the campaign against Allakhverdiyeva was a meeting she held with the British consul. Threats from activists affiliated with the Young Guard and other organizations soon followed, with questions as to why the museum was not staging “exhibitions about the Special Military Operation.” This campaign was followed by searches and interrogations. In 2024, Allakhverdiyeva resigned from the museum and left Russia. In the summer of 2025, she was placed on the country’s wanted list in connection with a criminal case over allegedly offending the feelings of believers.
The curator Dmitry said that, in his experience, the biggest problems are caused not by state officials but by informants:
“Every region has its own group of informants. They identify the participants in a particular event, comb through their social media to see what they've said about the war or the LGBTQ community, and look for ties to international institutions. Then comes a wave of denunciations. In my city, for example, this is done by a pro-government Telegram channel. One way or another, this work is coordinated by the state. As a result, institutions often postpone or cancel events. Recently they denounced a book festival held at GES-2, and it worked: many events at the festival were canceled, and the staff member overseeing it was fired.”
At the same time, Dmitry said there is also a more grassroots level of denunciations and intimidation:
“Last fall there was a peak in denunciations, and all sorts of people were sending me threats. When I looked through their social media accounts, it turned out they weren't even from my region. They were former servicemen from elsewhere who seem to spend their time monitoring people, apparently deriving some additional aesthetic pleasure from it. If you look at all the posts in these denunciation channels reposting events they dislike, you'll see countless outraged comments. People promise to file complaints with the prosecutor's office, and then you just sit there waiting for it to happen. I received dozens of threats like that. But if these people really wanted to have me imprisoned, they would have taken a closer look at what I do and found articles of the Criminal Code that actually fit.”
Some artists themselves have also become informants. Aleksandra said that one former student of the Baza Institute, which closed after the searches, has gained an unfortunate reputation within the art community:
“After the searches, she got very scared and immediately switched sides. She started painting little birch trees. But on top of that, she's making everyone's life miserable — she goes to every exhibition and reports people. She wanted to report me too, and I told her I'd report her as well. There aren't many people like that, but they do exist.”
Aleksandra believes these artists are primarily trying to shield themselves from possible repression. At the same time, she said, no one pays much attention to this particular artist's activities anymore: “People just say, ‘To hell with her.’ She's reported everyone — the Zverev Center, Garage — but the state doesn't seem to pay any attention either.”
How cultural institutions are responding
It is impossible to determine how many events have been shut down because of state pressure — many projects are canceled at the planning stage, while most bans are imposed through informal instructions from officials and security services or through pressure from pro-government activists. Even so, the fact that many events have been canceled has become public knowledge.
In 2022, an exhibition by artist Grisha Bruskin at the New Tretyakov Gallery closed ahead of schedule after complaints from activists and inspections by Russia's Ministry of Culture, which claimed to have found “anti-state” messages in the works.
In 2023, an exhibition by Rostislav Lebedev at the VS_Unio gallery was subjected to sweeping censorship immediately before its opening. Around 30 of the artist's works were removed, while the name of prominent independent curator Andrei Erofeev was completely deleted from promotional materials and press releases.
That same year, the Russian Museum canceled an exhibition marking the 65th birthday of Timur Novikov (an iconic artist of the perestroika era) just one day before its opening. The decision has been attributed to the museum's new director, Alla Manilova.
In the summer of 2024, ART4, Moscow's first private museum of contemporary art, closed after one a performance by artist Sergei Pakhomov provoked fierce criticism from pro-government activists affiliated with the ultranationalist NOD movement.
The same year, the Department of the Latest Trends at the Tretyakov Gallery was shut down, while the New Tretyakov Gallery ended its exhibition program. In effect, these developments marked the end of the possibility of exhibiting contemporary artistic practice at the country's principal national museum.
Dmitry believes that organizations can still resist the efforts of informants. He cited a two-year-old example from his own work curating a major project at a regional center for contemporary art. Since he knew he was being monitored, his involvement was not mentioned in any of the announcements that went out before the exhibition opened — only in the catalog, which visitors could see at the event itself. “In that sense, I acted behind the scenes. The chances of any informants actually coming to the exhibition were very small, so you could say we outsmarted them,” Dmitry recalled.
According to the curator, however, institutions have responded to the new reality in different ways:
“There are also more unpleasant cases involving institutional self-censorship. For example, in 2025 the artist Blue Pencil was preparing an exhibition at the Arsenal museum in Nizhny Novgorod, but the institution got so frightened that it didn't mention his name anywhere at all. Yet some time later, Individuum published Blue Pencil's book, a manifesto dealing precisely with censorship. And nothing happened! This is a constant pattern: institutional directors try to assess the risks, and they often overreact.”
Commenting on the dismissal of a staff member from GES-2, Moscow art gallery founder Aleksandra said that when faced with state pressure, major cultural institutions are reluctant to stand up for either their employees or for artists:
“Institutions behave according to the principle, ‘I'm just a kitty – what can I do?’ In my view, GES-2 today is the most clear embodiment of what institutions devoted to culture and the arts look like under Putin. Artists who, let's say, don't take a clear public stance, are eager to get in because that's where the money, exhibitions, and opportunities are. But the situation is similar at other major institutions as well. People cling to their salaries, and you can understand why — an institution will not defend one of its employees, even if they've worked there for a thousand years. You shouldn't expect any sense of decency.”
Pressure can also take a more overtly coercive form. One of the clearest recent examples occurred in May 2026 at the Kontur photography fair in Nizhny Novgorod. A day before the opening, unidentified people arrived at the venue and covered the booth displaying photographer Alexander Gronsky's work with white fabric. Gronsky is best known for his series of photographs exploring how the war has transformed Russian cities.
“On the night before the opening, stern men in suits convincingly suggested a new exhibition design,” Gronsky wrote. In the comments on the photographer's post, people joked that the men in suits had “created a new trend” and that the artwork had only benefited from their intervention.
Dmitry also said that foreign artists visiting Russia can become victims of censorship restrictions:
“Last year, one institution held an open competition for participation in an exhibition. The curators selected an excellent Chinese artist. He flew in, and then information came from the FSB that he had taken part in protest actions in China, so he had to be banished immediately. The artist spent literally six hours in Russia — he had only just checked into his hotel — and then he was sent back because the FSB had looked into his background a little too late.”
Not everyone involved in the art world, however, is overly concerned by the new restrictions. Veronika (name changed for security reasons), an artist and curator, said that while preparing a contemporary art fair in a major Russian city, she did not dwell on the risks or censor the works herself:
“Of course, we thought security officers might show up, but what could we do? Most of the artists taking part were people I already knew, so I had a rough idea of what kind of works they might bring. We selected the artists and organized the shared booths, but we didn't inspect every piece they intended to exhibit. It was obvious enough that nobody was going to hang a swastika or LGBT symbols on the wall. Of course, anything is possible, but if something like that had appeared, we would have removed it immediately.”
Veronika added that curators often deal with such situations on the spot. There have been cases in which exhibition organizers removed works at the request of security officers — but after the uninvited visitors left the venue, the works were put back on display or quietly sold under the counter.
How artists are responding
The atmosphere has had a profound impact on Russia's contemporary art scene. The Insider's sources say that fewer and fewer works even attempt to allude to the country's political or social situation.
But at the same time, other genres have emerged. Curator Irina says that “there's now a trend toward depicting children, with a huge number of works centered on family — apparently as a nod to traditional values.” “Nostalgia, old photographs — honestly, I'm completely tired of all that,” she adds.
There's now a trend toward depicting children, with a huge number of works centered on family – apparently as a nod to traditional values
Art theorist Boris Klyushnikov described the 2024 searches of artists' homes as a turning point: “I think we've entered a kind of Putinist formalism. It was after the Verzilov case that they split art into politically engaged contemporary art and everything else. Formalist art, on the other hand, is actually encouraged.”
Klyushnikov believes this is connected to the Putin-era elite's appetite for collecting art: “They go to fairs like Blazar, Cosmoscow, and so on. And what's being sold there now is art that's almost entirely formalist — a kind of zombie formalism.”
Curator Irina says that purchasing power in Russia has declined sharply, and buyers are disappearing as the country's middle class grows significantly poorer. Those who have benefitted from the war economically tend to be members of the elite and civil servants, and artists can often only sell the sorts of work that appeal to those buyers.
“That's what makes it doubly amusing when major galleries try to hint, in Aesopian language, that they're against the war while making their money almost exclusively from government officials and lawmakers,” Irina says. “Artists who work with major institutions while talking about independent art are, let's say, not telling the whole story. Because all the major sponsors and patrons still left in Russia are, one way or another, connected to the war.”
Irina offers a telling example of how artists are adapting to the new market:
“A man and his wife, who is an artist, decided to market her work to Russia's energy industry. She started painting power lines and energy infrastructure. After finishing the paintings, she put on a kokoshnik and wore it to Russian art fairs, partly funded by the government, such as Art Russia. Those kinds of works sell for millions [of rubles]. And portraits of Putin also sell very well.”
According to The Insider's sources, some artists are still trying to comment on contemporary reality through Aesopian language. “You can, for example, title an exhibition Freedom, Openness, or Dialogue,” Dmitry remarks ironically. Others, much as they did in Soviet times, have retreated into the underground, though the audience for this sort of semi-public art has naturally become much smaller. Some artists, Dmitry says, seek out little-known venues on the outskirts of cities and try to ignore censorship.
Artist and curator Veronika also told The Insider about works that rely on allusion and metaphor to address current events: “The people I know who work with political themes do so in a very indirect way. They turn to metaphor or what you might call ‘conceptual neutrality.’ An outside viewer looking at such a work wouldn't understand anything, and the accompanying text sometimes exists in two versions: a neutral public explanation and a more candid text intended for a narrow circle of people.”
As an example, the artist cites a work involving the performance of anthems based on Alexander Brener's letter opposing the war in Chechnya. The anthems themselves are performed in languages other than Russian, while the accompanying public text merely states that “the lyrics are based on Alexander Brener's 1995 letter to Khudozhestvenny Zhurnal.”
Another escapist means of avoiding censorship is to stage an exhibition devoted to a past era. “We've organized exhibitions about the 1960s and the 1920s. In such cases, there's no censorship — after all, we're talking about long-gone times,” Dmitry says.
As Dmitry explains, university instructors teaching contemporary art have increasingly shifted their focus to technological art and media art: “These fields are geared toward producing a very specific kind of knowledge that doesn't necessarily intersect directly with the political context. But even these people are afraid that their work could come under threat.”
An artist from St. Petersburg, who asked to remain anonymous, told The Insider how the city's contemporary art scene has become commercialized in recent years: “Art fairs and sales — that's what St. Petersburg lives on now. It feels like everyone is exhausted and focused on producing things that can be churned out and sold. We've lost the sense of play — I think we've forgotten why we're doing any of this in the first place. And, of course, so many artists have left, and those people are deeply missed.”
“Everyone is exhausted and focused on producing things that can be churned out and sold. We've lost the sense of play, and we've forgotten why we're doing any of this”
The artist links these changes to the risk of searches and arrests: “We've been crushed by this repression. There's a feeling that if someone creates something out of the ordinary, the searches will come afterward. Nobody wants to take that risk. Of course, there are still some deeply underground, punk spaces where anti-war statements can appear. But in terms of audience, it's what you'd call the very bottom layer of the internet.”
Some artists and curators, however, take a more optimistic view of the situation. Aleksandra believes that it is still possible to work as an artist and create free, experimental art in today's Russia:
“You simply understand from the outset that you've been excluded from the institutional sphere. Nobody is going to support you financially — you'll be making art with your own money. But maybe that's actually a good thing, because no one will be dictating the terms. Artists, including graduates of the Rodchenko School and the Joseph Backstein Institute of Contemporary Art, continue to produce works on a wide range of subjects, including the war and the militarization of society. You just have to accept that this kind of art will reach a much narrower audience.”
Living under this hybrid form of pressure has given rise to complex strategies of resistance. Dmitry said that although he continues to work on public events, he periodically has to reduce his visibility. It all depends on how active the informants are: “It's a kind of cat-and-mouse game. It's obvious that if I become more visible, the pressure from them will increase as well. You have to strike a balance between doing something and doing nothing.”
Art theorist Klyushnikov pointed to another emerging trend: the growth of self-organized educational initiatives in contemporary art: “In a way, art has become a cover for these collective gatherings. People simply need to talk, although political conversations happen as well. Art history has become especially important because you can show a work from, say, the First World War and discuss it, while everyone understands what you're really talking about.”

Treasury ‘contributed’ to assistant’s death by failing to tell her she wouldn’t lose job over complaint
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
15:22:04 BST
23:22:04 KST

Treasury ‘contributed’ to assistant’s death by failing to tell her she wouldn’t lose job over complaint
Chloe Moffat, 26, died a day after managers told her of an anonymous allegation that she had shared sensitive information
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The Treasury "materially contributed" to the death of a worker who took her own life following a meeting, by failing to clarify she would keep her job if allegations were proven, an inquest has heard.
Surrey Coroner’s Court was told on Monday that Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a director at the Treasury, died on May 20 last year. Her death occurred a day after managers informed her during a meeting of claims that she had shared sensitive confidential information.
Ms Moffat’s family said they will "continue to honour her memory and seek the changes needed to ensure that no other family suffers a similar loss".
A spokesperson for the Treasury said they were "considering the findings carefully".
Assistant coroner Anna Crawford said HM Treasury materially contributed to Ms Moffat’s death by not applying written disciplinary policy, which included informing her that the likely penalty if the allegations were proven was a written warning and not dismissal.
Ms Crawford said “it was agreed by everybody that Chloe enjoyed her job”, she had a good work record and had not previously been subject to any workplace disciplinary proceedings.
On May 19 Ms Moffat went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one meeting with her line manager, and a more senior manager was also present, the inquest heard.
She was told of allegations that she had shared sensitive personal information about colleagues, which she had obtained as part of her job role, within the office.
Ms Moffat denied the allegations.
She was informed that no final decision had been taken as to how the allegations would be handled but that it may be by way of a formal investigation or disciplinary meeting.
She asked if she would lose her job and the senior manager said “she could not predict the outcome at this stage”, Ms Crawford said.
She was told they were temporarily removing her access to the director’s email inbox.
Ms Moffat was shocked and upset during the meeting, the senior manager left, and Ms Moffat cried before composing herself, and it was agreed she did not have to work for the rest of the day, Ms Crawford said.
She texted a friend saying she thought she was going to be fired, then spoke to her mother on the phone, who tried to reassure her, and it was decided Ms Moffat would go and stay at her parents’ house.
The next day Ms Moffat took her own life.
The allegations were first drawn to the attention of Ms Moffat’s line manager and the more senior manager on May 8, and they took time to read the policy, however the senior manager described it as “high level”, Ms Crawford said.
There were then a number of email exchanges between the managers and HR advisers.
Ms Crawford said if the written policy had been followed, that instead of attending the meeting on May 19, Ms Moffat would have been sent a letter setting out the details and would have been advised that the likely penalty, if proved, would be a written warning.
Ms Crawford recorded a conclusion of suicide and made a short narrative that HM Treasury “materially contributed” to Ms Moffat’s death by not applying written disciplinary policy, in that they did not inform her that the likely penalty if the allegations were proven was a written warning and not dismissal.
During the inquest, evidence was heard that the information fact-finding meeting was not a one-off and was standard practice at HM Treasury and across other departments, which was a “matter of concern”, Ms Crawford said.
Ms Crawford said she would be sending a prevention of future deaths report to HM Treasury, the head of the civil service and to Acas.
In a statement to the press, Ms Moffat’s family said: “Chloe was a bright, caring and talented young woman who loved her family, her friends and her work.”
The statement added: “We continue to believe that HM Treasury failed in its duty of care towards Chloe.
“At a time when she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced that her career and reputation had been destroyed.”
It said: “Our hope has always been that some good can come from this tragedy. We therefore welcome any recommendations made by the coroner aimed at preventing other families from experiencing the heartbreak that we have endured.
“We hope that a prevention of future deaths report will lead to meaningful changes in how disciplinary processes are conducted and how employees’ welfare is safeguarded.
“Nothing will bring Chloe back. She was a much-loved daughter, sister and friend, and the loss we feel every day is immeasurable. We will continue to honour her memory and seek the changes needed to ensure that no other family suffers a similar loss.”
A Treasury spokesperson said: “We continue to mourn Chloe’s passing as a colleague and friend. Our thoughts remain with her family and friends.
“We take the coroner’s concerns extremely seriously and recognise it is important to act quickly. We are now considering the findings carefully.
“We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.”
If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch. If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

MAGA Superman actor Dean Cain’s attempt to embarrass Democrat backfires immediately
Trump and his allies have recently lashed out at Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Former Superman actor Dean Cain has been forced to eat his words after a failed attempt to discredit rising Democratic star Abdul El-Sayed.
Cain, a 60-year-old vocal supporter of Donald Trump, tried to go after the Michigan Democratic nominee for Senate in a social media post after El-Sayed, 41, made a jab at Trump on CNN Sunday.
“Has anyone ever seen a photo of Michigan Senate candidate Abdulrahman Mohamed El Sayed (D) playing High School football?” the Cain wrote in an X post. “He says he was captain of the team, but I can't find a single photo. Internet, please do your thing.”
Cain’s replies were filled almost instantly with pictures of El-Sayed in football gear, with X users pointing out that the politician had shared one of the pictures himself on Instagram in March.
“This literally took 2 seconds,” one X user wrote. Another commented: “Wow - that’s your (failed) attempt at a ‘gotcha’? I’d say stick with acting but nobody is interested in seeing that.”
One person wrote, “kinda weird that dean cain wants a picture of a high school aged boy, but a simple google search did the trick.”
Another X user found a 2002 article in the Detroit Free Press that mentioned El-Sayed playing on his high school football team, but it was apparently not enough proof for Cain, who responded to the post asking, “What newspaper?”
Cain, who announced last year that he was joining ICE to “help save America,” is known for playing Superman in the 1990s TV series Lois & Clark: The New Adventures of Superman.
The actor did not return The Independent’s request for comment. The Independent has also contacted El-Sayed for comment.
El-Sayed was captain of Bloomfield Hills Andover High School’s football, wrestling and lacrosse teams, according to his website. He has posted pictures of himself in his lacrosse and football uniforms on his Instagram page.
The popular Egyptian-American progressive has become a MAGA target after he recently won Michigan’s primary over moderate Democrat Haley Stevens. Trump, 80, and his allies have repeatedly attacked El-Sayed in social media posts, with the president pointedly referring to El-Sayed by his full name in a similar tactic to how he previously emphasized Barack Obama’s middle name, “Hussein.”
In a Truth Social rant Saturday, Trump posted a picture of himself and his wife, Melania, next to a picture of El-Sayed and his wife, Dr. Sarah Jukaku, with the caption: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.”
When asked about the post on CNN, El-Sayed agreed that the two couples are in “very different Americas.”
“Yeah, he’s right,” the former public health official said. “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you — or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things.”
El-Sayed continued: “So yes, you’ve got two different visions of America. Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?”

Spirit Halloween’s parent company buys Hot Topic

Spirit Halloween’s parent company buys Hot Topic
‘The best time for Hot Topic was the early 00s when they were staffed by only the coolest and meanest 16-20 somethings’
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Spirit Halloween’s parent company is snapping up a store known for its rock-and-roll vibe and pop culture savvy.
Spencer Spirit Holdings announced Thursday it will buy Hot Topic and two other stores owned by private equity firm Sycamore Partners, according to a press release. Spencer Spirit is paying around $350 million for Hot Topic Inc., according to Bloomberg, which includes Hot Topic, pop-culture trinket trove BoxLunch, and fashion brand Her Universe.
Sycamore Managing Director Dary Kopelioff said his company is “proud” of the way it’s grown Hot Topic Inc.
"We're proud of the value we've built together over more than a decade, and we're confident Spencer Spirit Holdings, Inc. is the right partner to carry this growth forward for the brands and their teams,” Kopelioff said.
Sycamore expects the deal to close by the end of September. It will boost Spencer Spirit’s total number of North American stores to more than 3,000, according to Retail Dive.
The private equity firm bought Hot Topic Inc. for $600 million in 2013, according to industry news site Retail Dive. At the time, the company had five brands: Hot Topic, BoxLunch, Her Universe, clothing store Torrid, and apparel and lingerie brand Blackheart.
Hot Topic opened in 1988, then joined the NASDAQ stock exchange in 1996 with its “HOTT” ticker symbol, according to the company’s About Us page. It went private in 2013 when Sycamore bought it.
The brand, known for its wide range of band and anime clothing, has transformed from a niche store for goth, emo and alt kids to a more mainstream establishment for everything from Disney franchises to K-Pop Demon Hunter gear, according to The Strategist, a New Yorker consumer review site.
Whereas the old iteration of the store was the type of place parents might be afraid of, the mainstream-ish bent of the current brand is welcoming a new group of fans, The Strategist wrote.
“I remember coming here when I was younger and the vibe was way more dark, but now it’s more bright and colorful,” a 20-year-old named Amberlyn told the publication. “Some people are like, I wish it was still the way it used to be, but I think it’s cool.”
Social media responses to the Hot Topic acquisition stoked nostalgia in some users.
“The best time for Hot Topic was the early 00s when they were staffed by only the coolest and meanest 16-20 somethings,” user cbih wrote on Reddit. “They'd [apathetically] fold shirts while calling customers posers.”

Russia’s National Wealth Fund totals $159.3 bln as of August 1 — finance ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:19:35 UTC
23:19:35 KST

MOSCOW, August 10. /TASS/. Russia’s National Wealth Fund (NWF) totaled 12.72 trillion rubles as of August 1, 2026, or 5.4% of GDP projected for this year, according to files released on the Russian Finance Ministry’s website. The National Wealth Fund equals $159.3 bln.
As of August 1, the amount of liquid assets of the NWF amounted to 3.69 trillion rubles (1.6% of GDP projected for 2026), which equals $46.2 bln. As of July 1, the amount of liquid assets of the NWF was 3.61 trillion rubles.
"In July 2026, the National Wealth Fund’s assets totaling 1,632.2 mln rubles were converted into 158.9 kg of unallocated gold, while assets totaling 529.7 mln rubles were converted into 47.1 mln Chinese yuan," according to the ministry.
The estimated amount of revenues from depositing NWF resources on accounts in foreign currency with the Bank of Russia recalculated to US dollars from December 15, 2025 to July 31, 2026 totaled $62.2 mln, which is equivalent to 4.97 bln rubles.
The exchange rate difference on the Fund’s assets nominated in foreign currency and revaluation of the cost of gold, in which the NWF’s resources have been invested, totally amounted to 67.2 bln rubles from January 1 to July 31, 2026.
A total of 189.7 bln Chinese yuan, and 141.2 tons of gold were on accounts of the National Wealth Fund with the Bank of Russia as of August 1.

Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said: "We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination."
Around 1,600 buildings damaged, including at least 61 completely destroyed
Epicentre of quake in San Jose Del Palmar
The epicentre of the quake was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles (400 kilometers) west of Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. The quake also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.
The quake ravaged cities across the west of the country, including Pereira, Quibdo, Cali and Manizales.

Venezuela was hit by twin earthquakes in June, which killed more than 6,000 people, mostly on the coast near the capital, Caracas.
Flights suspended at several airports in Colombia

'I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake', eyewitness says

“My entire house shook,” he said. “I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake.”
Colombia declares national emergency after deadly earthquake
ICRC says it is closely monitoring the quake affected regions
Manizales mayor urges people to remain outdoors because of possible aftershocks
Colombia declares national emergency after earthquake
Colombia government has declared a national emergency after Monday's deadly quake, local media reported.
Province of Risaralda reports highest death toll – 42 people – so far
The highest reported death toll was in the western province of Risaralda -- where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located -- in Colombia's coffee-growing region, where Governor Juan Diego Patino, speaking by phone to Caracol Television, reported 42 fatalities.
The powerful earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday killed at least 69 people, local officials said.
The 7.4 magnitude quake killed 40 people in the coffee-growing Risaralda region, 27 in Valle del Cauca department and two more in the city of Manizales, according to new tolls from these officials.
Local officials confirmed that at least 40 people were killed in the Risaralda region, where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Colombia's third-biggest city, Cali, is located. MOSCOW, August 10. /TASS/. The harvest of grain and leguminous crops in Russia since the beginning of 2026 has exceeded 72 million tonnes, surpassing last year's figure, the Agriculture Ministry reported.

The leaders in terms of yield are the Krasnodar Region, as well as the Bryansk, Kursk, and Kaliningrad regions, where farmers harvest around 6.0 tonnes (60 centners) of grain per hectare.

11 best induction pans, tried and tested in a real kitchen
From griddle pans to woks, these are the best pans to choose to cook up a storm on an induction hob
- Bookmark
I’ve got a confession to make. Until I first got an induction hob several years ago, I didn’t know induction pans would only work with certain pots and pans. This realisation led to something of a cookware overhaul, but first, I had to go searching for the best induction pans with which I could replace my original, defunct line-up.
You can find induction-suitable options for every kind of pan you might need in your kitchen, whether that’s a huge stockpot or a ‘do it all’ 10-in-one pan that can handle everything from stir frying to baking. So it goes without saying that the best one depends on the kind of meals you make.
Induction pans need to have a flat, magnetic base, such as cast iron or stainless steel, and, because the base itself is heated, rather than the surface of the hob, they need to be thick enough that the bass won’t warp. If the base is thick and does end up warped, it’ll cause uneven cooking and, eventually, the hob will stop detecting the pan at all (this I know from first-hand experience, unfortunately).
Whatever suits your kitchen, these are the best induction pans to choose, all tested on my home hob.

- Best overall – Our Place titanium always pan pro: £170, Amazon.co.uk
- Best budget buy – Salter megastone 20cm frying pan: £13.99, Amazon.co.uk
- Best frying pan – Circulon scratchdefense stainless steel frying pan: Was £78, now £52, Amazon.co.uk
- Best induction saucepans – Ninja ceramic pro three-piece saucepan set: £174.99, Argos.co.uk

Your questions about induction pans answered
What is the best induction pan?
If you can only buy one induction pan, I’d invest in the Our Place titanium always pan pro. It can cook almost anything, has a very effective non-stick surface and heats up quickly and evenly. If the always pan pro is out of budget, I also rate the Salter megastone 20cm frying pan, which requires little oil when cooking and is super lightweight. If you’re short on space or need to buy a whole set in one go, opt for the Tefal ingenio emotion 22-piece pan set, which has removable handles that be used interchangeably between the pans.
How I tested induction pans
I used all of these induction pans in my own kitchen over several weeks, to get an idea of which ones were worth a permanent place in my kitchen cupboard. With each pan, I cooked a range of dishes from casseroles to curries and assessed it according to the factors below:
- Design and ease of use: For each pan, I noted how it looked out on my hob, but most importantly, how easy it was to cook with. I paid particular attention to its weight and if I could move the pan around easily and whether it seemed robust.
- Versatility: Few of us have the space to store a huge number of pans in different sizes, so I rated any that could be used for cooking a variety of dishes. I cooked all kinds of meals, from bacon to stew, to see how well each one fared, giving an extra thumbs-up to any that were also oven-safe.
- Performance: By cooking a range of dishes, from omelettes to pasta sauces, I judged if the pans cooked well, if they heated evenly and if food stuck to them. I also noticed how responsive they were to changes in temperature, and if I needed a lot of oil to achieve my desired results.
- Ease of cleaning: I cleaned all the pans by hand to see how easy they were to wash, and if cooking residue came away easily with minimal scrubbing. For those that are dishwasher safe, I put them in the dishwasher more than once to see how successfully they were cleaned.
- Ease of storage: Though this comes down to personal preference, I gave extra points if the pans – and their lids – were easy to store or if I would need to clear out some cupboard space to fit them in my own home.
What pans work with induction?
Pans must be made of magnetic materials to work on an induction hob, so look for cast-iron and stainless-steel pans. Essentially, if a magnet sticks to the bottom of the pan, it will usually work well. However, always double check the pan is compatible with induction cooking before buying (check the packaging or the manufacturer’s website). Those showing a coiled spring symbol are the ones to look for. Thick-based pans work the best, as induction hobs heat the pan rather than the hob, and the magnetic field can cause thinner pans to warp over time.
Can you use induction pans on gas?
Most induction-compatible pans can also be used on a gas hob, so you may not necessarily need to buy a whole new set of pans if you make the switch. Stainless steel and cast iron pans should usually work on both, but if the pan is particularly thin or has a non-stick coating, an open gas flame could cause damage. It’s always a good idea to check the manufacturer’s guide to be sure before cooking.

The Independent’s product guides are carefully curated, featuring items that our experienced shopping team has personally tested and approved. Siobhan Grogan is a journalist with years of experience in testing products for the home, from the best tabletop dishwashers to the best mattress protectors, so is an expert in evaluating their quality and, ultimately, whether they’re worth your time and money.
