Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Monday met Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker at the presidential complex in the capital Ankara.
Earlier, Erdogan welcomed Stocker with an official ceremony.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Communications Director Burhanettin Duran, the president's chief advisor Akif Cagatay Kilic, and other officials were present at the ceremony.
Stocker is paying an official visit to Türkiye at the invitation of President Erdogan.
Multidimensional bilateral relations, steps to further develop existing cooperation, as well as regional and global issues were expected to be discussed in the meeting.
Relations between Türkiye and Austria have recently shown signs of renewed engagement, with both sides seeking closer cooperation on trade, migration, and security.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited Vienna in April, where he met his Austrian counterpart Beate Meinl-Reisinger as well as Stocker, highlighting efforts to strengthen bilateral ties while also discussing Türkiye-EU relations and regional conflicts.
Economic links remain a major pillar of the relationship.
Bilateral trade reached about $4.36 billion in 2025, up from $3.91 billion in 2024, according to Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry. Austrian government figures put 2025 trade at almost €4.3 billion (about $4.97 billion).
Austria is a significant investor in Türkiye, and the relationship is also shaped by a large Turkish community in Austria and substantial tourism ties.
More than 563,000 Austrian tourists visited Türkiye in 2025, while Austrian investment in Türkiye between 2005 and 2025 exceeded $11.2 billion.

Poland and Baltics tighten critical infrastructure security amid Russian threat concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:49:00 UTC
22:49:00 KST

Lithuania, Poland and other Baltic states are stepping up security around dams, power plants and natural gas infrastructure amid concerns that Russia could stage “false-flag” attacks intended to trigger confusion within NATO, Reuters reported Monday.
Lithuania has strengthened protection of critical infrastructure after its military intelligence reportedly obtained information that Russia was considering attacks in the Baltic region using captured Ukrainian drones in an attempt to obscure their origin.
NATO’s eastern-flank countries have also publicly warned in recent weeks that they have intelligence indicating Russia could be preparing to carry out provocations using kinetic means.
Since June 18, Lithuania’s military has been supporting the Public Security Service in protecting the country’s liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipėda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection substation with Poland in Alytus, a transformer substation in the Alytus district and the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Power Plant.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas signed an order July 17 extending the security support through August 19. The military is authorised to deploy a unit of up to 30 personnel, equipped with vehicles, as well as a vessel or boat with a crew.
Kaunas, the Latvian prime minister and four intelligence and corporate officials from across the region shared new details of intelligence assessments and measures being taken to protect infrastructure in interviews with Reuters.
“We are increasing the security of our critical infrastructure, we constantly exchange information with our intelligence on what to do next,” Kaunas told Reuters.
Latvia has increased security around all critical infrastructure, including a dam on the Daugava River near Riga and the Inčukalns underground natural gas storage facility, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told Reuters.
Poland investigates forged documents
In Poland, energy company Orlen is examining alternative natural gas import routes in case its usual supplies or infrastructure are threatened, a person familiar with the company’s operations told Reuters.
Orlen imports about 80% of Poland’s gas through the Świnoujście liquefied natural gas terminal on the Baltic Sea and an undersea pipeline carrying Norwegian gas that comes ashore nearby. Gaz-System, which operates the infrastructure, is working under heightened alert conditions, another person familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe, the state-owned company developing Poland’s first nuclear power plant, said forged company documents had surfaced in an apparent attempt to mislead stakeholders. The company said the trail led “east of Poland”.
The company is investigating the matter with intelligence and law enforcement agencies and monitoring the planned construction site for possible sabotage or other threats, spokesman Marcin Skolimowski said.
Poland’s electricity grid operator and a military unit also began increasing security in July around an electricity connection with Ukraine that helps stabilise the war-damaged country’s power grid, which is regularly targeted by Russian attacks.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:48:05 UTC
22:48:05 KST

Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners, in London on Aug. 10, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
LONDON — Nigel Farage ruled out entering talks with right-wing rival Rupert Lowe Monday — unless Lowe moves to expel a controversial ally.
The pathway to power for Farage’s Reform UK was already narrowing before new Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s takeover aided a polling bounce for the governing Labour Party.
While still polling in the single digits, Rupert Lowe’s splinter party has been proving it can eat into a significant chunk of Reform’s vote. Lowe formed Restore Britain after being kicked out of Reform — but he has been, at least ostensibly, dangling an olive branch for Farage to grasp in recent weeks.
Advertisement
On Monday the prospect of the two warring factions signing a make-up pact seemed to be at an impasse.
Farage used a press conference in Westminster to publicly state a new condition for holding discussions with “that party,” as he referred to Restore. Lowe must, he said, kick out Restore’s co-founder — a move Lowe has already rejected.
“I’m always happy to meet people and talk to people — within reason,” Farage said when asked by POLITICO what his conditions for entering talks with Lowe would be.
Leader of Restore Britain Rupert Lowe speaks to the media in Wigan, England on June 18, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images
“But I do think it’s fair to say that there are one or two people in the orbit of the upper echelons of that party who, if I sat down and talked to, I think our members and our voters would be utterly shocked that I’d done it,” he added.
“So we can talk to Rupert Lowe — that’s fine. But when you have co-founders, etcetera, putting out what I would call the ‘old theory’ — the old theory that we probably haven’t heard in this country since 1936 — and you have other adjacent publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country, just as an example…
“So the condition I would put on it is those people would have to be out of the inner circle — and I think that for me would be the only way we could sensibly proceed.”
Advertisement
The co-founder Farage referred to is Charlie Downes, who was this month accused of implying that Farage had been “bought” by Jewish supporters. Campaigners against anti-semitism accused Downes of perpetuating the “oldest smear” against Jewish people.
Farage’s attack on “publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country” is meanwhile a reference to Steve Laws, a backer of Restore Britain who is an advocate of “total remigration.” Lowe told POLITICO in June that Laws plans “no part in our decision-making process,” although Lowe said he is “very welcome” to support the party.
Lowe had already indicated his opposition to booting out Downes after the Telegraph first reported Farage’s rejection of talks. “Farage and Reform have also said that Restore Britain must outright sack Charlie Downes — putting a young Christian man out of work, just as he is looking to build his life and start a family,” Lowe wrote on X. “That is simply not how I operate.”
While still polling in the single digits, Rupert Lowe’s splinter party has been proving it can eat into a significant chunk of Reform’s vote. | Darren Staples/AFP via Getty Images
It’s the latest twist in a convoluted saga that is commanding attention on the right of British politics.
Lowe last week offered to put “past disagreements” with Farage aside so that the pair can work together. But he set five conditions for doing so, including the exclusion of Conservative defectors to Reform from a future Farage cabinet.
Prisons push
Farage’s comments came at a press conference he held to add to pressure on the new prime minister over Britain’s prisons, which have in recent years been hovering around breaking point.
Advertisement
Farage said Reform UK will begin talks with El Salvador about renting prison space so a future government he leads could deport all foreign prisoners to serve their sentences abroad — an echo of Donald Trump’s controversial policy for prisoners from the U.S.
Other possible countries that could forge similar deals, Farage suggested, are Kosovo, as well as Estonia or Lithuania.
Reform claimed the plans would free up 10,000 spaces in U.K. prisons. However, nearly a third of foreign nationals in detention are on remand, meaning they haven’t been convicted of a crime and are awaiting trial.
Pressed about the disparity, home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf told POLITICO: “That’s not the gotcha that you might think it is.
“The vast majority of those people end up being convicted — so in terms of the practical plan that we’ve laid out, it makes no difference.”

Network Rail fined £1.2m after railway station wall falls on elderly man
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:47:39 BST
22:47:39 KST

Network Rail fined £1.2m after railway station wall falls on elderly man
Edward Hanlon, then 81, suffered several fractured ribs, a punctured lung and a blood clot in his lung
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Network Rail has been fined £1.2 million after a railway station wall collapsed and seriously injured an elderly man.
Edward Hanlon, then 81, was walking along an adjacent alleyway when the boundary wall beside a car park at Rugby station, Warwickshire, collapsed.
Mr Hanlon suffered several fractured ribs, a punctured lung and a blood clot in his lung, and spent two weeks in hospital.
The Office of Rail and Road said the incident in September 2022 had a “lasting impact” on him physically and mentally, leaving him in “persistent pain” and preventing him from returning to “many of the activities he had previously enjoyed”.
Mr Hanlon died in January 2025 after a diagnosis of lymphoma, which is a type of blood cancer.
Network Rail owned the wall and was responsible for its maintenance, but the installation of a fence in front of it by a previous tenant led to the mistaken assumption that the fence marked the station boundary, the ORR said.
The wall was consequently omitted from Network Rail’s inspections, and its deteriorating condition was not identified, according to the industry regulator.
The ORR said Network Rail was fined £1.2 million at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court on Friday after admitting an offence under health and safety at work legislation.
Richard Hines, the ORR’s HM chief inspector of railways, said: “Our thoughts remain with Mr Hanlon’s family and friends.
“The sentence imposed by the court reflects the seriousness of Network Rail’s failings and the devastating consequences when infrastructure is not managed effectively.
“Duty holders must know which assets they are responsible for, carry out appropriate inspections, and take timely action to address defects before they pose a risk to people.
“This prosecution sends a clear message that ORR will not hesitate to take enforcement action where failures to manage safety expose workers or members of the public to serious harm.”
Gary Walsh, route director for Network Rail, said: “We are deeply sorry for the incident at Rugby station in September 2022, for the injuries suffered by Mr Hanlon and the distress caused to his family.
“Following the incident, we reviewed the circumstances surrounding the wall, took action to address the immediate risks and strengthened processes relating to asset records, boundary identification and inspection management.
“While incidents of this nature are rare, we remain committed to continually improving the safety of our infrastructure for passengers, neighbours and the wider public.”

Drought forces Basel ferry to suspend service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:47:00 UTC
22:47:00 KST

Drought forces Basel ferry to suspend service
The St Alban ferry in Basel has been closed since Monday morning due to low water levels and will remain so until further notice.
The other three ferries on the River Rhine are still operating, Dieter Bühler, president of the Basel Ferries Foundation, told the Swiss News Agency Keystone-SDA.
The reason why the “Wild Maa” ferry, unlike the other three, cannot set sail is not only the low water levels but also its geographical location. It is more exposed to the westerly wind than the others. As Bühler explained, when the wind blows directly towards the boat, the current in the Rhine is too weak to propel the ferry.
More
Sparse rainfall and heatwaves have put Switzerland on drought alert
The “Wild Maa” ferry connects the St Alban Valley in Greater Basel with the Wettstein district in Lesser Basel. The ferry association publishes information on the current situation on its website. The Basler Zeitung was the first to report on this.
Unlike the St Alban ferry, the low water level is not putting a spanner in the works for another local tradition: the Basel Rhine Swim is going ahead this year. The 46th edition of this traditional event is set to begin as scheduled on Tuesday, at 6 pm, the Swiss Life-Saving Society announced on Monday.

Revolut bags full French banking licence in European growth push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:46:51 UTC
22:46:51 KST

Revolut's French banking licence follows the bank receiving its UK banking licence back in March 2026.
Revolut announced on Monday that Revolut Bank S.A. received a full French banking licence following a joint assessment by the European Central Bank (ECB) and the French prudential regulator (ACPR).
This marks a significant milestone for the online bank and strengthens its position as one of Europe’s biggest retail banks. It also paves the path for further global growth, while allowing the company to focus more on localising its products for different markets.
“This achievement reflects months of close collaboration with the ACPR and the European Central Bank, whose rigorous standards have helped us build the right foundations for long-term growth in the region,” Béatrice Cossa-Dumurgier, CEO Western Europe at Revolut, said in a press release.
She added: “Our focus now turns to execution. We'll begin by serving customers in France before progressively expanding across Western Europe, while accelerating the localisation of our products and services to better meet the needs of retail and business customers in each market. This is the beginning of a new chapter for Revolut."
This follows Revolut receiving its full UK banking licence in March this year after a series of regulatory hurdles and delays.
The digital bank already has 30 million clients across Western Europe, with eight million coming onboard last year. It has more than 75 million clients across the world.
In the past year, the bank has shared that it would be investing more than €1 billion in Western Europe in Western Europe and is also hiring over 600 people across these markets.
Revolut has also said that it will be opening its new Western European HQ in Paris in 2027.
Revolut Bank S.A. will start serving European consumers in steps, starting with France, while other markets like Ireland, Germany, Italy, Spain and Portugal will also follow in phases.
“This licence gives us the foundation to build the next generation of banking for more than 30 million customers across Western Europe. France has become a leading financial hub, supported by a dynamic financial ecosystem and a robust regulatory framework,” Nik Storonsky, founder and CEO of Revolut, also said.
He added: “It is the ideal platform to accelerate Revolut's next phase of growth - bringing us one step closer to our ambition of becoming one of Europe's largest and most trusted banks."
Revolut’s Lithuanian entity, Revolut Bank UAB, will remain the focal point for operations for the rest of EEA. This two-pronged model is expected to help support the bank’s growth across Europe, with both entities subject to supervision by the European Central Bank and local governing authorities.

After Burnham’s ‘rip-offs’ crackdown, what more could PM do to help us save money?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:45:32 UTC
22:45:32 KST

In the long run, these so-called “everyday fixes” may not make as much difference to your wealth as increasing mandatory contributions on pensions or capping rents, but they will get rid of some day-to-day frustrations. Here are six other things he could fix while he is in the mood:
Ban booking fees on tickets
Buying a ticket for an event such as a gig or show doesn’t come with as many hidden costs as previously, thanks to consumer protection laws introduced last year. But the fact the fees are clearer does not make them all more palatable.
In the days when you could choose to go to a box office, or between having your tickets posted or emailed, there may have been a justification for some of the add-ons to cover different costs for the promoter, but when there’s no choice, it sticks in the throat. Retailers do not charge “transaction” or “order processing fees”, so why can they still be slapped on tickets?
Stop direct debit hikes when your energy bill is in credit
You pay your bill by direct debit and have been careful with your usage, so at the end of the winter, you are in credit – and then your provider tells you it wants to put up your monthly cost by £50. Of course, a rising price cap might mean you need to increase what you pay, but if you have already got a cushion, why should you hand over more?
According to the regulator Ofgem, providers held a total of £3.2bn of customers’ money in the year to March, with the average household £135 in credit. Yet some households on fixed tariffs with large balances are still told that their supplier wants to increase their direct debit. Yes, you can refuse, but the onus is on you as a customer to make the effort. Providers could be banned from raising direct debits by more than the price change, or when customers have built up a surplus that covers a set percentage of their bills.
Cut sneaky shrinkflation
We all know prices have been going up and sometimes a smaller pack for the same price is more welcome than having to shell out more, but when the cuts are sneaky, that’s bad for consumers.
In France and Austria, there are rules designed to make it more obvious to shoppers when they are getting less product for the same – or sometimes even more – money. Demanding a simple “new pack size” message on products would at least alert people to the change and mean they are making informed decisions about what they are buying.
Force companies to put a phone number on their homepage
You’ve got a problem with a company and you want to get it sorted – and then you realise you cannot find a number for it anywhere. There are communications companies that have no “contact us” link anywhere to be seen, and energy companies that send you all round the houses looking for a way to get in touch.
One of the recurring themes of Guardian Money readers’ problems is the struggle to find someone to help when something goes wrong. Clearly, once you have published a phone number, you need staff at the other end answering the phone and offering some joined-up thinking, so this is only the start of the solution – but at least customers would not feel like companies were trying to hide from them.
Bring forward plans to improve parking
Fines for charging an electric car, debt notices that should never have been sent, fees when you have tried to pay and the app has let you down … Guardian Money has heard from readers encountering all of these things and more when simply entering a car park. The government has promised to sort it out: a code of practice was drawn up several years ago but was not introduced, and a new consultation on it ended last September. Meanwhile plans for a nationwide app that would bring together all of the different parking company apps, making it easier to pay while out and about, were watered down.
Bringing forward and enforcing the planned code, so that drivers are not receiving bills for parking crimes they did not commit, would leave a welcome gap in the Guardian Money postbag.
Make insurers give you the best deal upfront
A lot has been done to improve the experience of renewing your insurance policies. Insurers are supposed to offer existing customers as good a deal as they do new ones, and your renewal letter tells you how much you paid last year so that you can see if the cost has gone up. And yet the annual dance continues: if you don’t call your insurer and query an increase, shop around or threaten to leave, you will probably end up paying more than you need to. It is a system that still penalises those who stay put.

UK water firm gives US$1.35 million payout to finance boss despite massive debt
Thames Water, amid efforts to get a rescue deal, drought and 571 million litres of water lost per day to leaks, also agreed other payouts
Thames Water has handed a delayed £1 million (US$1.35 million) “golden handshake” payment to its chief financial officer and agreed controversial retention payouts to top bosses despite its battle to secure its financial future.
The stricken supplier, which is sinking under a debt pile of more than £20 billion, disclosed in a letter to the Environmental, Food and Rural Affairs Committee that it had made the so-called signing-on payment to Steve Buck at the end of July from an emergency lending facility from creditors.
In the letter sent last week to committee chairman Alistair Carmichael, Thames Water chairman Adrian Montague said the payment was a “necessary incentive” to Buck in joining the utility when he was appointed in April 2025, but that it had been deferred when wider retention payments were put on hold.
It is understood the payment was made after legal advice.
Thames Water also said in the letter that it had agreed individual settlements over what it calls retention payments for a dozen top bosses, plus two who have now left the business, despite a furore late last year over them.

British radio station broke rules in mistakenly announcing death of King Charles: Watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

22:45:00 KST

British radio station broke rules in mistakenly announcing death of King Charles: Watchdog
- Radio Caroline accidentally broadcast false messages announcing King Charles III's death during a May programme, causing a 16-minute silence and national anthem to be aired.
- Ofcom ruled the broadcast breached rules on accuracy and timely correction, noting the station took too long to acknowledge the mistake.
- The error happened when a staff member played pre-recorded death files out of curiosity, then panicked and left; the staff has been reprimanded and files removed.
AI generated
LONDON – A community radio station breached the rules after accidentally announcing the death of King Charles III in a May broadcast, a British watchdog said on Aug 10.
Radio Caroline, a former pirate radio that now mostly plays rock music, apologised in May after airing messages falsely announcing the monarch’s death.
One of the messages had said “we have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III”.
The national anthem was then played, followed by around 16 minutes of silence before the regular programme resumed.
The presenter apologised 30 minutes after the messages were initially triggered, Ofcom said.
The regulator, which received two complaints about the broadcast, said the “very significant inaccuracy” and the “considerable length of time” taken to acknowledge the error breached two of its rules.
One requires news reports to be accurate and impartial.
The other requires significant mistakes to be acknowledged and corrected on air promptly.
Radio Caroline told Ofcom the error occurred when a member of staff accessed sound files pre-recorded in the event of the monarch’s death while carrying out maintenance on the studio computer, as the programme was being streamed remotely.
The staff member played the files “out of curiosity”, which stopped the stream from the presenter’s remote location and broadcast the files on air.
The person then reportedly “panicked and left the premises” after realising what had happened, according to the Ofcom statement.
Radio Caroline said the remote presenter “would not realise that they had gone ‘off air’ unless they were monitoring their output via an internet monitor”.
The presenter, believing they were still on air, was not actively monitoring their phone and did not immediately respond to calls from people at the station who had noticed the error, the report said.
The station said the person who played the files had been “reprimanded” and had “apologised”.
It added the pre-recorded files had now been removed from the studio computer. AFP

Fire Point Boss Says Home-Grown Ballistic Missile Interceptor May Be Operational by Mid-2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:43:59 UTC
22:43:59 KST

Ukraine is planning for an initial launch of its answer to the powerful US air defense system – the new Freyja interceptor missile – in mid-2027, the Director of the aerospace company Fire Point Denys Shtilerman said in a late Sunday comment.
Work for the weapons system that would partially or possibly even totally replace US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles that currently are the only means Ukraine has to intercept Russian ballistic missiles is going forward at a satisfactory pace, but much coordination work and sub-systems testing remains to be done before even an experimental home-grown Freyja might take to the air, Shtilerman wrote in an “X” post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are planning a full-scale launch of the anti-ballistic interceptor by mid-2027. As of now, the first cluster of integration work within the Freyja project has been completed. Ahead lies a major and technologically complex stage – the unification of all components [and subsystems] into a single complex [unified weapons system]. After that, the system must undergo a full cycle of testing and confirm its ability to intercept ballistic targets,” Shtilerman said in part.
The FirePoint/Shtilerman timeline was more ambitious than a Sunday prediction by President Volodymyr Zelensky, who stated that Ukraine hopes to field a domestically manufactured version of the US premier ballistic missile interceptor, the PAC-3 fired by the Patriot air defense system, in “12 months to several years.”
Zelensky in Belgrade: Vučić Refused to Let Serbia Foot Putin’s Bill
A ballistic missile flies in a high arc nearing space and on re-entry can reach attack speeds of six or more times the speed of sound, making the missile difficult to detect and intercept.
Ukraine’s search for ballistic missile interceptors is a matter of national security. Aside from the US-made PAC-3, Ukraine’s military has no practical means of stopping a Russian ballistic missile once launched. As a result, the Kremlin’s armed forces are able to fire ballistic missiles at targets inside Ukraine with impunity whenever supplies of PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine run low. Although imprecise, most ballistic missiles launched by Russia at Ukraine carry a warhead weighing at least half a ton.
Zelensky in Saturday comments to Kyiv reporters said an initiative for Ukraine to produce PAC-3 missiles under license is moving slowly because of plodding US participation in the project and “bureaucracy.” US President Donald Trump and key institutions had already made the political decision to transfer the necessary licenses to Kyiv, Zelensky said.
However, Trump has recently questioned whether he and the US would even agree to license Ukrainian production of the US high-tech PAC-3 missile.
“We have to be very careful about letting somebody build our advanced weapons,” Trump said in a July 31 Camp David comment to a reporter’s question. “We have not agreed to that. We’re talking about it, but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology. Those people whom you give technology can also turn on you. That’s possible. We have to be very careful.”
The major US weekly, the Atlantic, in an analytical article published on Sunday, reported US generals and executives at the US arms giants Lockheed Martin and Raytheon are concerned that, were Kyiv to receive full production blueprints for PAC-3 interceptor missiles, Ukraine’s skilled weapons manufacturers would quickly reverse-engineer US military technologies and set up production of a competing weapon costing half the price.
A pure Ukrainian interceptor missile, thanks to combat testing in a full-scale war against Russia, might even be more effective than the American missile, which has never been used in combat against a peer opponent, some Ukrainian military analysts say.
The White House, in February 2025, announced it was drastically curtailing deliveries of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine and would in the future only sell the missiles to Ukraine via Ukraine’s European allies at a 10% markup. Following the joint US/Israeli attack on Iran and war between those countries, Trump and administration officials in the Pentagon have blamed Ukraine for taking too many PAC-3 missiles from US stocks, and leaving US forces with insufficient missile stocks to take on Iranian missiles and drones fired at US forces and their allies.
The Kremlin has exploited a near-total absence of PAC-3 missiles in Ukrainian hands to bombard Ukrainian homes and businesses ruthlessly with its ballistic missiles. In July, according to a Ukrainian military count, Russia launched at least 195 ballistic and/or hypersonic missiles at targets inside Ukraine, of which only 29 were intercepted. In the first week of August, Russia launched 51 ballistic missiles, of which none were intercepted.
The weapons launched by Russia were primarily the advanced Iskander-M surface-to-surface missile, with salvos augmented with S-400 dual-use (surface-to-surface and surface-to-air as NATO’s SA-21) missiles and, possibly, North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles.
Following Russian missile attacks hitting Ukraine on Aug. 5-6 – killing 17 Ukrainian civilians and injuring 44 – Trump, in response to a reporter question whether the US should increase PAC-3 deliveries to Ukraine so that casualties caused by Russian ballistic missiles might be reduced, Trump denied America was under any moral obligation to sell Ukraine interceptor missiles it needs to stop the Russian ballistic missile bombardment.
“Look, we’re not involved. We’re separated by an ocean,” Trump said. He went on to say he thought thousands of war deaths in the Russo-Ukrainian War, every month, was deplorable.
In an Aug. 6 editorial entitled “Will Trump Leave Ukraine Without Patriots?” in the Wall Street Journal, the usually pro-Republican broadsheet called Trump’s active prevention of PAC-3 interceptor missile deliveries to Ukraine strategically foolish and morally wrong.
In an Aug. 3 editorial published in the Washington Post, Shtilerman argued that the multi-source/joint development of the Freyja was the only strategy by which Ukraine might meet the threat of Russian massed ballistic attacks, because only mass-produced, inexpensive Ukrainian interceptor missiles have a realistic chance of taking on the Russian ballistic missile threat.
Shtilerman wrote that the Ukrainian objective with the Freya system is:
“Not to build another Patriot, but to create an ecosystem in which no single manufacturer, factory or state determines the fate of the entire system. Network logic and redundancy are pervasive in the arrangement... Software and technical systems should not contain hidden dependencies on any single company or state, and they should be open to independent audit...The best weapon in insufficient numbers loses to a sufficient number of good weapons. Ukraine paid dearly to learn that lesson. Other democracies need to learn from our early mistakes.”
Maj. Gen. Vadym Skibitsky, vice director of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR, in comments published by the news agency RBK-Ukraina, on Monday said that the Russian Federation is increasing production of ballistic missiles and that Ukraine should expect more of the weapons launched by Russia in the future.
Current production of Iskander-M is about 65 weapons a month, he said, with the Kremlin able to add limited numbers of S-400 dual-use and North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles to the attacks as well, Skibidsky said.
Production of Iskander-M missiles has accelerated about 10% since the start of the year and Russian manufacturing of cruise missiles – a weapon Ukrainian air defenses are fairly efficient at detecting and shooting down – increased by about 40% over the same period, he said.
As of mid-August, per Ukrainian intelligence estimates, Russia has about 400 S-400 missiles, 130 ballistic “Iskander-M” and 100 North Korean KN-24 in stock, Skibidsky said. Future attack targets most likely will be the Ukrainian defense industry, railways, ports, shipping, logistics and energy infrastructure, he said.
Based on Russian missile production rates and probable targets, attacks on electricity and heat supply facilities are to be expected, and Ukraine needs to prepare for them, Skibidsky said.

Expert coach shares five kettlebell workouts to get you in ‘the shape of your life’
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:43:21 BST
22:43:21 KST

Expert coach shares five kettlebell workouts to get you in ‘the shape of your life’
In this week’s Well Enough newsletter, Harry Bullmore explores Dan John’s five-step kettlebell system for building strength and fitness, revealing how a handful of simple movements, loaded carries and smart progression can be combined into an effective, scalable full-body training plan for any level
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The article below is an excerpt from my newsletter: Well Enough with Harry Bullmore. To get my latest thoughts on fitness and wellbeing pop your email address into the box above to get the newsletter direct to your inbox.
You only get one body, and it’s with you for life. I want to help you build a body that you enjoy living in, and I don’t want you to spend much money in the process. From my experience, kettlebell training delivers on both fronts – and then some.
A kettlebell is a relatively inexpensive lump of iron with a handle that lasts a lifetime. Better yet, it’s versatile enough to help you improve every facet of fitness – strength, mobility, muscle, cardiovascular fitness and more. All you need is to know is how to use it.
That’s where coach Dan John comes in. John has been making people fitter since 1979, shaping the way we train with kettlebells and inventing many exercises now seen as commonplace, such as the goblet squat. Over the last couple of years, I’ve enjoyed a series of interviews with him in which he revealed his five-step method for starting kettlebell training – whatever your fitness level.
“If you were to stick me in a prison where all I had was a 16kg or 20kg kettlebell, and you told me I would only be let out when I was in the best shape of my life, I could pull it off,” John told me during our first meeting. Having since put his teachings into practice, I’m inclined to agree.
Now, his five-step guide to kettlebell training for beginners is ready to share. The links below dive into more detail on each step, while the article that follows contains a whistle-stop tour of the plan alongside sample workout videos for each stage.
- Part one: learning the three fundamental kettlebell exercises
- Part two: introducing loaded carries, which offer ‘the most bang for your buck of any exercise’
- Part three: the many benefits of training with two kettlebells, and how to do it effectively
- Part four: take your workouts outside and enjoy plenty of unexpected perks
- Part five: everything you need to know to transform your health, fitness and body with just a kettlebell or two
Dan John’s five-step guide to kettlebell training for beginners
John’s first lesson is that everyday fitness is a simple three-part formula: “Strength training, walking and caloric correctness.” Your priority should be to make strength training sessions a regular part of your routine, he says.
Next, establish a decent dose of daily movement through walking, then consume an appropriate number of calories for your activity levels. Brownie points are on offer if you can include some form of protein, fibre and fruit or vegetables with each meal. Now you are ready to train.
John sees the body as a series of interconnected systems rather than isolated parts, so he prefers to target movement patterns instead of specific muscles with his workouts.
There are five basic human movements, according to John: push, pull, hinge at the hips, squat and loaded carry. If you can touch on each of these on a regular basis, you will feel the benefits.
The good news is that you can hit all five with just three fundamental exercises: the kettlebell swing, goblet squat and press-up. You can find an example of how to weave these into a quick workout in the Instagram post embedded above.
Learning these movements is step one of training with kettlebells. (Although, if you do not feel ready for a dynamic exercise like the kettlebell swing, you can swap it out for a kettlebell glute bridge.) You can then combine these moves in any number of ways to create fun, effective and efficient workouts.
Step two in your introduction to kettlebell training is adding loaded carries into your workouts. This simply means picking up a weight and carrying it, whether you’re holding it at your side, at your shoulder or overhead.
“Loaded carries offer the most bang for your buck of any exercise,” says John. “The weird thing about the whole loaded carry family is, I don’t care what you do, you will benefit just by doing them. If you’ve never done a loaded carry, try it, then ask me more questions.”
Step three is incorporating a second kettlebell into your training, broadening your exercise horizons even further. There are three key exercises to learn here: the double kettlebell clean, double kettlebell front squat and double kettlebell press – the third entry being “the best thing you can do with kettlebells,” according to John.
“You can call the area from your neck to your knees whatever you want,” John says. “Lots of people call it the core, but saying ‘the core’ is like saying ‘doing cardio’ – it’s an overused term. The three words I use for this area are armour, anaconda and arrow.”
Armour means packing on muscle, anaconda is the harnessing of internal pressure (bracing) for stability, and arrow refers to the ability to move powerfully. John believes training with two kettlebells is largely unrivalled in its ability to develop all three areas, building a fit, functional and robust body.
Step four is to take your training outside. You don’t need me to tell you that spending time in nature is good for your health, so why not combine this with your regular workouts for bonus perks? There are some unexpected extra benefits on offer too.
For one, your workout starts early. Lugging a kettlebell to your chosen spot in a park is a decent warm-up in and of itself, and it covers your loaded carry work for the day.
Training outside also makes you more adaptable, John says. And adaptation is the reason we exercise, whether that’s wanting to look better, perform better or feel better, mentally and physically.
“Training outside makes you more like a jazz performer,” John says. “Maybe the ground is soggy so you can’t do a lot of ground work; maybe it’s unseasonably hot; maybe your usual spot has been taken by a family picnic. You have to adapt.”
Finally, we reach step five. You have the constituent parts of a successful exercise plan, and now you just need to put them all together. John gives an example of how to do so in this sample kettlebell training plan.
However, he also encourages intuitiveness among his clients. No one knows your body and what it is capable of better than you do. It is down to you to use the raw ingredients above appropriately and create a suitable exercise plan.
“As you learn more moves, you can figure out that one day a week is a mobility day, one or two days a week are ‘get sweaty’ days and one or two days a week are ‘get strong’ days,” John adds. “The piece of equipment remains the same – the kettlebell.”
“You also always have to leave something in the tank,” he continues. “If you work out so hard today that it impacts your workout tomorrow, you’ll actually end up regressing. It’s far better to have 365 days of training consistently than one incredibly hard session followed by nothing for the next few days.”
Therein lies the quiet beauty of the kettlebell. It sits in the corner of a room for most of the day like a glorified doorstop, then transforms into an entire gym when it comes time to exercise.
Having a whole gym on hand at any hour of the day allows for accessible, time-savvy workouts, and these in turn lead to consistency – the common denominator behind any successful fitness plan. To start transforming your fitness, simply grab a kettlebell and get into the swing of things.

Powerful 6.6-magnitude quake rocks Colombia, geological agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:42:57 UTC
22:42:57 KST

The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogotá, the US Geological Survey and Colombia's counterpart reported.
At least 111 people were killed and hundreds of buildings damaged after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, the country's President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Monday.
De la Espriella said that at least 87 people had been injured and that he had declared a state of emergency.
“You are not alone. The state is present and taking action,” he said.
The quake trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as the capital of Bogotá.
The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogotá, the US Geological Survey and Colombia’s counterpart reported.
The USGS said it struck at a depth of 107 kilometers and was also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.
The quake left cities across the west of the country ravaged.
A mix of residents and search teams picked through the rubble of collapsed buildings amid concerns by authorities of aftershocks.
Colombia's interior minister said more than 20 municipalities across the country had been hit.
Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in hills of the city as buildings collapsed. Residents in the city and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors.
“My entire house shook,” he said. “I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake.”
Colombia's Geological Service said on Monday that it had been “the highest magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade” and that it had been followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.
Authorities also reported that flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura and Pereira.
The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5,000 people.
At the same time the quake brought down buildings in Colombia, desperate families in Venezuela continued to search the ruins for the bodies of their loved ones.
In Pereira, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling down on travellers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic.
Pereira's mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that at least 18 people had died and that many more were trapped under “a massive quantity of collapsed buildings.”
In nearby Manizales, a city nestled in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Jorge Eduardo Rojas, the mayor of Manizales said two people had died in the city “because of the quake” and asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks.
Authorities in the rural state of Choco, the epicentre of the quake, reported injured people and damaged buildings in the capital, but provided few details.
In Cali, a city 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed.
Small earthquakes, known as “temblores,” are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare.
In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia, killed more than 1,100 people.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday the bloc was "ready to provide more support" after a powerful earthquake struck Colombia.
"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia after the terrible earthquake in the Choco region. We have already mobilised Copernicus, our satellite service, to help with rescue operations," von der Leyen said in a post on X.

Large earthquake hits western Colombia causing damage

13:42:00 UTC

Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026
A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.
Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.
Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.
The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.
The government has declared a state of emergency.
What is the latest?
Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.
He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.
"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.
"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."
What's happening on the ground?
The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.
"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."
Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.
Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.
The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.
And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.
Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.
"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.
What do we know about the quake's size and location?
The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.
The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.
The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.
The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.
The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors.
Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.
USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.
The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

34% of Italian sea, lake water samples exceed legal pollution limits: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:41:27 UTC
22:41:27 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
More than one-third of sea and lake water samples collected across Italy exceeded legal pollution limits, according to a recent report by an Italian environmental group.
"In Italy, even this summer, seas and lakes are increasingly under strain and vulnerable," said an assessment by Goletta Verde and Goletta dei Laghi 2026, two annual summer campaigns run by environmental group Legambiente to monitor the country's seas and lake basins.
The assessment found that 34% of the 391 samples collected from marine and lake waters across 19 regions exceeded legal pollution limits, accounting for more than one in three samples.
"Unfortunately, the overall figure is in line with last year and shows no improvement. The trend is also negative for lakes, where the 34% recorded in 2026 is the worst result of the past seven years (2020–2026)," it said.
The assessment noted that inadequate wastewater treatment is among the main factors affecting the health of sea and lake basins.
It also found that 54% of the 188 samples taken from river mouths were polluted or heavily polluted.
"Even in areas far from river mouths or discharge points, water quality is not at its best: 15% of samples taken directly from the sea or lake waters exceeded legal limits, with 5% classified as polluted and 10% as heavily polluted," the assessment added.
The report also raised concern over the lack of information signs at river mouths, saying 70% of those monitored had no signs prohibiting swimming.

Swarm Aero lands U.S. Air Force deal to speed up drone production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
12:36:54 UTC
21:36:54 KST

- Swarm Aero announced more than $10 million in contracts with the Air Force Research Laboratory to develop high-rate composite aircraft manufacturing techniques.
- The work will be performed at Swarm's Advanced Manufacturing Center in Fayetteville, Arkansas, an 80,000-square-foot facility opened earlier in 2026.
A California aerospace firm building giant swarms of unmanned aircraft has landed a deal with the Air Force to prove it can manufacture those aircraft faster and cheaper than anyone else in the industry.
Swarm Aero, a defense technology company that develops large uncrewed aerial vehicles designed to operate in coordinated fleets, announced more than $10 million in contracts with the Air Force Research Laboratory to develop and test a new method for mass-producing composite aircraft parts, the kind of lightweight, high-strength material used to build everything from fighter jet wings to commercial airliner fuselages.
The Air Force Research Laboratory, known as AFRL, is the Air Force’s primary science and technology organization, responsible for identifying and funding emerging technologies years before they become standard military hardware. Its involvement here centers on a manufacturing technique Swarm has spent the past four years refining, a high-rate composite production process the company says allows it to build large aircraft airframes at volumes far beyond what traditional aerospace manufacturing typically achieves, and at a fraction of the cost of comparable military aircraft built using conventional methods.
Peter Kalogiannis, CEO and co-founder of Swarm Aero, explained that the company treated manufacturing as a core design priority from its earliest days rather than an afterthought bolted on once a working aircraft existed.
“Since our first engineering hire, Swarm has invested in manufacturing and design in tandem. We are not designing or even building one aircraft only to then start thinking about how to manufacture it at scale. We have designed our manufacturing processes to enable us to deliver aircraft at the scale our customers require. Our team has a strong track record both in building large, novel aircraft extremely quickly and in delivering aircraft at volume. We’re looking forward to leveraging our manufacturing approach to build cost-efficient flyable aircraft components using our unique methods,” said Kalogiannis.
That emphasis on manufacturing speed reflects a broader problem the U.S. military has struggled with for years, the gap between building a single impressive prototype aircraft and actually producing enough of them to matter in a real conflict. Traditional composite aircraft manufacturing tends to be slow and labor-intensive, often requiring skilled technicians to hand-layer carbon fiber sheets and cure them in specialized ovens called autoclaves, a process that can take days per major component and makes scaling production to thousands of units extraordinarily expensive. Swarm’s pitch is that its high-rate manufacturing process sidesteps much of that bottleneck, and the company has already built infrastructure to prove it can operate at scale, opening an 80,000-square-foot (7,432-square-meter) Advanced Manufacturing Center at Drake Field in Fayetteville, Arkansas earlier this year, a facility the company says will eventually have the capacity to produce thousands of unmanned aircraft and create hundreds of skilled aerospace jobs over the next decade.
Oliver Palmer, Swarm’s Chief Revenue Officer and co-founder, framed the Air Force Research Laboratory partnership as validation from an organization with deep credibility in evaluating exactly this kind of manufacturing innovation.
“The Air Force Research Lab’s structures and materials and manufacturing teams have been consistent leaders in the industry and champions for introducing new processes that can reduce cost. We are honored to partner with them as we bring forward our novel manufacturing process. They both are tremendous partners and are well placed within the Department of War’s engineering ecosystem to evaluate what we are doing,” said Palmer.
Swarm Aero was founded in 2022 by a team drawing on decades of combined aerospace experience across companies including Scaled Composites, SpaceX, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, Airbus and Archer, along with leadership that previously managed major Air Force acquisition programs, including a former commander of Air Force Material Command who oversaw a $60 billion annual weapons acquisition budget and a former leader of the Air Force’s $24 billion unmanned aircraft systems portfolio. That background has shaped the company’s core pitch to the military, that large uncrewed aircraft paired with coordinated software can accomplish missions traditionally requiring manned fighter jets or bombers, without putting a pilot’s life at risk, while costing several times less than the crewed aircraft they could eventually supplement or replace.
The strategic logic behind that pitch has become increasingly urgent as Pentagon planners study potential conflict scenarios in the Pacific, where China’s growing military capabilities and the vast distances involved have pushed American defense officials to prioritize aircraft that can be produced quickly and in large numbers rather than relying solely on smaller fleets of extremely expensive, exquisitely capable platforms. A single F-35 fighter jet costs roughly $80 million to $100 million depending on the variant, a price tag that inherently limits how many a nation can afford to field, whereas a large uncrewed aircraft built through mass-manufacturing techniques promises a fundamentally different math, trading some of the sophistication of a manned fighter for the ability to field dramatically greater numbers of aircraft across a contested battlespace.
The company raised $35 million in a Series A funding round earlier this year, led by Two Sigma Ventures and Silent Ventures with participation from earlier seed investors including Khosla Ventures, funding that helped support the buildout of its Arkansas manufacturing facility. Swarm now maintains operations across Oxnard, California, Spokane, Washington, Fayetteville, Arkansas, and Washington, D.C., a geographic footprint that spans both its engineering headquarters and its growing production capacity, along with a presence in the nation’s capital positioned to maintain close contact with the Pentagon customers the company is ultimately building toward.

A pilates studio in Gelderland has been hit by three explosive attacks in six weeks, the most recent in the early hours of Monday, police have said.
The studio in Zevenaar, which opened a year ago, was first targeted on June 24, when a blast blew a window pane out of the front door and caused a fire to break out.

Five days later a second explosion blew a hole in the entrance. The word betalen (“pay”) was written three times on a window.
The most recent attack was at around 2.45am on Monday, when another explosion went off and a brick was hurled through a window, Omroep Gelderland reported. The explosion was heard throughout the neighbourhood.
The door and several windows of the building have been boarded up following the attacks. Police would not say if they were linked or if any arrests have been made.

Lebanon indicts ex-central bank governor Salameh over new alleged financial crimes
BEIRUT, Aug 10 - A Lebanese judge on Monday indicted former central bank governor Riad Salameh and a former commercial banker, accusing them of financial crimes including embezzlement and illicit enrichment, a senior Lebanese judicial source told Reuters.
Salameh, who headed the Lebanese Central Bank for three decades, has already been indicted and arrested in Lebanon over other alleged financial crimes committed during his tenure. He has denied any wrongdoing.
On Monday, a Lebanese judge accused him and Samir Hanna, the former head of Lebanon's Bank Audi, of embezzling tens of millions in funds from the Lebanese central bank, the judicial source said. The source said the file includes accusations that Hanna bribed Salameh while he was central bank governor.
It is the first time a commercial banker has been indicted in a financial crimes case related to Salameh, showing that Lebanese investigations into the former governor are expanding to the private sector, the source said.
Salameh did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Hanna could not immediately be reached for comment.
The former governor is currently in custody but is under medical supervision at a government hospital outside Beirut, after having missed a hearing over the case. Hanna, 88, paid a $1 million bail and is not in custody as financial investigations continue.
In January, Lebanon's current central bank governor Karim Souaid told reporters that the central bank had filed a criminal complaint against an unnamed former official of the central bank, a former banker and a lawyer over alleged illicit enrichment through misuse of public funds. He said the operations were carried out through four offshore shell companies in the Cayman Islands that he did not name.
Accountability Now, a Swiss foundation that has worked to investigate Salameh, said in a post on social media platform X on Monday that the indictment covered the suspected embezzlement of $154 million in 2010 and $102 million in 2012.
Salameh was detained for about 13 months over alleged financial crimes committed during his tenure and was released in September after paying record bail of more than $14 million.
He also faces investigations abroad, including in France, Switzerland and Germany. REUTERS

Driver who broke sound barrier attempts another speed record in Utah
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:38:55 BST
22:38:55 KST

Driver who broke sound barrier attempts another speed record in Utah
At age 64, Andy Green thought his racing career was behind him until JCB invited him to join their new project
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The sole person to ever drive a car faster than the speed of sound is returning to the salt flats of Utah this week, aiming to establish a fresh world speed benchmark.
Two decades after British driver Andy Green achieved a diesel-powered land speed record of 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) on Utah’s Bonneville Salt Flats, he is returning to the desert terrain on Tuesday. This time, he will attempt to surpass his previous achievement using a vehicle propelled by hydrogen.
Beyond pursuing a new title, the retired Royal Air Force fighter pilot hopes to demonstrate the viable potential of hydrogen as a clean energy option. Green described hydrogen as the "fuel of the future" during an interview with The Associated Press in July.
For his latest attempt, Green will steer the 32-foot (9.75-meter) JCB Hydromax, a slender, bright yellow machine crafted by British construction equipment producer JCB that looks much like a pencil. Drive comes from two modified construction machinery engines converted into hydrogen internal combustion units. Producing a collective 1,600 horsepower, the engines ignite a mix of ambient air and pressurized hydrogen gas to supply propulsion.
While aiming to eclipse his old diesel record, Green also intends to surpass the existing land speed marks for hydrogen internal combustion cars (185.5 mph/298.5 kph) and electric vehicles (341.3 mph/549.2 kph).
During practice runs last week, Green recorded a top speed of 368.347 mph (592.797 kph). However, to make the record official, he must replicate the feat on Tuesday under the observation of motorsport’s global authority, the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile.
"What the peak speed is, I can’t say. We just don’t know," Green said. "Part of the adventure here is we’re going to find out."
Tuesday's run will not come close to matching the supersonic velocities Green attained using jet propulsion nearly thirty years ago.
Guinness World Records notes that Green was already a supersonic military pilot when he saw a print advertisement stating: "Wanted: High-speed driver to break the sound barrier."
In 1997, driving a twin-jet vehicle in Nevada's Black Rock Desert, he broke the sound barrier and set the absolute land speed record of 763.035 mph (1,227.98 kph), generating sonic booms that rattled the nearby community of Gerlach.
At age 64, Green believed his racing career was behind him until JCB invited him to join their new project. The manufacturer has poured over $134 million into developing hydrogen engines, which it states generate zero carbon dioxide tailpipe emissions.
"If you’re serious about emissions, you have to be serious about hydrogen, and a land speed project is the perfect way to prove it," JCB Chair Anthony Bamford declared during the vehicle's May presentation. Bamford maintains that hydrogen technology is better suited to heavy industrial applications than battery-electric solutions.
Nevertheless, the environmental benefit of hydrogen depends heavily on its origin, with most supply currently derived from fossil fuels. To counter this, JCB contracted to purchase green hydrogen—produced via renewable energy sources—though it represents only a small portion of global production.
Operating hydrogen internal combustion engines carries specific safety hazards because the pressurized gas is extremely flammable.
"We're managing the risks very carefully," Green stated. Following extensive testing of the vehicle, Green spent several months studying its handling under local weather conditions, mastering the dual-engine coordination, and practicing parachute deployment to decelerate across the slick salt surface.
Drivers seeking speed records have gathered at the smooth expanse of the Bonneville Salt Flats since racing first began there in 1914. Situated roughly 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Salt Lake City, this ancient lake bed covers an aquifer that helps cool passing vehicle tires.
Onlookers are required to remain a quarter mile (400 meters) away from the 10-mile (16-kilometer) straight track, frequently relying on wide-angle binoculars to view the action.
Located near the Utah-Nevada state line, the landscape has served as a filming site for feature films such as Independence Day and The World’s Fastest Indian, along with the final episode of the television series Mad Men.
Green is scheduled to launch his attempt approximately an hour before dawn on Tuesday. The run comes one year after a fatal accident at Bonneville's annual Speed Week, where driver Chris Raschke crashed his rocket-shaped vehicle, Speed Demon, at 283 mph (455 kph) last August and succumbed to his injuries.

Is Andy Burnham seriously about to tour Britain like some medieval monarch? | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:38:12 UTC
22:38:12 KST

Andy Burnham is going on a “listening tour”, travelling the country on a bus to find out what real people are concerned about. I’ve heard commentators rationalise the idea in various ways: apparently it underscores the difference between him and his predecessor, who only ever relaxed when he was out of the country; what else is Burnham going to do in recess, with his cabinet already chosen – organise his Post-it notes?; he’s been out of politics a long time, and many people will be only dimly aware of who he is; his speeches to date have had a very urban focus, and particularly with farming being this season’s crisis sector, he needs to broaden his sphere of interest to take in rural areas. Truly, the prime ministerial honeymoon period is like a one-year-old’s birthday party – all you have to do is stand up and smile, for everyone to clap.
None of the rationalisations are in any way true: an in-person focus group, where you journey to discover a range of concerns you could figure out for yourself with one report from the Institute for Public Policy Research and half a brain, is exactly the kind of thing Starmer would have done, if he’d thought of it. There’s quite a bit to be getting on with, between now and September, since autumn’s looming crises – food shortages, energy price hikes due to the ongoing war in Iran – are plain, and there’s no better time to plan than when you don’t have the leader of the opposition yanking your chain. Burnham actually has tremendous household-level recognition, thanks to a combination of hinterland and eyelashes, as evidenced by the fact that even when contesting Makerfield he got mobbed every time he got out of a car. Now, the conditions devastating farmers, being the direct result of climate crisis, would be better addressed by a long-range strategy on the transition to renewables, not a chinwag.
I’ll meet the road show halfway, though, and accept that the thinking behind it is buried deeper in the squishy collective subconscious than the “marketing strategy for mid-sized building society” strata. This is the living definition of “peripatetic”, an adjective usually attached to kings. Medieval kings travelled around the country in order to collect their taxes by literally eating them from one noble estate to the next. Tax hikes could be exacted by simply adding to your entourage and eating more. King John’s train stretched two miles, bulked up by the mercenaries required to protect the pampered non-warrior class from rebel barons who were sick of having their food eaten. In a pesky feedback loop, the larger your entourage, the more you all ate, the more annoyed the aristocracy became, the more mercenaries you needed and the larger your entourage.
Burnham could be forgiven for thinking he’s more than a match for this death spiral, having the lessons of history right there, but can we forgive him for the emotional leap that put him on his tour bus? His first question seems to have been not “What would the leader of a mature democracy in an embattled period do?” but “What would be the first move of the King of the North?” His kingly role models must all come from the dawn of monarchy, since by the time you get to Henry VIII, he’s only really travelling to escape sewage overflow from his last great palace. But then “King of the North” has always had a very medieval overtone. A sign of the early modern period’s growing governmental sophistication was its ability to distinguish one bit of the north from another.
It is endearing, if also nerve-racking and painful, to consider the faith underpinning this self-fashioning – that leadership is an innate quality more important than sequential thought and planning, and that if the stars light upon a leader who can connect with his people, the nation will come together, good decisions will be made, and the rest is detail. One can but hope that’s the limit of the wishful thinking, and he’s not also banking on some dragons.

Türkiye's Parliament begins debate on National Solidarity bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:34:40 UTC
22:34:40 KST

Türkiye’s Parliament has begun debating the National Solidarity Bill, a key legislative component of the government’s Terror-Free Türkiye initiative aimed at ending the country’s decades-long terrorism problem.
The bill establishes procedures for suspending investigations, prosecutions, convictions and related legal proceedings once authorities determine that the terrorist organisation PKK/KCK and affiliated groups have ended their activities and surrendered their weapons.
Lawmakers stress justice and national unity
Speaking during the General Assembly debate on Monday, Felicity Party leader Mahmut Arikan said lawmakers were considering legislation that would shape both Türkiye’s past and its future.
Arikan said significant efforts had been made to resolve the country’s terrorism problem and noted that his party had openly expressed its expectations throughout the Terror-Free Türkiye process.
He stressed that a lasting solution would require strengthening justice, the rule of law, social cohesion and national solidarity.
New Path Party Group Chairman Mehmet Emin Ekmen credited President Recep Tayyip Erdogan with playing a clear and constructive role in managing the process and bringing it to its current stage.
He also thanked Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahceli for his position during the initiative.
Bill sets out legal path after disarmament
The legislation covers offences including membership in, aiding or promoting the organisation, as well as crimes committed as part of its activities and terrorism-financing offences carried out in its favour.
Its provisions would take effect after competent authorities determine that the PKK/KCK terrorist organisation and affiliated groups have ceased their activities and surrendered their weapons.
The parliamentary debate marks a significant legislative step in the broader Terror-Free Türkiye process, with lawmakers now weighing how the proposed legal framework can support a lasting end to terrorism while addressing concerns over justice, accountability and social cohesion.

Russia posts rising trade surplus in H1

Emre Gurkan Abay and Emir Yildirim
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
Russia’s trade surplus climbed 14% to $73.4 billion in the first six months of the year, according to its Federal Customs Service.
Russian exports rose by $23.2 billion to $219.5 billion, and imports dropped by $14.2 billion to $146.1 billion over the same period. The country’s total foreign trade volume rose 11.4% to $365.6 billion.
Russian exports to European countries decreased 5.6% to $28 billion, while imports from Europe increased 8.7% to $37.1 billion.
Russian exports to Asia surged 17.2% to $174.9 billion, and Asian imports to the country increased 12.6% to $98.9 billion.
Meanwhile, Russian exports to North and South American countries were down 12.1%, reaching $5.7 billion, while imports from these countries into Russia rose 4.6% to $7.9 billion.
The main Russian exports were minerals and mineral products worth $120.7 billion over the six-month period, while the most imported category of items was machinery, equipment and vehicles, totaling $70.9 billion, the data showed.
Last year, Russia’s trade surplus shrink by 8.2% on an annual basis to $139.3 billion.

Why choosing low-fat dairy is not necessarily better for your health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:31:09 UTC
22:31:09 KST

Why choosing low-fat dairy is not necessarily better for your health
For years, we thought low-fat dairy was the way to manage obesity. New research is increasingly questioning this logic.
Low-fat dairy products may not be healthier than full-fat, researchers say, challenging decades of common knowledge linking full-fat dairy to weight gain and cardiovascular conditions.
For decades, scientists and nutritionists preached switching to low-fat dairy to counter obesity and cholesterol, but new research suggests otherwise and goes a step further to indicate that, instead, a full-fat dairy serving could even offer some health benefits.
Research by Harvey Anderson, professor at the University of Toronto, adds to growing evidence that full-fat dairy can be part of a healthy diet.
The researchers found that eating three servings of full-fat dairy per day did not negatively affect body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood lipid levels, as per a report published in The Journal of Nutrition.
So, what did the research find and how? And does low-fat make any difference?
What does the study show?
The researchers at the University of Toronto assigned 74 adults with overweight or obesity to one of three dietary groups, studied between September 2020 and February 2023.
One group followed a low-dairy, calorie-restricted diet; the second group followed an energy-neutral diet with three servings of dairy each day; the third group ate an unrestricted diet with three daily servings of dairy. Those assigned to the dairy groups were supplied with full-fat dairy products during the study.
After 12 weeks, researchers found no meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or cholesterol levels between people following the low-dairy diet and those eating three servings of dairy each day.
The research cites food guides in Canada and the United States recommending three servings of low- or no-fat dairy a day for adults, noting that the countries are not recognising recent evidence that full-fat dairy may be beneficial.
The study found that participants consuming more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and better intake of calcium, protein and vitamin D.
“Those that had three servings of dairy didn’t have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance,” Anderson told the ScienceDaily website.
Why has full-fat dairy been frowned upon?
The basic nutritional logic has been straightforward: whole-fat dairy contains substantial saturated fat, and saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, known as “bad cholesterol”; therefore, cutting the fat content of dairy should reduce cardiovascular risk.
Dietary guidance treated saturated fat as a major health risk and encouraged people to switch from whole milk and other full-fat dairy to low-fat or fat-free versions.
The underlying logic was not entirely wrong. Saturated fat raises cholesterol, and replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fats, particularly polyunsaturated fats found in foods such as nuts, seeds and vegetable oils, is associated with lower cardiovascular risk.
However, a large Harvard analysis published in 2016, involving more than 220,000 participants across three US cohorts, found that dairy fat itself was not associated with higher cardiovascular disease risk, but replacing dairy fat with polyunsaturated fat was associated with a 24 percent lower cardiovascular risk, while replacing it with vegetable fat was associated with a 10 percent lower risk.
Prof Anderson, who led the latest research, said the evidence from human research has not always matched those concerns. Some studies, including recent research led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, have even reported positive or protective effects associated with dairy consumption, he noted.
How does new research counter it?
Existing popular understanding suggests that removing dairy fat was expected to help prevent excess weight gain. The new study complicates this assumption.
If three servings of full-fat dairy per day do not cause measurable increases in weight, body fat, or cholesterol, it suggests that the presence of dairy fat in a person’s diet does not automatically translate into the adverse metabolic effects that the old model predicted.
It also challenges the idea that the fat content printed on the dairy label is, by itself, a useful proxy for the food’s health effects.
However, the bigger question it posed was for the food matrix itself.
Older nutritional thinking often focused on individual nutrients: saturated fat was considered a risk factor, so a food containing more saturated fat was presumed to be worse.
But researchers are increasingly looking at dairy as a whole food matrix containing protein, minerals, vitamins, carbohydrates and fat. The way those components interact may affect how the body responds to the fat.
In simpler words, the health effects of a food may depend on how its components interact rather than simply on the amount of one nutrient it contains.
“With dairy products, it’s got two proteins – casein and whey – that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in,” says Anderson.
