Warship cut in two found off the Isle of Wight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:18:23 BST
22:18:23 KST

Divers have located the wreck of HMS Tiger, a Royal Navy warship lost off the Isle of Wight in 1908 after being cut in two during a training exercise, and the ship is set to gain legal protection under changes to shipwreck law now before Parliament, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The discovery was announced by ProjectXplore, a team of divers and historians who spent five years working through archives to narrow down the location. The same group found the wreck of the cruiser HMS Nottingham in the North Sea last year. Tiger had evaded searchers since her loss 118 years ago, when she strayed into the path of another warship and was severed. Fewer than half of her 57-strong crew survived.
The announcement is timed alongside government proposals to amend the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 through the Armed Forces Bill. Under the changes, military wrecks would be designated protected places automatically from the moment they are found, making it an offence to disturb or remove items without permission while still allowing divers to visit on a look but don’t touch basis.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Minister for the Armed Forces, said in the release that “Defence has a role to play in preserving our maritime heritage and the memory of those who gave their lives”, adding that the protections are intended to safeguard vulnerable and nationally significant monuments from the first day of discovery. She described the Armed Forces Bill as wide-ranging, spanning cultural heritage and improvements to the defence housing estate.
The current Act has significant gaps, according to the department. More than 129 sites have been designated in the four decades since it passed, either as protected places, which divers may visit, or as controlled sites, which require a licence from the MOD before any diving takes place. But the legislation does not cover wrecks more than 200 years old, offers no immediate protection to newly discovered wrecks, and permits only vessels lost after 4 August 1914 to be classified as protected places. Ships such as Tiger fall outside that date, leaving them either unprotected for years after discovery or pushed into the more restrictive controlled site category because no other option exists.
Extending the Act beyond the 200-year limit would bring vessels dating back as far as the Armada into scope, including former enemy ships, along with merchant vessels sunk while serving under Admiralty orders.
Leo Fielding and Dan McMullen, co-organisers of ProjectXplore, said in the release that documenting the wreck had been “the privilege of a lifetime” and that they hope the ship and the memory of those connected with her endure. The group described the proposed amendments as a constructive step in protecting UK maritime heritage.
Lieutenant Commander Jen Smith, the Royal Navy’s Deputy Fleet Wreck Officer, said protecting military wrecks benefits both maritime heritage and the diving community, noting that divers can still visit the sites. Her request of them is simple: “enjoy looking, learning and paying your respects at these incredible sites” without disturbing them.
Beyond shipwrecks, the Armed Forces Bill proposes improvements to service accommodation and an expansion of the UK’s Strategic Reserve, the pool of former service personnel carrying an ex-regular and recall reserve liability, which the department says would allow defence to draw on veterans’ skills in a crisis.
The waters around the Isle of Wight and the wider Solent approaches are among the most densely wrecked in British waters, holding losses from the Tudor period onward including the Mary Rose, raised in 1982, and numerous casualties from both world wars. The Protection of Military Remains Act has historically been applied to well-known sites such as HMS Hood and the ships sunk at Scapa Flow, with designation intended to prevent salvage and souvenir hunting on what are legally war graves.
Images: Dan McMullen and Guy Trees / ProjectXplore.

Erdoğan hosts Austria’s chancellor in Ankara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:17:53 UTC
22:17:53 KST

Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker arrived in Türkiye on Aug. 10 at the invitation of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan for talks expected to focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation.
The visit includes a comprehensive discussion of steps that could be taken to further develop cooperation between Ankara and Vienna, Türkiye’s Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said.
Duran said the talks would cover “all aspects of the countries’ multifaceted relations and include an exchange of views on current regional and global developments.”
Local media reported that Vienna’s interest in acquiring drones could be among the key issues on the agenda.
Austria’s parliament voted in 2016, with the support of all six political parties represented at the time, to halt arms exports to Türkiye. The decision was followed by calls to prevent the export of Rotax engines used in Turkish drones. Türkiye later began developing and producing domestically manufactured piston engines for its drones.
Stocker has served as Austria’s chancellor since March 2025. A member of the center-right People’s Party, he has been a member of the National Council since 2019.
He served as the party’s secretary-general from September 2022 to January 2025 before becoming acting leader following the resignation of Chancellor Karl Nehammer.

One million evacuated as Typhoon Dolphin pummels east China: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:14:34 UTC
22:14:34 KST

One million evacuated as Typhoon Dolphin pummels east China: What we know
Hundreds of flights have been grounded in China due to weather conditions caused by Dolphin.
China evacuates a million from homes as Typhoon Dolphin arrives
Provinces in eastern China have been inundated with heavy rain and flooding caused by Typhoon Dolphin, the strongest storm to make landfall in China this year.
Dolphin struck eastern China, including Shanghai, with winds up to 150 kilometres per hour (93 miles per hour), forcing more than one million people to evacuate their homes. The storm has disrupted flights and other transport while bringing heavy rain, flooding and the risk of landslides across the region.
About 40 percent of flights in Shanghai were grounded on Monday due to the weather.
After Dolphin made landfall late on Sunday, it weakened to below cyclone strength and is forecast to weaken further as it moves inland.
Here is what we know:
When and where did Typhoon Dolphin make landfall?
The typhoon made landfall in Yuhuan in China’s Zhejiang province about 5:30pm (09:30 GMT) on Sunday, according to China’s meteorological authorities.
On Monday, Shanghai was badly hit with residents circulating the hashtag “Shanghai turns into the sea” on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.
Last month, Typhoon Bavi also made landfall in Zhejiang, causing the evacuation of 1.7 million people.
Where is the storm moving, and how much damage will it cause?
Torrential rain was expected on Monday across Zhejiang, Shanghai, northern Fujian, northeastern Jiangxi, central and southern Anhui and much of Jiangsu.
Parts of central and eastern Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm (10 to 20 inches) of rain in all, according to forecasters.
China’s Ministry of Water Resources warned that the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao and Shuiyang rivers could experience major flooding while smaller rivers in the hardest hit areas could rise above warning levels.
Authorities also warned of a high risk of geological disasters in parts of Zhejiang with residents in areas under a red mountain-torrent warning told to follow local evacuation orders.
Since making landfall, Dolphin is forecast to track westwards before slowing over central and southwestern China and gradually losing strength, Wang Haiping, chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Centre, told state broadcaster CCTV.
The slower movement could prolong heavy rainfall and increase the threat of flooding and landslides, particularly in mountainous areas and along smaller rivers.
How have the authorities responded?
The authorities have warned of the risk of severe flooding and landslides as the storm moves further inland and continues to bring heavy rain to densely populated areas of eastern China.
Shanghai evacuated at least 30,300 people while, in neighbouring Zhejiang province, the city of Wenzhou relocated more than 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters.
Authorities also evacuated about 390,000 people in the Zhejiang city of Taizhou before Saturday evening.
In Fujian province, about 98,900 people were evacuated from high-risk areas after authorities raised the typhoon emergency response to Level III, the state news agency Xinhua reported.
Authorities moved offshore workers to safety, ordered vessels back to port and stepped up inspections of reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations.
People have been told to avoid going out of doors and tourist attractions, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai have been closed.
In Hangzhou, Zhejiang’s capital, parking fees in public spaces have been waived for drivers needing to abandon vehicles to seek shelter.
Transport has been widely disrupted across the region. About 1,400 flights have been cancelled from Shanghai.
Fujian maritime authorities suspended 55 coastal passenger ferry routes, halted 115 offshore construction projects and moved 290 construction vessels to sheltered waters.
Shanghai’s Yangshan port also cleared ships from its berths and moved more than 500 small and medium-sized vessels to shelter before the storm.
How strong is Typhoon Dolphin, and where did it come from?
Dolphin originally grew out of a tropical depression on July 26, moving at 45km/h (30mph) over the open waters of the Central Pacific Ocean as it embarked on a journey of several thousand kilometres.
Over the course of its journey, Dolphin strengthened to a tropical storm and then to a severe tropical storm before burgeoning into a typhoon and then a very strong typhoon on July 28.
As it came ashore in China on Monday, the storm packed maximum sustained winds of 151km/h (93mph) near its centre, equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane, the lowest category of hurricane.
Hurricanes, cyclones and typhoons are all essentially the same thing. The main difference is where they originate. All three are storm systems with winds exceeding 118km/h (73mph).
Typhoons occur in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and frequently hit the Philippines and Japan. Typhoon season is most common between May and October, but the storms can form year-round. The strength of a typhoon has various classification scales with the most severe storms named super typhoons.
Cyclones occur in the South Pacific and the Indian Ocean, often impacting countries from Australia all the way to Mozambique. Cyclone season typically runs from November to April.
Hurricanes occur in the Atlantic Ocean and Eastern Pacific and often affect the East Coast of the United States, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. The strength of a hurricane is measured on a wind scale from 1 to 5. A Category 1 hurricane will bring sustained winds of 119-153km/h (74-95mph) whereas a Category 5 storm can exceed 252km/h (157mph).
Different agencies use different wind scales. China does not use the Saffir-Simpson hurricane category scale in its official domestic forecasting or national standards.
Will Typhoon Dolphin become stronger or weaker now?
Since making landfall on Sunday, Dolphin has weakened and is expected to further weaken.
As of Monday, Dolphin is a remnant low, or a weakened, post-tropical cyclone that has lost the organised thunderstorm activity required to qualify as a tropical storm. It is expected to continue to dissipate and lose energy on Tuesday to 35km/h by 17:00 GMT.
Where else has Typhoon Dolphin hit?
The typhoon battered the outer Japanese Ogasawara Islands, also called the Bonin Islands – the first part of Japan it reached – with strong winds on August 4.
Dolphin then swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture over the weekend, injuring at least six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.
The outer bands of Dolphin brought heavy rain to northern Taiwan, including the capital, Taipei, from Saturday. Dozens of ferry services were suspended, and more than 180 flights were cancelled as the storm brought strong winds and downpours.
In the Philippines, Dolphin intensified seasonal monsoon rains that triggered flooding and landslides in parts of the country.
Five people were rescued and seven were still missing after a landslide struck three houses in the northern mountain resort city of Baguio on Sunday, according to officials.
Flooding also affected large parts of the main northern island of Luzon, including the densely populated Manila metropolitan region, displacing more than 12,000 people and forcing several northern cities and towns to close schools on Friday and Saturday.
The monsoon rains followed a tropical storm that killed at least six people last week, including four people killed in a landslide and rockslide in the provinces of Benguet and Rizal, Philippine officials said.
Why is this storm called Typhoon Dolphin?
The typhoon has been named after Hong Kong’s Chinese white dolphins.
Individual hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are named by the Typhoon Committee at the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), which maintains premade, rotating lists of names.
For hurricanes originating in the Atlantic Ocean, these lists comprise typically male or female first names that are easy to remember.
The WMO’s lists of names for the western North Pacific’s storms include local animals, plants and cultural items. Dolphin was Hong Kong’s contribution.
Where to track Dolphin
You can track Dolphin on Zoom Earth, an online platform with satellite imagery that shows weather patterns and is useful for tracking storms.

Oman says grounded tanker oil spill covers 400 square km
Aug 10 - Leaking crude oil from a tanker grounded off a nature reserve in Oman has created a slick covering almost 400 square kilometres, the country's government said on Monday.
The Caroline Bezengi is loaded with close to one million barrels of Russian oil bound for Asia and first reported difficulties on June 8 off Yemen, with two maritime security sources saying initial assessments indicated a blast had occurred onboard.
No party has taken responsibility for attacking the vessel.
Oman, in its first public disclosure on the environmental impact, said on Monday it was seeking to tackle the oil leak near the Hallaniyat Islands.
Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tarik issued a royal decree last year creating a nature reserve around the islands, an area that is home to wildlife including Arabian Sea humpback whales and Socotra cormorants.
The oil slick covers some 390 square km (150 square miles), Oman's Environment Authority said in a statement carried by the state news agency, adding that there was no concern for facilities in the area including water desalination plants and tourist facilities.
Environmental group Greenpeace last week estimated the slick at around 600 square kilometres citing analysis of satellite imagery.
It extends northeast of the islands and is within an estimated seven kilometres of the coast, the authority said.
A spill of this scale requires dispersant be sprayed across the affected area by aircraft and the use of booms and other equipment to collect the oil before it reaches the shore or sinks to the sea floor, said Tony Gutierrez, professor of environmental microbiology and biotechnology at Edinburgh's Heriot-Watt University.
"If this oil is kept offshore, the impact will be much less than if the oil reaches shallower waters and the actual coastline," he said, citing the impact on diverse marine life such as coral, birds and fish.
"You could find oil still there years later. And that's what happened with Exxon Valdez. Ten years down the line, there still were remnants of oil," he said, referring to a 1989 spill in Alaska.
An analysis by Reuters of satellite imagery and shipping specialists showed the spill from the stranded 274-metre (900-foot) tanker was still spreading at the end of last month, raising concern about possible environmental damage.
The Caroline Bezengi loaded at Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in April and passed through the Suez Canal at the end of May, ship-tracking data shows.
Built in 2001, it is part of the so-called shadow fleet of older oil tankers used by Russia which lack Western insurance cover and sail under the flags of various nations to obscure their true ownership.
It was listed on public shipping databases as flying the Cameroon flag but was among 39 vessels de-listed from Cameroon’s ship registry in June.
The ship is subject to sanctions imposed by the European Union, Ukraine, the UK, Canada and Switzerland.
Its registered owner is Rentoor Shipmanagement Ltd and its manager is Villar Shipmanagement Ltd, according to LSEG data. Reuters could not immediately reach those firms, which appear to be based in China. REUTERS

Kyiv under S-400 fire: how Russia has turned air defence missiles into a weapon of terror and why they keep coming
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
16:13:00 EEST
22:13:00 KST

Kyiv under S-400 fire: how Russia has turned air defence missiles into a weapon of terror and why they keep coming
Russia attacked Ukraine with 24 ballistic missiles on the night of 4-5 August, which the Ukrainian Air Force grouped under the combined Iskander-M/S-400 designation. Kyiv Oblast bore the brunt of the strike. With Patriot interceptor stocks running low, Ukrainian air defences were unable to bring down a single missile.
What makes the S-400 particularly notable is that it was designed as an air defence system to intercept incoming missiles, not to strike ground targets. It has nevertheless been repurposed by Russia, which has ramped up production, extended its range to Kyiv, and significantly expanded its strike capabilities.
Read on this Ukrainska Pravda story to learn what these missiles are, why they travel at such high speeds, and why their inaccuracy makes them especially dangerous to the civilian population.
How an anti-aircraft missile becomes a short-range ballistic missile
This is not the first time Russia has used air defence missiles to strike ground targets. In 2022, it employed older S-300 surface-to-air missiles against towns and cities near the front line.
Subsequent reports confirmed the use of the newer 48N6 missiles, compatible with later variants of the S-300 and the S-400. In 2026, Russia added the RM-48U to its arsenal, mass-producing the missile by converting decommissioned surface-to-air missiles. According to Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, Russia manufactured 200 RM-48Us in 2025 and intends to produce more than 480 in 2026.
Russia has turned the ad hoc use of surface-to-air missiles into a stand-alone production effort that enables it to supplement Iskander short-range ballistic missiles during combined attacks. The result is a greater number of high-speed weapons per strike, despite their inferior accuracy and destructive power compared with purpose-built ballistic missiles.
The names S-300 and S-400 are commonly used as shorthand for missiles, although they actually refer to families of air defence systems comprising radars, command posts, launchers and several missile types. Rosoboronexport, Russia's state arms exporter, lists four missile variants for the S-400 alone: the 48N6E3, 48N6E2, 40N6E and 9M96E2. As a result, recovering a piece of wreckage from a 48N6 missile is not always enough to determine which specific air defence system launched it, as these missiles are often compatible with both later variants of the S-300 and the newer S-400.
The oldest missile relevant to this story, the 5V55R, weighs around 1.66 tonnes and carries a high-explosive fragmentation warhead weighing about 130 kg. Its standard engagement range against aerial targets is up to 75 km. The newer 48N6 weighs around 1.8 tonnes and, depending on the variant, carries a warhead weighing between 143 and 180 kg, according to various reference sources.
Both missiles were designed primarily to destroy aircraft and incoming missiles in flight. Their warheads generate a large volume of fragmentation but lack the specialised penetrators or reinforced casings needed to breach concrete or underground structures. As a result, they are less effective than purpose-built surface-to-surface missiles against hardened point targets. Yet in urban areas, that limitation matters little. Travelling at high speed, the missile's mass and the spread of thousands of fragments can devastate a wide area even with a relatively modest warhead.
The 40N6 stands apart as the S-400's longest-range missile, with a claimed engagement range of up to 380-400 km against aerial targets. In November 2023, Ukrainian officials reported finding debris from a 40N6 on the Zaporizhzhia front. However, the presence of missile debris alone does not prove it was launched against a ground target rather than fired by Russian air defence units. Nor is there any public evidence that the 40N6 has been used systematically in ground-attack roles. Likewise, its maximum engagement range against aircraft should not be confused with its potential range in ground strikes, as the missile follows a different flight profile and relies on different guidance methods.
The S-300's ground-attack capability predates the full-scale invasion. In May 2011, three Russian air defence missile regiments carried out exercises at the Telemba training range, firing five combat missiles from a stationary S-300 system at ground targets. The Russian military claimed that all five had hit their targets. Results achieved on a test range, where target coordinates are known in advance, cannot be directly compared with long-range strikes under combat conditions. They do, however, confirm that the capability existed and had been practised.
The exact guidance algorithms used for ground attacks for all missile variants remain classified. The available technical information indicates that they employ inertial and radio-command guidance during the initial stages of flight. Once the missile passes beyond the radio horizon, however, guidance from the ground radar is no longer possible, and it continues towards the target using inertial navigation alone. This mechanism enabled the 48N6DM to cover more than 200 km in a strike on Kyiv, but it also explains why these missiles sacrifice accuracy for speed over long distances.
For this reason, describing these weapons as ballistic missiles comes with an important caveat. Neither the 5V55 nor the 48N6 is a true equivalent of the 9M723 missile used by the Iskander-M system. Instead, each follows a ballistic-like trajectory for much of its flight before descending into the designated target area during the terminal phase. There is no publicly available, verified data on the circular error probable (CEP) of strikes by these missiles, meaning the precise accuracy figures that occasionally appear in the media cannot be independently substantiated.
The absence of reliable accuracy data is particularly relevant when analysing individual strikes. Hitting a target on a test range or a large industrial site does not necessarily prove that the missile can reliably strike a small target at its maximum range. The longer it flies without radio correction, the further its performance diverges from that of a dedicated precision-guided munition.
Travelling at extremely high speed, the 48N6DM gives defenders only minutes to react. Ukrainian estimates put its top speed at about 2.5 km/s, which means it can cover 200 km in just a few minutes. During an attack on Kyiv Oblast in January 2023, the early warning system was not always able to issue timely alerts. The issue was not that the missile could not be detected, but that its short flight time left little time to determine whether an S-300 or S-400 launch was directed at an aerial or ground target.
Geography of the strikes: from Mykolaiv and Zaporizhzhia to Kharkiv
During 2022 and 2023, S-300 missiles were used primarily against regions close to the front line or the Russian border. Among the most devastating was the attack on a humanitarian convoy in Zaporizhzhia on 30 September 2022. Russia fired 16 S-300 missiles on the city and its outskirts, four of which hit the area around a car market and a convoy of civilian vehicles. The strike killed 32 people and injured 118 others.
Further south, Mykolaiv also came under S-300 attack. On 23 October 2022, a Russian missile struck a five-storey residential block. No fatalities were reported.
On 14 April 2023, Russia struck Sloviansk with eight S-300 missiles. Residential buildings, offices and commercial premises were damaged. The attack claimed 15 lives and injured 24 people, according to the final toll after search-and-rescue operations ended.
On the evening of 21 October 2023, two missiles struck a postal hub operated by Nova Poshta (Nova Post), Ukraine's largest private delivery company, in Novyi Korotych, near Kharkiv. Citing early reports, the prosecutor's office identified them as S-300 missiles launched from Russia's Belgorod Oblast. Bomb disposal experts recovered debris at the scene consistent with that assessment. Eight people were killed and 15 were injured.
These incidents demonstrate the key advantage of this type of weapon for Russia: the launchers are positioned close to the battlefield, enabling missiles to reach cities such as Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Sloviansk in a matter of minutes and leaving less time for warning systems to react.
When the S-400 reached Kyiv
On the morning of 14 January 2023, the Ukrainian command reported that S-400 missiles fired from the north had struck Kyiv. Photographs of missile debris showed markings that allowed experts to identify it as a 48N6DM. Russia's Bryansk Oblast was named as the likely launch area, although the exact coordinates and final conclusions of the expert analysis were not made public. This makes it more accurate to refer to the finding as a credible Ukrainian assessment rather than definitive confirmation.
The newer 48N6DM can travel significantly further than the older 5V55 and carries a heavier warhead. However, the S-400's maximum advertised range of 400 km should not be interpreted as the ability of all its missiles to accurately hit ground targets at that distance, as that figure primarily refers to the 40N6 missile's claimed performance against aerial targets. Regarding the Kyiv attack, Ukrainian experts attributed the strike to a 48N6DM missile that had covered more than 200 km.
In the summer of 2026, S-400 missiles are once again appearing regularly in Ukrainian reports alongside Iskander missiles. On 2 July, the Ukrainian Air Force recorded 24 missiles in the combined Iskander-M/S-400 category, four of which were intercepted. On 6 July, 23 missiles were recorded, but no interceptions of ballistic assets were reported. On 1 August, one of the 27 missiles in this category was shot down. On 5 August, none of the 24 missiles was intercepted. All four attacks were directed primarily at Kyiv or Kyiv Oblast. Based on publicly available data, it is impossible to determine what proportion of these missiles were S-400s.
The Russian attack on 14 July provided further physical evidence of S-400 use. A warhead and debris from an S-400 missile were found in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district. Since the exact variant was not determined, the evidence confirms the system's involvement but does not allow the missile to be definitively identified as either the 48N6DM or the 40N6.
The low interception rate during these attacks is a result of the missiles' flight profile, high speed and the limited number of systems capable of engaging them. Russia is taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of Patriot interceptors and increasing its use of ballistic missile strikes. Defending against these threats requires Patriot or similar systems, such as the SAMP/T, which Ukraine also operates. The result is a costly imbalance: even a missile with limited accuracy can force Ukraine to choose between exposing a critical infrastructure facility to destruction or using a valuable anti-missile interceptor.
RM-48U: from the disposal of old missiles to a mass-produced weapon
Debris identified as RM-48U was publicly shown in Ukraine for the first time after the combined attack on 20 January 2026. The missile is a refurbished dummy based on older 5V55 or 48N6 missiles withdrawn from service. It is compatible with S-300 and S-400 launch systems.
It was initially unclear whether the missile in question had been equipped with a conventional warhead or was being used as a decoy. In January, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine described RM-48Us in a report on the cost of the latest Russian attack as training missiles. By June, the same type was listed in intelligence data as the RM-48U missile designed for ground targets. This indicates that different variants or employment methods may exist within the same missile family.
The extent of the RM-48U programme became apparent only in 2026. Defence Intelligence of Ukraine reported that Russia had produced more than 200 RM-48U missiles in 2025, aims to produce over 480 in 2026 and has reached a production rate of up to 50 per month. As a result, the first publicly identified debris in January should not be interpreted as the missile's first deployment. It was merely the first case where its use could be tied to a clearly identified designation.
These figures change the perception of the RM-48U as a one-off effort to dispose of obsolete missiles. Instead, they point to a specialised production line that enables Russia to convert decommissioned surface-to-air missiles into offensive weapons or decoys. The RM-48U cannot match the Iskander in precision, destructive power or ability to defeat fortified targets. Instead, it adds more fast-moving assets to Russian attacks, further complicating Ukraine's early warning and missile defence efforts.
For air defence units, the difference between a live missile and a decoy becomes apparent too late. A high-speed target cannot simply be ignored on the assumption that it may not carry a warhead. It must still be tracked by radar, its trajectory assessed and a decision made on whether to launch an interceptor. This is precisely why the RM-48U retains military value even in its decoy configuration.
Not a replacement for the Iskander, but a second echelon of attack
For Russia, converting S-300 and S-400 surface-to-air missiles into ground-attack weapons is a practical solution. It enables Moscow to tap into vast Soviet-era stockpiles, including missiles nearing the end of their service life, and takes advantage of launchers already deployed near Ukraine. The RM-48U programme expands on this approach by establishing a structured method for refurbishing decommissioned missiles. As Soviet-era reserves gradually diminish, developing new anti-aircraft missiles requires considerable investment and lengthy production cycles.
However, this is not a cost-free replacement for purpose-built ballistic missiles. The 5V55 and 48N6 have smaller warheads, limited ability to penetrate hardened structures and lower demonstrated accuracy against ground targets. Their use also draws on Russia's air defence reserves. Their advantage is distinct: they pose a fast, additional threat that can increase the number of missiles in a single attack and complicate Ukrainian interception efforts, as they require a different response than that used against drones or cruise missiles.
Ukraine's response cannot be limited to expanding its missile defence arsenal. Patriot and SAMP/T systems depend on a steady supply of scarce interceptors. Other measures are equally important: improving launch detection, providing earlier warnings, dispersing personnel and critical industrial facilities, and targeting launchers, radars and production sites linked to Russia's missile programme. The RM-48U's mass production indicates that this threat will persist even as Soviet-era 5V55 stocks decline. Russia is moving from using accumulated reserves towards maintaining a dedicated capability to produce and deploy new weapons.
Arkadii Dotsenko
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

Bank of Russia advises lenders to support entrepreneurs affected by terrorist attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:11:53 UTC
22:11:53 KST

MOSCOW, August 10. /TASS/. Russia’s Central Bank has advised lenders to support entrepreneurs affected by terrorist attacks, the regulator reported on its website.
"Small and medium-sized enterprises that have suffered from the terrorist attacks on logistics centers, warehouse, production, trade, office, and other facilities will have an opportunity to have their loans and microloans restructured," the report said.
The Bank of Russia also urged lenders not to charge fines or penalties for overdue payments to entrepreneurs affected by terrorist attacks, and not to demand early loan repayment. "Lenders are recommended to refrain from charging late payment fees and penalties and demanding early repayment of outstanding loans. If lenders change the terms of loan agreements, they are advised to inform borrowers about new payment schedules as soon as possible," the regulator said.
The restructuring shall not deteriorate entrepreneurs’ credit histories, the Central Bank noted.
The Bank of Russia also advised lenders to approve restructuring applications of these borrowers whether they have the right to loan repayment holidays by law or not and treat such a restructuring as an independent measure to support business.
The regulator’s recommendations regarding loans held by entrepreneurs whose warehouses have been affected by attacks apply through August 31, 2027.

Labour leads Reform in yet another poll days before Nigel Farage faces crucial Clacton by-election
Voters will cast their ballots on Thursday in a race in which the former Ukip leader takes on Count Binface
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Labour has taken the lead over Reform in a fresh national poll just days before Nigel Farage faces the judgement of voters in a crucial by-election in Clacton.
The latest survey puts Andy Burnham’s party on 28 per cent, three points ahead of Reform on 25 per cent, Labour’s best position in an Ipsos poll for more than a year.
It is the fourth national poll Labour has topped since Mr Burnham entered Downing Street, ending the run that saw Mr Farage’s party lead in the polls for more than a year.
The findings will come as a boost to Labour, who Ipsos said were “benefiting from changing their leader”, and a blow to Reform as they spend their final few days campaigning in Clacton.
The Reform leader dramatically quit as an MP earlier this summer - before Labour’s ‘Burnham bounce’ in the polls - and could find himself left without a seat in Parliament unless he wins on Thursday.
While he is widely expected to win the by-election, with his main competition coming from comedian candidate Count Binface after other major parties refused to field candidates, Clacton voters told The Independent last week they feel like the town’s residents have not been respected.
Meanwhile, the Ipsos poll also found Mr Burnham has a significant lead over his political rivals including Mr Farage, when asked who would make the best PM.
Some 36 per cent chose the Labour leader, more than double the 15 per cent who picked Mr Farage or the 13 per cent who selected Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch.
Mr Farage faces a crunch test on Thursday when he attempts to win back his Clacton seat.
He resigned as an MP after he claimed that he was the subject of a “stitch up” over the parliamentary standards inquiries into a £5m donation from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne and gifts from his close confidante and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, after claims they had not been declared as required.
Mr Farage has denied wrongdoing and claimed he has been targeted.
Gideon Skinner, senior director of politics at Ipsos, said the new PM was “clearly much more personally liked than his predecessor was at the end of his term” and more than the opposition leaders.
But he warned his position was currently “part benefit of the doubt and part jury is still out.
“Although Labour has received a boost in voting intentions (partly thanks to more of their 2024 base returning to the fold), many of the underlying issues remain,” he said. “The Labour party itself is still less liked than it has been for most of the last 20 years, and 7 in 10 are still dissatisfied how the country is being run overall - the ongoing pessimism of recent times has dampened public enthusiasm that a new PM will be able to quickly turn around the direction of the country.
“For the moment we are seeing evidence of Andy Burnham’s personal popularity, but for this to continue in the longer term the public will be looking for tangible evidence of improvements in their day-to-day lives.”
The Ipsos poll of 1,033 adults between 30 July and 4 August found Labour 28% (+4 from June), Reform 25% (-1), Conservatives 18% (no change), Greens 12% (-1) and Lib Dems 9% (-2).

Two men have been questioned on suspicion of acting as accomplices for a man accused of stealing valuables from a cemetery in The Hague by selling the items to a gold dealer.
The 60-year-old man, who works as a shift manager at the city’s main cemetery on Kerkhoflaan, was arrested in June after police received a tip-off that items such as jewellery and gold fillings had been stolen during working hours.
The prosecution service confirmed on Monday that two other people who worked at the cemetery were suspected of money laundering “by selling valuable objects originating from the cemetery”.

The city council has launched its own internal inquiry and set up a hotline for families who were concerned that their relatives’ valuables may have been stolen. So far the hotline has received around 60 calls.

BoP proposed deal would leave Israel vulnerable to Hamas re-armament, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:09:19 UTC
22:09:19 KST

The Board of Peace’s proposed agreement to disarm Hamas would leave Israel restricted in its ability to deal with immediate and emerging threats, while allowing Hamas to remain armed with “personal weapons,” according to an assessment by Dr. Igal Shiri published by the Meir Amit Terrorism and Intelligence Research Institute last week.
The 15-point plan, which was rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, notably failed to see Hamas relinquish its weapons, only seeing the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza store the weapons and decommission them under point 8.
Shiri noted that a political crisis or the collapse of the NCAG, or a similar armed takeover of storage facilities like the one seen during Hamas’s 2007 takeover of Gaza, could result in Hamas being rearmed.
Additionally, Shiri warned that it remained unclear whether a complete inventory of Hamas’s weapons production facilities, tunnels and other infrastructure would be handed over, and whether these structures would be dismantled or completely destroyed under the supervision of parties not allied with Hamas, rather than only by Turkey and Qatar.
Unclear whether IDF expected to withdraw before or after Hamas disarmament
It also remains unclear whether the IDF would be expected to withdraw before or after Hamas disarms.
Critically, under the ninth point of the agreement, Hamas members would be allowed to retain “personal weapons” registered and licensed with the NCAG.
Shiri said such a process would do little to ensure the complete dismantlement of Hamas’s military wings or prevent current and former Hamas police members from rearming, particularly if they are allowed to integrate into the new security forces.
Netanyahu said on Sunday he would not allow a deal that promises only “fictitious disarmament,” where Hamas is allowed to continue holding arms.
“When I say Hamas is disarmed, that means the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons – all the weapons,” he said.
Shiri also pointed to Hamas’ declaration that it would continue to work to “liberate all of the land from the occupation on all fronts,” as reflective of the group’s continued commitment to armed jihad against Israel.
He argued that Hamas therefore had no intention of implementing the agreement in the spirit in which it was written, but instead could use it as an opportunity to reorganize and raise resources.
Fate of Hamas operatives unclear per the agreement
As to the fate of Hamas’s current commanders and terrorist operatives, including those who participated in the October 7 massacre, the agreement is also vague. It is unclear whether they will be allowed to stay in the Gaza Strip, though point seven would allow those in the Palestinian police who do not pass vetting to be offered alternative civilian roles.
“None of those shall be deprived of their financial rights, particularly due to political affiliation,” the agreement promised.
Finally, Shiri warned that the restrictions on the IDF’s use of force threaten its ability to respond to immediate and emerging threats because it fails to address Israel’s right to self-defense, only demanding its withdrawal in point 13.

Israel raises absurd new demands as Lebanon weighs ending talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:09:12 UTC
22:09:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel raises absurd new demands over Lebanese Jewish graves as Lebanon weighs ending talks
What began as negotiations ostensibly aimed at ending Israel's military presence in southern Lebanon and securing the release of Lebanese prisoners has become increasingly weighed down by a widening list of Israeli demands, some reaching back decades into Lebanon's turbulent history.
In the latest round of talks, Israel has asked Lebanon to facilitate the removal of the remains of Lebanese Jews buried in historic cemeteries in Beirut and Sidon and transfer their remains to Israel, according to reports citing sources familiar with the negotiations.
The proposal was raised during talks in Rome as part of what the Israeli delegation reportedly portrayed as a potential "civilian prisoner exchange".
Israel suggested that the remains of relatives of Israeli citizens whose families once lived in Lebanon could be transferred in exchange for the release of some Lebanese civilian prisoners held by Israel.
The demand comes as negotiations are already struggling over far more immediate questions, including Israel's continuing occupation of Lebanese territory, its near-daily attacks on the south and the fate of Lebanese prisoners.
Lebanon has been seeking the release of 34 Lebanese prisoners whose cases have been documented by the authorities. Israel, however, has sought to divide those it holds into two categories, according to reports of the negotiations.
The first consists of people Israel identifies as Hezbollah fighters, whose release it has reportedly refused to discuss. The second consists of civilians whom Israel claims posed a threat to its forces when they were detained.
Israel has also continued to refuse requests for the International Committee of the Red Cross to visit the Lebanese detainees or independently establish their identities and conditions.
Israel seeks Lebanese Jewish graves
Against that backdrop, the introduction of Lebanese Jewish burial sites into the negotiations has bewildered Lebanese officials and added another layer to talks that were already showing signs of faltering.
Israeli negotiators reportedly referred specifically to Jewish cemeteries in Beirut's Wadi Abu Jamil district and in Sidon, saying Israeli citizens of Lebanese Jewish origin wanted the remains of relatives transferred to Israel.
But the demands did not stop there.
Israel has also raised the cases of 11 Jews who disappeared or were killed during Lebanon’s civil war in the 1980s and again sought information about Ron Arad, an Israeli airman who disappeared after his aircraft went down over Lebanon in 1986.
Lebanese sources following the negotiations have described to The New Arab the demands as unrealistic and unserious, arguing that Lebanon does not possess records establishing where people who disappeared during the civil war nearly half a century ago were buried.
For Beirut, the growing list of demands has reinforced concerns that the negotiations are drifting further away from the issues for which they were established.
Those concerns have also been sharpened by Israel’s position on the so-called pilot zones envisioned as part of the negotiations.
Washington has informed Lebanon that Israel does not want to discuss establishing a second pilot zone in southern Lebanon, according to reports citing sources familiar with the talks.
Simon Karam, who heads Lebanon’s negotiating delegation, had gone further, telling associates after returning from Rome that he would not take part in another round unless Israel first committed to serious concessions on withdrawal and the pilot zones, according to leading Al-Akhbar newspaper.
Karam had also demanded that Israel halt demolitions in occupied villages and engage seriously on a prisoner deal, the paper added.
Instead, Israel wants to focus on direct coordination with the Lebanese army and on selecting a third party that would verify whether the army had fulfilled the requirements imposed on it in the first pilot zone.
Will Lebanon suspend talks with Israel?
The refusal represents another obstacle to a process under which Lebanon has sought Israeli withdrawals alongside deployments by the Lebanese army.
Official Lebanese sources told TNA that Beirut was still committed to negotiations and considered them "the only path to a solution", but warned that "it is not possible to continue holding rounds without tangible results".
The sources said Lebanon had delivered a clear message to Washington that "negotiations cannot continue in this way, without any Israeli response on the ground", and called for pressure on Israel to make the process reciprocal.
Beirut is now discussing several possibilities with the United States, including suspending the talks, demanding concrete Israeli steps before a tentatively planned eighth round in early September, or securing guarantees that such measures will be carried out as a condition for continuing negotiations.
Lebanon also rejects Israel’s attempt to make withdrawal conditional on first verifying Hezbollah’s disarmament.
"It must withdraw so that the Lebanese army can deploy and carry out its duties," the sources said, adding that a verification mechanism would then supervise the process.
President Joseph Aoun has nevertheless continued to defend the negotiating track.
Beirut Bar Association head Imad Martinos said after meeting Aoun on Monday that the president had been clear that the negotiations were "proceeding as they should", despite political and diplomatic obstacles.
Martinos said Aoun believed the talks would allow Lebanon to "preserve the land and recover its occupied territory", while stressing the need for Lebanese officials and citizens to remain united behind state institutions.
That defence of diplomacy is increasingly being tested on the ground, where Israel has continued military operations across southern Lebanon even as negotiations have proceeded, leaving Lebanese officials increasingly sceptical about what the talks are actually delivering
Overnight into Monday, Israeli forces carried out a series of explosions in Kfar Tebnit, Haddatha and between Taybeh and Deir Seriane, while artillery fire struck several areas and Israeli drones flew over the south.
On Monday morning, further Israeli explosions were reported in Majdal Zoun and Zawtar al-Sharqiya. Israeli soldiers were also reported to have infiltrated the western outskirts of Meis al-Jabal, while artillery fire sparked woodland fires between Bani Hayyan and Markaba.
In Khiam, Israeli troops were reported to be setting fire to homes on Monday.
Elsewhere, residents of Mansouri gathered near a Lebanese army position demanding to return to their village after being kept out following an Israeli evacuation order.
"We protest against the fact that the Israeli enemy is preventing us from entering our village and returning to our homes," said the head of Mansouri municipality.
He further called on the ceasefire monitoring mechanism to pressure Israel to allow residents back.

PM urged not to change scheme to stop PC Andrew Harper killers’ early release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:07:26 UTC
22:07:26 KST

Andy Burnham has been warned that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so PC Andrew Harper’s killers are kept behind bars would force another spate of early releases before the next general election.
Prison Service officials have told No 10 that adding an exemption so that those convicted of manslaughter, such as Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, remain in jail would mean further early releases would be needed within 18 months.
Governors told the Guardian the prime minister’s decision last week to exempt rapists and serious child sex offenders would force thousands of sentences to be recalculated in haste and could lead to the mistaken early release of some prisoners.
On Monday, Downing Street said the prime minister had “pushed hard on what more we could do” but it was not possible to exempt “one or two offenders” from early release, as manslaughter of an emergency worker was not a stand-alone offence. Instead, if they wanted to block the release of Cole and Bowers then every offender with a manslaughter conviction would be affected.
The government plans to release 5,000 prisoners early over a period of 10 months from October to free up places. Harper’s killers are due to be released in January.
Burnham is facing demands to exclude Cole and Bowers from the early release scheme. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures.
Despite the concerns from the Prison Service and a lack of obvious options, a No 10 source said the prime minister was “still pushing” for a way of keeping Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars.
The prime minister said last week he had “pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do” by exempting 1,000 rapists, child sexual abuse offenders and groomers from early release, which reduced the number of spaces to be freed up in the next 10 months from 6,000.
Blocking the early release of Cole and Bowers could mean delaying the release of at least 500 other offenders also convicted of manslaughter, a Whitehall source said. “People in the Prison Service are terrified by the prospect of another exemption,” they said. “They have told the PM that if they carve out manslaughter cases there will have to be another early release scheme before the general election.”
Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said ministers have been warned that delays to the early release scheme mean some prisoners could be released at the wrong time.
“We have expressed concerns to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) officials about increased ‘releases in error’ and ‘unlawful detention’ risk because of the government’s last-minute changes to the Sentencing Act’s implementation. Officials have assured us that ministers have been briefed on the increased risk environment,” he said.
Each prison will be expected to re-evaluate the sentences of every prisoner affected by Burnham’s changes. This could mean recalculating many thousands of prison sentences in a short period of time when staff are on holiday, Wheatley said.
“These late changes come at a time when many staff who specialise in calculating sentences and met the original deadline are off work, on a well-earned break. Because this is a time-pressured and manual process, involving paper files that can be inches thick, it carries an increased risk of error,” he said.
Ministers have been advised that they are at risk of a legal challenge if they try to carve out exclusions for Cole and Bowers but not others convicted of manslaughter. Nick Hardwick, who was the chief inspector of prisons for six years until 2016, said he felt “uneasy” at the suggestion the government could draw up exemptions from the scheme to satisfy a public outcry.
“I am appalled by what happened to PC Harper,” he said. “But we have to be careful about the principle here. We should be uneasy about politicians deciding what happens to particular offenders. It is something that needs careful debate. It should not be up to politicians to choose how long individuals spend in prison.
“If the government did change the legal framework to exclude these two men from early release, it could well be an example of ‘hard cases making bad law’.”
MoJ officials said prisons could run out of places in November if the scheme was abandoned.
Asked on Monday whether ministers were accepting the situation as it stood, Burnham’s spokesperson said: “I think you’ve seen from the prime minister’s words that he’s far from accepting the situation and, as he wrote last week, he wants to go even further. He’s pushed hard on what more we could do and his focus now is on fixing the prison system long-term to avoid a repeat of this prison crisis so that it never happens again.”
Pressed on whether the prime minister was admitting there was nothing more he could do, the official said: “He understands the public wants him to go further, and he wanted to go further, but on the wider issue … prisons would have run out of space, police would stop making arrests, it would be impossible to lock up convicted offenders and that would put public safety at untold risk.”

Trump took secret flight out of Turkey over Iran threat — report
US President Donald Trump reportedly departed from Turkey on a secret military flight in July instead of the flying aboard an older Air Force One as announced by the White House.
This was in response to a credible assassination threat from Iran, the Washington Post reported, as the monthslong warcontinued.
Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit in July. However, he unexpectedly announced he would used an older Air Force One when departing the country, "for old times's sake." The move had then raised question over the donated jet's safety.
Trump boarded the older Air Force One in front of cameras but was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, it said, citing corroborating material and a US official familiar with the operation.
Journalists aboard the decoy Air Force One, where they believed to be accompanied by the US President, said they had been advised to keep their window shades closed in the press cabin.
When they inquired about it later, Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight."
"But if I go, you go. Right?" he added.
Ayatollah Khamenei appoints new military leadership for Iran
Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has replaced six top Iranian military figures according to decrees made public on Telegram late Monday evening.
The move represents Khamenei's first senior military appointments since being chosen to replace his father, who was killed in the early hours of the war.
Khamenei appointed Revolutionary Guards General Ali Abdollahi head of Iran's armed forces and confirmed Ahmad Vahidi as commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Abdollahi previously led the Khatam al-Anbiya, Iran's military operations coordinating command.
Earlier this month, he warned regional neighbors that "any country serving as a defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war."
Hossein Taeb, a long-serving intelligence officer, was appointed head of the paramilitary Basij militias and Brigadier Ali Asmai was appointed commander of the IRGC's naval forces.
Two further appointments concerned deputy positions.
The shake-up comes after Khamenei appointed former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaee chairman of Iran's National Security Council on Sunday.
'Board of Peace': Gaza plan still operable, despite Israeli opposition — report
US President Donald Trump's "Board of Peace" organization contends that its "plans for Gaza" remain operable, despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's very vocal rejection of an Israeli withdrawal from the Palestinian enclave until the militant group Hamas is "genuinely disarmed."
The Reuters news agency quoted a board representative as saying, "The plan is very much still operative and advancing."
"The road map is between the Board of Peace and Hamas, and discussions with Israel are continuing. Israel is not being asked to rely on trust or to make irreversible moves before verified steps are taken on the ground," the official said.
Board of Peace head Nikolay Mladenov, a former UN special envoy for the Middle East and former Bulgarian foreign minister, told Israeli broadcaster N12 that "both Israelis and the people in Gaza have one shared strong interest, and that is to get out of this horrible cycle of violence that has cost so many lives and destruction to both sides."
Trump says if Iran is demanding compensation, then he is, too
President Donald Trump said on Monday that the United States would demand compensation from Iran, in response to Tehran saying it would seek compensation after US and Israeli attacks.
Over the weekend, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman on new shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz. But it said that reopening the waterway would depend on Washington meeting various conditions — including an end to sanctions, military threats and an agreement on compensation for damages resulting from the war.
Trump said that this was "never mentioned" in any negotiations with the US to date.
"But is an interesting idea because now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He cited specifically a 2000 terrorist suicide bombing of the USS Cole ship, but alleged there were "thousands of others killed in combat."
Trump's remarks come a day after he said he was not engaging in major talks with Iran, telling US media outlet Axios that the US was "low-keying" its approach.
The US and Iran have frequently put out vastly contradictory claims and counterclaims about the status and details of their talks and terms.
Iranian supreme leader calls for 'unity,' president says
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Monday that he had a nearly seven-hour meeting with Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
He did not, however, say exactly when or where they met.
Pezeshkian told the state-run IRIB that he and Khamenei discussed "people’s livelihoods, the state of the market, employment, people's housing." He said they also talked about "problems that are now being created as a result of the sanctions."
Most important, Pezeshkian said, was the importance Khamenei put on "unity and cohesion."
"All of the enemy's plans are aimed at creating division," Pezeshkian said. "What we have to do is prevent divisions from emerging."
It is only the second time the Iranian president said he has met with the supreme leader since Khamenei was appointed in March. He came to power after a US-Israeli strike killed his father. Khamenei, believed to have been wounded in the same attack, has not appeared in public since then.
Germany says US plan for Gaza could lead to disarmament of Hamas
The German government regards US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza as an opportunity to make progress toward the disarmament of Hamas, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Monday.
Asked about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's announcement Sunday that Israel rejected the US-led plan, the spokesperson said some disagreement was not surprising.
"With such a complex undertaking, it was perfectly clear there would be many, many unanswered questions," he added.
Late last month, Trump hailed a 15-point plan that would see Hamas lay down its weapons and the Israeli military withdraw from the Gaza Strip. It expands on an October 2025 ceasefire agreement that slowed, but did not end, the conflict in the Palestinian territory, about two-thirds of which is under Israeli control.
Despite the truce, Israel continued to carry out airstrikes in Gaza. Health officials there say more than 1,200 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed since October 2025. Five Israeli soldiers were killed in Gaza during that time. Hamas, which is classified as a terrorist organization by Israel, the US, Germany and several countries, does not disclose figures on its war dead.
On Sunday, Netanyahu said Israeli troops would not leave the Gaza Strip until Hamas had been "genuinely" disarmed.
Iran demands concessions from US before reopening Strait of Hormuz
A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States met its conditions.
"It is up to the US side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions," Esmail Baghaei said on Monday.
What are Iran's demands on the US?
In a statement over the weekend, a member of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and Revolutionary Guards commander said Tehran demanded that the United States:
- Never threaten Iran again
- Pay compensation for months of war damage
- Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip
- Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area
- Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets
The impasse over the Strait of Hormuz has led to a global jump in fuel prices.
Iran is holding talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including a possible temporary shipping corridor, but it has said any actual reopening depends on negotiations with the United States.
On Sunday, however, US President Donald Trump said the US is not engaged in major talks with Iran.
"We are low-keying it," he said, according to US media outlet Axios. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."
Trump also expressed his optimism that a satisfactory conclusion would eventually be reached.
"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," he said of the war.
Tehran: Ships will be expected to pay to transit the narrow waterway
Iran intends to charge commercial vessels for passage through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement Monday from the Foreign Ministry.
Iranian media cited spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying that Iran was working with Oman on "mechanisms for monitoring security, protecting the environment and combating crime at sea."
Fees would be for maritime services provided to ships, he said.
The dispute over transit rights in the strait, through which some 20% of the world's oil passed before the war and which is a key route for gas and fertilizer, is regarded as a key reason behind the continuation of the war against Iran.
Before the United States and Israel launched the conflict against Iran at the end of February, shipping through the waterway did no incur tolls nor fees for transit.
The Strait of Hormuz measures only around 39 kilometers (24 miles) at its narrowest point.
Since Iran and Oman each claim the maximum 12 nautical miles allowed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as their territorial waters, there are no international waters in the narrowest part of the roughly 21-nautical-mile-wide strait.
The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees a right of transit passage and prohibits a blockade of commercial vessels. Iran, however, does not accept this legal position.
The US goal is to restore pre-war levels of oil and gas transit through the Strait of Hormuz, US Vice President JD Vance said on Sunday.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello from the DW newsroom in Bonn, Germany, and welcome to our coverage of the war in Iran and developments from across the Middle East.
One issue DW is looking at is Iran's announcement that it intends to charge commercial vessels for transiting the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with a still-unreached agreement with Oman on the future management of the narrow waterway.

Fyodorov facilitated Palantir's involvement in Ukraine conflict — opposition politician
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:06:47 UTC
22:06:47 KST

MOSCOW, August 10. /TASS/. Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov was a conduit for US multinational corporations getting involved in the military campaign against Russia, Viktor Medvedchuk, head of the Other Ukraine movement and former leader of the Opposition Platform – For Life party banned by Kiev, said.
"Mikhail Fyodorov is a figurehead who became a facade concealing the real involvement of US multinational corporations in the war against Russia. [Palantir Technologies CEO and co-founder] Alex Karp and Eric Schmidt made the now former Ukrainian defense minister their courier, whose job is to run between Ukrainian offices and communicate decisions that the Ukrainian authorities are required to implement," Medvedchuk wrote in an article published on the movement’s website.
According to him, this explains the activity of the "cardboard Maidan" protests demanding that Fyodorov be reinstated as defense minister. Medvedchuk said that the former minister’s dismissal had taken on a significance disproportionate to the length of his time at the Defense Ministry.
The politician recalled that Fyodorov helped usher in new technological changes in the Ukrainian armed forces. In fact, the former minister was "the public face of projects in which drones, digital battle management systems and artificial intelligence were gradually combined into a single control mechanism," he said.
Palantir’s role
Medvedchuk noted that Karp proposed opening a Palantir office in Ukraine and providing software for warfare as early as 2022. While the software was already used in the United States and NATO countries, Ukraine became a testing ground where technologies combining intelligence, satellite, drone, radar and ground reconnaissance data, identifying links between objects and transforming analysis results into decision-making options were integrated into a system for data collection, target selection and combat command against Russia, he said.
Fyodorov promoted the system politically and institutionalized it at the state level, while Palantir created its software foundation, Medvedchuk added. Another company directly involved in these developments was Perennial Autonomy, which was formed out of the closed Project Eagle initiative created with the participation of former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, he said.
According to Medvedchuk, Perennial Autonomy’s task was to transfer autonomy directly to a physical platform, including computer vision, navigation amid GPS jamming, target tracking and automation of the final stage of a drone’s flight. "Project Eagle’s organizational architecture remained opaque for a long time and was developed as a multilevel network. Its key figure is Eric Schmidt, whose involvement in Ukrainian military developments was directly linked to Fyodorov’s activities," he wrote.
Other US companies are also involved in developing and testing these systems, Medvedchuk said. In this structure, Fyodorov served as the state organizer and public face of the changes, while their technological content centered on Palantir’s developments, he added.
"In May 2026, Alex Karp acknowledged that the company played a ‘very large role’ in a significant part of Ukrainian military targeting. At this level, Palantir became the de facto technological headquarters of the war against Russia – a center where intelligence data are turned into targets, targets into combat missions and missions are assigned to specific strike assets. Therefore, Palantir is in fact the technological flagship of terrorist strikes on Russian territory," the Other Ukraine leader said.

July was Ukraine’s deadliest month for civilians since 2022 — and Russia is scaling its ballistic missile salvos toward 200 at once
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:05:14 UTC
22:05:14 KST

Russia can currently fire a simultaneous salvo of 77 ballistic missiles, and it aims to lift that ceiling to 200. Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, who commands Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, told the Associated Press. He called the plan one of Ukraine's gravest weak points.
Ballistic missiles remain the hardest to stop
That shortfall has already turned lethal. Intensified strikes made July the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, the UN human-rights office in Ukraine documented. Air defenses downed just 29 of the 195 ballistic missiles Russia fired that month, roughly 15%. Another 40 fell short on their own. Yet the largest single-night launches recorded so far run to only a few dozen. That is well below the salvo of 77 that Brovdi describes, and a fraction of the 200 Moscow is reaching for.
"Even if they only manage half of that, it will all be flying at us."
- Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander, Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces
Production running ahead of plan
His warning tracks Ukrainian intelligence. Russia's defense industry is overfulfilling its monthly targets, hitting 110% to 120% on the main missile types. So said Deputy Military Intelligence Chief Vadym Skibitskyi in an interview with RBC-Ukraine. He put July output for the Kh-101 cruise missile at 140% of plan, the Kalibr at 111%, and the Kh-35 at 200%. A pause in strikes, he judged, is unlikely.
The pivot to jet-powered drones
Moscow's factories are also retooling around drones. Russia plans to assemble 11,000 strike drones of various types in August 2026, Skibitskyi said. That mix spans the Geran-1 through Geran-5, the Harpia, and several Gerbera variants. Output dipped in July as the industry shifted toward the turbojet Geran-4 and Geran-5.
Those jet models fly faster and demand different interceptors or short-range air defense. They already made up half of one recent attack. The concentration of jet-powered Shaheds, meanwhile, has climbed 2.5 times in recent weeks, Brovdi added. Taken together, the assessments point one way: more missiles and faster drones, launched in larger waves, against defenses Ukraine is scrambling to rebuild.

Lithuania may seek EU migration pact changes during 2027 presidency, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

Lithuania may seek amendments to the European Union’s new Migration and Asylum Pact during its 2027 presidency of the EU Council, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Monday, citing concerns about border security and recent migration incidents.
“There are many issues to consider. We will evaluate how the Migration and Asylum Pact is functioning, as it only entered into force on June 12 this year, if I am not mistaken,” Katelynas told reporters at the Lithuanian parliament.
The minister said one of the main concerns was that the pact could limit the ability of border authorities to operate effectively at the EU’s external borders.
“We saw this in Spain. However, the Spaniards took measures regardless when facing the tens of thousands who flooded Ceuta,” Katelynas said.
He argued that the pact should not prevent EU member states from taking measures to protect their security.
Lithuania will therefore assess how the new rules work in practice after it takes over the rotating presidency of the EU Council on January 1, 2027, Katelynas said.
“This is a pressing issue for many member states, particularly those with an external EU border who see these problems and are actively raising them,” he said.
After an initial assessment, Lithuania could compile proposals from member states and pass them to Greece, which will hold the EU Council presidency after Lithuania and also faces migration pressure, Katelynas said.
The Migration and Asylum Pact entered into force across the EU, including Lithuania, on June 12. The legislation represents a major overhaul of the bloc’s common migration policy and is intended to strengthen external border management, improve security and establish a more predictable system for solidarity among member states.
Katelynas identified migration policy as one of the key issues Lithuania is likely to address during its EU presidency.
His comments came after a recent migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, located on Morocco’s northern coast. Spanish authorities said tens of thousands of people attempted to enter the enclave from Morocco in late July, with more than 100 people reportedly dying during the crossing. Madrid moved to return migrants, and most have since left the enclave.
Under the EU’s solidarity mechanism, Lithuania plans to relocate 58 migrants from Cyprus and make a financial contribution of 1.14 million euros. The government has decided to meet its obligations under the pact through a combination of relocation and financial contributions.
More than 218,000 foreign nationals held valid residence permits in Lithuania as of May, according to Migration Department data.

The managing director of John Lewis has quit the job after less than three years in charge of the British department store chain, as the company faces “really tough” trading conditions.
Peter Ruis will leave the business in order to “pursue new projects”, John Lewis said in a statement on Monday.
He will be replaced by Will Kernan, a non-executive board member of the employee-owned John Lewis Partnership, which also runs the Waitrose supermarket chain. Kernan said in a statement that John Lewis still had “significant headroom for growth”.
The surprise departure comes after John Lewis’s chair, Jason Tarry, last week warned of “really tough” trading conditions in an interview with the company’s in-house magazine.
John Lewis had felt confident enough in the economic outlook in March to pay its 69,000 workers – which it calls partners – an annual bonus for the first time in four years after underlying profits rose. Staff shared a bonus pot of £35m, worth about one week’s extra pay each.
However, the US-Israeli war on Iran has caused a rise in inflation as oil prices have soared. That has put shoppers under pressure and raised costs for retailers.
Tarry indicated in the interview that “we have to adjust for an immediate future that we weren’t expecting even six months ago, let alone a couple of years ago”.
Ruis had returned to John Lewis at the start of 2024, after leading retailers including Jigsaw and Anthropologie. During his previous nine-year stint Ruis was John Lewis’s buying and brand director.
He oversaw investment in the 36 John Lewis department stores that remained after the company closed 16 during the coronavirus pandemic, and as recently as November he told the Guardian that he was looking at expansion.
Ruis will stay in post until 6 September. Kernan, a non-executive director since 2023, will take over in the middle of September as the retailer prepares for its Christmas peak trading period. John Lewis has started a search for a new non-executive director.
Kernan has previously served as chief executive of River Island, The White Company and the cycling shop Wiggle, and spent 13 years at New Look.
Ruis said: “After nearly three years of significant investment and modernisation, the business is now on a much stronger footing. I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved, and there is so much more still to come.”
 Kernan said: “Having served on the partnership’s board for three years, I have a clear understanding of the John Lewis business and a huge appreciation for the partnership’s values and employee-ownership model. We have significant headroom for growth and I’m looking forward to leading the team to ensure John Lewis remains the country’s most trusted and loved retailer, in store and online.”
 Tarry said: “Peter has done a fantastic job and will be missed by all of our partners. He’s injected energy and pace into the John Lewis transformation and we are sad to see him go.”
Separately, the Co-op Group on Monday announced that its chair, Debbie White, had decided to step down after two years that included steering the group, which runs convenience stores, insurance, legal services and funeral parlours, through a major cyber-attack.
The senior independent director Moni Mannings was appointed as interim chair to oversee the hiring of a new permanent chief executive after the March departure of Shirine Khoury-Haq amid claims of a “toxic culture”. Khoury-Haq said colleagues had told her they did not recognise the criticisms, and she denied her departure was in relation to the allegations.

Train punctuality reaches 5-year high

Train punctuality in Belgium reached 94.6% in July, the highest rate in five years, according to figures from national rail company NMBS.
Home News
Train punctuality reaches 5-year high
Published:
The punctuality rate indicates how often trains arrive on schedule – meaning with less than six minutes’ delay – in Brussels or at their final destination. Last year, the figure for July was 93.4%.
Almost 40% of delays in July were the fault of NMBS, with 27% caused by third parties such as people on the tracks or accidents at crossings and 16% the fault of network manager Infrabel.
Around 3,100 trains were partially or completely cancelled in July, representing almost 3% of all trains. Including these cancellations puts the total punctuality rate at 92.3%, higher than last year’s figure of 90.9%.

LONDON, August 10. /TASS/. By the end of the decade, the European Union will face a shortage of domestically produced launch vehicles due to growing demand for satellite launches, European Space Agency (ESA) Director-General Josef Aschbacher stated in an interview with the Financial Times (FT).
"ESA’s expectation "today [is] that Europe has a shortage of launchers around the 2030 timeframe," said Josef Aschbacher.
In this regard, the ESA has asked European launch vehicle developers to come back "in the coming months with estimates of what it could cost to expand their programs," the ESA chief said. Production of the Ariane 6 launch vehicle is expected to increase from the current 9-10 to 15 per year. This also applies to the production of Vega C rockets.
The results of these consultations will influence decisions on where the ESA will allocate additional funds to address the shortfall over the next decade.
Ashbacher had previously stated that the EU needs to develop its own reusable launch vehicle as quickly as possible to keep pace with Elon Musk and SpaceX.
Last year, participants at a ministerial meeting of ESA member states approved the largest budget in the agency’s history - 22.1 billion euros. This amount covers the period from 2026 to 2028 and exceeds the previous three-year budget (16.9 billion euros) by more than 5 billion euros. Of the 23 participating countries, Germany and France will contribute the most (5 billion and 3.6 billion euros, respectively), with Italy in third place (3.5 billion euros).
