While the world is witnessing a struggle for trade routes, Belarus and Uzbekistan are opening up new opportunities for transit between Eastern Europe and Central Asia. It took less than six days for the first through freight train, the Slavic Caravan, to deliver Belarusian products to Uzbekistan, covering roughly 4,000 kilometers. With minimal costs and maximum speed, the “caravan” has generated considerable interest from foreign media, and experts are already talking about the formation of an important regional supply chain connecting Belarus with the countries of Central Asia.
The first through freight train, the Slavic Caravan, departed from Belarus on 30 July, passed through Russia and Kazakhstan, and was already welcomed in Uzbekistan on 5 August. The new service enabled the export of Belarusian woodworking products, food cargo, and chemicals. Now Belarus awaits the Uzbek “caravan” with local products ranging from light industry goods to foodstuffs, including fruits that do not grow in Belarus.
What makes the new service special? According to Belarusian Railways, cargo has been delivered from Belarus to Uzbekistan by rail before. “But together with our Uzbek colleagues, we have developed a completely different, higher-quality service,” said Valery Verenich, head of Belarusian Railways. The key idea is that the Slavic Caravan travels the route without being broken up or making any additional stops. This makes it possible to cut delivery time nearly in half, while also ensuring the cargo is reliably preserved. Everything runs exactly on schedule.
“This train will operate on a schedule like a passenger train, meaning we will know exactly when it departs and when it arrives at its final destination, Sergei Verenich explained.
The train can also accommodate individual containers. This means that small Belarusian enterprises will not need to accumulate enough cargo to fill an entire wagon. Additionally, Belarusian Railways offers a consolidated container service for goods from multiple shippers. Moreover, plans are underway to expand the range of cargo and include wagons with containers delivered by road transport, which will allow shippers to take full advantage of multimodal transportation.
In the meantime, Belarusian producers have decided not to delay and have dispatched another “caravan” to Uzbekistan. On 3 August, Belarusian Railways announced the departure of a second freight train. Notably, the second “caravan” includes export goods that, transiting through Uzbekistan, will be delivered to neighboring Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. Thus, the geography of deliveries is expanding.
 
 
 
  
 
 
  
 
 
  
  
  
 
 
  
 
 
  
 
 
  
 
 
  
 
 
 “The Slavic Caravan not only facilitates the formation of a new transport corridor but also plays a vital role in the further development of trade and economic ties between Uzbekistan and Belarus, increasing trade, and realizing the strategic objectives defined by the leaders of the two states,” the Uzbek publication Aktualno noted.
The Slavic Caravan has also drawn attention in Türkiye. “Transporting a 20-tonne container via the new rail route is at least 1.5 times cheaper than by road transport. While the delivery of individual railcars could previously take up to two months, the cargo will now arrive in Uzbekistan in just 5 to 7 days,” the publication Yeni Şafak said.
“Belarus has introduced its first direct freight train service to Uzbekistan, opening a new chapter in transport and trade cooperation between the two countries,” Transport Advancement, an international news platform dedicated to the transportation industry, stated, assessing the significance of the new service.
“The Slavic Caravan does not create a separate economic union of four countries, but in practice, it strengthens the connectivity of their transport systems,” the Rossiyskaya Pressa news agency said. “Belarus and Uzbekistan gain a direct service for exports and imports, while Russia and Kazakhstan receive an additional steady transit cargo flow. For businesses, this means a more predictable schedule, fewer transshipments, and the ability to plan the supply chain in advance. The project’s main success will be measured not by the ceremonial departure of the first train, but by the regularity of trips, container capacity utilization, and the emergence of return cargo. The first successful trip has already confirmed the technical viability of the route. The next stage is to turn it into a sustainable trade channel between Belarus and Central Asian nations.”
Undoubtedly, the project’s success depends on many factors – primarily on demand and the readiness to satisfy it, the development of infrastructure and industrial cooperation, as well as the ability to expand the product range and involve SMEs by creating the necessary conditions. As of today, it is obvious that there is a demand from the business community, while government bodies demonstrate a commitment to giving momentum to trade and economic relations. In July, the presidents of Belarus and Uzbekistan signed the declaration on strategic partnership between Belarus and Uzbekistan, and today we can already state that relations between our countries are reaching a qualitatively new level.
“It is already clear that the Slavic Caravan run is not a one-time logistics success, but a response to an established business demand. Growing trade can transform this route into a vital component of Belarusian and Central Asian exports and imports. Amid the restructuring of global supply chains, it is services like this that will determine the competitiveness of manufacturers and the dynamics of trade in the region,” News Central Asia summarized.

Wildfires raging in western U.S., Canada amid severe drought force thousands to evacuate
Spokane, Washington — More than 40 large wildfires are burning in the West, fueled by severe drought, as over 100 blazes scorch parts of western Canada.
The Bug Fire near Reno, Nevada, has burned more than 15,000 acres, getting dangerously close to homes and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate over the weekend.
In Utah, two pilots were killed after their helicopter crashed on Friday while fighting the Widemouth 2 Fire, which has grown to more than 100,000 acres.
And in British Columbia, Canada, which borders Washington, the Bald Range Fire burned out of control, nearly doubling overnight as residents raced out. More than 20,000 people were ordered to evacuate the area of Summerland — 150 miles east of Vancouver — and officials say some residents had to be rescued.
"Aerial response teams were converted to emergency evacuation personnel," said Ravi Parmar, minister of forests of British Columbia. "Eighteen of our aircraft were used to rescue more than 50 individuals."
British Columbia declared a province-wide state of emergency Saturday as more than 100 wildfires burned across the province amid windy weather and prolonged drought.
Last week, fires near Spokane, Washington, showed how quickly conditions can escalate. Blazes there destroyed nearly 1,000 structures.
Some evacuations in Spokane eased Sunday, but the hardest-hit neighborhoods remain closed while crews check for hot spots.
Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said authorities were doing everything they could to get people back in their homes "as soon and as safe as possible."
Officials have not said exactly when families in the hardest-hit areas can go home. Crews are still monitoring for hot spots and removing hazardous materials.

AI access to data on nuclear weapons could turn against humanity — lawmaker

Unknown Publisher

22:02:37 KST

MOSCOW, August 10. /TASS/. The access of artificial intelligence to data on weapons of mass destruction poses a threat to humanity, Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on Information Policy Andrey Svintsov stated in a column published on the TASS website.
"Currently, the greatest concern is caused not only by the frightening speed of neural network development, but also by the accessibility of critical data on nuclear, biological or chemical weapons. Thus, global awareness could turn against humanity," the deputy noted.
He recalled that AI agents have repeatedly escaped human control. In particular, companies Anthropic and OpenAI reported cases of their AI agents escaping beyond the space designated for testing. "The Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol models attempted to carry out a cyberattack: Mythos 5 tried to deceive GitHub's file-sharing system and inject malicious code into it. When testers discovered this, the agent began to cover up its own activity history. The OpenAI GPT-5.6-Sol model twice violated protocol by 'gaining access to the internet in ways that the program prohibited,'" Svintsov stated.
The parliamentarian also drew attention to the fact that the problem of the rapid development of AI and its access to critical information is understood within the professional community. In July 2026, more than 1,200 employees of major US AI companies signed a petition calling on the government to adopt a mechanism allowing control over the pace of artificial intelligence development.
"Among those who signed the document are OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. According to the petition's authors, there is a 'real risk' that AI will begin to develop faster than humans can 'understand or control' it. But the legislative process risks being drawn out for a long time," Svintsov concluded.

British defence startup building missile interceptors hits £2.5bn valuation - just two years after launching
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
14:02:35 BST
22:02:35 KST

British defence startup building missile interceptors hits £2.5bn valuation - just two years after launching
Cambridge Aerospace develops interceptor systems to use against drones
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A British defence firm founded only two years ago has attained a valuation of £2.5bn ($3.4bn), following a funding round which makes it one of the most valuable startups in the UK.
Cambridge Aerospace develops and makes interceptor systems for use against drones and missiles, as well as a radar system and rocket motors.
Defence secretary Wes Streeting called the multi-billion valuation “a great vote of confidence” in Britain that would continue to put the UK “at the forefront of defence innovation”.
The most recent funding round for Cambridge was only in April of this year - the current one marks an increase in overall valuation of well over double since then.
Part of the reason for the rapid increase has been a series of Ministry of Defence contracts earned by Cambridge Aerospace, providing their interceptors for the UK Armed Forces.
The company employs more than 250 workers it describes as highly skilled or in engineering roles, while outside of Britain it operates in other European nations including Germany and Ukraine, as well as Australia.
Seb Johnson, tech business writer and founder of Scaling Europe, noted Cambridge Aerospace is one of three UK-based defence firms to have hit unicorn status - valuations of $1bn or more - in 2026, with the UK having previously had zero. Uforce and Kraken Technology Group are the others.
In May of this year, the government - then under Keir Starmer - signed deals to provide contracts worth up to £4m to 13 different businesses to work with the MoD, as part of a wider scheme to help startups and SMEs progress to unicorn status and aid wider economic growth in key industries.
Cambridge Aerospace was not listed as one of the firms awarded contracts on that occasion.
Professor Steven Barrett, an aerospace engineer, is the chief executive of the firm. “By bringing together the best talent in the world with a singular mission to protect Allied skies from threats we have achieved a huge amount already,” he said. “The addition of these funds will allow us to continue to scale our manufacturing and our delivery to meet the pace of threats, and the needs of Allied nations.”
Grant Shapps was formerly the chair of the firm but stepped down in June having breached rules on ex-ministers’ business appointments. Mr Barrett says Cambridge have “no plans to appoint anyone new” as a replacement and that Mr Shapps’ “role was only ever titular in nature”.
Mr Streeting added: “This valuation is a great vote of confidence in Britain. Cambridge Aerospace’s Skyhammer is an example of the low-cost interceptor missiles our Armed Forces need to deter adversaries and keep our country safe.
“It is exactly what our unicorn scheme is designed to create – British start-ups scaling into billion-pound companies, creating skilled jobs, cementing the UK’s position at the forefront of defence innovation.”

Israel’s siege cripples transport system in Gaza, risking return to famine in Gaza: Rights monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:01:45 UTC
22:01:45 KST

Burak Bir
10 August 2026•Update: 10 August 2026
The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor on Sunday said Israel is intentionally disrupting transportation and freight by destroying trucks and warehouses of transport companies, which pushes Palestinians back toward famine.
In a statement, the human rights group said: "Israel enforces a comprehensive policy that disrupts the entire supply chain, starting from the entry of goods and aid through crossings until they reach the population."
According to Euro-Med, even when trucks are permitted to cross into Gaza, it is not guaranteed that their cargo will reach those in need, due to the destruction or impairment of the transportation, storage, and distribution infrastructure.
Nahed Shuhibar, the head of Gaza’s Private Transport Association, told the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor that before the Israeli genocide, Gaza had about 1,200 trucks delivering food, medicine, fuel, animal feed, building materials, and other essentials.
"Since then, only around 400 trucks remain after Israeli bombings and destruction, with roughly 100 out of service due to restrictions on the entry of spare parts, tires, oils, and batteries," Shuhibar added.
"As a result, just about 300 trucks, which are only 25% of the original fleet, are currently operational."
Citing Justin Brady, head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs in Palestine, the statement said the Gaza Strip is facing a food emergency that could escalate to Phase 5 of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification if aid flow diminishes.
Euro-Med Monitor emphasised that Israel’s obligations under international humanitarian law stand, regardless of coordination.
"This includes avoiding attacks on civilians and civilian structures, safeguarding relief workers and their transportation, taking all possible precautions to minimise harm during military actions, and enabling the swift, unobstructed delivery of humanitarian aid."
According to the group, several newly imported trucks in the Gaza Strip have also been taken out of service.
Sharing Brady's analysis, the monitor warned that approximately 212,000 people, nearly 10% of Gaza’s population, will remain in a Phase 4 food emergency, the penultimate stage.
"The comparison with last year’s data reaffirms that the humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip remains critically severe," it noted, stressing that any reduction in aid volume could swiftly worsen living conditions, which are already very fragile.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority in Myanmar, face discrimination, persecution and statelessness.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya have fled Myanmar since 2017 due to violent crackdowns by the military and armed groups. More than 1.3 million have sought refuge in Bangladesh, with some reaching Indonesia and Malaysia after perilous sea journeys.

The Intrepid Humanitarian: The world’s most forgotten crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
13:01:26 UTC
22:01:26 KST

Share & more
Around the globe, few humanitarian crises are as neglected by the international community as that unfolding in the United States, one of the world’s top banana-exporting republics. Two weeks ago, I journeyed to the country's militarised capital, Washington DC, to shine a light on the terrible consequences of decades of political decline, institutional decay, and chronic flavour insecurity.
The crisis is all the more tragic because it was once thought avoidable.
Following independence from its former colonial master, Britain, the United States was hailed as the brightest democratic prospect in the troubled Caucasian bloc. Blessed with immense natural wealth and vast agricultural resources, many believed it would rise from a rudimentary First World level of political and social development to become a model Third World democracy, paving the way for other Caucasian states.
However, under a succession of aging, corrupt, and increasingly authoritarian regimes, public institutions have been hollowed out while members of a small elite have amassed massive fortunes. The result is one of the most unequal societies on Earth, with the top 1% owning the same wealth as the bottom 90% combined, and a humanitarian emergency impacting tens of millions of ordinary people.
Nearly 50 million Americans face food insecurity – a number equal to the entire population of Kenya. Millions of children suffer from malnutrition linked to diets almost entirely devoid of adequate flavour. Despite generations of African humanitarian assistance, much of the population continues to rely on traditional fast food, itself a symptom of deeper structural governance failures.
The country's current ruler, Donald “Papa Don” Trump, has accelerated this decline since returning to power last year. Like many First World strongmen, he has concentrated authority around himself and his family, weakened oversight institutions, and prefers to rule by decree, bypassing the country’s weak democratic institutions. He has also plunged the US into a needless war with Iran, which has left its economy and international standing in dire straits.
Fears of political violence
Civil society groups I met during my visit also expressed alarm that municipal and parliamentary elections scheduled for November could trigger renewed tribal violence similar to that witnessed following a shambolic and disputed 2020 presidential poll. In the discreet gatherings held only a few kilometres from the presidential palace, participants expressed fears that armed Shite Christianist militias loyal to the regime could once again be mobilised against political opponents should Papa Don reject the election results.
Such fears should not be easily dismissed.
Each morning, I watched as devotees of traditional religion gathered at the National Mall, a sacred area of the capital containing shrines to revered ancestors, where they performed elaborate jogging rituals. Participation appeared voluntary, although there is considerable social pressure to take part.
The country possesses perhaps the world's most entrenched cult of gun worship. Anthropologists believe this influential offshoot of Shite Christianity has helped normalise political violence while elevating firearms to objects of veneration along with the country’s military. This has fostered a primitive traditional custom of mass shootings in public spaces, as well as schools, where they have become a cultural rite of passage.
Yet amid the anxiety, daily life continues. Each morning, I watched as devotees of traditional religion gathered at the National Mall, a sacred area of the capital containing shrines to revered ancestors, where they performed elaborate jogging rituals. Participation appeared voluntary, although there is considerable social pressure to take part.
Some of the male pilgrims stripped to the waist during these activities, in an act of ritual purification. While scholars disagree over the origins of the practice, some elders I spoke to explained that exposing the body in this manner allows the ancestors to witness the physical effects of chronic low-calorie consumption and thus grant strength and endurance to the faithful.
Shrines and ceremonies
The Mall itself also functions as the symbolic centre of political authority. It is on a hill overlooking the shrines that rulers perform traditional religious oathing ceremonies before taking power, reinforcing the close – and in many ways destructive – relationship between state and faith that characterises much of Caucasian political culture.
Papa Don, for example, also doubles up as the Grand Covfefe of Shite Christianity, which has many adherents in the country’s dank interior. These adherents reject the counting of votes and believe the terror group, Al Jibra, is using math and Arabic numerals to bring Sharia Law to the United States.
The Mall has also recently become the focus of public controversy. The Reflecting Pool, a sacred body of water associated with national reflection and remembrance, was closed after a controversial government restoration project descended into scandal. Contracts worth billions of shillings were corruptly awarded to political allies of Papa Don as costs ballooned. Eventually, algae transformed the water into a neon green, which many believers saw as a sign of the ancestors’ displeasure, further weakening the regime’s already shaky claims to legitimacy.
The disconnect between rulers and ruled was perhaps most evident during my visit to two very different shrines commemorating the country's history. The first was the baked-mud hut that served as home to an ancient ruler, Woodrow Wilson. Despite lying outside the sacred Mall, the cramped dwelling has been carefully preserved by Caucasian tribes.
Wilson remains a deeply contested figure.
Although celebrated by some for guiding the country during the first internationalised Caucasian tribal conflict between 1914 and 1918, his regime also marked a turning point in relations between the United States and the generations of African humanitarian workers who had long helped build the country's wealth and institutions. African experts who had contributed to public administration were gradually pushed aside as Wilson surrounded himself with members of his own and allied Caucasian tribes, reversing years of patient capacity-building.
The second monument offered a striking contrast. Located prominently on the Mall, it commemorates the centuries of African aid to Caucasia, and to the United States in particular, telling the stories of millions of aid workers who laboured under unimaginably horrific circumstances to improve the living standards of Caucasian societies repeatedly devastated by inter-tribal warfare, famine, epidemic disease, and political collapse. They helped transform agriculture and industry, strengthen public health, transfer technology, and expand education.
Yet, while their contribution remains immeasurable, like so many humanitarian interventions, success has been undermined by a lack of political will.
Ensuring progress on rights
Today, many activists say that continued assistance to the Caucasia region should be conditioned on improvements in governance and human rights. Several suggested that future African support be linked to measurable democratic reforms, like independent electoral oversight and an end to the intimidation of opposition supporters. They also demanded the regime withdraw heavily armed paramilitary units such as ICE from the capital’s streets and end the politicisation and tribalisation of the country’s military.
Others called for emergency deployment of African math teachers to strengthen local vote-counting capacity before the elections.
Like others across Caucasia affected by conflict, corruption, and poor governance, Americans exhibited extraordinary courage standing up to the Papa Don regime.
No discussion of America's humanitarian predicament would be complete without mentioning the flavour crisis. Unlike other nations in Caucasia, the country has been spared the worst as aid workers have been largely able to circumvent barriers and smuggle in flavour – including under the guise of what locals now call "Soul Food". However, most Americans still consume far below the minimum recommended daily intake of flavour. Aid agencies continue to press for expanded access for humanitarian flavour convoys, particularly through the San Ysidro and Laredo-Nuevo crossings.
I was singularly impressed by the resilience of Americans in the face of all the hardships they continue to experience, which today also include drought affecting over 150 million people. Throughout my visit, I met ordinary people trying to care for their families, preserve their dignity, and build a better future under circumstances largely beyond their control. Like others across Caucasia affected by conflict, corruption, and poor governance, they exhibited extraordinary courage standing up to the Papa Don regime.
As my flight lifted out of Washington, I found myself thinking less about the country's eccentric rituals or colourful politics than about the quiet conversations I had with those people, most of whom simply asked that the outside world notice their suffering.
It is time we did.

Now open: A gorgeous new resort overlooking the waterways of Hoi An
NHAAN Resort & Spa Hoi An has rooms with direct pool access, a rooftop spa and a cocktail bar spotlighting the flavours of the coconut.
Hoi An, with its UNESCO-listed Ancient Town, is on most travellers' first-time itineraries to Vietnam.
And, if you’re planning a visit to the former trading port and need somewhere to stay, you might just want to take a look at NHAAN Resort & Spa Hoi An, Tapestry Collection by Hilton.
Newly opened at the start of August, the property is found along the Co Co river in Cam Thanh village, which is best known for its basket boat rides.
The gorgeous resort was designed by Vietnamese architect Vo Trong Nghia, with biophilic architecture that’s meant to create an open-air sanctuary that blends with its surroundings.
“Tapestry Collection by Hilton is a collection of independent boutique hotels, each woven with an original, vibrant story shaped by its locale,” Alexander Shockley, lifestyle and collection brands at Hilton in Asia Pacific, said.
“NHAAN Resort & Spa Hoi An is a compelling expression of what makes this brand resonate globally – uplifting design, food and beverage grounded in place, and experiences that invite local exploration and adventure. As we introduce the Tapestry Collection to Vietnam, this property brings the soul of Hoi An to life in a way that feels fresh, authentic, and distinctly its own.”
What to expect at NHAAN Resort & Spa
The 174-key property offers a number of room categories, including some with direct pool access.
As you may have guessed from the name, one of the highlights of the resort will be the spa, which is set to open later this month.
The eforea spa & health club is located on the hotel’s rooftop and offers views over the waterscape. The wellbeing offering also spans a 24-hour gym, and outdoor infinity pool and a yoga deck.
Plenty of tourists head to Vietnam purely for its food, and you can explore the region’s cuisine through the hotel’s four restaurants and bars.
At Plait Restaurant, guests can dine on locally caught seafood prepared over an open Korean grill, while Keng Restaurants serves Vietnamese specialties all day.
Bong Lounge, which has a design inspired by the 500-year craft legacy of nearby Kim Bong Carpentry Village, is the place to be for coconut cocktails.
For those who want to spend their days soaking up rays in the pool, you can grab poolside bites and drinks at Nipa Pool Bar.
On the flip side, guests are just a 10-minute drive from Hoi An Ancient Town, and you can also book in for pottery-throwing, woodcarving and lantern-making workshops through the hotel if you’re looking for cultural immersion.

Poland and Baltic states are preparing for possible Russian false-flag strike, says Reuters
Reuters has learned that Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are cooperating to shield their infrastructure from potential Russian attacks that could be staged as "false-flag" operations, as allied intelligence services have repeatedly warned.
Source: Reuters, citing intelligence officials from these countries, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The countries are strengthening security around dams, power stations and gas infrastructure amid concerns that Moscow could stage a "false-flag" attack using captured Ukrainian drones.
Last week, Lithuanian intelligence said Moscow was considering such a staged attack. Poland, Latvia and Estonia have also warned of possible Russian sabotage operations aimed at testing NATO's response as questions grow over the US commitment to the Alliance.
"We are not naive, we see the information, we read between the lines and we are doing our homework," Lithuania's Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Reuters.
"We are increasing the security of our critical infrastructure, we constantly exchange information with our intelligence on what to do next," he added.
Last month, Lithuania deployed troops to help riot police protect critical energy infrastructure: its liquefied natural gas import terminal, oil products terminal, a key power link with Poland and the Kruonis Pumped Storage Plant.
"We are clearly signalling that, if needed, we will be defending ourselves," Kaunas said.
Latvia has stepped up security around all critical infrastructure, including the dam on the Daugava River near Riga and the Inčukalns underground gas storage facility, Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told Reuters.
"A potential hybrid threat is more likely than it was before," he said.
Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe, the state-owned company responsible for building Poland's first nuclear power plant, said forged documents purporting to be official company records have emerged in an apparent attempt to mislead stakeholders. The company said they originated somewhere "east of Poland".
Marcin Skolimowski, spokesperson for Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe, said the company is investigating the matter in cooperation with the special services and law enforcement agencies and is also monitoring the planned construction site for signs of sabotage or other threats.
In July, Poland's power grid operator and a unit of the armed forces began stepping up security around the electricity interconnector with Ukraine, which helps stabilise Ukraine's energy system amid sustained Russian attacks.
"This is an area where heightened vigilance is required, so we are using all available resources," the grid operator's spokesperson Maciej Wapiński told Reuters.
The company expects that the military will help ensure the security of its critical infrastructure in other eastern regions of the country.
Background:
- In May, Moscow accused the Baltic states of planning to allow Ukrainian drones to attack Russia from their territory and promised to take retaliatory measures. This raised concerns that Russia could stage such an attack in order to justify its actions against these countries.
- Leaders of NATO's eastern flank countries have recently issued public warnings, citing intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing provocations on their territory.
- Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski had earlier suggested that Russia could organise a false-flag operation using Ukrainian-made drones.
- Media reports indicated earlier that the US had passed on a warning to Warsaw that Moscow is considering an armed provocation against Poland in order to "test NATO's resolve".

Powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake strikes Colombia, tremors felt in Bogotá

A powerful earthquake struck Colombia on Monday, with tremors felt in the capital Bogotá, across several parts of the country and in neighboring Ecuador, prompting people to evacuate homes and buildings.
The European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) measured the earthquake at magnitude 7.4 and said it occurred at a depth of approximately 115 kilometers. Witnesses in Bogotá told Reuters they felt the shaking.
Colombia’s Geological Service initially issued a lower preliminary estimate, measuring the earthquake at magnitude 6.7 and a depth of 82 kilometers. It placed the epicenter near San José del Palmar in Colombia’s western Chocó department.
Later assessments by both the U.S. Geological Survey and Colombia’s geological authorities put the magnitude at 7.4. Both agencies described the earthquake as relatively deep and located its epicenter near San José del Palmar, about 400 kilometers west of Bogotá.
The quake was reported at around 7:34 a.m. local time and was felt in Bogotá as well as Antioquia, Cundinamarca, Meta and other areas, according to local reports. Shaking was also reported across the border in Ecuador.
Residents in parts of Colombia and Ecuador evacuated homes and buildings as the tremors were felt, while emergency authorities activated response and prevention protocols and began assessing possible damage.
Authorities did not immediately report injuries or significant damage.
The earthquake comes weeks after two powerful earthquakes, measuring magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, struck Venezuela in late June. Those earthquakes destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5,000 people.
The varying initial measurements reflected preliminary assessments by seismic agencies, which can be revised as additional data is analyzed.

ASEAN closing ranks as cyberscam threat escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

ASEAN members closing ranks as cyberscam threat escalates
August 10, 2026
For years, governments across Southeast Asia largely approached the region's online fraudsters as a matter for the police, anti-trafficking agencies and border authorities.
But these bodies have appearently failed to stem the rise of international cyberscam cartels. The illicit industry is increasingly using international banking systems, cryptocurrencies, telecommunications networks, shell companies and trafficking routes, with some of its centers operating under the protection of armed or politically connected groups.
Now, ASEAN governments seem increasingly willing to tackle the threat as a united bloc.
Myanmar approves death penalty for cyberscam bosses
Signs of this shift were visible at the controversial meeting in Bangkok on August 6 between Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Min Aung Hlaing, the head of Myanmar's military government.
The two governments agreed to clamp down on scam centers along their shared frontier, exchange information and jointly disrupt criminal financial flows.
Thailand also offered support for Myanmar's participation in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial-intelligence bodies. Myanmar's military-backed parliament had already voted in favor of applying the death penalty on those caught operating online scam centers.
While visiting Cambodia late last month, Indonesian Deputy Foreign Minister Arif Havas Oegroseno also proposed a joint task force to combat online scam syndicates.
And last week, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Thai Prime Minister Charnvirakul held talks in Jakarta where they agreed their two countries must lead the way and strengthen ASEAN's resilience against scam groups.
Online scams grew into an 'economic security threat'
A UN estimate published last month put the annual losses from cyber scammers — many of whom are located in Southeast Asia — at between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion (between €76 billion and €98 billion) globally in 2025.
Artificial intelligence, cryptocurrencies, encrypted communications and deepfake technology have made their operations cheaper and harder to detect.
"Cyber scams in Southeast Asia have evolved beyond a conventional cybercrime issue and should be viewed as an economic security threat," Hai Luong, a lecturer at Australia's Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice, told DW.
Impact of cybercrime felt around the world
Governments in Southeast Asia have already had to respond to pressure from the US, the EU and China as their online cartels drew international attention.
In October 2025, the US designated Cambodia's Prince Group, one of the country's largest conglomerates, as a transnational criminal organization and imposed sanctions on 146 people and companies connected to it.
US authorities also charged Chinese-born Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi with wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies. Cambodia eventually revoked Chen's citizenship and extradited him to China.
Prince Group's business empire extended across real estate, finance and other sectors in Cambodia. US authorities allege that criminal revenues were mixed with legitimate commercial activities through an international network of companies.
Washington has also sanctioned other Southeast Asian individuals and companies accused of investing in scam compounds and laundering money.
The EU followed last month, imposing sanctions on Prince Group and Jin Bei Group in Cambodia and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army in Myanmar for alleged involvement in cyberscams.
Cambodia moves against US-sanctioned banks
In 2024, the United States Institute of Peace estimated that Cambodia's cyber-scam industry generated more than $12.5 billion annually, equivalent to roughly a third of the country's formal economy.
The collapse of several scam-linked conglomerates has raised concerns about how the economic shockwaves will affect the rest of the country. At the same time, other voices say negative publicity around scamming is hurting the country's tourism sector and keeping away foreign investors.
Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has acknowledged that the illicit scam economy is damaging legitimate businesses and has vowed a systematic crackdown on online scam networks, including greater scrutiny of the financial sector.
The National Bank of Cambodia has shuttered at least six financial institutions since the start of 2026. Three commercial banks whose licences were revoked in August had all been sanctioned by the US over alleged links to scam networks.
On August 4, the Singaporean government introduced legislation that would expand information-sharing between police and service providers, allow authorities to disable accounts suspected of facilitating scams and strengthen restrictions on financial, telecommunications and online services supplied to suspected offenders.
Criminal groups capitalize on government inefficiencies
As ASEAN nations try to clamp down on cybercriminals, the region's greatest weakness is its fragmentation, Sophal Ear, an associate professor at Arizona State University's Thunderbird School of Global Management, told DW.
"Criminal organizations operate seamlessly across borders while governments continue responding through separate agencies with different mandates and limited coordination," he said.
Ear added that the financial infrastructure used to move and conceal criminal proceeds can often prove more resilient than the law-enforcement architecture designed to dismantle it.
What is in ASEAN's anti-crime plan?
Now, the regional governments seem to be catching on — at least judging by ASEAN's new Plan of Action in Combating Transnational Crime for 2026–2035.
The plan calls for improved intelligence-sharing between national law-enforcement agencies and financial-intelligence units, joint investigations, better cross-border coordination and stronger capacity among anti-money-laundering regulators.
ASEAN has also recently established a joint working group to combat money laundering.
But ASEAN's consensus-based system still heavily relies on national governments implementing those commitments and sharing sensitive financial and law-enforcement information.
"In practice, governments should prioritize disrupting the financial infrastructure, labor supply chains, technological services and transnational business models that sustain scam operations rather than focusing solely on individual offenders," said Luong from Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.
Moving beyond money mules
Asha Hemrajani, senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, agreed that the region needs to take a "holistic, not siloed" approach to attack the entire cyberscam business model.
"The shared objective should be to identify and dismantle crime syndicate leadership, financial networks and enabling infrastructure, not just arrest money mules or raid individual scam compounds in Cambodia and Myanmar," Hemrajani said.
This includes official scrutiny of high-risk corporate structures and checking sources of funding, as well as a much tougher stance against money laundering, she added. Hemrajani also recommended ASEAN sanctioning business groups linked to the cyberscam networks, similar to how Washington cut off sanctioned Southeast Asian companies from the entire US economy.

First Lufthansa jet with Starlink wi-fi set to take off
Streaming and cloud-based work above the clouds: Lufthansa is launching its first plane equipped with high-speed wi-fi from the US provider Starlink – and Swiss International Air Lines (SWISS) is set to follow suit soon.
The Lufthansa Group is equipping its entire fleet with satellite internet from the US provider Starlink. According to Lufthansa, the first aircraft to take off with the new wi-fi service will be a medium-haul Airbus A320neo operated by the parent company Lufthansa on August 19. Lufthansa’s subsidiary SWISS is set to follow suit before the end of this half-year. Passengers will then be able to use high-speed internet on board via their own devices to browse the web, stream content or work on their company networks.
Lufthansa claims that the online bandwidth will, in many cases, exceed internet connections at home or in the office. The German group is thus one of the first airlines worldwide to offer Starlink. The service is provided by SpaceX, the company owned by billionaire Elon Musk, which has deployed more than 9,000 satellites for the service. Numerous airlines have already announced their intention to switch to Starlink. In Europe, Air Baltic is among the pioneers.
More
Smoking powerbank forces SWISS Boston flight to land in Dublin
Free of charge after registration
Lufthansa has announced that internet access will remain free of charge for all status customers as well as for passengers who create a user account for the so-called “Travel ID”. The company did not disclose the investment figure. The necessary technology will be installed in the aircraft during scheduled maintenance stops.
“By 2029, all of the group’s approximately 850 aircraft will be equipped with this technology,” explains board member Dieter Vranckx.
A spokeswoman stated that expansion plans are already in place for all the group’s airlines. In addition to Lufthansa’s A320 fleet, aircraft operated by the subsidiaries SWISS, Austrian and Brussels Airlines will be the first to be fitted.
User guidelines have been drawn up for the new service via the “Lufthansa Group WiFi” portal, which users must agree to before using the service. Among other things, passengers are required to always wear headphones when playing audio and video content, to refrain from making voice and video calls, and not to broadcast live streams from on board.

Pamela Anderson recommends Watermelon Granita for a cool, no-fuss summer dessert
My cookbook “I Love You” began as a box of recipe cards: a housewarming gift for my sons, inspired by our homegrown traditions and world travel.
Since I don’t have a strong sweet tooth, dessert for me is more about being social and having something to share over cards, tea and coffee. A treat for the kids and their friends.
This Watermelon Granita is something beautiful to pull out at a barbecue — either in paper cups or in crystal glasses on a long picnic table outside… the dessert itself is pretty enough.
Not all my dinners end in dessert, but I like to make sure all senses are firing, and a cool treat outside on a hot day is always appreciated.
Watermelon Granita
Serves 4 to 6
Ingredients
6 cups diced seeded watermelon
Juice of 1 lemon
⅓ cup granulated sugar
Directions
Combine the watermelon, lemon juice and sugar in a blender and puree on high speed for 1 minute. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a 9-by-13-inch baking pan. Cover and freeze for at least 2 hours.
Use a fork to scrape the frozen mixture to create tiny ice crystals. Return to the freezer and continue checking and scraping every 30 minutes or so until the granita is completely frozen as beautiful flaky crystals. Serve in little bowls.
___
Pamela Anderson, author of “I Love You,” is an actress, activist, and lifelong cook and homemaker. Above all else, she says, being a mother to sons Brandon Thomas Lee and Dylan Jagger Lee has been her greatest source of pride.

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Vermont’s state primary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
12:53:02 UTC
21:53:02 KST

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Vermont’s state primary
WASHINGTON (AP) — Vermont Democrats will try on Tuesday to do something they’ve been unable to do in five previous attempts: nominate a gubernatorial candidate who can beat Republican Gov. Phil Scott.
Voters will also decide contested Democratic primaries for lieutenant governor and state auditor and choose a Republican nominee to challenge Democratic U.S. Rep. Becca Balint in November.
Scott is one of only two Republican governors to serve a state that then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. But toppling him this fall will be no easy feat. He received 73% of the vote in his 2024 reelection bid, improving upon the 69% he won in 2022.
He’s also been a rare Republican critic of President Donald Trump. Scott not only endorsed former United Nations Ambassador Nikki Haley for president in the 2024 primaries, but he also says he voted for Harris over Trump in 2024 and for Joe Biden in 2020. He is unopposed for the Republican nomination.
Two Democrats are running to challenge Scott: economist Amanda Janoo and former child advocacy organization CEO Aly Richards, who boasts endorsements from former Democratic Govs. Howard Dean and Madeleine Kunin. Richards has raised about $453,000 for her campaign, compared to about $308,000 for Janoo. Richards also had about double Janoo’s cash reserves as of the end of July.
In Vermont, the governor, lieutenant governor and other state constitutional officers serve two-year terms. If Scott is reelected and completes another term, he’ll surpass Dean as Vermont’s longest serving governor since it became a state.
All 30 state Senate seats and all 150 state House seats are up in 2026. Democratic state lawmakers suffered significant losses in the 2024 general election, losing more than two dozen seats across both chambers, along with their supermajorities. This year could prove to be another difficult one for the party but for different reasons: Democratic incumbents in five state Senate districts and 11 state House districts face primary challengers. Republican incumbents face challengers in only one state Senate district.
For state legislative primaries, the number of winners in each contest varies by district. With multiple winners in many seats and relatively low turnout for down-ballot primaries, especially on the Republican side, determining the winners could come down to a relatively small number of votes.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for U.S. House, governor, lieutenant governor, auditor, state Senate and state House.
Who gets to vote?
Any registered voter may participate in any party’s primary. Vermont does not register voters by party.
How many voters are there?
As of July, there were about 501,000 registered voters in Vermont.
How many people actually vote?
About 23,000 Republican primary voters and about 33,000 Democratic primary voters cast ballots in the 2024 gubernatorial primaries.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
About 30% of the vote in the 2024 state primary was cast by mail. In the presidential primaries that year, about 24% of Democratic primary voters and about 13% of Republican primary voters cast mail ballots.
As of Friday, about 17,000 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election.
When are early and absentee votes released?
Vermont runs elections at the town and city level. There are 247 separate jurisdictions administering local elections, and they vary in terms of how and when they release results. In many of the larger jurisdictions, the bulk of results from both mail voting and in-person Election Day voting are released together in their first vote updates.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the 2024 state primary, the AP first reported results at 7:18 p.m. ET, or 18 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 11:45 p.m. ET with about 87% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
A candidate may request a recount if the vote margin falls below a certain threshold. In federal, statewide and state Senate elections, a recount may be requested if the vote margin between the winning and losing candidate is 2% or less of the total votes cast, divided by the number of persons to be elected for that position. For state House and local races, the required margin is 5% or less of the total votes cast, divided by the number of persons to be elected. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 84 days until the 2026 midterm elections.
___
The AP’s Matthew Junkroski contributed to this report.

Taylor Farms recalls jalapeno products over salmonella concerns
Taylor Fresh Foods, parent company of Taylor Farms, is voluntarily recalling some products that include jalapenos because of worries about a possible salmonella contamination.
The announcement comes a few weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled its iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico because of a potential link to a multistate cyclospora outbreak that has sickened people across the U.S.
Taylor Fresh Foods said that it was pulling some products including jalapenos from stores shelves after finding out that Coast Citrus Distributors was voluntarily recalling fresh jalapeños due to a potential salmonella contamination.
Guacamole, pico de gallo and taco dip are some of the prepared foods included in the recall. The list of recalled products were distributed by Taylor Farms in multiple states with a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026. The products were sold at stores including Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart.
Taylor Fresh Foods said that the Food and Drug Administration and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention were working with state and local partners to investigate illnesses in a multistate outbreak of salmonella infections linked to fresh jalapeños supplied by Coast Citrus Distributors. The company said that a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, a supplier to Coast Citrus Distributors, was identified as the potential source in the outbreak.
Taylor Fresh Foods said that it is no longer sourcing products from the farmer and will be filling orders from alternative suppliers. The company is currently not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.
Consumers who have any recalled product are advised to discard it immediately and not eat it. Refunds are available at the location of purchase.
Consumers with any questions can contact Taylor at 855-455-0098 Monday through Friday from 8am-5pm PT.

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Connecticut’s state primary
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two veteran Democratic incumbents in Connecticut face strong challenges in a state primary on Tuesday.
The contests take place as elements within the party look to redefine the Democratic brand ahead of the midterm elections by replacing old guard figures with younger and often more progressive alternatives.
Democratic Gov. Ned Lamont is running for a third term but must first clear a challenge from state Rep. Josh Elliott. Both candidates have raised just shy of $400,000 in contributions from individual donors. Nonetheless, Lamont, a wealthy former cable entrepreneur, has far outspent Elliott, thanks to $9.5 million in personal funds he’s invested in his campaign. Elliott has received about $3.8 million from the state’s public election funding program.
A primary upset by Elliott, along with additional Tuesday primaries in Minnesota and Wisconsin, could extend a progressive winning streak that began this summer with the defeat of Democratic incumbents in New York City and Colorado and continued with a high-stakes victory in the Michigan U.S. Senate primary on August 4.
The Democratic nominee will face Republican state Sen. Ryan Fazio in November. Republicans last controlled the governorship from 1995 to 2011. Lamont was first elected in 2018 with 49% of the vote and reelected in 2022 with 56%.
In the 1st Congressional District, longtime Democratic U.S. Rep. John Larson is running for a 15th term. Challenging him for the nomination are former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune and state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest.
This year marks Larson’s first primary challenge since he was first elected in 1998. He won a close primary that year with 46% of the vote but has not appeared on a primary ballot in his subsequent 13 reelection bids.
Bronin has slightly outraised and outspent Larson in the campaign overall, although Larson had a slight edge in terms of available cash heading into the primary campaign’s final three weeks. Gilchrest and Fortune trailed far behind in fundraising.
Larson turned 78 in July. In 2025, an incident on the House floor sparked concerns over his health and age when he suffered what he later described as a complex partial seizure while delivering a speech. He said the episode, which caused him to briefly but abruptly stop speaking, was related to a heart condition that he now treats with medication.
The district is heavily Democratic. Larson received 63% of the vote in his 2024 reelection campaign. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 61% of the district vote in the presidential race.
All 36 state Senate seats and all 151 state House seats are up in 2026. Democrats hold two-to-one majorities in both chambers.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 8 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for U.S. House, governor, state Senate and state House.
Who gets to vote?
Voters registered with a political party may participate only in that party’s primary. Democrats may not vote in the Republican primary or vice versa. Independent or unaffiliated voters may not participate in either primary.
How many voters are there?
As of October 2025, there were about 2.5 million registered voters in Connecticut, including about 878,000 Democrats and about 529,000 Republicans.
How many people actually vote?
About 114,000 Democratic primary ballots and about 94,000 Republican primary ballots were cast in the 2022 state primaries.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
Early voting was enacted in Connecticut after 2022. There was no statewide Democratic primary in 2024, but about 17% of the Republican primary vote in the 2024 state primary was cast early in-person or by mail.
As of Friday, about 43,000 Democratic primary ballots and about 3,900 Republican primary ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election.
When are early and absentee votes released?
Connecticut runs elections at the town and city level. There are 169 separate jurisdictions administering local elections and they vary in terms of how and when they release results. In many of the larger jurisdictions, results from a mix of voting methods are released together throughout the night.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the 2024 general election, the AP first reported results at 8:12 p.m. ET, or 12 minutes after polls closed. The vote count reached the halfway mark at 12:25 a.m. ET. By 2:06 p.m. ET the day after Election Day, about 90% of the total vote had been counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
Recounts in Connecticut are automatic if the vote margin is less than 0.5% of the total votes cast but does not exceed 2,000 votes. Recounts are also automatic in races where the margin is less than 20 votes or in the case of a tie vote. If a recount results in a tie vote, a runoff election (called an “adjourned election” in Connecticut) is held. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 84 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Will Syria's Deir al-Zour airport revival meet expectations?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10

Breadcrumb
Will the revival of Syria's Deir al-Zour airport meet expectations?
Last week, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa inaugurated Deir al-Zour International Airport in eastern Syria via video link on Wednesday evening, 5 August, following its rehabilitation and announced several projects that he described as the beginning of an integrated plan for the eastern region.
He said the reopening of the airport marked a transformation in the facility's role, making it a gateway connecting the province with its local and regional surroundings. He also announced the launch of a comprehensive development plan for eastern Syria.
The plan includes upgrading infrastructure, rehabilitating the healthcare sector, completing road and bridge projects, and establishing an industrial city, contributing to the creation of new jobs and strengthening economic development.
The reopening of Deir al-Zour International Airport comes months after growing demands from residents of the province to end marginalisation and improve services.
Security incidents and protests in recent months brought Deir al-Zour back to the forefront of political and public service debate.
The announced projects include the establishment of a major industrial city incorporating food and petrochemical industries to provide employment opportunities and strengthen local production.
They also include the construction of a specialised cancer treatment hospital at an estimated cost of $21 million, the launch of the international road project linking Damascus and Deir al-Zour at a cost of between $275 million and $300 million, the rehabilitation of roads connecting Deir al-Zour with Abu Kamal and Raqqa, and rebuilding destroyed bridges, notably the Al-Siyasiya and Al-Mayadeen bridges.
Omar al-Husari, head of the General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, also announced the establishment of an advanced air cargo centre at Deir al-Zour Airport to support agricultural, industrial and commercial activity and connect the province with domestic and foreign markets.
Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Syria's recovery would not be complete without the recovery of its east, adding that the time had come to "turn the page on marginalisation" the province endured for decades.
Deir al-Zour is one of Syria's richest provinces in natural resources, containing most of the country's oil and gas fields, as well as vast agricultural land dependent on the Euphrates River.
However, according to residents of the province, it has remained among the regions that have benefited least from its resources, before and after 2011 uprising began.
The province suffered widespread destruction as a result of battles against the Islamic State (ISIS), followed by subsequent military operations by multiple partie.
Large parts of the city's infrastructure, including roads, bridges, hospitals, and water and electricity networks, has been destroyed.
Hundreds of thousands of residents were displaced, while large areas continue to suffer from shortages of basic services and high unemployment.
Flooding of the Euphrates River several weeks ago further increased the hardship facing residents, causing significant economic losses amid severe difficulties travelling between different parts of the province because most of its bridges had been destroyed.
The government announcements come after the province witnessed protests and tribal and popular mobilisation for months, all calling for improved public services, employment opportunities, the reopening of Deir al-Zour airport, the rehabilitation of the road network, and the establishment of productive projects capable of employing thousands of unemployed young people.
Furthermore, major security incidents, accompanied by tensions and clashes, also renewed attention on the fragility of the economic and social situation.
Mohammad al-Hassan, a resident of the province, told The New Arab that the community had grown tired of repeated promises and were demanding fundamental changes.
He highlighted the need to improve service sectors such as rehabilitating hospitals, healthcare centres, bridges and roads, improving sanitation, clearing rubble, and providing employment opportunities for young people to prevent them from migrating to other provinces.
He added that implementing these projects, if carried out according to the announced timetable, could have a positive impact on the local situation.
However, al-Hassan stressed that "the real challenge lies not in announcing projects but in securing funding and ensuring implementation, especially since major infrastructure projects require substantial investment and security and administrative stability."
Khaled al-Jassem, from Deir al-Zour, told TNA that residents have a degree of optimism but were waiting for practical steps.
"The province has heard many promises over the past years, while services have remained modest, and electricity, water, healthcare and roads continue to be among the residents' main hardships," he added.
Al-Jassem said operating the airport had long been a demand of residents because it would ease the burden of travel and connect Deir al-Zour with the rest of Syria and abroad.
However, he believes that improving basic services and creating jobs remain the population's top priorities.
Many residents of Deir al-Zour say the announced projects constitute the largest development package by the Syrian government for the province in years.
It success remains contingent on the state's ability to secure funding and complete major infrastructure projects within the announced timeframes for a province that faces significant challenges after many years of war and marginalisation.

India: Student anger over alleged exam issues spreads to Jharkhand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-10
12:52:00 UTC
21:52:00 KST

India: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand
August 10, 2026
Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process.
Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly.
The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters.
The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi.
In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led "Cockroach" protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike.
Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated.
"The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW.
He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).
After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned.
But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs.
What sparked the protests in Jharkhand?
The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July.
Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated.
Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure.
But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem.
What are the protesters' demands?
The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated.
They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery.
The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies.
The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken.
"The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW.
Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India?
The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers.
That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan .
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters.
But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined.
Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi.
"Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system," Bora told DW.
"They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future."
Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights.
Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition.
"Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW.
"The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added.
Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12.
"The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment.
Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government
The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media, hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession.
The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission.
But India's youth are refusing to stop there.
Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure.
For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest.
"We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW.

Has the army turned the page on control of western Sudan?
Sudan’s military repels a series of offensives by the RSF paramilitary in a strategically significant region.
Khartoum, Sudan – A Sudanese army-led counteroffensive in the western region of Darfur has led to a series of gains for government-aligned forces over the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group in recent days.
In early August, Sudan’s military and allied groups repelled two successive attacks by the RSF in the strategically important Bir Saliba region. It lies about 30km (nearly 20 miles) north of el-Geneina, the capital of West Darfur state and the RSF’s last stronghold in the region.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Sudan army drone attack on Darfur kills 35, rights group says
- list 2 of 4Women expose rape as a weapon of war in Sudan
- list 3 of 4Sudan war threatens ancient Meroe pyramids
- list 4 of 4Sudan’s war threatens an ‘entire generation’s’ future, UN warns
Government-backed forces have tried to put pressure on RSF supply lines by seizing control of crossings and desert routes along the border with Chad. The strategy could signal a shift in fighting towards el-Geneina.
Leading to el-Geneina, the Bir Saliba region is of strategic importance. It has a network of roads that link the state capital with areas in the northwest of the region, particularly Jebel Moon and Kulbus, according to General Bahr al-Din Adam Karama, the governor of West Darfur state.
Attempt to encircle Bir Saliba
Darfur Regional Governor Minni Arko Minnawi announced that Major General Mahdi Adam, known as “Jebel Moon” and one of the RSF’s most prominent field commanders, was killed in fighting in western Sudan. The RSF has not officially confirmed his death, but if true it would represent a significant loss for the paramilitary group and leave a leadership gap along this key western front.
Minnawi said the Joint Force of the Armed Struggle Movements, a coalition of former Darfur rebel groups that signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement and now fights alongside the Sudanese army against the RSF, also thwarted an attempt by the RSF to encircle Bir Saliba. One RSF force advanced from north of Kulbus while another moved from the direction of Sileia in the Jebel Moon area before launching a large-scale attack on the Joint Force.
“[The RSF] bet on the element of surprise to break through the Joint Force’s defences, but they received another lesson,” Minnawi said.
Battlefield gains
Major Mutawakkil Ali Wakil Abu-Ja, the Joint Force’s spokesman, told Al Jazeera that the Joint Force destroyed more than 38 combat vehicles and seized 27 others in the campaign.
The commander of the attacking RSF force was also killed, he said, with fighters fleeing the battlefield and leaving their dead comrades behind.
Abu-Ja said efforts were under way to secure the western axis and increase pressure on the RSF before what he described as a decisive battle for el-Geneina.
Air strikes on a convoy travelling near the border with Chad have further isolated the RSF and struck a key supply route for the paramilitary group, Major General Othman Siraj said.
Pressure on multiple fronts by the army was preventing the RSF from regrouping its forces and paving the way for what he believes will be the final battle for el-Geneina.
Fadel Kaya, a leader and adviser with the Sudan Liberation Movement/Army – Transitional Council (SLM/TC), a Darfur rebel faction that split from the original Sudan Liberation Movement and signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement, told Al Jazeera that the Joint Force’s victories in West Darfur indicated that the RSF had shifted away from trying to gain territory to retreating from key positions.
Drone warfare
In North Kordofan state in central Sudan, the RSF had turned to drones to compensate for the loss of the strategic route linking Omdurman and el-Obeid. This had served as a major supply artery for the RSF before the army recaptured it on July 27.
Amin Ishaq Zakaria, a SLM/TC spokesman, told Al Jazeera that the RSF’s increased use of drones reflected “a predicament on the ground and an inability to engage in direct confrontations after losing vital positions”.
Sudanese armed forces had seized a number of attack drones along the Jabra al-Sheikh axis during the counteroffensive, he added.
The International Organization for Migration reported on Saturday that the recent escalation in fighting has seen more than 6,650 people from 11 villages in the Sirba region displaced.
More than 13 million people had already been displaced since the war between the military and RSF began in April 2023, according to United Nations estimates.
The RSF and its allies have also established a rival administration, known as the Tasis government, in opposition to the Sudanese government based in Port Sudan.
Al Jazeera reached out to the RSF and Tasis government about the fighting in the Bir Saliba area but received no response by the time the report was published.
